The game is a small, yet super fun indie game. I've played it for about 4.3 hours in about one day. It's essentially a running, 2D platformer with Mario Kart-like elements (one where you use a missile that homes on the lead player, similar to the dreaded Spiny Shell!). I'm a Mario Kart fan and a Mario platformer fan, so a hybrid of my two favorite games is a big delight. Despite its simplicity and how easy it is to pick up, there's plenty of strategy behind this, especially concerning item use, as all items have their own perks and strategies. The only downside personally is that I'm required to play online to unlock some characters and costumes, as it stops leveling up after a certain point, and I don't like playing with randoms online. I played offline with my twin, and we had a total blast with the game. Hopefully, mods will get bigger with the game, as it's also fairly easy to mod some aspects of it, including the music.

TL;DR: If you like tower defense games, this is an enjoyable TD with a twist. But it has its problems.
The graphics and music are well done in the 8-bit era style, nothing to complain here.
The gameplay reminded me of Orcs Must Die (or Dungeon Keeper even). You place traps that finish your enemies in various, graphical and delicious ways. In addition to the traps, the levels can have boulders and pits which you can use to your advantage.
However, due to the nature of traps, the game lacks some depth. Why? Well, it all boils down to fact that traps have very limited range of operation AND the path is one-way (i.e enemies just run from start to end). Some traps operate on larger area, but the trigger area is usually quite small, like one tile. This means that the path can actually be considered a single line on which you place the traps, and each trap can only affect one short part of the path. And because different traps benefit from proximity, the most efficient solution is usually a small "death alley" where you grind everything to pulp (or toss/drag the in the pits).
In many TD games you can use the tower range to your benefit by placing towers in such places that they cover as large area as possible, and areas as early AND as late as possible (to make use of giving your tower more time to work on the enemies). In Dungeon Warfare there is simply no such thing. (Well, there is, but it's more like a special case).
Once you realize this, it eats a bit of the experience. Even the most fancy and complex levels can be solved with concentrating on a small space, effectively ignoring much the level.
The game does get a bit more complex in the end. And for the record, I haven't completed the game yet, I think I'm at 70% or so.
Some random issues:
* Start of the game was quite heavily tutorialized, but nothing annoying
* Trap tiers and upgrading traps was NOT tutorialized, didn't learn this until later on when wondering what the "tier" means
* Going back to old levels to finish the optional gem levels is a bit stupid as all your upgrades make the game super easy (why not limit traps and/or slots per level?)
* Music is slightly repetitive... I cannot understand why many indie games have such a short soundtrack. Easy way to add value, folks!
Despite all this I'm still enjoying the game quite a bit, and wholeheartedly recommend it. It's just that with some design changes the game could be even better. Maybe for DW2? :)

A great tower defense game with a huge variety of towers, enemies and possible strategies.
This is a hidden gem of a very good tower defense game, comparable with Defender's Quest and Gemcraft, but ten times less known. What can you expect from the game?
- A huge variety of upgradable towers, unlocked gradually so you can learn about each one
- Respeccable skill points that you can (and must) distribute according to the map you're going to play
- Challenge modes that make the maps more difficult in exchange for better rewards
- An endless mode with ever harder waves
- User-created maps and a map editor
Most of the fun comes from the well designed towers and traps. In their most basic form, TD games have usually three types of towers - the reliable peashooter, the slow firing group damager and a slowing tower. In Dungeon Warfare you can of course use these basic towers and combine them with traps such as:
- Spikes shooting from the ground
- A harpoon pulling an enemy towards the abyss
- A push trap that pushes whole groups in the direction you wish
- A blackhole that sucks nearby enemies onto a single tile, making them a better target for the following AoE attacks
- A lich that turns any enemy it kills into a zombie fighting on your side
- A rotating spintrap rising from the ground and hacking everyone who comes near into minced meat
- A hex trap that turns an enemy into a frog
There are many effective combinations you can find and there is no set way of finishing a level. For example so far my go-to killzone consists of a chessboard of spintraps and spikes with a blackhole at the beginning and a spring trap at the end. The spintraps and spikes deal most of the damage to groups, blackhole pulls enemies periodically back so they have to travel through the kill zone again and the spring trap throws any straggler back into the fray. Sprinkle with a few liches to further slow down enemies and a gold enhancer and put a grinder at the end for any heavy units that make it through.
Another favourite strategy that some maps support is a using lot of push plates and harpoons combined with a slow trap, disposing of enemies by pushing/pulling them into the abyss. This is especially useful for large groups of slow, heavy enemies. It doesn't however work on thieves and horsemen who are too fast for the push plates and run through. Those must be disposed with a spintrap/flamethrower or spikes. The abyss also doesn't pose danger to flying enemies, those are better killed with a lightning trap and bolts.
All enemies have their weight and pushing/pulling traps have their force, so light enemies will get pushed further/faster than heavy ones, something you have to take into account. You can upgrade your push traps to have more force, but if there is a walkway behind the abyss, light enemies might get pushed too far and land safely on the other side, while if the trap is too weak, heavy knights and golems don't even move. Of course this can also be used to your advantage, as you can create endless cycles forcing groups of light enemies to go through your killzone multiple times...
You get the idea.
Graphically the game looks very simple, but unfortunately the screenshots don't make the game any favor as they look very chaotic. When in motion the game is quite clear and you know what is happening.
Don't let the screenshots dissuade you.
All in all Dungeon Warfare is a very good entry in the TD genre, well worth playing.

8/10 - Jet Set Radio, originally on the SEGA Dreamcast, and called Jet Grind Radio on the Dreamcast in North America, is back! And in glorious HD. Part action/platformer, part in line skate video game, Jet Set Radio is a unique and extremely fun title. One of the first titles to ever use the now common cel-shading graphics, it certainly has a unique visual style, even today. You play as part of a group of young in line skaters, bombing the system by skating around in different urban environments in Tokyo-to, and tagging different areas while running from the local police, and competing with other gangs. Not the type of gangs you'd think of. Just groups of rival graff heads looking to lay stake in different areas by putting up their own signature tags. This game was fresh more than a decade ago, and still a blast to play today. It's also accompanied by an extremely catchy soundtrack filled with artists ranging from genres of J-Pop, underground hip hop, and more. This version features nearly all of the music featured in both the PAL and North American versions. The 1 Japanese only track is still missing from the game.

There are few decent options for either medieval combat or first-person melee games out there. Chivalry is far from perfect and could really use some updating instead of them just moving on to release another game, but as it is you could do a lot worse. Chivalry is easy to pick up, but incredibly difficult to be good at, with a complex system of swings, thrusts, feints and blocks that means you will tear through several wildly-swinging heavy knight noobs only to be felled by a single man-at-arms who intercepts your every strike. Two teams, four classes and an impressive library of swords, axes, maces, spears, bows, crossbows and so on. Map design is pretty decent, and the melee system itself is fairly complex: difficult to learn, but very rewarding if mastered. The voice work is pretty amusing: You will hear almost constant, comically long yelling from people as they charge into battle. Be sure to look for servers that cap the number of archers there can be on a team, or risk being buried in arrows by people too chicken to swordfight.

Gemini Rue is a point-and-click game, with a furturistic-noir feel to it. The dark and mysterious atmosphere created by the extremely good soundtrack, gorgeous visuals and outstanding voice acting create a world that immerses you on such a high level you forget you are sitting in front of a computer. Just because this is a point-and-click game, does not mean that it's a game for kids or noobs. There are gunfights, which are both intense and challenging to play as ammo is limited and you can only take 4 shots. Lack of quick-thinking  will lead to death. The plot line is in no way cliche, it is paced out extremely well and characters are interesting, accompanied by the excellent voice acting. The hints and information build up on a very solid story, and the plot twist is unpredictable, punchy, and shocking - the elements of a perfect plot twist. As you travel through this 7 hour game as Azriel Odin, trying to find his lost brother or Delta-6 trying to escape.

Wow, I was really impressed with this game. The demo made the concept seem fun enough but I wasn't sure how much they could really do with it, and needless to say I was surprised. Pretty much every level plays with the core concepts in a new way, and the introduction of new drilling abilities allows you to go back to old levels and solve them in new ways. There's loads of replayability here, too. You can complete a level normally, you can complete it with the treasure chest, and you can complete it with the maximum (or more than the maximum!) number of blocks. And each level will play differently depending on what you're trying to do; a lot of levels you can only clear normally the first time through, which is maybe a bit annoying, but the game's short enough and powerups come quick enough that it barely matters. There's also 30 extra levels beyond the main game and a level editor/community level hub, so if you can exhaust everything the developers put into the game you still have plenty to keep you entertained.
The game does have a few weak points to it but they're generally more nitpicks than anything. Though the game is technically a puzzle platformer, it's much more puzzle than platformer, and the least fun levels tend to be the ones that have a platforming focus, as tetrobot is not an especially good platforming character. He has a long airtime but a low jump (necessary for puzzles) and a large hitbox (and anything that can kill you also does, too) leading to some clunky platforming sections, most notable in a few of the bonus levels. As well, the bonus levels have some meta-puzzles to them that I could do without/didn't bother trying to figure out myself because I'm lazy, but the main game is kept clean of them so I can't complain too much. A checkpointing system would've also been helped on some of the longer levels, as accidentally getting yourself killed several minutes into a complex puzzle and being forced to restart can get tedious. Thankfully most of the levels are kept either short or relatively danger-free.
Minor stumblings aside, this is a great game and a worthy addition to any puzzle game enthusiast's collection. You get quite a lot out of it for the low price, as well. It's an indie game that loves indie games and does what it wants to do quite well, allowing it to stand up with the games it references.

It's been well over a decade since something this exciting has been around on the MMORPG market.  While everyone else sells out to new balance systems, Boundel keeps things real with only guarded safe zones to protect you from her world.
Murderers and Criminals are marked red and are fair game.  Even in the relative safety of the city, one can attack or possibly kill another player before they are KOS.  It makes for great danger and risk, which is also quite enjoyable.  The world is big enough that one can find an XP niche and go hide for a time to get stronger.
The world feels neither enmpty nor crowded, vast for adventure, but sensible and navigable with some exploration.  Signs and roads provide the way.  Terrain is natural and flows well, circling round the main villages so that one can literally see where one is going by climbing a mountain top.  Awesome, in the true sense of the word.
The spells are especially enjoyable, as one must aim like in FPSs.  Some are quite speedy, which satisfies my button masher.  Whilest many are timed and aimed for patient players looking for DoTs or devestating DD.  The skills are fun and without classes the player can try them as they please.  I enjoy the way the aggro works, even if it is a bit off at the moment.  Sometimes mobs do suprisngly intelligent things.  I was able to kite to 10 without much trouble, but then I got to lizards and they link.  This means intelligent pulling is a must.  That's a lot like Everquest was back when it was great.
The graphics look like circa 2000ish, but they are beautiful, with sweeping landscape, rolling moiuntain ranges, deep oceans, and the immense clip plane.  Something about it is nostalgically wonderful.  It's clean and fast for good PvP.  It's got a certain efficiency that works well with many systems.  It doesn't have a lot of pretty environment, but it's easy on the hardware, well balanced for good play.  That being said, it's still well made and feels real.
Some players are kind, others are vicious, & that is the point.  No quests means freedom and fun.  Gawd I am sick of quest grinding!  So Boundel is perfect for the mature mmmorpg player.  Is it confusing?  Yes.  Is the English rough?  Yes.  That is part of the fun!  All your Boundel are belong to us!
This game is worth your support and I would have gladly paid $50+ for it 10 years ago.  At $5 it seems priceless.  If you don't enjoy a real-life experience this isn't for you.  No whining.  You die and lose your gold if you forgot to bank it.  There will be gangs in the future.  It is up to us to shape the community.  Plus with a LAN mode, if you don't like it you can go offline and play!  Sweet.
Boundel is truly one of the brightest indie stars to watch throughout Early Access.

This is one of those games I wasn’t really hyped for or interested in for a long time despite it haunting my wishlist for a while. At first it looked like a Diablo clone set in Divinity’s universe which would have been enough for me. Instead, it became more of an older school Baldur’s Gate/Icewind Dale type game with a bit of an XCOM flair to it. There’s many comparisons to be made but funnily enough, the game evokes the feeling of Morrowind and its general open endedness. It is a pleasant surprise.
Y’see, in Morrowind, you could literally kill anyone. Even the self-proclaimed living god Vivec. You’d be met with a type of error message telling you to reload or “continue in the doomed world you have created”. However DOS2 here actually doesn’t care who you kill, because progress can be found on journals, diaries, or keys on anyone’s body.
Character creation is a fun process. Not a lot on the physical customization because you mostly just play through a tiny avatar through most of the game, but the nuances come in the skillsets and “Origin” characters. You can customize your own but the game comes with about five of their own, and mercifully you can customize their actual class so you can change the Enchantress’s build to suit your personal playstyle (mine being rogue/assassin like people) regardless of how she usually starts as a default NPC.
Choosing one of them may be to your benefit as they get extra dialogues and experiences. I chose Lohse, an entertainer/bard type girl who once met a dwarf she was familiar with and despite the grim surroundings, had a bit of a musical duet together for about fifteen seconds and it was quite a sight to see. You’d miss such an interaction if you went just for a personal custom character.
The game begins on a prison ship, and Act 1 is placed on the prison island altogether. I didn’t like the idea of being shackled for a while but the game does a great job of giving you plenty to do in what is essentially the game’s over extended tutorial. The amount of freedom I was able to acquire was staggering, even in the confines of the ship itself which is only the first twenty minutes of the game or so. In it, I could bash down doors, find a secret key for some extra loot, and even backtracked to murder a guard that was rude to me earlier, after♥♥♥♥♥♥had hit the fan. It was awesome, and in that moment the game took me.
There’s a guy named “Griff”, the inmate who essentially ‘controls’ the other inmates, even going so far as protection rackets and food supplies (he runs the kitchen). There was a chestpiece called “Griff’s Shirt” on the ground, and he’s flanked by another vendor who occasionally patrols away.  On a hunch, I decided to sneak behind him when that happened and steal his shirt. It worked! The item’s blurb says “It was Griff’s. Now it’s yours.” Then I saw the patrolling vendor run over yelling “Thief! There’s a criminal about!” I just ran off, not wanting to test the game’s impressive AI to see if it could find me as the thief if I lingered in the area too long. I returned later, wearing his shirt and nobody was the wiser (which may in itself be a weaker point in the AI).
There will be some spoilers for Act 1, though my actions are hardly the only ones you can take.
To continue on the same line of how insane this game is with options, with the help of one of my online friends… They led me to getting my collar removed, to which I was thrown into a dungeon for that. I don’t know how non-thieves get out of that but I was able to lockpick my way out, retrieve my gear, find a waypoint which allowed the transport of my teammates into the dungeon itself and we… proceeded to absolutely demolish the guards from the inside out. We basically cleared the island. It was great.
There are so many nuances to the game that aren’t outwardly apparent. You may notice as you traverse the landscape that your characters will get a variety of buffs like “wet” and “warm” which might turn to your detriment in combat when enemies cast spells to take advantage of those. The game is littered with oil spills, blood splatters, firey explosions and puddles. Each one can be affected by a spell type. One time, I had my mage set some enemies on fire but when it turned out to be to my detriment (my melee characters couldn’t reach some of the enemies), I had her cast “rain” which didn’t just put the fires out, but actually creates a smoke screen which limited the enemies’ vision.
So many enemies use a spell to summon a slick of oil then promptly set it on fire. They’re not idiots.
Combat in this game does an excellent job of making sure you’re both aware of your surroundings, and then actually capitalizing on it.
There’s more to it the nuances than your combat. I was speaking to a lizard-raced bodyguard in a cave who was very standoffish to my own character. On another hunch based on some of this guy’s dialog, I switched to a different party member and spoke with him again. I switched to Ifan, an ex-soldier. Being a soldier himself, the lizard-man actually respected Ifan more and had more dialog to give and even had an extra discount on the few wares he sold.
Most of my RPG life is spent in the perspective of my own, and it is a bit refreshing to see that exploring other personalities is typically rewarded here.
As I said, I’ve only played through most of Act 1 so I do not have the full picture as far as the game will give me, but I am excited to find out, and more excited to the fact that there isn’t much I can get overtly wrong here.
If I had a complaint, it’d be the same complaint I have in many open world RPG’s. At a certain point my quest log gets bogged down by errands and scavenger hunts and it’s hard to tell which ones will be worth my time and what wouldn’t be. It’s also the one thing I feel I can actually get wrong - after having most of Act 1 down I still find myself with more than a few side quests, like finding a woman’s missing child and I’m not sure if I’ll be missing out on any potential rewards if I just give up and move on in the story.
It’s a minor point to be sure considering the freedom the game is able to give you.
There’s so many other side stories I could give. Like how my multiplayer friend had the only pet pal perk, spoke to some dogs and then I ran back towards them and they all went hostile. Or how my dwarf teammate met up with an old friend and had a chuckle. Or what the pet pal perk even does, talking to dogs is just pure gold. Many other stories to be had and I can’t wait to hear others.

A note before my review: I laughed out loud when I saw this game on Steam. I hadn't heard of ETS and haven't played simulator games in years. I saw a truck sim game and thought "who the hell wants to drive around and make deliveries in a truck?" Well, apparently I do!

The added ability to listen to internet radio makes it so much better. I personally like driving around jamming to some 80s rock, it's a perfect compliment to life on the road.

Classic game that I spent hundreds of hours playing back in the day - in a lot of ways a big improvement over its predecessor, the graphics and interface are much more friendly, the combat is much improved (although a certain amount of cheesiness of tactics is opened up in terms of using your archers range advantage to create one sided results in many battles if you have the patience). The only downside is the much simplified economy, which is far less interesting and challenging than the original.
The general idea of the game remains the same - build up an economy, raise troops, go out and conquer more neutral counties/countries to build even more armies so you can defeat the active AI opponents that are doing the same. Unlike the original there are a number of different maps to conquer, rather than just the single England and Wales map, although the gameplay doesn't really change all that much between each map (you don't grow different crops or find different resources or build different military units).
As noted the economy is much simplified - for agriculture you only have two options, grain and cows/dairy. Even worse the lack of weather (except as special events) and fertility/crop rotation means that in practise you just always switch over to pure grain production as soon as you can as it frees up the most workers to your military industrial complex, as the risks of the previous title in specializing like this just aren't there.
On the upside the combat part of the game is much improved however, with the ability to position and move your troops much more fluidly, so you can try to outflank the enemy, or bottleneck the enemy in defensive terrain (ideally with melee troops defending a bridge while your archers and crossbows rain death on them).
Particularly for sieges this can get cheesy as you can dodge incoming fire with a bit of practise while the AI just stands there as you shoot at it, although this requires a lot of patience...especially when you have dozens of counties to capture during each campaign. Overall it plays much more like an proto-RTS game in this phase, and is much more fun and interesting that in LotR1.
As a whole then the game is far more accessible and friendly to play, so it would probably be the recommendation for someone that hasn't played the series before, although due to its age it likely is going to have an audience mostly limited to those that played it many years ago, who don't need a review to know what the game is like.

I love Fallout. Well, I loved Fallout 3. I didnt get into the others so much but the post nuclear/disaster/world gone to♥♥♥♥♥♥scenario called out to me. Moderated help chat. This is a key in any game that people are new to and I think should be a staple in ANY MMO. The GM's are friendly but also help you when you need it.
Crafting. I have honestly never played a game with better crafting. Literally everything you can think of can be made. Want a shirt? Craft it. Need new shoes or pants? Craft them. I've heard some people say SWG had the best crafting system but I didnt play it so I cant comment.
The classless system. This in my book is a bonus. You can be whoever you want. Want a guy that beats the crap out of things with a 2x4 and shoots pistols? Thats ok. A lot of people get confused by now having a rigid class to stick to but I think its a breath of fresh air.

My only dissapointment is that Icarus studios sold it. A lot of people grumbled about the micro tranasctions but in my opinion you either buy them or you dont.
Anyways if you like fallout then I think you should enjoy this. Plus its free to play now so if you dont like it it wont cost you anything :) Its the closest to the fallout MMO your going to get for a while.

Ahh, yes... where to begin. This game is not about space ninjas, not anymore. It's about grinding for good loot, sometimes far longer than you would think you could possibly justify just for a single item, then you use it and realize that it may be the most busted thing you have ever seen. Seriously, I don't even want to know what the PvP is like, I just enjoy the flow of battle while taking on the different races that inhabit this galaxy. This game can make you feel like a total bad♥♥♥♥♥ or it can bend you over and show you who's in charge (there is a middle ground where you feel like if you slip up once you'll die, and that feeling usually proves to be correct the next time you slip up). This game is mostly fair in PvE, the risk is usually proportional to the reward. The quests can be annoying to an extent, and you may start a quest without knowing that the warning you recieved that you cannot continue normal play before completing the quest was actually quite warranted because you just jumped into a quest that will take at least an hour to complete. Then you have the buggs, there are a lot of them. These bugs usually aren't big, and just elicit a chuckle from the player. Then there are a few that are rare but rather nasty, like a few that can make certain missions impossible. Note: for those missions that are bugging out on you, bring someone along. That has helped me and some of my friends get through some rather nasty bugs. Overall, this game has it's ups and downs. But in the end, I'll keep coming back to it because of the feeling of pure bad-assery I get from this game.

Disclaimer: I played this for hundreds of hours pre-Steam.
All I can do is agree with majority of the constructive negative reviews:
AMAZING game completely overshadowed and ruined by the microtransaction model.
Amazing game, as in:
Very decent themepark PvE progression and endgame system.
Very decent open world, instanced and large scale PvP system.
Very decent sandbox, trading and crafting system, definitely one of the best since Star Wars Galaxies.
There is so much to do and it combines so many great things from other MMORPGs that only focus on 1 of them and the best thing of all is that it actually does very decent at all of them.
You'd never be bored with how much content there is, whether you're a PvEer, Sandboxer/Trader/Crafter or PvPer.
It also looks very decent graphically and is quite well optimized.
But people, PLEASE stop denying it's Pay2Win.
It simply is, so severely much, that the fact you'd still defend it means you're either paid by them or delusional (or someone who really can play this at least 12 hours every day a week without any sense of social life, a job or school).
Someone who pumps 200 bucks into their character is going to be super tanky to you in PvP and will kill you within 5 seconds.
For you, as a Patron (not even Freebie), it will take at least 3-6 months to get to that level.
And another thing is:
This isn't Free2Play, this is pretty much Free2Try with a subscription that you simply can't do without.
No you can't, stop saying that you can, unless you're a masochist that never intended to play the game further than leveling to the level cap, you are going to need it.
The Patron doesn't only give you massive boosts, it also unlocks very important things that aren't even available as Freebie: plots.
I honestly think this game should have just been a standard 12-15/month without microtransaction shop (or perhaps with only 100% cosmetic items).

*sigh* another open world PVP game.
Seems like every fledgling dev wants to make an open world PVP game these days.  Like some dream akin to a young boy wanting to be a rockstar.  The vocal minority of  bloodthirsty gamer/murderers fill forums demanding it... over and over... stating anything that isn't open world PVP isn't realistic or hardcore enough, a fallacy that sounds pretty convincing to those that lack experience.  Open PVP is actually incredibly unrealistic and there has yet to be a system implemented that mitigates the outcomes in a realistic way.  You would think with this dream of FFA PVP that some developers would actually improve the formula but it's always the same lawless unimaginitive garbage with next to no AI.  And yet with the endless FFA PVP games that flood the bargain bin of Steam no one seems to get the clue.  Why do they keep failing?  Well that's simple.  A) Because not that many people actually want it (see vocal minority) and B) because once it does get off the ground, the type of player base they attract are not the community building type.  In fact from my decades of playing MMOs I've found open world PVPers to be the whiniest most immature group of foaming at the mouth imbeciles. Script kiddies, cheats, etc.
Another major problem with open PVP games is so much development time and resources are spent trying to plug all the holes for the crap show that will inevitably ensue, that the development of PVE elements and mob AI suffers dramatically.  Which is why these PVP games feel like a barren wasteland.  Boring.
There's actually a study out there about open PVP games and how the players that are attracted to them share a similar psychological makeup as wife beaters and rapists.  It's not really surprising.  People are playing these games to play out their urges to murder, anonymously, without consequences in a video game.  Sure it's not real but they DO want to ruin your fun.  They get off on it.
Anyway on to the actual state of this game.  Seems very empty and barebone.  There are a couple of things I like so far, the ability to make my own server and the music in this game.  Once the game is further developed and there's a reason to make my own server, I might give it a thumbs up... but with the reservation that it's yet another open world PVP game.  Someone please just make a solid, challenging, group oriented PVE game for once.

The voice acting is really good too.  A lot of people I talk to say that male Shepard's voice actor isn't great, I disagree.  Not every line needs to have passion and over-acting in it.  I will say that he shines when playing as a renegade, however.
The gameplay, is nothing to write home about.  But it's solid, which is a welcome improvement considering how awful it was in "Mass Effect".  It feels like "Gears of War" except not as slow and with magic powers.  The harder difficulties are really fun to play.  Dying never feels cheap.  A little thinking and planning is required.
There are lots of ways to play this game (story choices, different fighting classes, varied difficulties), so multiple playthroughs are needed to experience everything.
Like I said, this is one of the best games of all time.  It is a must-play game.  I recommend playing "Mass Effect" before playing this game.  It will create stronger connections with the characters you meet in "Mass Effect 2".

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding cheese cake recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1 cup digestive plain sweet biscuit crumbs
3 tablespoons sugar
3 tablespoons melted butter
40 ounces softened cream cheese
1 cup sugar
3 tablespoons flour
1 tablespoon vanilla
1 cup sour cream
4 eggs
Directions:
For The base:.
If you're using a dark pan, preheat the oven to 350. If you are using a shiny pan, 375.
Combine the crumbs, melted butter and 3 tbsp sugar well and pat onto the bottom of a 9 inch springform pan. I also like to very very lightly butter the sides of the pan so that the cheesecake will not stick later on.
Bake for 10 mins in your preheated oven and remove. Let it cool while you prepare your batter.
For the batter:.
Make sure everything is at room temperature.
Combine sugar, cheese, flour and vanilla in a big bowl and mix on medium speed till well combined. Don't forget to scrape the bowl as you're doing this.
Mix in the sour cream till its incorporated well. Then, add the eggs one by one, mixing well after each addition.
Pour the batter into the springform and let it bake for 1 hour and 10 minutes After the baking time, turn off the oven and leave the door ajar. Let the cake cool in there for about 1 1/2 hours.
Remove the cake and let it cool thoroughly. Refrigerate overnight.
Release the sides of the springform.
Eat.

This is most certainly THE best attempt at following up on Dungeon Keeper 2 in an attempt to create the long sought after DK 3 which many of us had waited for.  You'll slip into a nostalgia coma as soon recognise every single component in this game from your previous DK experience.  They nailed it!  But this is also where the problem comes in.
The game is a graphically pleasing, humour-filled remake of DK and not so much a sequel. Sure enough there is a bloody good load of newly added components, such as the titan creatures and a "leveling" scheme which allows you to unlock traps, rooms and the odd creature using points called "sins".   Heck, they even have the original voice-over from the old DK games! Nostalgia overload.
The campaign is "alright" and provides you with around 9 hours worth of gameplay - less if you are just one of those gamers who nail-it fast.  I completed the campaign a day after I bought the game and then, you are stuck with very few options.  The sandbox modes are pretty much blank maps with infinate gold that allows you to quickly dig out enough space and place all of your dungeon rooms and summon all of your creatures - provides you with around 30 minutes of entertainment.
Multiplayer is an excrutiating experience.  For those of you who have been playing games outside of steam's DRm, you'll remember those horrible tech nightmares where you had to go and mess about with your port settings, enabling UPnP on your routers and so on - the days we all thought were long gone since steam (and other DRM's) provided a platform that negates this.  Well, in the spirit of nostalgia you may well enough enjoy that experience in this game again.
Multiplayer is stock standard, once you get it working.  Play against other opponents and squash them.  Whether it is you and a mate vs the AI (the developer's definition of Coop...if you can believe that) or whether it is two of you vs two other dungeoneers - all modes we should be fairly familiar with.
The actual coop which was hinted at during the kickstarter, though not reached, also seems to be not in the pipeline for the near future.  Now this does not mean it is off the table entirely, though it doesn't look to be soon.
The expansion, "Heart of Gold" (released two or three days prior to this review) adds about 4 - 6 hours worth of play in a campaign, some dungeon visuall candy for multiplayer and the odd spell here and there.  It's not an expensive expansion and therefor the little content can be quantified.
Overall, the game's base price vs what you get for it is not good at all.  This is the kind of game we should be looking for during steam specials.  You will barely get a weekend's worth of playing from both the game and its current expansion and multiplayer is unlikely to entertain you for very long if you get past the uneccesary setup hassles.
In summary:
They absolutely succeeded in providing a nostalgic experience in the spirit of Dungeon Keeper. No one can compete.
However, the game falls horribly short in providing an entertaining experience for more than an approximate 15 hours worth of play (more, maybe, if you really really like repeating the same actions).
No Coop (and mplay coop 2v2 does NOT constitute coop at all).
The game's development does not seem to be entirely finished and there "appears" to be some level of new content being planned.  This may very well be a boon to the current state of the game.  Though, if not getting this title on a good special I would suggest that you seek out the most recent reviews of newly added content on our usual trusty sources (i.e IGN, Gamespot, Gamasutra, Cooptimus).

Conan Exiles...or should I say, ARK 2.0..
TL;DR
Conan boasts a VERY pretty world (not just the dongs, breasts, and bushes), but the whole world is pretty to look at. The building works a million times better than ARK, giving you A LOT of freedom on how you want your structures to look. The combat feels fluid MOST of the time, however, stay away from bows/crossbows until they get some work. The enemies are challenging, but beatable. Structures can be destroyed, but it takes the 3rd tier of weapons and tools to do so, which is I think 25 levels in. All in all, if you like survival/crafting/pvp games, this is one that should not be missed!
Conan is in it's early stages still, meaning there are a handful of glitches, bugs, issues, exploits, and things that need work. That being said, Funcom is working on it. Some issues are taking more time than others, but they're communicating what issues they are working on, have worked on, and plan to work on in the future. There is a lot of fun to be had, whether you like crafting and building, PVE and taking on enemies of all sorts, hunting, or I believe their working on questing as well, or even PVP, which is a blast.
Pro's:
-Crafting System feels rock solid and rewarding
-Building system is fun, and allows a TON of customization and has very few limitations.
-Combat is fun, and though still early, works well.
-You're not required to JUST PvP. Enemy camps of NPC's and even friendly NPC's that offer rewards for talking to them offer a varied experience.
-Religion system unlike anything I've seen. The more devotion you give your "god" the better items you can craft and recieve from your god, ultimately leading up to being able to summon an Avatar of your religion.
-Thrall/Slave system. Capture slaves and make thralls that will either work for you and help you craft, or you can get fighters that will defend your base while you're away, as well as archers that will work as turrets if placed in the right spot.
Con's:
-Still early access, has a ways to go in order to feel complete compared to some other big name Survival games (ARK, RUST. etc..)
-Ranged Weapons, bows and crossbows, need a lot of work. There is no audible sound that lets you know if you hit your target. The animation feels VERY stiff. The fall off on arrows (thought I think they're patching that in a day or so) is REALLY harsh. Every other arrow fired is invisible.
-Animals can destroy bases REALLY quick, making it difficult for new players to establish themselves.

+ Runes (difficulty settings for increased exp bonus) are all available at the start, so seasoned TD players can instantly start the game at a suitable difficulty level.
+Towers are reasonably well balanced. Generally towers work well when used in combination with others, e.g. a choke point with a spike trap and demons to prevent enemy movement.
+ Simple physics system with numerous towers that take advantage of it, e.g. harpoon trap pulls enemies towards it and potentially into a pit, spring traps can launch enemies to another part of the maze, etc.
- The retro graphics style, while not bad, does make it unclear at times what's happening. It's at times impossible to mouse-over a specific entity for more info.
- No zoom function. Not a massive problem, but it would have been a nice addition.
- All units seemingly share the same soundset - golems that fall to their deaths will use the same scream as a peasant.
- Consumable trap feature (basically the "spell" slot) - while it's not a bad thing, I would have liked to see this as an optional feature. The way I like to play TDs is to do all the planning (building of towers) and then just watch the carnage without having to micro-manage the battle using spells. The game is balanced around using these, so simply not using them is not an ideal decision. I recommend adding a rune that disables the consumable trap slot entirely, maybe for something like 1.2-1.35x exp gain.
Recommended if you enjoyed Kingdom Rush, Gemcraft TD or Orcs Must Die. This game is on par with those, if not better.

- Original Review after a couple of hours of play -
The server was moved after several days of being offline, and I was finally able to give the game a try.
My impressions -
Positives:
+ Good variety of creatures
+ Leveling seems fairly easy, at least in the beginning
+ Can pick the skills you want to use
+ No quests means you can really go do whatever you want
Negatives:
- Mob AI is pretty bad.  Lots of them just stand around while you hit them, others kill you off with no warning or follow you forever
- Mana regeneration is very slow, at least in the early going, which means you spend a lot of time just kiting in circles or standing around doing nothing
- Abilities need better descriptions and equipment/skill points need explanations
- Server stability - The server went down and/or I was booted at least 5 times in the few hours I played
- Toxic community - I was pk'd by two different people multiple times that could oneshot me, as they obviously outleveled me by a huge amount (had mounts and everything, so there was no way I could run away either), and just rode over and attacked without a word.  I also had numerous other people decide to grab the loot that the mobs I was killing dropped, and/or "help" me kill something that was nearly dead only to grab the loot.
Verdict:
Considering the cost, I'm pretty impressed with the framework here.  The game has potential, but until some of the issues are fixed (especially the "free" looting issue and the fact that there seems to be no penalty for killing people that are trivial to you multiple times, both of which I can only see getting worse with a higher population), I can't really recommend it.
- Updated Review -
I've been playing some more, and did manage to find some people that didn't try to kill me on sight, and even a couple of generous players who offered tips and a mount, which was much appreciated.  Having said that, the community is still an issue.  Though this has become less frequent after gaining a fair number of  levels, I'm still one-shot killed at times, often by people I didn't even see approach despite watching for them (I have a feeling this is due to the "recall" points, as people pop out of thin air when they recall), and I've been killed while still logging in several times as well. I'll readily admit I'm not much of a fan of pvp in the first place, but I can't really understand how "pvp" where one player kills another in one hit over and over again would be fun for anyone.
I'm also finding (in line with what's mentioned in the comments) that there's less variety in mobs than I originally thought, as a lot of areas are just empty, and the pve seems to be pretty repetitive, as even though I'm still at a fairly low level compared to a number of players, unless I aggro a huge group of ranged mobs or fight a dragon, I'm already not finding too many challenges.
Having said that, I'm now close to 20 hours into the game, and have been enjoying it more than I was in the beginning, so I'll change my recommendation to a "yes" with the caveat that there are still a bunch of issues with the game that hopefully will be addressed in the future.

As a longtime fan of Bullfrog's Dungeon Keeper series, I came into WFTO with lofty expectations. It's for this reason that I feel it would be impossible for me to write an unbiased review of the game based entirely upon its own merits, so I'm not going to try.
This *is* Dungeon Keeper 3; and thus far, it has satisfied or exceeded my expectations on every level.
If you're like me and you've been waiting for all the bugs and nasty bits to be hammered out before you spend your money, the time has come. With the release of the Gold Rush patch and DLC, the game is technically solid, artistically inspired, full of content, brimming with devious personality, and one hell of a good time for god-game enthusiasts.

I tried to give it a chance. This game has every possible element I enjoy: cyberpunk, skill-based, shootem' up. It's execution RUINs this, however.
The storyline and plot is pretty much non-existent. Basically what it boils down to is this: "Find your brother." Simple enough, and overdone. The entire plot gets constantly blasted in your face with seizure inducing cyber-punk themed screen flashes. I didn't have a problem with the screen flashing, but when your entire story can be summed up to literally 1 frame that's put on the screen for miliseconds at a time, the plot shouldn't really be a selling point for your game.
The maps are super repetitive, and throughout the entire game the same color scheme is repeated without any real change to the environment. It feels like it's trying too hard to be aesthetic, and it's attempt detracts from the overall experience by being, to put it quite simply, boring/bland to look at. While initially cool, I can only spend so much time looking at the same floor panels.
The combat definitely has some complexities, but the issue is that things are either too fast or too small to notice. While it may seem like the issue is on my end, I have a decent monitor and play many different twitch/skill-based games that I don't have this problem with. The number of times I died in this game and actually knew the cause was greatly outnumbered by the amount of times I had no idea... which is problematic when the entire game is based around having the skill to outmaneuver obstacles. Inevitably this makes victory in the game feel more about luck than being able to learn and improve.
The game also doesn't seem to adhere to it's own rules. As an example, there's a gunship that moves around the map. In order to survive, you have to stay out of the spotlight to avoid it's gunfire. However, the spotlight's circle is not the AOE at which the gunship will start firing. You can be outside of the light and still get shot at. From a mechanical gameplay perspective, that doesn't make sense. It should only fire if you step into the circle. By itself, it may not seem like a big deal but when you take it into account the number of similar problems, the experience starts to erode. You're in a stage with a couple of gunship spotlights, a couple of enemies, and these things called "leeches." Suddenly it becomes close to impossible to predict how close you can get to the light without triggering the gunship damage (let alone being able to see the spotlight amidst all the color flashes) and how to manuever away.
Enemy variants are unnoticable. What it can be boiled down to is whether the enemy is melee or ranged. Sometimes they have a shield, sometimes they don't. However, it's still difficult to tell how much health an enemy has. How then do you know who to eliminate first? You can't really know to risk charging an enemy, if your hits are going to be ineffective.
Finally, the powerups and skills can be a bit buggy. I've had times where mind controlled enemies will attack me, and sometimes they won't. Also the slow-down-time skill lags the game beyond what I think they intended with inconstitent freezes and unpolished bugs. For a game as short, small scaled, expensive, and simplistic as ruiner, it should be an absolutely polished experience.
The game is incredibly short, too. If you're okay with replaying the game a lot, then you might get your money's worth. Personally, I just don't feel like it's worth it. Even on sale at $13.39 USD the game just didn't really feel all that great. If the game was as polished as similar games in the genre (like hotline miami) then I mightn't have a problem with the price tag. This just feels like too much, especially full price.

I can't recommend the game because it has bugs, bugs, bugs, and the developers apparently are completely uninterested in fixing them.  Everybody reports the same bugs, over and over, and nothing is done, month after month.  It's a bug farm.  Skip it.  With that caveat...
The gameplay is pretty non-traditional.  If you want to play a game for a couple hours, this isn't it.  Instead, you'll log on maybe twice a day for a few minutes each time.  Successful game play will necessarily span weeks (and months).  Progress is fairly quick at first but the costs of upgrades, etc., are exponential.
There are two currencies in the game -- gold and supplies.  You can pay real money for gold.  You can exchange gold for supplies and/or speeding things to completion, but it's very expensive.  You can use supplies to build units, build buildings, build defenses, and updgrade everything.  In effect, supplies are the only real resource.  You do create supplies at a constant rate, which can be improved, but it's always at a pretty slow rate.  Think of it as a constant trickle; what you need to do something interesting is a full bucket.
The game itself is a fairly simplistic build, attack, conquer.   When you conquer, all you get is supplies and increased community ranking.  When you are attacked and defeated, all you lose is supplies and decreased community ranking.  So when you see somebody with a lot of supplies and a really low ranking, they're good for the picking.
Strategy is fairly simple.  You can decide when (and if) to launch your various units.  They are not controllable once launched, so, yes, it's very frustrating to watch your tanks beating against a brick wall while a machine gun right next to them is blowing them to pieces.  That frustration is not rare.
tl;dr - free, play over weeks to months, not much strategy, simple - tons of bugs

An over-hyped "bullet-hell" top down shooter with an appealing art style. The actual gameplay becomes much more puzzle-esque than I would have liked. This is not the straight-ahead action title I thought it to be, but a 'thinking' shooter. The intro segment was very sparsely populated with enemies, holding your hand as you navigate from room to room picking off a handful of enemies with a few long corridors in-between.
The actual game begins as you are locked into a tiny room, with a timer counting down as the character who just 'trained' you says 'hey you die when my timer runs out, oh by the way fight this powerful boss in a teeny room as the game throws handfuls of enemies at you. Dash around the screen and time the dashes just right and perhaps you can get close enough to enemies to whack them with a pipe or spew 8 to 30 bullets out of a ranged weapon (all of which have extremely limited ammo in single-clips in a single clip before they are to be thrown on the ground empty and useless.
The controls aren't quite 'clunky', with a mouse and keyboard, but playing this with a steam-controller is nothing short of infuriating. I could see picking this up later when I'm done stewing that the game went straight from intro to controls/attacks and dumps you into a challenging boss fight. How about letting me clear a couple levels of normal baddies before tossing me into a timed boss battle as 10 other baddies continue to jump into the fray from gates that I can not pass through.
I appreciate what this game tries to do, but in execution it falls short of satisfaction immediately with awkward pacing and an AI system that will hold you down and butt-♥♥♥♥ you within seconds. This is very much a "bang bang you're dead" style of gameplay that expects you to perform "devil may cry" type on-the-fly offensive/defensive maneuvers. However, for all the finesse it requires, your enemies advance upon you so quickly in teeny-tiny rooms that you aren't going to have much of a chance outside of the slo-mo feature to execute anything very graceful.
I'm 31 years old, allow me to rattle off a list of games that got this style of gameplay right back in the mid 1990s on the original Playstation (PS1) console:
1. Silent Bomber
2. ONE
3. Fighting Force
I'd rather play any one of those games than this. It's just not fun.

The Good:
-Beautiful art design
-character customization
-99% voice acting, even for animals
-soundtrack is memorable
-playing with friends makes the experience 10x better
The Meh:
-Story is basic, feels forced
-Origin characters feel forced and shallow with a couple exceptions
-Illusion of choice.  A fair bit of railroading, but done in a way that most people wouldn't notice
-Game can be unstable, with random CTD during dialog
-Quests are unnecesarily vague in many cases.  I'm all for a game not holding my hand, forcing me to gather clues from reading journals, talking to people, etc., but for many quests I hit a wall, and lost interest in continuing, hoping to stumble upon the next step.
-Crafting system is inefficient, and dated.
The Bad:
-Bugs galore, from quest-killers, dialog glitches, suicidal AI pathing, and quest log incoherence.
-Combat system is clunky, sluggish, and punishes you for it's own flaws.
-Initiative system is terrible.  Watch as your character gets shuffled down in real time so you miss 2 whole turns before acting, despite having a stellar initiative score.
-Unlike a truly freeform game like D&D tabletop, your choices are dictated by the parameters of the game architecture, rather than a human GM.  This makes predicting the outcome of almost any decision you make difficult, even if something makes sense.  Save-scum often, which isn't that fun, and breaks immersion.
-No confirmation system in iventory management, crafting, or bartering.  This adds a level of difficulty in tedium that is unnecessary.  It's like having to make DEX checks while trading so you don't sell the wrong item.
-Artificial difficulty curve that takes away from the overall experience of the story, which isn't so great to begin with.
-Lazy storytelling that makes me feel like I'm playing a mediocre D&D game with a novice DM.
-Arx is so buggy, even post-update (10/8/17), it is an exercise in frustration that had me eager to just finish the game and get it over with.
-As of today, final battle crashes mid-fight during second phase.  Tried it several times, but it is unplayable, which has killed my interest in what happens at the end.
Overall: 5/10
I can understand why this game is getting so many accolades, but I feel that there needs to be more objective reviews out here. It is unique in a very important way: Couch Co-op.  It's one of a tiny handful of games that my wife and I can play together, and for that, we are both having fun despite the myriad flaws present.  Also, I admire Larian Studios' passion and dedication to their work, which seems a rare commodity in today's game industry.
EDIT 10/8/17: Final battle is buggy, crashes, and isn't actually that well designed as far as final battles go.  Game overall is a glitch-fest, combined with lazy, forced game design.  I may recommend it when an enhanced edition releases a year from now and everything is ironed out.

I was never one to show much interest in simulators based on things like farming, construction, or bus driving.  Seems like everytime you turn around there is a new simulator on something that would seem boring or mundane so I am not sure what motivated me to try a trucking simulator, but I am sure glad I did.  Starting with nothing you get to build your own trucking company by taking various jobs until you have enough money to invest in your own equipment, employees, and facilities.  As you level up you gain access to new and different forms of cargo that will allow you to gain xp and money much faster.
Driving a truck around may seem very boring, but I found it to be both very relaxing and sometimes challenging.  You have access to wide variety of radio stations so I just pick one with hits of the 60s, 70s, or 80s and just enjoy the drive.  Parking and maneuvering these massive trucks with trailers around cities with tight roads or crazy AI drivers will keep on your toes even after playing for hours.
Although I do recommend this game I have a few minor gripes I wish to point out.  First, the game lacks any form of a visual damage model.  I know the point of the game isn't to hit other vehicles or objects, but sometimes accidents happen and some sort of visual damage model would have been nice.  When you are invovled in an accident you just get a percentage of how badly you hurt your truck, but you will never see any visual damage on your truck or in the world.  My second gripe is the current "world" of ATS is very limited.  Although the devs have very grand plans in place for this game they haven't seen the light of day yet.  The driving distance between locations isn't currently that long and I've seen more of the desert than I care to at this point.
Minor gripes aside, if you are looking for a game that allows you to get behind the wheel of an American big rig then ATS will let you play out your trucker fantasies short of the ability to pick up hookers hanging out at truck stops.

The first Original Sin game was fantastic, although I didn't end up finishing it because it became too easy as your characters grew more powerful. Original Sin 2 not only rectifies this problem, but it takes just about everything to the next level.

Strategy means everything, and if you're not thinking about your parties positioning, you will get wrecked, at least in the tougher battles. I think terrain & environmental hazards could be a little more punishing than they currently are; again, going back to OS1, they were significantly more relevant to the combat. That being said, at least battles aren't over in the first turn in OS2 like they were in the first game, where you could very easily stunlock entire groups of enemies using weather effects.
On top of that, it's refreshing to see a real, old school style morality system, where you're free to kill any NPC at any time, and not have a stupid karma meter telling you how good or evil you are. You make decisions, and you get on with the job.

My choice for Game of the Year so far. My expectations were high and this game surpassed them in almost every regard. There is a bit of a steep learning curve. However, once you get past this, you are for a very special treat. If you are new to RPG's, hang in there. It is worth it.
Pros:
- The game never breaks immersion. You feel clever when you solve puzzles and complete quests.
- The turn based combat feels great (with the exception of the new physical/magic armor system)
- Exploration is rewarded
- Outstanding VFX to go along with combat abilities
- Many different options for solving quests
- Great voice acting
- Amazing story
Cons:
- Physical/Magic armor system. I don't think this was the right way to fix the CC issue that the original game had. It overly complicates combat interactions and makes an already complex system more difficult to understand
- The difficulty curve is quite high at the beginning
- UI with the Rune system. Frustrating to manage runes. When you want to place a rune into a piece of equipment that another character has in their inventory (not in their gear), you have to exit the UI and move it first.

There are many tower defense games available on Steam. In my opinion only some of them are really good. Dungeon Warfare belongs to this group. Although it uses simple pixel graphics the game is very addictive and offers a wide range of options when it comes to setting up your defense grid and define your play style.
The game features a balanced but very divergent choice of traps and weapons.
Enemies offer interesting and challenging abilities and remain fair except for a few last waves in a few levels.
The game also offers some rpg elements. By beating levels you will earn diamonds that can be used to upgrade weapons and traps. Upgrades can be changed for different levels or different play styles. Twelve runes can be individually activated or deactivated for each level to make the game harder and earn more diamonds.
The game also comes with a simple to use level editor and a Steam workshop that offers levels from other players. Designing individual maps is simple.
If you like tower defense games don't pass on this one. It's great!

Blocks that matter is a brilliant addition to any puzzle gamers library.  Jumping around a slime figuring out how to arrange your array of wood, stone, metal, and sand blocks in order to get them all back before you reach the next platform is a thrilling expierience.  Every puzzle completed feels like an accomplishment:  Rewarding and fun.   The addition of stars for completing a level with the most possible blocks and the treasure boxes add replay to each of the puzzles.  I have only played 30 of the campaign levels and still find myself engrossed in what challanges lay ahead.
The game is in no ways flawless, as the story is entirely seperate from the players control, predictable, and segments of dialog replay upon every single re-entry into the level that they occur in.  The player is expected to use their "look key" (Default C) to view the entire room ahead to know weather or not they should keep 3 sand blocks and a stone or 1 wood block 2 stones and a sand, and is rewarded with re-starting a puzzle if they choose wrong.
While at times leading to frustration, and leading me on through a predictable storyline, I find myself entranced through the game living up to its words and displaying its ability to live up to the challange of both a puzzle and a platform game.  I award thsi game 8.325 repeating stars and reccomend it to anyone who likes to mix puzzle-platform games.

Okay, since I've clocked over 10 hours for this game, I think I'm qualified to review it ;).
First off, this game is perfect if you're sick of fetch quests (or quests in general) in MMOs which most of the time are very stupid and cliche. In this game there are no quests and you set your own goals, it's a great sandbox.
Lack of lore information may be offputing to some, but IMO it's more fun to create your own lore using that thing us, old farts call "imagination" :).
The content in this game is great, there are so many available items and gear that I've barely scratched the surface of it all. And to think this game was made by just one person (aside of music) :)...
The only issue for me is the lack of player housing (unless I'm missing something, there is none but it can be added in future) and the performance (despite server supposedly being in German and me being in Poland, I experience quite bit of lag and have to restart game every so often as the games tries to fry my CPU and turns into the slideshow).
Overall, despite the flaws I've mentioned in the last paragraph, I recommend this game wholeheartedly. This is the only MMO that actually made me immersed in its world and when I play it at times I forget it's just a game. Then I notice the HUD.

While I generally think this game is a thumbs up, I can't say I am entirely happy with the level of polish... or lack there of.
It truly feels like a sequel or spiritual successor to Dungeon Keeper 2, but seems to lack a little of the heart that went into that title. It has a similar sense of humor, but maybe a bit more drab than the old DK franchise. I can see that the devs loved DK and wanted to make this as close to that concept as possible, but in too many places it falls just shy of the potential.
The old Dungeon Keeper games had some bad bugs in them that made them almost inplayable at times and unfortunately this game does follow that same trend as well. That being said, the devs have not given up on this game and appear to be trying to fix, improve, and expand on the game months after it's full release, so here is to hoping this game gets enough love from both players and devs over time.
All said, it does feel like Dungeon Keeper 2.5... I just wish it had felt more like Dungeon Keeper 3. But still a fun game and if you want to try something new or something old that feels new again, give this game a try. Worth a play.

Archeage was designed to be an MMO with a small but dedicated player base and the S. Korean version of Archeage succeeded as just that, a game with a small but dedicated player base willing to pay a fortune in subscription fees and micro-transactions for cosmetic items, potions, and equipment upgrades. As of this review, the NA version of Archeage is not dead and still receiving updates but when I look at Archeage I still see wasted opportunity. Archeage had a lot going for it but the failures of Trion and XL and the ingrained pay-to-win elements of the game have killed the fun and made the game unplayable. The current state of Archeage is horrible and I wouldn’t recommend playing it. However, I really want to emphasize that you really missed out if you didn’t play Archeage when it was freshly released.
In my opinion, Archeage simply never got enough attention and resources. Trouble on launch day is expected but Trion’s initial launch of Archeage featured massive downtimes, queues and rampant exploiting that never got resolved. Worse, all launches of fresh start servers would also be plagued with worse. Whether this was intentional is hard to gauge but It appears as though the game was just treated as money machine rather than as the ward of passionate developers. Trion either always underestimated player interest in the game or was skimping hard on its server and staff. At the start of each release, Archeage’s servers would always be filled to capacity and new servers would always have to brought in to lighten the load and even after introducing new servers there would still end up being server queues. The last fresh start releases featured absurdities like players being unable to get into the game for a month and getting a free month of subscription as compensation and players only being able to play for exactly 2 minutes before being booted off and having to wait hours in a Queue again.
Archeage had the obligatory grind to max level and a few PvE instanced dungeons but the main focus of the game was the PvP experience. Archeage featured 2 continental factions and a pirate faction and these factions were at war with each other. However, the game also allowed for player killing within one’s own faction which encouraged guild-play and even unholy alliances between guilds of the 3 factions. The way Archeage’s factions and PvP functioned coupled with the intense competition for resources and profitability of trade-pack carrying between continents created perhaps the best PvP play in MMORPG history. The combat was the standard MMO system with tab targeting and skills on a bar but this standard system, while not all that innovate, worked perfectly for Archeage. The intensity of Archeage’s PvP was greatly increased by the overpopulation of the servers. Grinding for gear required control over territory and hundreds of players fought just to hold onto grinding territory. The most profitable skills, Trade, and fishing required traveling through PvP land areas and an insanely massive PvP ocean area that separated the 3 factions.
However, Archeage’s excellent PvP was spoiled by its “pay-to-win” elements. The difference between high-level equipment and low-level equipment was massive, the difference between being able to beat a dozen max level players by yourself and being one knocked out in two hits. This difference in gear value was supposed to be balanced by the production of this equipment coming down to luck and costing a fortune. However, many of players would simply be able to buy up all of this equipment by selling APEX (tokens players purchase and sell to other players so that they buy subscription status and get benefits). Archeage basically allowed players to become practically unkillable within a month of a server starting and with most of the fun ways to make money were linked to PvP. This pay-2-win was disastrous as players who didn’t spend a fortune or have a no-lifing guild would struggle to even inflict damage in PvP. Worse, Trion also did a horrible job at cracking down on exploits, including exploits that allowed the worst of the player base to duplicate APEX and teleport valuable trade packs across the ocean. Trion would actively crack down on people bringing attention to exploits and has even given exploiters amnesty for being power users/spenders.
Currently, Archeage has a problem where PvP is not profitable. Archeage has a “labor system” which gives players points based on how much they’re online that they use to collect resources. I don’t know Archeage’s stated purpose for the labor system but I’d imagine that this came from Trion/XL wanting to encourage players to be efficient with their labor and participate in PvP instead of just doing repetitive tasks in safe areas. However, currently, Archeage is nothing but convoys of alts moving trade packs and fishing in safe areas (safe fishing was made very profitable). Alts have always been a problem and now Trion has openly declared the use of alts within the rules and now the use of alts is now not only more profitable than PvP but much more convenient. Trion seems to be just milking the games whales for whatever is left.
A few minor things of note about the game. Archeage has a garbage story but that doesn’t really matter. The game's music is pretty alright and the game lets you compose music and play music on a variety of instruments. Archeage is an M-rated game but the community managers coddle the player base, an example of being the CM’s recent crackdown on the discussion of controversial topics like Donald Trump. Archeage has an incredibly massive world and you can climb to the top of any mountain and swim to the bottom of the ocean and best of all, most of it is PvP. The game looked great on release, was well optimized and it aged well. The game has a serious problem with power-creep so casuals and players joining older servers don't really stand a chance. A mediocre player with advanced end game gear can take on dozens of maxed leveled players.  You can play as a flat character that has a battle mech.

TLDR: Buy the game if you loved DK1 and / or DK2. If your new to the "franchise" buy it still, you won't regret it, especially if you love dark humour and room building.

The Dungeon Keeper and DK2 aspect of this game is there, the room building, even the imps have the same animation. I was so surprised how close to the "old thing" it was, and how well the old games bugs and glitches were fixed.
As I said, it's quite the nostalgia trip.
One thing to note though, and I'm sure the devs of this game are aware and trying to fix is that this game has a minor memory leak on longer sessions. Approx. 6 hours in you'll start to freeze lag etc, but is easily fixed through killing the program and starting again, just remember to save your progress. :)
One thing that I'd hope is that this game would somehow intertwine the story of where DK2 was headed, as the story was awesome, even though the animation was crap in todays world. But I did feel like the story did somehow intertwine a little with DK2 and DK1 especially.

I picked this up on a whim since it appealed to my love of both tower defense and pixel art and discovered an awesome gem of the genre! I'm now at 100% achievement progress!
Dungeon Warfare may not do anything revolutionary or groundbreaking as far as the genre goes, but that's not what I'm looking for... for a genre with seemingly simple paradigms for mechanics and gameplay... I've sadly come across too many otherwise enjoyable games ruined by poor execution of some facet of the experience (usually by trying to be what they're not). Sometimes, I just want to play a pureblooded tower defense; build some towers and watch the enemies get burned, impaled, shocked, or thrown to their doom, without other genres muddying the waters. This game provides exactly that.
What makes this game so good is it boils down the essence of the tower defense experience and everything it does is well executed and enjoyable. Tower defense done right. And because of that, I've had the most fun with a tower defense game that I've had in quite some time!
TL;DR highly recommended for any fan of tower defense!
-- pros/cons --
+ difficulty curve almost perfect (only a couple spots required persistence to progress past)
+ satisfying tower combinations
+ solid progression system
+ little to no grinding to progress
+ great pixel art
+ all traps can have purpose depending on playstyle
+ maps provide ways to use their inherent dangers to your advantage (mine carts, pits)
+ traps both for the ground and walls so pathway space isn't wasted
- minor UI/UX annoyances
- only one tier 4 upgrade of each trap type made my OCD go wild
- would have preferred chiptunes for soundtrack
hats off to the developers, thank you for such a great game!

If you haven't played a Paradox game before: Crusader Kings II is a fairly good introduction to the grand strategy genre; you don't have to conquer the world, you don't really "win" the game. You essentially play from the point of view of the dynasty that controls a historic geographic area...I say that instead of "country", because you can play as the leader of a individual county or district,  or the leader of a group of counties, the leader of a group of groups...etc. there are some other variations available from mods and DLC's of course. So you could "win" the game by keeping your dynasty alive and in control of just one county until the end of game time, or you could win by conquering huge portions of the map... there is also considerable non-typical gameplay involving intrigue, religion, relationships (personal and political), illness, technology... In short, it's a little bit of everything. if you are put off by the "real-time" aspect, don't be; you have complete control of how fast the in-game clock runs, you CAN play it fairly similar to the way a pure turn-based game plays...hmm. I bet there is a mod for that? Speaking of mods... if you think of it, there probably already is a mod for it; if not, it's honestly very straightforward to make your own mod. I don't say it's simple, it can be very time consuming and can get complicated, but there is nothing hidden, no cheats required to make your own mod. oh, one other thing: there are a lot of DLC's. some are expensive. You don't need them to enjoy the game. if you do need the stuff in the DLC... you CAN make it yourself.
If you HAVE played EU, Vicky, HOI, etc; buy it.

When it comes down to what's one of the best Western RPGs, Oblivion will always be on the list. You can wander around for dozens of hours - and I mean that *literally* - without even following the main storyline or any of the DLC. With mods like Triple O (Oscuro's Oblivion Overhaul), Beautiful People (Ren's Beauty Pack compiled with other various customization mods), FCOM (google it, first link in the results) add so much replay value beyond belief. You might even find yourself sidetracking alot due to finding new locations or helping out people in town.
When/If you use mods, I highly recommend using the OBMM (Oblivion Mod Manager) for sorting, converting and activating custom content. TESNexus is THE site for Oblivion mods and no where else. Due to the [older] retail versions not having any DRM, some mods may conflict with the Steam version. To my knowledge I've had a few crashes but nothing major. The Fast Exit plug-in with Oblivion Script Extender (OBSE) works great.

An excellent squad based shooter mixed with RTS elements. One player becomes the commander, researching techs for better equipment and vehicles, managing resouces, building pre-set vehicles for faster construction, setting waypoints for ground units and helping to protect the main base. Meanwhile, players on the ground build the projects set by the commander and defend valuable buildings such as barracks and vehicle depots. Combat, for the most part, if fun and challenging with multiple classes and multiple guns for each class. Anti-Armor classes, Base Infantry, and Medics keep pressure on the front line while Engineers contruct turrets and keep bases and resource collectors safe. Sniping is perhaps the most difficult, and yet the most rewarding, since the maps are so large, sniping is a real challenge, but can turn the tide of battles.  As for faults, graphical fidelity is rather low with any given map's group texture being the same texture streched across miles, finally, many maps feature long and dull tracts of land that brings about boring combat. However, despite these few gripes, Empires is an excellent game with many facets that has kept me playing.
