I hadn't heard of this little gem before but glad I saw a friend post some screenshots of it.   First off let me say that this game is still in very early access.  Also even when playing local your internet connection must be stable for you to play.  I found this out the first few times I was trying to play and I had something downloading in the background.   I disabled the background download and then was able to connect with the local server.  I have plans on picking up another copy for my daughter for us to play LAN with once I try it out some more.
As of this writing I have about 90 minutes in the game.   I will say at this point don't go into the game expecting any fancy graphics, currently they are very bare bones.  Your character is going to look off, but I am sure that will vastly improve over time.  Also there isn't any hand holding in the game yet.  You are going to have to experiment.
One of the things I found out very quickly is that there are a mixture of mobs all around.  You might be fighting a level 3 Zombie one moment and then a level 15 Zombie Lord shows up.  The first time or two this happened I had my butt handed to me but I quickly learned the game is currently all about kiting.  Once I started doing this I was very easily able to takle mobs way above my level.  At level 5 a level 18 witch wasn't much problem as long as I paid attension to the attack queues.
One of the things that took a minute to get used to but now I love is that this isn't like WoW, you don't lock onto a mob.  You have to manually make sure your spells are aimed at the mob.  Missing is a very easy prospect if you are not careful.  But I like this as it adds some more realism (well when talking a fantasy game, as much as it can be I guess).  Still if you learn to kite and watch the attack warnings you can easily kite a much level mob without much problem.
Performance wise, the game is what you would expect for a $5 game that has just been released to early access, however I didn't have many performance issues that were not network related.  The rig I played on was an i7-860 2.8ghz, Nvidia 960 with 16GB RAM so no where near type of the line.   Framerates were low but once again this is in very early access and $5 invested.
I will say that the game pulled me in after I got the ropes.  Still not really sure what I am doing past the kiting of mobs, but fun none the less.  I recommend the game, even at this stage, $5 already better than many $50 games I have tried.  I haven't checked to see if there is any crafting yet.  I didn't see any indication that if there is going to be that it is implemented yet.  Crafting isn't really my cup of tea.  None the less crafting aside, I will say that I enjoyed this more than I did with Wurm Online (stand-alone) which I ended up getting a refund on and paid a good deal more money for.
I am not a great reviewer.  Often I just ramble.  But let me close with saying that $5 is worth a chance on this game, even if you let it sit in your library for a few months.   I have a feeling that it is going to shape up to be a nice little niche MMO/LAN RPG.

Don't let this mod fool you. It may look like a Command & Conquer look alike, but there's more to it though.
At the beginning of the match, your goal is to either reduce the tickets of the opposing team or destroy their command vehicle.
There's 4 classes to choose and each have their own ways of doing things. Not only that, but they also have the ability to learn new skills and perks in combat. There's skills that go with classes and skills that are class specific. Oh and the Engineer counts as a medic too.
But that's enough about the soldiers. You must be wondering what makes this an RTS mod because, I'm making it sound like a first person shooter. Well, that's because it's both an FPS and an RTS mod.
The RTS part is that whoever gets in the command vehicle, is. . .you guessed it. The commander.
The commander is in charge of managing your team's base. You have to upgrade, research and build to help your team. But in order to build something though, a soldier has to be near the position you want to build on. So send in an engineer and tell him what you need building. If your engineer will listen that is.
Yes this mod is team work heavy. It's vital if you want to win. Otherwise I can't guarrantee you'll win even a single match if you can't cooperate with your other team mates.
So if you want to play a mod that's both an FPS and an RTS, give Empires a try. But I'm sad to say that this mod is almost completely dead. You'll be lucky to find a server with players in it.
Also, I recommend getting some training before you try out being a commander. Commander is hard figuring out once you try being one, so get some commander training or else you'll never know what you're doing. As well as get bashed by your team mates for being the worst commander ever.

This game is a testament to what can be both good, and unbelievably bad in gaming.
I -LOVE- tower defense games, to the point of friends making fun of me for playing anything in the genre now matter how bad it looks. I picked this one up on a whim and right off the bat I could tell this game was set up with a mobile market in mind.
They build RNG into your potential power by making upgrades random drops, and build the maps around having gotten said random upgrades. So inevitably, you will reach a spot where the towers you have are simply not good enough, and to proceed you will have to grind and spend time PRAYING for a specific tower that you want to drop so you can upgrade it.
It is a black spot in the genre, and this game should be avoided on that basis alone. The rest of the game is bog standard tower defense, and not interesting enough to make this system worth my time. Do not purchase.

Do you like strategic roleplaying games like Baldur's Gate, Planescape: Torment, Arcanum, Fallout 1 & 2, Dragon Age (the first one), or XCOM 2?
Well, you're going to love this.
This game combines the roleplaying depth of Dungeons & Dragons with a strategic feeling similar to XCom 2. Practically speaking, what this means is that outside of combat, you can do damn well near anything you can think of. In combat, you can do the same. If you want to break into that house, kill that lady, steal that gold, and escape into the night, you can. If you want to be the daring hero, and save shackled stowaways on a sinking ship, you can. This game gives you the freedom to truly explore the "RP" factor of Roleplaying games. Very few games these days can hold a candle to the amount of roleplaying this game encourages.
I think a number of groups of Dungeons and Dragons players will likely abandon tradtional and even virtual play, and just move their games over to Divinity: Original Sin 2. It's easy to learn, hard to master - not unlike D&D - and it's also aesthetically gorgeous in both music and graphics. Can't recommend this game enough. Buy it.

If you have the patience or a friend to teach you how this game works, it´s a game you can easily spend hundreds of hours in. If you are into strategy games I can definately recommend this one. It´s not the easiest to learn, in fact, after fifty games you will still learn more about this game, and with the continuous supply of DLC you will not get bored of this game quickly.
Now, why is this game so great?
+ A big map that gets expanded occasionally. You can start of as a viking king in Norway and eventually rule India, or start as a Russian Slavic pagan and become emperor of Europe. And who knows what Paradox is preparing to add next?
+ A hundred of options with a thousand of choices. Whether you start off as a viking or a muslim, you will encounter similar problems. However, every religion, culture and country has it's own way of solving those. And as your character develops he will unlock (or block) other options. You'll never stop exploring these options.
+ Easier and harder gameplay is possible, so whether you are new or experienced you will always find your challenge
+ Great multiplayer, especially with friends. Whether you like PvPing or play versus the computer, a good multiplayer match will always keep you interested. Connecting to other players has been made easier (compared to how it was in the past), and is easily done via steam.
+ Events and results are random. You'll never know what happens, for you could be killed by bandits during your hajj to Mecca, or you could suddenly get an extra 100 gold.This can be very frustrating, or very interesting.
+ You can create your starting king with the ruler creater DLC
+ Loads of DLC that add new and interesting things to the game. When playing multiplayer, only the DLCs owned (and activated) by the host are available. If you play with friends, have the person who hosts most often get some DLCs, so the others won't need them.
+ Starting date can vary from 769 to 1337 (there currently are six bookmarks, respectively the Early Middle Ages (769), the Viking Age (867), the High Middle Ages (1066) , the Alexiad (1081) the Age of the Mongols (1241) and the Late Middle Ages (1337).
+ No game will every be the same. After a hundred years into the game, you will notice considerable differences in each game.
A game would not be realistic if not without flaws, so here are some of the downsides
- Event and results are random. You'll never know what happens, for you could be killed by bandits during your hajj to Mecca, or you could suddenly get an extra 100 gold. This can be very frustrating, or very interesting.
- Multiplayer can sometimes be unstable, especially if you play with more than 5 people. Desyncs will happen every now and then (usually you can play for an hour or two), and you have to restart your game to properly solve it. This is less common if you play with less player and if the internet connections are good. (If you have good internet, and so do your friends, this is MUCH less likely to happen.)
- At first, this game might be very complicated and confusing. I recommend playing with someone with experience, if possible.
- Once you get to a certain size, you will become quite unstoppable (although there are a few big armies coming to Europe, like the mongols, that might make you lose lands again).
Overall I would easily recommend this game. Once you grasp how this game works, you will be able to spend hours and hours of your time into this, exploring the near unlimited amount of options, and seeing how every game is available. If you play with friends, get a co-op game going.

This game proves that Tower Defenses still have a lot of potential.
Thanks to its top-down view, the game can rely heavily on traps and pits and it changes everything.
You can push enemies into the pits with moving walls, or fire hook arrows to pull them into the abyss.
The game also let you create small packs of auto managed soldiers, to stop the enemies... except some of them who will run faster to get killed by the next trap you put on their way.
Some traps can feel less useful than the others, but once you have tested them enough, you can find them good uses.
On the downsize, it's just a "level after level" kind of game, and if you are stuck on a level (generally because you want to use a strategy which is not the best), you can be blocked a long time.
I highly recommend to watch youtube videos to discover new strategies, even for levels you already completed, because you can play levels a lot of different ways.
The game looks to be between 20 and 30 hours long, and if it's you are an experienced Tower Defense player.
If you have played over 100 Tower Defenses (like me) and think you know everything about the genre, you will still be amazed by how many new stuff this game contains.

When it comes down to what's one of the best Western RPGs, Oblivion will always be on the list. You can wander around for dozens of hours - and I mean that *literally* - without even following the main storyline or any of the DLC. With mods like Triple O (Oscuro's Oblivion Overhaul), Beautiful People (Ren's Beauty Pack compiled with other various customization mods), FCOM (google it, first link in the results) add so much replay value beyond belief. You might even find yourself sidetracking alot due to finding new locations or helping out people in town.
When/If you use mods, I highly recommend using the OBMM (Oblivion Mod Manager) for sorting, converting and activating custom content. TESNexus is THE site for Oblivion mods and no where else. Due to the [older] retail versions not having any DRM, some mods may conflict with the Steam version. To my knowledge I've had a few crashes but nothing major. The Fast Exit plug-in with Oblivion Script Extender (OBSE) works great.

I got this game gifted, off the recent Humble Bundle, so maybe I'm not in the best position to review this, but you're reading this, so I already did. Deal with it.
I don't think Blocks That Matter are worth €5 of your money. Why? To begin with, it's not a very complicated game. It's a puzzle platformer, based around manipulating blocks, that might as well been a Flash game. But it's not a very well designed puzzle platformer either.
The "premise" of the game is ridiculous: two devs (who are basically Alexey Pajitnov, creator of Tetris, and Markus "Notch" Persson, creator of Minecraft; the game doesn't attempt to hide this) create some small robot who has to solve puzzles to go to portals and to then go to more portals and for some reason rescue the two heroes. (I didn't really pay attention to the story, it's a
.) Yeah, could do better in terms of plot development.
The Tetris and Minecraft references are very prevalent in the game, and by very prevalent I mean
. You got blocks. Of different types, which behave differently. Blocks, which look very much like in Minecraft. And behave quite a lot like in Minecraft. (gravel and sand fall down, wood and stone doesn't, obsidian is unbreakable, etc.)
And then you can use these blocks to build structures. But only structures shaped like Tetris blocks.
That's the game.
I'm sure there are more kinds of blocks with properties that I couldn't dream of (the game even shows me some of these new blocks I can't do anything with in the first levels of the game, as if to taunt "you can't do this yet! better backtrack later!"), but the gameplay is frustrating. I'm probably bad at the game, but to be fair, getting stuck in a level and having to restart it by
(or blowing yourself up, in this case), is not good design in my book.
The music is okay, the visuals are okay, but all this to me is a mix of two already-existing games, just in the puzzle genre. There's zero originality in this, and I doubt I'll play this longer, it's just not fun to do.
You can buy this if you don't mind all of the above though I guess. (especially if you're smarter than me)

An interesting post-apocalyptic game. Usually when I think of post-apocalpytic games I think of a generic zombie shooter, so when I went into Fallen Earth, I was surprised (Granted there is a part of the main story where they kind of have zombies). Fallen Earth is a open world MMORPGFPS. It's alittle more hardpressed towards the survival aspect then the shooting aspect. Crafting is a big thing in Fallen Earth and is probably one of the funnest thing to do. Almost everything you can get, can be crafted. From weapons, armor, and even your ammo. Sure you can buy most of your items from the auction house, but there's a certain feeling of just crafting it yourself that is so amazing in the atomsphere that Fallen Earth has created. The combat is a twist between a FPS and a TPS. You can shoot in a third person camera view but I perfer playing in a first person view, Although it feels just a tad bit off and could use some work  it's generally pretty good. Although not the most innovating or new, that's not really what Fallen Earth is about. In my opinion Fallen Earth is about the grander feeling of the atompshere of a Post-Apocalyptic world. Not saying anything about it being a hardcore role playing game but if you can get past the generic combat, it is quite an intriguing game. Theres plenty to do, and even from a story perspective, with all of the side quests and even the main quest is kind of interesting, it caters to a wide audience. If you're looking for an openworld MMO that focuses on elements other than combat, than look no further.

This is a really good puzzle platformer and anyone who enjoyed Portal, Braid, Limbo, Antichamber, or countless other games like those would enjoy this one.

I have a slight warning, though. Level 34 is brutally hard and nearly had me rage-quit. It feels out of place with the rest of the game, as it pulls a Super Meat Boy kind of platforming skill for a few minutes. Still, after that level, things come back to normal and the game is far more focused on puzzles than platforming. I completed the entire game in about 8 hours, mainly because I used no online sources for hints and pushed through the Chocolate levels(bonus ones).
I'm disappointed that the game comes with its own bonus levels as well, but locks them until you complete certain objectives in the game. I would have liked them to just open when you beat the game.
Anyway, pick up this game if you like puzzle platformers. It is not at the top of list of great ones, but is decent fun, and is a great sale purchase.

Golem Gates is an interesting blend of RTS with Card Game. However, unlike most RTS games there's no base building (outside of some minor stationary defensive weapons), and instead your strength and power rely on your Glyphs, which are essentially your cards. By building a good deck of glyphs that mixes spells, creatures, traps, and buildings, the objective is to overwhelm your opponent's army and destroy their Harbinger to win.
Instead of resource gathering like most RTS games, you regenerate mana over time, which you use to activate all of your glyphs, and you can increase that by capturing certain points on the map. This creates a unique gameplay experience where your strategy comes almost entirely from unit placement and proper glyph management both during the actual game and before you begin with building a proper deck. At the end of any game you get glyphs to help create that perfect deck.
Overall the game is very fun. There's a versus modes, both with team vs team gameplay possible as well as free-for-all. Additionally, there's a coop survival mode where you attempt to survive 15 minutes with an optional friend against a neverending horde of enemies on a randomly generated map. Definitely a unique, thought out experience.

Pretty short game, but if you can get it for less than a dollar or two (or free while Indie Gala was giving it away) I'd recommend it. I imagine it'd be more fun with other players, but I wasn't able to join any of the servers.
The UI is pretty awful, especially the Armory. The hit detection is iffy. The weapons all feel about the same (upgraded sniper rifle does 2 hit kill, but so does my starter pistol so what's the use of upgrading?). Story is pretty meh. Nazis want to steal a sphere that's making everyone turn into mutated monsters, they want to use it to win World War 2. A few German soldiers, some Americans, and a Russian soldier all team up to try to destroy the sphere before it gets in the wrong hands.
There's only 10 levels, I think, and they're all exactly the same. Different backgrounds, sure, but each one consists of you walking to the right until you reach the end. You kill enemies to earn XP and occasionally an enemy will drop a weapon. There's two weapons that sometimes show up in maps that aren't available in the Armory, a flamethrower and a lightning gun. Both are fun to use and very overpowered.
Occasionally a boss will show up, usually just consisting of throwing all your grenades and then running away, firing a few times, running away, firing a few times, etc. etc. Not the best gameplay, but also not the worst. There's also Mechs in the game, but I only saw them in the Arena mode, not in the main campaign, which is a bummer. Though the one Arena match I tried, the Mech died extremely fast, so oh well.
I feel like the game would've been much better if it was 2D, instead of 3D (not only do you walk left and right, but you can walk up and down, which causes a bit of the hit detection issues, I think).
The animations were pretty good, and the enemy designs were cool for the mutated creatures. I appreciated some of the small touches too, like the wounded guys on the ground that were receiving CPR from nurses, but you'd notice them open one eye occasionally. Think of the CPR pool scene from The Sandlot. He was basically doing that.
Anyway, decent game, I don't regret spending the hour it took for me to beat it. Would've been nice if it had a bit more to it, maybe secret areas or something. I'm sure it'd be a lot more fun if you play it with a friend, too.
Also, ignore that I have 10 hours in this game. I've left it idle to collect the cards, but they take a very long time to drop. It really did only take me an hour to beat the game. Oh, and by the end of the game I reached level 10, but it looks like the last weapon upgrade you unlock is at level 45. I doubt most people will ever reach that. and as far as I can tell those weapon upgrades just give you a different looking skin/weapon attachments that don't do anything extra.

I seriously can't imagine why so few people know about this game.
This game has everything you could want from a Tower Defense game and it may very well be the most strategical one I ever played. A lot of TD games are either too easy or too hard but this game just gets it right:
Most of the levels are easily winnable on the first try, which is a good thing because of the "rune" mechanic. Runes allow you to customize the difficulty in a really big way, making even the easiest levels challenging if you include all 10 of the difficulty-increasing ones. There is, however also one that allows you to play "endless" mode and another one that significantly decreases the difficulty at the cost of the experience you gain from it, which I find really helpful for players that get frustrated when playing the same level over and over without success. This makes for a perfect difficulty progression.
Another important aspect that really sets this apart from most other TD games is that the variety of towers - or rather:  traps - is remarkable as there are traps that push enemies, traps that pull enemies, traps that spawn minions to stall enemies, AOE traps, traps that counter fast enemies and so on.... This makes for very strategic gameplay because you need to have a good trap composition to counter every type of enemy that comes within a certain level.
As if it didn't have enough replayability already, this game has a built-in easy-to-use level editor and there are already a lot of user-created maps on the workshop. This is pretty cool but I haven't used it a lot as of the time I write this review (7-8 hours in).
My only real complaint previously was the lack of key rebinding options but that was fixed soon after I posted this review initially.

I'm gonna start this review off by saying I am a huge, huge fan of strategy games. One of my all time favorite video game franchies is Nintendo's Fire Emblem series of games, a strategy role playing series where every action and battlefield decision counts because of permadeath as a feature (at least, if you're playing these games the way they're meant to be played. Valkyria Chronicles is among one of the most unique SRPGs I've ever played, so let's jump right into the review
In Valkyria Chronicles (VC) you play as Welkin Gunther, a young aspiring biologist with a family legacy of military service whose dreams get put on the backburner when his home country is attacked, forcing him into active service.
The world/setting of VC is heavily inspired by that of Europe during World War I (with tongue and cheek references such as the war being called the
War. Thematically wise, the game deals with surprisingly serious topics such as racism, with major side characters getting development through side missions and thus character arcs. The other playable characters do not get too much development but one group of them does through the
dlc that comes included with the Steam version. Overall, I believe the story is decent, with enough status quo changes and plot development to keep us invested in the story.
The artsyle of the game goes for a watercolor esque approach and I have to say it looks quite nice. The world and maps look very detailed and the perspective shifts from the hand drawn looking strategic maps are excellent to see translated into 3D when moving your units in real time. The music transitions from subtle subdued melodies to louder anthems when transitioning from strategic to real time movement as well which is quite nice.
The gameplay in this game is simply fantastic. As mentioned before combat shifts between an overhead hand drawn map of the current game map with your and enemy unit positions clearly denoted, and you must move your units in somewhart real time to position them to kill enemies and take objectives. Movement works somewhat like superhot, with enemies only firing on you when you move. Different unit types are encouraged (e.g. Lancers specialize in taking out tanks but are very inaccurate, scouts have a large movement gauge but low defense, etc). Unlike many SRPGs your actions are limited by the amount of action points you have, so it is possible to move the same unit multiple times per turn if their movement gauge is high enough but conversely you may find that you will not be able to move all of your units in one turn. Ultimately, this system forces you to optimize your actions and encourage smart decisions. Unit diversity is also encouraged as no two are alike: one scout may hate grassy, nature-filled areas and perform poorly in combat there while another may excel there but hate metal, concrete structures and perform poorly there. Some may be old and suffer penalties in accuracy for their age. This truly helps to make you invest in your units.

Tower defense veteran here. Dungeon Warfare plays out similarly to a 2d version of Orcs Must Die, without a controllable hero. The scoring is also calculated in the same manner - Enemies have a score value and that value is multiplied by the # of different traps involved in their demise. You earn bonus points and gold for killstreaks.
There is a rune system (similar to the trait system used in GemCraft games) for added challenge that adds a multiplier to your level score. If you beat a stage, the resulting score is given to you in EXP, which allows you to level up, which gives you increased skill points, starting gold, and trap slots (up to 9). You cannot repeatedly farm a stage for EXP, as only increases in your highest score will net more EXP. Every level also has an endless mode, which is unlocked if you  complete the stage with 4 or more runes. Endless mode is a great way to earn extra EXP, as your score for it is separate from your normal high score. There is also an individually selectable rune to make the game easier, for those who want to progress without as much challenge, but you will earn less points.
Difficulty is fairly well balanced. Most of the early stages are a breeze, but later ones will keep even good players up to devise better strategies. There are also interesting achievements to seek out if you are inclined.
Graphics are gritty, fitting the theme. The game has a dark, medieval steampunk look. Nothing looks impressive or detailed.
The music is redundant. I found it to also fit the theme, but there weren't many tracks. Sounds are limited, but great - especially when units fall into pits.
Enemy variety is important for TD games and there is plenty in this one. There are some that will annoy you, like the horse or dwarf. It's good for a tower defense game to have threatening enemies. Trap (tower) variety is great. There are plenty of interactive cooldown traps to keep you busy.
There is also a map maker included. You can create and play content made by others.
Since music and graphics are the only arguable weak-points, and those matter least to the tower defense genre, I can say that this is one of the best tower defense games released this year. I didn't encounter a single bug throughout my time with this game. It's well-done.

Honest Reviews by Taroth:
Valkyria Chronicles HD Remaster
Biases: I've owned this game on PS3 since its release. I've completed the game at least 5 times before touching this PC version.
Upgrades: Honestly, there is almost no notable difference between the PC version and the PS3 verison. Graphics are updated, but not enough to matter. All DLC is included in this version so that gets a thumbs up for sure. The DLC does little to add story content (Edy and Selvaria are side stories), but it adds some great combat.
The original game is one of the absolute best tactics RPGs I have ever played! Some background - I started playing turn based tactics games with Xcom in 1994 and I have played just about every tactics game I can get my hands on from Fallout Tactics, FF Tactics, to Disgaea, Phantom Brave, and even D&D tactics on the PSP! I stomached Suikoden tactics.... a horrible game! So, by calling this one of my favorite of the genre should carry some weight.
Why do I love this game?
1. Combat:
The combination of classes, random leveling traits, and the real time movement/combat 3rd person shooter aspect just seem to be perfectly combined in this game. VC 1 is a genre changer, yet it has never been replicated. This game is lightning in a bottle..... combat, tactics, character development, and the plot all work to create a unique gameplay experince and charm that few other titles in the genre have.
The combat system is easy to understand but difficult to master. It is tactical, tense, and exciting. I hate..... HATE vehicles in tactics games- yet they do a great job with the tanks in this game. Recruiting is fun, developing characters is fun, combat is a joy!
The other thing about combat is that people complain they might lose towards the end of a battle and have to replay 45 minutes to an hour and a half of gameplay. This might happen to you. I can think of 2 or 3 combat scenarios in which I lost on my first playthrough (not including DLC). I did not mind replaying missions. If you don't enjoy the combat system, then wiping will be a major issue for you. If you are into tactics games and don't mind replaying missions (I'm looking at you again Fire Emblem), then this is right up your alley.
2. The story:
I can't believe I am saying this about a game not titled Fire Emblem, but I loved the story. It took me a long time to get behind, but in the end this game has a truly fantastic storyline! It touches on racism, war, death, and mysticism. The timing felt slow to start, but it really works to build the characters (only a few main characters) up to set the stage for major plotlines down the road. I grew to loathe the empire and really enjoy the various personalities involved in the resistance. There is a history and life to every aspect of the game. Even your engineers who help with research trees and equipment manufacturing have a backstory. The reporter who follows your battalion also develops.
Be warned, there is a ton of dialogue and plot in this game, but it does pay off.
3. Graphics:
I grew up with JRPGs (yes even those BEFORE FF7 made them mainstream in the US). That said, I am not an anime lover, nor do I find the humor and exageration of anime style games/movies/shows all that compelling. For some reason though, the grapics in this game really grew on me. The way the game feels more like a manga or comic book really works for the presentation. It is almost like playing a tabletop game with character cutouts, although everything moves and reacts in real time. Typically anime art does not bolster the enemies in a way to strike fear into me as a player (I'm more akin to the dark souls style of art for RPGS than the anime style). However, I can say that in the end the art direction in this game is spot on for the type of story they want to tell. A more gritty style would have removed the charm of some characters- who are over the top architypes, but still endearing.
4. Controls:
Use a controller. Okay, that may be harsh. I am several years into this game and only had a PS3 controller to use until now. I didn't give the mouse and keyboard a chance in this version. The controller based controls feel natural and smooth. Hopefully mouse/keyboard is just as good.
5. Overall:
The complete package results in one of those games that I will suggest to other people to play. I rarely do this and can list those games quite easily (FF7, Demons Souls/Dark Souls, Heavy Rain, Axiom Verge, The Witcher Series, Mass Effect 1, Orcs Must Die! 2). Not many make the list of games I strongly recommend, but Valkyria Chronicles does. I even hunted down a PSP and a copy of VC 2 just because this game was so great......
Do yourself a favor and avoid any releases beyond 1 and 2. The rest of the series has lost the magic of the first.
In conclustion, Valkyria Chronicles is a true gem.... one of the best RPGs of the PS3 generation and easily the best turn based tatical RPG of its generation. The combat system is a refreshing change from the Fire Emblem/Shining Force approach to combat. This variation is welcome, fun, challenging, and exciting all at once. There is a depth to this game that many don't appreciate until they try EX mode combat. Let me say this game sort of defines why steam needs a neutral button and not just thumbs up/down.
On the one hand I do love the game; but on the other I am massively aware that the bulk of my love comes from the nostalgia trip of how much I loved Dungeon Keeper (and DK2).
If it were not for Dungeon Keeper I'm not sure I could like this game half as much as I do. I am keenly aware that this game was made by fans of Dungeon Keeper; and for what it is there is an amazing wealth of throwback to the game it is trying to emulate.
Unfortunately it also suffers from everything you would expect from what is essentially a "mod team" that is trying to convert itself to an actual development studio. The amateur mistakes show through with poor game balance and narrow strategic layers that never reach the level of variety as the original DK's pulled off. The costs of spells, the speed of unit deployment, the limited number of strategies that the enemy AI is able to cope with; the list of cons is fairly long.
Basically what the game ends up being is a very polished shell with Dungeon Keeper logos painted all over it but inside is just empty and hollow.
To their credit this team also continues to expand on the game, and I'll admit there has been improvement over time. But the reality is that it's a very long time coming. For a released game we're still seeing things added that should have been in from day one (and that was years ago...).
In summary this game is a labor of love from a devoted team trying to recreate Dungeon Keeper and if you are a fan of that old series and can afford to throw money in their direction. Do it. This may in the end be the only close successor the gaming world will see (at least in this decade). Just be aware that the game is heavily flawed and I'm not sure the dev team has the experience needed to ever make it as-good-as Dungeon Keeper really was, so we (as a community) must either foster them in the hopes they improve or just play it for what it is and cry over what's missing.
On a side note if you have not played the originals; find them. Get Dungeon Keeper and Dungeon Keeper 2; they are available on GOG, and worth the effort. Despite the slightly aging graphics they are still fantastic games. Then come play War for the Overworld with us and pray it continues to reach for the glory of what Dungeon Keeper once was.
As-is I'll continue to play War for the Overworld occasionally and hope the team behind it continues to learn and improve on it (which they have done for many years now, impressively for a team with no official training or past game development experience)

ros:
- The game is the first game (Besides Lugaru, their earlier game) that has had this fantastic and intuitive combat system.
- It is quite unique to find a game where you have the same chances to die as the AI enemy has, and all that keeps you alive is skill. Take for example Call of Duty where you have much more health than the AI opponenets. Of course there is also a need of skill in Call of Duty, all i'm trying to say is that Overgrowth is very unique on those two exact points. And for this point i count it as a pro, but someone else could easily count it as a con, so as i said in the beginning, these are just my opinions.
- I've always loved gladiator games/modes and the arena mode in Overgrowth is a great idea. But as much as this is a pro, it's also a con, becuase i feel that they could have improved the mode so much. For example they could have added the actual possibility to achive something like a new rank, so you could compete global. Take for example the Fifa Ultimate Team mode, they feature divisions, and if you win enough games out of 10, you move up. They could add things like this to make the game mode a game for itself.
- Superpowers without superpowers. I love how you can jump high, long and run on walls, but what i love even more is that everyone else can too. You're not overpowered in any unfair way, it is just plain fun! Just as before this may be a pro for some, and a con for others.
- The realism. The fact that some kicks and punches are more lethal compared to others, and it is a mather of the placement. The fact that if you get kicked into a wall you are most likely to suffer dramatically more damage, and you're most likely dead if it was the second kick or punch. Just as before this may be a pro for some, and a con for others.
Cons:
- Lack of worked through gamemodes. As fun as the game is, no matter how much you like it. Killing the same old rabbit without achieving anything just becomes boring at some stage.
- Multiplayer. I really wish that they at some point will add multiplayer to the game.
- The fact that they haven't made one proper level yet also is a bad disappointing.
- The sounds aren't really that satisfying, you could really wish for some better sound effects when the combat system is so great, but the sound just dosen't match you lethal and awesome kicks.
Finally my score for this game would be 8/10

Great game. If I were to grade the game strictly on its own merits it would easily be the greatest source mod. However, alot of the "veterans" of the game create an atmosphere which quickly turns away potentially new players. This game has a "commander" who essentially places structures and issues strategy for a team to follow. If you're a new player, never ever even try to command. You will be criticized harshly if you make even one mistake. Essentially this leaves players in a catch 22. You can't gain experience as commander unless you are allowed to command in atleast a 5v5, but if you play a 5v5 you  can't command and get better due to veterans criticizing you to the extent that you just leave. Alot of veterans believe the game is dead/dying due to new players performance as commanders (noted on multiple occasions that vets would blame bad comms for the reason why people would turn away from this game.) This is simply not the case. The game is dying for two reasons. One, source engine is getting old, and two, the majority of the veteran community is extremely unforgiving towards new players. Overall the game itself 10/10, but combined with the  community its probaly closer to 7/10.

Alexey Pajitnov (designer of Tetris) and Markus Persson (designer of Minecraft) were kidnapped because they were supposedly collaborating on a new game. Instead they were working on a miniature robot that was a blend of their two computer games. Tetrobot was activated in their absence and had to go rescue them from "The Boss." Definitely cliche.
As Tetrobot, you start out only being able to jump but quickly get a drill attachment. With this drill you are able to drill and collect certain blocks in the level, similar to Minecraft. Throughout the game, a couple of upgrades are added to Tetrobot to allow it to drill and collect different types of materials. With this collected matter, Tetrobot can regurgitate the blocks onto the paying field following a couple of rules:
1) The first block must be anchored to the level. It cannot just be put into mid-air. Subsequent blocks must be attached to blocks currently being placed.
2) Groups of four blocks must be placed. No more - No less. This creates "Tetronimos" I-J-L-O-T-S-Z.
Collecting and building platforms to get through the level is the goal. There are couple other things such as undrillable blocks, falling blocks, slimes and TNT. Each level also contains a Treasure Chest. Collect this chest and bring it to the level and you collect the "Block That Matters" for the level. The blocks that matter all pay tribute to different games.
Finally, every level has a star available. If you finish the level with a set level of blocks in your inventory you get a star, i.e. finish using the minimal number of blocks left on the board. Finish at the minimum get a gold star. Finish below the minimum and get a green star.
Rescuing Alexey and Markus will probably only take 3-4 hours. One of the Steam achievements is to complete this part of the game in one session. However, to get 100% (all the BTM and stars) will take significantly longer. I have played about 15 hours and still have 16 stars to collect and 14 bonus levels to complete. This is a fun little puzzle game that can provide a casual distraction to full out rage quit.

How it feels. It feels like a Conan game. It really does. There is a great amount of gore, you look like some poor deprived barbarian, and the nudity. I don't need nudity in a game, but when basing a game off of Conan you need to.  My first experience to the world, like most people probably, was the 1982 Conan the Barbarian movie. Not the greatest movie ever by any means, but very enjoyable. The one complaint though is that it is a movie about killing people, and I swear there are more sex scenes than killing scenes. Having said that. The nudity in the game, to me, is sort of a callback to that. In a weird way it helps build the world.
Cons:
Bad Optimization. So I have the recomended everything. My computer is nice and beefy and by all accounts should be able to play the game on ultra settings. But it just can't. It runs perfectly fine until I get near water, a forested area, or a city. At that point it is trying to load in so many things (even on medium it has actual blades of grass) that the frame rate tanks. It is impossible to play on ultra outside of the desert. High quality is still bad but not nearly as bad, and usually what I keep it on.
Bugs. Like every early access title it has beautiful bugs and glitches for us to explore. And by beautiful I mean mind numbingly dreadful. It isn't nearly as bad on single player so right now I have to say, play on that or co-op.
NPC AI. So all the animals are great, there really is nothing wrong with them. But. The NPC people are another story. Specifically the ones in the camps near the desert. They don't do anything. They just stand there, holding swords. Never moving. They don't even react to animals coming into their camp. The only thing they react to is a player, and you have to be very close for them to react to that. I would personally like to see them at least walking around the camp. They don't need to do backflips for me, or chop down a tree, but some movement and a care when something aside from me has entered their camp would be nice.
Can't move things. So I made a camp fire and a bed roll. And I wanted to move them. Maybe I missed something? But I can't move them, I have to dismantle them, which doesn't even break them down into all of their parts. A campfire cost 50 branches and 30 stone. I got 12 stone for dismantling it. It'd be nice if I could pick them up and move them, or at least got a better ratio back when dismantling.
Dehydration is a little too fast. So, you don't actually run out of water that quickly. I only did once and I am convinced it was a bug because I have never run out of water that quickly again. But when you run out of water and you start to die, it is just a little too quickly for my taste. You start the game in a desert, and it feels like one. There is rarely any water. I honestly died 9 times of dehydration before I was finally able to find water. Anytime I ran out of water there was just nothing I could do, I had to sit and watch myself die because there was no way I could find any water in time.
Final Point. Night is too short. Weird complaint I know, but it goes by so quickly. I haven't ever exactly timed it, but day seems to last about 30 minutes, maybe less. Whereas night only last about 5-7 minutes. I won't say the times should be equal because night is much harder to work in, but it'd be nice if night were about 10-12 minutes long. Just to give you extra uneasiness if you are caught outside during the night.
All in all the game is fantastic, and I really look forward to future updates. I'd honestly say the game is worth the $30 I spent for it. I have generally had an amazing time playing and I certainly feel as though I have gotten my money's worth out of playing it.

Blocks That Matter is a puzzle game with some platforming involved. The Adventure Mode has about 40 levels total, and there are also about 20 optional bonus levels to be unlocked as you collect hard to reach blocks locked in chests through each area. You are also given access to several bonus levels that have tie-ins to other games that were included in the same Humble Bundle that must also be unlocked. If all of those levels were not enough, you also have access to numerous player-made levels that are available for download in-game. The artwork is cute and interesting to look at, but is not rich with much animation. The main character is a small robot by the name of Tetrabot, and it looks very much like a little clothes washing machine. The puzzles aren't too complicated, but I do find myself restarting each level many times in order to get them right. Especially the last ten or so levels are quite difficult and will require your focused thoughts and attention to hit upon a solution. Your goal is to manipulate blocks in the environment in order to gain passage to other sections of the levels and to exit through portals. The music is very good, and of the ambient chiptune genre. This is a relaxing game, and even its storyline is cute and fun. The chests (containing video game history trivia blocks) scattered throughout each level are mostly very difficult to reach, but they are not required to proceed. The premise of the game is very creative and does not resort to cheap gimmicks or pretentiousness to accomplish its goals. All puzzles are intuitive and logical, challenging the player in the most adequate of ways. Some levels are significantly more difficult than the majority, and you will retry many, many times, until you are able to pass it, but this does not subtract from the overall quality and enjoyment of the game. For completists, there are dozens of hours to be spent with Blocks That Matter, with all the additional content made available as bonuses and for free. The ending was adorable and continued to showcase the artists' distinguished style. Even for someone such as myself, who does not enjoy puzzles as a whole, appreciated, rejoiced, and experienced hours of entertainment from this puzzle platformer gem.

A fantastic RPG with tons of choices to make regarding the story, the environment and the encounters. You can start the game with a character that somewhat resembles a familiar archetype, but it's very easy for every character to quickly become a custom hybrid. Your companions each have their own distinct personality and their own story to explore.
The game doesn't hold you hand too much, you have to explore the environment, and talk to NPCs to find sidequests instead of just looking for quest markers. Some destinations do get marked on your map, but often you rely on journal notes.
The combat is a familiar turn-based format, but features a system with a ton of different ways to use the environment or combine spells for different effects. Each character also has a physical armour pool and magical armour pool to work through before damaging a character's health pool. Both types of armour can be healed by various spells and effects, and both prevent different types of damage and status effects.
Overall, D:OS2 has all of the elements that make up a great RPG game. An engaging story, and a rich world to explore, full of rewards for exploring it. The combat is fun, and rewards creativity, and there are a lot of ways you can fight battles. It's sure to clean up come award season, and is definitely a contender for game of the year.

A novel and surprisingly engrossing and addictive tower defense game--albeit, more accurately, dungeon defense.  Pesky heroes are assailing your various lairs en masse and it's down to you to devise elaborate combinations of booby traps and minions to keep them at bay.  Unlike most tower defense games where you're given a bevy of said towers to line some paths and periodically make some mazes, Dungeon Warfare's arsenal plays much more heavily into utilizing the surroundings and managing the different sorts of heroic intruders battering at your dungeon doors.
One of the most ready examples of this are the pits and chasms that you'll find in many of the locales; there are a number of physics and movement related traps that can push, catapult or pull intruders off ledges and send them tumbling into the abyss (the harpoon trap being particularly brutal and fun--firing a big tethered javelin into enemies and 'reeling them in'.)
Different enemies have different properties, so a heavily armored knight is a bit harder to push around than their lighter fare.  Horsemen try to rush through your arsenal to batter down doors and bee-line for your inner sanctum, dwarves seek out your barricades to sap and destroy, adventurers try to duke it out with your minions and are generally nimble, etc.  Similarly, stages can include tracks with mine carts circulating them to plow enemies around in dangerous intersections, spiked walls ready for you to shove lines of troops against them, etc.  You'll also find giant boulders you can set tumbling to crush everyone in its path.
There are quite a few different traps and setups available at your disposal which can compliment one another fairly well.  I'm pretty fond of a lair that brings about a little necromancer who will go about raising slain enemies as a tiny army of skeletons.  Many of the traps bring Orcs Must Die to mind--but they're solid to take inspiration from (such as the springboards that launch enemies into pits, for instance.)
Accompanying the traps are a bevy of cooldown-based powers you can utilize ranging from giant bear traps to bombs to eggs which hatch minions when enemies draw near or power-ups for your traps.  There is also an excellent 'trap mastery' system wherein you can invest gems to unlocking upgrades for your traps, reducing cooldowns / costs, making them do more damage, etc. (gems being earned by completing stages well and leveling up.)  You can also put gems into basic upgrades such as being able to sustain more enemies in your sanctum before losing, or starting the stages with more gold to work with--and leveling up also gives you more gold to start with as well.
Additionally, there are 'runes' which can be activated for stages to make them more challenging (faster enemies, fewer resources, limited load-out of traps, etc.) in exchange for more experience bonuses.  Completing a stage with four runes active unlocks the ability to play that stage in 'endless mode' for additional challenge.  Between the runes, large variety of traps and tools, I feel like there's plenty of mileage to be had--and that's before taking into consideration that the game includes a pretty easy to use map editor and Steam Workshop support.  Cool!
It's hard to fully do the full aesthetic experience of Dungeon Warfare justice in text and I feel like the screenshots don't necessarily do the game justice--but when you've got an elaborate gauntlet of death traps going full-force and a hoard of invaders trying to barge their way through it, it really gets quite rad.  It may seem a bit low-fi at first glance, but when grinders and darts and spring-loaded spikes are firing away while lightning arcs are chaining between knights and necromancers and demons are keeping footmen mired in boiling oil, it's all to fun effect.
If you're the sort that typically gives tower defense style games a pass, I'd urge a bit of a longer look at this one--I was very surprised by how deep it got its hooks in me; it is definitely the sort of game that if it clicks with you, you'll want to keep pushing on for 'just one more stage.'
Edit: Since release, Dungeon Warfare continues to receive excellent developer support by way of additional polish, making it all the more an excellent little game to revisit in your library!

An absolute pile of trash for many, a MARVELOUS GEM for others. I am with the others on this one.
As another review had stated, it is quite a different fighting game STILL IN ALPHA in terms of mechanics besides the part where you smash the other person into submission. Unique combat at its finest when either your rabbit avatar is facing the opposition with bare hands or armed with a variety of weapons the enjoyment out of winning is always there.
Currently no story has been impletmented but i have no griped against it knowing that fact before and after purchasing this game.
The game does not allow you to just throw out blows randomly like any street fighter game, it will only allow you to attack while near the vicinity of an enemy. Nor is blocking an infinite 1-Button forever guard, you will have to carefully time it or dodge to get the better of your foe and even reversing the blow into a throw to your advantage.

Combat with weapons gives a real sense of danger as each blow may cripple you or end you. The game shows many signs of injury as your character bleeds profusely from surface impacts and weapon injuries. Parrying or dodging during armed combat is even more important as you will die very quickly if you don't. Along with close combat is the ability to throw your weapons usually resulting in fatal injuries or a carefully timed catch leaving you to deal with 2x the armaments from your enemies now.
Punishing the game is when you're not careful about your methods of attack or are unaware of your environments. I have fallen on my head countless times in game and knocked myself out resulting in a loss while trying to kick an opponent into the wall, I have chuckled nearly everytime but am sad at such a ridiculous loss. I have also kicked an enemy away only to realize i propelled myself head first into a very solid wall behind me also resulting in a loss.
I really hope to see more from this game as it is an amazingly FUN game to play, add a few different modes or features and more connectivity in the future of this game and it will forever stay a classic in my library.

VC is a tactical RPG unlike any other. Its most original aspect is how it blends the classic turn-based system of the genre with action and FPS elements. While it is pretty close to X-COM in conception, instead of moving your characters through a square grid in this game you actually move them in a full 3D environment; this allows you to be creative in reaching your objective without exposing yourself to enemy fire or finding cheeky angles to shoot them from while being under cover.
The game's overall difficulty is slightly milder than the average of tactical RPGs. Just like in FFTactics there are short battles called skirmishes you can repeat how much you want to gain exp and money, so if you have any difficulty beating a certain chapter you can always grind in skirmishes to level up your classes and make the battle much easier. The Steam edition also includes all of the DLC of the original PS3 version, which are relatively easy, give tons of exp and drop some extremely broken weapons that will make the early game a total breeze.
The game is completed with awesome visuals and canvas effects that makes it look like a sketchbook. The white border around everything can feel unnecessary though, but there are mods out there that allow you to easily remove it.
Don't miss on this Sega classic if you never played it!

Did you ever love playing a tabletop RPG (DnD, DCC, MCC, etc) but the logistics of getting one together was hard? Look no further adventurer, for Divinity: Original Sin 2 creates a tabletop experience right from your 'battlestation'.
Naturally, the game is challenging and open, there are many options of how to play and what to do in any given scenario. Kill everybody! What the hell right, they're in
way after all right? Or, befriend as many people (monsters, creatures, and animals as well) as is possible! What the hell right, they're part of
adventure after all right? Dialogue is so well done in this game, so profoundly voice acted that most characters have a unique feel and attitude as well as conversation choices (often per Origin character, meaning the five Origin characters have unique interactions with the world).
Character creation is fluid, meaning, at a certain point in the game you have an opportunity to re-spec each character in your campaign into a better presentation of what you wanted in the game. For example, didn't like the summoner healer and instead wanted a summoner ranger? Well, why not! Or perhaps a jack of all trades? That is probably one of the more enriching experiences of the game, feeling as though one did not ♥♥♥♥ up in terms of how they allotted skill points.
One of my favorite elements is the use of surface elements (blood & water, or either electrified, ice, fire, poison, oil, and cursed ground -- you'll see that for the first time and it is an intense experience especially on harder difficulties).
But beyond that, the playing with friends experience is open and ongoing. Say a friend can only hop in for a few hours on the weekend, while you've played 34 hours in 3 days? Well, they can jump into one of the characters you have, re-spec them to their liking, finish a couple quests and get out all while continuing along your level base and campaign. (and you can do the same to their campaign, should they ever make one)
PROS:
- Great character development and voice acting
- Awesome fluidity in how to build characters
- Satisfying and intense turn-based combat (on Tactician it is hard, but not impossible)
- Rewarding unique playstyles without catering too much to cheese (without giving it away, the game will sometimes know if you cheese certain puzzles)
- Ongoing joining/leaving process for party play with friends
- Brings visualization to the tabletop experience (imo, but still)
- An absolutely enormous amount of content
- Challenging and fun (or frustrating and befuddling) puzzles!
- Connecting the dots on quests can be sometimes misleading, meaning the player needs to actually put in the work to logically figure out what the questbook/discovered dialogue related to the quest means in order to complete it -- this is not always straightforward and direct.
CONS:
- There actually are some bugs, believe it or not, and because of that remember (REMEMBER!) to save OFTEN
- Somewhat slow-paced (not a personal con, as tabletops are slow-paced, but I have heard this be a turn off so I include it)
- Some quests are easy to miss or hard to figure out due to the last point on PROS, (not a personal con, but it is something that may frustrate people who aren't used to having the game hold their hand through exploration/decision making related to important quests)
tl;dr: great open RPG with turn-based combat akin to tabletop gaming, think outside the box and be rewarded, discover more about the characters and races and be rewarded (or disgusted). Combat is wonderful, albeit tricky, and full of dazzling experiences. Great for picking up and leaving off with friends who have busy or demanding schedules.
If you're a fan of turn-based RPGs then give this one a go on sale, or if you're a die-hard tabletop RPG person pick it up when you can. If you have friends you can convince to play this with you, do that, probably one of the best buddy-gaming experiences I have had in a great while.

ArcheAge was the very best in mmorpg. It was like a second coming of star wars galaxies: Open world pvp, unrestricted class mixing, physical trade and trade caravans, gorgeous graphics and beutiful races with cool dungeons, lots of exploration and a remarkably robust crafting system.
Why is it bad?
Pay to win. Completely, unapologetically ruined by extremely bad payment model. If your guild does not put in real money to get exclusive items/packs/patronship, you will not be able to compete.
I was a guild leader on Tahyang for the Prowletariat, we went from a 4 person guild to 70+ before we all quit. We grew fast and became powerful because we worked hard to get land at the start, we was lucky to find a massive area without anybody else and we claimed it quickly and used our land to grow. However, that all changed when they opened the cash shop...
How was my small guild able to compete at the end? Money. We put in a lot of money and that made us powerful because we had a tonne of land and gold, we were able to farm materials and we had many premium items that boosted your power (for example, trees that guarenteed a thunderstike which gave you thunderstruck wood which was required material to build top tier veicles/ships).  We put up with the system for about 4 months after they implemented the premium crap in the cash shop before we realised enough was enough. It just wasn't fun anymore.
The final straw was how they handled the broken cash shop incident:
1) Trion released a premium box that had a chance to give you the rarest, strongest most powerful gear in the game (at that time) for your class. These divine weapons were unparalled at that time as was the armor set.
2) This wasn't a problem at first, it was an extremely rare drop....
3) Until somebody found out if you used the box with a single slot in your inventory ,it had a 100% drop rate on the divine weapon/armors.
4) This glitch got passed between major guilds on the enemy faction.
5) Suddenly, we went from even battles to a single healer/tank combination being able to destroy 20-30 players at once simply because our gear was incapable of taking it on. At the point where the healer was able to TANK THROUGH 20 players smashing her face in with everything they had and just..heal it off constantly...we thought trion was going to fix the problem and roll-back.
6) It became a widespread issue. Power shifted sides as the guilds who cheated got the upper hand, I and my co-leader decided that we would not be abusing the glitch and thus ordered everyone to do the same. Therefore we had a massive disadvantage in combat, but we expected trion to address it!
7) Trion announced they would NOT be rolling back the servers, that they could NOT remove the items from players, and that they would, going forwards, be taking no action.
8) We had a guild meeting and we packed our bags and left within a week. The guild disbanded, and the greatest 6 months of my mmorpg time ever were over. (I played on trion's launcher, I recently tried to go back again and join a guild etc on the new re-launch servers but Trion quickly started re-releasing cash shop pay to win items again and we decided not to continue)
TLDR: The game itself is an incredible PvP Sandbox with some exceptional questing, dungeons and raids/world bosses. The payment model is awful and if you cant pay, dont bother.

Hello everyone, I come to you today hoping to write a review that is both biased, yet informative though I will throw some of my own feelings into the mix and will try and keep it short. I hope you all enjoy!
TLDR;Great potential, still flawed, lots of fun, If you dont pick up early access at least keep it on your radar for full release!
So I want to just throw this out there, I am not a big fan of the whole "Early Access" thing, dont get me wrong there are a few times where I have supported them (This being the obvious case). I played maybe 20 hours of Ark back when the game was released, couldnt really get into it for the most part, I had a big minecraft phase and also play a lot of other games that are similar so survival/crafting games aren't new to me.
I always had Conan Exiles on my radar but wasnt sure if I wanted to pick it up ($40CAD for early access NFW), there was a patched version of it that they unfortunately forgot to put their Denuvo antipiracy in, I will admit I instantly downloaded it and fell in love with the concept. After doing some research into the game and finding out that upon release the Dev's are patching it almost daily, now I know what your thinking "Oh but Binson, they are always small patches!" and yes, you may be right. However to me this shows that the Dev's want this game to be 100% on release but they also want to make sure they are resolving issues in the early access and they go back and forth with the information instead of just putting out a couple patches of an early access or demo, fixing those bugs and then your all good! In most cases, this does not work... EVERYONE who knows anything about how computers (Hardware & Software) when 1 thing stops working and gets fixed 10 other problems surface, anyways enough about that.
This game looks ok, the enviroment and atmosphere itself is beautiful but the textures are still choppy (Expected, Early access) it is still pretty buggy and is not optomized very well at all unfortunatelly so there is a lot of "screen tearing" and drops in frame rate regardless of how powerfull your machine is, though I find its only really bad in areas you havent been to yet, They have a stat system which I enjoy (STR,AGI,STM,ect.) and their crafting system at the start is fairly easy to use, once you get into the blacksmithing and forging some things can get confusing but you will eventually get the hang of it.
All in all I think this game has started off on a fantastic platform, it does need a lot of improvement but the Dev team is working tirelessly working on bug fixes. As my final opinion, as much as I love this game and the fact im still giving it a "thumb up" I would wait, at least keep it on your wishlist, follow the patch notes but as it stands right now DEFINITELY PURCHASE FULL RELEASE!

Great art style, great music and fast gameplay. Even when the same enemy types are being re-used by the end of the game, it still manages to stay fun. There are a few random difficulty spikes on a couple of bosses; there's no voice acting making the cutscenes sometimes feel awkward and the story has missed potential. I also encountered one strange audio glitch which caused an explosion to play at a much higher volume then everything else every time I loaded in the final boss fight.
The only problem I had with the combat was that it's difficult to know when you're getting hit. There's no sound effect or on-screen notification other than your health bar decreasing - the overuse of the colour red also contributes to this confusion. The first few hours of the were pretty unpleasant until I learned to keep an eye on my health and learned when to dodge.
I want to explore more of RUINER's world but the hub area, which is trivial in gameplay, is disappointingly the only part of the game which is on the surface. Most of the game is underground exploring factories - which is fun and suits the game's theme well - but it still would've been nice to see more varied areas in both look and design.
Overall, however,  I enjoyed my time inside RUINER's cyberpunk world and want to spend more time in it.

This is one of the best, if not the best, pure tower defense games in a very long time.
Depth:
There are numerous enemies with lots of different abilities, defenses, speed, etc.
20 towers, each customizable by placing points into them.  Most of them have 3 upgrades in game, a few only have 2.
I counted 47 levels, but the map is kinda a mess so I could have easily missed one or two.
Challenge:
You can adapt any of the levels  to be as easy or difficult as you'd like.  Need to just beat a level to get the rewards (new tower or gems) but having problems?  Tone it down a bit with the "Breeze" rune.
Looking for a challenge?  Load up to 10 different runes increasinng the difficulty greatly, but also the reward!
Looking to go nuts?  Turn on the "Endless" rune and get ready for an increasingly difficult grind.
Replayabilty:
With all of the customization available, you can replay this game until your mouse breaks, buy a new mouse, then keep playing some more.  There is no end to the fun.
I highly recommend this game.

Great tower defence game but could perhaps do with a few tweaks.
For instance having to replay a level because I didn't know it would throw a wave of 20 suicide bomber dwarves at me at the end that would shred my barricades instantly is slightly tedious. Being able to view all the wave lists before you start rather than just see the first six would be a good change.
A lot of the levels are clearly designed for you to use barricades to create a long and winding path of death to make the enemy march through. Or they have mine cart tracks to direct them onto. However due to the dwarves blowing up barricades it's often better just not to bother even trying to direct them. On endless mode it quickly becomes pointless having more than one or two barricades meaning that a lot of space on the level is unused. A lot of time is just spent with the repair tool hovering over what few barricades you do have and that gets a little tedious too.
I kind of think that the fully upgraded turret wielding version should be indestructible as it would give you a lot more options and makes levels more fun. Also it is kind of odd that you can build floor traps on top of this barricade which do nothing, except the lightning turret with AOE. It would be good if it could also use the AOE affects from some of the other traps, like poison, fire or bleed.
Once I had worked that much out and defeated the suicide bombers I got up past a million points on endless on one level only for my portal to be swamped by riderless horses that just charged through everything with dead riders but without a scratch on them. The giant stone golems and the heavily armoured knights fell before they'd even reached my main line of defence but the horses? Despite repeatedly running into walls and bouncing around all over the place whilst on fire and frozen with three harpoons in their backs and non stop lightning bolts frying them they still made it through. So yeah I think they might be a little bit over the top in their current state. Their speed and fact that they don't stop to fight liches or demons makes them powerful enough without also have more health than Jesus... and like Jesus you have to kill them twice.
Also when you do reach that stage in the game where the entire screen is filled with enemies you can't really see to build or upgrade anything. A build mode toggle option to hide all enemies whilst you place a turret would be nice. As would the ability to see the number of kills per turret or damage dealt.

This is the dungeon keeper clone that we've been waiting for!
War for the Overworld is an attempt at creating a modern Dungeon Keeper. For those who are not familiar with Dungeon Keeper, it was a game released in 1997, where you played an evil dungeon overlord. You would build a dungeon with different  rooms that attracted different creature types, and you would use those to fight the heroes of the land and rival dungeons. Controls were indirect, you could not give orders to individual creatures, but you could pick them up and move them about, and you could use other means to make your creatures go where you wanted them to go, but unlike a regular RTS, you could not give direct orders. You could also not recruit specific creatures, but instead creatures would be drawn to your dungeon based on what was in it. War for the Overworld does not change any of this. At its core, it's basically Dungeon Keeper with a fresh coat of paint.
Several attempts have been made in the past to make a "modern Dungeon Keeper", but most of them have, quite frankly, not been very good. As this game is so similar to Dungeon Keeper, there will be a lot of comparisons between the two.
The graphics in War for the Overworld is actually quite good for an indie game. The models are detailed enough, and the textures are also relatively detailed. It won't rival the latest AAA games, but as long as you don't expect that, it won't disappoint. The game also has a very cohesive art style, nothing looks out of place, despite the different creatures looking radically different from each other. One thing I would complain about is the game being a bit too dark. It's not a major issue, and a dungeon should be dark, but some more light would have made the game look more pleasing.
The sound felt a bit weak. Nothing had much impact, and you don't get enough feedback from the sound to really feel like you're doing things. It's nothing game breaking, but it is one of the areas in which the game could stand to be improved.
The story in this game is nothing to write home about. You're awoken and told about the emperor of the land, and that you should go and kill him. There's a bit more to it, but that's basically all you need to know. The story is basically just an excuse for "go kill good guys".
Where Dungeon Keeper 1 played up the contrast between the good guys and the bad guys (that is, you and your creatures) for comedic effect, War for the Overworld plays it more straight, similar to how Dungeon Keeper 2 did it. Which one is better is a matter of taste, but I preferred Dungeon Keeper 1. The game is not devoid of humor, but it's not as much of it as in DK1.
As mentioned above, War for the Overworld plays very similar to Dungeon Keeper. Build your dungeon, attract the creatures you want, and then attack. Everything feels a bit faster in War for the Overworld than it did in Dungeon Keeper. Your creatures level up faster in the training room, claiming land feels faster and so on. I would say that this is an improvement. Unlike Dungeon Keeper, where you had to research the "Call to Arms" spell in order to attract your creatures to a certain point on the map, you have access to a similar thing right from the get-go in War for the Overworld.
Going into enemy territory is a bit more dangerous than you might expect. You can't pick up creatures that are not on your territory, so if one is in danger, you'll have to use magic to save it, and hope that it is able to make it out of there on its own. And the game encourages you to use your magic liberally. You have a separate mana pool, and it is refilled quite fast, so using spells in combat is almost a must.
Creatures are also handled differently than in Dungeon Keeper. Now you have two broad categories that can basically be seen as intelligent creatures and animals. Intelligent creatures will be this games counterparts to goblins, warlocks, trolls and so on, while animals will be things like giant spiders and other more animal-like beings. Intelligent creatures requires regular pay, can work in different rooms, and can use your training room. Animals will wander about, and the only rooms they can use is the portal that attracts them (you need to build this one, while the portal that attracts intelligent creatures is already on the map), an arena (this is how you level them up outside of combat, but they are damaged in the process) and the room they get their food from.
If the game has one flaw, it is its difficulty, or lack thereof. While Dungeon Keeper was not a hard game, the only way you would realistically lose in that game was if you ran out of gold, War for the Overworld is even easier, giving you plenty of gold to spend, and far less to spend it on (training creatures, for an example, is free). Gold is used to build new rooms, and when it's payday (at which point all your intelligent creatures will go to the nearest treasury and take some money). Not once during the campaign did it feel like I was running short on cash.
War for the Overworld is a really good game. It sticks really close to the Dungeon Keeper formula, but does a few things to speed up the gameplay. Is it better than Dungeon Keeper? Well, that's a matter of taste. I would have an easier time recommending this game, but due to nostalgia, I still think I like Dungeon Keeper a bit more. But anyone who wants to play a game like Dungeon Keeper, or who want an interesting take on the RTS genre should check it out. Just beware that the game still has some bugs (nothing game breaking, but they were common enough to be annoying).
