So here we are. Another day, another World War 2 metaphor.
Well hold on to your horses there, little Jimmy; 'cause this one is actually quite exceptional. So, while you're blasting dudes in Call of Duty: Next One, I'm chilling with my WW2 anime about war waifus who fight racism in between laser fights and strategy gameplay.
Yes, this game was made in Japan. No, some memes from Japan are simply unavoidable; i.e the beach episode, the awkward phrasing, singing over flashbacks, copious Steve Blum usage, etc etc. But for all of these memes, I've got to hand it to the localization team here. What could've been the land of the rising memes actually flipped to something quite meaningful and interesting. Bravo.
So, how is the actual game portion? It's interesting in its own right, but not fully realized. Most of the gameplay is done on a unit to unit basis, meaning individual moves can cause you some real trouble. You slowly build up your arsenal and realize the potential of your characters, but even then it feels cumbersome most of the time. Capturing points, flanking enemies, and destroying tanks all feels rather cool; but chugging across massive battlefields, missing easy shots, and getting absolutely dumpstered by a swarm of enemies doesn't feel so great.
The reason why this game shines like it does is that it takes a very interesting approach to storytelling. Of the games I've played I'd say its a good bit like Valiant Hearts in a strange way. This game is more about people than it is about the war. Sure, the war is a motivation for a lot a characters, but most of the time it comes down to ideas. There's seldom just "the baddies" and "the goodies" at play here.
The game introduces you to different perspectives little by little, and it tries its best to make people seem well... human. The soldiers are bakers and dancers, teachers and builders to name a few; and all of them rely on you to not mess things up. More than anything, I appreciated that they kept the preaching to a minimum. The only thing the game actively beats you over the head with is that just because someone's different doesn't mean you get to be a jerk... Which is obviously still a relevant lesson today.
It's a very interesting beast. But I can say what you put in is what you get. If what you see here is a game about Japan's take on WW2 that's light on the gore, and the killstreaks; with big mouth billy basses masquerading as one note personalities flinging bb gun pellets at eachother, then there really won't be much here for you. But I can say I put in five bucks for this game. I invested into these characters, their struggle, and even their rinky-dink bio pages, and I came out pretty satisfied with the journey and the destination. Not bad for a meme.

I want to like this game but I can't. I purchased this because I am a fan of Skies of Arcadia—three characters from that game appear in Valkyria Chronicles—and I like tactical combat in vein of XCOM. Valkyria Chronicles gets some stuff right, which makes it seem like a pretty cool tactical/RPG hybrid, but I can't stand the stuff this game gets wrong. Specifically: the cliché characters, the asinine story, and lack of any gameplay balance. I can overlook the writing if the gameplay is solid, and vice-versa, but that isn't the case here.
The story is an awful mess of magic, cartoonishly evil nazi-like empires that kill civilians for no reason, and a rag-tag group of freedom fighters that somehow are able to win against an overwhelmingly superior foe. Basically an entire check-list worth of stuff that makes me groan. At least you can skip cutscenes. Get ready to mash enter as there are mountains of cutscenes.
The gameplay, which could be decent, boils down to upgrading scouts and having them run across the map to capture a flag in as few turns as possible. Why bother using all those other cool guys and gals you've recruited when getting the best rank requires speed running every level? Why bother using your tactical acumen and strategical thinking in order to take down a well-equipped enemy? Better just run through the level instead.
There is a mod that fixes the gameplay by changing up basically everything, but I have yet to try it out. If I do, I may change this review. As a vanilla game, I can't recommend Valkyria Chronicles.

What a shame. This is a pretty tower-defense with decent but grindy and mobile-oriented mechanics (all of the sorts of traps littered into f2p games on mobile platforms, designed to entice you into paying money to speed up gameplay), but with the only way to get them on PC being to rather tediously grind for them. This still would have gotten a thumb's up from me despite the grinding (because it was enjoyable to play through the campaign, and I liked the art and core gameplay loops), and I was sort of slowly grinding my way through the final achievements, when the servers were unceremoniously shut down for this SINGLE PLAYER GAME, which breaks the achievements and makes the gameplay lag.
It was barely excusable to have this game have an online component when the servers still worked, but it is inexcusable for this company to continue to sell an game whose abandonment degrades its performance. It also never got the updates and bug fixes that other platforms got, and the developers ignored the bug reports from Steam. Don't put it onto Steam at all if you don't want to support it here, or stop taking money for it when you discontinue support, please. Without the server requirement and with updates done in parallel with mobile (or even freezing updates here after the major bugs were fixed), this game would have been a good example of a completed and satisfactory tower defense game. Without them, it's a black mark on this developer's record.

The main quest itself is interesting enough to anchor your attention to the fact there is a demonic invasion that's going to ravage the countryside (pretty sure it's a matter of Story and Gameplay Segregation) as you progress as main quest is being completed and the guilds' and DLCs' questlines are also worthy enough to grab your attention and are enjoyable to play through and are longer than Skyrim's.
Class system might be restricting but even that isn't taken too seriously in the game and you can still level your non-class related skills like with Skyrim and Morrowind. I will have to said about the wizards that they are easy for anyone to level up but difficult to use when using ranged spells given the nature of NPCs' combat behaviors (hello hammy enemies and allies, espiecally vocal humanoid demons) as well as personal protection.
All in all, this is enjoyable game despite its graphic, age, and AI combat behaviors.

Although I've been having a decent amount of fun with this game, I can't recommend it based on it still being incomplete. There's still far too many bugs in the quest system.
In most games, completing an objective that is part of a quest you have not unlocked yet is not an issue. Once you accept the quest, it recognizes your current progress and incorporates it. In DoS 2, doing this is likely to permanantly break the relevant quests. What's more, these broken quests will auto-complete at the end of the current act with negative completion entries. It's entirely possible to save someone, only to complete an act and have your journal claim you abandoned them to their fate.
There are minor mechanical issues still existing as well. Barrels exploding fluids onto surfaces two floors above them, enemies healing from elements with 50% resistance, quests that require teleportation not accounting for retribution damage, an infinite ashen idol of rebirth bug that leaves your character permanantly unable to leave combat..
To top it off, the only bug Larian has recognized so far is an infinite damage loop. Despite sending in several reports that would "be replied to within one business day" I've now gone a week without a single piece of acknowledgement of the slew of quest related issues I'm experiencing.
TL;DR wait for them to fully finish the quest system, at least. So much outside the main line is in near shambles right now. The game is still fun, but you'll be constantly frustrated by impossible quests and a tarnished log.

: I have only experienced 4 hours of this game at the time I write this. I have yet to play through everything or even get the chance to use every tower. If my views change as I play more, I'll update this review.
If you like Tower Defense games, you will like this one. It doesn't do anything to revolutionize the genre, but throws in some cool towers/traps that add a nice twist, such as being able to push and pull mobs into pits. The pixel style is simple but both looks good and has good animations. The style most likely contributes to the games excellent performance, even when there are a lot of moving and effects on screen. The addition of a map editor is excellent, as most of my time so far has actually been making and playing my own levels. You can also share these levels to the Workshop as well as download and play the creations of other people, giving the game great replayability.
Like I said, the game performs great. I had no issues with anything slowing down, glitching graphically, etc. I was also pleased to see the game ran perfectly despite my two monitor set up. It naturally assumed a Borderless Window sort of mode at 1920x1080 without any adjustments necessary. It's easy to click out to other windows if need be (which with games like this, I'm usually multitasking) and there were no issues using ALT+TAB to get in/out of the game.
I think it would be nice to be able to zoom out a bit more than you are, but I don't know if that's technically possible with how the game is made. You do get some fairly large levels to play sometimes, and scrolling around and keeping track of things sort of artificially (perhaps intentionally?) makes the game harder.
Upgrading traps sometimes has the button appear underneath something else, such as a little dropdown at the top of the screen that shows you stats/info about the turret itself. You can still click the button easily enough, but it's just a nuisance that you can't really see what you're doing.

To all you ex-Dungeon Keeper 2 players looking to reignite your love of the game....Buy this game! But beware things are a little different this time.....
At first, I was weary of the deviations from DK2 (of which there are many), and wasn't exactly sure if I liked it or not, but over time, I've come to believe this game is actually an improvement on the original.
Pros:
+Relive DK2 fun in a new and challenging way.
+Map editors
+Great game mechanics (skills trees, mana locking, sanctuarys etc.)
+Multiplayer
Cons:
-Relentless AI (surely this can be toned down?)
-The add crash or glitch (particulary on multiplayer)
The single player is great fun, and a great way to learn how the new game functions. My main grievance is just how relentless the AI is. It really is ridiculously hard sometimes.
Features such as mana locking and skills tree seem annoying at first, but you begin to realise that it's a mechanic that actually makes gameplay far more enjoyable in the long run.
For me the multiplayer is the best (and sometime worst) part of the game. This is the closest I've come to reliving those glory days of LAN'ing DK2 with friends, so I can't recommend this game enough for this reason alone. My main frustration comes from the odd crash when a large battle starts (which lets be honest, was far more regular on the orginal DK2). The game is far less geared toward defence (compared with DK2), so rather than lengthly stalemates, games can be won/lost within half an hour or so.
In short, this game is will delight those familiar with DK2, but will still provide a new challenge with it's tweaking on the mechanics. There are still the odd glitches which need to be ironed out, but these are few and far between, and don't effect the overall enjoyment of the game.

It\'s fun.. If you want to turn the game into a science of precise timing that requires hours of practice. At first the game was awesome, it was a game of accurate swings and feinting and large amount of people would turn this game into a medieval movie. Buuut nowadays a large amount of the playerbase uses this method called dragging, allowing the player to swing their weapon incredibly slow yet still dealing full damage.
Sure, dragging requires alot of skill, and I\'m sure their proud of themselves in their own special way. But In my eyes it created a far steeper learning curve that I\'d rather not devote my game time to. But the absolute worst part of it is that dragging and some of those related techniques completely destroy the immersion of this game(in my opinion).
At the start of this game(shortly after it was released), charging the other team with 10+ teammates was exhilirating! You had to stab, slash and swing to get to the objective. Blocking, feinting, kicking and dodging were extra mechanics that could give you the edge in the fight. If you wanted to test your skills in a more private setting, then you could hop on a duel to fight someone solo.
Nowadays, since dragging was embraced by the developers and was even given as a hint to players on loading screens, things definitely changed. When you join a populated server, instead of people jumping at you, in the hopes of removing your head; you will get people waddling around like drunk crabs slowly twirling their weapons slowly with a pile of dead bodies around them. When you jump into a duel, instead of a head to head clash of positioning and accurate strikes from a bloodthirsty warrior; you still get something similar to those skills but instead of a warrior, you get some contorting wierdo that hits you with a flurry of deccelerated and accelerated swings that makes me think \"How does this make sense?\". Sure you could learn to counter them, but it is stupidly annoying nevertheless.
To sum it all up: If you want this game, then you are going to have to enter the world of dragging or else you will rarely see a positive KD ratio. Just look it up on youtube and ask yourself \"Do I want to do this?\".
In conclusion, you are looking for an immersive medieval experience that will engross you on your free time? DON\'T CLICK THAT PURCHASE BUTTON!

I liked this game.  What really sells it is the storytelling.  It's sort of like a turn-based XCOM game mashed together with a season of anime (seriously you don't realize the amount of cutscene story animation until the final credits roll and it recaps for quite a while with cutscene replays).  It's also got this really good pencil-shader thing going on, which looks great.
Tactically it plays a bit like XCOM in that it is turn-based movement and you can cover behind certain objects.  However there are a couple differences.  Instead of action points being on an individual basis, it is on a group basis, so it allows a certain character to move multiple times in a turn, at the expense of others being static for that turn.  Another difference, which takes some getting used to, is the reaction fire.  This means if moving across an enemies field of fire, they will attack you constantly during -your- turn.  This can be avoided by keeping out of range or executing commands quickly (it is unusual for a turn-based system).  Terrain varies over the course of the game (city, rural, desert, forest, etc), and occasionally there will be things like rooftops or trenches that can be used for advantage.
You play a subset of 9-10 characters in a given battle, out of a roster of 20, which itself is taken from a larger pool of about 30+ (not sure, it is a lot).  Each character has a personality and a story.  Certain characters like (or dislike) others which makes certain groupings better at times.  There are also a bunch of upgrades and leveling that can be done on the main characters and equipment.
That said there are some annoying aspects of some battles.  The system grades the battle performance (A, B, C, ...) and although the rating is irrelevant for story progression, getting a good rating can help acquire some rare items in the back half of the game.  Thing is, the rating is based exclusively on speed, not on keeping your squad alive (and it is possible to lose members).  In some battles it can be just ridiculous to finish at any speed, much less at an 'A' rating speed, due to enemy respawn or other things, so you'll find yourself searching online for tricks/techniques in some cases.
As far as the story, it can be cheesy and unnecessary at times (eg. Hans), but it can also bring in serious topics (like oppression, concentration camps, eg. Darcsens).  Overall it does a good job, and can really draw you in by the end.  Sort of like a good anime season.  It is one of the few games I've ever watched the full credits roll (and final cutscenes).

I'm really unhappy to be writing a negative review for this game.
The simple problem is that it takes way too much time/effort(and some money) to become competitive at the high levels.
At a minimum cost you are going to need to pay the monthly membership fee to get labor points, which is used in crafting. There are lots of different ways to craft, but without crafting you wont be making money, and therefore won't be able to get the gear.
Gear is extremely expensive, expect to do a lot of grinding on really boring crafting activities that seem cool at first, but get old fast. I played this game at the max level for about 5 months, on membership the whole time, and by the end of it my gear wasn't near half what it should be to be competitive in pvp and endgame content. Which means it will take years of these crafting activities to get the money to buy the gear that is acceptable at end game.
The economy is neat, and the fact that players can steal from each other is also great, but when you constantly get one-shotted in pvp, and it takes years to not be one-shotted, it kind of defeats the purpose of having cool systems like that.
The community is a mix of toxic and really cool. In faction chat expect to hear constant propaganda (yes, propaganda), for high level guilds trying to maintain their reputations after stealing or doing something else shady, including constant power struggles. People who speak out against them are often put on the guild's kill on sight list, as well as publicly ridiculed by them in faction chat. However, my guild that I found was great. The people were nice, extremely helpful, friendly, and made the experience fun. You will be able to find cool people despite the jerks.
All in all I would say avoid this game if you are looking for a new mmo to play, the time cost of getting strong is just way too high, and the annoying high level guilds are mostly horrible people. If you are a returning player, and have really nice gear, feel free to give it another try.
Also I played it mostly on the glyph launcher, so the steam hours on my account aren't accurate.

It also has a very immersive storyline and fictional history which is based off of a sort of WW2 era in Europe. Characters are also nice and well built as after you've gone through many operations with them you begin to care for them instead of random grunts dying left and right without you worrying about them in the slightest. The strategy in Valkyria Chronicles is also paramount to winning, heading straight into an enemy encampment armed with cannons and machine guns isn't going to get you far, you need to think about what you can use to counter it such as a tank that can punch through a heavy defense like a deployed gatling gun that can easily shred your troops or using sandbags to advance slowly while lobbing a few grenades here and there. Approaches to simply taking over a single camp determines what your losses and damages are. Another feature I truly love about this game is the RPG elements. You can upgrade your weapons tiers and upgrade your tank's armor, weapons, accuracy, swap it out for a quad - linked machine gun or a flamethrower. You can upgrade things with money earned in the battlefield. You can also "level up" your squad using XP earned in battle to be used to unlock new battle orders or unlocking "potentials" in your troops and having clearance for using weaponry such as grenade launcher attachments to a rifle or a flamethrower attachment under a machine gun. The campaign is extremely immersive and the episodes in between long operations that can take anyway between 20 minutes to over an hour make it seem rewarding. If there was one thing I could complain about this game is the tank controls can really screw you over, its still WASD however the tank can still jerk to the right or left exposing the dreaded weakpoint the vechicle (the radiator), and also an extremely annoying glitch where climbing up a ladder somehow drops an enemy (or a trooper of your own) down to the bottom of the map where he cannot be recovered and is no use (I mean maybe it can scout but...). The game is well worth it, has some replayability with you trying to beat the campaign again with all your equipment and XP carrying over so you can try to get an A in each mission or you can do the "skirmish" missions and the DLC missions that come with the purchase of the game which are quite difficult.

I'd been meaning to try Warframe for a year or two, then some friends said "hey, come play Destiny 2!" The resulting YouTube review-watching session led me to Warframe. One week and nearly 40 hours of playtime later, I knew I was hooked.
Yes, it's grindy, which is part of why I'd put off trying it for so long, but the moment-to-moment gameplay is pretty fun, and the grind (almost) always feels productive. There's a fair bit of RNG to the drops, but (at least fairly-early-game where I am) the drops are generally at least useful, even if they're not what you were hoping for.
The premium currency is never *technically* required to progress (surviving with only 2 warframe slots would be painful though) and can even be earned in-game by trading with other players (gathering trade-worthy items looks to be yet another grind).
Yes, you can "pay to win" to an extent, but paying is FAR more "speed things up" than "get what free players can't", and the near-exclusive PvE gameplay softens the blow of being matched with someone who out-classes you.
There is a bit of a learning curve, and the in-game tutorial, while fun, doesn't cover as much material as it probably should. Definitely check out a guide or something for equipment modding and especially how damage works. That said, the curve is more long than steep if you're used to dealing with RPG-like stats (like in Borderlands, or other MMOs), but you'll probably want to keep the wiki handy for reference.
A word of warning: the devs have their own launcher for handling game updates; on first launch, there was around 10GB more to download.

When I bought this game (on sale), I thought I was picking up something a little bit akin to Shadowrun. A dark, punk style universe where I can cause some mayhem and destruction for a few hours.
Instead, the game turned out to be incredibly repetitive and boring. The level design is linear and simplistic, with the player getting stuck in ambush areas while enemies flood the room. The combat style resembles Diablo more so than anything else - just click away, with no thought whatsoever to strategy or tactics, until everyone is dead.
Melee is the main method of combat, with gunplay leaving a lot to be desired, and your character can barely interact with any items in the world. You can open some containers, that's it. There's no other mechanics in the game whatsoever.
The worldbuilding is essentially non-existent, and I was taken aback by the poor dialog, and uninspired characters. For example, right in the first level you're freed from digital slavery by a mysterious woman, who immediately sets up the lamest plot possible:
Ok, well, if the character's brain was hacked, and he can't even remember that he
a brother, then how does the kidnapping make any sense? All in all, a forgettable game, not nearly worth the price tag.

I'm giving this game a tenative positive review given that it's still in Early Access like so many products on STEAM. In it's current state the game is like a horizontal as opposed to vertical scrolling version of Ikari Warriors (for those who have played that, if you have you are officially *OLD*). It's functional but a bit basic where you wind up switching between a pistol, machine gun, and grenades to kill waves of identical looking enemies while occasionally popping an explosive barrel. The game truely needs more enemy variety in this state but I can only hope that is coming.
Premise-wise the game has you playing as a "German Soldier" in WW II, coveyed in the modern reinventionalist stance popular with Japan that is trying to seperate this from the Nazis. While playing a Nazi in a heroic context outside of the historical war could be thought provoking, and I think the world is ready for that, this is not the game to do it. The plot has very little to do with the war as a whole and your killing monsters for the most part. The only part of the game that some might find disturbing in this context from what I've seen is the first level where all of the bad guys have pronounced noses (a sort of Jewish stereotype) where the main character your playing has no real nose at all. Some may read into this, but it's never explicitly stated who your fighting, just people of this village where wierd stuff happens before the aliens and giant spiders show up.
To be fair if they never specified your playing as a German soldier and armed you with vintage WW II weaponry there would be nothing even remotely controversial about this. There isn't anything offensive here, as the game seems to be intentionally walking the fence, as far as I've seen the Devs are correct and there isn't even a single swatstika on display though given the fanaticism that caused WW II I'd find it hard to believe anyone trusted with a special mission as this seems to be wouldn't be a loyalist of the National Socialist party, which of course doesn't mean someone is neccesarily a genocidal maniac (it being a workers rights movement by and large which got derailed by the leadership). Even if one argues for what would be a rare exception you'd at least be dealing with an ultra-nationalist in the military. But as I said this goes well beyond the context of what I've seen in the game.
With some work "Burgers" could be good, but it lacks the charm or quality of "Castle Crashers" so far, but it could get there and become a shooter version. Shorter levels, more enemy variety, more background scenery to give it personality, etc... and this could very well turn into a great little game.

Let me say that I go into this quick review with a bit of a bias... This has been my most anticipated game for the last 2 years.
Finally being able to get my hands on a Steam release and even the alpha lives up to everything I had hoped for.
Being a ninja rabbit (or the other animals featured in the game) is such fun. Much joy. Many gameplay. Wow. The parkour elements are incredibly fluid and fun to execute. The climbing, wall running, and jumping all feel so satisfying that you'll find yourself doing it over and over again even without a clear goal to do so.
The combat system is fantastic. Technically very simple - very few buttons are used. The system however is incredibly deep and complex - very hard to master. All the characters, aside from being able to carry out loads of moves, can also pick up weapons to use in combat. Those can also be thrown (Which is a lot of fun)
The one mode which convinced me this game has neverended potential is the versus mode. Although only one map is featured, and the mode is literally "Player 1 tries to kill Player 2 while Player 2 tries to do kill Player 1" when me and my sister played it for the first time we spent 40+ minutes on it, constantly having fun. There was always some new combat move to execute, there was always some discovery to do - turning on slow motion and throwing swords at each other and watch them bounce back and kill us in recoil, chasing each other whilst throwing combat knives, doing nothing but jump kicks, etc.
The game at the current state also features some stealth elements, allowing you to sneak up on enemies and take them out silently rather than engaging in a fight.
Best part? You can mod and change everything as you please.
Want to make a map with 20 rabbits fighting to the death with dog bones on top of a giant mountain? You can.
Want to make your own story map with characters, dialogue, jumping puzzles and combat? You can.
Want to download mods and maps and new characters or try making your own? You can.
I could go on for ages, but even for an alpha this game not only offers a lot of content, but provides something I really enjoy in games - The ability for the player to make their own content. To make their own world and fun, and I dont mean this in terms of the editor but in terms of gameplay. Hours can be spent on creating characters with various weaponry and then fighting them on maps you designed, Wolfire designed, or the community designed, OR hours can be spent doing parkour and slow motion flips as a ninja rabbit.
If this doesn't convince you to buy this game - I dont know what will.
Totally worth the 30 bucks and I cant wait for more and more and more content to be continouly added such as the campaigns, more arenas, more versus maps (although you can already play Split Screen on any map downloaded) and of course the online multiplayer.
Already a candidate for game of the year.

It\'s fun.. If you want to turn the game into a science of precise timing that requires hours of practice. At first the game was awesome, it was a game of accurate swings and feinting and large amount of people would turn this game into a medieval movie. Buuut nowadays a large amount of the playerbase uses this method called dragging, allowing the player to swing their weapon incredibly slow yet still dealing full damage.
Sure, dragging requires alot of skill, and I\'m sure their proud of themselves in their own special way. But In my eyes it created a far steeper learning curve that I\'d rather not devote my game time to. But the absolute worst part of it is that dragging and some of those related techniques completely destroy the immersion of this game(in my opinion).
At the start of this game(shortly after it was released), charging the other team with 10+ teammates was exhilirating! You had to stab, slash and swing to get to the objective. Blocking, feinting, kicking and dodging were extra mechanics that could give you the edge in the fight. If you wanted to test your skills in a more private setting, then you could hop on a duel to fight someone solo.
Nowadays, since dragging was embraced by the developers and was even given as a hint to players on loading screens, things definitely changed. When you join a populated server, instead of people jumping at you, in the hopes of removing your head; you will get people waddling around like drunk crabs slowly twirling their weapons slowly with a pile of dead bodies around them. When you jump into a duel, instead of a head to head clash of positioning and accurate strikes from a bloodthirsty warrior; you still get something similar to those skills but instead of a warrior, you get some contorting wierdo that hits you with a flurry of deccelerated and accelerated swings that makes me think \"How does this make sense?\". Sure you could learn to counter them, but it is stupidly annoying nevertheless.
To sum it all up: If you want this game, then you are going to have to enter the world of dragging or else you will rarely see a positive KD ratio. Just look it up on youtube and ask yourself \"Do I want to do this?\".
In conclusion, you are looking for an immersive medieval experience that will engross you on your free time? DON\'T CLICK THAT PURCHASE BUTTON!

This review is based on the Overgrowth Alpha (3.January 2014):
Right now Overgrowth is already much fun for players trying all of the mechanics. I personally got it because Nerdcubed did a Lets Play on Youtube on it. It looked like much fun playing with the sandbox and the new arena.
Arena: The new arena gameplay is pretty dope. I love the fights without weapons, because you have to fully use all the mechanics in combat that your rabbot has. Also the polearm fights are awesome, I just throw it and then try to retrieve it while not getting killed. One vs One fights are too easy right now. Just jump towards them and kill them with a precise kick.
Sandbox: The sandbox does not have a hughmangous amount of stuff to do, but it is fun and I enjoyed playing it. Play with the mechanics, build your own challenges and fight against an army of rabbits and wolves.
Also it is possible to download custom made maps through the SUMLauncher (retrievable through the "secret" Overgrowth Alpha forum at Wolfire Games). Some of them are already great, some don't even launch on my computer. Much work to do, but awesome already.
So if you're up for some fun and combat with a rabbit, this is cool. It's still an early Alpha, that is to be remembered while playing. But I think the developers are on a good way and this game will be great fun with a good story coming in the full customer version.

Valkyria Chronicles is a story rich, visual novel-like turn based tactical role playing game (if one could call it that) in which the player needs to complete different missions with assets of their choise, i.e different unit classes, weapons and tank upgrades.
Each turn the player will get a certain amount of action points that they need to use to take out the enemy as tactically and wisely as possible.
It's like any strategy game in which you need to use your head and be clever to win, with the exception that the player has time to think and consider different approaches more carefully, as there is no hurry to make the move. That is good, because the game tends to get more and more challenging the further the story goes and versatility of deployed units becomes a huge asset. Scouting, sniping, using grenades and anti-tank lances, pushing, flanking, covering, pulling back and moving behind cover at correct times and trying to predict the enemy is vital especially on the later missions.
Each deployable character has a unique personality, voice, appearance, and even a disposition towards each other, which may affect their performance on the field. The main protagonist and tank commander Velkin in his tank, the Edelweiss, can activate orders which in their own way work as bonuses for the team, such as damage boosts.
Between the missions the story goes on in forms of short cutscenes and visual novel-type conversations. The (Japanese) voice acting is excellent (who even plays this game with "engdubs" :D that's pleb tier), the characters are unique and charming each in their own way and the story itself is just mindblowing.
The story, of course, is the single most strongest point of this game. After playing, I highly suggest looking into the anime or manga versions, as they open up the story a bit more than the game does.
This is absolutely one of my favourite Japanese game releases since Chrono Trigger.

Crusader Kings II is one of those games that I'll fully admit I didn't like when I first started playing. As you can see from my hours played my perception changed quite a bit from those first few hours. This game has a steep learning curve, and there are still things that I am figuring out even 450+ hours in. Give this game some time and look up some tutorials online and I guarantee you that this game will suck you in and keep you engaged like a fantastic book.
In Crusader Kings II you are the head of a medieval dynasty and the only goals that exist are the ones you make up for yourself. Do you want to unite all of Ireland? Go get at it. Do you want to restore the Roman Empire? Much harder, but still possible. Do you want to avenge the death of your beloved son by slaughtering the family of the one who ordered his assassination? Sharpen your swords. Do you simply want your family to survive until the end date, regardless of how powerful or weak you are? Hey, that's an option too.
Odds are, throughout your family's history there will be numerous twists and turns, stories of great triumphs and great tragedies, histories written about the ruler who was benevolent and beloved by their people and the ruler who was an absolute tyrant, despised by all in life and in death.
There is honestly so much I could write about this game, but we'd be here all day. Yes, the interface is kind of clunky. Yes, the game is extremely unfriendly to newcomers. Yes, there are some mechanics that are absolutely broken (Decadence, anyone?). If you can look past some of these flaws, what you have here is a game worthy of your time and has so much to offer. (I would suggest waiting for it to go on sale. This game plus all of it's expansions are spendy). The best way to experience Crusader Kings II is to experience for itself.

Did you ever love playing a tabletop RPG (DnD, DCC, MCC, etc) but the logistics of getting one together was hard? Look no further adventurer, for Divinity: Original Sin 2 creates a tabletop experience right from your 'battlestation'.
Naturally, the game is challenging and open, there are many options of how to play and what to do in any given scenario. Kill everybody! What the hell right, they're in
way after all right? Or, befriend as many people (monsters, creatures, and animals as well) as is possible! What the hell right, they're part of
adventure after all right? Dialogue is so well done in this game, so profoundly voice acted that most characters have a unique feel and attitude as well as conversation choices (often per Origin character, meaning the five Origin characters have unique interactions with the world).
Character creation is fluid, meaning, at a certain point in the game you have an opportunity to re-spec each character in your campaign into a better presentation of what you wanted in the game. For example, didn't like the summoner healer and instead wanted a summoner ranger? Well, why not! Or perhaps a jack of all trades? That is probably one of the more enriching experiences of the game, feeling as though one did not ♥♥♥♥ up in terms of how they allotted skill points.
One of my favorite elements is the use of surface elements (blood & water, or either electrified, ice, fire, poison, oil, and cursed ground -- you'll see that for the first time and it is an intense experience especially on harder difficulties).
But beyond that, the playing with friends experience is open and ongoing. Say a friend can only hop in for a few hours on the weekend, while you've played 34 hours in 3 days? Well, they can jump into one of the characters you have, re-spec them to their liking, finish a couple quests and get out all while continuing along your level base and campaign. (and you can do the same to their campaign, should they ever make one)
PROS:
- Great character development and voice acting
- Awesome fluidity in how to build characters
- Satisfying and intense turn-based combat (on Tactician it is hard, but not impossible)
- Rewarding unique playstyles without catering too much to cheese (without giving it away, the game will sometimes know if you cheese certain puzzles)
- Ongoing joining/leaving process for party play with friends
- Brings visualization to the tabletop experience (imo, but still)
- An absolutely enormous amount of content
- Challenging and fun (or frustrating and befuddling) puzzles!
- Connecting the dots on quests can be sometimes misleading, meaning the player needs to actually put in the work to logically figure out what the questbook/discovered dialogue related to the quest means in order to complete it -- this is not always straightforward and direct.
CONS:
- There actually are some bugs, believe it or not, and because of that remember (REMEMBER!) to save OFTEN
- Somewhat slow-paced (not a personal con, as tabletops are slow-paced, but I have heard this be a turn off so I include it)
- Some quests are easy to miss or hard to figure out due to the last point on PROS, (not a personal con, but it is something that may frustrate people who aren't used to having the game hold their hand through exploration/decision making related to important quests)
tl;dr: great open RPG with turn-based combat akin to tabletop gaming, think outside the box and be rewarded, discover more about the characters and races and be rewarded (or disgusted). Combat is wonderful, albeit tricky, and full of dazzling experiences. Great for picking up and leaving off with friends who have busy or demanding schedules.
If you're a fan of turn-based RPGs then give this one a go on sale, or if you're a die-hard tabletop RPG person pick it up when you can. If you have friends you can convince to play this with you, do that, probably one of the best buddy-gaming experiences I have had in a great while.

The levels are all unique and challenging in their own way, and often require a little outside the box thinking to beat them. The difficulty level is adjustable per-level in this unique mechanism called "runes". Basically, you make the level harder on yourself and you get extra XP because of it.
I recommend running through all the levels with the newbie rune enabled (the top-left one) to unlock all the towers, then run back through all the levels increasing the amount of difficulty runes you enable.
Don't forget you can reset the towers you've upgraded and choose which towers to upgrade per-level.

If you like puzzle games, this will be right up your alley.  Blocks That Matter has plenty of puzzles to solve, with a level editor and community levels available to provide even more content beyond that which is included in the game.
The controls are fluent, the graphics are simple and effective, the music is good, and the gameplay challenges you to think not only about minimal use of the resources on hand, but also where they should go so that you'll be able to recollect them later.
The community levels are fully integrated into the game, you can just scroll through a menu and select one to play it.  No messing around with having to unzip files and put them in the right place, the game makes the whole process seamless.  Also, you can see the community's rating (both upvotes and downvotes) of any given level to help you decide if that level is worth your time, and then contribute to that rating once you've played the level.
As the system requirements would lead you to believe, you really won't need a very beefy gaming computer to run this game smoothly.  It runs perfectly well on a computer I built in 2004.
Overall, Blocks That Matter is an incredibly good game, astonishingly so given its price.

[Review written for 1.3]
Engaging RTS / dungeon management game where you get to play the bad guys.
Negative reviews are primarily concerned with WFTO at launch. Game is fully polished and well-optimised now, which makes for a much more enjoyable experience. Worth the full price, extremely worth during a sale.
War for the Overworld is the spiritual successor to the cult hit Dungeon Keeper, a series by Bullfrog (later snapped up by EA - which is why DK3 never. ;_;).
You play as an 'Underlord', a wibbly wobbly non-corporeal being that seals its essence in a Dungeon Core (the room you start with in every game). Lose that and you lose the game; protect it at all costs.
But in order to enact your will (and defend said Core), you gain access to an assortment of rooms,
-
Backers and early buyers remember the... fiasco that was WFTO's launch (although they did explain why it released the way it did, which was understandable); it's come a long way since then. Virtually all bugs have been fixed, many quality-of-life features have been implemented/improved and the optimisation is much better.
-
Although a successor to DK, there's nothing else like this on the market at the moment. WFTO isn't a carbon copy of DK either; it has its own fantasy, creatures and ideas (most notably, Potions and Rituals).
-
One of the major attractions, you can build your Dungeon however you feel like (within the constraints of the map terrain, of course). If you want a massive open-plan ground, meticulously divided rooms full of doorways and corridors, then you can do it. (A more recent addition was Wall prop efficiency; to offset the fact you have less building space, rooms with reinforced walls will operate more effectively.)
-
[outside of the Campaign]. Every game, you'll start with no abilities or rooms unlocked, spending Sins (points) in a three-column Tech Tree to unlock stuff. You can rush for a specific tree's Titan, or you can spread Sins across all three trees. That said, I don't think it's perfect (see below).
-
With Richard Ridings as your Mentor (the same VA for the DK Mentor) and the dark, tongue-in-cheek (and occasionally just plain silly) humour, it'll catch you out once in a while.That, with the excellent(ly awful) voice acting for the good guys makes for fun outside of the gameplay.
-
Hotkey support was enabled a while back, but the lack of visibility is a significant issue to learn hotkeys, especially if you're trying to micro combat / efficiency. Could easily be fixed by displaying the relevant hotkey in ability tooltips.
-
. It's alright, but once you get to grips with the game, it becomes a lot easier to fight against. Also, there's no difficulty mode for the campaign; although the early missions are newbie-friendly, the difficulty curve rises quite significantly, particularly if you're new to this genre.
-
. Following on from the previous point, the game introduces many additional utilities you can make use of. That in and of itself is a good thing; the lack of introduction and usage of them isn't great. There's still a few rituals and potions I never make use of, while others are pretty overpowered for their investment. There are user-written guides that provide in-depth explanations, but it shouldn't really be the place of the community to tell you how something functions in the first place.
-

Having tested a defensive strategy against Master AI, I can confirm that defensive strats do indeed work (Avarice + WDs, all I'm saying), though I can't see them being as effective vs players. Nevertheless, Although there are options and optimal choices do vary from map to map, I still feel more could be done to promote tech / build diversity. Possibly passive buffs (and nerfs?) for certain units when you invest into certain trees, or passives that only activate from speccing into multiple trees to complement your playstyle.
-
I have 8GB RAM (DDR3, meh clock speed), but on larger maps I will start to lag; it's still playable, but everything goes slower and commands won't always register. For optimal experience you'll want 12 or 16GB, but it's fine on small/medium sized maps.
Congrats for getting this far!
Overall, I would strongly recommend picking this up (especially if it's on sale, but the devs definitely earned the money asked). Many of the negative reviews were released at launch, present issues that have since been addressed in virtually all cases. Most of the bad points are fairly minor, primarily to do with communication and visibility.
Yes, it's not Dungeon Keeper 3; but that's fine. I personally believe it's better that WFTO is its own game, drawing inspiration from DK but not trying to become it.

I came to this game hoping for something like Dungeon Keeper. I got something like Dungeon Keeper, though not exactly what I expected. The game certainly brought back memories, but is different enough to feel unique and fresh, actually solving a few problems I had with the original Dungeon Keeper game. It's hard not to make the comparison, and for the sake of it I will be trying not to (for a bit).
War for the Overworld is, mechanically, solid, I've not encountered any bugs I remember. The game is not so much; at your leisure as it is at your throat with objectives on some levels, though there are more relaxed ones. It has an unusual style of graphics and some very strange creatures (See the Part Rock-Hammer part Demonized Kirby workshop enthusiast, the Chunder). And such delightful oddities enhance the experience, like being able to turn prisoners into gold statues that you can mine. That sounds like a cheat, but no that's a spell. The pacing of the game itself is reasonable, you're never left with nothing to do, and the times where you feel there's too much is clearly deliberate and in order to provide challenge, which there's a fair amount of, not hugely but enough to at least make you feel like you're not just walking through it. The dialogue from the minions and enemies is quite amusing (May I suggest torturing a dwarf and listening?)
Now in terms of flaws I'll be making direct comparison to Dungeon Keeper, because honestly, it's where my expectations come from.
The three criticisms that aren't just a direct comparison to Dungeon Keeper are:
First; that I don't, in all honesty, feel that evil. Yes there's toture chambers and prisons and YOU CAN TURN PRISONERS INTO MONEY (Did I mention that?) But honestly it's hard to feel like a badass overlord/underlord, when you're taking orders, yes, the guy giving you orders sounds like a deliciously evil warlord, but I'm still taking orders, which is hard to make...well cool. Why can't I be the one who is a deliciously evil warlord?
Second; It's pretty complicated, as a game there are so many things to build, it feels like it's been overcomplicated with all of the buildings of obfuscated uses, and many of them don't feel like they have uses, like the Tavern, which serves cooked food to your minion, but they'll just as easily go off to the Hatchery and eat a micropig live (Which is a lovely touch by counterpoint).
Third; I'm on level 7 and I'm not playing War for the Overworld, I'm not even playing a dungeon management game, I'm playing an RTS where you have no base and are just wandering from crypt to crypt with about 4 necromancers and a buttload of skeletons, raising skeletons from the crypt so I can go raise some more skeletons. I played this level for 15 minutes and got bored of the repetetive nature. It's dull.
My direct comparisons to Dungeon Keeper are pretty simple; it lacks the style of dungeon keeper, it has it's own but it pales by comparison. The animations of things even as simple as a slap with the Hand of Evil seems to lack something by comparison, I can't put my finger on what though, I think the Dungeon Keeper version ultimately just felt like it had more soul in it, like it wasn't ashamed to just be a power fantasy for the player, it didn't need or want a complex plotline; you were evil, and you were doing what evil people love to do: conquer the world!
I think, all in all, most of my criticisms can be summed up in four words: Dungeon Keeper is Better, and it's funny that a game almost two decades old is still one of the best in it's category. But to the point my verdict on this game: It is itself, it's not a copy of Dungeon Keeper, and it does well to establish itself as something new and unique, and it definitely has it's moments of brilliance, but there's a lot of unexceptional stuff in here as well, things I myself don't enjoy.
I struggle to find myself choosing between recommending it and not, I'll put a word in for it; it's good, but I seriously cannot put myself through that crypt level that's just awful.

I feel this does not capture the spirit of the first Dungeon Keeper, but I also feel like it surpasses Dungeon Keeper 2, but not enough for me to give a recommendation.
The main problem I have with this game is the pacing. Every mission you unlock something new, leading to a rather spikey learning curve as you are supposed to juggle the intracies of new rooms and creatures on gameplay while being introduced to new rooms and creatures and mechanics. The game wasn't even challenging. You aren't ever wanting for resources, nor do you need to carefully build defenses, or carefully gauge how much of whatever room to attract various minions.
Prisons and torture are pretty useless, but more units never hurt anything. Traps are overpowered, and you can rally click your way to victory without breaking a sweat. I enjoyed the narration though.
The entire game feels like a tutorial, and there's never any added difficulty of learning to use your arsenal well. When you finally get all your toys to begin playing with, the game gives you the credits and a thanks for playing! Well, you're not welcome. Ok, maybe a little welcome. It was still Dungeon Keeper after all.

Overgrowth provides a gaming experience you cannot get from ANY other game. The meaty, brutal, bloody combat and insanely fast movement and fighting makes the game PERFECT in every way as a straight up combat game. The fighting controls consist of left/right click for attack/block, but you choose your direction of attack based on which direction key you're hitting at the time. Combine this killer combat control with a ton of badass weapons and a GREAT blood and "slash" system, and you have yourself endless gruesome combat.
Movement in Overgrowth is very polished and extremely fluid. You play as a rabbit like creature, so it makes sense for various flips, wallruns, ledge climbing, and super high jumps to be used commonly in the environment. I always enjoy running around the map trying to pull off cool parkour runs.
The editor in this game has to be one of the best, if not THE best editor for any game in terms of what all you can do. And trust me, there is no limit. Although the awesome editor for the game comes with a price. The learning curve. If you only plan on making simple maps or freerunning courses, then you'll adapt pretty quickly to the editor. Spawning in AI and weapons is extremely easy, but the more complex things you want to do, the more you need to learn about the editor.
Now that the game has been released on steam, there is no reason NOT to purchase it. This game is one of my must have's and first installed when I switch PCs.
TL; DR, This game provides a combat experience like no other, an editor to die for, and parkour elements so longed for in other games; All wrapped up in a neat, mod capable, well performing, and constantly updated bundle.

What to say about this one? well I can't really say I was too disappointed by this game because it is the true Dungeon Keeper successor and I was never able to play that game due to it being too old and too finicky with modern systems to get running but I really wasn’t impressed by anything in this game either. It has good intentions but it's really not all that interesting, even going along the campaign and unlocking new abilities, traps and room types the game never got more exciting than the 'oh yay new dungeon management game, im sure this will be good!' thrill at the start.
Here are categories on why I was barely able to enjoy the game:
What storyline? It's so bland and forgettable I'm pretty sure it's there so the devs could say 'we made a storyline!'. I can sum it in afew sentences. Your evil and stuff, you get betrayed by alot of other evil people you have kill on the way to the top, once you kill all forces of good and become the most evil dungeon lord you get betrayed in a very obvious way you could have predicted way ahead of time and poof game done, yep… seat clenching. It is a shame because surely someone can think of a neat storyline for an evil dungeon lord coming from the bottom all the way to the top of the world? Even if it was taken non seriously like a joke, “They made fun of your really cool hat, knocked over your letter box and keep killing your zombie collection for fun, they must pay!” might have been better. Meh, not a big gripe for a game like this but it never really feels like I have any incentive to killing all these 'good' characters and ruining their world other then, your bad mkay? kill stuff cas the game gives you no other options, ugh. What did they look at me wrong? call my mum a bad name? Not put the toilet seat down?! Why do I hate them to the point of torturing them!? The game never explains that, if it even could, it's not very fulfilling at all and it just made me want to end the game as quick as possible.
It took me barely 8 to 10 hours to get done, not alot of depth, not alot variety, a very linear experience from one click spot to the next, I don't know what more to say about this that wouldn’t repeat the storyline section, with no engaging storyline to follow the campaign felt pretty bland and meaningless. I was only doing it to get my monies worth out of the game about half way in and it just left me so unsatisfied at the end I ditched the game right after finishing it and never plan to come back to that waste of time and effort. If you’re looking for an amazing single player experience in this I’m sorry look somewhere else...
Oh boy is this a major gripe. This must have been made on an old Unity engine cas as far as advancing gaming graphics goes it looks terribad, and I really wish I was exaggerating. Great models and textures but not the right game engine to show them off in! Even the lighting in this is nothing special, there is no real visual evidence that your dungeon is as evil ,dark and monster filled underground hell as it is supposed to be, I was never really fully immersed by it and that's such a disappointment. Oh yea and don't even get me started on the joke of an anti-aliasing option... it's either have sharp visuals with jaggies for days or mega FXAA that blurs the whole game to such a degree you can barely make out the details of a single object or texture *shudders*. Just, no, if you appreciate graphics like me you will have a depressing time here, again all this is to blame for the crappy Unity engine they chose.
Performance, oh boy! You can imagine a game that's not open world with not much going on and poor visual fidelity will run great right? Well no, not at all, no hopes, again the Unity engine strikes to make this game run dreadfully on my gtx980 with 16gbs of RAM semi top of the range rig. On the last few missions my frame rate got down to a solid 12! I crap you not, 12!! If I was lucky I got 17 fps. With no optimization to be heard of this game will run like the alternative name for a donkey as soon as your dungeon gets to any decent size. I could have turned down the graphics maybe, but it already looked bad enough with no blurry AA on I didn't dare try, and on a gtx 980 why the heck should I have to?! Top of the line graphics cards aren't cheap for a reason right?
Moving off the biggest gripes, the variety is pretty good, a large range of different room types which also equal a different minion type for most of them, spells, traps, side powers you can call on to help you out abit and even little ease of life constructs. The enemy sends you a decent variety of enemies to annihilate and you even fight other underlords at afew points, this is all great, if it weren't for the insanely boring combat that you have to endure with to progress...
About all you can do is possession control a minion for some FPS interesting involvement but that gets boring quick due to a single minion never being able to make that much difference even while played by you. The only other thing you can do to help combat is the healing and rage spells and zapping enemies with lightning if they go on any of your territory and slip by, other than that it's just misc helpful spells to run the dungeon and spamming the attack banner around so your stupid minions actually move and attack everything else, nothing goes much deeper than that. Maybe I wasn’t being creative or was missing something? But I doubt it because I tried everything I was given, waiting for a crud ton of minions to spam then just blob charging them at the enemy was the only thing that seemed to work so I went with it for the whole campaign, not very engaging. =/
I guess after all that the only final conclusion can be... don't waste your time and effort on this, really just don't. This is quite frankly the most boring dungeon management game I’ve played so far, it does nothing new from Dungeon 1, Dungeon 2 and Impire, I can actually say that Dungeon 2 is more fun purely because of interesting mechanics and a playable dungeon lord that always gives you something to do! This game however will consistently show you how bland an unengaging, unsatisfying management game can be. Other than building 5x5 basic 'blocked' rooms and doing some spells and building traps I never really felt like I had any reason to be in this game 'helping'. A disappointing shame but it happens, bad engine and not enough thought and depth put in by the devs. Even the management in Overlord 2 was cooler lol, the minions in that game had personality and where so loveably evil and fun.
Buy this when it's majorly on sale if you really want or find something else because this really is a hit and miss for me and mind you I have played every dungeon management game I have found so far so hopefully everything I said holds enough water for you to believe me, because this review is in -your- interests.

Crusader Kings 2 is one of my all time favorite games. I got it back in 2012 I think, when the map was about a fifth of the size it is now. The support this game has gotten from the devs is a serious credit to them apart from the (Questionable?) DLC. But I'll get into that later.
First and foremost the vanilla game is about being a christian ruler in medieval Europe. The base game itself is fantastic and if you get it on sale you are in for a treat. Many hours of gameplay from the base game. DLCs are something I got as they were released and because of the time between them I didn't really see their total price. Looking at them now, Ehhh, I can see why people are apprehensive. It's a lot of money. I honestly think it is worth it especially if you can catch this game on a big sale.
With the DLC practises e.t.c out of the way onto the game in general:
The positives:
It has a lot going for it. Rule as somewhere, with a historical ruler or your own madeup dynasty and character, and try to lead your family to greatness. Many people can get caught up with the conquesting and stuff but this game is about putting family first. If you don't look after the family it's going to be GG.
The multiplayer is one of the best, mainly because of the hours of fun I've had in it, especially if you have a group of friends to play with. You can get one person to buy all the DLCs and then everyone gets to use them for free in the lobby. I'm the designated host of my group because of my long term investment into the game which means none of my friends need splash the cash on the DLCs. The connection is very stable between clients, rare desyncs to happen however and the sending of save games at hosting is very fast, even with my awful 600kb/s speeds.
The depth you can go into is incredible. Have affairs, murder your brother, raid your neighbour, go on a pilgrimage, borrow money from the Jews on the hollow promise you'll pay them back then immediately expell them after they show you their hidden Jew-gold. Which brings me to my next point. SJWs, PC peeps and the faint hearted will have an awful time with this game simply because it is historically accurate. Woman are oppressed in almost every culture and religion, Jews are treated like complete♥♥♥♥♥♥and the small are bullied by the big. It is a really brutal society.
Now as much as it hurts me... I'm going to have a few digs at the game...
The negatives:
The seduction way of life is completly broken. FIx your ♥♥♥♥ing♥♥♥♥♥♥Paradox. You are usually decent at fixing this stuff but a English king cannot travel to ♥♥♥♥ing Italy every weekend to have a go at the Italian queen. All the while on the way back he ♥♥♥♥s the German kings five daughters and has a go at the French queen. It's ridiculous and needs to be nerfed HARD.
Educations on children need to be looked at because something funky is going on there. Every now and again my Midas Touched ruler (best stewardship education) who is educating his two heirs will finish education with really good traits. Good so far right? Ok well then the game decides I have it too easy and gives one syphilis and kills him and the other becomes a detached priest.
As much as I love a hard game, crusader kings can sometimes go too far. If you are playing multiplayer with a group of four or so friends you will see this. The game will pick one person and ONE PERSON ONLY to pick on and make life almost impossible for. It has killed my strong and quick character two days because of a wound. The first day it got infected, the second day I died. That was it. Game over. Crusader kings just didnt want me in that game for some reason. Other times it will wait. You will notice you are getting the bad events while other people are finding gold in wells out in the backarse of nowhere when suddenly syphilis stricks you down and you are out of the game because your lustful, fertile character somehow didnt make a child.
TL;DR game has some balancing issues and SOMETIMES wonky AI but the multiplayer, historical accuracy and depth more than make up for it IMO. I honestly think this game is worth your money. Even the DLCs

Prime World Defenders is a good game in it's base but is unfortunately crippled by it's progression system making it an absolutely unrewarding grind to play.

When completing a mission (the first time) or playing one of the "random" side mission you are rewarded an item card, this can be a tower, a spell, an item that is a tad better for upgrading, or one of the game's currencies.
The issue with this system is that you getting the cards you need is completely random, so you can find yourself in a situation that you do just not have the cards you need. And even when you get the card you need, it will be so underpowered in comparison to the cards you started upgrading that they are pretty much obsolete. Speaking of obsolete, some towers even when fully upgraded get straight up outclassed by the "rarer" ones, that is after you started upgrading those repeating the cycle.
It's a horrible system that turns the game from enjoyable to frustrating.

Unfortunately that is not the only issue the game has. The magic system for example (again cards you need to upgrade) is completely useless since the spells do not scale with the waves, hardly making a dent some waves in.

There also is the issue that there are no fine controls in the game for the towers, you can not set a tower to attack the enemy the furthest along, or maybe the weakest. This adds another layer of frustration especially with the boss fights where towers tend to lock on to the boss and les all the weaker minions pass.

It is a shame really, the base game is good and with some minor tweaks it could have been darn solid. But do yourself a favour and don't loose yourself in this frustrating mess.

I like this game, but it has many problems people won't simply dismiss.  I for one can forgive them but it confuses why these problems exist.  Problems like animation, hitboxes, crafting system.  They all seem outdated and worse versions of what other games do.  The first person animations are monstrous, but the third person animations are alright.  The hitboxes can be a bit wierd but bearable.  The crafting system is a click, wait, get kind of system, where you get the materials, hit craft, wait a while (5 min to 10 hours depending on the item.) then you go and get it from the menu.  Also something that bugged me was that this game came out in 2009 originally and that they had the nerve to put a price on this game before it went free to play.  This game is a good free to play but paying for it is a horrible and idiotic idea, simply because the polish in this game is next to nothing.  This game does get in depth later on though with factions, vehicle (Better vehicles I should say, since you get a horse ealy on.), and more advanced and better looking weaponry.  The quests are interesting and sometimes challenging but luckily I had friends to help me out, this also improved the amount of fun that I had with this game. When you first get in it may look like another hotbar World of Warcraft like game (I actually like WoW it's just that many MMO's borrow so much from it that it gets boring.) but all those keys are 100% option for a more "magic" oriented player.  The tutorial is horrible, boring, and useless aside from simply teaching new players and should be skipped if you have played before.  Now onto the better parts of this game.  It progression is slow but it feels good to finally get that first revolver after using pellet guns for a while.  The custimization in this game is good ingame but in character creation it is limited but acceptable.  The towns feel alive due to all the other players going around doing their missions, crafting, learning, etc.  Now for a more personal opinion, I found this game alright, it gave me fun times with my friends but sometimes I would get locked getting resources in an area for crafting and trading.  I saw myself just joking around a lot before heading out to do a mission, which my friends would have fights over because some would go ahead of each other and it honestly annoyed me.  This game also has PvP which I never participated in since I had no real reason to.  This game gave me some rewarding progression (Which was created from the effort and time put in),  confussion as to why it isn't more polished and improved, and a annoying but sometimes fun time with my friends. If I would have to give this a score it would honestly be a 5/10.  I see the appeal here it's just I can't get over why it is like it is now: a messy MMO shooter with mechanics which could be improved easily.  I recommend this game to someone who takes MMO's as serious as a mature Arma player.

Prepare to rage when you play this game. That is right gamers I am going straight into this review with a warning because Mutant Mudds Super Challenge is not just a name, oh no it is actual fact! I mean come on developer…you are not getting with that damn title at all. This will be that game to make you break a controller in half, but not really since they are freaking expensive. Let’s get into this review.
You see that menacing image of those silver faces of evil…yup that is the game ready to mess your whole world up with much destruction to your mental state. Mutant Mudds Super Challenge brings a classic style to the new age of gamers from the days of yesteryear where this game takes its difficulty from. This is a cross of Ninja Gaiden and super Mario brothers with a dab of contra. The funny part about the game is that there is a pattern that any gamer can follow, but it all comes down to our human error in the end.
Some enemies will go left to right or up and down. There are many occasions where they jump into the background and they move so slow that you can’t really blame the game if you get caught by that pattern. Your biggest enemy in this game is the environment itself and that freaking jetpack that makes you feel safe, but not really. It is all about timing and being patient until you know the game and you can then do a speed run.
I am not going to make claims that I went far into the game, oh no. In fact, my fellow writer Mr. Trickster played for three hours with over 80 deaths and I played for a full hour having 50 deaths under my belt and it was a fun nightmare. That statement may sound confusing, but the game is not bad at all. It brings a level of difficulty and challenges you the right way that many games have lost through all the hyped up graphics. The best part about this game that it is available on handhelds which you can take the rage with you on the road.
Since I am not alone in this review, I have a quick statement from Mr. Trickster who also dabbled in Mutant Mudd Super Challenge.
Well, let’s compare with a good platformer like mega man. It was challenging because of the placement of the enemies with the level design complimenting that challenge by either making it harder to get through easier enemies or making it easier to get through harder enemies. MUDDS does the opposite, having some enemies make it near impossible to pass without getting hit (the ghost levels) and just have bad enemy and bonus door placement overall
That is a good point there should be a balance between difficult and nearly impossible to succeed. At times that would sound like whining, but I did notice some hiccups with the controls that make it difficult to gauge my jumps and the hit detection in some areas made me question how did I get hit. The part of any game is when the foreground covers where you are going, I used to hate that in old titles when trees you pass will block your line of sight and since you jump to the background that tends to happen a lot. This is not challenging that just causes a problem.
This is where I am at a crossroads between a difficult game that is fun versus a difficult game that is impossible. I understand you want us to earn the win, but if you make a game that has certain control issues and poor designs in combat or environments then it becomes something evil in a sense.
Graphics wise the game is visually beautiful and the added bonus of unlocking many sprites from different games kept me going, to an extent. I had to take many breaks from the frustration and I can’t help but keep going back to that frustrating aspect. I thought Ninja Gaiden for the Xbox was hard on the first level, but you sir are scary.

Conclusion:
Mutant Mudds Super Challenge should be taken with caution and be prepared for an engaging and frustrating time with some rewards, but many tears. In that, we give it 3 Paws out of 5. I have been sceptical that FunCom could pull this off after their Age of Conan game - which started out rather bumpy.   Now that I have experienced Conan Exiles I am happily surprised - and very excited for this new comer to the MMO genre.  This is the game FunCom should have done long ago.  If they keep adding new content, new items, more land mass and new areas - this game will be the game Bethesda should have made with Skyrim.  Skyrim is a great game - but it sorely was lacking due to the fact that it was a solo game.  If Skyrim had the coop/multi-player ability that Conan Exiles does it would be the game.  As it is FunCom beat Bethesda at their own game.  This is without a doubt one of the best games I have ever played in Early Access(beats ARK by miles at this stage of the game).  Just awesome.  Keep it up Funcom and you'll have an instant classic - just like Bethsda did with Skyrim. I highly recommend this game!
Oh yeah, don't be turned off by the mixed review rating.  I was fence sitting becuase of some of the reviews saying things like - terrible FPS, too glitchy, and too much like ARK and RUST.  This is not ARK, this is not RUST.  This is a Conan based survival game that puts ARK and RUST to shame.  FunCom is doing everything right in this game and I suspect with the speed at which they are patching this game will just get better and better in the next couple of months.  For a game in basic Alpha I'm shocked - shocked that this is their ideal of Alpha and Early Access, because I've played released that are not as well made as this game is at this early stage of development.  So yeah, this game just rocks.  As I said earlier - I highly recommend this game.

While the story and themes aren't necessarily super exciting, Blocks That Matters makes a lot up in the gameplay department. The object of the game is to control a little drilling robot and solve a slew of increasingly mind-bending puzzles. Your Drillbot can drill certain blocks (dependent on the quality of its drill) and then use those blocks to create platforms. Different blocks have different ways of behaving with certain situations and objects. You are also going to need quick fingers and lightning fast reflexes if you want to solve the puzzles in the "most efficient way" to earn a Gold or even the Green star!
The game is notably short if you don't have a obsession for completing everything and gaining every little golden star in the game, but at the same time it doesn't drag things endlessly and spread itself too thin. Almost every new puzzle requires different kind thinking. In the casual category, this game shines!

Dungeon Warfare is an amazing take on the tower defence genre. This type of game is probably my favourite genre bar RPG. The game does a very good job of introducing different traps each level, allowing you to get to grips with each of them so you know how best to use them.

I liked how you could spend gems which you gain for completing a level and going up a level on upgrading your traps.
