I saw the name "Burgers" and I bought it instantly because I figured it must be entertaining at least.  Well, it's not very good, I don't know what game the other reviewers were playing  but I sure didn't have the same experience.
First of all, the animations are great.  I actually admire the amount of work that went into the animations.
But the game falls short after that.  I didn't find the levels to be very well thought out, basically just a simple straight path with the same enemy types over and over, I got all the way to the first boss, being extremely careful the whole time with hundreds of ammo.  The boss had several attack moves, but easily avoidable, so without missing a single shot, the boss took all of the machine gun ammo and all grenades, leaving me with just a pistol with 1000 ammo in it.  The pistol does not do much damage at all, and it would probably take 20+ minutes of shooting slowly to take him down.  I had to stop after pressing the shoot button a couple hundred times.  It would be a different story if you had the ability to be swapping out weapons or could build up some sort of strategy up to that point, but there's no way to have unlocked something else by this time.  Just sit there and pew-pew-pew your way through, taking tiny scratches off this boss.  It's just boring gameplay all around, and feels unbalanced as though they never even played their game from the start.
On the third level in the graveyard, there is a giant message that says "SNIPER RIFLE BEST USED HERE" and a picture of a sniper.  But it's not possible to even have a sniper rifle at that stage at all, it's all locked.  You just have to ignore this.
In your "armory", it lists a number.. mine says 317 right now.  What does it mean, I wonder?  There's no dollar sign or anything beside it, no tool tip, is it money?  Experience?
In addition to that, there are buttons in the menu to join online servers but none of them work.  When you first boot up the game, it says "CONNECTION STATUS: Disconnected" in the top left corner.  But it's not possible to actually connect to anything, I tried every single server.  Not a huge issue, though.
When you press the escape key in-game, it brings up the menu.  But it doesn't pause the gameplay at all?  I guess the developer hasn't figured out how to do that yet.  Not an issue for online games as it wouldn't make sense to pause it, but for single player matches it's awful to have no way to pause what you are doing.
There are just weird problems everywhere, like if you click on the options menu, it reads "create room" on top, for no reason at all.  That's how rushed of a release this is, they didn't even check over the options menu for obvious mistakes.
So, overall I found the game to be very poorly made, yet it shows promise.  They could turn it around and fix things...  but then now let's talk about the real reason I came here to complain.  I smell something fishy.
First of all, the whole store page is full of positive reviews on the very first day, everyone is just LOVING this game, somehow.  We've got steam accounts that only have 1 or maybe 2 games in it, buying this game and reviewing it.  Steam accounts that have ONLY started playing games on the day of Burgers' release.  That's highly suspicious.
Secondly, I videotaped myself playing the game, and my content was banned from the community.

Overgrowth is just fantastic! I've put probably over 100 hours into it (Steam says otherwise because this game was available way before the release on Steam) for good reason. The parkore is very smooth and fun, plus you get to jump super high because you are a two legged animal. The combat is where this game shines though. It has very butal fast paced combat, where you can engage enemies with various attacks and counters. Now it isn't a button mashing game where it is dish out as much attacks as you can, you need to actually go at enemies with tatics (especially groups of them or wolves). Then there is weapon combat (which I like the most). Battle with weapons can be extremly fast paced. This isn't like some games where it take five to ten stabs with a sword to kill some one, nope it is one slice with a broadsword, one stab or slice with a regular sword, around two stabs or slices with a spear, and about five to six cuts with a knife. There is also stealth in this game where you can choke your opponent out or cut there throught open with a weapon. The AI is also pretty smart but could use improvements (mostly just their AI for running and getting help). There is also tons of moddablity with this game, you can download custom items, hotspots, and maps with the SUM Launcher. Over all I give this game a 4/5, thirty dollars is a great deal, espesially compared to all of the cappy AAA titles that cost sixty dollars (looking at you COD: Ghost).

Crusader Kings II is one of those games that I'll fully admit I didn't like when I first started playing. As you can see from my hours played my perception changed quite a bit from those first few hours. This game has a steep learning curve, and there are still things that I am figuring out even 450+ hours in. Give this game some time and look up some tutorials online and I guarantee you that this game will suck you in and keep you engaged like a fantastic book.
In Crusader Kings II you are the head of a medieval dynasty and the only goals that exist are the ones you make up for yourself. Do you want to unite all of Ireland? Go get at it. Do you want to restore the Roman Empire? Much harder, but still possible. Do you want to avenge the death of your beloved son by slaughtering the family of the one who ordered his assassination? Sharpen your swords. Do you simply want your family to survive until the end date, regardless of how powerful or weak you are? Hey, that's an option too.
Odds are, throughout your family's history there will be numerous twists and turns, stories of great triumphs and great tragedies, histories written about the ruler who was benevolent and beloved by their people and the ruler who was an absolute tyrant, despised by all in life and in death.
There is honestly so much I could write about this game, but we'd be here all day. Yes, the interface is kind of clunky. Yes, the game is extremely unfriendly to newcomers. Yes, there are some mechanics that are absolutely broken (Decadence, anyone?). If you can look past some of these flaws, what you have here is a game worthy of your time and has so much to offer. (I would suggest waiting for it to go on sale. This game plus all of it's expansions are spendy). The best way to experience Crusader Kings II is to experience for itself.

The game this would be most similar to would be the XCOM series, a turn-based war tactics game.
But where XCOM has a retro futuristic aesthetic dealing with an alien invasion, Valkyria Chronicles tells a war story closer to that of WWII with an anime flair.
Watercolor aesthetics through their canvas engine provide a stark contrast to the heavy themes covered within its story. While predictably melodramatic and cliched at times it doesn't shy away from topics of race, genocide, history being written by the victors and the tragedy of war. The way in which these were covered were far better than I went in expecting given the aesthetic.
The watercolour aesthetic bears mentioning again, it looks fantastic and has held up well given the age of the game. Aesthetics over graphics every time. It also helps that the game runs fantastically, a VERY good quality port.
Gameplay wise I would say it is as satisfying as XCOM with some differences, while it is turn based, you gain control of the character you pick for that AP point and have a number of actions you can carry out, and reaction fire from enemies happen in real time.
Where VC stands out against XCOM is in the development of characters and the storyline. In XCOM you only get attached to characters insofar as you have developed their stats. VC manages to develop personalities, and their quirks can inform gameplay decisions as well. I found myself becoming very fond of some characters, and knowing who played well as who (as well as which members of my squad were racist and should be benched).
There are some issues, you are unable to save mid mission which can be frustrating on longer missions, especially if you give a command in error. You also lack the ability to replay a mission to obtain a better rank until newgame+ which is frustrating. When I finished the EXELLENT campaign I didnt feel like going through the whole thing again, where as I may have replayed a mission while it was fresh in my memory to improve.
Also the game doesnt do a good job of explaining some of their systems or method of ranking. The prime example being the rankings, I thought a complete victory with removal of all combatants was important. It turns out that blitzing past many defences to secure the objective can score a MUCH higher rank, this changes the style of strategy one employs considerably (Dont get me wrong, these kind of all or nothing plans are glorious fun).
Finally, without getting into spoiler territory, I really appreciated having a complete ending, nothing left hanging in the air, nothing pointing with a wink at a potential sequel, a complete and satisfying story with a conclusive ending.
Highly recommended.

So far I've recommended three games that are each very good in their own right. Unfortunately, not every review can be positive, just not like every Tower Defense can be good. And Prime World Defenders is an example of how to do one wrong, in my opinion.
The game is a spinoff of Prime World, an MMO also on Steam (which probably should have sent off some alarm bells right away). It takes place in the Prime Zone, a stretch of land that was struck with a miniature apocalypse, where pockets of energy have appeared and dangerous mutants roam the land. You play as a new recruit to a group of treasure hunters slash do-gooders who explore the wasteland. I didn't find myself particularly interested in the story, though, and it didn't help that the voice actors didn't appear to be either.
Defenders starts off perfectly fine, and annoyingly it takes a while for what I disliked most about to rear it's head. The game looks nice, there's some interesting maps, and every map has some special conditions you can pull off for some rewards. But inevitably, I ran into the big problem: this game is grindy just for the sake of it. Your towers have a card gimmick to them, and you're rewarded one or two after every mission. To make your towers stronger, you can sacrifice junk cards you don't want for a slight stat boost, and you can also 'evolve' them by pairing them with another card of the same type. This is absolutely necessary, since that's what allows you to upgrade them in stages.
So if you find yourself needing a card, your course of action is to play stages hoping it will appear - if it does, the game also shuffles up rewards to make getting it random too. You can try again for a fairly sizeable amount of silver, a resource the game wants for everything, including evolving cards. The game offers a shop, too, where you can spend silver on mostly random boosters, or use stars, a harder to acquire currency, on more specialty items. This is probably reminding some of you of something, and it likely won't surprise you to hear Prime World Defenders also has a mobile version, among others. There's no micro-transactions in the Steam version, but when the framework of the game still seems built around them it's hard to say that's a positive change.
What's really damning though is that the version of the game on Steam has basically been abandoned. The last time the developers were seen about the forum was apparently two years ago, and there are bugs that haven't been fixed. Meanwhile, the versions of the game that do have micro-transactions are still supported, with fairly obvious implications as to why. I bought Defenders in a bundle, so I don't feel as ripped off as I could have been, but it's hard to recommend a game the developers seem like they could care less about, especially compared to the ones I've talked about and a lot of the ones I will.

This game's story is actually pretty difficult.
So you load the game and have a jolly old time playing the first six chapters or so. The game is your best friend. This game is really good, you say, as you get to know the characters and get attached to them. You learn the mechanics, and you're certain you've bought a great game.
Then in Chapter 7, the game betrays you. It slaps you in the face and kicks you in the stomach, forcing you to fall on your♥♥♥♥♥
The game starts to kick you. It kicks the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of you. You beg it to get back up. Each beg makes the kicking harder.
"Let me get back up!" you scream in a desperate attempt to stop the pain.
"EARN IT, NERD!" The game replies, as it mercilessly continues to pound your ribcage and torso with its unforgiving boot.
It goes on. The pain is unbearable. With nothing else to do, you scream for the pain to stop.
The game doesn't say anything, it just laughs at your misery. It likes this. It likes to see you a broken, bloody mess on the floor.
But you don't give up.
Motivated by the best story and the best characters that have ever graced a video game, you don't give up.
You brace yourself for the pain of each impact.
You've been kicked so hard for so long, you start to go numb. But around this time, is when you learn.
You learn the kicks. You learn where they come, you learn how they come. You've gone numb to them, so now they can't hurt you as much.
The kicks keep coming. But this time, you take it. You take the pain and you tough it out, because that's what this sadist seems to want. You're used to what it has to dish out.
You try again, saying "Can I get back up now?" in a raspy, injured voice.
It backfires. The game is personally insulted. It starts to kick you harder. It puts all its energy into each hit, hitting new, and bruised areas. Soon it starts to stomp on you instead. It's reconsidering whether it even wants to let you get back up.
Maybe you should just give up. But no. You've gone too far to do that now.
The characters flash in your mind. You remember why you're laying here, being beaten in the first place.
You keep taking the kicks, and now the stomps. You've learned the hard way from the kicks, the stomps aren't as bad of a challenge now.
You're used to it. Used to having the living♥♥♥♥♥♥beaten out of you.  You're used to the numbness. The numbness is now your strength.
"GET UP, SCUMBAG!" The game taunts you. You make the mistake of taking it, and you try to get up.
It puts a boot right into your nose, sending blood spilling down your mouth. You're back on the ground now, dazed from the impact.
The game laughs at you. It's taken pleasure in what it just did.
You know that you can crawl away, but you don't. You don't because of the story. It all started because of the story, and the characters. You're far too attached to back out now.
You ignore the game's laughter. You start to notice that you're getting stronger. The laughter doesn't matter.
"EARN IT, YOU ♥♥♥♥ING SCUMBAG!"
Enough.
You're done. You've been taught everything you need to know.
Aching from the pain, you slowly begin to stand. Slowly this time, soon you're on one knee.
The kicks start to stop. The game knows what you're doing.
But now, the game punches back, a harder than ever this time. You refuse to let this one hit its mark. You swipe his fist out of the air, inbound to your cheek, and shove it away.
Blood still coming out of your nose, bruises covering your body, you start to rise.
You get up.
On two feet, staring the game dead in the eyes, you speak three words.
"I got up."
The game smirks, and for a moment, you think it's going to start beating you again. But it's not.
The game steps forward and stands next to you.
"You earned it."
It offers its hand. You take it, and smirk as you give the game a handshake.
You won. You completed Valkyria Chronicles.
Rather, you conquered Valkyria Chronicles.
Returning to seriousness, some of the game's missions really like to put the player in an awful spot then say "Good luck, nerd." The difficulty spike in Chapter 7 is higher than any other game I have ever seen, and for every mission beyond that, the Empire always has better gear and more numbers than you. But, the only thing keeping you from putting the game down for being so hard and unfair, is the characters and the story. It's just too good.
Great game, proceed at your own risk. But, the handshake you receive at the end of the game is one of the most satisfying things you will ever experience.

First off let me say that this game has beautiful graphics and so much potential. But the issues that I have are not with the numbers, stats or game balance.

This game feels devoid of any true substance. I have many suggestions after playing this game, all on the aesthetic side as I feel that the math and stat mechanics are very solid. Please take my suggestions into consideration.
After playing Conan: Exiles for a little while I realized that I was yearning for more character personality and animations. There are not nearly enough animations and clever camera use to make surviving in the Conan universe a cinematic and meaningful experience, not yet anyway. I want to see my character uncomfortably laying down on a stone bed, poking his testicles on branches while he forcefully rips bushes out by the roots. Show me his hands as they become bloody from toil and hard labor. Don't cut corners with a quick nab of a rock. Make the character actually have a limit of rocks they can carry based on their strength or something. Show the Rocks piled in my character's arms while I move him back to my build site, where I drop the rocks and hear a sigh of relief escape my character’s lips. I want to see a stronger connection between the players and the characters they create in this game.

Meaningful representations of the player character's states should be represented. When the player builds a campfire, have an animation play where the character extends their arms out to warm their hands. I personally would see this as a reward in a sense. My character is enjoying the warmth of the fire and I can see that. Move away from the MMO feel of this game where visuals are taken for granted and often simplified. You (The developers) go through great lengths to add detail to the characters such as physics based anatomy and gore which is in my honest opinion fantastic! but you are missing a connection to where that blends in with the Survival aspect of the game. You have given my character a♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ great, now let me use it. I may find a suitable woman to bear my children and thus help me raise warriors and laborers to carry on my character's name. This could ultimately be a way for you to add in some new mechanics. Having children might mean that when your main character dies, you assume the role of your eldest and continue playing. The blood that stains the character’s skin is a nice touch but why simply make it fade away? Keep that dirt, sweat, blood and sinew on the player until they can get to a water source and rinse off. I for one love seeing my character trek through the wilderness covered in the blood if his/her enemies.
Loosen up the character animation in combat. I want to feel capable and powerful. I feel that you should stop making the combat based on stats and more so on physics and one to one action. In my opinion the combat should be more akin to Dying Light but with attention paid to the animations so that third person feels visceral and cinematic. Add grappling and tripping. Make it so that you truly feel the gritty reality of combat. Force the player to use basic actions such as Roll, dodge, tackle, sweep etc. to fight. Imagine a scenario if you will, where an enemy tackles your character to the ground. You can reach for something, cover your face, strike or tackle back in an attempt to roll the opponent over. Reaching for a nearby stone might enable the player to strike the opponent in the head, giving them an opportunity to get up or roll the enemy over and cave his/ her head in. I hope you get where I’m going with this. Make the combat more Conan and less EverQuest.
The last things I’d like to touch on is the use of weapons and damage. Since weapons degrade and break down, it makes sense to not even allow players to become attached to them. Repairing weapons makes no sense to me to be honest. The one thing that I loved about Conan, was that he used whatever he had at his disposal to end his enemies and would often use his bare hands. While one might argue that the player is not Conan, that resourcefulness should be present in gameplay regardless. Force the player to prepare for a hunt and build their supplies in the safety of their camp. Remove this ability to repair your stone axe with more stone out in the field. Make it so that twine is what is used to repair the axe at least, so if the stone axe head comes loose, you can use twine made from plant fiber to strap it back to the stick. The player should have to rely on their supplies, and if they do not have any more weapons then they should have to improvise out in the wild.
Damage feels way to MMORPG here. Make the damage more realistic and based on physics and type. If a Hyena charges at me and I thrust my spear into its face, it should die. There should be a satisfying animation where my character forcibly removes the spear from the Hyena’s head with an equally satisfying fleshy sound. If there are multiple Hyena’s my character might not be able to remove the spear in time and will need to leave it and switch to the dagger. Again, with the tackle example, the Hyena can attempt to pin my character to the ground but my experience has taught me to use the momentum of the Hyena and stab with the dagger. Just writing this feels much more fun and cinematically entertaining than what is currently in Conan: Exiles. Make damage less EverQuest and more Conan. Just because something can die quickly doesn’t mean that the game will be boring.
I truly hope that these suggestions will find their way into the game. I feel Conan: Exiles is honestly nothing special because it lacks moment to moment excitement and any meaningful aesthetic connection to the character one creates. This game is missing elements that truly make a great survival experience and leave the player saying “Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥that was cool!”.
Less EverQuest, More Conan!

Auction House: Used to sell whatever Items that are tradable, though most people I have noticed that are new to this game even older members tend to get two things confused at times, first.
Remember that theres differences between Not Tradable and Not sellable. Not tradable means exactly what it means, you can't trade it with other members of the game like yourself, and Cannot be sold, means you can't sell that item to the Merchants in-game. This doesnt mean you can't place this in the AH unless it states its both Not Tradable and can't be sold. If it just says cant be sold, you can trade the item with players but cant sell it to the merchants. if the item says it cant be traded but doesnt say it cant be sold, that means you cant trade with Players but you can sell it to Mercs. If both are displayed, best th8ing to do is either two things, stash it somewhere or right click the item to delete or Scrap it for parts, if given that Option.
Most players have a hard time figuring out where best to scavenge loot, whether its for crafting or selling. Try looking in the outskirts of Embry, Oilvile, Pass Chris and other towns, Oilvile contains alot of Copper and Lead deposits for example.
Waypoints.
Waypoints is VERY important in this game if you have a hard time keeping track of where your favorite spots are, rather its for looting and killing. To use Waypoints go to your Menu and locate the name Waypoints click it to open another window you can create a Waypoint or Add another. To create your own you can locate your Radar and click the globe icon to bring up your strategic map, from there, you can uncheckmark the Overhead to view detailed Information of where your at, and you can right click where ur Marker is at to add a waypoint, you can edit name to easily find it in your Waypoints Manager Window.
Copy recipe Links or AH links to Chat Windows
If you are near a AH or chatting in a Chat Bar, you can link recipes by going to Menu locating your Recipes and find the desired recipe and look at the bottom of your recipe, you will see an icon that looks like Shuffled cards, next to that icon is a chat bubble you click that to add it to any Recently Active Chat windows, then Enter it to show Full recipe to someone, But NEVER shout out recipes in the HELP section, since this will get you muted or possibly banned from Help for Spamming in the Help channel. Just like Adding Recipes you can also just directly link the Item itself rather the full recipe which is useful in the Auction Channel so you dont spam and make anyone mad. To do so, locate any recipe, find the actual item you want to craft, look at the Icon of the Item point your cursor to the thumbnail of it and you will see a Red pin like picture in the picture of it, you will then notice it will show a detail information of it, when it does that, hold down your Ctrl Button down on your keyboard and click your left click on your mouse to see it directly link to your active Chat Window. Works great for asking in the Auction Channel when saying WTB or Wanting/Willing To Sell

Cyberpunk + Hotline Miami = Match made in HEAVEN?
Not quite, sad to say.
RUINER's world and story falls short of Cyberpunk gems like Shadowrun and Deus Ex, while its gameplay feels like an unsatisfying imitation of Hotline Miami.
Reikon put real effort in trying to establish Rengkok as a living and breathing cyberpunk dystopia. But it never felt real to me. The player is allowed to roam free in Rangkok South - similar to the hub zones of Deus Ex and Shadowrun. However, this hub zone equates to little more than running to a spot to trigger an unvoiced cutscene or a mission start. It's shallow and pointless. At one point there is a police crackdown - however we do not get to experience the effects of that crackdown beyond being told that it is happening and seeing a few extra patrol drones flying overhead. Lack of depth reverberates throughout the game. Bosses are never explained. Instead of having a personal reason to care about them, they are just bigger and badder baddies on a carousel of faceless baddies.
Despite the techno-abundance of new gore-splattering fantastical future goodies, the gameplay just isn't all that satisfying. The soundtrack didn't drive my adrenaline in the way that Hotline did. Slashing or shooting an enemy didn't generate the same gut-punch. Bodies and viscera would fade, meaning that the player never gets a chance to reflect on the aftermath of violence. Ruiner does not create Jackson Pollock recreations via the medium of human viscera. The noticeable recycling of map elements is difficult to justify in a 3-4 hour game. Perhaps it is unfair to expect this game to be too similar to Hotline, but Ruiner creates these expectations through embracing an extremely similar combat and play style.
I really wanted to like this game, but the unfortunate truth is that I just didn't enjoy it. Each and every element within Ruiner is executed better by other recent games.

Golf with Your Friends is everything you want in a casual game. It's amazingly fun on multiplayer and I've already racked up 32 hours on the game since getting it in late August. I love casual games and Golf with Your Friends manages to achieve that perfectly and despite being early access, it's still an incredibly fun and creative product bursting with life.
My only criticisms come from three aspects of the game which I feel might be fixed by the time this game is fully released:
1. A restart option needs to be available in Classic. Many achievements rely on playing in Classic and when I'm trying to achieve par with a friend online, once we realise we won't get par or under, we have to 'Retire' and then set up a lobby again.
2. The game can be very glitchy. The ball can sometimes just randomly stop, get stuck in terrain when it shouldn't (Haunted's carpet floor is particularly bad for this). Likewise, on Twilight's final hole, once you reach the floor, your view is impaired with either water or blackness. This obviously needs to be fixed but I have every faith that these problems will be sorted.
3. Haunted isn't fun. This game is meant to be a challenge, but it's also meant to be fun - discovering new trickshots and cheats,♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off your mates by getting THAT ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t hole-in-one etc. Whilst all the other courses manage to brilliantly balance between challenge and fun, Haunted is just a mess. It's almost impossible to score a hole-in-one and everything is just very awkward and frustrating. There is nothing wrong with an annoying hole, but Haunted is too difficult and there is nothing fun about playing it in my opinion.
Other than these three aspects, this game is frankly excellent. A brilliant early release which I can't stop playing. I cannnot wait until we get the full game with the level editor and more courses.

Fantastic little tower defense game, one of the best among the top-down point-and-click ones. I'd rate it right after Defense Grid. It's the traps that fling enemies around and the environmental hazards that make it special, they are very fun to put into place and the effects can be downright hilarious. Orcs Must Die had those first, but if you want the same kind of action without the running around (which for me detracts from the strategy, rather than adds to it), this is the game for you.
The progression system is pleasant and very flexible: new traps are unlocked by completing specific levels, and all levels you finish give you upgrade points to improve turrets. The twist is that those are not just passive upgrades: you unlock lvl 2 of your pusher traps, but you still have to upgrade them in the course of a level using gold from killing invaders. You can redistribute your upgrade points between levels to specialize differently. You can also increase the difficulty of a level by choosing challenges that grant you more XP if you win.
Level design is good with a lot of variety; some involve a little bit of mazing using barricades. Traps can mostly be placed in pre-existing walls — a few can be placed on the floor — so you don't get the type of freeform design present in Defense Grid where you can build elaborate mazes and your turret themselves act as walls. Perhaps some levels could allow you to place walls, or even some track sections! (Yes there are deadly minecarts running around.)
Overall the gameplay is solid and interesting, so much so that while playing it I find myself wishing to see it used as the base of a larger game of dungeon management. It's a well-crafted and super fun tower defense. Buy it now.

Rarely have I been this excited about a Greenlight game getting onto Steam. I love, love, LOVE Dungeon Warfare. As a Tower Defense game, it does everything right: It's easy to learn and challenging to beat. It features new variations on a classic theme.  It offers on-rails or creative placement, whichever you prefer. Most important: It's just plain fun.
There are nice touches here that weren't in the Greenlight version. First, there is a feature between levels that allows you to actually increase the difficulty of your game in up to 8 different ways (for example, by reducing your lives to only one, reducing the number of traps you can use, or increasing enemies' strength, speed, or health). Why would you want to do this? Because each additional, potentially crippling selection will increase your xp multiplier! In short, as long as you have the cajones, you can gain some serious xp and, thus, level in fairly short order.  Conversely, you can also make things a bit easier for yourself, at the cost of 40% off any experience you might earn for that board.
That said, the game still offers balance, and I've never felt overpowered, even as a level seven player on board three. Each level up grants you an ever-increasing number of gems that can be spent to power-up your traps. As new areas are conquered, branching paths open up, offering more variety. Beating each area offers its own rewards, ranging from gems to opening up new trap slots.
Speaking of variety, there are a number of interesting traps on offer, from push walls to floor spikes; from barricades to melee fighting, demon-spawning portals; from darts to spin blades. The fun comes in trying different combinations, along with using the environment. Watching a well-placed push wall shove an enemy into a bottomless pit, for example, is quite satisfying (and the humorous sound effects really make the moment).
There are a couple of things that could be improved upon (navigation of the playfield could be better implemented), but the simple truth is this: As I write this, Dungeon Warfare is only on its ninth alpha release, and it's
in better shape than most full releases. I can't wait to see what's coming.
For fans of the genre, this is well worth the full price of $11.99.

Prime World Defenders is a good game but it does have the annoying remnants of a free-to-play system that make the game a bit irritating at times. You unlock towers and spells by progressing through the game, like many other tower defense games, but in order to upgrade those towers you need to get duplicate 'cards' and combine them. You get random cards from beating randomly generated 'grinding' levels and from buying booster packs. You can get common towers easy but the rarer towers (the ones that you really need to perfect some levels) will elude you for a good portion of the game. Eventually you will max out everything and then the game is really enjoyable although easy at that point.
Each level has two challenges that encourage you to play in different ways and after beating the game once you unlock a harder difficulty to really test out your skills (think new game +). The towers and enemies are fairly standard by tower defense...standards but I didn't really have a problem with that. There are boss fights every few levels that require a bit more strategy until you unlock a tower that absolutely shreds bosses to pieces when upgraded. Some kind of infinite survival map would have been a good inclusion, there are 250 wave survival maps when you finish but with a decent enough strategy you can easily beat them with minimal effort.
Overall I'd recommend the game if you don't mind grinding a bit in the early/mid game to get the towers you need to upgrade.

Scheherazade is not a good game.
Among several small sins, there are two parts that absolutely sink a what otherwise could be an interesting title:
-	The Game Mechanics. Oh the game mechanic. Never have I toiled so hard to accomplish so little. At first it looks like the game offers several character paths to embark upon, depending on the skill set, but quickly you realize the Difficulty checks are so high, and the base state increases are so low, your only reliable way of passing tests is getting a random selection of ANY skills to max, and then spamming the aspirations they drop for the general bonus to every other check. It’s so incredibly unrewarding, it made me lose all will to progress, which was already dwindling because of….
-	The Main Character. Jesus Christ the Main Character. She has all the traits of a Mary Sue, while also having no actual character traits. She’s incredibly intelligent, adventurous,  “witty”, "loveable", headstrong – and a heiress to a fortune, of “pure heart”, and with a mysterious destiny before her. She’s so absolutely impossible to relate to, I cannot comprehend how can any of the characters (or players) stand her.
Oh, and I forgot - she's also an ambitious independent woman in an age of inequality. How revolutionary! But fear not, when the situation strikes, when romance needs to happen, she has no qualms about tossing it all away to ask in a quivering voice “M-m-mummy-sama, c-can I grab your h-hand so we don’t get l-lost in the dark?”
Yeah, there is a Mummy in the game. The MC doesn’t seem to be all that phased by that fact. I guess I can see why, since the Mummy isn’t all that particularly interesting. None of the characters seem too interesting, even the romance choices. In a visual Novel. But I guess that might be just my opinion.
But anyway, add to all that some minor other annoyances, like dialogue choices not making any actual difference, bland art, cluttered interface, convoluted plot, and you got yourself a game that dreamt big, but fails to deliver on every possible level. Not worth the time, IMO.

I love this game, I didn't even find out about it until years after it's original release but now I'm blown away that the mechanics haven't been copied over and over in triple A titles.
Basically it is a turn based tactics game that you play in 3rd person view.  That probably makes no sense to anyone who hasn't played this game but it's essentially XCom meets Borderlands.  I chose borderlands as a FPS because it has a bunch of non-standard guns and RPG elements that contribute to your accuracy, range, etc...
The game adds a lot of anti-cheese mechanics like reflexive fire and patrols.  However, the missing element that would've made it even better was a teensy bit of randomization at the start of a level.  As it is, you can cheese a lot of it by knowing exactly the patrol spots every turn and knowing the exact cone of cover fire that entrenched units have.
Also, a few characters get ridiculously strong by the end of the game and you can go back and replay levels with them to perfect everything.  I don't think that's particularly cheesey as you would expect early levels to get easy once you're leveled up.  Some people might find it cheesey though.
All that being said you don't have to use cheesey tactics if you don't want to.
The story is one of the best, the artwork is great, the gameplay is original and inspired, great replay value, great additional content levels, and most importantly fun to play.
All in I would say I give it a 9/10 I think the 1 tweak that it needed was mild randomization at the start of the level.  Just something as simple as enemies facing in a random direction chosen out of a 45 degree angle would've drastically changed how a level is played as you wouldn't be able to easily predict (and avoid) their sight cones anymore.
As many others have put in their reviews I too have an appetite for more content of this type.  I would love to either see additional entries from this series ported to steam or for an indy developer to take up the mantle and make something similar.

A direct and to-the-point game, which deserves a direct and to-the-point review.
A brutal twin-stick action game, think Hotline Miami - but with a plethora of weapons, multiple dashes and unlockable abilities for a breakneck-speed and fun as hell combat experience.
Minimal, in a very refreshing way. The setting is a distillation of Shadowrun, Blade Runner, Ghost in the Shell, Neuromancer and several other sci-fi and cyberpunk classics. It tells you almost everything you need to know about the world purely through the oppressive red neon-tinted visuals alone.
The plot itself is marvellously simple. You are dumped in the midst of a high-tech, dangerous corporative compound with but two words imprinted over and over again on your mind:
. That's all that there is. Regardless of where the story eventually goes, that's all that it ever needed to be.
Wonderful. It evokes the same frenzied, non-stop beats as Hotline Miami, but with a distinctly Asian-Cyberpunk flavor to it. Does much to enhance the setting and fuel the action.
Let's see... The environments and bosses get repetitive after a while? And the game doesn't have an actual final boss at the end - not in the way that it maybe should.
That's it?
It's great! If you like twinstick action, arena-style combat, oodles of violence, oppressive cyberpunk-industrial setting, great music - Do get Ruiner. You won't be disappointed.
And remember:
More fun with more people, and is still fun a year later.

In

. By doing so, you have the chance to kick some nasty-looking alien butts, gather an almost entirely new crew, make love and shed tears of joy, shake your @ss in the finest clubs of the Pirate Queen Aria T’Loak, make friendly conversations with an oh-so cheerful Reaper about things like

Although gameplay-wise this game isn’t the most refined installment of the series (that title goes to Mass Effect 3 in spite of its horrible running animations) and the devs ripped out some RPG elements and the sense of exploration of the first game completely (actually, the latter part is not necessarily a bad thing, considering the tedious straggling across stark and empty terrain with the almost uncontrollably bouncy Mako was very...well, tedious as f*ck), overall Mass Effect 2 is hands down the best game in the trilogy. It represents a huge and very welcomed quality shift in the shooter part of the game, fighting and kicking butts here are far more fluid and enjoyable than it was in Mass Effect 1 with those clunky controls; the level design is finally decent and the new maps are especially memorable; and the soundtrack is so good, that I would say it’s beyond my comprehension how anyone could make such a thing...I declare here and now, that the composer Jack Wall must have been on demigod level when he composed those wonderful tunes.
Of course the real bread-and-butter here are the characters. Except Tali and Garrus, they are all completely new and fresh-feeling faces. As I was getting to know them better realizing how distinct, flawed, interesting and (in deep down) fragile personalities they are, I just couldn’t help loving them more and more, which obviously applied to the game itself. This is the greatest achievement of ME2, the genuine and extensive relationships between the main hero and the seemingly plot device NPCs, the potent world-building through its characters and their lovely recruitment and loyalty missions.
The biggest faults of the game aren’t even present in the actual game, which creates a kinda weird situation when it comes to evaluating it: The Reaper threat is always just lurking in the background, the main storyline doesn’t push the larger narrative forward (I mean what do we know at the start? The Reapers are coming, we are screwed, what are we going to do to stop them? No idea. At the end we know almost exactly that, nothing more...still have no idea what to do with the Reaper threat.) and the game introduces 10 completely new characters only to push the burden of closing their story arcs onto the third game. I’m sure that this situation (meaning ME2 is essentially not else than a long and exceptionally good side trip) created a big room of creativity for the devs to fill at ME2, and restricted their possibilities badly at ME3, ultimately making the second game better and worse the third.
In the end, what really matters is that Mass Effect 2 is an
, and it goes without saying that it is absolutely recommended to experience at least once in your life.

[Spoiler-Free Review]
Foreword: The game is not reccomended for a few major reasons:
1. It lacks serious mechanical polish; if you played the first game, expect to be disappointed by many of the mechanics.
2. The game is seriously bugged, the majority of quests are very likely to break and become uncompletable-- Including the entire endgame sequence.
3. Acts 3, 4, and the endgame lack the content and polish of the first two acts, and were clearly rushed out the door.
Pros (Reasons to Purchase)
+Combat is turn-based, tactical fun
+Game has very acceptable voice acting, no particularly bad examples stand out
+Art direction and visual design is top notch
+OST, while not as good as D:OS1, is not bad with many fantastic tracks
+World is vibrant and full of characters you can interact with
+Game allows you a great degree of freedom in exploration and progression
+Memory Slot system is much better than D:OS1's School system
+Early game is very polished and expansive, lots of content and choice
Notables (Things You Might Want To Know_
=The writing is very hit-or-miss, but is excellent compared to AAA RPGs
=Combat is very easy to those familiar with cRPGs and played the first game to completion; but is very challenging for those inexperienced with tactical combat or cRPGs.
=Potential party members seem very abrasive and offputting early on before their stories develop
=As of the time of writing, support for content creators is barebones but growing
Cons (Reasons to Think Twice)
-Game's Quest Log system is broken, almost every quest in the game can and will break, have wrong entries in the journal, become unresolvable, or just outright disappear
-Game's combat is significantly streamlined
-The new Armor System was not properly fleshed out, leading to a lot of issues
-Several mechanics are redundant, forgotten, or outright removed (Accuracy, Initiative, Attributes, etc)
-Itemization, Crafting and the Economy are much worse than the previous game's
-Character Building is very boring compared to D:OS1; there isn't nearly as many elements to work with, and lots of choices have been streamlined away
-Lategame gets more and more restrictive and unpolished, things become a trainwreck by Act 4
-Devs are on a spree of nerfing/removing/restricting things in the game rather than fixing balance or overhauling anything; does not set a good trend for the game's continued development and community support
If you really want to buy it, or liked the first game, just do a bit of research about what changed and the game's current state before you end up in a 4 man coop party 49 hours later unable to complete the game, and half of you end up quitting or refunding before they bother to release the first major patch a month later.

This is not a worthy successor to the Dungeon Keeper franchise. The parts are all there, but they're either faulty or shoddily put together. Even if you're an RTS or Dungeon Keeper fan, "War for the Overworld" will be an exercise in frustration and annoyance.
First and foremost, the game is lacking in terms of presenting the player with useful and sometimes necessary information. What can this creature do? How strong is that creature? What skill will they get and what do they do? What can the heroes do? Who knows? I certainly don't, because the game never bothers to tell you. I've played it for over 60 hours and have no idea of the relative power levels between creatures in the game. Not that you really need a balanced army or anything, but it'd be nice to know what your guys can or can't do. In Dungeon Keeper, you knew bugs were crap, bile demons were badass and that mistresses and vampires could wreck most things in 1v1. Here, I have zero clues what my gnarlings can take, what beasts are good or what the chunder actually does. No clue whatsoever. Just mass creatures and call to arms to their base, then hope for the best.
In terms of the story itself, you've been relegated to the role of underling to the narrator, who's the main character of the game. He's the one interacting with the overlords and heroes of the game, he's the one telling you what to do and he's the one setting the agenda. You're just along for the ride. Now I know how my imps feel, always getting told exactly where to go and what to do. Maybe you can find enjoyment in that, and if so then this is the story for you, but I couldn't. I want to be the main character in the game I play.
The game is horribly optimized, to the point where I can't tab out and back in without it grinding to a screeching halt and you need to restart. I've been able to play Starcraft 2 with the highest settings, skyping and having a browser up at the same time without performance issues. I've played Crusader Kings 2 grand campaigns with no real issue. I've played Grey Goo and Planetary Annihilation without it killing my computer, but War for the Overworld is slow and sluggish. It's incredibly slow and sluggish. You will also run into a lot of lag-related issues ingame, like the fog of war not dissolving when you explore, your creatures losing their focus and just standing around like idiots, creatures seemingly starting to teleport all over the map or even creatures starting to ghost (by which I mean they stand still and you can hover your mouse over them to see their info, but you can't interact with them because they're not really there, but the game just hasn't updated their location, so you're stuck with their ghost for a couple of seconds before the game eventually rectifies this). You're also going to see visual bugs, like creatures freezing mid-animation. You can also run into visual problems where the minimap doesn't load, where the UI doesn't load or where certain rooms and backgrounds won't load, so you're stuck with black nothingness in the middle of your dungeon.
Lastly, the game starts to suffers from increasingly heavy UI lag, where you press a button and sometimes need to wait for a couple of seconds before it actually interacts. Sometimes you have to press a button three or four times before it actually gets pressed. In stressful situation, I don't need to tell you how annoying it can be to try and reposition your creatures whilst casting spells and fighting your own UI and the game's lag.
The AI doesn't work. In Dungeon Keeper, you told your imps to do something and eventually they'd come around to finishing it. Not so much in War for the Overworld. Your imps will start a diggin task, stop and run to the other side of your dungeon, stop again, run to a random room and turn, run and chop once at a gold square, run back with the handful of gold, start reinforcing some random wall for a bit, then stop and run back to the original position and claim a square or two before going back to digging for a bit. It's beyond frustrating. At first I thought I just overloaded them with tasks, but no matter how little you give them to do, they won't ever do it faster or more efficiently. I tried maxing out the number of imps, but it made literally no difference. You keep your five original imps, but just ignore them and do everything yourself. It'll save you time and headache. This is a kiss of death for a dungeon building game, in my opinion.
Imps are not the only ones with a severely lacking AI, though. Some creatures won't ever do what you tell them to, ever. Beastmasters will not train in your training room unless you stand over them and cast spells to force them. They won't fight in combat more than occationally, instead going to the back of the fight and walking around in circles. You will also have creatures that get so sleepy, hungry and are so greedy, that you will never see them do anything but beeline between their beds, the tavern and the pig pens, trying to satiate their desires.
Sometimes, when the game slows down too much, the AI stops working altogether, and you will have to restart before fighting any battles. This is because your creatures won't actually fight, the AI can't use any skills in this state, but will opt to stand around, walk back and forth and sometimes losing and regaining the call to arms flag trigger.
Finally, I need to bring up the one way you can control your creatures in this game when not standing on your own lands, the call to arms flag. Sometimes there will be areas in the game where your call to arms won't work. You place it like always and everything seems fine, but your creatures will suddenly lose interest and walk away. It's beyond frustrating.
In conclusion, I recommend against getting this game. Don't buy War for the Overworld if you're a fan of Dungeon Keeper, because this is such a poor substitute you'll be pulling your hair in frustration. Don't buy it if it's on sale, it's not worth a dollar of your money. It's not fun. It's not challenging. It's buggy, it's simplistic and it's been done before and done better. The AI doesn't work, the UI is slow and unresponsive, the story is not even revolving around the player and you'll play the game from beginning til end without ever having to learn anything about it. Just go through the motions, call to arms in their base, rinse repeat. Do yourself a favour and play something else.

I had a lot of different conversations with my Steam friends lately and one of them reminded me of some good games, that have been released recently, but I couldn't manage my time properly to finish them.
One of such games on my list was Ruiner. The game I purchased on the day it was released, tried and liked it a lot. I was charmed with all this neon style, 80th era, blade runner cyberpunk style, and then I got stuck on one of the hardest levels in game and dropped it. Like I said already 1000 times before - end of summer/september-october was a very busy gaming period, so I almost forgot about Ruiner during this period.
So, what can I say about Ruiner? Well, its a cyberpunk game. Yes, another one in 2017, this year is sooooo full of cyberpunk titles and Blade Runner references and I can't be sad about it. It's really amazing, that this beatiful genre/culture is still viable. It's a brutal bloody non stop top view action shooter set somewhere in a distant future. The main hero is an augmented wired semi-human fighting his way to reveal the truth about the corrupted system and rescue his kidnapped brother.
At this point, you should already understand that this game is all about its gorgeous style, first of all. Dark, moody interiors with a bunch of neon lighting, astonishing soundtrack, progressing your character, leveling him to unlock new powers, hordes of enemies and non stop action. Speaking of enemies, I really loved the variety and creativity of the bad guys you will be forced to face in game. However, not everything is perfect in this game. Don't expect huge variety of locations/ landscapes or whatever. You are literally locked for the whole game in one big dark industrial zone with a minor changes on different levels and appearance of new more difficult enemies. The whole point of the game is pretty much obvious, like in every top down kill-em-all\shoot-em-all action games - run through the linear corridor levels, find a boss at the end of this level and put a bullet between his eyes.
However, the whole mechanics and ideas in this game works pretty much amazing in this game and you probably will not notice all these things, 'cause you will simply enjoy the gameplay, enjoy the music, fighting, shooting and progressing through levels. For example, I really liked the idea of weapon grinders. Imagine, you have an insane fight in the narrow room, with no chance to escape or run away, until you kill everyone's alive in there. At the end of the fight, the whole room is filled with blood, guts, ripped off arms, legs and...weapons, dropped from the enemies. But you can't carry them all, you are only allowed to carry two types of weapons - one blade and one gun. So, here comes the weapon grinder in the middle of the room, you activate it and it simply grinds all the leftover weapons in the room and you get karma points for that, which you can spend to level up your character.
Ok, to sum everything up!
You should grab this game if you:
+ Enjoy cyberpunk
+ Love action shooters/brawlers
+ Into all this Blade Runner thing
+ Like moody games with its own atmosphere and mindblowing soundtrack
You should pass if you:
- Expect a long game, game can be beated in one session, or two if you feel tired, somewhere around 4-5 hours
- Don't like a challenge in game - sometimes it can be ridiculous difficult, even on the lower difficulties
- Looking for a rich story game. Story is quite obvious and simple without any twists or 'damn what I have just seen' feeling
Enjoy!

Dungeon Warfare is an amazing Tower Defense game.
I have been playing Dungeon Warfare from the moment it became available. I have spoken with Groquest, one of the game's developers, for over a month about the game. Thanks to him, I was able to make videos on Youtube (linked at the bottom) about the game, and they show just how far Dungeon Warfare has come. Initially the game was pretty bare bones, but it was still immensly fun.
There are many different traps in the game that are unlocked by completing levels. The traps range from dart traps that shoot adventurers, to sticky traps that slow them down, to harpoon traps that fire into adventurers and pulls them into pits. There's something extremely satisfying about hearing an adventurer fall into an endless pit after being harpooned in the chest.
I highly suggest this game to anyone looking for a strategy game, or a tower defense game. I have always been a huge fan of TD's, including Bloons, Orcs must Die, GemCraft, and many more. I often find myself playing a level or two every night just before bed. I definitely recommend this game. If you're looking for more of a review, here's a link to my YouTube playlist for the game.

Before to start the review, I’d like to say that I’m really big TD lover from the age of Warcraft3.
As you know, most of the types of TDs that you can find in the market today, has been defined at that time.
Personally, I suppose there are two categories as a big picture, and those are like below;
1.	One – way TD
You can only install the tower along the path which is fixed, the only thing that you can arrange is ‘when’ you install ‘which’ tower.
This type of TD is really easy to build for the developer, because of easiness of leveling the difficulty.
It is really predictable, and there are no many options for the players to get the goal.
2.	Maze type TD
You make your own path with the barricades or obstacles, the only thing which is fixed is entrance and the exit of enemy.
This type can be provide wide range freedom to the player, because this TD is all about “how”.
But it’s really hard to get a proper leveling.
Because depends on the players’ skill, it can be too easy or too hard. And also, it’s really difficult to design vary maps.
Usually in this case, the differences between maps are only types of enemy or types of tower that you can build.
This limit is also connected to the difficulty of the leveling itself.
Actually, I prefer the Maze type TD, but it’s really hard to find in the market recently. Because of the limit that I’ve mentioned above, it’s almost not proper as the product to sell.
Because its natural defect on the volume of the game.
If you want to sell a TD to the gamer, you have to put “reasonable number of maps” in the game. But not like one way TD, maze TD’s maps can be really similar each other in the different meaning. Because for one way TD, developer can set only one path in one stage, but in the Maze TD there are so many possible ways to play in one stage. So to say numbers of map set itself, one way TD has really big advantage.
Sorry for so long prologue, but I just like to explain why I like this Dungeon Warfare this much.
This TD is ultimate-proper hybrid which is mix of those two types,
DW, it’s not fully maze type, but it is providing maximum level of the freedom for the player with the aspect below.
1.	There is no tower type limit for stages, except very beginning of the game.
2.	Always there are bypass to make a way.
There are many kinds of obstacles in the map tile set that player can use. it can help player to make a maze or can be irritating.
3.	But as a design of map, each map has its own character because of fascinating unique features that you would never find in another TD.
(You never miss the mine cart)
Not only the map design, but also there are many attractive in many aspects.
1.	You can set the difficulty very specifically. Normally TD has very simple difficulty level, but in DW, you can set many kind of abilities of enemy.
Especially what I love is the “weight of enemy”. This thing can affect hugely to the game.
This is a really good example that simple physics how could help make game fun. Bigger unit is slower, heavier ,and harder to throw into the air.
It’s really natural, but I couldn’t stop laughing when I saw this.
2.	There are many kinds of towers that you can get.
I played only 14 hours, and I’m really bad at gaming unfortunately, even I love so much.
So I couldn’t go that far. But already I have 9 types of towers, and each of them are very fresh. Especially Harpoon, Push, and the spring.
I will not mention the specific function of those here. Because if you see the towers in the game that I’ve mentioned, you would know what I mean “fresh”.
3.	User-friendly UI.
Except mini-map, which I want to complain about, There is all the needed user interface. Very comfortable to play, and very noticing.
4.	Volume of game.
I wonder why this game has the early-access tag. This game seems already finished to build, well defined, and has enough volume to play not like other early-access.
I heard there are 30 maps, and with the difficulty set up that I’ve mentioned, I think it can guarantee more than 30 hours of playing time.
But also there are a few things must be improved further.
1.	Music
I know this is indie game, and there are no many developers to serve on this minor issue, but still it will be really nice if this game has more music.
Although the main-theme is well made for an old gamer, but only one theme for almost 30 stages is still not satisfying.
I’m playing with my own music, so actually this is not a big issue, but..
2.	MINI MAP!!!!!
Please put a mini-map in the UI. It’s really hard to notice if only one enemy sneak out from my maze in the big map. This defect can be more noticeable when you play multi-entry stages.
Especially when you play one-life mode, this can be really critical.
So I reviewed this game with my humble word, but I’m pretty sure that I couldn’t express enough the wonderfulness of this game.
Go and get it, and it will give you the maximum fun for 10 bucks.

Dungeon Warfare is the game where you kill or you die.
To more accurately describe the game, Dungeon Warfare is a tower-defense game focusing on installing traps in pre-defined dungeons in order to kill waves of enemies. The game starts you out with access to only two basic traps: The floor-mounted spike trap, which periodically juts up deadly spikes to damage the enemies above it, and the the wall-mounted dart trap, a device that continuously fires darts at whatever direction it is pointed at. As you progress through more of the levels, more traps types become available. Want to push enemies into a bottomless abyss? The pusher trap's got you covered. Want to burn them? The flamer will take care of that. Want to summon demons to fight for you? You can do that too. Each trap type is unique and varied, with over 13 different types as of this writing and more on the way. The fact that you can only take a limited number of trap types with you into a level means that you will need to plan out your defenses ahead of time. Often I've found myself having to decide just how I was going to deal with that massive wave of peasants in wave 5, for example.
Speaking of enemies, the enemies that you are fighting are more "good" than most things usually found in dungeons. In Dungeon Warfare YOU are the big bad evil guy, defending your portal from the legions of good. From the humble peasant, slow and weak but deadly in large numbers; the rough and tough warriors, able to take a beating; the theives, quick enough to bypass most of your traps; the mighty knights, that push your damage skills to the test; to the haughty nobles, that have more gold than they know what to do with; with over 12 different enemy types, every enemy in Dungeon Warfare is unique and presents a different challenge to the player.
The game deals with progression well, allowing the player to learn how to deal with each new enemy type over the course of levels. The game utilizes an experience system to reward the player with bonus starting gold for all levels, as well as "gems". In this game, gems are the currency used to upgrade the trap mastery of each trap, with increasing cost per level. For example, raising your spike trap mastery to level 5 takes 10 gems, as 1 (Level 2) + 2 (Level 3) + 3 (Level 4) + 4 (Level 5). The effects of trap mastery are twofold. Immediately, each increase in level affects the stats of a particular aspect of each trap type: For spike traps, it is a percentage increase in damage, for dart traps, the cooldown time between shots is decreased by a percentage, etc. There is no need it be worried about spending your gems on the wrong upgrades; at any time between levels the player can reset their gems at no cost, allowing them to mix up their play style for the next level. The second effect is that for every 5 levels in a trap mastery the player gains, the player unlocks a new tier of upgrades for that trap. These are straight upgrades that the player can spend gold on during a level to upgrade a single trap, and the upgrades often cost less than it does to place a new trap, although sometimes more can be better; again, depends on the playing field of the level.
On the topic of levels, for that matter, the game boasts a count of 29 unique maps as of this writing, with more levels being added each week. Also, while not currently implemented, the game will include a level editor that will allow the player to make their own custom levels and share them through steam workshop. Level layout will determine your strategy, forcing you to adapt. Some levels have natural defenses in them, such as bottomless abysses, thin corridors, and minecarts running through the map; figuring out how to best use what you're given is up to you.
In Dungeon Warfare, your experience total is the sum of all of your best scores across all levels, meaning that it pays to go back and revisit a level to boost your score. What seperates this from most games is the Modifier system that the game uses. In each level, you can choose from nine different modifiers that make the game more (or less!) challenging. Each modifier changes different aspects of the game: The "Nil" modifier decreases the bounty you get from killing enemies by 10%, forcing you to be frugal; the "Anchor" modifier increases enemy health by 5%, and enemy weight by 100%, making shoving them into the abyss much harder; the "Breeze" modifier is for those that are having difficulty, increasing the spawn times between waves, lowering enemy speed and health, but also cutting your score by 40%. All the modifiers affect your final score with multipliers, and up to 8 modifiers can be stacked (with the exception of the breeze modifier) to provide a massive challenge that, should you emerge victorious, gives you a outrageous multipler of x5.23 for your final score for the level. Be warned, this challenge is not for the weak; you will need all the skills you can muster for this monster difficulty.
All in all, Dungeon Warfare is a promising Early Access game. With more content being continuously added, massive replayability value, and a creator that is vocal and very visible to the public, this is one game you don't want to miss. Now get out there, and wage some DUNGEON WARFARE!

I’m finally done with this game, and while it has some issues, I must tell this was one of my most enjoyable gaming experiences lately.
I highly recommend this game, but you should be warned about a couple of things. First of all, this is a very long visual novel styled game. If you don’t like the style, you won’t be able to bear with it, believe me. It also has an awful amount of stat rising that may be really unnerving at times. I tend to hate VNs with stat rising, but believe me or not, I liked it in this game, because it wasn’t all about stats, and the so called “inspirations” you gather are a pretty good idea – you’ll understand if you play. Though, I must admit I’ve played on easy mode, and I wouldn’t try any other – some of the stat checks were really tight even on easy (but well, I’m not very good with stat management).  I don’t really think you can have a really middle ground opinion about the game, to be honest – either you love it or you hate it.
What do I love about it? Well as I’ve said, the stat system is quite enjoyable to me. But more than everything, I love the story and the characters. The characters are cheesy and over-the-top, in a good way. I mean, you couldn’t expect a 18 years old girl to speak god knows how many languages, be able to repair vehicles, do magic tricks, use guns, fight thugs… This is impossible in the real life! But it seems so natural in the game. Besides, I really like her – she has that silly crazyness about her. And I like the other characters at least as much as her, if not more. Well, not everyone, of course, but the cast is quite lovable. I like the romance option characters, except maybe for Nigel who isn’t my kind of character. I went for Ahmose’s romance/ destiny in my playthrough – he’s really lovely and I must admit I have a thing for undead romance options, so yeah. But let’s not dwell on that.
I genuinely like some of the other characters Sadie can meet, like Rashad or that sly Zul.
Well now, in my opinion the game is all about the story, the characters, the romances… basically, the content. The “packaging” on the other hand may not be so pretty. What I mean is that the art is fine, but nothing more than that, except maybe for the maps for every region – these are actually really neat. The music isn’t exceptional either. Some tunes are pretty, some are annoying, some you don’t even notice. Overall,  the music would benefit from some polishing, and I would have enjoyed some more emotion filled tunes at some points of the story.
But overall, the game was so much fun and enjoyment I would recommend it to everyone, as long as they like VNs.
PS: it’s a shame the game doesn’t have a “story mode” without skill checks, so you could replay it fast in order to get other endings, but I see how it would be impossible to make since lots of things depend of the success or failure of the skill checks.

By far my favorite Survival game. It's impossible not to compare this to ARK, so I won't.
The leveling curve and play balance is much better. The start of the game isn't as relentlessly punishing, but it'll never get easy no matter how much you progress via levels and equipment. Anything can kill you if you aren't careful.
Thralls are great. Everything you feel is too slow or teedious can be improved with Thralls. Finding, capturing and breaking them is a lot of fun. Them having set spawn points is not. Once you've been through a camp and not found the thrall you want, there's no reason to go back.
Default XP gains are a bit too slow. Most servers I see run between 2 and 3x XP gains, which is still slow but feels much better. You won't spend days with a roof-less house that way. Enemy leash distance is also way too long and very uneven. Sometimes you get chased to eternity.
The building system is great, the ability to rotate or control elevation with the mouse wheel is very useful. There is a high number of building tiles too so good variety. It isn't perfect though. Placing slanted roofs properly is a pain. Doors won't place if stairs lead into them, etc... Nothing that can't be fixed though. There are a lot of cosmetic construction items that do nothing. It would be nice to get some sort of buff from being in a well decorated house, akin to the dancer buff.
It feels like there is much more to do in this game than most other Survival games too. On top of the usual building, grinding and PvP, you have bandit camps to raid, caves and ruins to explore. Even huge dungeons with bosses that require some serious preparation and team play.
While not the best game visually, it's still very pretty. Ultra runs great even on a modern but modest machine (reduce shadow quality though). The map design and the art direction is excellent. Some of those bandit camps and ruins are breathtaking.
Performance isn't steady though. I run my own server on a box I slapped together, and the game just halts for a few seconds when a backup is created. Loading certain map elements or large player constructions is also extremely slow. And the laggier your server is, the easier it is to beat enemies as they seem very slow to react, while on small, fast servers, combat becomes much more hectic and dangerous.
Balance wise, enemy respawns don't seem to be on a per-enemy basis but instead be at set interval, which can result in full repopulation minutes after a clear. Equipment wear is much too fast and equipment values are all over the place. The construction unlocks don't flow and will often leave you with annoying gaps or multi-level periods of saving points before the next thing of interest.
Overall this game is a solid 8/10. A lot of fun, excellent for those who enjoy Survival sandboxes, RPGs, dungeon diving or Conan in general. Hopefully the devs fix the few issues it has and put out a lot of content for it.

Pros:

Cons

I just spent a great $20! If you are a Tribal Fan...this game is for you. I started in T2...Tribes 2 V2 was my favorite, and still is, but this feels VERY close. Not many character models yet, and you can clearly tell the textures and stuff aren't completed yet, but the Physics and guns work amazingly accurate. The Jetpack is amazing, has a few mechanics to make it it's own, like all momentum being based on the direction you are facing, not just which direction you were going, your jetpack has more power and thrust if you AREN"T holding a direction to move...you are meant to reach desired altitude before going in directions, but as you are moving fast generally from the very well laid out map slopes and curves, it is very easy to launch forward without having to hold W once you jet off the ground. It does have several packs you can use like Energy pack, the Farming pack to constantly plant base turrets, shield pack, stealth pack...and each pack has 3 perks to choose from, so it's very cool. As for the CTF, which is all I've played so far, it feels far better than Tribes: Ascend, which seemed to not care much for anything other than someone grabbing a flag and reaching the base. You are far more dependant on Inventory stations again, far more dependant on that Generator to protect your base from Cappers and Rapers....the compitition is back, and I hope people fall in line soon, cause it shouldn't be missed! Sorry if you like point and click games such as Call of Duty where you only have to aim forwards and sometimes do a quick stab...Sorry Halo fans, but you still can't come close to keeping up with having to MA someone 20+ yards away with a PROJECTILE! Give it up any FPS that claims to have skill...git gud at Jetpacking, MA, Projectiles!

American Truck Simulator and Euro Truck Simulator 2 are the best trucking simulators. Even if you're not a fan of that kind of games, be sure to check them out, it's surprisingly addictive to deliver cargos across huge open worlds on fully customisable, highly detailed trucks. Both games are continuously supported by the developer and have many years ahead to grow and expand. Regular patches add new trucks, features, roads, and regular DLC's add new territories and customization items, so there's always a good reason to come back after awhile and explore something new. Both games share many similarities, such as interface, engine, physics, that's because, I believe, they will be somehow merged together one day to become a kind of World Truck Simulator. There's already an online feature called World Of Trucks, that allows players to complete online contracts and share different kinds of media. There were some rumors about Euro Coach Simulator as well, which should add a bus driving mechanics, but it's unclear how or when it's going to happen. Mods are available too. A lot of mods of any kind, that add even more trucks and territories, so you will never be bored of anything.

There should be a "maybe" option but yes, I do recommend although it could be greatly improved. The building system is great but not as great as Rust's system, which summarizes all of your building options into one single item. It's kinda annoying that you have to craft the parts first, then put it into your tools belt or whatever it's called and then start building. A single item like the Building Plan in Rust would be a much better option.
Also, PvE isn't hard: it's annoying or boring depending on the situation. At first levels mobs aren't really a threat. Then there are mobs such as spiders which are way too annoying, especially since shields aren't really useful. If a mob attacks you and you block its attack, right after you hear the sound of it hitting your shield you'd think "oh hey time to attack and then block it again". But nope, you'll receive damage even if its attack animation is ending. And if you wait for it to end so you can attack, the next attack animation begins right after it and there's not enough time for you to block it. So what you have to do to defeat those mobs is simply attack them over and over and never try to use your shield.
This is pretty lame for many reasons but mainly because:
a. Mobs have the same kind of attack and they'll do it over and over again instead of switching to a different attack or even trying to avoid you or something. Spiders, for example, will throw poison balls and cripple you and if there's a few of them away from you then you're screwed. They'll keep throwing it instead of trying to reach you or using some other attack. You'll be poisoned so you won't be able to sprint away from them or avoid their poison balls and you'll be dead soon;
b. Shields don't really work as explained above and not only that, they don't really last too long;
c. There are many glitches such as mobs teleporting right next to you, your character not being able to hit mobs due to terrain while they can hit you etc.
A good PvE system allows even low levels to defeat higher level mobs as long as you find a good strategy for it. It keeps PvE exciting since you don't need to reach a certain level to make sure you won't die simply because you'll have more HP and better armor.
Another thing I forgot: items in general break way too easy. I mean do I really have to believe that after a few swings on naked people my iron sword would break? And then it costs a fortune to repair it.
