I  first played this game  before it was released on steam. I still have  that copy. I enjoy it very much.  We follow Sadie, a daughter of famous archeologists, during her archology studies and the adventures she gets into.
It's adventurous, it is humorous, the setting is refreshing, it's sparkling and fun.  I have a great sense of adventure. It s a stat raising game. I LOVE stat raising games and this one  makes  stat raising really functional by having trials you need to overcome on a path of choice.  The game combines so many things, and you can choose "routes" to change Sadie's  "dream". I love that. It guarantees replayability, making the game fun each and every time.  My favourite paths for Sadie is Nigel because I really love the character and find him well matched and I trully enjoy the progress and the adventures Nofel and Sadie get into all the time.
In most otomes you chose a route. Here in this game that skillfully combnes elements known to me from  otome, visual novel, stat raising and adventure games, you can LITERALLY chose a route and then follow it thorugh in various locations Sadie travels to as part of her quests. Storywise, a lot of effort went into this because whle the game has an overarching story of Sadie, it branches out into so many paths you can have Sadie follow, it's really incredible for me. I love the sense of travel and adventure!
Also, the many endings you can achieve depending on the fullfilmment of the dream points and depending on difficulty levels make it really enegaging.
Sadie is a really nice main character, intelligent, spunky (if a little reckless sometimes?), kind, polite, educated, has a strong presence and I do care for her. I really enjoy travelling and adventuring with her.
The design is interesting, we chose adventures and activities from various maps and the maps are varied. when an adventure ends, it shows up as a newspaper heading. Those little touches make it so much more fun. Because this game has so many elements to it, I never feel bored and never have a sese of routine. It's exciting all the time for me.
This is such a thoroughly engaging and fun game for me. I have been told there is a sequel planned that will continue from the ending chosen by the player. I generally don't like sequels but I look forward to this one as I really like the characters, the setting, the great flow of the text, engaging stories and setting and stat raising. There is really a LOT packed into this game and it is a real keeper for me among the many games I ever purchased in my life.
I enjoy it when I can. I have had this game for a few years already  and I still haven't reached 100% completion. It's immersive, it's fun, humorous and adventurous and one of my best purchases ever, a game I really love for the sense of great fun and adventure and extremely rich content. It feels like a genuine labour of love and it is very fun to play.

TLDR:
ArcheAge has seen many improvements since launch and is a way better game. Play with friends, be social, and take
your time with the game. In-game has improved dramatically. Ignore the stigma and try the game.
FULL REVIEW:
My friends and I were beta players, buying the most expensive founder's packs, in full hype mode for the game. It was a blast during beta, but after release we all left feeling disappointed in what the game was starting to become. Now after a long break and many disappointing attempts of finding anything close to what AA offers, interms of freedom and PVP, we are happy to say ArcheAge is in a good place right now. A lot of balance changes to combat, gathering, crafting, and in-game store has made the game a joy to play again. Trading needs a bit of tweaking, but TRION is working on getting that balanced fairly soon with XLGAMES.
ArcheAge is the only MMORPG I have played in years that gives me such a satisfying feeling after playing. Nothing is just given to the player, everything must be earned. ArcheAge rewards dedication and people who play smart. Making friends and playing with others is essential to the ArcheAge experience. I've played both as a patron and F2P player and have not felt like I've been gated. This is mainly due to the fact I play with some friends and we're always sharing resources, whether it's labor, money or materials. This isn't a game meant to be played alone. Finding a guild or group of players you can share your endeavors with is key to your success but more importantly, your enjoyment of the game.
The cash shop has seen dramatic improvements since the days of release. Most things can be purchased with merit badges or loyalty. I feel the shop is now tailored to push people to sub rather than throw money at it. I understand that TRION and XLGAMES have a business to run first and foremost and F2P ( in every F2P MMO in my opinion) is more of a unlimited trial, encouraging players to ultimately sub. Which you should absolutely do if you enjoy the MMO you’re playing. It makes no sense to me that a person would spend dozens of hours playing for free and be so reluctant on spend money for a sub when they have the opportunity.
ArcheAge takes time to get into the flow of things and to understand the systems in place. No other MMO can hold a candle to the level of freedom ArcheAge gives players. Racing to endgame is not the way to play and will ruin your experience with ArcheAge. Rushing this game will leave you frustrated and jaded. I implore people to give ArcheAge a shot and take your time with it. Play with friends, meet new people, be social, and I’m sure you’ll have an amazing experience with all ArcheAge has to offer.

This review is based on the Single Player mode only (30+ Hours):
While Conan Exiles may seem to hard to play at first with a little bit of time it becomes a very rewarding experience. Of course the game is still in development so there are some things that need improvement and bugs that show up now and then, but with a good graphics card you can play the game with very little lag. I play the game on a PC that has 16G of Ram, a Intel Core i7, and a Evga Geforce GTX 960 graphics card. With that and the settings all turned up to ultra, the only lag that occurs is when I try sprinting from a stand still, otherwise the gameplay is great.
Pros:
Great Graphics
Great Sounds/Music
Fairly good character customization
A Good selection of craft-able items and structure building options
Great selection of enemies/aggressive creatures ranging from real (Rhino, Antelope..etc) to unreal (Dragons, Monsters, Giant Spiders...etc)
Lots to explore and secrets to uncover
Online servers give access to PVP and the ability to play with friends or random people
Cons:
No start up tutorial
Potential lag (especially if playing online)
No offline single player mode
You can't interact with the Map (such as there are no indicators, no ability to zoom in...etc)
Unneeded and frankly stupid Nude character options
Not much of a story/plot to the game (this will improve as more quests become available...etc)
No in-game help book (such a thing would explain things like the effects of corruption and info needed to harvest certain resources...to name a few)
Unneeded and stupid setup with recipes -
-(Instead of just unlocking recipes permanently by level, they add an additional unneeded amount of work by making you use points to unlock recipes, then have to reset the points (for free) when you want to unlock a different recipe, basically just wasting your time.)
Of course I am sure there are many other pros and cons that could be added to these lists, but the point for me is that the pros out weigh the cons. I know the game will continue to develop and It is my hope that it continues to get better. I would give Conan Exiles a 8/10 rating and would definitely recommend it to anyone, I believe it to be with the $30 I paid for it, especially if it continues to improve.

Want the ultimate jetpack joyride? Look no further than Midair, a rollicking combination of altitude and heavy artillery by developer Archtype Studios. The basic concept is capture the flag with the added element of flight, which allows the battles and maps to both be exponentially more interesting. But although each round is unique and exhilarating, I think Midair has a lot of unexplored potential that could make it even more fascinating.
One pre-existing aspect of the game that I really like is the weapon selection. I can personally feel a real difference in my performance based on weapon choice, so I always appreciate it when the various guns are noticeably unique and cater toward different people. I, for one, like rapid fire weapons with high damage, so I loved the machine gun. You also get plenty of exposure to and practice with the different firearms in the practice tutorials, which are quite long but very instructive and entertaining. The game also connects players across multiple network servers, so you can join parties with other online gamers in real time. You can even live chat your teammates and opponents during rounds, which improves communication and can even determine the winning team.
Midair clearly has enough going for it to be a very fun video game, but I believe there are ways it can expand and engage players even more. As I said previously, the tutorials were engaging; in fact, they were such a blast that I found myself wishing that some of the gameplay mimicked the training rounds. For instance, I got to jetpack up air chutes, shut down enemy turrets, and even slide down huge hills using the “ski” function of our equipment. I never (or rarely) got the chance to do any of these things during actual fights, so it would be great to see some of those elements integrated more. Also, in order to play in a real battle you must join a server with other gamers already on it, and that often limited you to playing with certain people and certain maps. Perhaps it was just because I was playing before Midair released to the general public, but there was a large number of empty servers that contained fascinating maps, and because no one else was playing on them, I was unable to explore those different settings. If an individual game mode was developed that was more missions objective based instead of group warfare, gamers could work on their movement and weapons skills on a more personal level and at a slower pace. Finally, the weapons selection is amazing, but it would be even better if there was more character selection and customization to go with it. Ideally, different characters would have unique capabilities and weaknesses, so players could find their ideal match.
All that being said, I still believe Midair has enough energy and variety to stand on its own as a great game, even if no further changes are made. Sometimes, all you want to do is play a simple round of capture the flag while hovering a few hundred feet above ground. My only suggestion is to develop the characters more and allow other modes of gameplay when network servers are empty or depleted, but the only direction Midair can go from here is up.

This game is really good one time through because it's very long and packs a lot of story content.
+ Excellent character interaction
+ Well written dialogue, great humor
+ Long play time with multiple interweaving stories. Overwhelming at times.
+ Music is nice and atmospheric.
+ Choices open up alternative paths, such as skipping skill checks.
+/- Art is ok. The sprites are ok. The ending CGs are kinda meh. It looks really flat overall.
- Text heavy. This game is meant to be played in breaks because there is too much information to digest. A lot of stuff flew over my head. I would have LOVED a term library- such as what Hakuoki uses, so that I could have had a better understanding of the archaeology terms and of the time period.
- The romance endings end with cliffhangers hinting at a sequel.
- No scroll back to see missed dialogue. Quick load is useless. It goes to the load menu instead of auto loading your quick save. The skip/quick save/quick load are inexplicably hidden at the bottom right corner in TINY MOLECULAR FONT.
- The menus are clunky. It was easier writing down dates in a notepad. There are no warnings about automatic events, unless you write down the specific dates.
- Stats are complex. There are too many stats and not enough time to pass events.
Here is a breakdown:
- Stats are valued at 100 = 10. To pass events, you need to pass a 10+ score. 5+ stress increases that number.
- You use +skill cards to make up the rest of your score.
Example: Checkpoint says 23 Occult Lore // 100 Occult Lore = 10 points // 1 card has +13 General and +7 Occult Lore = 20 Occult Lore // base score 10 + card score 20 = your score 30
- On Easy difficulty, the highest checkpoint (Turkey, Dream, and Main events) goes to 65+ (5-15 stress). On Hard difficulty (or a lot of stress) goes well over 100+
-
- The game lets you carry 10 cards initially. To increase your carry limit, you need to successfully pass Dream/Main Events. Passing them rewards you with great cards (20-90 general)
- There are time limited sections. You must constantly cycle through raising a stat, farming cards, passing events, passing hidden automatic checkpoints, lowering stress, and repeat to the next section.
- Skills are grouped under trees. The tree has a separate 100 value. A high tree score makes it faster to train the skills under that tree. You can only earn tree points passing
. It's NOT randomized, but there are NO complete guides so you literally need to make your own walkthrough to know what checkpoints give out what skills and tree points.
Example: Occult Lore is under Wits. // 100 Wits = +10 Occult Lore w/ stat raising // Spend 10 turns raising Occult Lore to 100
In conclusion, the game was too text heavy for my tastes on top of a difficult stats system that I couldn't really enjoy myself.
If you are a completionist, this game will leave you unfulfilled. Stats and achievements are still bugged, including some that effect which endings you get. There are no complete guides and with so many endings, you will not see all of them.

Midair easily takes the mantle of the best Tribes game without Tribes in the name. And with the death of Ascend it's the main hope for most Tribes fans. So what's it like? In a lot of ways it feels amped up from previous games. On the first day, skiing feels a lot harder than Ascend style movement as you really feel your momentum. By the second or third day, once you've gotten used to using the terrain to turn, and realize that directional jetting is in fact incredibly powerful, more powerful than any other Tribes title (Ascend, TV, T2, or T1) something clicks and you start hitting ridiculous speeds even as a beginner/intermediate. Although these high speeds often end in catastrophe, hitting a wall or somesuch. But you really can go ridiculously fast without being a top tier player.
Similarly, discs fly faster and because of that midairs start coming more regularly once you get the hang of the weapon. But of course if you're playing with good players, that means that you'll get absolutely thrashed if you fly in a straight line. That's where the more powerful directional jets come in--duels become a dance of dodging, energy management and terrain usage that tops any of the old games. I say that as someone who spend probably a thousand hours in arena and duel gametypes of T2, TV and TA. This is the single best Tribes game for the pure combat experience.
This review is written during early access closed beta. For those wondering if they should buy in now or wait for f2p release, I'd say it depends on what you're looking for. The part of the game that feels complete is skiing around, grabbing flags and killing people. Base play, in contrast--knocking down generators, putting up turrets, spawning vehicles, etc--doesn't feel there yet. A lot of it is there on paper, but they're only just starting to tackle balance issues like being able to deploy tons of turrets within close proximity of each other. You can still have fun games, but if you're someone who loves those aspects of the game, it might be worth waiting to see how those aspects get fleshed out. Otherwise, it's a great game as is. Duels are super fun and so is the process of relearning to ski. Fully recommended with the caveat that it depends on what part of the game you're looking to enjoy at the moment.

All of potential romance options are intriguing (but mummy for the win!) and likable. As for protagonist... Well. I like her, but she has pretty annoying moments and I can imagine that some people may not find this as charming and funny as I did.
Pros:
+ game length
+ many routes
+ many adventures
+ good writing
+ good graphic
+ interesting and deep characters
+ challenging...?
Cons:
- ... too challenging, I'm afraid, especially if you decide to play your first game on normal (or higher) difficulty. I can imagine that constant failures can scare some people off
- stat raising aspect - I personally like it, but I think it may be a little over complicated for most people and, to be honest, some stats didn't really seemed very useful
- some adventures seemed to be dragging too much, while other felt a little bit rushed.

Overgrowth is a sandbox fighting / plattforming game in which you have a wide range of melee weaponry besides hand-to-hand combat. You control a human-shaped rabbit and fight other rabbits, wolves and dogs in a variety of maps and levels.
Aside from the unusual setting, the game's strong points are its combat system, its fluid movement and the outstanding modding tools. Unlike other games of the genre, Overgrowth's fighting doesn't have a health system, but instead it calculates the damage to the model's skeleton and muscles in a realistic manner.  There's some parkour involved as well, which adds to the vertical gameplay and the combat itself.
On top of all that, there's always new content from both the developers who are actively working on the title and the wonderful modding community. Maps and new weapons / characters are always being made and, in-game, you're allowed to edit the levels adding weapons, enemies or even objects to make every playthrough new and more challenging (this IS a sandbox game, after all).
Many new features are yet to come, as the game is still in its Alpha state, although I can surely say that it has a bright future not too far away. Purchase this game if all the features mentioned previously seem appealing to you!

Hand of Fate is a solid mix of TCG, text-based RPG and good 'ol hack 'n slash. The game has strong replayability due to random card draw mechanics and lots of endgame content for the perfectionists. Side quests and multi-storylines are handled very well with the token system. Combat is less chance-based like traditional D&D or Pathfinder games and more skill-based as combat is handled in real time. The dealer's personality is endearing. The bosses and suits are varied enough to promote different combat approaches. The achievements worked well with the ability to customize one's deck before a game.
But not all designs are good designs. There are glaring annoyances that tend to stick out more the longer one plays the game.
Chance-based encounters that require three or four draws to accomplish, chance-based encounters that require you to FAIL half way through to get the token, and chance-based encounters that has a chance to change its outcome are major grief points of this game. The treasure chest card, for instance, requires three dice rolls (chance draws) and even if one succeeded in getting all the cards right, there's still a chance that it will spawn a mimic which inflicts direct damage to the player without triggering combat, no question asked. And then, there's the minotaur card that involves FOUR dice rolls after a GODDAMN BOSS FIGHT to clear it.
Combat encounters are not fool-proof either. Over the years, I have grown a passionate hatred towards games designed to lock away the player's skills at endgame. Hand of Fate's endgame involves fighting an overwhelming number of mobs (up to 20 at once) that renders coup de grace mechanics useless, in a cramped space that makes dodging nigh impossible, and each of these mobs either has long-range attack, or unblockable counters, or both. Let's not forget that they either have poison, shield block, damage counter aura, immunity to shield bash, or AOE unblockable mid-range attack (I'm looking at you, lava golems). In such encounters, one cannot dodge, cannot counter, cannot coup de grace, cannot shield bash, and cannot attack while these craps (shield, damage aura) are on. The point of having these mechanics is moot when the game deliberately forbids the player from using them later on.
The dire lack of crowd-control capability on the player's end really hurts at endgame. There are a grand total of FOUR crowd-control weapons in FORTY equipment cards one can use in any given match and only two of them (Thunderbolt and Flaming Mace) can inflict meaningful damage. I am going to recommend Hand of Fate but that recommendation does come with one big caveat.
Namely that the difficulty level in this game is all kinds of messed up.
If you go through the game on the normal difficulty then you will, unless you get very unlucky, easily breeze through every single "level" with a minimum of challenge. That is until you hit the final "Level" and suddenly hit a brick wall of challenge.
Since the way that each "Level" works is a set of "Floors" that are made out of encounter cards, when you step on a card you lose one food and that card is revealed. If it is a event you play it out and if it is a encounter you fight the enemies(The combat itself is a piece of♥♥♥♥♥♥. You move across the floors until you hit the Boss card, fight the boss and you have won.
The problem with this is twofold, the first is that you only really need to worry about Food, if you run out of food then you start losing health and when you have it you heal every time you move. So there is no real reason to worry about money unless you want to complete a certain event that needs money. Since there are plenty of encounter cards that give you gear. The second problem is that when you trigger the Boss card no matter what happens that level is over. If you die it is over and if you win it is over. So you can have a floor of maybe 20 cards and hit the boss on your third move since there is literally no way of knowing where they are. It is really annoying and becomes even worse on the last Level.
The game also has "Curses" that it puts on you as the game goes on, most of them are not really a problem, until the last level. Where you have a curse on you from the start that literally just takes money or food away from you every five steps. There is no way to avoid this and it is insanely expensive to get starter curses removed. So you are basically in a position where you are in a death march trying to reach the Boss before you are chipped to death by the game.
It would not be such a problem if the rest of the game up until then had been anywhere near as hard. Instead it really is a brick wall of difficulty.
I guess reading all that would make you wonder why the hell I would still recommend the game. Mostly the reason is because, in spite of the game getting ♥♥♥♥ed up at the end, it was a pretty fun game. The voice acting is solid and the presentation is great as well. Whilst the combat is nothing amazing it works well enough and the moment to moment gameplay is fun.
It's just a damn shame that they screwed up the ending so badly.

Good Robot is an alright game, but not much else.
The Soundtrack, aesthetic and occasional text you get in shops varies from alright to fantastic.

On the other hand the secondary shotgun weapon near the end of the game, kills missiles, does good DPS and it's knockback can be used as a pretty good makeshift dodge at times.
A note for the devs, if you ever make Good Robot 2 make the corridors much much bigger, give us essential upgrades from the beginning and make the game more instant response, bullet hell action where death is merely a minor annoyance instead of an unfair Dark Souls with limited lives.
In short, if you have time to kill and are more into the electric side of music perhaps you could have fun with this game if you're good at Dark Souls. You should probably wait for a discount though.

This game is not what I was expecting.
There is no saving, just like Tetris. If you die, you start from nothing.
It's a very simple game, just random level layout. The layout is not complex at all and each level is farily short (5 screens worth).
At the end of each level, you can choose to purchase a set of random upgrades or items. These upgrades go buy buy if you die. Again there is no saving.
You can purchase hats for your robot for each level, but they do nothing but change your appearance and the hats disappear after the level is complete. You can buy a hat at the begining of each level.
Throughout the level you can obtain, money, primary gun and secondary gun. Guns are replaced so you can only have 1 of each, and you can't choose from a list og gus you've collected because you can't collect them. Guns go buy buy if you die.
Upgrades incluse increase damage, rate of fire, shield capacity, etc. They are expensive and you can typically accumulate enought money to purchase 1 upgrade per level, but that is if you don't need to replenish your health. The store at the end of the level, where you purcahse the upgrades or items is random, so you don't always get to choose an upgrade or the option to replenish health/shields.
You can also get shield, which is just health. You'll need to get health throughout the level or purchase it at the end of the level in order to survive through the levels.
After a level is complete you can decide to go through 1 of 3 gates. The gate you choose decides what your next level challenge will by. They can be more money/items, more enemies, harder enemies, boss, and maybe others. The gates appear at random, so you don't get to decide which three gates appear.
Game mechanics are simple, just fly around and shot either enemy robots or wall mounts that produce enemy robots. The contoller version doesn't allow for finer motion of the gun, I'd recommend mouse and keyboard, you you get this.
I guess the biggest disappointment is the lack of any kind of saving or progress retention.

Divinity: Original Sin 2 is my 2017 game of the year. If you’re looking for a rich and compelling story with challenging turn-based combat and an RPG experience as rewarding and fun as some of the most popular RPGs out there then look no further than Divinity: Original Sin 2.
The story is really well written with many different ending outcomes depending on the choices you make and don't make. The world feels alive and there are many ways to complete quests with or without combat. As you progress you definitely feel the fear and oppression within the world with each NPC you meet having their own take on what is happening in the world and their own opinions of your character.
Character creation is in depth and allows for many possibilities. There are five races to chose from; Human, Elf, Lizard, Dwarf and Undead, with Undead allowing you to play an Undead version of any race. Each race is definitely unique in terms of look, racial passive abilities and how they are perceived and treated within the world. Depending on the race and gender you choose NPCs will react differently to you and new dialogue options open up. You can also choose specific background tags for your characters which open up even more dialogue choices.
There are wide range of base classes available but you aren’t locked into any specific class preset. You can customise your stats to create whatever class you want. Want to be a heavy armour wearing rogue? A robe wearing warrior who dual wields? A ranger who can also sling fire? The possibilities are seemingly endless.
You can choose to travel with up to three companions but there is nothing stopping you from going it alone. Each companion has their own backstory and motives and will often stop to ask you whether they can talk to an NPC before you as that particular NPC is important to their personal stories. Companions also have their own personalities and can react positively or negatively to actions you take, if they stop liking you enough then they can permanently leave your party. Each companion is voice acted really well and since playing with silent companions in Early Access the voice acting is really appreciated. As well as companions every NPC is voice acted with some performances being better than others but on the whole the voice acting is really well done. You can also chose to play as either one of the companions allowing you to experience their stories first hand.
The entire game can also be played with three other people cooperatively with each person being allowed to explore different areas at the same time, meaning that if one player gets into combat then the others won’t if they’re somewhere else. The game also features a Dungeons and Dragons esque Game Master mode allowing you to create your own campaigns using the game’s assets and DM for a party of players. Assets can be added, removed and edited on the fly and any campaigns you create can be shared with other players.
Overall Divinity: Original Sin 2 is definitely worth the asking price. There’s loads of replay value and many hours worth of compelling and meaningful story to experience. If you love story rich RPGs then you’ll love Divinity: Original Sin 2.

This game really feels like a free to play game stripped of all it's microtransactions. You might think that sounds like a good thing but what is left is a confused and horribly unbalanced game.
I spent my first 8 or 9 hours breezing through the game at a steady pace before hitting a brick wall of challenge which is insurmountable without resorting to endless grinding. Your towers come in the form of cards. You need to collect several of the same cards to upgrade them and progress however the only way of obtaining cards is by finding them at random or by purchasing them with in-game credits. You can't choose which ones you buy with your credits though, that is also left to chance. You'll soon run out of credits though and In a freemium game you would be able to purchase in-game credits to top up if you wanted, in this game however, the only way to earn credits is by grinding. Grinding can often be fun in a game, here it is so ineffective that it feels like an utterly pointless endeavour. You grind away hoping to be rewarded with the cards you need to upgrade and progress yet all the end of level rewards feel about 3 levels behind where you need them to be, meaning the cards you want, the cards you NEED, rarely come up. By the time you've fully upgraded a few towers the game ramps up the difficulty and they are rendered ineffective. You need to upgrade the new towers. Your magic abilities are absolutely useless, the fuse and evolution function is over complicated and there are frankly just too many towers with too many different enemies with the same levels rehashed over and over. It's a mess to be honest and the in-game currency, leveling up system along with the grinding nature of the gameplay and 'daily rewards' and 'special offer's' on items all scream freemium. Yet this isn't a freemium game, so it's all a bit redundant.
All in all then Prime World Defenders' as a game is basically thus: Want to obtain more towers? Grind. Want to unlock new abilities? Grind. Want to upgrade your towers so you can beat the level and progress? GRIND. Just don't expect grinding to get you anywhere.

Scheherazade at the Library of Pergamum is a gem of a game that works like a cross between a deck building and management game and a visual novel. You follow the heroine (let's call her Sadie), a New York scion and a junior year student of archaeology, in a series of adventures around the world that brings her in touch with a huge cast of characters. You spend game time between raising your many stats and collecting "inspiration" cards, which will help you move through the various capers that form the plot of the game. Sadie is part Indiana Jones and part manic pixie, and has both a deep passion for archaeology and a knack for attracting trouble. Sounds familiar? Though the story draws from every possible cliche (from the tragically lost parents to your typical temples of doom), it manages to come through as smart, humourous and engaging. The designers gave a lot of attention in capturing the mood of the period, both in the game's writing and its amazing soundtrack.
Note that despite its visual novel feel, the game is quite challenging. To resolve each caper, Sadie must pass through a number of checks that depend on her skill level and her card inventory. Difficulty rises very fast, and the player must plan ahead from day 1 (most plot lines advance even in failure, but some do not, and how successful you are impacts the game ending). To complicate the situation, the skill system is far from balanced (but far from broken, as well), and the game doesn't make a good job of explaining what you need to be doing. I personaly enjoying the difficult aspects of the game, but I can understand that strategizing and number-crunching may not appeal to everyone. The price may also be an issue; I got the game in a 50% discount, and I think it was totally worth the money,
So if you like visual novels, enjoy the grand adventure movies of old, and don't mind a little (or a lot of) challenge, this game is for you.

Scheherazade is one of the more involved otome games I've played in a while. In this one, you play as Sadie, an aspiring archaeologist, as she goes on adventures in various locations around the world. Like many similar games, you have a year to build-up certain skills in order to achieve the best ending on the route you choose. Unlike others, you also have a card based element to the game.
In order to successfully pass an adventure, you need to not only build-up your skills but also gather cards (or inspirations as they're called in the game) to play during the capers. This involves some strategic thinking, which I loved since in a lot of otome games the skills building can get a little monotonous when you're just spamming a certain trait.
I also love the time period (1931), supernatural elements, and that you don't have to chose a romance route in order to get a good ending. However, the romance options are wonderful. So far I've loved the ones I've played through. My only frustration is that it's near impossible to figure out how to get someones best ending.
All in all, this is a really great game.

This game is Indiana Jones, film noir, and comedic hijinks all in one. The last time I loved a game like this, I was playing a AAA title. 15 seconds in I was chuckling and didn't stop until 3 am when I made myself go to bed.
Pros:
-protagonist  is fun, capable, and witty
-lots of palatable history (if you like history) and myth (you probably like myth)
-refreshingly novel feel of 1930's, complete with 1930s slang (lots of moxie to go around)
-refreshingly novel best friendship that feels genuine, when best frindship between girls is often overlooked.
-supporting characters, from protagonist's best friend to one-time side character to the antagonists, feel like real people who have lives off-stage. I cannot say this enough: CHARACTERS ARE AMAZING.
-the "map" interfaces for the different locations are beautiful, and really help immersion
-the adventures around the world really do capture the essence and culture of their locations
-high replayability (because there's no way you're going to get to do all the adventures in a location in one playthrough)
-love interests are actually interesting--and entirely optional! A satisfying ending is achieved no matter what.
-romances are not half as cheesy as they could have been, especially for the medium
-witty exchanges everywhere (but does not interfere with serious scenes). Unless slapstick is your thing, you will be very amused.
Cons:
-art is not the best, but passable and overshadowed by other good stuff
-New York music is repetative, but you get a break when going abroad
-story is a bit convoluted, and
-lots of text, but usually enjoyable to read--at least in the first playthrough
-the skillchecks are difficult, and take a lot of getting used to to find a good strategy, but not impossible, and still usually fun. (I recommend writing down what checks come up on an adventure beforehand)
If you don't like history, you won't like this game, but you don't need to know history to have a good time. I am desperately hoping for a sequel.

Although I do not recommend Midair in Early Access at this time (early Sept '17) I hope this can be seen as a constructive commentary on the game thus far. There are some strong positives and some concerning but fixable negatives. For the time being I have got a refund on the Early Access, but I'll be checking back to see if things have improved.
It's clear a lot of work has gone into Midair, formerly Project Z, and that there is also a lot left to do. At this stage it feels like a proof of concept of a Tribeslike game. It certainly has issues but there is also a lot to like.
Having played Starsiege Tribes, Tribes 2, Tribes Vengeance, Tribes Ascend (and Legions) I know that what is and what isn't Tribes has always been divisive and there opinions aplenty. I managed to enjoy all those games even if T1 & T2 still feel superior, Ascend's Weapon unlocks were the obvious low point of the saga.
The problems I see with Midair right now are not ones that cannot be solved. Heres a list of the issues as I see them.
- Movement does not feel right. Skiing and jetpacks are present but feel off. Perhaps because the Jump isn't integrated into Jetting perhaps? A separate unjetted jump should exist, but I think had jump also scripted into jet in T1 & T2 (almost 20 years, my memory is hazy). Lateral movement in the air feels slightly superior though, so that's a small plus. Ground movement when not jetting or skiing feels a little slow. As such the player controls felt a little awkward.
- The UI is firmly in placeholder territory. It's just nasty. I do not believe the current elements can be tuned to improve them. For example, modding your loadouts does not need to fill the screen. Instead players should have an onscreen display that allows them to keep situational awareness of the game world.
- The HUD isn't great either, but is more functional than the rest of the UI.
- Player avatars profoundly disappointing. I was pleasantly surprised by the art style of the game buildings and vehicles, which I liked even though I wasn't sure at first, but I really do not like the player models. This may be a question of taste. It's possible to match the colourful style without making the players look a doofus generic cartoon character. Helmets at a bare minimum would improve matters, as would the traditional 5: Light female, Light Male, Medium Female, Medium Male and Generic Heavy (which both genders use).
- Armour weights tied to a gender and race is jarring. I think this might also be a problem tied into the current player avatar design. I honestly don't care what gender or race I play as, but swapping between Light, Medium and Heavy armours I would like to have the same voice and gender. And yeah, I know all cappers will be female Lights because size. 1998: pick your voice, gender & appearance, 2017: get what you're given.

Well that's a lot of grumbling. So what did I like about the game...
++ Despite my issues with the avatars, I like the look of the game world a lot. It's a simplistic art style that works well. With the speed necessary for a Tribeslike game, being able to resolve opponents and teammates in a fraction of a second is key. I think this is the Midair team's best decision (aside from making a Tribeslike game, of course!).
+ Similarly the vehicles and base assets are also great. You should have no difficulty recognising what vehicle you're up against, even at long distance.
++ From what I saw, most (probably all) of the weapons I remember are present. What I tested felt like they needed tuning. Not a huge issue and one that will evolve over time. Mostly damage values, area of effect sizes, rate of fire... all that sort of thing.
+ So too are at least some of the equipment modifiers.
+ The map design, while occasionally and unapologetically designed around skiing, looked pretty good. I will be interested to see how the Midair team reinterpret some of the classic maps but also what new designs they come up with.
++ It's the most Tribeslike game I've seen since T1 & T2.
So in the end. Is it Tribes? No, not yet but it's so very, very close. I do want it to suceed, but I reserve recommending it unless you personally have the time to dedicate testing an unfinished but promising game.

Hand of Fate is a game with charm and mystery where you unlock cards with unique stories and the Dealer narrates the whole thing and he sometimes relishes in your misery although his game is quite fair for the most part.
Story wise the game varies quite a bit in terms of quality, there is storylines that are quite entertaining and have various layers of depth, specially the ones that you unlock by the end of the game and you will most likely only finish long after finishing the main story, and then there is others that are not much more than get x of this or pass a test x amount of times to get some minor item and sometimes a cool new quest.
The game is divided in 2 main parts: the game board and the combat sections. The game board is the best part of the game by far and it is where you will spend most of your time by building your deck in story mode with cards you unlock, making choices in the various events and storylines chosing what risks to take and playing the shuffling card minigame.
All that is great however the combat is a very simplistic arkham combat style however as you unlcok more cards you will get gear with special abilities that change how the combat feels however there is curses that degrade your experience so that is mixed bag opinion, definatly the weakest point in the game.
Hand of fate is a good game that is dragged down by an average combat system and some bad design decisions in the later sections where they sacrificed gameplay for story which in part gives the best storylines in the game but they are hidden behind some fairly mundane events that are extremely dificult and sometimes just annoying to complete, which makes them be completely missed by alot of players outside of completionists which is a bit sad.
Anyway even if you dont feel like completing in which you will definatly miss some cool stuff you will still find a fair bit of enjoyment. Also the dlc is something that you dont necessarily need to buy unless you want to 100% the game in terms of achievements since the storylines that come with that are pretty mediocre and the stuff you unlock from that is fairly average.

I am one of the many (or not so many? Dunno...) that owns this game since the Bedrock Beta so I can tell you pretty well some negative and positive things about this game, but mostly negative....
First and foremost I must admit that the guys at Subterrenean Games are working hard and passionate, however there are - as mentioned before - some very negative things that destroy the enjoyability of this game for me and will probably also for you...
The Beta was actually an entire mess, there was almost nothing that actually really worked it even crashed regularly and gameplay lagged as hell...
So that what was actually called a "beta" was actually a public alpha version, but this wouldnt be a major problem if Subterrenean wouldnt have rushed the game out.
The game has been hastly released with alot of bugs from the "beta", apart of the lack of optimization for systems other than the developers.  The next disappointment was that who purchased the underlord edition didnt got everything as advertised. The soundtrack for example was missing and there was also no advertised guide. The soundtrack was added later (you buy something but you dont get the product you paid for...), dunno about the guide and I also dont care anymore...
It took approximately 2 major updates (1.1 and 1.2) and several minor patches before, so that the game could be called "somehow" - and only somehow - a working game.
Well, at release of the game (version 1.0) I've first started playing the single player campaign of WFTO, however I gave up on playing the SP campaign because the campaign wasnt very balanced apart of the bugged necromancer mission (I think that was level 8...).
With 1.3 I was thinking about to give the SP campaign a new try, but before I wanted to play-test some skirmish matches against the AI because the long-awaited map-editor was also released with 1.3. That was a good chance to try both things...
After creating my own map and playing it I've noticed a bugged minion and worker AI and a major slowdown of the FPS. I was really hoping with patch 1.3 that such performance and AI flaws would have disappeared but they didnt. Since the Bedrock Beta there were performance and AI problems. Of course they appeared less with every major update but the latest problems in 1.3 are enough for me, my patience is literally exhausted - especially if you go through this since the Bedrock Beta, sorry Subterranean but I'm fed up from this...
Pros:
+ Richard Ridings as narrator
+ Gameplay is almost the same as in DK1/2, although a bit faster than in the predecessors
+ Sounds effects and sound atmosphere are very well done
+ The AI is very efficient (but also see Cons)
+ Different salutations by the narrator (Richard Ridings) at game startup, depending on the real computer clock
+ Beasts are well chosen and animated
+ (Patch 1.3): Map editor with mirroring function
Cons:
- Minion leveling isnt well balanced, there is also no visual difference between a lvl 1 minion and a lvl 10 minion except the number stating the minion level... a level 10 minion could really need some anabolica that should lead into a visual difference...
- The skirmish AI is very efficient but NOT very smart, the skirmish AI is good in going on your nerves but if you counter the skirmish AI it doesnt really know how to handle this situation.
- The skirmish AI doesnt use nor place any defenses (doors/traps)
- The skirmish AI doesnt use/activates artifacts
- I disagree on certain regular minions in regards of their look (chunder f.e. rather looks like a ugly thin toy and not big fat bad♥♥♥♥♥like a bile demon) but this "look" topic is a matter of taste...
- There is almost always somewhere an AI bug destroying the enjoyability of this game and which also often leads into performance issues, although the campaign might be unaffected by this because the campaign is rather more scripted than based upon the skirmish AI...
Let's sum it up
Bedrock Beta = Paid Alpha which was also known as Steam Early Access
WFTO 1.0 - 1.x = Paid - almost have it working stable but still being a - Beta
WFTO 1.x - ? = Final stable release... (ETA?)
All what I wrote sounds very negative but if you are a passionate DK 1 and/or DK 2 player and you still dont own WFTO you should get it in a sale. People that are interested in this game but never played a dungeon game like Dungeon Keeper before should wait maybe for the next 2-3 major updates. I will however start up the game again when the next major patch (1.4 maybe?) will arrive but until then I dont have the desire to start playing it again...

Review date 2016/01/03, version 1.3, Win OS, only 36 hours under the belt. DK fanboy. 7/10 if they fix the stuttering.
It really does feel like you're playing Dungeon Keeper. It has a somewhat more serious tone than the originals, whether or not that's a good thing will be personal preference.They're apparently already working on patch 1.4. There are few issues  as far as I can see that would negatively affect the gameplay - the only one really that got under my skin was the stuttering on the larger maps. Decent graphics & music creates a nice atmosphere. The game is more fast paced than DK2 - I'd recommend setting the game speed to about 60-70%
My single player experience : The first half has a distinct DK1 feel to it, while later on with the bigger maps it plays more like DK2.  The campaign was a little short for my liking but I would happily buy an expansion to extend that playtime. Some levels are pretty challenging while others are too easy.
Minions : A lot of people didn't like that you had so many "human" minions in DK2 and I feel they have a nice balance here. When you upgrade your beast lair and build a fighting pit, you get 4 different types plus beastmasters who whip them all the way to the pit so they fight each other for xp, the beastmaster also gets xp from this. You have 2 rally flags, one for beasts and one for all your minions so you can use your beasts to ward of small groups without interrupting your minions. Beasts don't collect wages, just the beast master.
Undead : Personally I like the way they handled it. Vampires are created by making 3 sacrifices and having a ritual charged. They eat live prisoners. Corpses from the battlefield, torture chamber & prison (after a vampire feeds or they they lie there too long because the prison is full) are taken to the crypt where your necromancers raise them as ghouls (skeletons) who then permanently follow the necro that raised them. Prisoners eat the rats and will not die in your prison.
Potions : A new feature where at the cost of some gold you create potions to be used similar to spells. Build an alchemy lab to attract crackpots who will brew them for you.
Another absolutely great new feature is the ability to create dirt blocks. In DK2 I'd often lose an hour of play because some dwarf decided to tunnel into my dungeon and I would restart the level. How I wish this was a feature in DK2.

What do you get when you mix a CCG, ARPG, and a frustrating helping of three-card Monte?
Normally it would be a mess, but in this case it somehow ended up being Hand of Fate and it's not too bad.  If it weren’t for a fairly broad spectrum of small to mid-level annoyances in design, I’d have to brand it a landmark game in the realm of indies.
It’s actually pretty surprising how straightforward Hand of Fate is when you get in to it.  It is very easy to avoid any of the more complex deck building processes if you want, and jump in to the game.  You start out with a dealer explaining how these cards are a game and you’re playing it with your life and all that standard RPG buildup.  What actually happens is that you have a deck of cards that represent all of the potential gear that you can get and all of the potential encounters you can come across.  All of your encounters are shuffled together with the dealer’s additions (like shops and other more nefarious options) and laid out across the board as a path for your avatar to step across.  Every step consumes food, which heals you, and running out of food causes you to lose health that persists between each encounter.  When an encounter calls for a reward of equipment, it is pulled from your shuffled deck of equipment and can have things like armor, weapons, and artefacts (limited use spells) which you then throw on your character.  Likewise, whenever an encounter hits you with food, gold, curses, blessings, or even combat, those options are again pulled randomly, but this time from a dealer-chosen deck.    Some of the encounters involve choices the player makes, and can also require payment of your resources like food, gold or equipment.  Others may have you picking “success” and “failure” cards shuffled three-card Monte style for an outcome.  Many encounters combine these elements and often end up with you in combat, but that’s where everything changes.
In combat, you experience one of the weaker portions of the game.  It isn’t necessarily bad, but it does share its design with the long line of games mimicking Arkham Asylum where the player essentially smashes the “attack” button while waiting for a green prompt to counter attack and a red one to get out of the way.  What makes this less-than-stellar isn’t necessarily the concept, but the execution.  The attack animations are limited and aside from triggering special weapon effects and artefacts, little else is required in combat other than timing things properly.  Aside from that, hitboxes and visibility are two areas that could have used a lot more attention before release and fights vary greatly from painfully easy to seemingly very unfair.  It looks, feels, and plays like an afterthought, but the game ends up relying heavily on it to keep the pacing up, so it ends up detracting from what is, as a whole, a good design.
Hand of Fate started strong, and I think there are many tasty meaty bits in the way that the stories play out through the cards.  There’s some strong writing throughout and it’s the interactions with the encounter cards and the subsequent unlocks they create are well thought out.  However there are several little problems (aside from my combat gripes) that made the latter portions of the game range from annoying to infuriating.   The first thing that I noticed getting me fired up was how much things started feeling like they were beholden to a random number generator.  The shuffling of success and failure cards gets far too fast to have any chance to follow, so that turns into a pure guessing game.  That carries over into some encounters that halt all progress in their quest chain until you can somehow manage to luck your way into a card pick in your one chance to do so during each run.  The second thing that plagued the end of the game was the massive ramp up in difficulty.  I went through the vast majority of the levels without dying, but in the final few, I started being screwed over by combinations of limited resources, excessively bad curses, RNG not going my way, and of course having to use a clunky combat system against much tougher enemies.  The final boss fight, not to spoil things, has you fighting a large number of very tough enemies consecutively, which is not like any previous portion of the game.  In every other encounter, you fight the people on screen and then end and move on.  The final fight has you fighting four whole waves without the benefit of healing in between.  I generally don’t have an issue with games, in general, being difficult, but I do find it very frustrating when difficult spikes where it really doesn’t need to.  I had to lower the difficulty level of the game to beat the final boss and I did it with literally one health point remaining.  In addition, in finally accomplishing that, it didn’t count as far as the achievements are concerned - so somehow I have to fight all of the luck-based elements of that final level *and* beat the final boss for the game to really “count” it.
Even with all of that, I think the game wants you to focus more on the card encounters rather than the idea of getting to the end boss or overarching “story”.  The vast majority of the writing exists within those chained quests between cards and that disparity is equally represented in the achievements.  Only one of the 53 achievements has anything to do with beating the final boss.  The “Endless Mode” option that sits below the “Story Mode” seems like the place to go to get the best experience out of the game and wash the taste of that nasty boss fight out of your mouth.  It’s probably most telling that the achievement for that end boss fight has only been completed by 4.9% of the owners of the game.
There were moments as I lost to that end boss maybe the eighth or ninth time that I considered maybe not recommending this game.  It was a very trying time and not one I enjoyed in the least, but I really don’t think it’s fair to judge a game by such a small section.  There were many enjoyable portions throughout my time playing and, if nothing else, I at least *saw* the ending – which is a very short and simple piece.  What matters though is that the game is worth playing, especially now that it’s regularly on sale for a really affordable price.  I think relegating yourself to an easy mode toward the end is probably fine – though I question the idea of stripping away the achievement for it when it has no text implying that the difficulty must be higher.  It’s just clear to me that a standout indie title like this could have been so much more with just a little bit of care put in to resolving all of these relatively small issues that crippled the end of the game.

It didn't take me long to realize that I would like the genre of sandbox / survival games since they are based around probably the one thing I like to do most in any MMO and that is crafting.  In Conan Exiles, and other such games, that is pretty much point and purpose of the game.  Sure, there is some underlying story line, but really from the moment you get into the game, the big focus is on building (gathering up resources and crafting) up from nothing so you can take on the additional challenges any story.  Conan Exiles does perform in that area, as it has a list of things to make such as weapons, armor, and the building blocks for whatever you want to call shelter, be it a small hovel, or a massive castle.  Also, there are a few Tiers of items, stronger, more damaging, or just cooler looking in the case of stuff you put into your home.  Of course, there is a need for this as there are several things that would love for you to be there next meal, or just don't want you around outright, and saying get off my lawn just doesn't seem to be enough for them.
Personally, I'm having fun in the game.  I playing it with my son, who’s 19 so the fact that there is nudity and proper physics for certain body parts, is more of a joke then a source of embarrassment. There are two things to understand about my idea of the fun I’m having in this game.  One is that I realize that I'm playing an Early Access Game that came out a few weeks before I wrote this.  Which means there are bugs, lots of them, and I'm not talking about the type you can smash with a hammer, or poke with a sword.  I've gotten stuck in the ceiling of my house when respawning, seen rocks and grass just floating in the air, and been stopped by what I can only imagine is invisible terrain.  The good news is day by day these things are being found, looked at and fixed as players are reporting them.  Somethings are easier to fix then others, which as the patches come in people seem to wonder why problem y got fixed before x, but to me it seems to be nothing more than the development process and how things work in teams.  Patching for some people is an issue, as though out the week, there seems to be a patch every day.  To me, that is something to be expected in an early access game.  We are somewhere between alpha and beta in this experience, I don’t mind the constant flow of patches, as you read though the comments others do, everybody is different, but keep that in mind.
The other thing, as I said, I’m playing this co-op, with my son, and not joining one of the public servers.  Because of this I’m having a different experience the some of the other people that have given reviews.  In my opinion it’s a better experience as there will always be people who are trying to exploit even released games, and during early access, just like there are many outright bugs, there are plenty of exploits.  The good news is, since they are being found out by some people’s bad behavior, the devs can look for ways to fix what is happening while still maintaining the concepts of the game.  I’ve also taken things one set further, and set up a private server for my son and I to use.  This helped alleviate another issue that was fixed in another game that used the same game development engine.  When you play just a normal Co-Op game, there is a tether of sorts to the person that setup and brought everybody into the game.  Because of this, when that person gets too far away from you, your character gets pulled towards them.  Annoying, yes, but again, early access.
There will come a time when things should be working quite will with very few bugs.  But looking at the number of things they still want to add to the game, we’re still far away from that time.  Because of that, if you’re not the type that wants to deal with an unpolished game, you probably want to stay away from this one for now.  Yes, there is plenty about this game that works, but the number of active bugs and exploits will probably irk you to no end.  Otherwise, if you can handle the bumpy ride, watching things be added, fixed, removed, re-added, and otherwise tuned, come on in, just mind the crocodiles and the ostriches.  Partially the ostriches, the crocs will kill you exactly like you think they will do, nobody expects to die to a ostrich…..

This game is very much a work in progress, uncompleted title. Early Access in this case really means it, the game's pretty rough around the edges and still has a long way to go.

That said, it's worth keeping an eye on and it's already pretty fun to play. If you don't mind paying to get in now during development it's absolutely worth it; if you don't want to deal with bugs, unfinished or unbalanced content, or other issues then absolutely wait a bit before jumping in.

Pros:

It's beautiful.
Building and working with the world is intuitive and easy. Dealing with the rigors it presents, not as much; it's brutal, often extremely difficult. I got frustrated at first by dying repeatedly, until I realized that I was enjoying solving the problems that led to that demise and was actually able to work toward real goals that I defined for myself.
The music is either very simlar to Funcom's Conan MMO's music, or is the same music. Either way, it's terrific. Sound in general is pretty well done, and audio cues are well executed.

It runs very well once it's up and going, aside from some minor hitching every now and then, and it's stable; I haven't had a single crash.

The world is large, with plenty of secrets to discover and explore. The building tools allow you to work pretty easily within the guidelines of the world to integrate what you want to build into the landscape.

Cons:

Load times are abysmal right now. It takes my system ~4 minutes to load my current game.

Combat needs some work, as to enemy animations. Player characters look and move very well, but enemy human NPC's have animations that don't fire and they respond oddly. Animals are generally better, though,  and most work just fine.
Weapons are balanced strangely. The Pike I can make at level 15 is better than the spear I can make at level 28, for example. The sword I can make around 15 is just as good as the cutlass I can't make until 10-12 levels later. A lot of skill points seem to need to be dedicated to build a functional base, and some building materials take a staggering amount of time and resources to use. All of this will be addressed later, I'm certain, but for time of this review it's a big enough issue to be  aware of.

Combat is about on-par with Skyrim's whack a mole melee. I expected better, and I think there's something in the works, but for now it's functional but lackluster. Archery is very disappointing in particular, being awkward to use as well as expensive resource-wise.
Some bugs, but not as bad as I expected. My current game has a massive tree that I started building around, but then the tree disappeared after a few hours of playing; it randomly reappears if I leave and come back, but when it's gone the game actually lets me build and do things where the tree would be. That's bad when it reappears, and that ground is suddenly inaccessible again.
Building is generally pretty good, if resource-heavy and slow, but the inability to move things you've built needs to be changed. Also, if you accidentally demolish the wrong support piece anything on it is trashed with it; if that includes a crafting station or box with resources on it, that's all lost. It works pretty well as-is, but definitely needs work to be more user friendly and is somewhat lacking in options to allow for more versatile structures at the moment.

Closing thoughts:

I play singleplayer, and have raised the XP rate to give a more natural progression curve without the need for excessive grinding. I also lowered the spoil rate a bit, although food isn't terribly scarce, and very slightly bumped the respawn rate for resources. This sort of versatility and customizability means I get a game I'm comfortable with, at the rate I play, with minimal hassle. I can make a more hardcore, slower game, or a more casual builder out of it, and it's all up to me.
I haven't played ARK or Rust, since those get constant comparisons here, and this is the first game of the genre I've really delved into. It's fun, albeit with high and low points, but I'm never without something to do or without something I want to be doing. For a game as early in development as this seems to be, and with so much coming to it in the future, I'm pretty excited about where it's going. It's already good as it is, if rough, and there's a lot to look forward to.
Recommended, but know what you're getting into first and wait if you're not comfortable with the game in its current state.

How I wish I loved this with no misgivings. In theory, it's got it all: Prohibition! Travel! Archeology! Intrigue! Romance with a mummy!
In practice: overly complicated interface! Unbalanced stats system! Info dumpy dialogue that lasts so long I could go make a sandwich! And a heroine, Sadie, who is inexplicably both a Girl Genius and Too Stupid To Live.
Don't get me wrong: 1931S:TLoP has merits, and it's commendably ambitious, which is why I'm not giving it a bad rating, but a lot of things drag it down.
The UI issues alone make it exhausting to play, and eat up a lot of time. Like other stat-raisers, 1931S:TLoP has menus for the MC's traits/skills, jobs/tasks to raise them or get other perks, etc., but the UI design is far from intuitive. It's very pretty, but lacking the functionality that keeps the mechanic from being boring.
Let's say you want to raise one of Sadie's skills. From the map screen, you navigate to the skills menu. Instead of an at-a-glance list, there are buttons for each skill category. You must then hover over each, look at the sub-skills that pop up beneath, and if the one you want isn't there,  move on to the next. There are dozens of sub-skills, too, so unless you've got a photographic memory, good luck remembering which one belongs to where.
(On a technical note, sometimes when you hover over a skill category and then try to click a sub-skill, the list disappears, so you have to go right back and try again. Arg.)
When you finally find the stat you want, you click it, then wait for a list of tasks to pop up in a sidebar. It should be as easy as clicking what you want to do, right? Nope! Clicking the task drags you back to the main screen, where instead of doing it, you're faced with all the tasks that take place in the same area of the map. This then requires you to skim over the descriptions of the jobs that are available to find the one you need, click it, then wait for a bubble to pop up to let you know it's done.
So, to sum up, it's open skill screen>hover over one of several categories>select one of 5-6 sub-skills>select task>open task screen>find task in group of 1-8 tasks>select task>complete task>repeat.
Then you have to do this all over again. And again. And again. Three of these tasks in an in-game day, often. In another game, you'd learn the available jobs, the stats they raise and their locations pretty quickly, thus cutting down on some of this time suck, but your character regularly ends up on a new map with new tasks that are grouped differently and raise different sets of sub-skills, so you have to learn them all over again only for that information to become useless the next time the MC travels.
Sound tedious? It is. This problem could be remedied by a simpler menu designed for function instead of form, but as is, it's a mess, and I'm sure I spent more time going between menus than actually advancing story. At first it's not so bad, but a full day of tasks that takes about five seconds in a game with a better interface takes about thirty in this one. That adds up fast.
The unbalanced stat system is also a pain. You train a skill as high as it can go and still need to use "Inspirations" (skill point boosting items) to complete adventures, but you can only carry so many Inspirations at a time, and each one is only useful for a few skills. I guess this is fine if you're planning on a specific strategy, and playing through a single storyline, but if you want to keep your options open and explore--as one might in their first few playthroughs--it's limiting.
It also suggests, to me at least, an incredibly broken system. Even if you max out a skill, it only goes as high as 10 points, yet some of the challenges require scores of more than 100, and the boosts carry between 1-10 points. So, if you come up against a 100 point challenge, best case scenario, you'll STILL need at LEAST 9 Inspirations to complete it. Adding insult to injury, you only have space for a limited number of boosts and those have to be acquired through the same slow system as skill points.
This is bad enough, but many storylines don't have a break between skill checks, so even if you horde enough Inspirations for a high score in Grace, if the next skill check requires an equally high score in Riding, you're screwed.
It's ridiculous. You don't pay someone a penny, tell them that's all they're allowed to earn and then demand they give you a dollar. Like...??? Why would you do that?
The less technical aspects of the game also suffer from some problems. The writing isn't bad, but it can get dull.
As you'd expect in a VN about archeology, there's a lot of history/myth relayed through dialogue, but it goes on forever and grinds things to a halt. (Not good, considering the menu/stats issues already make the game feel slow.) It seems like characters spend more time reciting textbooks than being characters, and my eyes glazed over more than once even though I'm interested in history and myth.
In contrast, the relationships you can pursue are refreshingly breezy. They're a bright spot in the game and make it all worth while.
Finally, we come to the main problem with the writing: Sadie. I want to like her. I do. But: when she's not being unrealistically competent, she's holding the idiot ball.
Running into danger that ought to get her killed despite other characters' reasonable caution, she stumbles from disaster to disaster wide eyed and stupid, yet survives without a scratch. It's bewildering, and makes me long for the sense of danger in other games of this genre where doing boneheaded♥♥♥♥♥♥WILL get you killed.
She's the hero, I get it. Heroes are lucky, and do "brave" things that are also dopey but live to push the plot. Still, even Captain Kirk has a transporter accident or ten, and when Harry Potter does something dumb, it has consequences. That's not the case here, and it's disappointing. Sadie is Teflon; nothing negative sticks to her, even when it logically should, or when it would make a more compelling story. Even things like failing challenges and maxing out your stress score have NO impact on anything at all.
(It's also annoying that she'll give other people a hard time for doing the same stupid things she does but nobody calls her on that hypocrisy.)
I should also mention the lack of same sex and love interests of color, which bothers me. (Ahmose technically counts as a PoC, I suppose, but he's bandaged head-to-toe so it feels like a bit of a cheat, really.)
Additionally, there's some unfortunate implications in that, despite traveling to places like Egypt, New Orleans, Peru and Turkey, where white people should be outnumbered, they're still the central focus and the non-white folks who show up are either thugs and thieves who try to kill you or bit characters who get one line, with rare exception. This is a highly problematic oversight, to say the very least. I'm sure it was unintentional, but still, the dearth of fleshed out, non-villainous PoC makes me uncomfortable.
***SPOILERS***
Adding to my discomfort is the story's climax in which Sadie has the opportunity to use a magical relic to potentially keep the Nazis from truly coming to power in Germany but instead goes, “LOL no *destroys artifact*” because reasons. There's a very thin rationalization for this but, uh...perhaps not the best plot point to use, there. It's pretty difficult to enjoy the game knowing that the narrative unintentionally makes Sadie—and you, as you can't do anything to keep her from this action—complicit in not stopping the rise of Nazi Germany.
***END SPOILERS***
Aside from these things, it's not a bad game, just has a lot of little finicky issues. I'm hopeful that the sequel will be more intuitively designed/streamlined, which will definitely make for a more enjoyable experience. I'm sure that even if the sequel's dialogue remains as overstuffed as 1931's,  it'd feel like less of a slog with a better interface.

Very fun visual novel with more freedom and options than are standard for the genre and tons of replayability.
In Scheherazade, you play as a brilliant girl archaeologist/explorer from a distinguished family in her first year of college (basically, a young female Indiana Jones).  The game will take you to several locations around the world, each with its own set of missions and tasks from which to choose.  Each story or side mission will have a series of "obstacles" to overcome, each of which can usually be tackled using a couple of different approaches, depending on which stats you've been favoring.  You raise your stats at various locations around town (unlike most visual novels, which have 3-5 stats, there are probably 30+ stats here), but there's also a twist on this mechanic: in addition to your permanent personal stats, you can also obtain "inspirations," which are essentially cards that will give you a one-time boost to certain stats.  Inspirations vary in type and quality, so it will be up to you to explore each location for the best combinations!
I really enjoyed the story and characters.  Although the plot in certain mission lines can get rather convoluted, it's always a fun ride when Sadie's at the helm.  Some scenarios just plain made me smile. :)
Since this is a visual novel at heart, the gameplay consists of reading, making choices in menus and maps, etc.  The game takes place over one year of in-game time, and there are so many different quests and branches from which to choose, it's not possible to see everything in one playthrough, even on Easy difficulty.  Although there is a charming tutorial, expect to spend your first couple of in-game weeks flailing about and generally failing objectives as you get accustomed to the flow of the game.  There are multiple romance-able characters, but even if you choose not to romance a certain character (or any of the characters), full friendship routes are still available, so the characters don't totally disappear from the game like in some visual novels.  This means that, while I enjoyed the romance aspect, even if you choose to remain single, you still get a complete gaming experience.  I just finished my first playthrough, which took about 19 hours, and I'm looking forward to jumping right into a second to explore some of the content I missed the first time around!
As far as technical things go, the location maps are super impressive, the menus are well-done, and character art is generally good (although the CGs are not always great).  The music is lively and era-appropriate; at the beginning of the game, it really impressed me.  As the hours wore on, though, it did get rather repetitive, so a few more tracks might've been nice.  I noticed that a few lines of dialogue seemed to have the wrong speaker's name on the text box, but this was rare, and the only bug-like thing I encountered (trouble getting achievements to register) was promptly fixed by the developer a couple of days after launch, so everything seems to be very stable.
To summarize, Scheherazade is a fun, extremely meaty visual novel game that oozes atmosphere and charm and even manages to incorporate a considerable degree of strategy in the form of stat-management mechanics.  Recommended for fans of VNs and those who want to explore a girl-Indiana Jones-type plot full of adventure!

I've been playing Midair since the kickstarter instant access release.  I'm impressed with the transparency the dev team has had with the community.  There's been frequent updates and constant communication on their end.
With that said there are a few things I'm disappointed in.  First, the marketing for this game is almost non-existitent.  I've talked to old tribes teammates and they didn't even know this game was still being developed.  Unless your among the crowd that paid money during the kickstarter you really don't know anything about this game, and the population after the Early Access Release shows that.  There may only be couple of servers with people in it at any given time.
My other complaint is this game is also a direct copy of the old Tribes/Tribes 2 games.  There's almost no originality at all.  Exact same weapons, same classes, same vehicles, same packs, and same deployables.  They just renamed some things and that's it.  Also, you can tell that most of their playtesters were old Tribes 1/Tribes 2 players and they heavily influenced the direction the game was going in, they've been wanting another Tribes game with updated graphics and that's basically what midair is.  What the devs didn't consider that there's a reason why all the old tribes games are dead right now with only a few people playing.  I would have liked to seen some new aspects added and this be a "tribes-like" game, rather than a full blown tribes game with updated graphics.
My last complaint is during the Instant Access/Alpha stages.  I rarely got to play in a game with more than 3 or 4 people in the game.  The only games that would go on is PUG (Pick up Games).  Which at that early stage of the game, there's no need for any pick-up games unless those are strictly playtesters on a set date testing things out.  All the pick up games did was drive new people away because they couldn't get in the passworded servers and divide an extremly small community.
With all that said, I still recommend this game and I'm rooting for this game to be successful. I'm just not so sure the right steps were taken to ensure that, but regardless I'll be playing.   And I'll bring some old teammates over to play as well.
