The Mass Effect series has been my all-time favorite video game series ever since the first one.
Let's start with the obvious, which are the downsides:
Mass Effect 2 is unlike the first one, and consequently is less of a BioWare game at heart than it could be, clearly showing the signs of transition between pre- and post-EA acquisition.
World exploration has been highly minimized in favor of action sequences, whether centralizing scenes with shootouts or with much more intense scenarios for the vehicle sections.
Going from point A to B revolves more around the action of that path, rather than a combination of full control, observation and going in unprepared.
The RPG elements are also dumbed-down, in particular with the equipment by making minimal changes between outfits and weapons, leaving only the character-building experience with dialogue sequences.
All this being said: the improvements definitely make up for most — if not all — of these downsides.
The enriched universe shown in the first game is still present in this title, which still leaves you with the same amount of awe.
The dialogues, despite feeling like two robots speaking to each other most of the time, is filled with character, where each line tells you just enough about the world you're playing in, and they're super well delivered thanks to the amazing voice actors like Jennifer Hale (if you played femshep), or Mark Meer (maleshep), or even the other awesome members of the main cast, including and especially Martin Sheen. Sure, the exchange between two parties doesn't feel like two human beings talking, but their amount of detail definitely make up for this fault.
The characters themselves are mostly unique; they have many facets to themselves that are progressively presented to you as you develop tighter bonds with them, and generally never feel unnatural.
Finally, despite the locations being abruptly cut in portions (sometimes by giving you menus of where to go next), they don't cut too much to prioritize cinematic display, which although is something inherent in video games nowadays and they're specially gorgeous in this one, is something that easily breaks the pacing. Mass Effect tackles this appropriately since most of the cinematics involve player prompts, so there's never a moment where the game forces you to put down your controller (or stretching yourself in your chair) unless you want it to.
All of this while you experience an epic story of a Commander that participates in something much more interesting than a mere "saving the Galaxy" (which the 3rd title unfortunately definitely uses as the main theme), by jumping between solar systems.
I'm a video games fan, so I'll play mostly anything, even if I end up highly disliking a game; before I judge them critically, I must give all a fair chance by at trying to play it from beginning to end.
Mass Effect 2, however, is the only game in my library and past experience that gives me a profound amount of pleasure while playing it.
If I was allowed only one part of my memory wiped, I would definitely use that to my memories of this series, so that I could re-experience it "for the first time" all over again.

The gaming landscape is vast enough that truly unique games can still emerge from the field, either through never-before-seen designs or groundbreaking combinations of existing systems. Hand of Fate exemplifies the latter, a game composed of familiar parts assembled in such a way to create something singular. But its success stems only in part from its uniqueness, because the expert care and polish that it is presented with makes it an absolutely engrossing experience from start to finish.
You have been invited to the table of the enigmatic Dealer, a reclusive mystic who challenges guests to games of cards. We’re not talking bridge or blackjack here though, we’re talking games of life and death. The Dealer’s deck approximates a hero’s journey through treacherous lands to vanquish deadly monsters, full of ambushes and chance encounters. To embark on these journeys, you must assemble your own deck of equipment and events which will determine what you find as you fight your way to your nemesis. Your success will rely as much on luck as it does your skill with both card and sword.
As much as I love waxing poetic about games, I’d be doing you a disservice if I didn’t spell out exactly how the game is played. Before each round you build two decks using cards you’ve unlocked, one of items and one of encounters. The Dealer mixes in non-optional cards like bosses and enemy ambushes and then lays out a grid of cards from your encounter deck to explore. Moving your token onto a card brings up a short text segment about what’s happening to you, often with choices to make and risks to take. For combat, you are moved to small arenas where you battle enemies in third person with your arsenal of weapons, shields, armors, artifacts, and blessings.
It’s a board game, one formed at random from your choice of deck and different every time you play. It’s dynamic as well, for some of your choices force new cards to overlay existing ones, usually to continue plot threads or give you destinations for quests. Some of the items you find can reveal important cards in the layout but in general they’ll be face-down, forcing you to explore carefully. Each area has an exit to another grid of cards until you reach the end and locate the boss. The end effect is a very roguelike dungeon crawl, working your way through unknown environs toward a goal while maintaining the resources to get there without dying.
Death will end your attempted run, lest you forget this is a roguelike, and death can come in a number of ways. You have three figures to track as you trek, your health, your gold, and your food. Health and gold are just what you’d expect but food complicates their management, because every time you move to a new card you must consume a unit of food. Eating restores a small bit of health but when you run out, you’ll lose health for each step. Buying food from shops or seeking it out as rewards is key to survival, especially since food itself is used in many encounters to barter for better options. Encounters themselves will likely never kill you outright but can put you in terrible positions by sapping your food, your gold, or even your maximum health.
Combat is the most obvious place you can die, but if you’ve ever played an Arkham or Assassin’s Creed you should be well-prepared for this. Generally you’ll be facing crowds of enemies but your spry avatar can interrupt most attacks with his own, block and counter with his shield, and execute downed enemies with a lengthy series of blows. Using only the directional stick and attack button you can float from foe to foe, beating them down in a ballet of brutal swings. Special powers granted by artifacts and blessings can have a big impact here as well, dispatching some enemies outright or even earning you extra gold or health for attack combos or kills.
While all of these elements form a unique and engrossing whole, it’s the presentation that elevates Hand of Fate to the next level. Aside from the combat interludes you spend the entire game seated across from the Dealer, and he is not a quiet fellow. He’ll muse about the potency of his minions, judge your actions, drop hints of concern, and so much more that you would expect from a fully-formed character. With mere mentions he hints at a wider world and tale beyond the table, and then he just as easily chides himself for making a card too powerful. The Dealer also manages his table with magical flair, moving and shuffling cards through grand gestures and the delectable sound of cards fluttering against each other.
There are other aspects of the presentation that charm, such as the crisp graphics and expert sound design. The only place the aesthetics falter is in the battle animations, which look far stiffer than the feel in practice. Outside of that though, it’s a polished, charming title that will last you a great many hours. Story mode encompasses twelve challenges, and there’s an endless mode where you can continue to chase down new cards and secrets. With so much offered in such a gratifying package, it’s hands-down on of the most unique and enjoyable roguelikes I’ve tried.

Alright, so as roguelites go, this one is a little bit short. A lot of stuff is done right, but the flaws really stand out in this game.
Starting with the positive, the production values and the feel of the game are quite well done. The weapons are satisfying to use and the simple art style works very well for the kind of game that is is. At its best, gameplay is frenetic and you are heavily punished even for slight slip ups (and heavily rewarded if you keep on top of positioning the enemies). Also, the game has hats in it.
Now for the rest: first, this is a very easy rogue-lite. I was able to beat the game on my second try, come on. While short, it isn't really all that short: about double the length of the original Binding of Isaac. Nor is it that the game simply is too forgiving. Instead, it ties into the next two problems.
This game lacks variety and randomness that keeps rogue-lites replayable. There are only a few different kinds of enemies and the designs for them (and the bosses) are so basic they might as well have been randomized (they are not). This does mean that once you figure out the mechanics of the game, you can keep yourself alive pretty easily as you are not as much at the mercy of the RNG as in most other rogue-lites (even if you can't find the weapon that you want, it might show up in a vending machine, and in any case, there are not that many and they are not really that different from one another). It doesn't even have that many hats! You're quite likely to see every single hat in the game in a single play-through.
The game rewards spam and standoff fighting far too much. That one reviewer who complained that weapon range is laughably short... well... that is only true of some weapons and not even your starting ones. Many of the weapons have no boundaries to their range, and can easily hit targets off the screen. You can avoid a lot of fighting by just spamming your weapons down unexplored areas and hoping they hit something. This is pretty boring, you have nothing to dodge, and it makes the game easier than it would otherwise be. With the cash magnet, there is no real downside to doing this (and you can confirm your kills without actually checking out where you shot at). If vision range were extended, this would at least feel less cheap and boring.
Finally, there is some minor, but annoying breakage to the game. It doesn't perform well on my Surface Pro 3. Performance does degrade gracefully (the game starts to stretch time, rather than drop frames or stop the world), and this was well done. However it would be nice if this thing could actually run at its full speed most of the time, as gameplay is both more difficult and more exciting when it does. Also, the hat-related achievements currently seem to be broken.
If this game is on sale, go ahead and get it, you'll have enough fun to justify this. However, if you want to play a rogue-lite game, pick up something better and more mainstream, like Enter the Gungeon, Nuclear Throne, or Binding of Isaac: Rebirth.

With very Fallout 3 and New Vegas style gameplay, an open world, post-apocalyptic setting and a first person/third person camera, many would say this game is copying the two latest Fallouts. But I disagree. This game OBVIOUSLY takes inspiration from Fallout, but it features a more in-depth system. With leveling, skill perks and harvesting random things in the wasteland (trash, plants etc.) for selling, you will find hours of in-depth, time-consuming activities to find. And for those perfectionists out there, there are around 650 achievements/trophies that are here on Steam that you can strive to gain. The quest ideas DO seem recycled and executed poorly, though. By this I mean killing 10 to 15 monsters in a secluded area and then returning to a quest-giver to recieve your reward. Though countering that, the quests have a pleasing level of challenge and usually vary. You'll see a couple of bounty quests here and there and then an extermination quest, so you'll be doing 10 different kinds of quests before you see another of the same kind. The Free2Play it's self is nothing short of fun, considering that 95% of the game's elements are still playable to unsunscribed users. Though I do wish there was a more in-depth trading system, no one said improvements can't be made. But finally, for those people (like me), who find a game's graphic's style amazing to make the game better, you're in luck. With changing times of day, many, many parts of the wasteland can be viewed in different ways, except for caves and things of the sort. Near cities at night (my absolute favorite time of day, in real and video-game life) beautiful light arrangements are shown. While they may seem bland and boring to others, nothing makes night-time more beautiful than lights coming off of a lit city.

A cheerful visual novel with a little more stats-juggling than usual.
There is a difficulty system, so if you aren't into stats juggling you can just pick easy and still have fun. The game also show you which stats are used before you pick a storyline and it helps a lot. There are also "Inspirations", single-use stats booster you can get on the map just as easily as a regular stats increase, which is a welcome addition.
Interface is pretty but could use some work, especially the map where it can be easy to click on the wrong locations due to their proximity. The skill screens could use more information and a better sorting (alphabetical?). The diary screen should omit the empty dates as they look ridiculous, and the fonts make it slightly hard to read. On the nice side, that mean you have easy access to story recap. The backgrounds are evocative and really pretty.
Probably should get a new artist for the character art, though. I meant it. The eyes!
Characters are fun to interact with and well-written, and they all have fun dialogues. There are a lot of different stories that make multiple playthroughs viable and enjoyable. The game is bigger than it looks content-wise.
As a visual novel the game's strength is firmly on the interactive novel side with its cheerful writing. There is a lot of that.

Then we come to the second game. I would say that it focuses more on the individual that is Shepherd and you, as the player, and the choices you are bound to make or have made.
Can't say much more specific, since it has been some time now that I have completed the game, but still, I would always recommend this, and the whole trilogy, to anyone. Definitely am going to play through it again, before playing the 4th installment, Andromeda.

While I do enjoy this game I must give it a thumbs down because while this game looks like Dungeon Keeper... it is not Dungeon keeper.  While this game has all the trappings of DK series, the goofy monsters, the dungeon building, the game voice narrirator,  this is not a true DK3.
The glaring difference between this and the previous 2 DK games comes in the level of level creativity and ability to explore.  This game quickly becomes a giant dogpile of troops rushing to the end.  It lacks the exploration element in DK 1&2 that are so essential to the overall feel of the game.  The zerg rush of the game gets so bad that rooms like the workshop are utterly useless.  You can't build doors and traps because you are constantly summoning your monsters to engage the enemy or rush the end lair.  You can't take any time because the AI is too agressive or the level is under a timer.  Unlike the games predecessors that allowed you to meticulously plot your dungeon, explore every nook and crany for all the secrets and craft the army you want you are in an RTS scramble to build as quickly as you possibly can and that saps alot of the enjoyment out of the game.
I hope that if they release DLC (a 2nd campaign) the creators really sit back and change the whole tempo of the game.  While the game looks like Dungeon Keeper it plays more like the Warcraft franchise.  If I wanted to play Warcraft/Starcraft I would have picked that up instead of DK3.

Just finished this game on my first playthrough. 130 hours of my life gone, and I don't even feel bad.
This game is a throwback to the glory days of crpgs like Baldurs Gate, Fallout and many more. Decisions matter, your party matters, everything you do matters. Not only that, but it also offers a rich world, where things happen around you wether you intervene or not. To top it off, the game looks great and has the best soundtrack and sound design I have ever heard.
On the other hand you have some minor continuity issues that can prop up if you take the open invitation of the game to play your own way to the extreme and some clunkyness with the UI. Nothing too major, those are things I can tolerate in a game that comes along fully voiced.
Comparing this title to other so called RPG's of modern times bar the Witcher series reveals a lot about the state of the industry. Larian gives the big names like Bethesda or Bioware a run for their money with this masterpiece.
In closing: My characters girlfriend, a demon-posessed bard that turned into a demon hunter once I helped her purge the demon from her soul played a heartfelt song (Yes, they recorded it) in front of the throne of the last living god. Can't recommend enough.

That being said, I loved Dungeon Keeper and this is more of the same. I will forever miss the comedic cut scenes between levels in the campaign of DK II but we can't have it all, can we?
I do find umbrage in the way AI is handled. Specifically, I find it a little unbalanced that the computer players can produce the enitre contents of their dungeon in under a second while I have to slowly rally my troops or click them, ten at a time, to the desired location. This is especially frustrating in later levels of the campaign or when playing master difficulty in Skirmish mode.
My glee returns however with the addition of new spells. Some of which feel spectacularly more sadistic, such as turning enemy captives into gold statues. I do like the new shrines and I am honestly one of those folks that wanted to see the ability to add walls.
I don't see myself wasting as much time with this one as I did with DK, but is that because I already played DK? Is it because the content isn't there quite yet? This remains to be seen, but for now, A Solid Buy.

I admittedly started playing this with fairly low expectations and it really caught me off guard.
A unique approach at puzzle/platforming that involves collecting and rearranging blocks with a variety of properties to progress to an exit and collect special hidden "blocks that matter" along the way.  Blocks can only be placed in tetromino patterns, making most of the puzzles deceptively difficult -- and therein lies what for me is so addictive.  The levels rarely seem difficult, they simply are.
Complete with extras that even further test your ability to think outside the box (pun intended) and a level editor that makes level creation and sharing seamless.
Definitely recommended if you like puzzle/platformers (and frankly, I generally don't.)

Game is repetitive and featureless.  It's cute, and entertaining at first... but it is lacking in mechanics, common features, and frankly any reason to keep playing.
There is no weapon encyclopedia or catalog, or similar.  You just have to remember what each weapon does.  And no collection.
There is no enemy compendium or similar.  You'll just have to remember (which is not hard, since there is little real variety).  No collection.
There is no variety. Levels differ in graphical background only.  Modifiers are nearly non existent.
There are no unlockables.  Of any kind.
One character.  Few ways to differentiate between runs (in terms of upgrades).
No further development.  Devs consider the game complete, have stated as such.  They ignore criticism and suggestions categorically.  They are not interested in furthering this game at all.
There is NO STORY despite the description.  Just the occasional single liner joke that you are meant to "piece together" to "discover what happened".  Except not really.  And there's nothing more than "world was ruined, you're still here.  Be a good consumer lol corporations mannnn." (oops, spoilers? =p )
No goal.  You just try to get a high score.  That is it.  You really see everything there is to see pretty much the first time you play it.  You confirm that the second time you play.  You feel disappointed the third time.  You see all the different ways the game could be worlds better the fourth.  You hope it will be better the fifth.
You wonder if it's too late for a refund the sixth.
Edit: it's worth noting that most of these thumbs up reviews are from months ago... and in all that time have barely more than an hour of play time.  Think about that.

In Valkyria Chronicles you take control of a squad of soldiers in a fictional World War 2 type setting. The game has a beautiful watercolor/line art, art style that is quite impressive. Gameplay consists of a overhead strategy game with a slight twist. When moving individual soldiers the game goes to a 3rd person camera and you get direct control over the unit's movement, aiming, and choice of weapon. Overall the gameplay is very enjoyable, and you can replay missions and try to improve your mission rank by trying different tactics or coming back with better units. I haven't finished it yet, but the story seems good so far. Like a lot of anime series it has a habit of switching from light-hearted scenes to very dramatic ones which keeps the story from becoming boring, and the characters all have distinct traits and back stories which gives the story and characters a little more depth. On the technical side of things I haven't had any crashes or major bugs, the only issue I've encountered was the screen not displaying correctly, which was an easy fix thanks to Steam users posting how to fix it in the Discussions hub. Overall I have really enjoyed this game and would recommend it to anyone who is a fan os strategy games.

Only three states are currently available, and who knows which will be offered from this point on (I don't expect them to be offered free, though it'd be nice). The optimization leaves a lot to be desired with framerates frequently dipping into the 40s in more populated areas on my i5 / GTX 970 system. The road system is also occasionally wonky with a lack of merging lanes, intersections on divided freeways that are all but impossible to enter realistically without getting hit by traffic, and general scale issues.
The company appears to be aware of some of these issues and has stated that a fairly major update is in the works. The actual driving and business management simulation aspects are nicely done and offer a tremendous amount of gameplay as-is, so I have no problem recommending ATS if it's something you might be interested in. The program is stable, runs fairly well, and looks nice enough (though there's certainly room for improvement). Mods are also supported and there's already a nice community churning out quality additions.
I play using a 360 gamepad and it works just fine, so don't think you absolutely need a wheel to enjoy this game.

Very fun game, has a short, but fairly hard learning curve, and then almost infinite potential for improvement.

On the surface, fairly simplistic.
Here's a basic run down (and a rating out of 5) for classes:
Engineer - revives fallen teammates, heals injured teammates, builds and repairs structures (commander dropped) as well as his own (walls/turrets/cameras/radars). Has seismic grenades which are excellent at taking down enemy structures.
Ease of learning (highest is easiest) - 5/5
Ease of reaching potential (highest is easiest to get really good at) - 4/5
Anti-infantry - 2/5
Anti-tank - 2/5
Anti-structure - 5/5
Solo potential (how useful the class is when played alone) - 3/5
Group potential (how useful the class is when played in a squad/with teammates) - 5/5
HIGHLY RECOMMEND ENGINEER TO NEW PLAYERS!
Rifleman - mows down enemy infantry with ease, provides surpressing fire and long distance fire as well. Important in close combat, but requires engineer support to be fully functional. Has regular and sticky grenades, which can stick onto enemy vehicles and explode causing high damage.
Ease of learning - 4/5
Ease of reaching potential  - 3/5
Anti-infantry - 5/5
Anti-tank - 1/5 (3/5 with stickies)
Anti-structure - 1/5
Solo potential - 1/5
Group potential  - 4/5
Scout - infilitrator/spy/assassin/James Bond. This is an almost purely support class which is highly useless but  cause can cause a lot of hassle when paired up with another class. Besides regular SMGs available, this class has a scout rifle, a "sniper" rifle as referred by some. Has a hide ability, as well as radar stealth and enemy detection. Has smoke/concussion/stun grenades Generally avoid this class unless you know what you're doing.
Ease of learning - 3/5
Ease of reaching potential - 2/5
Anti-infantry - 3/5
Anti-tank - 1/5 (2/5 with stun)
Anti-structure - 3/5
Solo potential - 2/5
Group potential - 4/5
Grenadier - it's in the name. Has a pistol, a dumbfire (or guided) RPG, a mortar, and mines. Has good vehicle related skillsets.
Ease of learning - 2/5
Ease of reaching potential - 1/5
Anti-infantry - 4/5
Anti-tank - 5/5
Anti-structure - 4/5
Solo potential - 3/5 (add +1 if you've mastered this class)
Group potential - 4/5 (add +1 if you've mastered this class)
Onto vehicles:
Jeep - basic transportation vehicle carries from 2-4 people (including the driver), has no mountable weapons
APC - spawnable-in transportation vehicle carries 8 (including the driver), carries an MG and Grenade Launcher
Light Tank/AFV - available by default first tank in the game. Carries standard cannon, a dumbfire missile, and a standard machine gun
Medium Tank - carries advanced weaponry, has increased armor, but reduced speed and manouverability
Heavy Tank - carries even more advanced weaponry, even more increased armor, but further reduced speed and manouverability
Artillery Tank - fires up in the air in an arc. Has no short distance capabilites, is usually useful and weeding out the enemy out of a specific area.
The game has a lot of depth to it which is not obvious on the first play through.

The game is in a very Alpha state, but it does offer a lot of value as an early access title. I've been following the development on YouTube but have been hesitant to pick it up until now. No, it's not because I'm a cheap ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ who needed a five dollar price cut, but more for the sake of convienence. Now that the game is on Steam the magic of auto-updates can allow ease of use for me the end user. Anyways enough about why I haven't purchased until now. Lets talk about what this game has to offer.
PROS:
The Engine- From what I can tell and what the developers say this engine is built from the ground up specifically for this game. I can safely say you won't find any rehashed or recycled objects here. With so many indie developers building on pre-made assets, it's nice to see a game with truely original content.
The Mechanics- Being a melee combat game in this day in age normally means more of the same... Overgrowth is not the same. The fighting is dynamic and based almost entirely on proximity. If you try spaming the attack button nothing will happen, you must first be within range of your enemy. Why is this a good thing, you may ask? Well in my opinion it is amazing! Gone are the days of accidently attacking for no reason and looking like a fumbling idiot. Immersion is important to me and not being able to attack unless near an enemy is a big Plus in my book.This also means that the combat always makes sense and your AI oponents have some inteligence. They also know when it's appropriate to attack.
The Art- Wolfire provides Art asset overviews on their YouTube channel which give even more insight to the creative development cycle. They also have a short graphic novel on their website which is very well done and worth a read. Seeing the art move from a concept to the end product always puts a smile on my face and I'm excited to see how this all ties in with the eventual lore and story of the game.
The Potential- This game has huge potential to become more than just kicking and punching. If they integrate a story with a fully realized world, characters, voice acting, scripted scenes and an interesting and engaging adventure... well... then this game would probably enter into the realm of some of the greatest games of all time. They have an extremely well made engine and set of mechanics to build off of plus the lore of the web comic. I am very excited to see where this game goes.
CONS: I'll keep these short and to the point since this is an Alpha build and should not be judged to harshly.
Settings- The settings menus do nothing at this point in time so you have to play the game as is. This is said to be fixed in the next update so I'm not to worried about it.
Stabilty- It's Alpha and it crashes unexpectedly.
Final Thoughts:
And that's about it for the time being. I highly reccomend picking up the alpha if you are at all interested in the concept and or are just looking for a new fresh melee combat experience. Keep in mind that these are my views and opinions and you should create your own opinion based on more than just what I have to say. Check out the Wolfire YouTube page for yourself and look at what other people have been able to do with the game. Keep an open mind and give this game high consideration for your next purchase.
Alpha Score 8/10

Ruiner is a top down shooter set in a well realised stylised cyberpunk world.
Most of your time will be spent within industrial complexes, a series of narrow paths connecting open areas where the majority of the combat takes place.
The combat is wonderful to behold due to a combination of tight controls, surprisingly difficult encounters (depending on difficulty setting of course) and the wonderful visuals. The visual/sound effects very effectively sell the weight and power of the weapons and abilities in use and make combat very satisfying.
The music is very effective at building the mood between combat areas, and great at getting the blood pumping in action sequences.
Ruiner is a small game, which is a shame. There is a city hub between the major mission sections of the game and the developers have done a fantastic job of making a lively and moody isometric cyberpunk sprawl, complete with characters. Unfortunately, you dont spend a lot of time in this area and there is only the one hub. Ruiner gives you a taste of the wonderful world they have crafted but I wanted to delve into it more. It would have been nice to have more than one hub, allow the player to explore more visually distict areas, Ruiner is saturated in red, but it might have been nice to see some neon.
Overall I very much enjoyed the game however, it is clear that they went for quality not quanity and what they have is polished to a mirror shine. I should also note that this game manages to look beautiful and runs like a dream. No issues with optimisation here.
I am hopeful to see DLC or a future game explore this world further.

An enjoyable spiritual successor marred by bad performance issues.
I have a system with a GTX980, i7-4790K, 16GB of RAM and I have this game installed on an SSD. On the later campaign maps my FPS drops to 16-30FPS depending on my zoom level, changing the graphical settings does nothing but even if it did it still wouldn't be excusable. I get a better frame rate on Witcher 3 with most of the settings cranked up to max for goodness sake.
I'd absolutely love to recommend this game but if I'm having these sorts of issues with a system such as mine I dread to think how this game runs on less beefy systems because even my fully expanded Pet Dungeon is averaging out at 20 FPS.
Here's a quick list of things that stuck to me after playing the whole campaign in one sitting:
The good news?
- It's practically Dungeon Keeper 3, if you've played the previous games playing this will be like riding a bike.
- Richard Ridings is as good as ever.
- They absolutely nailed the sound design.
The so-so?
- Greater degree of micromanagement:
- I really don't like how doors function in this game, there's no 'only open for my minions mode'. You either keep it open or lock yourself in.
- Prisons offer a greater variety of choices but it's always a manual process as to what you do with them. If the developer insists on these not automatically turning into undead like before there should at least be a means to auto-allocate them to the torture chamber, crypt or turn them into gold.
- Imps and traps are tied to a limited mana pool, ultimately limiting the number you can have of either but this also means too many imps affects the number of traps you can create and vise versa. Not only that, imps don't seem to get any sort of speed increase as they level up.
The uh-oh?
- Aforementioned performance issues.
- Campaign is seriously lacking variety. Albeit, there are some call-backs to the sort of thing you'd see in DK1&2 but there isn't much of a sense of exploration and it's sorely lacking in surprises. You won't be running into ball traps or neutral rooms in this game. The maps also often feel a little cramped in regards to how much space they're offering you to build rooms of an acceptable size of quantity.
- Unit balance seems all over the place and level 10 units feel weak. Battles seem to be about whoever has the most amount of units regardless of level.
- And then there's some somewhat niggling issues like your minions getting upset and leaving a fight (or ignoring NPCs altogether) because they want to get fed or paid. I was warned that my minions were starting to revolt on the final level simply because there was such a prolonged period of fighting before you were granted the opportunity to send your minions back home.
I really like this game and want to see it become the DK3 everyone wanted but it still needs some serious work. I certainly don't regret my purchase but these shortcoming need to be noted. If you really want your Dungeon Keeper fix but already played DK1 and 2 to death you still might get some enjoyment out of this. The core is all there, it's all the ragged edges that need smoothing out.

An interesting CCG/action game. The tutorial is clear and teaches you the basics in a step by step fashion. I liked it. The game itself is very addicting.
The story mode is a blast. I played 5h non-stop when I first launched it. You always want to progress further and the game gets harder after every win.
There are 12 different dungeons with 12 bosses at the end. When you kill a boss, you unlock new cards, new quests and new equipment that you can possibly find if you put them in your deck. After you complete the 12 dungeons, you will face the main boss, the Dealer, and this dude is REALLY hard to kill and it's even hard to get to him. So you will have to grind a little bit. You will need to complete some quests in order to unlock the most powerful cards.
And on top of it, this game is heavy on RNG, so prepare to be disappointed pretty often.
The combat system is very similar to the Batman Arkham/Shadow of Mordor games, but it's very simplistic in that regard. All you need to do is to attack/block/roll over/counter. The fights are quite mechanical and straightforward. If you have bad equipment and you face a strong pack of enemies - you will gonna have a hard time, or at least it will take you much more time to beat them than it would have with a good weapon/armor/shield.
The gameplay feels fluid. There are some annoyances that requires you to click some dialogue options everytime you step on certain cards. It get tedious really quickly.
If you only care about completing the main story mode, this game can be done in about 8-12 hours, but if you want to complete every single achievement and get the best score in the "Endless" mode" - this game can provide tens or even hundreds of hours of fun.
Really looking forward to Hand of Fate 2, will definitely try it sometime in the future.

I'm really on the fence with this game, however, sadly my frustration with Hand of Fate outweighed my enjoyment towards the end of the game. It has an interesting idea that entertained me for the first few hours, but repetitive events and combat grew stale quickly. Those looking for a true adventure will likely be disappointed.
Hand of Fate has a multitude of issues. There are many bugs in the game, combat is very flat and rarely works in a way that is satisfying to play (enemies will slide accross the field when you roll into them, you will sometimes take damage from nothing, etc), and RNG based mechanics can be downright frustrating.
Unpolished combat from a smaller studio is understandable, but many of the design decisions here are unexpected and akward. I don't really mind RNG, but when it decides whether or not you can continue with certain events, or just plain kills you in one hit because of a string of bad luck, I no longer feel like I have any impact on the game. Towards the end of the game I felt like I was playing a slot machine.
Going in, I expected a "choose your own adventure" style of game. However, the vast majority of cards in the game are surprisingly dull and often have little impact. The risk of turning negative effects from cards made me skip them quite often in favor of rushing to a boss. Part of the reason for this was the truly odd choice to balance all the cards in the game so they never get more powerful; the sense of progression is almost non-existant because of this. "The Maiden," a card received at the beginning of the game wound up being the most useful card I ever had.
The difficulty scaling in Hand of Fate felt a little off balance. The first 12 stages felt all too easy when RNG went my way. The biggest challenge was not putting down the controller after a cheap death and realizing that I had to replay the entire level. The final stage has a massive difficulty spike, which honestly wouldn't even be that bad if you could challenge the end boss directly instead of replaying a long pointless level.
In essence, while I did enjoy parts of the game, and would recommend it to those who enjoy heavy RNG elements and light "choose your own adventure" style gameplay, those who prefer skill based games with interesting and diverse gameplay should steer clear.

One of the main reasons I purchased this is because I was a MAJOR fan of Dungeon Keeper back in the day. I loved the series and played it a lot as a kid and always remember it being one of my personal favorites.
When I started playing this one; all of the memories came back and it was a great feeling. The ability to play a game that dated to my childhood, and for it to be updated with more stuff than what was available before; especially multiplayer. They did a good job of keeping to the way it was remembered back in DK 1 and 2, as well as adding some more unique features in that keeps it entertaining.
The graphics received an over-haul, and it seems to perform alright on almost any modern machine  (I can also get decent FPS from my laptop if I close out everything else running - mind you the laptop runs 16GB DDR3 RAM w/ AMD graphics). It does get sluggish quite a bit as you build your dungeon, even on a pretty high-end desktop. Changing the graphics settings from Ultra down to normal or even low sometimes still doesn't fix the sluggish frame drops that you'll receive. The game needs more optimization which I hope they start focusing on.
The music keeps to the theme, and the sound effects are great. The only sound I do miss, is the mistress that entered your dungeon from having the torture chamber (the crack of the whip and the mmmm lol). The original announcer is back, along with the funny jokes and commentary that anyone who played the DK series loved.
I only wish that the multiplayer support was there a bit more. I attempted to search for an online game last night, and I found one server total which was a 1v1 match and was full, so I just went back and did a skirmish with the CPU. The community aspect could be a thousand times better, and right now it is almost next to impossible to get anyone else in an online match unless you are playing with a friend.
Hopefully with more updates, this game becomes extremely popular. It is showing a lot of promise, and has great potential. Keep up the good work, and thanks for bringing me back to my childhood.

I just want to start this with the fact that my play time on steam, currently at none, does not reflect the time I've played it since I've played a good bit on a console. Hand of Fate mixes a lot of ideas that seem like they wouldn't work. A brawler, card game, rpg, choose your own adventure game, it sounds like it could very well be terrible on paper. It isn't though. It's actually very entertaining, with the card game elements acting as a sort of adhesive bringing everything together. Cards determine your equipment, encounters on each level, and influence enemy encounters. Because of that, you can be stuck with fighting a kraken with a basic weapon on the first level of the game. Unlike in a turn based rpg though, you actually have a chance with the brawler mechanics coming in to play, giving the player control over how they handle the situation. Maybe run around the arena to fend off monsters, or go into a frenzy of dodges, counters, and hits to kill off the monsters. The smarmy card dealer also adds to the fun of the game, his sarcastic, witty, or even possibly rude comments (depending on your view anyway) potentially driving the player to succeed just so you can rub it in his smug prick face. I've enjoyed every minute I've played of this game, and hope to play Hand of Fate 2 as soon as I can get it.

The Good Robot is an excellent shoot 'em up experience with moody lighting and feel that strongly resembles the masterpiece Badland. Your good robot looks like a very aggressive Clony, not trying to avoid risk but instead thrown against it shooting everything frantically. Dozens of evil robots roam the tunnels you travel, waiting to make you their prey and you have to crush them mercilessly using two weapons your robot carries at any time. In the early levels of the game, the activity is relaxed, opponents few in numbers and the navigation of the central character very easy. In the advanced levels though, the action turns into bullet hell, enemy shots fill the screen, the adrenalin is elevated to the max and the good robot conducts incredible choreographies trying to dodge the shots and int the same time, hit his moving targets.
The combination of mouse and keyboard to operate your killbot reaches absolute perfection. The accuracy of the shots is almost frightening thanks to the movement of the cursor. Furthermore, the elaborate maneuvers of the robot are very easy to execute. The cramped underground environment does not leave much room for maneuver, on the other hand favors the use of rock formations as a shield to take cover from the enemy fire and then appear suddenly in front of your enemies before they can shoot you again.
The strengthening of your playable character has many enjoyable aspects. At first, you can buy primary and secondary weapons to equip, choosing those that suit your operating style best. The best feeling i had from a weapon in game i got it from the heavy machine gun while for secondary weapon i always prefered guns that fired rapidly and cover more area when impacting the target. Besides the above, the armor shields were essential for the survival of the robot from track to track and i always replenished them before reaching the next level. Without warranty, the bonus that works like continue, giving you a second chance, you will not go very far. In addition to all that, strengthening the fire power and rate of fire speeds up the extermination of enemies and enhances the splendor of the fighting.
There are two negative aspects of the game for me. Unlike roguelike masterpieces like Rogue Legacy and Binding of Isaac, there is no development system for the playable character past each playthrough. Either you buy all the accessories that are transforming your character to the ultimate war machine or destroy more robots than stars is our galaxy, your robot will start from scratch the next playthrough and the only evidence of your achievements is the score on the leaderboards . A second problem of Good Robot is the relative monotony of levels who become repetitive and tiresome after two - three hours of playing. If with future patches the developers improve these issues and add multiplayer mode then the Good Robot will take his place to the best titles of his category.

So this is what the first hour of play is like for someone with no experience of survival games, but who has fond memories of old Conan movies and generally loves the fantasy genre.... (Survival game fans will probably scream in rage that I "don't get it" - but that isn't the point of the review. This review's for you if you have no idea what a survival game is, but fancy a bit of Conan in your gaming.) ....
1) Buy game. Give it a few hours to download - it's 19GB. While it's downloading, remember all those cool Conan movies you used to love...
"Between the time when the oceans drank Atlantis and the rise of the sons of Aryas, there was an age undreamed of. And unto this, Conan, destined to wear the jewelled crown of Aquilonia upon a troubled brow. It is I, his chronicler, who alone can tell thee of his saga. Let me tell you of the days of high adventure!"
2) Launch game. Wait for a while as the game "retrieves character information" or something like that. No idea what it's doing - but hey, think of it as building drama!
3) Design character. Watch slightly lame intro where a poorly voice-acted Conan saves your life and mutters something about meeting you later, with the grim warning that it may have been kinder to have left you to die. Spawn by a big stone of epic graphics glitches; interact with it and get an ominous voice telling to go forth down any road and umm, something vague but dramatic sounding. So far, so good.
4) Follow "any road", like the voice said. Try using the controller in 3rd person view, but find that's unplayable, and go back to first person with mouse and keyboard. Find some cool ruins that look like an ancient tomb or temple. Remember that bit in Conan the Barbarian where Conan found an ancient sword in a spooky tomb, and excitedly run off to investigate the ruins. Find there's nothing there. Then find you've lost the road. Then die of thirst.
5) Respawn somewhere you don't remember. Follow "any road" again. Wander for ages while nothing happens. Bring up the map; find there is no marker for your location on the map. Wander a bit more. Die of thirst again.
6) Respawn. Check map. Realise you're on the edge. Wander, check map, wander, check map. Realise you can actually wander off the edge of the map - which is what you did before. This time, wander onto the map. Wander around trying to work out what you can or can't pick up. Make a stone axe thing. Think that dark patch on the map may be a river, and try to get there. Don't make it in time. Die of thirst.
7) Respawn. Make a dash for the river, make another axe, fight a couple of lumpen creatures. Make it to the river. Take a drink! Hurrah! (By now Conan would have epically vanquished a multitude of foes, seen them driven before him and heard the lamentations of their women - but you, you managed to drink some water!) Realize you have no real idea what you are doing. Pause game, switch to browser, quickly run through some online help guides.
8) Go back to the game. Discover you had died while paused, and respawned. Wander… axe... wander... lumpen creatures... and get back to the river. Wander some more. Kill animals (rabbits, baby turtles, and more of those lumpen bipeds). Realise the lumpen foes give you more XP, so kill some more of them. Collect lots of sticks and rocks. Use axe and pick to hit trees and rocks. Level up a few times.
9) Wander some more. Find a couple of barbarian types by a fire. Approach, wondering if they will talk or be violent. They attack. Well, one does; the other just sits there dumbly while you bludgeon his friend. Approach second one. Maybe he'll talk? No, doesn't seem like dialogue is a thing here. He attacks you, too. Bludgeon him, too. Realise that combat in this game is nowhere near as good as combat in other open-world fantasy games, like Shadow of Mordor or Skyrim. Realise you will soon die of starvation. Remember that the online guides said you should cook meat on a fire. The barbarians had a fire; you've got some meat. Stand stupidly by the fire clicking everything you can to try to work out how to cook the meat. Fail to work out how to cook meat. Realise you're now definitely going to die of starvation. Realise you don't really care.
10) Consider your future in this game. If you bludgeon enough random critters you'll level up enough to make, pretty soon, a storage chest, and then maybe a bed. Farther in the future you can imagine - if you batter enough creatures and press E on the environment repeatedly to gather twigs, stone, grass, etc. - you might even be able to build a shack. That shack will then give you a base to do the same again, over and over....
11) Realise that Conan was probably right in the intro - it would have been kinder to leave you to die. Decide starving to death is probably the best option. Quit game. Uninstall game. Request refund from Steam.
12) Write snarky review.
"Between the time when the oceans drank Atlantis and the rise of the sons of Aryas, there was an age undreamed of. And unto this, you, destined to pay thirty quid so you can wander aimlessly picking up twigs and rocks...."

I like the faithfulness of this game to the original. They kept the flavor of the original game, making it easy to make the transition. So far as I could tell, there's all the same elements of the original game, dungeon building, room optimizing, cheating your minions out of their pay, slapping and torturing them, etc.
There's also some very good new features, like control groups and invisible-fence-for-imps, that were missing from the original. The graphical update makes it a very nice looking game, although by no means cutting edge or demanding.
This does mean, however, that the game is not much of a change from the original. There's no radically new gameplay, just some tweaks, a graphical update and a new story.
Also, the minimap is unnecessarity pixelated, and the game uses so much memory! It uses 2.5GB more memory than Tomb Raider 2013, and about 1GB more memory than vanilla Rome II. I can't imagine what all that memory is used for, since Rome II handles more units and has better texture. Given this and some other reviews, I'm inclined to think that optimization is not very good, and systems with slower/less RAM will stutter due to paging issues.

The whole point of the "Dungeon Keeper" genre is to have the time and dungeon space to build up sneaky traps and defences, and only then let the goodly heroes wander haplessly into your carefully constructed dungeon. Then you laugh as they fall to your devious trigger-trap combos. (remember those?)
This game attacks you within seconds of the game starting, breaching your marshmallow-tough walls from all sides, ruining the whole point of the game.
You can't build an effective dungeon because there isn't enough space and there are more holes than a swiss-cheese in the dungeon soil so you can't build rooms.
It is not supposed to be a frantic click-fest!
They have totally broken a game whose genre is all about designing traps and slow careful exploration.
The other main game mechanic of "Dungeon Keeper" was creeping about, picking off enemy scouts without raising the alarm, and carefully expanding your dungeon without the goodly heroes ever noticing your progress until it was too late for them.
This game mechanic has also been destroyed by WTFO, which is now all about the enemy AI attacking immediately, and heading straight for your dungeon heart in an endless torrent. Yes, they implemented the 1st person posession spell, but now there is no reason to have it as there is no sneaking about to do.
I even waited until they got as far as Ver 1.3 to let all the bugs get ironed out, but that was a mistake too. It is still very buggy.
The devs have spent way too much time upgrading the graphics of Dungeon Keeper, whilst missing the whole point of what the game is supposed to be. As a result it is very pretty, dialogue is great, and yet the easy-bit, the gameplay, is totally absent.
I didn't want a shoot-em-up game, I wanted a dungeon-design game and I feel ripped-off.
Don't waste your money.

Good Robot is one of the more unique rogue-like games I've encountered. The game plays well with a controller and the procedurally generated maps provide a fresh experience each run. The music and artstyle are pretty polished and since I have a lot of things going on in my life, one of my favourite features is that you can stop in the middle of a run and continue it later. From what I've seen so far, there is a good variety of upgrades and enemies you can face. The hats are a nice touch with the added benefit of protecting you from damage for one hit. The game can be difficult at points when it turns into a bullet hell with all the enemies shooting at you. There's also the added difficulty of only seeing the enemies in the area your flashlight covers. I get bored easily with games.  I often play for a week and give up.  That is why reviews are perfect coming from me.  I tell the reality of games.  So before I dive deeper let me say this is a great game for early access.
Building:. Good as is, but will not win people over with what it has.  Pieces can be extremely frustrating to snap together.  Certain pieces would seem to go together but don't.  The amount of pieces is very limited and needs to be doubled at least to have a good chance of standing out from the crowd.  Half walls, arches, glass etc.  All need to be added and much much more.
Combat:. A super simplified Skyrim.  Needs much more work on the ai and the mechanics(especially the archery) of the game.  Stealth should be more streamline and sneak attacks should be utilized.
NPC:. Clunky and unrealistic.  99% try to kill you, which is fine but make it seem more real.  Not blobs with the same few attacks and tactics as everyone else.  They need a retreat tactic.  Backup tactics.  Swimming ability, for animals and people.  Utilize defense and numbers.  Not chase, slash, chase, slash, chase slash.
Story:. Most basic of story.  No real direction, no rea purpose other than don't die.  More obvious clues or more clues.  More friendly NPCs to point the way.
Interface:. Too small to use a TV in living room.  Chat should be adjustable.  And STOP using crappy cheap looking fonts.  Go back and play Skyrim and watch what happens when you level up, when you speak to someone, when you fight.  That game doesn't look cheap and it's simply because of how they utilize the space on the monitor and stay away from cheap looking fonts that make me feel I could remake at home with crayons.
Conclusion:. This may seem like a hate fest but far from it.  I believe this game is great for what it is, early access, but the devs need to know this stuff or they won't see or know what needs fixed.  I suggest everyone get this game, try it out and give constructive criticism.  It'll make this game the best we've seen.  The devs are doing great with updates.  If they listen to the people and keep up the hard work this game will dominate.  No doubt!

The developers of this game have been working on it for 7 years and they still haven't gotten very far. Trust me, it's a fun game and it's nowhere near bad. Is it really worth the $29.99 though? Let's see it's pros and cons.
+Amazing combat system
+Very good parkour/traversal mechanics
+Great maps
+Good map editing system
-Can get very repetitive
-Very glitchy and lags a lot, even on amazing gaming PCs, at times the game just shuts itself off and creates a pop-up asking you to send a dmp file to
, (sending a dmp file does nothing)
-Game has been stuck in development hell for a VERY, VERY long time
-I think it's safe to say this game will probably be finished in about 5 to 15 years or maybe even more. I'm seriou, it's very glitchy, and with every update, there are minor changes.
So back to the question. Is Overgrowth worth the $29.99?
Verdict: No, not really, Overgrowth is going to take a very long time to finish, and if you buy it now, you will probably lose interest after the first few hours of playing. Overall, it's a 5.8/10 for me.

Divinity: Original Sin 2 is my 2017 game of the year. If you’re looking for a rich and compelling story with challenging turn-based combat and an RPG experience as rewarding and fun as some of the most popular RPGs out there then look no further than Divinity: Original Sin 2.
The story is really well written with many different ending outcomes depending on the choices you make and don't make. The world feels alive and there are many ways to complete quests with or without combat. As you progress you definitely feel the fear and oppression within the world with each NPC you meet having their own take on what is happening in the world and their own opinions of your character.
Character creation is in depth and allows for many possibilities. There are five races to chose from; Human, Elf, Lizard, Dwarf and Undead, with Undead allowing you to play an Undead version of any race. Each race is definitely unique in terms of look, racial passive abilities and how they are perceived and treated within the world. Depending on the race and gender you choose NPCs will react differently to you and new dialogue options open up. You can also choose specific background tags for your characters which open up even more dialogue choices.
There are wide range of base classes available but you aren’t locked into any specific class preset. You can customise your stats to create whatever class you want. Want to be a heavy armour wearing rogue? A robe wearing warrior who dual wields? A ranger who can also sling fire? The possibilities are seemingly endless.
You can choose to travel with up to three companions but there is nothing stopping you from going it alone. Each companion has their own backstory and motives and will often stop to ask you whether they can talk to an NPC before you as that particular NPC is important to their personal stories. Companions also have their own personalities and can react positively or negatively to actions you take, if they stop liking you enough then they can permanently leave your party. Each companion is voice acted really well and since playing with silent companions in Early Access the voice acting is really appreciated. As well as companions every NPC is voice acted with some performances being better than others but on the whole the voice acting is really well done. You can also chose to play as either one of the companions allowing you to experience their stories first hand.
The entire game can also be played with three other people cooperatively with each person being allowed to explore different areas at the same time, meaning that if one player gets into combat then the others won’t if they’re somewhere else. The game also features a Dungeons and Dragons esque Game Master mode allowing you to create your own campaigns using the game’s assets and DM for a party of players. Assets can be added, removed and edited on the fly and any campaigns you create can be shared with other players.
Overall Divinity: Original Sin 2 is definitely worth the asking price. There’s loads of replay value and many hours worth of compelling and meaningful story to experience. If you love story rich RPGs then you’ll love Divinity: Original Sin 2.

Valkyria Chronicles is a charming combination of military and drama elements packed in a turn-based RPG. Story is well made (though some parts are cheesy), there is large character diversity (50+ characters in your squad, each member is unique, has own traits and backstory), enormous possiblities of weapon, armor and tank modifications/upgrades, numerous missions which require a lot of time to win, skirmishes and challenges give extra money and experience. Combat is well made (except scouts being overpowered and tanks having an odd weak spot) and players will get into difficulties sometime. I don't know how to describe AI, sometimes it acts recklessly and orders units to run at your line of fire, sometimes it learns your mistake and makes you pay for it (for example, I spent half an hour on a mission and I thought it was almost over, but enemy reinforcement arrived - a lancer which ran to back of my tank, I didn't have any infantry on its right side, so the lancer needed just one shot to make game over), also a good thing is that there is unlockable hard difficulty. Including DLC-s, 50+ hours are needed to complete the game, but that depends on personal preferences. There are more types of ground (city, desert, forest, plain), numerous obstacles and buildings, rows, which make combat interesting.
One of few bad sides of the game is bit cheesy story. Valkeria Chronicles is a turn-based tactics game. During your turn, you spend movement points to take control of a character, in which time you can move around, fire once, and continue to move until out of stamina. Characters have some individual traits, but job classes share the same level, so it has more of an Advance Wars feel. Permadeath is possible, but you have the ability to rescue characters, so it’s not as brutal as classic Fire Emblem.
Enemies can fire on you during the movement phase but you can take your time aiming and calculating damage, so think of it like VATS from Fallout 3.
The story in VC1 is decent, although not as complex as your usual JRPG. The narrative style, however, is pretty cool. 100% playable in Intel HD graphics.

There's no tutorial, but the game does a good job of teaching you through doing; enemy types are introduced gradually, and you learn pretty quickly that - for example - you can shoot down missiles. Still, some things could likely use a bit more explanation than they get; hats aren't just cosmetic, they'll also negate the first hit you take. The doors leading to different types of areas are pretty easy to figure out, though there are a couple that aren't super obvious. Still, if you're paying attention that's not going to be a problem.
Basically, buy the game already. It's 10 bucks! It's real good!
EDITED TO ADD: Upon starting a new game, I bought a hat, and noticed that the little text snippet reserved for amusing anecdotes on other vending machines flat out says "hey this hat'll block your first hit", paraphrasing. So... User error. Disregard.

Good Robot is a lot of fun.  How fun?  Well, the last time I enjoyed a shoot-em-up this much, I was a kid playing Galaga-knockoffs on a monochrome monitor in my father's office.  The game has a lot going for it, including:
- Visuals!  If it moves, kill it.  If it glows, dodge it.  (If it bounces, panic!)  The backgrounds are sparse, but that's a good thing when you're tracking a dozen enemy robots and dodging a screen full of projectiles.
- Sound design!  The game continues to track your bullets after they leave the screen, and you can tell if you've killed something by listening for the tell-tale sound of an exploding robot.  Even better, you can tell whether the the robot dropped cash or loot.  And the music is darned good, too.
- Controls!  You can switch between gamepad and mouse & keyboard on the fly.  Let go of the mouse and pick up the pad--or vice versa--no menus necessary.  You don't even have to pause the game.  (But you probably should.)
- The thrill of discovery!  What do those little icons on the doors mean?  Why not go through and find out?  The game is semi-random, but the patterns are fairly simple.  It's easy to pick up and learn as you go.

Positive:
-True F2P.
You can avoid spending a single dime and, in about a month of average gameplay, you can already be approximately "middle class".
-Very little exclusive(cash only) content.
Unless you count purely cosmetic stuff, as far as I can remember, the only game-affecting cash item was a Prime Extractor or something that nobody needs anyway.
-Relative diversity of gameplay.
Has flying minigame, spying minigame, PvP, raids, "open world" minigame, treasure hunting etc.
-Runs on potatoes.
Pun intended, but it can be played on budget laptops with either bottom-end dGPU and even most iGPUs. At 720p and 30> fps, of course. Though it's best not to visit Earth(the starting planet -.-) or Plains of Eidolon(on Earth -.-) if you are running 4GB RAM or below.
-Abundant online community(almost no wait times).
Unless you want specific premade games. Pubs are most generally easy to find.
-Mostly PvE.
The game is built as PvE and does not force you to play PvP.
Negative:
-Warfarm\Bugframe
95% of the game's content is farming. The last thing I recommend is putting effort into it. There will always be the drones to do it for you, even if they dare to "report" you to their momma. Likewise, almost 5 years out and it's still in beta. Yes.
-Narcissistic developers
They have the morale integrity of a shoe. Like Trion games, they have a boner for streamers, and so I would VERY MUCH advise you to stay AWAY from any Warframe streamer or Youtube channel. There may be one or two decent, but, face it, most are fugly. Those, who aren't - were either banned or have quit. And the most popular - are some of the worst examples of creatures humanity has to offer.
-Lack of proper endgame.
The game generally scales into three categories:
1. Things you have to farm
2. Things you can solo.
3. Things you can't solo or shouldn't solo.
As it stands, to feel actual action, intensity, thrill - your best bet is to take a bunch of utter noobs and go to some "high level" mission. Watch as they struggle to kill enemies, die and make your gameplay all the more impactful. However, bear in mind that this scenario is an ABSOLUTE waste of time with zero pay. Because, mark my words, there will NOT be equal endgame content for a non-premade groups of players to properly enjoy and be rewarded for.
The game's difficulty follows a principle: "Either you oneshot stuff, or stuff oneshots you". There is no real progression besides that. No strength in numbers, no tactical enemies or good AI. So, to add to the previous point of action, you may think that a Corrosive lvl 100 Sortie boss is hemorrhoid, but... only if it ends up as the aforementioned simulated noob scenario. In the end, it can be cheesed, because, due to the "oneshot rule" - it has to be cheesed. There is no other way to fight it.
Conclusion:
If you like games, like Marvel Heroes or Trove, basically mindless grinders with little coherent action, but ample opportunities to get some pixels, upgrade your character/account, hunt some heroin dragon and enjoy the beautiful scenery/graphics...
In other words, if you have nothing better to do with your life....
I recommend this game.
If you want to try something new, spend some time on vacation or otherwise - STAY AWAY FROM IT. You don't want to be sucked in, and unless you go all in, there is no point for you to even start. Save yourself the effort and "download" something else.

A spinoff of the mediocre MOBA, PW:Defenders is a decent enough tower defense game. What killed the game for me is the constant bugs and sudden loss of data.  Towers don't always hit their mark, bonuses are either not correctly applied or explained incorrectly, daily rewards and store offers disappear/reappear randomly, and achievements will stop functioning after a certain level.  This prevents any further progress through Steam's system, though they can still be earned in game.  Not long after losing the ability to gain Steam achievements my data was completely lost with no hope of recovery.  Still not sure how that happened, probably an error on their server regarding saves.
Looking to the forums shows absolutely no further dev interaction, patches, or support.  This is essentially dead software.  If you are hoping for patches or fixes, either the community will have to find a work around, or you're♥♥♥♥♥♥outta luck.  I bought this on sale for $2.00, and certainly got my money's worth out of it.  Even if I didn't complete it.  But at current full price of $10, it is definitely not worth it at all.

To start out with, I'm not basing this review off of any of the rumours or heresay, that speculate on whether Trion Worlds or XL gaming are in control of this title, who ruined it, or any of that nonsense. This review is based SOLELY on my on experience with this game.
ArcheAge is an older style of MMO. Theres very little hand holding, they don't flat out tell you how to do everything. You have to go through quests to figure things out, and if you want any sort of success you have to join a guild. This isn't a typical free to play MMO either, it's free to play in the same sense that world of warcraft is free to play. The only difference is that in ArcheAge your not limited to level 20.
ArcheAge is a subscription based game, your not really going to get the full enjoyment out of it without paying a subscription, and considering that the subscription isn't that much more than blizzards, you really don't have anything to complain about. yes there is a cash shop, yes it does have boosts and benafits for paying players, but most of these are for accelerating the gameplay.
There is NO instant gratification in this game, you WILL spend hours upon hours upon hours playing it if you want any sort of progress. There is a grind to it, but it's the sort of grind that isn't nearly as bad as it could be BECAUSE your able to do it with friends, which is HOW IT'S MEANT TO BE PLAYED. This game really encourages you to cooperate and work with guilds, families, it strongly punishes players who try to solo and be that "me against the world" stereotype.
Combat in this game doesn't follow the normal archetype system. Theres classes, called professions, that are constructed by players based on the specific talent trees you pick. Anyone who's ever played RIFT will see some similiarities there. However, customization of your character is all about your particular play style. Specifically, the actual abilities you select and how much you use them. For example, if I take talents that focus on stealth, melee combat, and ranged combat, But put more points in ranged combat than I do in the other two, then my character will lean more to ranged combat, simply because he'll have more skills to use towards that. Furthermore, if I want to be effective as a ranged character, I have to use my ranged abilities. Those abilities level just as your character does, the more you use them the higher level they beome, and thus the more powerful they get. You can't just click up your abilities and expect to hit hard with them, just like in real life, you have to practice to become stronger, and this applies with everything in the game.
Unfortunately there are some builds and setups that are clearly stronger than others, with certain weapons providing greater bonuses and thus being obvious choices. Because of that, a lot of pvp combat can see unfair, depending on how you like to play. However, I believe the game makes up for this by, once again, encouraging working with others. Instead of trying to fight players by yourself, try and make friends and always run with a group, whenever you intend to be in an area expecting a fight. It makes life a lot easier for you, trust me.
Further reinforcing the team work over all idea that seems to be this games theme, naval combat, something this game is able to boast about that no other MMO (so far as I've seen) can say, requires multiple people on a single naval craft to be effective. This is because the ships have multiple stations that have to be manually controlled by players to make the vessel effective. You'll have your captain, the guy driving the ship, and your crew who will usually be doing anything from manning the cannons to watching the radar, to even running repairs, depending on how dedicated you are to the fight.
However the Naval combat, and the guild wars combat for that matter, aren't something you can just hop into. They require significant amounts of preparation and contribution from those who intend to be involved. You don't just GET ammo for your cannons, you have to make it, and theres different kinds used for different situations. You can't just fix the boat either, you have to have a special, and quite frankly expensive, material in order to run repairs. The ship itself is also upgradable, with components that help you specialize with it for different roles, and all of that takes materials and work to put together.
And that is the biggest part of this game right there. The crafting. You will spend WEEKS, not even exagerating, doing everything from farming enough materials to build something, to putting those materials together in the actual construction of that building! And your limited by the Labor system, which is this little bar at the bottom left of your screen that goes from 0 to 1000 for non subs, and 0 to 5000 for subs. Understandably, subs have it easier, and that's not a bad thing, nor is it pay to win as alot of people seem to think. In truth, it's a way of limiting players who aren't paying for the game from getting through the content as fast as those who do pay. ArcheAge doesn't limit your character's level, like WoW does, so they have to find another way to stop you from enjoying the full content without paying for the game. Thus they slow you down, and force you to really put in copious amounts of time for everything you do.
See now what I was saying about increasing the game speed? Those boosts and things you see in the cash shop, are for the most part intended to help you with the constant and unending grind that is this game. Some people find this to be tedious and unattractive, but I beleive it's a matter of perspective. I personally find that achieving success over an enemy after putting in all the hours and work to reach that goal is quite the most fulfilling experience one can get from an MMO. And the grind itself I find to be plenty enjoyable, so long as theres friends to talk with and help out.
The biggest problem this game has is it's population. The majority of new players go to the fresh start servers, which sadly leaves the legacy servers severely hobbled. And because the population of the legacy servers is so low, you rarely get the enjoyable experiences that I've mentioned here, as one guild or another tends to grow to exceptional power and thus become inconquerable, because nobody else has the numbers to beat them.
All in all, this game isn't nearly as bad as some people would have you believe. By no means at all can it be called perfect, it has many many problems, not all of which i've even encountered. But for the price associated with it, it's really a good game. I mean, for around 15 dollars a month I get to enjoy playing with friends in a world where my efforts can help bring us to glory and conquest? Far as I'm concerned, that's worth it.

This platform/puzzle game surprised me.  I didn't expect to like it as much as I did.  The concept is pretty simple; collect blocks and dispense them in such a way as to help you get to the end of the level.  As you progress you will find that you must utilize the unique properties of the blocks to solve the stage.  In addition, there are challenges available for finishing the stage with the most collected blocks, as well as reaching a treasure box within the stage.  This gives the gamea  bit of replayability.  While most of the stages allow you the freedom to study the stage without any urgency, there are a handful of stages that require twitch reflexes and excellent timing (Big Mama, Child's Play).  These stages were challenging, but feel a bit out of place when the rest of the game is so much more cerebral.  The forced scrolling stages allow you to skip the stage, which is appreciated, but in other cases you will be permanently blocked until you can get the timing down.
Overall, this is an easy recommend for puzzle fans.

Good Robot presents itself as a Rogue-like, and indeed it is. But it's quite unique when compared to most self proclaimed rogue-likes. It's extremely arcadey! You gain nothing with each session except experience, unlike other games that give you extra characters, different perks, unlock upgrades to be obtained in the game etc. This game doesn't want you to keep playing under these pretexts, it wants you to keep playing because it's a tempting challenge. I always died with the impression that I could beat that if I were more careful. You know, the kind of difficult people enjoy and take it as a challenge and makes you want to try again. This is the replay mechanism on good robot. You can see this mechanism in effect on strangely unrelated games like Dark Souls and Flappy Birds. I can't believe I just put those two games in the same category.
But, as I said, it's a very arcadey game. It even has SCORE, good heavens (at the time of writing this edit I'm at 16th place of the global rank) It does what it does very well and nothing else. The visuals are pretty cool! but there is very little meaningful variation. You fly and shoot the whole time. But the combat is truly great; the immense variety of weapons, weapon combinations (you can have two at a time) , enemies and upgrade choices is a guarantee that it will take a long time for the game to be mastered by the player.
I don't have any real solid criticism that couldn't instead be characterized as "I would have done it differently", which is not criticism. Mostly, I would add more depth, make it less arcadey and less likely to be released by a small team. Yup, sounds like me. But a few simple things could be added without jeopardizing the project, like a different weapon system and the persistent perks between game sessions. But, reiterating, this would be a different direction, not better or worse.
Edit: I finished the game and my opinion did not change much. But I can add a few more words on it. I found the end game quite anti climatic, specially considering I was reading every flavor text I found. I also noted that weapon pick ups are not as simple as I first thought. There really is a huge number of weapons and they don't seem to be uniformly distributed in the game. I say this because I found some very powerful stuff as I progressed through the game, stuff I never saw in the earlier levels. This prompts some possible different strategies, because I was completely ignoring the weapon store! using my money purely on upgrades. But I'm digressing now.
The fact that I'm still thinking about the game and possible strategies after getting that lame ending is a good sign.
