And you're left to destroy all the robots on a number of environments that seem to have killed all the humans. Your robot has two weapons - a primary rapid firing weapon and a slower heavy hitting weapon and matching primary and secondary is the key to beating a lot of the levels. The robots that you are up against are varied and have different behavior and weapons. You'll often find yourself trying to find a strategy to overcome the combinations of enemies as you can get some very interesting emergent mechanics arising with the different enemies working together. The game has some influences from the old PC game Descent, but as this is a 2D game, it's considerably easier to play. Old 8-bit games such as Robotron and Paradroid on the C-64 as also evident with the visibility of the robots and how your skill in nipping in and out of robots and bullets to avoid trouble. There are elements of a "bullet hell" shooter as well, but as you are more mobile than the bullets and have environmental cover to hide from.  It is extremely survivable as long as you keep moving to use the environment to your advantage.
In addition to the shooting, you can also collect and buy weapons to upgrade your weapons. There also shops for upgrading abilities and also buying "invulnerabity hats" which protect you from attacks. You lose your hat when you are hit. This hat mechanic also adds an additional difficulty level to to the game where you get achievement for keeping your hat. The highest achievement is to keep the same hat to finish the game - which means that you have to avoid being hit in every level. No mean feat, but it does add a considerable challenge for the seasoned gamer. There is also some very good humour text in the menus and news reports reflecting the corporate news media trying to cover up the crisis. Complete with retractions and churnalism.
The graphics are well done with lots of atmosphere for the various level and robot designs. The level scrolls around with parallex layers and fogging and the lighting cone from the robot is a nice touch. The visibility means that you have to keep looking around you to avoid being ambushed from side passages.
The levels are procedurally generated and are different each time to keep the game feeling new. You have a choice of levels to move onto as each are themed - some have certain classes of enemies, some have more money to buy stuff with, some have "special robots" and other have environmental hazards. The final level you choose is the boss level and from there you move onto the next world.  It's nailbiting stuff as you have to juggle your money to replenish your shields and 'lives' whilist buying weapons and performance upgrades. And you can find yourself making life difficult if you can't adapt your playing strategy when a new design of robot turns up.
The music is an electronica soundtrack which changes from world to world. World 3 has a Chinese design and the music has various Asian themes built into it. So there's quite a bit of variety to the music. The sound effects are just what you need for a shooter such as this with audio cues for events you need to watch for such as robots spawing in at the factories and when you find yourself surrounded by heat seeking missiles you need to shoot.
The overall impression is of an extremely well designed game that draws upon some games from the past to bring them up to date. I've played this for about six hours now and it's proving difficult to put down. There are some some minor issues that the developer is currently patching that don't affect the game, but given that a very small team of put this together and did such a good job, it's well worth the asking price.

How many of you enjoy card collecting games like “Magic: The Gathering?” How many of you play “Defense Grid” and “Sol Survivor” religiously like your life depended on it?  If you raised your hand to both of those questions, then there’s no doubt in my mind that you’ll take a liking to “Prime World: Defenders”.  This game reminds me a bit of “BattleForge”, a card collecting real-time strategy game that I was heavily invested in for quite some time.  In this case however, you’ll be collecting cards that will form your tower defense arsenal and be tasked with slaying mutants and baddies by the thousands.
Overall, I really enjoyed my experience with this game.  I’ve thrown hours into this game and have been showing no signs of slowing down any time soon.  “Prime World: Defenders” is an incredibly addicting game that I’m glad to see has brought something new to the tower defense table.  Yes, it’s a bit grindy…but I’m finding it to be the good kind of grindy.  I also want to praise the game for not including any sort of real money store or microtransaction system, which would be very easy to do in this particular type of game.  Everything purchased in the game is done via coin, which you’ll be earning as you play.  The mission generator (which you’ll see after the first few missions) adds almost unlimited replayability to the game.  My only real complaint (if you could call it one) was that the combat and tower animations were a bit generic.  While pretty, I didn’t feel “wowed” by the towers I placed or the enemies I saw…they just simply served their purpose.  If you’re looking for the bottom line, then I’ll simply say that I highly recommend it, especially for the ten dollar price tag that it currently advertises.

This is going to be a review of a game that is not yet finished. A lot of people are saying good stuff about it and I have to agree with them. However there is one thing they avoid to say or maybe they feel emotional attachment to the game therefore they won't say it.
I on the other hand will say it because it was my +/- 20 pounds that was wasted here.
This game has a big potencial but the biggest "flaw" its it biggest "strength"
After watching some videos about the game I was really hyped about it. WOW! We need more games like this! Third person melee combat / action adventure ( perhaps later RPG dunno... its in alpha ).
I was expecting to have awesome combat system you would expect from a fighting game ( like DOA 5 or SF or Tekken you name it... ) but it fails to fulfill my expectations. Combat is fluid yes but it feel unfair! Here's why :
1. There is no tutorial at all ( maybe because it's alpha )
2. You have only 2 BUTTONS?! One for attack and one for block ( so forget combos ) sure you have jump and crouch too...
3. You have to be at the right distance from your enemy to perform CORRECT attack. If you are close you will either punch or kick with knee. If you are further away you will do roundhouse kick... etc. If for example you want to punch or do a swift kick YOU CAN'T!!! Because enemy won't stay in the same spot to let you come closer! SO IT FEELS CHEAP! I got so angry that the character wouldn't do what I wanted him to do because I was either not facing enemy properly or distance was too short or too long. So it comes down to timing and observing what your enemy will do while try to position yourself so you can counter.... This system doesn't work and causes massive frustrations.... SURE it's fast and can be satysfying if your character will perform well ( or actually do what you intended to do ).
AT LEAST put a lock-on system for newbie players so I can always FACE the enemy and focus on either attacks or defending! ( Just like in Dark Souls ). Seriously there is no way to control whether you going to punch or kick... it happens automatically by judging distance.
Other than that I have no problems with this game. Graphics are good for alpha and animations look ok ( but i would slightly slow them down ).... This game has a potential to become some special ( it would be nice to see really good campaign and possibly co-op whether split screen or online ). Tons of mods will save this game for sure.

So yeah I feel dissapointed... I hope it will turn out good in the end though. I can't recommend it just yet.

Hexoscope combines hex-grid pattern-matching/swapping with pipeline type puzzles to create a really soothing, comfortable little game with an astonishing electronic soundtrack.
It is difficult to come up with new basic concepts for a puzzle game, but sometimes combining two already existing ones results in something great. Hexoscope is like that; it mixes tile swapping with pipeline/plumbing puzzles, and glues them together with a nice little trick as a base rule: you need to build the pipeline in order to activate more tiles to swap.
The game offers 6×12 stages of increasing difficulty, where each stage only determines the shape of the board and the puzzles themselves are randomly generated. Sometimes the result is almost obvious, sometimes you need to build your pipeline in a certain direction to acquire a tile you need to progress towards your real goal.
This means the replay value is quite high, and thanks to the great electronic soundtrack it can be difficult to put this game down. Considering its super low price tag, Hexoscope is a steal, even at full price.

Starsiege: Tribes was the game that got me hooked on PC gaming way back in 1998. When I was younger, I would stay up for 2 or 3 days straight swapping between Tribes and Age of Empires. Whenever I was inevitably kicked off the family computer, I'd pop in Final Fantasy VII on the classic Playstation. Oooh yes, the good old days.
Midair brings those nostalgic memories back, but in a fresh and vibrant way.
Right from the start you can tell Midair is it's own thing. It belongs in the FPS-Z genre, and it's really not just another Tribes clone.
Midair has made jetpack flying feel unique and new, yet pulls a few tricks from the Starseige: Tribes days.
...  isn't the right word. You'll see what I mean when you start trying to take turns mid flight. I guess, a better way to put it would be to say it
like your armor has
to it. Remember skiing in Starseige: Tribes? Ya know, the OG of FPS-Z. Well, Midair feels a bit like that, but a little more refined.
OH, one thing I can say for certain, and it's not a major announcement, but I gotta get it off my chest..  is that Midair alpha is
already better than Tribes: Ascend.
Let's talk about the Ring Launcher. Personally, I love it. I think the devs did a great job with reimagining the Disc Launcher. It fits right in with the other iconic FPS-Z disc launching weapons. The reload animation is awesome, the trail it leaves behind when you fire it is much easier on the eyes compared to the old Tribes disc launchers. It just
right. The only con I have right now is getting use to calling it a Ring Launcher instead of a Disc Launcher.
Grenades -  I like the explosion animation, but I don't like how you throw them. It's a little janky. This is a Closed Alpha review, so I'm sure many things like this will get tweaked.
Overall, I really like it so far:
- It's gorgeous.
- The maps feel well made.
- The weapons, though similar to Tribes, have their own distinct feel to them in Midair.
- Skiing and utilizing your jetpack stay true to the FPS-Z style, but may be tougher to master.
- Annnd one of your taunt animations is to flip somebody off. It has that TF2 style of humor.
I should add that at this point in development, the game isn't well optimized. It's making my PC run warmer than usual and FPS is capped at 120.

TL;DR: Midair is a true successor for Tribes 1 & Tribes 2 Classic for the FPS-Z genre. Far better than Tribes: Ascend and not using the money grabbing tactics that Hi-Rez used. By purchasing Early Access, you are buying a 'Progression Pass' which will unlock all gameplay content FOREVER. Many folks from the Tribes communities had an issue with the price before, and now I think it is very reasonable for you to buy in as this is the price it'll be staying at until the full free to play release.
If you've never played any of the above games, Midair is very friendly to newbies on the learning curve compared to past titles and great fun as soon as you manage to hit a disk in someone's face. The movement might seem difficult at first, but in the end will the reason why you keep opening the game up.
I've followed this game since its beginning all the way back when it was planned as 'Legions: Overdrive 2.0', and then 'Project Z', and then finally 'Midair'. Releasing on steam is only the latest step on a long eventful journey. You will not find a developer team who are based all over the world that has spent more of their free time and passion on making a 'indie' title with AAA production values. That being said, the game is still in a unfinished state from a full release hence why it is still in early access, so don't be surprised if you find bugs or the game balance is a little off, BUT! the developers want your feedback, no matter how small or insignificant.
About Midair's gamemodes: Midair has a strong gamemode called 'LCTF' and is what I suspect will be the main gameplay mode for those who just want pure jetpack 5v5 Capture the Flag. It is pretty much feature complete and over half the maps for the mode are finialised with more on the way. 'Base' or just 'CTF' is trying to be angled as the main gameplay mode for all, which involves greater numbers of players, generators to power the base and vehicles to use. While I think this mode will be fairly popular, I don't think it'll catch on massively with competitive play and LCTF will be the main competitive mode. 'Arena' is another gamemode similar to Clan Arena from Quake, once you're dead you're out of the round, first team to 5 rounds wins. 'Rabbit' is final gamemode and involves only one flag and your objective is to hold the flag as long as possible to score points. More gamemodes are planned, with a vote planned for the kickstarter backers soon, with three gamemodes on offer: Jackpot, Hunters or Duel.
In terms of game performance, the game runs really well on the GPU, but if you have a weaker CPU your fps will be lower the more people that join. This is probably the weakest part of the plan to make the game Free to Play, as I have an i5-2500k @ 4.5ghz and struggle to maintain consistent 120 frames once there's more than about 12 players and it only gets worse the more players that join, so for a full CTF server, it will be struggle, especially if you are competitive. Optimisations will be coming, but because of the load that Unreal Engine 4 puts on your machine, I doubt this will improve much. Currently I have a thread on the Midair forums that goes indepth on graphical options using Unreal Engine, so if you are struggling to run the game, try my configurations out:
So what isn't in the game yet that will be in the full release?
- More completed maps.
- Demos.
- Parties.
- Clan support.
- In depth stats.
- 3 additional weapons.
- Cosmetics.
What will probably be coming after release (in no particular order)?
- Matchmaking.
- Community map making.
- More gamemodes.
- Advanced demo tools (keyframes etc).
- UI Customisation.
- Additional Weapons.
- More cosmetics.
Now is a great time to jump on the bandwagon and try Midair out, it's only going to go up from here.

Pro - Its Dungeon Keeper all over again!
Con - Its Dungeon Keeper all over again...
Now, don't get me wrong, I love the original Dungeon Keepers. Love the humour, the creatures and minions. And when I learned about this game, I was thrilled! A new dungeon keeper?! Awesome! And when I first started playing, I was happy as the nostalgia washed over me...
The thing is, this isn't 'Dungeon Keeper 3.0'. Its not even 'Dungeon Keeper 2.5'. Its 'What if we remade Dungeon Keeper 2 with new graphics and new names/creatures so we don't get sued'.
This, in itself, IS NOT A BAD THING. But if you played DK2 to death, as i did, then you will notice that it tries to be more of the same, and it doesn't always succeed.
I do heartily recommend this game, as it was fun whilst it kept my attention (almost 9 hours). But it did only feel like I was only adding to the hundreds of hours I'd already put into DK1 + 2 - and as such, It was just more of the same for me. At the end of the day, it replicates the originals so well/much, that I may as well be playing the originals - something I haven't had the urge to do in 15 years. Yes, there are new mechanics added, but its like saying that adding a 'go faster stripe' to a car changes the car; It doesn't.
Conclusion
- If you've never played the originals, and think you might enjoy this, give it a go.
- If you tried playing the originals, enjoyed it but the outdated graphics ruined it for ya, give this a go.
- If you played the originals when they came out, loved them, and want more, give this a go.
- If, however, you played the originals and want something MORE than an almost 20 year old game with a fresh lick of paint (however awesome it was) - might wanna give this a miss.

This game kicks you into the fuzzy nightmare of a hacked brain. It's jarring, ridiculously fun and, so far, looks fantastic. The art direction is consistent in using bright colors and contrast with deep shadow to highlight and compliment the game's very consistent, creative universe. This obscene lighting makes it feel like you're on mescaline in a fun house, but done it's done well: like glowing pinstripes, not 3 coats of neon paint. The hidden paths often use shadow or over-saturated, very bright areas to blend into the scene.
And then there's the music. This is the first game to made me want to purchased the soundtrack so I could support the artist. It's the techno anthem to a 90's Fetish Ball heard from a padded cell in the building one over. It's flows and mutates perfectly with the game, like a supporting character.
The music really takes the game over the top.
The game is fun to play, sure, but it's fun to just stop and listen while you play. I had to stream the game so I could share it with non-gaming friends who enjoy this kind of music.
It's certainly not deep, but I'm only a few hours in and I'm already getting paranoid and don't trust anyone. (That's my normal state of mind, though, so it might just be me.) I constantly click my thumb sticks on accident and trigger abilities, but it usually helps. Other than that it's a complete gem. I have the attention span of a over-caffeinated ferret, but I'm probably playing this one straight through.
The combat is fast, easy and fun. It's a twin stick shooter with a melee weapon and a gun you can grab from the piles that accumulate while bashing, slicing and mowing your way through a bunch of baddies. It's forgiving in that you can make a few (or a baker's dozen) mistakes in a battle and not immediately get beaten. And you can respec your skills on the fly, changing what skills and even upgrades you have based on your opponents and play style. Checkpoints are decently spaced. All in all, it's very gamer friendly. I have not fiddled with things, but I assume you can set it to make it quite challenging if that's your cup of tea. I'm quite happy with the purchase.

I was a bit sceptical at first playing this game, since it looked like a regular turn based card game. Seeing there was the odd combat in the trailer, I decided to give it a go.
Lets just say I was pleasantly surprised and got caught up in it :)
Hand of Fate is a card game, but only on the "map" to describe it. Here you will be playing against The Dealer. The game offers some strategy, since you can't just jump around and do everything, as your character eats food at every card tile. If you have no food, you start losing hitpoints and die.
Various cards you jump into can be loot, combat and the regular "chance" based draw. Drawing a failure at these chance draws can result in just skipping it, taking damage, losing equipment and so on. Rather painful, but with a keen at some times you can notice where the success cards land.
Combat leads you to a small map where your character is battling enemies. This function in the same way as a Hack'n'Slash game. Any equipment you gained from the card "map" helps you here. It's a bit repititive, but things escalate as you go further into the story and more is unlocked. Boss battles are also part of the game.
All this combined was a nice little gem for me and thus I can recommend it.
The downside:
The game is completely RNGesus based, which means you can run into some rather mean encounters even at the beginning of a new "map". This gets worse as you unlock more and more encounters and equipment, so while the encounters and boss battles are doable, it's very painful with starting equipment for example.
The combat can feel a bit sluggish at points, but I've heard this is better in Hand of Fate 2.
Combat also "relies" a lot on having a shield, since that is the only option to deflect ranged or do counter attacks in melee. If you don't have a shield, you manually have to determine when an enemy is about to hit you. This is painful as you're forced to evade insted, rolling away and sometimes this is tough to control due to character and camera.

It's XCOM, except you control your units as if it were a third person shooter and isn't grid based. There's cover, there's half cover (albeit implemented pretty terribly in this game), there's stupid % misses and hits, there's levelling (although this is only for unit classes, not for individual units), there's choosing your roster (which you can't rename unfortunately), there's a decent story and you actually come to care for your characters.
It can be fairly challenging, with some missions requiring a few tries, and since permadeath isn't hard to avoid it's not necessary to restart a mission because someone died, but rather because you failed your objectives or got wiped. This, I feel, is good because it took me a long time per mission, and since I was playing with a friend we were constantly discussing our tactical decisions each turn. A few mission I managed to cheese completely, but overall that isn't very easy to do and presented a decent challenge, with quite a few missions in the second half of the game requiring ~3 tries.
Art is like the screenshots, a very distinct art style, and the music is good too. Overall, would recommend if you're a fan of turn based strategy and don't mind anime-like story and art.

This game is not without flaws, and your enjoyment of it can depend greatly on how you like it's mechanics. Most crucial among those is a progression system that allows you to level up your towers between missions through a collectible card system. You can buy additional cards as well as boosters with ingame currency (no microtransactions whatsoever in the steam version) and use those to evolve your towers, unlocking the ability to upgrade them during missions, or infuse them, making them more effective. Different tower cards also have different rarities, with some being straight upgrades from their common versions. This leads to the first major flaw with the game, as the card rewards for side-missions are random, leaving you hoping for a specific tower to drop because at some point in the game, about 10-12 story missions in, you will hit a brick wall of difficulty. Once you get the next 'tier' of basic towers properly evolved and infused it becomes easier again, but getting these towers is mostly a case of farming sidemissions in hopes that RNG will bless you with the right rewards. I feel the upgrade system worked well inherently, but adding tiers to the towers completely broke it.
Difficulty tends to be all over the place in general. For example, finishing the normal mode of the game unlocks a heroic mode and two extra long survival missions. But with the towers required to beat the last level I had zero difficulty in the survival missions, often mashing the rush button to send in more gits because my towers ground everything to paste from start to finish. The heroic modes also felt hugely dissapointing, as I was able to blitz all of them with next to no effort up to the last level, which I overcame with two retry's and a bit of tweaking the tower placements.
The missions themselves however, are well-built for the most part, with the only hiccup being the randomized levels you get for your sidemissions. The game essentialy re-uses previously finished levels and adds random buffs to some tiles and inpassable rocks to the other. This meant you couldn't rely on a single layout and had to adapt, which greatly increased their replay value. Admittedly it could benefit from removing the first few levels from the map pool, since they're so small you run out of things to build or upgrade halfway through the harder sidemissions and can only sit and cast the odd spell, waiting for the waves to inevitably overrun your defense.
The towers themselves start out rather bland with the basic all-round tower, the slow tower and the anti-air tower, but later tiers add some much needed variety, with the highest tier offering some interesting options to mix and match into all new ways to make the Touched's lives impossible.
The Touched is the generic enemy faction in this game and consist of a collection of fantasy villains like kobolds, ogres and trolls. The only remarkable enemy is the pink floating marshmallow... thing that occasionally teleports forward and suddenly sneaks past your defenses. No really, you'll know it when you see it... and then you'll rage.
The game has a story and a linear set of missions to follow along with that, but it's cringeworthy at best. There's no major twists, even if the game tries very hard to set one up for you. The voice-acting is mostly terrible, with a special place in hell for the short snippets played during the missions.
TLDR: the gameplay is good, but beware that the difficulty can spike wildly between missions and most of the times the only solution is to farm sidemissions. Also there's a story, but who plays tower defense games for the story?

In Hexoscope your goal is to build a path from the power generators to the power receivers. In each level you start at the power generator and start placing connectors next to each other to make a path towards the receiver. You move connectors by swapping the position of two connectors. The catch is that you can only move connectors that are either connected to the power generator or are next to a connector that is connected to the power generator. This means that you will have to create paths to different parts of the level to retrieve a connector piece that you need to complete your path to the receiver.
Despite being only $0.99 Hexoscope is a very good puzzle game.

The most interesting feature of the game comes from the many unique encounter and equipment cards that you gain as you work your way through the main campaign. You can build your own adventure by selecting which cards you've earned that you want to include each time you set off on another story.
The deck that you build modifies your experience each time you play. The story encounters build on each other and present you with these mini quest narratives that you have the chance of furthering each time you play a portion of the main story. Some of the best equipment you can add to your deck come from these events, but you can't just select what armor or weapons you want to equip at the start, depending on what cards you include in your deck gives you a chance to find them in your next playthrough.
For me the game started off very easy and after about halfway through the difficulty ramps up and becomes a lot more punishing. The combat encounters can become repetitive after a while as the fighting gameplay is not very deep and boils down to simply attacking, dodging, and countering. Some of the weapons and armor have unique abilities and attributes however this does little to change the feel of fighting the same handful of enemy models repeatedly. I feel like this weaker aspect of the game is more than made up for through the many events that enfold through each playthrough especially thanks to the mysteriously voiced narrator, The Dealer who guides you through his game.

If I told you this game is Rogue meets a collectible card game meets Arkham Asylum and that it's
, I wouldn't be surprised if you didn't believe me. None of the elements are particularly deep, but the combination is. The game starts with a standard set of equipment cards and a deck of encounters. When beginning an adventure, the Dealer shuffles your encounter deck with some of his own and deals out (face down) a pattern that serves as your map. Each turn costs food to explore the next location (by flipping over the card). You might get enemies to fight, a shop or the exit. But sometimes you get a challenge that awards you new cards for your next adventure.
Some of the challenges award you with the next part of a story. Each story is
interesting enough to not mind losing all your health and starting over. This isn't amazing writing, but just solid, workmanlike storytelling, which is rare enough in games. But you'll generally want to keep going in order to continue collecting more cards. You'll be collecting equipment, blessing and curses that change the rules of the game.
Fighting enemies works a lot like the Batman brawler games. Success depends on reflexes, pattern memorization and having the right equipment. (It also helps to use a controller. Mouse and keyboard works, but combat is tuned for analogue stick and buttons.) One of the little pleasures is equipping a weapon, shield, armor or helmet that not only helps you fight better, but also changes the way your character model looks. In particular, I always am happy to get a helmet that replaces the fairly ugly default head. There's a clear effect in combat for each equiped item, blessing and curse. And the results of combat, particularly health lost and gold found, translate up to the card game. There are even maze encounters that challenge you to dodge through a series of traps to collect treasure of various sorts.
All the while, the Dealer provides running commentary. It repeats quite a bit, but I always want to turn the sound on because the canned phrases are delivered so well and there's always new dialog added as you find new encounters. In a very real sense you are playing against the Dealer who wishes for your destruction, but always plays fair. Even the occasional three-er-four-card Monte you are forced to play from time to time can be won consistently if you watch carefully.
In the end, this is a game that manages to be more than the sum of its gameplay elements.

I would highly recommend this game, especially if you enjoy fantasy RPGs but are bored with what's already out there.  It succeeds where many RPGs fail.
Pros:
-The combat system is great!  Spell synergies, interaction with the environment, teleporting enemies, and summoning familiars are a few things that really vitalize each encounter and make it feel like there are myriad ways to win.  Combat is NEVER a grind, each battle is unique and you are never mashing a button to win.  If you lose, try a different strategy, sneak to a better starting position, or change equipment.
-Voice acting and writing seem much improved over the first installment.  I played a bit of Divinity Original Sin 1, but couldn't stay engaged because the writing and voice acting seemed a bit bland to me.  In DOS II, I haven't heard a single line yet that pulled me out of my immersion and every performance is quality.  Writing is smart and often times very funny. I will say the main plot isn't totally drawing me in yet, but I'm only just starting Act 2, so there's much left for me to see.
-One thing I really like, though a somewhat small detail, is that armor looks different when worn on different people.  Like a dwarf wearing a robe will look different than an elf wearing the same robe.
Cons:
-You basically HAVE to save scum your way through this game.  Any time something goes right, save.  It takes some training if you aren't used to that and can be really frustrating at first.  They really should have a more sensitive autosave system because it should be saving every 2 minutes.
-Some bugs with abilities I've noticed.  Sometimes an item will give you an ability, and when you equip it a glitch makes it so you don't get the ability.  Or you will remove the item and still have the ablity.  I expect this to be fixed at some point, but it's worth noting.  Not gamebreaking at all, but can be slightly annoying.
-If you are playing with a controller...don't.  Basically anything you have to do in a menu will take 10X longer to do and there are actions you can't even do when using a controller.  It's nice that they have the option to use one, but they need to do some UI tweaks and give it the same functionality as using mouse and keyboard before it's practical.
-Early game is very difficult since you don't have any good equipment and there are few options for battles to gain EXP, unless you want to just attack a random NPC.  Takes a while to get the hang of combat if you aren't used to it, but Dark Souls was the same.  Just have to tough it out.

Valkyria Chronicles is a fresh and interesting take on the turn based strategy genre that is executed sub-par, resulting in a rather average game.
As far as I know, Valkyria uses a unique combat system that mixes in turn based moves with a weird (slightly artificial) real time movement system.  You have a certain ammount of turns you can spread out amoung your forces however you see fit, but multiple turns on the same unit decreases thier overall movement.  After your moves are used up, its the enemies turn and vice versa.  The common, expected elements are here: cover, supressing fire, different unit types and weapons.  Then there is the single tank, which functions as an all powerful super unit, you get to use which drastically changes the standard formula and adds a lot of fun.  There are lots of things to level up and collect which is great, and bonus missions to explore, altough these are just reskins of previous missions.  F
While these are strong elements to a strategy game, there are a fair share of negative elements that balance out the fun.  The gameplay can be a bit janky-- the tank in particular has its own mind and will sometimes go where you want without problem or will spend all of its movement poitns just kind of vibratingn in place while you yell at the screen.  There are obvious strategy elements mission such as the ability to cover corners which is bigger than you think when the game insists you use your tank as a mobile barrier.  Finally, the real time system is implemented poorly as the enemies are always firing back regardless of whether or not you are spending movement points. This means merely looking around or changing weapons as you plan is punihed and essentially fatal in some cases.  The way it is implemented is silly, the real time system feels like it could have been polished in a single day, it's so close.
More than anything, the battles are SLOW.  There is no speed up button for enemy phase and that is desperatly needed.  It becomes a slog later on as the battles get bigger and the battles have huge inactive segments.
The story exists. It's bland and nonoffensive. This could have been a much more compelling game with a better story, but with the uniqueness of the mechanics the focus isn't on this element.  Overall it neither gains or loses points on this fact.
Valkyria is an interesting game.  One that I could go on forever talking about what worked and what different because there are such huge swings on both sides.  What does that mean for you?  If you can find it cheap and are fine with playing through a quarter of the game just to get a feel for it, buy it.  Valkyria quickly loses its sizzle with the frustrations piling up and the level times and speed quickly killing any interest to play.  It's honestly a game I would love to play through all the way, but I don't think I could manage it.   Likewise, I would only recommend this game to players who realize they are going to grow bored fast, but can appreciate the few hours of fun playtime they had.
It's a recommendation, but it's a very tentative recommendation.

Good ideas, bad execution. I see why many people are into it, but also why most people aren't.
The core gameplay is IMO the best element. Turn-based mixed unit tactics with a single tank and accompanying platoon of infantry. Unfortunately, the missions seem to be designed with the idea in mind that you play through them multiple times until you can cheese spawns and AI behavior, rather than requiring a significant increase in skill. It is possible that hard mode expands on the gameplay, but it is locked behind completing the story.
The menus and controls are clunky. It's clear the game was made for console and limited efforts have been made to port it, but even compared to console games it takes ages to go through a simple upgrade menu or switch between game modes. In some menus you can see personality traits, but not what those traits mean.
The story and characters are as good as in an average anime. Fun though thoroughly unrealistic WW2 mixed unit tactics mixed with some awakening of ancient power nonsense. It is mostly presented through talking heads, through about five separate cinematics between missions, one or two of which is fully (though not particularly well) animated with the in-game 3D models. Menuing between each minute-long cinematic takes about ten seconds, when all that occurs is a change in scene or animation/talking heads.
A system exists for the personalities and traits of your squad and how these translate into battlefield advantages (though this is entirely deterministic), but other than the main characters they're all thrown at you at the same time, statistically nearly identical, and looking up their individual traits is a chore.
The music is okay, but gets repetitive quickly. You spend 90% of the time listening to the same three tracks, and they aren't (IMO) good enough to carry that much time. Especially since you always hear the first couple of seconds.
The graphics are good, for a ps2 game. Animations are stiff and form a small set. The art style is pretty, as you can tell from the screenshots up top, but it can be hard to tell whether obstacles are passable.
Also, tanks can't cross trenches. That is literally what they were built for.

There's an upgrade to this visual range but it costs nearly as much as a damage upgrade at first and wasting money on anything as useless as being able to look further in a game where upgrades both cost a lot and make very little difference. We're talking 10% more damage or slightly faster fire rate for what amounts to 3 full "cash" levels.
Enemy health scales so you have to keep up with your damage, and at some point you'll find you're no longer one-shotting small enemies that also get much better at dodging your shots. And then the game just starts cheating and has enemies that constantly double or spawn more enemies.
The sound effects sound like they were made in half an hour in a freeware 8 bit sound generator. The music ranges from unlistenable sing-songy nonsense to decent.
I like Shamus Young. I followed the game from the beginning. I'm sorry but I'm very disappointed.
Fans of Dungeon Keeper must purchase. There are some added complexities that I think make the learning curve a bit steeper, but it's great and we should keep digging.

BUT...
The baddies are in a constant state of "better than you can ever be" near the middle of the game. As you are upgrading towers, like in other tower defense games it should be EASIER to take out baddies so they just throw more baddies at you so you can then upgrade towers more, but in this game they not only throw more baddies at you but the baddies are near invincible and require HOURS AND HOURS of grinding to finally beat. Even with upgrades and such, the starting "prime" money/resources at the begining of each level is insanely low for the amount of powerful baddies that show up even in the first wave... The amount of prime you get from each kill does not go up with the difficulty increase and health increases the baddies get as the game progresses, so it makes it even harder to upgrade towers and such without pointless hours upon hours of grinding. Also, the types of towers that show up after the midpoint are completely random, so you may get some decent towers in a playthrough or you may never see those towers at all!  It just feels like a poorly executed port from a mobile platform "free to play, but pay to win" type game at that point. I mean I had towers upgraded that could do 5000+ damage in a single shot and it couldn't take down the weakest swarmers.
I really cannot recommend this game because of the insane difficulty curve that spikes in at the midpoint of the game; it goes from being fun, to being a decent challenge, to being an automatic rage quit. Maybe I will revisit the game and give a better review if the devlopers ever fix the balancing issues. (DEVS? If you are reading this, play the game 'Defense Grid" that is how a tower defense game should be done.)

This is an early access review.
A note regarding early access: Please do not buy early access games if you do not understand the concept of early access (which a lot of you don't, and are leaving unjustified negative reviews because of it). The price you are paying for early access games do not reflect the quality and value you will receive in the final product. Early access gives you the chance to pre-purchase and support the developers by acting as a tester of sorts, and having the ability to offer them feedback and ideas throughout your play time.
Having been a fan of Funcom's previous Conan game (Age of Conan) I decided to support them by buying the Barbarian Edition of Conan Exiles during early access. I was really impressed with how they interacted and took on board ideas from fans in the past, so I jumped at the chance to help out by playing this game during early access.
This is a survival-crafting-adventure game, kind of like a mash up between Minecraft and Skyrim. The atmosphere and style is great, and really throws you into the ruthless world of Conan. From the very beginning I felt like everything in this world was out to kill me, and my survival instincts kicked in. So far I'm really enjoying this game and having a lot of fun.
Once the bugs are squished and more and more features and content are added, this will be the go-to survival game.
At the moment the two biggest issues would be optimisation and server stability. Even high end systems are having trouble running this game at a decent FPS without sacrificing graphical quality, and playing on multiplayer servers can only make the problem worse.

The 3D graphics are superb, the gameplay is fun, but might be a bit grindy for some people, the sound is great with excellent music.  Every thing else is done right and very colorful!  All the menus are pleasing to the eye and the world map is awesome!  The choice of creatures is the best feature and they are all rendered in stunning 3D!!!  The towers and animations look great!  The list goes on and on...
The only negative thing that I found was that you can only grind the maps so many times before you stop getting silver and experience points for beating them.  Then you have to move along to the next map and grind that map to it's max times.  I think you can grind each map around 10 times or so.  I haven't counted, but it's enough to get some of your perks leveled up.  The cards really only represent the towers and do not come into play during combat like the card game Magic.  You will stack them to level your towers and magic, so to speak.  There are special cards to find and add to your towers too.  This is all done outside of combat.  Combat is your typical tower defense setup, but leveling towers happens outside of combat.  Makes sense and is pretty cool! :-)
The game is a little hard, but easier than some of the other TD games I've played.  I'll have to play some more and then come back and review it.  I do like it a lot so far.  The game is solid and has not crashed on me yet.

TL;DR: The price tag of this game is INSANELY LOW for the quality/quantity of puzzling. Buy it quick before they come to their senses!!
The Hexoscope boards contain randomly-generated pieces which each have lines pointing in various directions. You swap pieces to create an uninterrupted line between the terminals. A new mechanic/obstacle is introduced in each section.
As you progress through a level more pieces are unlocked which you can then use anywhere else on your chain. I've found a good strategy is to get as far as possible via one route, then if you get stuck double-back via a different route using the pieces you gained on your first push.
You can play levels on Normal or Turbo (timed) which gives you more points. The points system seems arbitrary though. You can repeat levels to get more points and they just accumulate for no apparent reason. No harm in it I suppose. People like points. Perhaps they'll develop a purpose if/when the Steam achievements arrive.
The colour and layout of the levels is crisp and sharp as a puzzle should be. The general game UI is beautifully done; level overview looks professional and intuitive; pull-out sliders on the level screens are pretty slick. Solid programming with no glitches whatsoever. The devs have taken the time to craft every facet of the game for smoothness and efficiency which makes a nice change from some of the ropey UIs I've seen lately (mentioning no names).
As expected, the background music is atmospheric and forgettable like most other puzzle games I've played. You don't want anything distracting while you're trying to concentrate.
Hard, challenging puzzles. There's no Eureka moment, it's more a series of small victories as you gain territory. Rage-quit is neutralised because if you really get stuck you can simply reset and try again with a different set of pieces. You really should resist the urge though because there always seems to be a way to swap a piece in the middle of the chain to open up the route again if you concentrate hard enough.
I'd like to address some of the negative reviews that say "I just reset till I got an easy solution". These people obviously haven't played further than the first few levels. Once you get onto the decent sized boards resetting will only give you a slightly better foothold, the benefit is minimal. I've long since stopped bothering to reset the start, I just take what's there.
Because the levels are randomly generated there can never be any guides or spoilers which is a rare quality in a puzzle game.
There's no native Linux support. It would be nice to have it, but I've discovered that this is one of the few Steam games that runs flawlessly in a VM. Not only that, but when I fired it up in a VM I was pleasantly surprised to find my previous progress from bare-metal Win appeared from the cloud, even the board I was in the middle of playing. Nice.
6 trading cards. No achievements yet but judging by the discussions on the community hub I suspect these will be coming soon. The game has plenty of potential for achievements so I'm looking forward to bagging some in the future.
6 sections with 12 puzzles in each, so 72 levels total. There's a good 15 hours of gameplay in a single playthrough but due to the random generation of levels there is UNLIMITED REPLAY VALUE. That's right, this is a $1 game that you can play forever!

I play a lot of $1 puzzle games, they're my favourite thing, and I'm usually happy to get 2 hours of gameplay out of them. Surely Hexoscope must be the best value game on Steam. They could charge $10 for this and it would still be a bargain.
This is now a permanent fixture on my Favourites list. I'll be dipping in and playing a couple of levels every day for months to come. I can't recommend this highly enough, it's just brilliant.
Here's a hot tip: if you like Hexoscope then check out Meld. It's also a hard join-the-hexagons puzzle game but the mechanics are totally different, it's the perfect complement to this game.

Seinarukana is a lengthy game with 6 possible routes. It's about 50% visual novel and 50% SRPG, imo. Your choices and gameplay matter for which route you get. With that said, each route simply focuses on a specific heroine in your harem, and the mechanics for getting the end you want is fairly obvious. It's technically a sequel to Aselia the Eternal, but other than taking place within the same universe (er.....multiverse) and a couple small easter eggs (
) this is completely stand-alone, and you won't lose anything from skipping the first one.
On the strategy side, units take turns traveling on points along fixed lines, with each point having small stat modifiers and healing/leveling/etc. taking place in towns. In this series, units are generally squads of 3 characters, with an 'attacker,' 'defender,' and 'supporter.' When your squad of 3 sprites meets an enemy squad of 3, they proceed to take turns beating each other up within that 'encounter' in a different screen. The vast majority of your tactics lies in how you organize your squads and their abilities (and there is a dizzying plethora of abilities) rather than how you move them, although that's important too.
I personally enjoyed the story of the first game a bit more. The dark tone and sense of desperation that persisted for so much of Aselia was addictive. Additionally, the harem cliches are slightly stronger in this one, which is always a bad thing in my book. However, I still enjoyed the characters, and I don't want to give too much away, but while I like the Iliad better, the Odyssey has some charm as well. So in the end, it's an apple and an orange.
The SRPG side is significantly improved from the first game. They got rid of the stupid mind mechanic and added something called combat mana. The outcome of each encounter is no longer predetermined. Your typical encounter now plays out in 10 turns (each side takes 5), so skills no longer have multiple 'actions.' Your skills cost 'combat mana,' and your characters only charge 2 combat mana per turn, so if a skill costs more than that, it won't occur. You can change the positions in your squad every turn, and the AI NOW CHANGES POSITION TOO! This adds a small element of luck since the enemy behavior differs from squad to squad.
Unfortunately, a few issues from the first game are still present. In particular, the awkwardness of constructing buildings and manually leveling up your characters to prepare for unknown threats while trying to finish a mission as quickly as possible has not gone away. The weirdest part of it is that in the first game, you were often trying to survive the onslaught of an enemy horde on your decrepit villages, so towers were ubiquitous. In contrast, in Seinarukana, every mission is an offensive campaign, your buildings will only last for two or three missions max, but it offers a smorgasbord of defensive buildings. I literally built defensive buildings on one mission in this entire game, and even on that occasion, it panned out that I was just overreacting and didn't need them.
tl;dr
- Story was good but not amazing? Like a 6-8/10
- Tactics is a lot better, but still has a couple of flaws.
- If you enjoyed the first one, it's almost guaranteed you'll like this one too.

First off, this was translated by Aroduc so if you like previous translations from Seiha then get the game. I know that on the blog for the translation there were complaints about removing flavor text from the second page of abilities to display what the ability does. I PREFER the way Aroduc translates because having what the abilities do is FAR MORE IMPORTANT imho than random flavor text. That bein said, Aroduc does try to localize sometimes so if you are a 'purist' then you probably won't like it.
Second, this is one of the only game heavy VNs licensed in English in existence right now. So if you want a VN with good gameplay, BUY this to send a message to the industry for more. In addition, if you are put off by typical JRPG games due to grinding, this game does not require heavy grinding but rather smart gameplay.
This game is still a VN however, as evidenced by the very long intro (2-4 hours before a real battle) and numerous dialogues in between each campaign. Plot wise it follows the standard 'call to action' -> 'journey' -> 'climax' -> 'denoumont' format of fiction. It does try to put in a few mature real life scenes. It follows the setting of introducing characters in a school setting to try to connect to (I guess the target audience) and then transports them to the actual story setting like Muv Luv does.
With regards to the gameplay I would describe it as a simpler Madou Koukaku/Nobunaga's Ambition without empire building and better battle mechanics. Madou Koukaku is an anime fantasy themed Total War like SRPG (except not translated into English). Nobunaga's Ambition is a Total War like game as well.
For a more mainstream comparison, imagine controlling armies on the world map from Fire Emblem Awakening and having turn based Rock paper scissors combat instead of a tactical grid.
Do note that this game took a long time to get onto Steam from release so art assets are dated somewhat. I think the art looks fine as it is. As a disclaimer, if you are looking for Eushully like quality or more modern art quality you will be dissapointed. I would say the art quality is a notch above Recettear and around the same as Fire Emblem: Shadow Dragon.
Lastly if you are looking for the non all ages version you should buy from other sites. Or honestly you should just go and buy Sakura Dungeon or something because that will get you want you want for far less effort. I think the all ages version is fine so far and they added new scenes for the all ages version.
Advice for playing: - Turn off combat animations in settings after the first campaign (cutscenes prior to that won't make sense without animation). Save frequently! If you lose a battle you have to restart the campaign. Also build artificats early on that increase Mana conversion rate, you will want it later.
_____
Aside: I kinda wish they made a 2D campaign map though, Madou Koukaku had a prettier 2D map and honestly for indier games like Nobunaga's Ambition or Seinarukana 2D looks so much better than 3D and it's cheaper too. Oh, and if you are reading this JAST: I would love a translation of Madou in English because machine translation is unintelligable.

I would say this is not a real review at this point, and will be updating it as I get further into the game. I'm only writing this now because literally no one else has written a review yet :/
First thing first, this is a visual novel(VN) so if you don't know what that means or don't like visual novels you probably shouldn't start here, mostly because this is a sequel to another game, Aselia the eternal. For the longest time I thought it was only thematically a sequel but that isn't the case, it is a true sequel. You could play this before Aselia, but I loved Aselia so much I would hate you if you did that :[
Special note: this is the All ages - Special edition, If you want the adult scenes purchase it on j-list.
If you are still reading this and are like "I don't know about VNs but that combat system looks interesting", after 3 hours of gameplay there have been 2 choices and only scripted battles. From my experience with the prequel the battles will be much more important and take up a larger portion of the game, but if you just want the strategy game portion and are the type to skip cutscenes, there is a lot to skip.
If I haven't dissuaded you yet let's actually get into what makes this game good so far. I really love how much detail the Eternity Sword games have to their world. It takes it's time establishing it's characters and their relationships, what they eat, how they live, the language they speak, the day to day chores. This was what grabbed me so hard about Eien no Aselia and that level of detail is here as well. It would be annoying if the sped through the first chapter to get to the fighting faster, because the characters motivations wouldn't be as developed.
That said I feel there are a few things that take me out of it. There was one scene that confused me because it jumped away from the protagonist to see a conversation we wouldn’t know about, which is fine, except the protagonist was on their way to that room and it seemed for a bit he was listening in to it but he wasn’t and it made me kinda glitch out
if you wanna see in my video my reaction, it is a like 5 minute scene and i don’t figure it out until after the scene.)
I also felt that certain characters we see in chapter one should have spoken in Phantasmagorian (their special made up language) so we wouldn’t know anything about what they were up to the first time through, but oh well.
The art has a similar style to it as the previous title but it shows that it is a newer title in how clean the art is. Art is too subjective for me to say it’s good or bad, I like the designs of all the charactors, if you want to see for yourself the art check some videos.
The music isn’t anything really special, but the use of the music is on point and I would suggest playing it with the music as it really helps set the emotional moods and makes it more immersive.
All in all it is a worthy successor to Eien no Aselia, and I’m looking forward to finishing it.

Hexoscope is an inexpensive puzzle game where players form combinations of hexagonal chips in order to create a chain from a power source to a power receiver. It has been developed by Studio Binokle and published by Sometimes You.
Gameplay is very simple. You click on the chips and swap them with the correct piece and combine them. You arrange the patterns so that they line up. The process continues until you have successfully created a chain from the source to the receiver. The gameplay is simple but addictive.
The color palette is very simple and easy on the eyes. I appreciate that the design is clear cut and something that most will not have an issue with. I haven't tested the game with a color blind gamer but I believe that they should be fine with the game.
Dmitriy "Cyberworm" Vasilyev has created a nice and relaxing soundtrack for that is unique to the game. It accomplishes the task that it needs to and is easy listening.
Hexoscope has Steam trading cards but lacks achievements. I would ideally like to see the developers add a number of achievements to the game. This would encourage people to purchase and play the game. I am of the opinion that puzzle games should always have achievements.
If the game had achievements it would get a resounding purchase recommendation. Hexoscope is a fun puzzle game that is accessible to all ages and all groups of people. If you're a puzzle fan then I'd suggest that you seriously consider the inexpensive purchase.

Who remebers Populous? It's basically a modern version of that with even older school retro graphics blended with a modern layout and feel. Hard to decribe but it actually works well.

The modes are however not set on a selection of people, but your entire team as a whole. So not much micromanaging here aside from setting the occasional waypoint and using fire pillar and lightning strikes to burn your AI opponent to the ground.
The developer(s) shows a lot of restraint in the overall gameplay and I appreciate what was built upon an already successful formula. I need to keep playing more to see how the mechnics evole as the game progresses, but already I am quite happy with my purchase and it brings back awesome feelings of nostalgia from when I was a young lad, sneaking onto my parents computer to play Populous at 1am on a school night.
Conclusion: Great fan service to a classic series. Effective and entertaining "god" simulator. Grab it if you enjoy high level strategy and casual rounds you can jump in and out of when you have some time.

Crusader Kings II is one of my favorite games, but it was not love at fist sight.
The tutorials do a great job showing you how the game works, where the stuff to click on is, and what things do but then you jump into a game look at it and say...
"Well, now what?"
This game does not hold your hand and give repeated idiotic advice like so many games love doing nowadays, you jump is with both feet and you are free.  That freedom is both exhilarating (I can do anything!) and frightening (but, what the hell do I do?).
You are the ruler of your Kingdom, or territory, or Empire, whatever you have chosen to play, and your goals are really up to you.  Marry off your heirs. become King or Pope, whatever you want to set as a personal goal, go for it.  This can be a bit rough to get started but one you get going it has that beautiful "Just one more turn.." feeling that keeps you glued to the game.
I have spent hours making sure my rulers children find the right partner in marriage, I have followed the rise of a ruler that married young and he and his wife fell madly in love and had many children before she died tragically of an illness and the liege never remarried, his heart forever broken.  The story you find inside the bloodlines of your kingdom drive you to keep playing and there is love and passion, hatred and betrayal, and the depth of all you can do just makes each play different.
The internal story that you create is both the games greatest strength and weakness, if you are unable to link events together into a cohesive tale then you are just going to stare at the screen and wonder what the heck the point of any of it is.

I would highly recommend this game to fans of grand strategy, and it could even be a good gateway to those who are interested in the genre.

Valkyria Chronicles combines strategy elements of conventional tactical role playing games with real-time action sequences. The game is set in a fictitious continent reminiscent of 1930s, Europe divided in two and ruled by the Empire and the Federation. The Empire has set its sights on invading a small neutral country called Gallia, which is situated in the middle of the two great empires. The game follows a hero named Welkin and his fellow soldiers of the Federation's 7th Platoon that are fighting against the Empire, who is intent on unifying the continent under its power.
Built upon the new "CANVAS" engine, Valkyria Chronicles' ground-breaking 3D graphics resemble a watercolor painting in motion. Gameplay is centered around a new type of tactical battle concept. Known as "BLiTZ," this battle concept gives players unique freedom to strategically move around the environment and attack enemies using real-time controls.

Well this is a difficult game to review.  There are so many things that I love and hate about this game but overall I would say that I would recommend it.  Even though it is Free 2 play, I would put some money into it with one of the deals that they offer to get the best experience.  I am a brand new player to Archeage but I have some experience in other MMOs like TERA and WoW.  Have to say hands down that the concepts that this game puts out is THE BEST.  Housing, Player based economy, warring factions, PLAYER PIRATES, and tons of other great features.  Then it goes into the BAD features of the game.  Cash shop and the Auction House.  Personally I like the Auction house but I will get into why I think its ruined later on.  Cash shop is the biggest issue.  I play on new servers which from what I read up on doesn't have the full cash shop implemented which means that its fairly less P2W.  I would strongely advice NOT playing on legacy servers.  I feel bad for people who worked hard on them but its completely broken and no skill/effort involved with getting gear.  Now onto why I think the AH is ruined even on the new fresh servers.  They have a currency called "APEX" coins and a loyalty status called "Patron."  Basically Patron is REALLY important if you want to be successful and grind less, pay less, and get more stuff overall.  APEX coins can be bought with real life money to pay for patron.  This is the big issue with the Auction House because you can buy APEX coins with in game free currency.  I think if APEX coins were REALLY hard to craft rather than have to be bought with real life money that it would be alright.  That means someone who has a big wallet can pour in the money to the devs so that they can basically do whatever they want and be on the top.  Gold is everything in Archeage with the Auction House.  Yet its so easy to get with APEX coins that it completely breaks the game.  I completely understand why its like that because Archeage is a F2P game and I would probably never had played it if it was subscription based.  I just wish that they would think of another pay model, maybe make a few servers subscription based while others F2P.  That way they can get exposure while more serious players can get onboard the sub servers to have a fair and less P2W experience.  Besides that, game is great.  Decent graphics, I would have to say that its probably on par with TERA on that part.  The combat seems okay, give it a 6/10.  I haven't faught any big bosses or done any dungeons yet so I will update if I really enjoy it.  Mostly just grinding quests that are the same thing over and over again to get to level 50.
Overall Rating - 7.5/10 (Fresh Servers)

- Farming, crafting, mining, ect.
- YOU CAN PLAY CUSTOM MIDI/MLL MUSIC
- Great lore
- Demon characters (Just look at my name)
Cons:

Despite only using steam to play it for 6.6 Hours, I've taken much more time to play the game through the actual trion launcher. it's an amazing game, it has the pay to win aspect to a minimum and as a free to play player such as new people; they can get all the in game pay items for free from saving gold.
Disclaimer: The patron bonus (In-Game Buyable "Subcription") Which can be boughten with in game farmable gold, gives most of these Pros' a major boost in usefulness and makes most cons' go away.
-Pros-
~Gold comes easily- usually racking up enough to get Paid for items at max level. Farming is really easy as well.
~Community is nice- always enjoyed speaking in Faction chat and world chat.
~Classes are well balanced and there are a TON! You get 3 Slots for classes, and you can mix and match to become whatever you want. Really cool concept if you want to be a multiclassing Swordsman/Bard/Ranger-Healer/Buffer/Tank.
~Character Design is really smooth- and with enough time you can re-create just about anything
~World Boss Raid System- where do i start on this one. You'll here calls such as "Get ready for rift raid". Good drop rate, and i used to host a lot of them on the Server Kyrios. Fun, and not required.
~Gear and Level scaling- this one is simple to grasp and understand. Every level a piece of gear goes up by, it has enough stats that it will always be better than what you had, but not to a point where your mixed and matched with Horrible Boots and a Magical A$$ Chestplate.
~The Coin Purse System- if you kill an mob enemy you get a coin purse, where you spend a point of labor (I'll explain labor next) and you open to gain money at a shot at items. Loot Box Jr. If you may call it such.
~Labor System- You get a cap of 2000 labor. (5000 for Patron) 5 Labor per 5 Minutes so 1/1 Minute labor for being logged in. Logged off you get none. (Patron gets 10/5m While Online and 5/5m offline.)
-Cons-
~Labor System-If you're not a patron, nor play a lot. This'll definitely become a problem for you.
~The Coin Purse System- it has a chance to become a major waste of labor if you have bad luck with opening them.
~Storyline- There isn't much story in the game but it does have it's own feel with lore. So don't expect a full book written story when coming into the game. However, it does give a short briefing in the beginning and then funnels you down the storypath. Kinda Forced.
~Mana/Stamina Consumption.
Let me explain this one shortly- Your Energy/Mana/Stamina bar is shared if you start sprinting; so sprinting or even fighting will drain it by a ton. Mana Cost on most abilities boosts the more you use it, so combos are kinda forced to use, even if it lowers DPS.
~Time. Over time this game has sightly started to turn into a cash grab with all of the new "Store Bought Chests" and loot boxes, costumes, consumables, housing/buildings, vortexes, all these arbitrary things that not everyone needs. You can ignore it; like i did. But i am opinionated when it comes to a good MMO. It has a feeling that they will turn into a Money wanting game like RIFT did. (Same company).
-All in All it's an amazing game, looks great, feels fluid and fun, easy to pick up and hard to put down, some downsides here and there but nothing is perfect. So give Archeage a try, it's one of the better F2P games on the MMO-Board

Now, there's a decent amount of people who have played Dungeon Keeper and Dungeon Keeper 2 who also grabbed this game. I am one of those people. I LOVE the DK franchise.  Anyways, going to try not mentioning DK/DK2 from here on out. Well, until the end, anyway
War for the Overworld is a dungeon building and managing god game.  You create your dungeon, create rooms, get minions, and level them up to get an advantage over your enemies. You create room, traps, use spells and Constructs. Depending on what you like and what your playstyle is, you can use or keep from using certain rooms or minions in sync with your playstyle. Hell, you could go all turtle style on your enemy if you wanted to.
This game also gives you a decent amount of defensive structures you can use, but from your limited resources, you won't be able to spam them all over the map. Which wouldn't be fun in the first place. Imagine a game where the enemy has turrets ALL over the map. Personally I'd just give the person a win and leave the current game. :P
Every game/movie/series has cliché's. This one is no different in that aspect. Lies, deceit, hero(es)/villain(s) gone batshit insane, plot twists, manipulation, 180 degree turn in personality, and so on and so forth. The usual. Though you can still get genuinely surprised by plot twists. Hell, I can see them coming miles away, and still get surprised. Must be the way the plot twists are handled.
This game breathe new life into the dungeon creating and managing-genre, which were severely lacking since the before-mentioned franchise. Which is kinda sad, as this type of genre is very fun.
Now, this game was officially released on the 4th of April, 2015. Personally though, I feel as if this game is kinda still in the "just came outta beta" phase, where they add content, fix bugs/glitches, etc. I love free stuff. Hell, even if it's paid DLC(as long as it's cheap enough) I will most likely buy it, though free DLC/content is always welcome, especially for this unpolished gem of a game. In maybe a year and potent and efficient polishing, this game could and will be a lot more than what it is now, and even more worth the money I spent on this unpolished-so-far gem.
Now, onto pros and cons:
Pros:
+ Fun to play
+ Real Dungeon Keeper(2) atmosphere, and graphics to match
+ Hilarious voice acting (Love ya, Richard!)
+ Very good camera options
+ AI is fully capable of tearing you a new one
+ Large creature/minion variation
+ Can train minions/creatures to max level
+ Infinite in terms of different plays you can do
+ Pretty fun campaign, though not exactly jaw-dropping
+ Did I mention voice acting?
+ Cool soundtracks
+ Devs are talkative AND are both responsive and positive with feedback you give them
+ Updates are scheduled and released and regular intervals, unlike for some other games I know
+ Very interesting map designs
+ All kinds of different map tiles, and how you interact with them
+ The devs and a lot of us are passionate about this genre, and are huge fans of the Dungeon Keeper franchise (Omg, I mentioned it, please don't hit me)
+ The mouse is a hand, which truly every evil Underlord(Keeper) needs!
Cons:
- Lacking in terms of campaign duration
- Not possible to change difficulty for campaign
- Can be a bit difficult at times to select a minion/creature, or even simply hover over it to see status
- Lacking multiplayer/skirmish maps
- Only 4-players max currently, hoping/wanting to see more
- Missing tooltip for when selecting AI's during skirmish, what their preferred strategies are, etc.
- Seems laggy at times
- A tad lacking in content, but this will come in time
- Better minion/Creature overview is lacking
- Kinda hard to select tabs at times because of small UI buttons (Rooms, Spells, etc.)
- Some of the mechanics in the game are poorly described/explained
- The mouse is at times hard to use, as the ingame hand you play with is a bit weird in terms of unit, room and environment interaction
Conclusion:
This game is good, fun, and catches the DK/DK2 type of gameplay. It's not perfect. Nothing is. But if you are thinking spiritually, this game could one day become the spiritual successor of Dungeon Keeper 2.
Anyways, this is my short review of War for the Overworld
Cheers,
Yakamaru

TL/DR: 7/10 This game is fun, pays a nice homage to the Dungeon Keeper series, but still has several bugs ranging from minimal to highly frustrating.
Pro Tip: Do not set the Zoom Level in options to be low. This is counter intuitive (atleast ot me)! the higher this value, the more you can zoom out.
PROS:
Very similar to Dungeon Keeper
appox 10 hr campaign
other game modes: skirmish, survivial, multiplayer
Nice economy feature: Each imp and trap reserves a small portion of your mana pool and caps at some percentage. This means you cant have a million imps and traps, instead only a dozen or two of each.
Skirmish mode has about 10 maps ranging from 2 to 4 player and ranging in size by atleast a factor of four.
Nice feature which encourages non-open floor plans; room pieces (like a torture device in a torture chamber) get increased efficiency for each bit of wall within 1 square.
Somewhat akin to Horned Reaper in DK2, there are three creatures which you can summon, but not control, which are at the apex of each skill tree. Unless you are rushing, I havent found them all too useful tbh.
Traps have two modes, which are interchangable by only a mouse click. The modes differ per trap, but are often more complex than just a defense/offense mode.
Additional creature class called beasts, which are summoned by a room (not a portal).
CONS:
Imps often poorly priorotize work, ie. reinforce walls (or do nothing) instead of claiming nearby tiles
No full page map
Creatures are hard to distiguish from one another.
Creature and room tooltips often do not appear when curser remains over them. I feel like the game is missing in game tooltops to better explain many creatures and rooms.
Strange room/trap/spell/potion research tree which is confusing and annoying if you dont have all the room types built yet
Campaign difficulty sways from trivial to really tough with few in a happy medium. Further balacing is needed.
Even after 15+ hours im not totally sure what some of the more advanced rooms do. Certaintly they arent critical for success.
No Bile Demons, or farts.
Not much (if anything) in the way of creature types which hate each other or fight. This differs from DK series where one might omit particular rooms to assure a happy dungeon.
Doors are useless, and two traps in particular, cannon and well of souls, are OP.
Leveled up imps do not have speed or teleport. But, there are new magic imps which work at a faster rate.
Enemies dont die in prison and turn to skeletons, they stay in jail forever. Enemies which die in the torture chamber turn to stupid ghosts which vanish after a short time. They are best used by posessing and then kamazeeing through the other keepers dungeon - but largely useless.
In skirmish, AI often amasses a dungeon and army faster than humanly possible - which can lead to some frustratng early battles
A few QOL improvement ideas:
-There is a nice feature which you can group creatures into a warband and set a rally flag for just them. For example, warband 1 would be selected by clicking CTRL-1 then clicking the minions, and then sent to a rally by clicking 1 then then clicking on the map. I WISH that after clicking 1, before setting the rally point, all the minions in that warband would appear as distinct white dots on the mini map
- You can select all creatures of a type into a warband by CTRL-1 then clicking thier creature type in the HUD rather than each individual one in the dungeon. I WISH I could toggle to automatically add all new creatures of that type which appear in my dungeon (or are converted in torture chamber) to that warband automatically.
- I WISH I could toggle a rooms activity priority to surpass a rally point. For example, set my archive (library) to priority, so that if I use a Rally ALL point, a few inclined creatures would stay back and do research. This would be really nice for research, trap manufacturing and torturing at the very least.

The "Early-Access" caveat is becoming more and more of a bad joke, developers, if we can call them that in many cases, are using it to release pure garbage and then giving the promise "it'll get better", well this game is just another example of that. I am well aware that they are releasing almost daily updates, but the question does have to be asked. With this being so, they must surely have tested this inhouse and seen how badly in plays, why the hell release it yet?
Sorry but users comments about it having an "engaging and fun" combat system are talking rubbish, with the current state of the game it's a case of run up to the NPC and spam the mouse button, hoping you manage to hit him enough times to kill him before he kills you. Don't bother with your shield, it'll break after a couple of attacks and doesn't often block the attack anyway.
Some of the problems I have ran into already in the 2.8hrs are as follows, in no set order:
-Terrible rubberbanding
-NPCs stuck in walls, trees, the sky, the floor. With this they are still able to attack you, but you cannot fight back.
-At times you will go to attack, only to find yourself launched around 50-100m away
-The durability on items seriously needs looking at. An NPC with a small stone axe attacks you, your equipped with a metal shield only to find it break after maybe 4-5 attacks?
-Constant crashes
-Terrible lag (even if being ran on a LAN)
-It constantly freezes. Open up your inventory and wait a couple of minutes for it to unfreeze, oh and BTW while you were waiting, an NPC spawned next to you and now your dead.
-The NPC models, unless you are directly infront of them don't actually run towards you, they slide (basically their animations don't trigger), this is also a problem while they are attacking you, at times they will simply freeze in a stance.
Like I have said above, I understand this title is "Early-Access", but it's not acceptable from a company that is more than a single guy in his basement. I also understand this review will probably get down voted because I am telling people the truth, rather then simply lying and going with the general view of "this game has promise".
Save your money and if this is still around in 6 months have a look then, hopefully Funcom will have actually sorted out the problems, I'm not a fan of either but If you want a survival game, go play rust or ARK until then.
