I first picked this game up back in 2012 or 2013, when it was still just called "Reprisal", and just recently got it on Steam; it was a
different than it is now in 2012, in some ways for the better and in some ways for the worse. The current UI of the game seems very generic Web 2.0, more suited to a tech startup website than to a game, and it's a little incongruous with the game's graphics. I felt like it had a lot more character in its older incarnation, and the grammar seems worse in this one (not a single apostrophe! The horror!).
As for game mechanics, the terraform tool is kinda janky and only works half the time. It's also a pain to terraform a large area at once, and I tend to accidentally destroy houses/buildings with it by holding down too long. The frame of view is obnoxiously small and panning around is
slow — you can move it with the minimap in the upper corner, but it pauses everything while you're moving it.
However! It's not all bad. The graphics (with the exception of the aforementioned UI) are very nice, and the pseudo-Grecian architecture and lore are a great touch. It's not an exceptionally challenging game, but it makes you think, which we can all use once in a while. The new universe system is interesting and definitely wasn't there before, but I think it's really cool, at least in an aesthetic sense (I haven't gotten the chance to try it out as I'm still working on the first planet).
So yeah, I'd recommend it, but it's not without its issues. The mechanics need some work and it's not enough to keep me playing for more than half an hour or so at a time. But it's fun, and it's relaxing, and it's $7.

The only way to make it easy, is to turn off the quick spawning of all populatants, then you can start winning again.
There are four basic things you can do as far as gameplay: fight, build, lead, and use your God like powers, which there are plenty of. You can even turn your leader into a hero and he'll do some real damage. And there are dozens of worlds and hundreds of maps in each, so I don't know if I'll ever finish it. I recently bough Shadow Tactics Blades of the Shogun, and while that game is fun, it wasn't the pace I was looking for after playing Streets of Rogue, so I immediately bought this game, expecting nothing but top down melee/shooter combat, and this game delivers.

The skill tree is unique in that you can slot an unslot skills at will to suit the situation. That said, I almost exclusively use the dash ability coupled with reflex booster (aka controlled slow time) and the melee weapons, because its easier to start a "finisher chain." This game has super addictive finishing moves you can trigger when an apponent is staggered and the finishers give you increased speed/damage which makes it easier to stun the mobs and perform more finishers.
The bosses are pretty tricky, but once you learn the pattern it generally becomes a question of how to do a crap load of damage first, which is where the reflex booster comes in really handy. However, I feel sometimes the controlled slow time is like activating easy mode mid boss fight. Bring a flame thrower or the freeze ray gun, and they do stuuuuupid damage to the bosses in slow time, so much so it almost feels like boosted reflexes should drain more energy while in use, but this may change late game when the player is generally taxed more heavily.
This game has a Speedrun Mode in order to add replayability, but I honestly don't see that adding much replay value compared to if this game added a Rogue mode with randomly generated levels and perma death. I may just love games like Nuclear Throne and Streets of Rogue a little too much, but I think this game would be one hell of a Rogue Like and I would happily pay 25 to 30ish dolllars US for the Story Mode, Speedrun and a Rogue mode.
Speaking of the Story, seems pretty good so far. The story elements are delivered through text and character art, the choices are meaningless it seems, but I do like the different art on the main character's LED helment (honestly the lack of real choice would be less important if the stuff displayed on the visor was more diverse), I haven't finished it yet, but I will say it makes me incredibly wary when I can't actually say no to someone ever since playing Bioshock one... and I'm intrigued as to who is actually calling the shots.
I will update if anything changes as I progress.

Although the game is still VERY early in alpha, this game is shockingly entertaining and fun! Overgrowth creates a large focus on its custom combat system, which is quite sophisticated. Unlike most fighting games, Overgrowth uses a skeletal structure within the model of each character to determine damage depending on location of a hit, rather than the traditional health system. This means that enemies can be taken out in as little as one percise hit. Overgrowth Alpha features sharp weapons, such as the dagger, a quick blade that can be used on an enemy after a sneak attack from behind, the spear, which is a good weapon for distancing melee attacks, and the sword, a brutal one-hit-kill. Each blade can be thrown. Aside from combat, Overgrowth already features an in-game map editor. Overgrowth's map editor is inside each map chosen from the main menu, so there is no need for extra software. Many of the physical aspects are customizable. Each character can be resized and rebuilt to fit a character of your liking, added with the ability to attach any object to the skeleton.
One of the most exciting features about Overgrowth is the ability to parkour your way around each map. Objects can be scaled up and over with ease. Pair that with an amazing combat system, and that sounds like a great game to me!

Valkyria Chronicles is one of those games that you'll never seem to forget. From the combat missions to the optional story content to the squad roster system, Valkyria Chronicles touches on a lot of things without ever getting too complicated. After playing through it again recently I still love it as much as I did the first time and have decided to write a review for it.
The combat is very straight-forward but even so it can pose quite a challenge at times. For the shooting you actually manually aim which is rather uncommon but other than that there's pretty standard turn-based strategy mechanics in place. The combat system really comes alive with the different squad members and their own unique traits. Some of them get lonely, some hate being around others. Some enjoy being on grass, some have pollen allergies. Figuring out a good combination of squad members for each battle is tricky and can take a few tries but is almost always rewarding.
That being said, the story is really the most engaging part of Valkyria Chronicles. The characters are well developed and the overall plot, while being somewhat cliche at times, flows really nicely. The story follows a war called the Second Europan War and has some strong parallels to WW2. The scale of the story isn't the same as WW2 however, as Valkyria Chronicles focuses on a single small nation trying to maintain its sovereignty. And it truly feels like a realistic conflict. As in real life, there are bad guys but also sympathetic characters on both sides. The heroes aren't infallible and the villains definitely aren't pure evil.
What I found to be the most interesting part of the story was the romance between our two main characters, which is probably the best I've ever seen in a video game and one of the most satisfying I've ever seen in any medium. It develops gradually over the events of the game and never feels too forced. Just to be clear, the romance is a very significant part of the story (arguably the mot significant part).
Technically speaking, this game is kinda dated. The art style maintains its charm even after all these years but this is still a port of a 2008 PS3 game. The hitboxes can be annoying and the game does crash occasionally.
Overall, Valkyria Chronicles is well worth it if you're interested in a game for either an interesting story or thoughtful turn-based combat. I can't recommend it enough.

There I was, 48, the Strategos of Nikaea in the Byzantine Empire. In my youth I had been weak, slothful and wounded, and all of this had made me very depressed. Fortunately, my first wife gave me a hunting dog, and training him and hunting him had improved how I felt, so I was now diligent and had gone from weak to actually being strong.
Although I had got maimed in a battle, life was good, and I had a good son lined up to inherit this all. I was in good terms with the emperor, and married to my second wife.
Then I turned 50 and things got a bit worse.
My wife died and I got hit in the head in another battle I fought in for my dear empire. I was incapable to lead, and my son had to be my regent. I married a Germanic princess who's not even 20 yet, just because. I was a bit unhappy, as for many years I could not do anything, my passive son wouldn't approve anything I wanted to do.
Then things went from "worse" to "Insane Crapstorm".
My wife got possessed and replaced my son as the regent. A few slow, grinding years later she claimed Jesus talks to her, and she also became a lunatic.
I was 53 or so, married to a Germanic possessed lunatic strategissa-regent on her 20s. The slow grinding years turned to slow grinding decades. She humiliated me in front of my court by cracking nuts with my teeth. On top of that she cheated on me with my courtiers, but still managed to give me a son too.
But suddenly, hope rises like the sun, as my son asks me if I want something done to bring her regency to an end. I nod my approval and fall asleep. She locks my son in the dungeon for this. I cry.
Several years go by, but then my magistros notices I am being mistreated! I nod my approval and fall asleep again. She locks my magistros down in the dungeon with my son.
The years go by. No one else seems to notice that placing a cloak on the strategos's face in front of his court, and cracking nuts with his teeth is not OK.
Suddenly my dear wife kicks the bucket at the age of 42. I cheer and almost cry of happiness. Her Regency of Terror is at an end! I only wish she'd died through assassination or some vile disease instead of old age. With my new regent I free my magistros and son, and life is good again.
At the ripe age of 83 I lie in my own bed, the old battle wounds aching and I know my time has come. I die peacefully, knowing that my dear Germanic princess's son is fourth on the line of succession, and that he will likely get assassinated and replaced by an older sister should he ever get near to inheriting it all. I also know my eldest son will reign well, and that he will never marry a Germanic princess.

Decent tower defense game, but completely abandoned by the developers.  As a result, many steam achievements won't unlock (although they do unlock in game, they just have difficulty  syncing up), and this is likely to never be fixed.  End game grinding is a bit tedious, as you're stuck with one of two options to obtain rare towers -- endless survival grinding for a chance at a rare card, and then a chance to pick that card from a set, or logging in every day to get a "daily bonus" which has the possibility of being a rare card.
It has a lot of card fusing and upgrading, which is kind of a side point to the main game, but it allows you to individually customize your tower set to only upgrade what you use, which is pretty nice.  The unfortunate part of this is the lack of a reliable method to get said towers.  As far as gameplay goes, it's a pretty well done TD, although your ability to path monsters via tower placement is virtually non existant, and your towers are confined to rails along the sides for the most part.  This is it's only real drawback, in that it's more like Kingdom Rush than Defense Grid.
All in all, decent game, but it unfortunately will never be great with a developer team giving it any post-release attention.  8/10.  Good for probably 40ish hours, with some additional hours if you enjoy the grind to max out your towers.

I bought this for 89 cents this morning, intending to play a puzzle or two and quit. Now it's 4 hours later, I'm 20 or so puzzles in, and I. Am. Addicted.
Hexoscope is a tile puzzle game with the goal being to build a red tiled path between two or more specific tiles. All tiles in between have different directional lines etched into them, allowing you to create one, continuous path. This is a design trope going back all the way to Pipe Mania (and can be seen in games as current as Loop and klocki), but Hexoscope throws in a couple of creative twists.
First, you cannot use a "black" tile unless you turn it blue...but you cannot turn a tile blue unless you successfully create a path into it with at least 1 red tile (or more in later levels). This results in some apparent roadblocks that might lead one to think that a board is unsolvable: Don't fall for it, because that is
what this evil little puzzle game
you to think!! You'll have to backtrack, figure out how to change color on single tiles that can't seemingly be changed, open multiple paths to give yourself the most tiles to choose from, create circuitous paths, or even swap out tiles you've already placed in order to open up new areas to grab the one tile you
need and
rebuild what you've destroyed...whew!...but,
when you've solved that board, it will have been properly good and spanked, and you will be its master. Until the next !$*#& board.
There are some really thoughtful touches, too: It autosaves on exit. It also allows you to undo your moves all the way back to the beginning of the board. I've asked for a similar "redo" button, as the developer seems pretty active on the discussion board (one player has asked for a fullscreen mode, which he has already confirmed will be in the next update). I'll update this review if that feature is added.
The one minor flaw is the game's web-translation of its tutorial, but I honestly had no trouble figuring it out and I'm pretty thick. And although it may seem near-impossible, I've not had to restart once. I've had to undo moves many times (once, all the way back to the beginning), but I've never had to re-roll a board  (and the developer has
).
With the exception of the poor translation though, I'm impressed with how polished it is, especially for a dollar game. I have encountered zero bugs, and the developer seems committed to producing a good experience. Hexoscope is simple in concept, but it will make your brain hurt in the best possible way, and completing a puzzle feels good because of that pain. The music is ethereal and not distracting, the design is crisp, there are timed and untimed modes, and more than one puzzle is unlocked from the start. Although there are 72 boards listed in the menu, elements are randomized, so you could probably play this for a
long time before getting bored (if ever). The amount of strategy in this little game really surprises me.
Hexoscope is my new addiction. It's at least a $5 game in a $1 package, and it really deserves a look from puzzle fans. Highly Recommended. (Edited on 19 Oct 2016 to fix a grammatical error)

Despite being only $0.99 Hexoscope is a surprisingly good puzzle game.
In Hexoscope your goal is to build a path from the power generator(s) to the power receiver(s). In each level you start at the power generator and start placing connectors next to each other to make a path towards the receiver. You move connectors by swapping the position of two connectors. The catch is that you can only move connectors that are either connected to the power generator or are next to a connector that is connected to the power generator. This means that you will have to create paths to different parts of the level to retrieve a connector piece that you need to complete your path to the receiver.
I am a fan of puzzle games and I enjoyed Hexoscope. The game's mechanics are interesting and fun. The game is surprisingly challenging at times as you need to really think out how to make a path that reaches the receiver but also gets you to the pieces you need to finish your path.
While Hexoscope is a fun game it is not perfect. First it is not the type of game that I would play for more than a half hour to an hour at a time. It is the type of game that is fun for a couple puzzles at a time but them gets a little repetitive. I plan on playing a couple puzzles a day and then coming back to the game a different day. The second issue comes from the randomized levels. While the game usually creates layouts that are challenging but not too challenging, the game occasionally creates really challenging or really easy levels. This means that the game's difficulty tends to fluctuate quite a bit.
If you like puzzle games and the game's concept interests you, I can't see you not enjoying your time with Hexoscope. The game is only $0.99 after all.

This is a great game in concept, marred by some lack of thought in the execution.  I would still recommend it, doubly so if you see it on sale.  Expect to get frustrated and maybe not play through it all the way, but tower defense games are usually just time-wasters anyway, right?
This is a solid tower defense game, made unique by the collectible card aspect which allows you to collect your towers as cards, and to upgrade them by sacrificing other cards.  Match two of the same card and you can "evolve" a card, and thus level it up (up to a max of level 3).  Burn a pile of otherwise-useless artifact cards, or some lesser cards that maybe you have too many of, and you can increase the level of your cards, making your towers do more damage and adding range.  The RPG aspects people speak of are pretty minimal, in my opinion.  You, as a character, do gain levels, and this allows you to buy some abilities such as larger card carrying capacity, passive buffs, and more spells/towers to pick from during a battle.  There are spells which, although pretty underpowered particularly in the second half of the game, add some extra bits of strategy when your towers are ALMOST good enough.  The comic-book-esque cutscenes are kindof neat, tho the story isn't exactly going to be the driving force for playing this one.
The balance is pretty well thought out, with one very glaring flaw.  If you are semi-lucky and get some good rare cards early on, or maybe if you stifle your spending of stars on your stats and instead spend the stars to buy card sets, you can pound through a pretty intense game.  If, however, you don't get at least a lightning or dragon tower by about the third boss, the game becomes impossibly difficult because it's balanced for actually having these top-tier cards.  If you don't have the rare towers, you may find yourself doing a fair amount of grinding, which really starts to suck the fun out of the game.  There are a couple 250-wave levels which are a good means of getting cards and money and experience, but you can't access these until you beat the first half of the game, which really sucks when you just need to build up to beat the last few maps.  They definitely could have put more effort into making the game adapt to the cards they've let you have, rather than assuming you're just going to grind until you get them.
A couple tips for this game: if you can hold off evolving a tower card to level 3, you'll get 5% more powerful towers if you evolve four level 1 cards into two level 2 cards, then evolve those into the level 3.  Takes four of the level 1 cards, which can be tedious to get for the top-tier towers, but that extra punch helps for the second half of the game.  Additionally, to help combat the wunky randomness of buying a set of cards for 3 stars and finding out you wasted your valuable stars, you can go to your %appdata% folder and back up the "Prime World Defenders" folder inside it, and restore it if you get dealt a bad hand.

Hexoscope has some nice simple mechanics that certainly has some depth, but it's reliance on randomly generated boards often makes the individual puzzles feel dull and lifeless. I found that if I got stuck I could just reset the level until a board came up that was easy to solve. I would also be given boards that were unsolvable from the start. The random generation also really impacts the difficulty curve as you might get a real tough layout for one level then get a real easy one for the following one. It would have been a better game if the puzzles were premade entirely with the random generated boards being their own mode.
Still, if you're looking for a puzzle game that has some real nice music/sound design, a great presentation, and is inexpensive then you should consider picking this up. Just be aware that it is very possible to get lay outs that are either impossible to solve or beyond your current understanding of the mechanics.

This game promised to be the 'Spritual successor to Dungeon Keeper'. What I got was a game that forced me to rush and I couldn't sit back and enjoy.
I wanted to love this game. Back in my youth I played the origional Dungeon Keeper to absolute death. What I loved about that was the humour and the ease of building a dungeon and that if you wanted you could sit back and stratergise and do well, or speed out and rush and hit the objectives hard and fast before your opponant knew what was happening.
WftO however seemed to rush me to constantly rush and attack and make rash choices about where to dump rooms or dig, or force me to build defenses with no proper set up. I found myself unable to plan leaving rooms exposed and routes to my dungeon core easy to exploit.
The humour is there, but it feels forced, thus making it not that funny at all.
In just 2 hours, I'd already gotten through 6 of the 13 levels without trying hard at all. At that pace, I'd not even have gotten 6 hours out of the main campaign. Even buying it on sale, £15 for 6 hours gameplay is pushing things.
The problem is, there isn't really anything massively wrong with the game. Its well made, the graphics are nicely designed, the interface is easy to pick up and use.... Theres just a large number of small problems that chip away at the enjoyment and feel of the game making it one I can't recomend, even to fans of the genre.

There is a lot to say about this game, mostly postive, but I will try and cut it down to basics. I cant really do an average rate of each element yet because this game is so under-developed. It is very much alpha, and will probably be some time before we see a full-release. That alone can be a negative for most. Im going to tell you why its not.
1. The developers are doing something amazing here. This is already one of the most complex combat games I have every seen. Its one of the few games out there that repects physically to the full extent durring combat.
2. It has a continuely growing gameplay and updates are added frequently. They are not only building a storyline game, but a mod friendly, developer game. Right now, you can change everything. They give you as much ability as them, and that is currently what the game is.
3. The vast ability oft his game is more than a few blank maps, 1 model enemy, a few weapons, and thats it. There is some of the most creative maps I have seen in a combat game in awhile. The time era here is difficult to pin, (Because all characters are animal :P) but they only have swords, axes, spears, hammers, etc. that makes the games combat a little more interesting, and forces it to be more detailed.
4. Despite the fact that you play as 7 foot tall rabbits, dogs, cats, rats, etc, this game is very realalistic. You can literally kill yourself by jumping of a high structure and snapping your neck. The sword fighting is also very detailed. Ending a 3 minute battle with no hits with a slow motion throat slit of your enemy is satisfying to say the least.
If you dont like waiting for a game to have its release, and hate waiting on developers, maybe this game isnt for you. But its a shame is you dont, because you have no idea what your missing out on. When this game has its full release and has an amazing story, the best combat ever, beautiful graphics, and is rated extremely highly. Go ahead an buy it then. Im just trying to say you're gonna miss out on some very intriguing gameplay pre-release, and getting to keep updating with developers to witnesss one of the best games ever be made. I would highly recommend this game, especially if you enjoy fantasy RPGs but are bored with what's already out there.  It succeeds where many RPGs fail.
Pros:
-The combat system is great!  Spell synergies, interaction with the environment, teleporting enemies, and summoning familiars are a few things that really vitalize each encounter and make it feel like there are myriad ways to win.  Combat is NEVER a grind, each battle is unique and you are never mashing a button to win.  If you lose, try a different strategy, sneak to a better starting position, or change equipment.
-Voice acting and writing seem much improved over the first installment.  I played a bit of Divinity Original Sin 1, but couldn't stay engaged because the writing and voice acting seemed a bit bland to me.  In DOS II, I haven't heard a single line yet that pulled me out of my immersion and every performance is quality.  Writing is smart and often times very funny. I will say the main plot isn't totally drawing me in yet, but I'm only just starting Act 2, so there's much left for me to see.
-One thing I really like, though a somewhat small detail, is that armor looks different when worn on different people.  Like a dwarf wearing a robe will look different than an elf wearing the same robe.
Cons:
-You basically HAVE to save scum your way through this game.  Any time something goes right, save.  It takes some training if you aren't used to that and can be really frustrating at first.  They really should have a more sensitive autosave system because it should be saving every 2 minutes.
-Some bugs with abilities I've noticed.  Sometimes an item will give you an ability, and when you equip it a glitch makes it so you don't get the ability.  Or you will remove the item and still have the ablity.  I expect this to be fixed at some point, but it's worth noting.  Not gamebreaking at all, but can be slightly annoying.
-If you are playing with a controller...don't.  Basically anything you have to do in a menu will take 10X longer to do and there are actions you can't even do when using a controller.  It's nice that they have the option to use one, but they need to do some UI tweaks and give it the same functionality as using mouse and keyboard before it's practical.
-Early game is very difficult since you don't have any good equipment and there are few options for battles to gain EXP, unless you want to just attack a random NPC.  Takes a while to get the hang of combat if you aren't used to it, but Dark Souls was the same.  Just have to tough it out.

Tower Defense crossed with a Card Collecting game; an unusual mix that strangely works well together. You have a set campaign of around 20 quests to complete before you, with some side quests you can do between main quests to gain further experience. There is some backstory to the whole game but its not overly interesting only appearing after winning certain levels. You use the drops, silver & stars earned from each win to upgrade your towers & magic, increase your deck size & obtain other perks.
Initial levels in the game are very, very easy to complete, making me think this might be a 'one session to complete' kinda game. Once you hit around level 10, the levels get much harder though. If you have been unlucky on the drops or have put your upgrades into tower cards you shouldn't have you can find yourself grinding out upgrades to get through the next level. This isn't overly frustrating though as the maps are randomly selected for each difficultly level & can have random modifiers to block certain tower squares from use. This adds new challenges for existing maps. There are also some unique boss levels where you have a set amount to build & take down a large enemy - those are fun!
There are a LOT of different towers you can build up in your deck. For tower defense veterans, most of the common suspects are there in some form (guns, flamers, slowers, long range), plus some other more unique configurations. Not sure exactly how many tower types there are but would estimate at least 20. The quality of the card determines how far you can upgrade, with each upgrade generally improving DPS/Range/Efficiency etc.
For those who like a strong mazing component to their tower defense, then this game might not be for you. There is some maps with a smaller level of mazing but most have a set path design. The strategic importance in PW:D is with your card selection to match the incoming enemies & what you put your limited upgrades earned towards. Better choices will make moving up the levels much easier (unlike my poor effort of a play through lol!), & bad choices will make the game feel next to impossible to beat.
The HD support (or lack of) I found a bit disappointing. Running PW:D in full screen ends up stretching the desktop down to 1280x720 - windows like the Steam window open in the background always get shrunk down & I need to resize. It looks fine at the lower resolution just a minor frustration. Again, a minor frustation I found was the menus between games. There is a lot of going in and out of different sections to get your upgrades done, check your towers etc. This could have been simplified to fit more cards on one page, and have main functions and browsing together to save going back and forth.
Overall, I have really been enjoying this one. Its a challenging & addictive tower defense game with a card twist! Lots of achievements & one that is well suited to load up for a quick 10-20min TD session.

I'm starting to see why the metascore is quite low. Despite it being low, the game has it's good moments. At start, I loved the game, I still play it from time to time. The idea of having different towers and magic abilities, which you can customize, is great. Towers and magic are aquired through cards. When it comes to customization, it means you can customize what towers you take with you and you can reinforce these towers with fusing different cards. The crafting isn't hard to grasp, you either improve a card or evolve a card. Evovling meaning, ie. a tower can be upgraded to the next level, meaning you can in-game upgrade the tower. There are 3 tiers when it comes to evolution, default, upgraded and max evolution.
It is a great game, but playing and progressing requires you to play same map, again and again. At some point through the main story, you will get the next map which you can finish, if you can't you have three different challenges from where you get more cards, easy, medium and hard. These kind becomes your bread and butter, grinding these challenges for more cards, so that you can progress and make better towers.
At some point, you will notice that there are very little variety to the game. Challenge maps will be recycled, which imo, isn't too bad. But you will see same enemies over and over again, in different colors. The challenge will be different, even though you have the same enemy, but the only difference is that the monster can tank more damage.
If you don't mind the grinding and similiarites through the game, I would recommend this game. Good game with an good idea, but somewhat poorly designed. I think the metascore is true and correct, but that doesn't mean the game is bad or not fun. I would recommend watching some gameplay vids, before considering buying the game. Still a decent tower defense game.

Chivalry: Medieval Warfare, is exactly what you must be thinking, a Call of Duty with swords and bows. ¿Never played Call of Duty though? The idea is simple, recreating virtually a medieval battles (village invasions, attack a castle, etc.) in which you play either with teams or free-for-all jumping in a massive slaugther, and very accurately, meaning, you can accidentally send your teammate's head flying away if you are not careful.
Friendly-"fire"...hmm...friendly-stabs are quite the frequent thing as we humans are imperfect, makes you wonder how many people were probably actually killed on accident because of a badly-timed sword attack. Doesn't hurt to send a little "Sorry!" on the chatbox though! It is also possible some people who must have absolute almighty skill for all games  and NEVEEEER hit someone, since in all in his life already knew how to play this game might be set off by this and start ranting and what not on the chat, ignore and keep on, it's part of the fun, all those little accidents. You'll get better with practice, promess.
While the controls is something you need to get used to, this game is pretty fun. Running around, beheading people, blocking attacks with your shield, cutting limbs, using the ballista, aiming well your bow. As I said the controls are somewhat difficult to get the hang on at first, it will take a few hours of gameplay to adquire the most basic bit of skill, but it is worth it. This is a game where there's no tutorial skipping. Feels really like a medieval battle, and no, there's no magic, demons, or dragons. Just regular people, with old-fashioned ye olde beheading swords.
If you are quite the wealthy fashionista, this game also has an in-game store where you can purchase other kinds of weapons and armor to suit your taste.
Is this game for you? Do you enjoy multiplayer battle games and want to try something different? Give this a try, specially when it is on sale (that's when I picked it).

The survival gaming market has taken off in the past year, with what is seems a new one each week. Some are quite successful as they take a strength and run with it, while others attempt to copy another and fail.
Conan has done something different. They took some of the best features in other games and mashed it into a interesting, competative game.
While in Early Access, you will have issues at times with FPS and crashing. I've placed just under 3 hours into the game and have experienced only one single crash. The bouncing FPS does happen, each and every game which can ruin the experience at times.
My main issue, early on thus far is the lack of intro. The game simply just drops you in and says, play. No help tutorial, just go out, walk around and figure things out. Which after the first hour, you do figure things out. Once you do figure out how to "LIVE", the game does make you want to keep pushing forward, harvesting as much as possible to unlock new features, new things to build and what you want to kill next.
My main tip is, don't go all crazy and kill at first sight in the beginning.
This game can potentially eat your life away.

The metacritic rating for this game is certainly correct. As someone that likes TDs, likes the art style, atmosphere, and music, I have trouble giving it more than a 6/10 simply due to all the gameplay ruining engine glitches. It probably doesn't even deserve that. Without the engine glitches, it might be a 7/10 or 8/10 TD.
There's a good assortment and variety of towers in PWD - nothing that leaps out as being incredibly unique, but they've got splash poison, single target poison, splash fire, single target fire, AA poison, etc.; what is unfortunate about the tower system is it comes down to luck whether you actually find all the tower cards or not. Even after playing through the entire game, then grinding another hundred levels and buying as many cards as possible in the store... I still did not unlock every tower. Bummer. Aside from that, some towers are slightly unbalanced. If you find some electric tower cards early and max upgrade them, building nothing but those towers and invis detectors is sufficient for beating all but ~3 levels.
I'm skillful enough at TDs that I had no trouble beating the game and collecting all achievements - which brings me to the next problem. The achievements unlock in-game, but some do not unlock on steam. There I am, in-game, and I can clearly see I've got an achievement from beating a level with certain requirements met (like holding onto a large amount of prime energy - used for tower building) - got it in-game, but not on steam. There's an elaborate reset procedure that you can do to give yourself a second chance to unlock such achievements, but if one of the two grindy achievements (win 500 games, build 10000 towers) locks itself down, you'll have no way to unlock them without the help of a tool like Steam Achievements Manager.
It's quite aggravating staring at a list of 134 achievements, 132 of them legitimately unlocked, and 2 of them frozen. You know that you can get (and deserve to get) the final two, but they are utterly frozen and unresponsive. If you do reset them and start from 0, they will likely freeze again at some point before reaching completion. Therefore, to get them you are forced to "cheat" (Steam Achievements Manager), all because of the company's incredibly shoddy programming.
Speaking of programming - this game is not epicly high quality like Defense Grid or even Defender Quest. A lot of the time projectiles or magic don't even register. I've landed an 8-wave wall of fire down on groups of enemies, then watched in bafflement as only the final wave caused damage, leading to leaks. For a few of the tougher levels, it can come down to luck on whether the damage you're causing actually registers. About a third of the time invis detectors don't even bother detecting invisible units, so for invis-heavy levels you have to layer quite a few of them all around or once again you may have leaks. (Or just use more electric towers.)
The game is missing some important hotkeys as well, like a sell button/key to rapidly sell towers. Instead you have to click on a tower, wait for an animation, then click a tiny sell button. It also lacks an 'Auto-Send-Next-Wave' toggle for those that prefer the challenge of waves coming as fast as possible. Instead you're expected to mash the 'Next wave' button, wearing out your keyboard or mouse.
Overall the game might be okay for a novice TD player, which doesn't get annoyed by engine bugs that are sure to♥♥♥♥♥♥off a veteran - but if you watched TotalBiscut attempt to play it, then you'll realize the difficulty curve is a tad too steep for novices. Quite unfortunate, as that leaves a very small audience that will fully appreciate the game.
The paper voice acting is also far below the standards of much older TDs like Defense Grid. Overall it left me uncaring about the storyline.
5/10 or 6/10 seem like fair ratings for the game, until they patch some of the engine glitches. But the company does not seem interested in doing so at this time. Every time I see a changelog I get hopeful, but then I check and everything is still just as broken.

Ultimately I do not want to recommend this game but it has merits. As follows;
Pros
- Great immersion, voice acting, unique premise and mechanics.
Cons
- Combat
While combat starts off interesting as the game progresses it eventually becomes rage inducing. The developer didn't allow players to target enemies specially and while that is okay with most enemies that do not block where it becomes painfully obvious is against reptiles. They have shields and turn on a dime due to having no turn animation to follow your movement. Hitting their shield resets your hit counter so it's nigh impossible to keep your hit counter up for damage boost. This is especially true considering the targeting system which is also like a roll of the dice. Pressing the cardinal directions towards a group of enemies makes the game pick a target through unseen mechanics and this results in a lot of missed hits and getting hit in the back when you didn't mean to do it at all. The game also locks you into animations which screw you over even more. For example when you don't mean to do a prone attack or when you try rolling and you are off by 45 degrees (recall it's only cardinal directions) and you get killed.
Adding insult to injury is there is one encounter where you have to fight a group of four reptiles and get your hit counter up to 30. Talk about ridiculous. This single handedly stopped 3 of my runs due to this nonsense. Considering the game is so chanced based having encounters like this is more like a slap in the face feeling than a good feeling. Monsters will also sometimes be pushed by your dodge roll so you get smacked anyways. I'm wondering why they made combat like this. Minotaurs are also extremely hit heavy and require a lot of patience.
A Hand of Fate is good and addictive but the combat is not mature and it just devalues the entire game. Overall good but not overall enjoyable.

Graphics are fine, pixel/retroish but not outstanding in any way. The music isn't memorable in the least if there even was any (I honestly can't recall any). Sounds are alright. The game could certainly use more polish to develop its personality.
If you're missing Populous or games of that ilk, I'd recommend this heavily. If you've never been a fan of that genre, I doubt this'll convert you. Definitely try to catch this on a sale as there's some real fun to be had here.

Pac Man, a pizza guy(A story is that Pac Man was made when designer have Pizza on dinner). Developed by Namco and first released in Japan in May 1980.  It was created by Japanese video game designer Toru Iwatani. It was licensed for distribution in the United States by Midway Games and released in October 1980. The player controls Pac-Man through a maze of various dots, known as Pac-Dots, as well as four multi-colored ghosts: Blinky, Pinky, Inky, and Clyde. The goal of the game is to consume all the Pac-Dots in a stage in order to proceed to the next one. Between some stages, one of three intermission animations plays. The four ghosts roam the maze, trying to kill Pac-Man. If any of the ghosts touch Pac-Man, he loses a life. When all lives have been lost, the game ends, doh!

This awesome game is about rabbits brutally stabbing each other to death with various weapons and/or beating the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of each other with their bare hands. The combat system is probably the most intense and fast paced I've ever seen. This game also has some of my favorite fighting mechanics in any fighting game, ever. The rabbits and other animals move blindingly fast, and attack unrelentingly, with each single move possibly ending in death. If Tony Jaa was a rabbit he would be in this game. It's like my dream Redwall game but totally not for kids(although those books were pretty damn violent). The graphics are aesthetically pleasing, but the really impressive part is the near perfect animation of the characters. They move so freakin'  fast that it's hard to appreciate all the work that's gone into animating these animals, but when viewed in slow motion (available at any time by pressing tab) you'll see each character inflict gruesome wounds on each other and block/ dodge in a convincing dance of death. When you see detailed blood streams running down your rabbit avatar's face and dripping onto the cold snow after a gruesome fight you'll see what I mean.
I played the alpha for this a bit prior to the steam release and while there's not really anything concrete to do yet I'm super excited to see where this goes. There's plenty of user created maps and stuff to mess around in too. Unfortunately the game kind of comes off as an early tech demo but so far the combat and parkour elements are super fun by themselves.
This game is a sequel to Lugaru HD, which came out quite a long time ago but featured the same peculiar rabbit on rabbit combat. The creator is Wolfire Games, who were responsible for organizing the first Humble Bundle. Into the first level, seems fairly okay, dialogue lines are being repeated randomly, adnimations are a bit wooden, but whatever, nostalgia overload - graphics are pretty awesome and Richard Ridings sounds awesome - I could see it being stellar. Second level, well I had to play the first one again for whatever reason, but when it eventually loaded the first condition of with selecting a "Vein of Evil" couldn't be done because it wasn't an option on the panel, trying to exit the game I had to force quit because once again the menu wouldn't load.
I can't believe after a couple of years this game is still unplayable. I've seen how much work the devs have put in, but I just get the impression it launched too soon (maybe for cashflow reasons), and it's several revisions in and still pretty unplayable, at least for me.
I want this game to be good, guess I'll check back in after another few versions to see if it's sorted yet.

I'm just writing a very brief review, in no way am I actually giving this game justice with my words, but I feel I have to write something as this game has consumed my life for the past 4 or 5 days.
Let's get started with the fact that I have not played any of the previous Divinity games, however I am a huge fan of CRPGs, stemming from the time I originally sat down and played the Dungeons and Dragons dungeon crawler: Pool of Raidiance - Ruins of Myth Drannor. Since that time I had backtracked, played through Neverwinter 1 and 2, though never actually completing them, as well as Wasteland, the Fallout series, pretty much most of the 'mainstream' crpgs most people are familiar with.
A few days ago a friend tossed me this game as a gift, honestly I am very thankful as this game has breathed new life into my fascination to this genre.
From the get go, the game is not forgiving, if you ignore obvious signs, you will die. Even on the normal difficulties if you lack in perception, the game has no qualm about stamping your expectations in the dust. And even if you are paying attention, it still does so. The way it handles ground effects, along with most spells being aoe, and actually having an impact. So you better think twice about casting that poison spell with your undead mage because he may be low health, but you may end up be using 3 resurrection scrolls instead of just one. Or you may send the dominoes of chaos smashing together to kill literally everything on the battlefield, as well as yourself.
Difficulty doesn't spike horribly though, once you get the hang of things, it's actually a breeze if you're used to any kind of tactics, especially in classic mode. Though I give credit to the enemy AI. There are times they are smarter than their own good, geeking the mage rather than going after my tanky knight front and center.
However this is a downside as well, because if my undead is under an enchantment to appear for all intensive purposes, as an elf. How yould you know it was undead to cast that heal spell on it?
But I digress, I have 60 hours in the game, I had finally after a lot of exploration started exploring the place after the initial island, and I am loving the game even more. Again, this isn't even half of my feelings, there are obviously some negatives, but they have already been stated by someone else, or I feel they are not an issue.
I heartily reccomend, I got it as a gift, and I actually wish I had been able to buy it myself.

Overgrowth piqued my interest a long, long time ago. I forget where I first saw it, but I believe it was a website dedicated to showing off new indie ideals. Overgrowth became immediately interesting to me, being that it is a game about animals kicking each other in the face. However, with the myriad of other games on the market, I lost track f it until now.
Let me preface this part by saying: if you can't handle a game with ALPHA BUGS and a game that ISN'T PERFECTLY OPTIMIZED, then this game is not for you. If you can deal with that, it comes with a ton of maps, and a pretty awesome editor. Though I have only scratched the surface, spawning 5-6 wolves in a map, and growing your rabbit character to the size of the Incredible Hulk, is immensely satisfying. The controls are solid, except for the few moments where you are going too fast or simply misjudging jumps. These end up being the most hilarious moments. Going for a jumping kick, and missing by a quarter-mile, then slamming into the wall---killing yourself.
So all in all, would I recommend this game to everyone? Maybe. I looked over the game, and found it to be substantial enough to warrant a purchase. I like the developers attitude for the game, and I like where it is going. I mean come on, its the guys who do the Humble Bundle, so clearly they know the Indie market pretty well. However, if you don't like to spend a lot of time with a level editor, and need a guided campaign, then the arena mode is certainly not enough. If you do buy it, hopefully the community will figure out how to get the pre-order code for the secret forums from Steam. That place holds the key to all of the modding information, and bug/optimization suggestions.
Just a note to close: I have run into some optimization "issues". Combat with 5+ seems to slow down quite a bit. I generally get 100-120 fps everywhere. Blood seems to really cause some issues on my rig. I am going to work on that next, and also I have noticed some buildings take a toll on the game. Also, make sure to map your shadows and ambient occlusion (and SAVE IT) because the game will constantly try to calculate it if you don't.

Valkyria Chronicles is one of those gems that people overlooked when it released. From the cover, it looks like your average JPRG - truth be told, I didn't feel like buying the game at first either, simply because of how much it looks like every other generic JRPG. But since it was on sale, and I felt like getting games to stuff up my Steam library after getting a new laptop, I gave it a try. And after around 50 hours of gameplay (with 5 hours of them being a second playthrough of this game due to the stupid file system which I will talk about later), I can conclude that this game is worth every dollar I paid.
Because the truth is, this game might look generic, but it'll be one of the greatest strategy(?) RPGs you'll play.
// PROS
- Great visuals
-> The cel-shaded graphics look beautiful, and still looks great in today's standards for a 7-year old game.
- Low system requirements
-> I have a non-gaming laptop, and it can still run the game at a steady 30fps without any problems.
- Great setting and plot
-> Basically the setting is WWII in an alternate universe, with a great story experience that you'll never forget.
- Immersive gameplay
-> There are generally two ways to experience the game - and the proper way of doing so blends turn-based RPG and shooter gameplay together perfectly.
- Memorable characters
-> The main cast of characters are relatable and all have distinct personalities that you'll come to love, and even the side characters you get to organize into your squad doesn't disappoint either. #Edy4Lyfe
- Great replayability
-> After you finish the game's story mode, you can start NewGame+ to get A-Ranks on the rest of the missions, and you even get to keep your progress with upgrades and such too. Or, you can try out the DLC missions, or even just go for the rest of the medals.
Of course, nothing is perfect - and definitely not this game either.
// CONS
- Annoying RNG
-> You'd spend most of your time in combat trying to score critical hits - but I suggest you save everytime you go for an all-or-nothing shot, because the amount of times the RNG (Random Numbers Generator, or basically "dice-rolling") system will troll you over is abysmal. Especially Largo. ♥♥♥♥ Largo.
- The "other" way of playing this game
-> "Alicia Rushing" is the act of equipping your Scout Leader Alicia with the best equipment, and giving her a Defense Boost order to run through missions at ridiculously high speeds. Yes, it's effective and is probably the most logical way of getting A-Ranks in this game, but it ruins the "tactical" part of the game.
- Illogical Save System
-> IMPORTANT NOTE - DO NOT SAVE YOUR DLC PROGRESS ON YOUR STORY SAVE FILES. It will overwrite your story progress, and you'll have to start over again. I don't know why SEGA decided to not let us save DLC and Story progress separately, but just don't do that.
- The Batomys mission
-> I hate the Batomys, the community hates the Batomys, and once you've played this mission, you'll also hate the Batomys.
// FINAL VERDICT
Valkyria Chronicles is an experience that you'll regret you missing when you look at the list of existing JRPGs. It's fun, it's memorable, it's replayable, and most of all, it's cheap and comes with all the DLC released. So just buy it already.

First thing you're gonna do when you get in-game is head straight for the tutorial. Upon entering, you get a rather basic series of text pop ups from some character you have no idea who they are, telling you vaguely what to do, and then they bugger off, leaving you pretty clueless on really what you need to do at all. Not only this, but the AI you'll be going against in the tutorial isn't limited in their abilities like you are, because you haven’t got to that part in the tutorial that you can unlock them yet, so more often than not, you're going to be obliterated by this AI in the tutorial. Since there's no cap on what they can do, or anything slowing them down, it’s a pretty unfair setup against a brand new player to the game when you’re meant to be teaching them what to do.
After a very unfair tutorial, which spans over quite a long time if you include all the hours you likely spent attempting to figure out what to do, you'll finally get to unlock the universe. The universe acts as a global scoreboard, but by then you might walk off and do something else because you're already bored with it.
Once you figure out what you need to do, it's a relatively simple game to play, and there's little progress or real grit in it to hold your interest for long. In short bursts, yeah, it can be a neat little thing to pass the time, but so is Sudoku or a cross-word puzzle, both of which I'd put it on par with.
One issue that really stood out to me though is the lag. When flattening or rising the land in large quantities the game would lag terribly for me, and this is certainly not down to my computer as I can play AAA games with ease. It's pretty aggravating when speed is usually the thing to need most of to beat the AI,  and certainly broke the immersion for me while trying to flatten a mountain and the in-game pointer is trailing behind where I just moused over.
It's not necessarily a 'bad' game, but there's really not that much there. It'd probably do better as a tablet or phone app rather than a full PC game. Maybe consider getting it when it's on sale, but it's not really worth going for it otherwise.

Hand of Fate is a button mashing good time!
(Though you can use skill to dodge, block, and reflect attack, the button mash approach works best for me.)
In all seriousness, this is a well thought out game. You build a deck of encounters which is then dealt at random to generate the map.
Each card will either open a combat map, a shop, or some sort of choice / challenge.
As you succeed at the various encounters, you unlock new cards which can be included in your deck resulting in a satisfying roguelike game.
Though I love the game, there are some flaws to be aware of.
Rather than RNG, you choose from shuffled cards. I find this REALLY hard to follow which makes the challenges much hard.
The combat maps are very limited. You will quickly come to recognize them.
The random nature of the shuffle can lead to some very hard runs, but this is common to all roguelikes
No character customization at all (though you can customize the gear available)
Definitely worth picking up at bundle price and I look forward to Hand of Fate 2!

Valkyria is one of the great masterpieces of video gaming. Everything about this game, from the atmospheric art style that mirror's the main character's sketchbook, the unforgetable character that you grow to love and hate, and the innovative gameplay that freshens up the classical tactics game formula build together to make this game a heck of an experience.
Where its sequel, Valkyria 2, arguably has deeper gameplay, this version has characters and a story that grabs you and holds you. There are a couple of funny cameos, in the form of Vyse and Aika from Skies of Arcadia. It even has, what I would call, the most heartbreaking moment in gaming history. Anyone who has played the game knows what I'm talking about. There is no way that you can see that scene without your blood running cold.
Don't miss out playing this game. While it may not play quite as slick as it did on the Playstation 3 and the controller support can be a bit wonky, it is still a ton of fun to live those experiences and fight through a war with a squad of individuals who group up around you. Fight for Gallia's freedom with them.

Okay first of: Is this a good game? Yes it is, definatly so.
If you enjoy games like baldurs gate, fallout 1,2 and tactics, Pillars of Eternity and so on then you will definatly enjoy this game. But what surprises me the most is the amount of fantastic well written meaty goodness the story has.
A few bugs are present sure, and there are some other things i dislike about it but that wont affect you one bit.
the only note worthy "bad" thing is that as amazing as the start and mid part of the game is, the ending seem a bit well weak. not directly bad, just rushed perhaps. But the guys made a fantastic tactical rpg with rich story, amazing music, well written romance side quests (at least the ones i have tested). It is just sad that their epilogue doesnt really appeal to me, mainly because of the lack of a few choices to wrap things up with.
Combat: Combat is fun and fast paced, tactical and can be hard as well as long. The whole Elemental magic, terrain exploiting, combining spells for maximum omph and so on is fun. Having a Geomancer make the ground slick with oil, only to have a pyromancer to set it ablaze alongside the enemy. Or have the Aquamancer flood the battle field with rain only to have an Aeromancer send down lightning bolts to electrify everything thats in liquid... yes liquid this means massive blood pools from critical hits or killed mobs can also be used for this. But do not take Warfare, Hunter or Scoundrel lightly these martial skills are not worse than spells, they have definatly their own uses to even the battlefield with knockdown, sleep, aoe damage and more.
Overall better than Divinity: Original Sin at least in my eyes, infact the mid part of the games beat the crap out of any other game i have played in the last few years or so. I am tempted to go 10 of 10, but there are those few little bits of meh that pulls it down to a 8. so yeah 8 of 10 (but could so easily be a 10 if the ending got a bit more polish)

This is probably one of the best games I've played. Let me make the list.
Pros:
Realism - Like some others have stated you will bring stuff to where it actually goes, like construction equipment will go to construction site, etc.
More Realism - Now I know some people say the AI is broken, but when I play it works really well. They slow down and even stop when your merging onto a highway, they will let you take your turn at a stop sign, as long as you use your turn signals then the AI works great, and much more!
Even more Realism - Working mirrors (that you can adjust so you can see out of them better), looking out your window, when it rains you can turn on your wipers and if you don't then you can't see as well out your window, while driving you need fuel, you can get tired (I don't know yet on what happens when your tired haven't had a 24 hour drive yet), traffic offenses (they don't go full on all the laws in the us I don't think because then it would be a little to hard to start), when your in the county you can see crop dusters actually dusting their crops, and lots more.
Mod Support - When a game adds mod support it allows the community to really get into the game because they can make content for it for other to use and make their experience more enjoyable. Like say you want a feature in the game but isn't in the game yet/won't be in the game, you can use a mod someone made and have that feature. They even help by letting you know when a mod is incompatible so you don't go searching for hours with tons of mods installed for the mod that breaks your game.
Trucking - It's as the title and description say, you're a truck driver. (Idk if this is a spoiler but I'll assume it is) You start off with no money but your a driver for hire, earn enough money to buy your own truck and be your own boss. (Or get a bank loan and buy a truck. :P) I got most of the DLC when I bough the game as most of it is free. (Unless somehow Nevada isn't in yet and I have it for some reason. :P) If you think the drive times will be realistic because the game is very realistic then don't worry, they don't want you to spend 20 hours on one delivery. It goes much faster.
And Lots Lots More!
Cons:
The only con for me is turning needs a tiny bit of work, like I'm use to the wheel auto-correcting when I let got of the turning button but I guess it's more realistic that you have to turn the other way to stop turning.
My Opinion of the Game:
A must buy if you like a nice relaxing game. Just you and the open road. But is still very fun. And I'll let y'all in on a funny place to sit online, if you go to Oxnard, the GPS takes you a route that most people at one point have no idea how to drive on so there is just a 50 truck pile up. And sometimes someone will be going 100 miles an hour and fly off the cliff. Lol. Definitely recommend this game. Fun times.

I've read the reviews complaining about the map being reletively small, especially compared to its older brother Euro Truck Sim 2.  These people aren't following the Devs announcements, or even the news on the title screen.  Nevada was released with the game followed closly by Arizona for free. It's smooth twin-stick shooter combat meshes well with the rogue-lite procedural level generation and perma-death possibilities. I was surprised to find that although it is a procedural game, it's well structured. With choice options at the end of each level to progress to harder bosses (or run through mobs for more cash). EDIT: To clarify things, I owned Overgrowth a year before it came out on Steam; my Steam playtime is irrelevant.
I make a point not to review games that are in alpha or beta until they're released, but I'll make an exception for Overgrowth for two simple reasons: (1) it's good enough to justify a $30 purchase even in its alpha builds, and (2) I consider it to be an absolutely enormous leap in the slow evolution of fighting games.
When you preorder Overgrowth, you get immediate access to the current alpha build, so you can test everything out right away as the developers add stuff. This alleviates the usual problem with preordering games, that is, putting down money for a product that doesn't exist yet.
The game itself currently boasts some of the smoothest, most fun, most intense combat of any game, ever, and I don't say that lightly. Overgrowth, like many indie games, uses physics as a driving mechanic. When you get kicked, your character reacts dynamically with a blend of animation and ragdoll. When you get stabbed, likewise. Dealing kicks and punches and slashes feels incredibly good -- the combat is fast-paced and frantic. Against more than one opponent, you'll almost inevitably lose unless your opponents are significantly slower or weaker than you, especially in a weapon fight.
Let's talk about weapon combat for a moment: it's just as fast as the unarmed combat, maybe even faster in the case of the fencing swords and knives. It's one or two hits to a kill, so blocking and dodging is absolutely essential. The fights are cinematic and extremely satisfying (this applies to unarmed fights as well), especially if you hit the slow-motion key (currently tab by default) just as either combatant dies.
The parkour can't go without mention. Though at this point in the game's development, the parkour is its weakest point (momentum doesn't carry while climbing), it's still ahead of many games with parkour elements. Wall-running, wall-jumping, and movement in genreral feel great. Everything flows together without the need for extraneous button-pressing, and when you do press a button, the resulting blended animation is a pleasure to watch. The only bad thing about the parkour, climbing, still isn't bad at all. It's still faster than most games, and still feels better than most games.
I can't recommend Overgrowth enough. You could buy it for the combat alone (setting aside that there's going to be an actual story, with the writer's skill already demonstrated in a full-length comic over at Wolfire's home page). Overgrowth's combat, in my opinion, is the most fun of any melee combat game ever made.

I have been playing this game on and off for the past 4 months. It has consistently been a lot of fun, and i'm glad they brought it too Steam so it can reach a wider audience.
TL;DR - Fun, very fluid and brutal 3rd person fighting game with rabbits and wolves, is definetely an alpha so expect bugs and a pretty good PC too run it.
This game at this current stage is basically an arena brawler with rabbits and wolves that are somewhat "humanoid", there are a number of different preset scenarios with slightly different objectives. For example, reach the coloured block without being killed, which is quite difficult when there are rabbit guards with broadswords and spears!  There is also a proper arena mode where you are in an actual arena and will fight waves of different rabbits, this is random and will spawn you with either a friendly NPC or on your own and is a lot of fun.
The fighting mechanic is pretty unique and reminds of me of kung fu movies, it consists of left clicking to attack and right clicking to block and shift to duck and roll, but it is very challenging at times and looks AMAZING when you finally master it. It also shows blood stains on the characters and on the walls when you get hit against them, and sound effects are pretty good as the actual hits that you manage to connect sound very satisfying and brutal.
Yes the game WILL CRASH and yes it is a bit BUGGY, but overall the fighting mechanics are beautiful in action and it feels so satisfying roundhouse kicking a rabbit into a brick wall. The game also needs pretty much a dedicated gaming PC to run well, and i find particularly the areas with multiple guards wielding weapons to take a slight hit in frame drop but otherwise it's great and will only continue to improve as more and more content is implemented.

Hmmm. Archeage. Well as you can see I have over 7k hours played. Overall I definitely recommend the game for pvpers. HOWEVER, you need either a lot of time or a lot of money to catch up to Legacy servers. I will forever try out fresh start servers everytime they come around.
Is it P2W: Yes.
Can you play to win: Somewhat. I put some money into the game and a ton of time and I am only 6.9k gs. Where I see really pay 2 win people (>$100k players) at 8k gs plus.
Can I compete in PvP against anyone: yes. Once you are over 6k gs on legacy you can definetly be competitive.
Why should I play: Are you a pvper? then yes? Do you not pvp? then no.
Rating
-Best pvp mechanics ever: 1v1 8/10, smallscale 10/10, open world 10/10, Raid v Raid 8/10, naval combat 10/10
-Professions 8/10
-server stability: 7/10
-XL/Trion game management: 6/10
-AA community: 6/10
-Sandbox elements: 8/10
-Themepark elements: 4/10
-Dungeons: 2/10
-Raids: 10/10. Most endgame content can be competed over. Doing a Kraken can turn into ours of Faction v Faction or Raid v Raid
-Class balance: 8/10 If you really take the time to learn the different kits, then Archers, Mages, Melees and Healers all have viable build for any type of pvp. Some are better suited for different situations. However unlike most MMOs, each class requires skill in order to stand out. If I consider the best mages, archers, melees and healers Ive met. They are all equally as difficult to fight. For average players, their experiences may differ. I played at a very high skill cap and understood the kits of my opponents. Most people think paladins or Drs are cheesy 1v1 classes, but nothing compares to a skilled daggerspell, defiler, lamentor, etc.
Best way to get started: Wait for a fresh start server release and get patron. Otherwise expect to put $100-200 into a legacy server and find a mentor to get started.
What to look out for: In 3.5 it appears the gap between the haves and the have nots are going to get worse. Ways of non swipers to gain gold are going to become more difficult. So people like me who dont necessarily need to improve my gear wont really be effected, while fresh players will be facing Mt. Everest to catch up.
My recommendations to Trion/XL: Merge legacy servers, Make tradepacks MORE rewarding not less, Lock transfers longer so guilds cant hop to lower populated servers to free farm, Reduce the ammount of tiers and grades on armor and weapons so you can retain a higher population, Remove all regrading items from the cash shop (The release of red regrade in RNG chests killed freshstart server). ALLOW a feature to block other peoples regrades and a feature to disable a players ability to regrade. Regrading is terrible already, Somehow I have spent over 400k gold trying to make an epic weapon and never made one, while other people on FS made legendary weapons by the 2nd week.
Summary: With all the trash elements of the game, the pvp is top notch. This game is completely carried by the amazing combat mechanics and while many will disagree the balance. You can literally play any type of damage and be top tier. If you really take the time to learn the kits every class is broken. Archers can 2 shot with concussive snipes, Mages can global with godwhisp animation cancels, melees can blow you up in a chained trip lock down. I enjoy playing every type of dps and even healing. Hope this helped =)

Owing to the succession laws of my country, a technicality prevented my ascension to absolute power over the land. Fearing the backlash from the nobility, I was unable to turn the influence I inherited from my merchant father, whom my mother married "Matrilinealy", into a physical act of power in the form of an armed coup. Also, owing to the cultural convictions of the populace, armed rebellion was a distinct probability, indeed built in to their constitution as a check against Tyranny.
Upon mulling this over, I hoped to find an etymological kink in my alarming realization that I AM a "Tyrant". While I couldn't rid myself of the label, I did notice that in the Greek tradition, while a "Tyrant" IS someone who achieves power outside of the methods a society has deliberately created, the negative connotation we experience was not necessarily (although, admittedly, often enough) felt by them. Indeed, when a Tyrant was welcomed and appreciated, it was during a time where the current system was not functioning. If I could capture that word, and guide it properly through it's emotional course, I started thinking that I might be able to channel the best and worst definitions of that word in a manner that serves my needs.
Thus, I sent my Chancellor to sow dissent in the regions of the empire with the strongest religious tendencies, warning of affiliations between the Emperor and Islam, confident that the difficulties in disproving such a connection makes proving them with factual evidence unnecessary. Between assignments, he labored to please god find some interpretation that will allow me to pursue my aims with a semblance legitimacy.
My Marshal was sent to repress rebellions in territories that were under no threat of doing so, with instructions to warn the populace against the imminent threat of an Islamic uprising secretly backed by an Emperor who wants to disarm it's citizens. By militarizing locals in the name of justice against Tyrant Emperor, he will be in a better position to evaluate where and how many weapons are being stored.
My Court Chaplin was sent, alongside gifts of money I just happened to want to donate, to the local religious leaders to demonstrate the support my efforts afforded their congregations in the form of masses of passionate, scared, angry zealots, and that reciprocation would be mutually beneficial.
My Spymaster was sent around the land to spread rumors that the Emperor, actually, was not at all legitimate on the same grounds that I actually am not. I have a game I like to play where I accuse someone of something I know they are innocent of that I may see what genuine denial of guilt looks like, especially if it is something that I am guilty of committing or plan to commit. When he dismissed the accusations as "beneath his dignity", he gave me leave to do the same when the time came to overtly assert myself. Regarding the issue itself, enough of the populace believes our Emperor is as illegitimate as I am in fact that it shouldn't be regarded seriously now.
My Steward was sent to collect taxes in the poorest regions in my grasp, with instructions to apologize for having to collect but their Emperor insisted they do so.
Now, to let the damage fester, I will continue to fight the version of my Emperor that my minions have created, and declare victory when thwarted and claim credit for anything positive done by the Emperor, especially if I did not support it, and preemptively call hypocrite anywhere I engage in hypocrisy.

Ok First it should go without saying but I will say this up front so there is no question.  This is an Early Access game and as such it has it's share of bugs and issues to work out.  Please do not play this game expecting any kind of a finished product.  I purchased this game with the knowledge of EA games already so I come with the expectation that there will be annoying moments in game and things that need to be fixed.
With all that said, for an EA product it is well done in it's state.  There is a lot of work to be done but it's a compelling enough game as is that it's worth playing even now with all of it's blemishes and kinks.   There are plenty of posts and articles out there that list the bugs that exist now and the problems some people have with it so I won't go into detail here.
What I do love is playing in the Conan Universe in the form of being an exile in the land, in survival mode.  I love survival games and open ended building and exploring games such as this and I love Conan so this was a win-win for me.  The game is not a block build type such as empyrion or others but more modular as in, you build with parts like walls and such.  This is an important point as I am sure there are some that would find this unappealing.  That being said, it is quite flexiblle in how you build your structures.
Survival wise it's dangerous enough that it keeps you on your toes but not at the level of games such as the Forest where your heart is beating rapidly every time you're out in the wilderness in the dark worried cannibals or mutants are going to get you (mind you that's not a bad thing just showing the contrast)
I have not yet leveled to the point of summoning a diety but it's something I look forward to.
Note-  I have only played solo so far so keep that in mind also.
I recommend this game to anyone that is familiar with EA games and is ok with watching development of a game happen as they play and is willing to report bugs or at the very least, put up with them as things unfold.

Words that could describe this game would be the following:
Grindy, Addicting, Long Haul, Third Person
Over the years playing Warframe, DE comes through with new content time and time again to keep the game alive. Even when just shooting baddies from different factions, or going about mission to mission hunting down that one prime piece, it doesn't grow tiring to most. If you're someone that doesn't like waiting real time hours for things to build (ranging from 12 to 72 hours), there's always platinum (in-game currency bought with real money or traded for items in-game) to rush items or venturing out to pass the time.
While the game isn't for everyone - admitted truth, tried getting a few people into it before, some people stick with it and others find it isn't their cup of tea - it's at least something worth trying to play. The beginning is semi-grind heavy considering Mastery Lock for items, but if you can pull through the long haul the results are worth it putting time and modding into your arsenal of weaponry.
All in all, while the game has some minor quirks, I still give it a 9/10. Here's to the long haul and more future content beyond what they've already brought - the landscape Plains of Eidolon - and to the many that come to join the community.

What can be said about Pac-Man that hasn't been said dozens of times already? The game isn't a classic for no reason. The gameplay is addictive and iconic, and as soon as you hear those jingles, beeps, boops, and waka wakas, you'll very likely find them stuck in your head for the rest of the day, if not longer.
So how's this PORT of Pac-Man, then?
Well, as far as the game itself is concerned, it's Pac-Man! Looks nice, plays great, sounds like the Pac-Man you'd expect.
That said, the "ARCADE GAME SERIES" version of Pac-Man here does have a couple of kinks in it, the main one I found being that you do have to play it while most of the screen is taken up with artwork like an old school arcade cabinet, but the game itself is as playable and addictive as it's always been.
Despite that, if you want some old school arcade fun to pick up and play without having to worry about the modern video game stresses of story modes, load times, and so on, then this is definitely worth the purchase.

It's Pac-man.
That alone should sell you on this, especially if you can get it for a good price.
Unfortunately, as many others have noted, it's also possibly the most bloated copy of Pac-man that anyone has ever seen. This is a game that came out almost 40 years ago. Even with nice new menus and interface, it shouldn't take up more than 50 MBs of space on your HDD. Somehow, Namco managed to make the game almost 1 GB in size.
What is all that space being used for? Who the hell knows. A spiffy new menu, overlays, artwork...even factoring in all of these things, there's no way the file size should be this darn big. When space is a commodity for most people (HDDs cost money and don't last forever, after all), this is an egregious oversight.
The game plays pretty well aside from some trouble picking up your movements, but I attribute that to simply being a classic retro arcade game designed to make you pump quarters. It's essentially a rom with nice, pretty new overlays, and that's not necessarily a bad thing – or at least it wouldn't be bad if it wasn't also taking up an incredible amount of space.
This might be enough to elicit negative reviews from some gamers, but there's just no way I can give Pac-man a bad review. Even if he's fatter than he has ever been before and probably needs to lay off of the power pellets, I still love Pac-man. I will always love Pac-man. I just can't quit you, Pac. I just can't quit you.
