Ruiner is a twin stick shooter set in a well realised stylised cyberpunk world.
Most of your time will be spent within industrial complexes, a series of narrow paths connecting open areas where the majority of the combat takes place.
The combat is wonderful to behold due to a combination of tight controls, surprisingly difficult encounters (depending on difficulty setting of course) and the wonderful visuals. The visual/sound effects very effectively sell the weight and power of the weapons and abilities in use and make combat very satisfying.
The music is very effective at building the mood between combat areas, and great at getting the blood pumping in action sequences.
Ruiner is a small game, which is a shame. There is a city hub between the major mission sections of the game and the developers have done a fantastic job of making a lively and moody isometric cyberpunk sprawl, complete with characters. Unfortunately, you dont spend a lot of time in this area and there is only the one hub. Ruiner gives you a taste of the wonderful world they have crafted but I wanted to delve into it more.  It would have been nice to have more than one hub, allow the player to explore more visually distict areas, Ruiner is saturated in red, but it might have been nice to see some neon.
Overall I very much enjoyed the game however, it is clear that they went for quality not quanity and what they have is polished to a mirror shine. I should also note that this game manages to look beautiful and runs like a dream. No issues with optimisation here.
I am hopeful to see DLC or a future game explore this world further.

ArcheAge is a PvP oriented game dominated by grind, powered by the endless pursuit of higher level gear and capped off with an extremely oppresive mechanic know as "Labor." The game itself has some superb ideas, most player driven and would be incredibly fun to play if it wasn't so deeply flawed.
This is a resource that is tied to almost every single aspect of the game: World loot, money bags, resurection (getting back XP from PvE death), gathering, crafting and all the systems based upon them.
Labor is gained in several ways, non-patrons can only attain it by being logged in at a rate of 5 labor per 5 minutes (cap of 2,000) or by buying potions in the cash shop whereas patrons gain it at a rate of 10 labor per 5 minutes with an offline gain of 5 per 5 (5,000 cap) plus the cash shop.
I have yet to discern a reason for this system which couldn't be done with cooldowns or limitations, other than it being there to sell labor potions or patron. Even opening collected loot and money bags requires it, both of which increase in requirement as you gain higher levels yet the rate you gain labor is constant and in a game of PvP dependent of gear, well you do the math.
In a word, tedious. Quite literally "Go here, Kill this X times" through a variety of climates and geography. There are dungeons in the game but you'll never see them until endgame.
Extremely dependent on your chosen classes, three in total with a choice 10 with up to 120 total combinations. Unfortunately out of those maybe 20 are actually useable and 10 of those being the most powerful.
The combat is driven by a fairly robust combo system that works across the various classes with various effects. Some combine for more damage, others create new status effects or simply prolong them. Sounds good in theory but in practice you'll be using one or two of the most effective combos.
The entire backbone of the game, so far (as of level 45) I've only seen one or two fights against players of my own level but a lot more of higher levels just ganking. Not really that interesting as a whole, it boils down to who can stunlock and burst the most.
Player driven with interesting things like treasure hunts, building vehicles, houses and farms, trade routes and piracy. All of which is effected by the previous mechanics and the labor system.
Overall ArcheAge will appeal to those who don't mind putting a lot of time, effort and money into something to gain the rewards but it is fleeting. New players are hopelessly outclassed by the higher geared players who prevent any progression by hampering trade, locking out bosses or simply ganking them as zones turn into "War" mode.
There are good ideas locked away behind these issues which, if handled correctly, could lead to a thoroughly enjoyable game. Just not this one.

Back to WFTO - I do recommend the game as there's some good fun to be had (again) treating this as a DK 2.0 reboot.
Some solid work was put into the game assets. The writing (in large measure) is also well done and they brought in Richard Ridings once again as mentor, and general grumpy evil scolder of things.
This isn't DK3 because that would involve finally breaking out onto the surface. From what I'm seeing that's not going to happen, unless WFTO is expanded - that would be great and all former DK fans would appreciate it.
Unfortunately there's also some (IMO anyway) glaring contrived things, most notably - sand.
Sand is being used to artificially separate enemy assets from the player. You can't claim it, replace it, put down a sheet of steel (or stone, wood, magic or anything else) to create a connection to take over enemy tiles beyond it.
It's downright stupid, frankly. I think the developers may have decided to use this because they didn't want to go to the effort of dealing with (a lot of added) level design complexities and logic where the player can capture (or cross and continue to capture) empire tiles beyond the single sand tiles carefully laid out as this silly barrier.
I'm calling this out because it may seem low priority but it's actually not. Part of the interest for many of DK is taking over every inch of the underworld, one map at a time.
Another issue more toward "imposed balance" is mana (and worker) caps. They've done the system in a way explicitly limiting the players ability to create truly massive defensive systems sprawled across the underworld.
There are other things lacking as well.
But, it's 2015, the game as-is has without question had a lot of work put into it much of which is good quality. Far more than not it is definitely an updated take on the DK series with some things that used to be fun not implemented or allowed at all.
For long time DK fans it's still worth a romp and visually it looks great. I still have my original DK1 + 2 CD's, bonus packs and maps I made sitting on a NAS. And I've played both as recently as last year on W7. Takes just a little work then the games work perfectly.
For those without DK experience you should go get and play both of them if you really want to understand and appreciate where WFTO is coming from.
It should (or hopefully) be possible to use an editor to change the core campaign maps to eliminate the stupid sand or (even better) change the properties of sand to make sense (claimable).
The DK editor doesn't by default allow saving campaign maps but that's easily gotten around and allowed players to fine tune campaign maps to suit how they wanted to play it, in every regard.
Hopefully the WFTO map editor is at-least as capable. I've no idea, yet.

I've been able to relay some information to him to help fix minor bugs, typos, etc, as it is his first full game release as the process has been a good learning experience that can only improve not only in this title, but in future games as well.

As other reviewer's have stated, there are some minor spelling errors and the like, which don't detract terribly from what's being said or overall experience of the game. Solid RPGmaker Title so far, it feels like it has a lot of character to it.
If you're looking for the kind of game that Steam RPGmaker games offer, this is a solid one. The combat system is competent, and has had its moments so far where it gets genuinly fun, and it hasn't ever quite gotten boring yet, though your mileage may vary, with parallel mana and energy systems, so you have one resource for spells and abilities that only replenishes at specific locations like Inns, and another that instead starts low in every battle and builds up when you deal or are dealt damage, which fuels an entirely different set of abilities you can use. It's a fun system, and the combat seems very much focused on normal encounters being less difficult, to focus on the Bosses and similar opponents. It all works, and the game is clever and satisfying with they way they provide you with progression.
As for the story- It spends the first large chunk of the game switching between two disparate story threads, one about a down-on-his-luck hunter who's getting followed by a weird magic dog, and the other about a kid from a backwater village who none-too-subtly has a big destiny ahead of him, despite the boy being somewhat of a kindhearted idiot. The story has a great tone of subversion and messing with you, and a fun deadpan sense of humor that lets it keep a strait face where it counts, so the genuine parts of the story aren't undermining what's funny, and the funny parts don't undermine what's genuine. It's very competently handled, and it gives the game a fun character that I'm excited to see more of.
And, as a plus, the assets for characters, attacks, and monsters all seem to be custom, or at least modified from the generic assets you find in rpgmaker titles, and all look pretty good. There's a lot to like for a low price tag.

PROS:
- Decent Story and Storytelling (not the best, but drama is suitably introduced for overaching story and motivations, and the "main" characters are developed enough to establish interesting personalities)
- Combat System (Fluid, easy to understand, allows for variety of ways to deal with enemies but also allows for use of tested and true ATTACK ONLY strats to pass on the less interesting parts of the game)
- Magic and Skill System (lots of variety, most characters are not bound to exclusive magic/skill sets)
- Equipment (enough interesting gear to make me want explore the world)
- Story Guidance (whenever lost, special saving spot Crystal shows you the way - also, before final battle, a sage character can give you hints of where to go to acquire and see all gear)
- Comedy and Silliness (not the major point of the game, but a welcome addition)
- Absolutely NO Grind unless you want to grind
CONS:
- Story and Storytelling Gaps (some of the party's character motivations are never properly developed, others are hurried along)
- Shortness (14 hours of game to do everything, talked to everyone, etc etc)
- Railroading (open world map is small and scarcely populated with no random encounters, little to no diversion towards current objective, small quantity of side quests and optional areas)
- Too Focused Lore Development (lore and context given only through dialogues and only regarding current story, no world history books to explain the importace of certain locations and characters, without expanding to other things)
I think that's it. Overall a nice game and I enjoyed it, it scratched that nostalgic feel I have about 90s SNES JRPGs.

I am a fan of RPG Maker games, but I normally played those that have steam achievements.
Although this game does not have steam achievements, I bought it due to the low price of under $2, but did not have high expectations. I just thought that it was another average, low price game to spend a boring evening.
I was pleasantly surprised!!! This game is beautifully made, with a very interesting storyline that keep you guessing who the bad guys were. Furthermore, when you follow the initial storyline, you get to play and see events through the eyes of different heroes, and also learn their specific strengths and abilities. This particular game also have an interesting twist in term of spells and special abilities. You need to find and equip yourself with different spell books (Fire, Water, Wind, Earth, Light and Dark) of different levels (ranging from Level 1 Spellbooks to Master level Spellbooks). The spells that a player can cast is not attached to a particular team member, but they are attached to spellbooks. This means that you can strategize and trade these books to various team members. Similarly, special abilities are attached to weapons instead of being learn by party members. So wielding different weapons will enable the same party member to have different sets of special abilities. Hence, spells and abilities are novel in that they are attached to objects instead of people. I love it.
I have played about 15 hours but am still not close to the end. I am at the point where I can enter the final battle. However, I am a completionist, and would like to get all the best tomes (spells), legendary weapons and best armors in the entire game. Interestingly enough there is an NPC that is close to the final battle to tell you what BEST items you are missing, the quests that are involved, and the location where these items can be found. Currently none of my items (spellbooks, weapons and armors) are among the BEST, and I realised that I have another 10-20 interesting sidequests to do instead of jumping into the final battle. Well, I might not even survive the final battle if I do not do all these sidequests. In retrospect, I enjoyed these game very much because there are many interesting things to do still.
I wrote this review because I only see 1 review for this game, and would like to recommend this game to other RPG gamers. I will also update my review when I finished getting all the top tier items, and finished the game.
For under $2, such an interesting and high quality game is definitely worth it.!!!

Fallen Earth is an entertaining MMORPG set in the apocolyptic future. You play as one of countless clones with an unknown past and future, searching for more than an identity. With countless factions to join, aid, and/or harm, you the player are able to advance and change the storyline of the world. With countless means of combat from guns, explosives, mutations, psionics, and even swords and axes, you can find all a manner of ways to customize your battle experience. With a crafting system that will let you make almost everything in the game as well you can be certain you will almost always be able to make and use anything you find and/or see. The use of third person view for exploration and interaction and first person view for combat may be of some concern for some players, along with the need to explore select areas in groups, but otherwise, the game is easy to get used to and play on your own.

This is probably one of the best games I've played. Let me make the list.
Pros:
Realism - Like some others have stated you will bring stuff to where it actually goes, like construction equipment will go to construction site, etc.

I started playing ETS2 a couple months ago, and bought ATS on a whim. Turns out, I enjoy it more than the former! The reasons why are similar to those of many of the other reviewers of this game. I find it very relaxing to turn on some music and just make a few deliveries. It helps me calm down after a stressful day at work. Granted, these sim type games are not for everyone...which is fine. If you are, however, one of those who enjoy these sorts of games, or have enjoyed ETS2, you should definitely go for this one!
My only complaints are these: One, the AI drivers are awful. I don't know if the devs programmed them to be texting on their phones while they drive (which would be realistic, admittedly), but I for one see enough of these people in real life. The AI will merge directly ahead of you...or directly into the side of your trailer.
Two: The freeways. I am American and have been driving on the Interstate system since I was 15, and have never encountered a T-intersection with a stop sign to get onto the freeway, which is present in several locations in ATS. Making a left turn in these intersections is harrowing, as you must wait what seems like forever for a break in traffic that MIGHT be long enough for your slow-accelerating truck to merge safely - and even then, the AI traffic may just crash into you anyway. It just seems like overpasses and on-ramps should be used in these situations, as they would IRL.
Three: This is not really the fault of the developers, and it's not really a complaint, as I understand the restrictions; but three states is just not enough, though it is a great start! I only hope that future DLC map expansions, which I wouldn't mind paying for, come relatively soon. It would just be disappointing if it was another ETS2 situation (when exactly is France becoming available there?)

Okay first of: Is this a good game? Yes it is, definatly so.
If you enjoy games like baldurs gate, fallout 1,2 and tactics, Pillars of Eternity and so on then you will definatly enjoy this game. But what surprises me the most is the amount of fantastic well written meaty goodness the story has.
A few bugs are present sure, and there are some other things i dislike about it but that wont affect you one bit.
the only note worthy "bad" thing is that as amazing as the start and mid part of the game is, the ending seem a bit well weak. not directly bad, just rushed perhaps. But the guys made a fantastic tactical rpg with rich story, amazing music, well written romance side quests (at least the ones i have tested). It is just sad that their epilogue doesnt really appeal to me, mainly because of the lack of a few choices to wrap things up with.
Combat: Combat is fun and fast paced, tactical and can be hard as well as long. The whole Elemental magic, terrain exploiting, combining spells for maximum omph and so on is fun. Having a Geomancer make the ground slick with oil, only to have a pyromancer to set it ablaze alongside the enemy. Or have the Aquamancer flood the battle field with rain only to have an Aeromancer send down lightning bolts to electrify everything thats in liquid... yes liquid this means massive blood pools from critical hits or killed mobs can also be used for this. But do not take Warfare, Hunter or Scoundrel lightly these martial skills are not worse than spells, they have definatly their own uses to even the battlefield with knockdown, sleep, aoe damage and more.
Overall better than Divinity: Original Sin at least in my eyes, infact the mid part of the games beat the crap out of any other game i have played in the last few years or so. I am tempted to go 10 of 10, but there are those few little bits of meh that pulls it down to a 8. so yeah 8 of 10 (but could so easily be a 10 if the ending got a bit more polish)

The character & class balance isn't exactly ideal, definitely encouraging you to play favorites; with the ranking system in particular encouraging an unusual playing style. The sequels apparently tried to address this & introduced new classes too but I've not played them because they're PSP exclusive.
It's recommended to ignore the ranking system, avoid unnecessary grinding and play blind on your first playthrough. There's New Game Plus so you don't miss anything by doing so.
There were definitely issues at launch but I think any that could be replicated consistently & easily were fixed by patches that were unusually effective for a port of a Sega game.
That said I never tested the issues the port had at high framerates.
The fact Vanquish, which was worked on by the same porting team, had similar issues caused by certain mechanics being tied to framerate suggest that Sega could save money on post-launch support by hiring a better QA team.
Better QA could have the added bonus of not launching a game with bugs that prevent it from functioning offline after a 2 week delay specifically for "optimisation and bug fixing", but I digress.
I don't use mouse & keyboard so I've not had reason to test any issues caused by those controls.
I also don't know if the Ladder to Hell glitch where characters could clip through the map while trying to climb a ladder was ever fixed but I don't think it was something that was encountered consistently.
The port's missing some aesthetic improvements made to the PS4 version but support for high resolutions and (unofficially) mods which allow you to replace the character models with more detailed counterparts from in-engine cutscenes mean PC has overall the best looking version of the game; and it can run at 60fps or beyond.
In comparison PS3 runs the game at 720P 30fps with drops while PS4 runs it at 1080P 60fps with rare & slight drops. I think PS4 Pro gets locked 60 in Boost Mode. This is aside from pre-rendered cutscenes that are 720P 30fps on all formats.
Both PC and PS4 bundle all the PS3 version's (paid) DLC with the base game and feature "true" achievements whereas the PS3 original made do with in-game ones.
That about sums up my "review" of the game itself and its port.
However I don't recommend supporting Sega. If possible I'd recommend buying the physical PS4 version (used) or even the PS3 original as long as you aren't bothered about resolution, framerate or the DLC.
This isn't because of this, unusually well made & supported by Sega's standards, port. Rather it's because of Sega's decision to ship their current PC line-up with Denuvo; & their inconsistent practice on disclosing its inclusion whether through incompetence or intent.
If Denuvo or proper disclosure of 3rd party DRM doesn't bother you then feel free to buy the game, though I don't know why you'd have waited so long to own it, but personally I'm extremely wary of any DRM that might make games that use it cease to function in future.
I fully expect any future high profile Sega releases on PC will use Denuvo & I don't trust Sega to pay to have it patched out of games they can no longer profit from.
Certainly the 1 year lifespan of Sonic Runners, a freemium game with IAPs which launched in 2015 and ceased to exist at all in 2016, suggests Sega has no qualms about killing a game that's either costing too much or just not making enough money.
To be clear: this port of Valkyria Chronicles doesn't include Denuvo. However Sonic Mania launched with Denuvo recently at about the same price as Valkyria Chronicles, Bayonetta and Vanquish.
As such it seems entirely likely that any future releases in this price range will see Sega take the same DRM strategy; or perhaps these ports only evaded it by being smaller franchises that Sega was less certain would make investing in Denuvo protection worthwhile. Sega's "big" PC-centric franchises already use Denuvo.
Should I have to root against games I like being successful? While that's what I'm now doing I'd rather not feel forced to do so. If the choice is between future PC ports using Denuvo with no clear long term support plan or nothing; I'd take nothing.
Sega's mismanagement of their PC ports and of the Valkyria series in general isn't worth supporting for reasons beyond Denuvo.
I don't see why the apparent surprise success of this port resulted only in a PS4 port of the original and a Sony-exclusive "spin-off" action RPG which seemingly nobody wanted.
If the rumored Vanquish & Bayonetta PS4 ports are real then it's quite possible PC gamers are being treated as guinea pigs to test less refined versions of planned HD ports.
Why did the sequels have to remain exclusive to PSP (the 3rd not even localised) rather than being next in line for PC ports? Certainly it would take much more work to make them "presentable" but I'm not sure that they'd have to be as long as their gameplay was still decent.
Why did PC ports of Sega's console games seemingly go quiet for so long after Valkyria Chronicles/Sonic Lost World? Maybe Sega assumed that if a niche game like Valkyria Chronicles can shift a few hundred thousand units then a Sonic game would sell several times as much. Clearly it didn't work that way.
I'm also hugely disappointed in Sega's refusal to offer any DRM-free PC releases. I don't even mean their current games: I can see why they'd take steps to protect them (no matter how limp wristed). However several of their PC games were in pirates' hands before Steam even existed, never mind Denuvo, so any protection current DRM might offer them is essentially moot.
When a game is still well-liked over a decade after its launch, like this one will soon be, I see no reason Sega couldn't sell a DRM-free version on either GoG, the Humble Store (who already sell Steam keys for Sega games) or another platform that offers DRM-free games. Not doing so is simply turning down willing customers.
If even companies as infamously belligerent in their protection of their franchises as Disney and Warner Bros have seen the benefits of offering certain games on a DRM-free store-front then I can't see why Sega hasn't.
TL;DR: fine game, decent port. Don't recommend supporting the publisher.

War for the Overworld is the closest game you'll get to Dungeon Keeper 3, until EA decide to do something great with the property.
It shares many similarities to the classic Bullfrog games, but with a lot of bells and whistles (spells, potions, devices etc), giving the game depth and better control over your army. Some technical problems; nothing game breaking, or causing the game to crash, but you might see weird stuff happen occasionally.
If you want another Dungeon Keeper experience then buy it and enjoy. If you want a strategy game, you might find the games rough points distracting.

Fantastic game. I wasn't sure what to expect coming into it. I just heard people talking very nicely about this game whenever it came up (generally). I'm going to add to that growing crowd and say how phenomenal this game was.
Let's get the first thing out of the way: this is a narrative-heavy game. You *could* skip it all in theory (which is a nice option the game has!) but I find it superior to enjoy it at the slow-burn pace it sets, because it always remains compelling with the twists and turns it throws your way. Each character this game throws your way has their own charm, and unique traits about them that makes you want to learn more about who they are as people. In that sense, its like a good Fire Emblem game. (cough, 7). Its pretty heavy on the optional cutscenes, but to their credit they are usually interesting and help progress the plot along in an exquisitely paced way while developing the main set of characters fantastically! One of the few problems this game has is perhaps too many side-characters. You can still get a decent story out of them, but sometimes you just wish you could get more development and attention for them. (which the game actually does address in some nice ways, such as optional side missions that do have a meaty amount of dialogue and character building for them, so its definitely assuaged...).
Basically any flaws this game has in terms of plot can be easily remedied by the solutions offered in-game, unless you dislike the entire plot to begin with (in which case... If you are set on being against the plot and setting of this game, I'd question why you're even looking at a review for it in the first place?)
The plot itself, in case you decided not to read the game description, effectively describes the entirety of a war between nations, but places special emphasis on a few characters (Welkin, Isara, Alicia, Largo, Rosie- Err... maybe not just a few) in a single militia underdog squad. Its amazing how they managed to capture the soaring complexities of a war between nations and successfully condense it into being a relevant, poignant, and empathetic experience for the player. You feel among your brethren with squad 7, the readings, notes and journals give you history, context of the nations and... really everything you could ever want to know about the nations and world you inhabit, and the people (be they friends or foes) you're forced to share it with. You learn more and more about every single character and major player in the war and the world as the game goes on. Its really quite incredible how they managed to pull this off. There's only one moment where I feel things were a little rushed in the game, maybe 2, but they put it in good places within the story to where they could feasibly play it off with the subsequent events (that I will not spoil; you'll just know them when you see them).
The action and combat system isn't a traditional turn-based type, it somehow combines a turn-based system with an action-RPG combat system into a wonderful and pleasant meld of intense-enough combat to always keep fights fresh. Once you take your turn, you can't afford to be too complacent or you *will* take a lot of fire and even have your characters die before you can retaliate. This happens ESPECIALLY when against tanks. If you act quickly and efficiently though, you can destroy entire enemy squads without even a chance for retaliation. There is also enough weapon diversity to keep one satisfied, though for me the choices were *usually* obvious, There were times when I did switch my loadouts however, and that's something to be noted at the very least. It is also challenging in similar ways to most SRPGs like Fire Emblem or X-Com in that if your character ends their turn in a wrong place... well, yeah. you'll probably have to rescue them or even restart if things *really* go south. One thing I *do* have to say is, while the maps and combat themselves are challenging, the game itself is *VERY* forgiving with how it handles character-defeats (no perma-death until an enemy walks over their corpse or 3 turns has passed, MUCH more forgiving than Fire Emblem). If one wants a high level challenge from this game, I'd personally use a self-imposed challenge (like every character KO= death = reset, or even an ironman) to truly get a brutal and hardcore SRPG experience.
The soundtrack is always satisfying, good enough, and never really gets old, which is quite impressive to its credit. It gives the war proper respect, and provides each battle with weight and its own unique flair. It is also not an "empty" game either. You'll hear plenty of radio contact (enemies and allies alike) and its quite interesting to hear what's being said between commanders, common soldiers, officers and the like. It does this without interfering with the gameplay, like background noise that adds to the ambiance of a battlefield. The soundtrack also knows when to bring its best- you won't truly connect with it until it plunges a knife right in your heart as tragedy strikes, or when the game lets you feel your greatest triumphs and you feel an adrenaline rush that you can't even describe. Once the soundtrack hits you, you're hooked on the game till the end.
Oh, and the graphics are amazing for a port like this. Fantastically clean, pleasant to look at. There's minor issues I can state here, like textures with leaves and whatnot, but overall its crisp enough to give a nice experience. There's also very few glitches and bugs but they generally do not break the game or affect anything. I can't even remember most of them because they were usually forgotten about.  BUT, there was 1 or 2 times where glitches hit me hard. Be very careful with going up the stairs on the multiple-bunker levels. That's all I'll say.
I'd go on, but this review is already a wall of text. All I can say is: pick up this game. Its worth your money. I feel horrible getting it for 6$ on a sale; the people who ported/remade/whatever this is deserved full price for it.

I bought this game with no expectations, but ended up pleasantly surprised.  For a first effort and for the price, Dragons' Twilight is a definitely a game worth checking out.
The maps are a bit sparse and there are a few grammatical/capitalization errors. However, what the developer does do with the more limited game map is fairly impressive. Never did I feel like there wasn't enough to explore.  The story also  is quite engaging with some rather decent character development. This development does fall away a bit toward the latter part of the game, particularly with the introduction of more characters. I actually found myself wanting to know more about certain characters and their connections to one another.
I think one area where the game does shine is in the "no grinding." Grinding, in these games, is often a gratuitous way to extend the game. Sprawling, maze-like dungeons are common and commonly detract from the overall game and story. That is not the case with Dragons' Twilight. Each dungeon area serves its purpose with none of the dreaded "when will this end" feeling you get in many games where, as the game goes on, dungeons become longer and more tedious. This lack of massive dungeons and lack of a need for grinding is incredibly refreshing.
Another area where this game shines is in the skills and magic features. Magic is attained not by leveling up, but by equipping different tomes. The same goes for skills, which are only attained based on the type of weapon and the gear that characters can equip. This makes the choices for what gear to equip, along with what party members to include far more interesting and flexible. Where one character might work wonderfully in one dungeon area, he/she might be a detriment in the next.
I would definitely recommend this game. It's by no means perfect, but it is quite engaging.

The original Mass Effect isn't very fun. The lore and universe it sets up are amazing, but your inventory fills up so fast that micromanaging it becomes necessary at annoying times, sometimes it feels like you pick up more junk items here than in Diablo, the romance options were pretty lame, the combat was just lame, vehicular segments were the worst (climbing up tall hills/mountains at -just- the right angle to try to get over them, copy/pasted buildings on various planets with very slight differences to their arrangement of furniture and such, side quest overload at the Citadel with almost no side quests anywhere else in the galaxy, and...yeah, it just wasn't very good. I'm glad it happened, though, because it meant Mass Effect 2 happened, and boy did I have a good time with it. Oh, and the ending song on Mass Effect 1 is totally great in my book. <3
Mass Effect 2 doesn't do much for the lore, in all honesty. You get a little more info on mercenary groups and an organization called Cerberus, and that's about it. Mass Effect 2 is all about gameplay, and it fixes everything I complained about above. Those things are either gone or made better so that you have a good time. Far more romance options with more interesting characters, all fresh maps, the vehicular stuff in DLC is easy to maneuver around in, side quests are all over the place instead of conglomerating 75% or so of them into one map you pick them up at, the combat lets you use special abilities more often while still balancing it out and making it so much more fun with shields, barriers, and armor on the enemies, and instead of mountains of useless items, you pick up a gun, and it's added to your loadout you can choose from on a mission. That's it. No tiny incremental stat gear like in Mass Effect 1 where you waste your time dealing with paltry differences in gear.
Mass Effect 2 is head and shoulders above Mass Effect 1, and it is the best game in the trilogy for me. Mass Effect 3's ending was a travesty, and though it had some solid gameplay, I still enjoy 2's better somehow.

Anyway, as other people already pointed out, metascore of 58 doesn't do this game justice. It's a solid 70+. "Must buy" for fans of a genre.

Prime World: Defenders is basically the same old Tower Defense game all over again; however, it's quite well executed. You have more control over which towers you upgrade and how; you have a talent tree, and you have some randomness as to when you might acquire new towers. Throw in randomized levels with the random loot system, and you have a lot of re-playability at various stages of the game - where you might decide to take a break from progression and go hunting for new cards on the side.
Another thing I find awesome is the music - it's way better than what you usually find on video games, and compliments the gameplay quite well. There's a decent storyline, and the gameplay is rewarding - this game rocks. The only down side is that the makers of the game are no longer standing behind it (no forum activity or work on game) and some minor (but widespread) bugs are still in it. The bugs won't hurt you much though; you can still enjoy a great game at a great price.

If you're a fan of choose your own adventure games, if you're a fan of 3rd person medieval combat, if you're a fan of scaling difficulty then this game is for you.

Crusader Kings 2 is a PC grand strategy game that takes place in medieval Europe from the years 769 to 1453 as of the latest Downloadable Content (more on that later). You have the choice of playing any rank of noble from this time period, the objective being to grow your dynasty and its prestige while surviving a deadly period of history. This is accomplished by warfare, intrigue, and diplomacy or any combination of the three.
The game captures the spirt of the time period well, through several game mechanics that help you to understand the Middle Ages. Your character can die at any time from warfare to a sudden case of slow fever. In most games, this would be an annoyance, but the succession mechanic means that death has a meaningful impact on gameplay. You might find that your first son (who you are now playing as a result of your character’s death) is challenged by a younger son for succession rights of your domain. This can turn ruling a peaceful kingdom into a desperate struggle for at any moment.
Where Crusader Kings shines the most is in its ability to generate meaningful scenarios no matter what you do in the game. In order to do well in the game you need to keep an eye out for rival characters and kingdoms that covet your land, and build alliances with other dynasties through marriage or mutual need. Certain characters or vassals will even try to betray you for personal gain or simply because they do not like you. Staying in power is a constant battle that requires you to pay attention to what is going on in the world around you.
This being said Crusader Kings 2 is not for everyone playing the game requires a willingness to learn about medieval concepts such as succession laws and understanding ranks and relationships of nobility such as dukes, barons, earls, kings and emperors. The game also throws many terms at the player such as demese, levy, retinue, and de jure claim which can be difficult for a modern mind to understand. Furthermore it can be difficult to wrap your head around all of the diplomatic, military and intrigue actions you can take in the game. However the game provides tool tips, a decent tutorial, and generally does a good job of explaining what is going such that a determined player can make sense of the game given enough time.
Furthermore I would be remiss if I did not mention the business model of the game, the vanilla version of the game currently sells on steam for $39.99 but if you want all of the downloadable content the complete package goes for $159.99. Most of the DLC adds unnecessary fluff such as character portraits for different nationalities, extra emblems for dynasties and titles, music and unit models but it also includes DLC’s that will allow you to play as a trade republic, Viking raiders or an ahistorical scenario in which western Europe is invaded by Aztecs to name a few. The game has frequently gone on sale on Steam for as much as 75% off on everything so pick it up while it is on sale and then decide if you want to purchase the extra content.
I have never played a game quite like Crusader Kings 2, it uses a similar mechanics to Paradox’s other grand strategy game, but the inclusion of characters with motivations and goals makes it feel less like you are playing as and against faceless government entities slugging it out, and more like a huge drama out of Game of Thrones or a Shakespeare play. If this game interests you at all I recommend looking into it, as it is excellent example of what video games have the power to accomplish.

Okay, I've reviewed Galaga and Dig Dug in the ARCADE GAME SERIES, so PAC-MAN is the last to cover. Everybody should know this one, but if you're pretty young and don't, you go around a maze eating dots while avoiding ghosts. There are power pellets that let you turn the table and temporarily eat the ghosts. Eat all the dots and move on to the next level, where there are more dots.
As with Dig Dug, it has full screen but doesn't have proper full screen, still having a border around the game. The game has a deadzone issue where 360 controllers cause your PAC to pull to the left, which is a disaster in a maze game where the controls need to be tight or you die. Controllers are not fully supported in general and not given prompts.
Once again, I can't recommend this, as it's a low-effort emulation with no frills and basic issues that keep it from being purely enjoyable. Pick up PAC-MAN Championship Edition instead, or just find another means to get your PAC-MAN. It's frustrating to see Namco-Bandai treat Namco's games so shoddily, and at $4 it's just inexcusable.

Wikipedia has a great read on this game!
Pac-Man (Japanese: パックマン Hepburn: Pakkuman?), stylized as PAC-MAN, is an arcade game developed by Namco and first released in Japan in May 1980.[2][3] It was created by Japanese video game designer Toru Iwatani. It was licensed for distribution in the United States by Midway and released in October 1980. Immensely popular from its original release to the present day, Pac-Man is considered one of the classics of the medium, and an icon of 1980s popular culture.[6][7][8][9] Upon its release, the game—and, subsequently, Pac-Man derivatives—became a social phenomenon[10] that yielded high sales of merchandise and inspired a legacy in other media, such as the Pac-Man animated television series and the top-ten hit single "Pac-Man Fever".[11] Pac-Man was popular in the 1980s and 1990s and is still played in the 2010s.
When Pac-Man was released, the most popular arcade video games were space shooters, in particular, Space Invaders and Asteroids. The most visible minority were sports games that were mostly derivatives of Pong. Pac-Man succeeded by creating a new genre.[12] Pac-Man is often credited with being a landmark in video game history and is among the most famous arcade games of all time.[13] It is also one of the highest-grossing video games of all time,[14] having generated more than $2.5 billion in quarters by the 1990s.[15][16]

Never left a review before, so I hope this will be helpful. First things first, this game is not for everyone. It is truly a SIMULATOR. If you just want to drive a big rig around and crash cars and things of that nature, you're going to have a bad time. Unless you really enjoy simulation games, you're not going to like this.
Besides that, if you do enjoy simulation, WHAT ARE YOU WAITING FOR? ATS is a fantastic simulator, there honestly isn't too many cons for me, many more pros. The only thing I really have to say about it is, at this point it really isn't a finished game. It was only released a few months ago, so there's still a lot more to be added on to it. But for the time being, it's still amazing. The graphics are absolutely fantastic, and so is the attention to detail. Especially on the trucks. You can keep the control scheme as simple or as advanced as you'd like. The only thing I'd have to say, is that the AI drivers are horrible. But then again so are real drivers so, eh. The only con for me are the speed limits. Sometimes they can be hard to notice, and a lot of time the speed limit drops immediately, for example from 55mpH down to 30mph, so if there's a cop around, prepare to be ticketed. War for the Overworld is a real-time-strategy / dungeon management game which was developed and published by Subterranean Studios. The game was made possible through Kickstarter and seeks to establish itself as the spiritual successor to the original Dungeon Keeper series of games, going so far as to hire the same narrator from that series. The game and its devs were also praised by Peter Molyneux, the original creator of Dungeon Keeper.
The plot is pretty straight forward and borrows heavily from the Overlord series' plot line where the player takes on the role of a newly resurrected evil overlord who seeks to rebuild his domain and take vengeance against the currently ruling human empire.
+ Good artistic design that manages to capture the look and feel of Dungeon Keeper
+ Nice graphics, specially for a Unity engine game
+ Excellent voice acting from Richard Ridings (the Dungeon Keeper narrator)
+ The game was able to preserve DK's gameplay while making a few improvements of their own such as the 'Sins' system.
+ Skill / Tech Tree system that makes for several variations in dungeon builds (Sins system)
+ Good sound effects and atmosphere
+ Good variety of monster / minions with different skills and abilities
+ Fun campaign maps and missions
+ Fast paced action
+ Constant updates and interaction by the developers with the community
+ Good game time
- The tutorial missions does not cover a lot of the game's mechanics
- The gameplay is essentially RTS but with the Combat / Minion control being woefully underdeveloped
-
performance drops during late game situations: (specially when there are a lot of units on the map)
- Tool Tips is lacking: For example, if you move your mouse over to the Spells Tab, It should show  something like this “Spells Tab (B)” so that the player immediately knows that its bound to the B key but it doesn't so you'll have to refer back to the Controls Menu to see which key is bound to which UI element. This is very inconvenient specially for a fast paced game like this.
- First Person / Possession mode needs a lot of work: particularly, the fact that the character models of the currently possessed minion sometimes clip over the camera.
+/- Demon hand: I know its part of Dungeon Keeper's legacy but it would have been nice to have an option to use the regular mouse cursor.
+/- Story is predictable specially if you've played Overlord 1 and 2.
. War for the Overworld is certainly NOT Dungeon Keeper 3 but its the closest one out there. The developers are certainly passionate about this game and should no doubt be praised for making a much better spiritual successor with such a limited budget unlike that
that should be buried deep beneath the earth and forgotten.

The original Mass Effect isn't very fun. The lore and universe it sets up are amazing, but your inventory fills up so fast that micromanaging it becomes necessary at annoying times, sometimes it feels like you pick up more junk items here than in Diablo, the romance options were pretty lame, the combat was just lame, vehicular segments were the worst (climbing up tall hills/mountains at -just- the right angle to try to get over them, copy/pasted buildings on various planets with very slight differences to their arrangement of furniture and such, side quest overload at the Citadel with almost no side quests anywhere else in the galaxy, and...yeah, it just wasn't very good. I'm glad it happened, though, because it meant Mass Effect 2 happened, and boy did I have a good time with it. Oh, and the ending song on Mass Effect 1 is totally great in my book. <3
Mass Effect 2 doesn't do much for the lore, in all honesty. You get a little more info on mercenary groups and an organization called Cerberus, and that's about it. Mass Effect 2 is all about gameplay, and it fixes everything I complained about above. Those things are either gone or made better so that you have a good time. Far more romance options with more interesting characters, all fresh maps, the vehicular stuff in DLC is easy to maneuver around in, side quests are all over the place instead of conglomerating 75% or so of them into one map you pick them up at, the combat lets you use special abilities more often while still balancing it out and making it so much more fun with shields, barriers, and armor on the enemies, and instead of mountains of useless items, you pick up a gun, and it's added to your loadout you can choose from on a mission. That's it. No tiny incremental stat gear like in Mass Effect 1 where you waste your time dealing with paltry differences in gear.
Mass Effect 2 is head and shoulders above Mass Effect 1, and it is the best game in the trilogy for me. Mass Effect 3's ending was a travesty, and though it had some solid gameplay, I still enjoy 2's better somehow.

Kudos for remaking Dungeon Keeper. It was really time for a new game using this brilliant game principles. The Kickstarter campaign made clear, that there is a huge demand for this kind of game. WftO has two problems though: abysmal QA and completely missing the pace, that made DK great:
Updates tend to break the game, make certain levels unplayable because no one seems to test how an "rebalancing" idea they implement actually fits into the single player campaign. I don't know if they don't test at all, are only interested in multiplayer game or someone who already mastered the game tries it out briefly. But when you are new to this game and think about investing money into this: Don't! You are not their target audience. They are themselves their only target audience. This would fit to an free, open source game, but not to a product that sells for money.
DK had a brilliant feature, that made this whole "evil overlord" concept possible: you could play at your own pace. You could play aggresively with early attacks, before the enemy builds his base, or you could fortify, build up everything and flood the enemy with your über-army. You could be as unfair as you wanted to be. I agree that this is very hard to implement, but WftO fails miserably. It dictates the pace all the time: Timers don't give you time to build up your dungeon, Enemy attacks disrupt you all the time. There is either an oversupply or far to little gold. It treats you like a kid with a short attention span, constantly forgetting what your task was. And in doing so it just expects a certain playing style. It's not hard to play a level: it's hard to find out, how the developers expected you to solve the level, without giving you a chance to develop your own solution and this feels strange.
Would be a good free game, doesn't feel like anything someone makes a living with.

After picking up ME1 & 2 as a sale bundle, I breezed through the original thinking it was a clunky Knights of the Old Republic clone. After being urged by a friend to continue on and play through ME2, I couldn't be happier that I did. Mass Effect 2 improves upon the original in every way.
Gameplay: This second game in the trilogy shifts the action from RPG-Shooter to Shooter-RPG and it's definitely for the better. The combat feels similar to the first, just inifitely tighter. Squad combat control is intuitive and the powers are fun and useful. Most importantly, the combat is balanced and fun. The RPG elements are limited to skill selection and dialogue options. The dialogue options are limited to angelic paragon or efficient ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, but both are viable.
Graphics: I played this in 2016. The engine is definitely beginning to show its age, but still holds up well enough that the graphics are never really an issue. The controls can be a bit sluggish thanks to the engine, but no big issues.
Story: I think ME2 does a great job of making you care about your companions, especially compared with the first game. Not only are the companions much more interesting and dynamic than in the first game, but each has an accompanying "Loyalty Mission" to delve deeper into their backstories and affect the final mission outcome. The main story is decent and somewhat mysterious. Plot holes and inconsistencies are there if you look for them. The narrative isn't as compelling as chasing Saren was in the first game, but it moves along well enough and with enough gravitas to keep things interesting.
It took me 28 hours to get through the main mission, loyalty side missions, and many side quests. You can pick this up for $5 or $10 on Steam sales, so there's no reason not to dive into this excellent Shooter RPG.

Fantastic game. I wasn't sure what to expect coming into it. I just heard people talking very nicely about this game whenever it came up (generally). I'm going to add to that growing crowd and say how phenomenal this game was.
Let's get the first thing out of the way: this is a narrative-heavy game. You *could* skip it all in theory (which is a nice option the game has!) but I find it superior to enjoy it at the slow-burn pace it sets, because it always remains compelling with the twists and turns it throws your way. Each character this game throws your way has their own charm, and unique traits about them that makes you want to learn more about who they are as people. In that sense, its like a good Fire Emblem game. (cough, 7). Its pretty heavy on the optional cutscenes, but to their credit they are usually interesting and help progress the plot along in an exquisitely paced way while developing the main set of characters fantastically! One of the few problems this game has is perhaps too many side-characters. You can still get a decent story out of them, but sometimes you just wish you could get more development and attention for them. (which the game actually does address in some nice ways, such as optional side missions that do have a meaty amount of dialogue and character building for them, so its definitely assuaged...).
Basically any flaws this game has in terms of plot can be easily remedied by the solutions offered in-game, unless you dislike the entire plot to begin with (in which case... If you are set on being against the plot and setting of this game, I'd question why you're even looking at a review for it in the first place?)
The plot itself, in case you decided not to read the game description, effectively describes the entirety of a war between nations, but places special emphasis on a few characters (Welkin, Isara, Alicia, Largo, Rosie- Err... maybe not just a few) in a single militia underdog squad. Its amazing how they managed to capture the soaring complexities of a war between nations and successfully condense it into being a relevant, poignant, and empathetic experience for the player. You feel among your brethren with squad 7, the readings, notes and journals give you history, context of the nations and... really everything you could ever want to know about the nations and world you inhabit, and the people (be they friends or foes) you're forced to share it with. You learn more and more about every single character and major player in the war and the world as the game goes on. Its really quite incredible how they managed to pull this off. There's only one moment where I feel things were a little rushed in the game, maybe 2, but they put it in good places within the story to where they could feasibly play it off with the subsequent events (that I will not spoil; you'll just know them when you see them).
The action and combat system isn't a traditional turn-based type, it somehow combines a turn-based system with an action-RPG combat system into a wonderful and pleasant meld of intense-enough combat to always keep fights fresh. Once you take your turn, you can't afford to be too complacent or you *will* take a lot of fire and even have your characters die before you can retaliate. This happens ESPECIALLY when against tanks. If you act quickly and efficiently though, you can destroy entire enemy squads without even a chance for retaliation. There is also enough weapon diversity to keep one satisfied, though for me the choices were *usually* obvious, There were times when I did switch my loadouts however, and that's something to be noted at the very least. It is also challenging in similar ways to most SRPGs like Fire Emblem or X-Com in that if your character ends their turn in a wrong place... well, yeah. you'll probably have to rescue them or even restart if things *really* go south. One thing I *do* have to say is, while the maps and combat themselves are challenging, the game itself is *VERY* forgiving with how it handles character-defeats (no perma-death until an enemy walks over their corpse or 3 turns has passed, MUCH more forgiving than Fire Emblem). If one wants a high level challenge from this game, I'd personally use a self-imposed challenge (like every character KO= death = reset, or even an ironman) to truly get a brutal and hardcore SRPG experience.
The soundtrack is always satisfying, good enough, and never really gets old, which is quite impressive to its credit. It gives the war proper respect, and provides each battle with weight and its own unique flair. It is also not an "empty" game either. You'll hear plenty of radio contact (enemies and allies alike) and its quite interesting to hear what's being said between commanders, common soldiers, officers and the like. It does this without interfering with the gameplay, like background noise that adds to the ambiance of a battlefield. The soundtrack also knows when to bring its best- you won't truly connect with it until it plunges a knife right in your heart as tragedy strikes, or when the game lets you feel your greatest triumphs and you feel an adrenaline rush that you can't even describe. Once the soundtrack hits you, you're hooked on the game till the end.
Oh, and the graphics are amazing for a port like this. Fantastically clean, pleasant to look at. There's minor issues I can state here, like textures with leaves and whatnot, but overall its crisp enough to give a nice experience. There's also very few glitches and bugs but they generally do not break the game or affect anything. I can't even remember most of them because they were usually forgotten about.  BUT, there was 1 or 2 times where glitches hit me hard. Be very careful with going up the stairs on the multiple-bunker levels. That's all I'll say.
I'd go on, but this review is already a wall of text. All I can say is: pick up this game. Its worth your money. I feel horrible getting it for 6$ on a sale; the people who ported/remade/whatever this is deserved full price for it.

[I'm probably about 25 hours into this game as I sit down to write my review. I've played the game enitirely in off-line mode, so I can't speak to any Steam-related issues or capacities.]
I'm a big-fan of the tower-defense genre, and have been playing them from way back in the Warcraft 3 modding-days, when there were dozens available, and many had very innovative concepts. Prime World: Defenders does a great job at incorporating many different Tower Defence elements into one game, in a way that is mostly smooth and satisfying.
I'll highlight those positive tower-defence elements in this review:
-Levels are loseable, due to failed strategy, random difficulty changes, or not having leveled up enough. This makes winning more rewarding, and the game more depthful.
-Many towers are availble in the game, and you get to select up to 7 of them for each battle, making your strategy personal and adaptable.
-You can use spells in addition to towers to add an extra layer of strategy and the need for awareness.
-You can "rush" the next wave of enemies for a bonus of money to build your towers. This adds both more strategy, and an ability to get in over your head.
-There is a leveling up system for your towers and spells, which adds elements of both luck and personalization to your resources.
-There are a modest variety of monsters, and while I wouldn't mind more, each type has strengths and weaknesses and the balance works well for the game.
-Ability to replay levels, either for resource farming, or to improve scores/records and secondary objectives.
-Each time you play a level, the map is generated to have differences in the tiles. A tile could be open, boosted, or blocked. This significantly changes the strategy and difficulty of the level. The type of monsters, and the order of waves also changes/
Also positive: I find the graphics to be both attractive, and more importantly, clear- I can tell what is going on with the battle at a glance. There is a story, which while not particularly incredible so far, takes place in an imaginative world.
The negatives are as follows:
-Sometimes you end up having to grind in order to buildup the resources you need to develop your towers and be able to move forward.
-Maps are reused frequently in the beginning, and while there are changes to both the map tiles and monsters, it grows tiring to keep replaying he same maps if you choose to grind early on.
-Sometimes the display radius of a tower does not display properly, or does not seem to match up with the tower's ability to hit monsters.
-The tower and spell-leveling systems are very simple, but poorly explained. I was very confused in the beginning, and there are still some nuances regarding cost that I have not worked out.
-The "percent efficiency boost" that notifies you what leveling up a tower or spell does is sometimes innaccurate.
Overall I feel this game is a solid investment for fans of the genre. I think it is depthful and strategic, and brings in a lot of nuance and a fair amount of challenge. The downside is that you may spend significant time grinding instead of moving forward, so the game might be a poor choice for people who want to play and beat a game, quick and simple.

An excellent game with the best plot of any game I have played so far! This game combines the tactical elements of a turn-based strategy game and the intensity of a FPS game -- each turn, you can select units to take action in the command window, and then each unit takes action in real-time as in a FPS game. Don't worry, they allow you abundant time to take aim, so non-FPS players won't be at a disadvantage. There are around 20 levels in the main campaign, and each of them is thoughtfully designed and do not feel repetitive at all. Each unit has its distinct strengths and weaknesses, so tailor your squad to your preference and to best tackle the situation. There are also extra reports, skirmishes and DLC for additional gameplay. The hard/expert level skirmishes and the Edy challenges will give you serious headaches if you want an increase in difficulty, though I recommend finishing the main campaign first.
The plot is great, with emotional moments and a few twists. The characters are well developed and each has its own unique personality and traits (unlike most war-themed games); they also created likable villains with compelling backstories and understandable goals. The tanks and other war machines in the game look very badass as well! If you want to learn more about the characters or the war machines, you can read the glossary/weaponary/personal tabs.
I have played the game for over 120 hours, and I hope you can enjoy the game as much as I did!

This game feels suspiciously like a mobile IAP-based game that was translated to PC...
First though, the good -- the game looks very nice indeed for a tower defense game. Very high production values when it comes to visuals and overall presentation.
But back to the mobile app part -- unlike your typical tower defense game, which focuses on strategy and proper tower placement / usage, this one features a very heavy emphasis on grinding for permanent upgrades to your towers, which makes it almost as much of a hybrid RPG game as a traditional TD one. The game features a booster / upgrade store, and it is this part which feels distinctly like a remnant of a mobile port. As the levels progress, the same types of creeps gain increasing amounts of health, while the strength of your towers remains constant - thus the need to spend substantial amounts of time grinding previous levels for money to buy upgrades. One might imagine that a mobile version of this game would include the ability to buy these upgrades on the spot in exchange for real money...
I'm kind of ambivalent about whether or not to recommend this game. The hybrid TD-RPG concept can work well and be enjoyable, but in this case, I think my problem is mostly with the balance and unnecessarily high grind requirement.

1st of all I have to mention - you will find like 50 different Pac-Man games, and a lot of them maybe better than this one, or simply different but as enjoyable, yet ALL of them lack one simple thing - they are NOT that one classic pure original Pac-Man - and this one is released by Bandai Namco ¯\_(ツ)_/¯.
It's up to you to decide if you need this one in your library, or you want to buy a pack of various pac-man mods for the same price.
+Visuals: Looks exactly as it was back in the days, juicy colors and a lot of video settings.
+Soundwork: Authentic sounds and music, nothing to add.
+Gameplay: In addition to the flawless port of the original game where you have:
-Leaderboards: everyone who plays with default game settings participating in global leaderboards
-Custom settings - lives, starting the level, bonus lives for better user experience.
-Good party game - short game sessions, good for hot-seat session to challenge your friends :)
-I find this PacMan like super hard, I don't know if it's my crooked hands, lack of reaction or casualty, but it's like super hard to advance to the levels above 5 because of how everything speeds up.
+Steam achievements - a lot of them!
-No steam cards - :(
-Non-remappable controls - Personally I find the default controls enjoyable, yet in 2017 you may spend 5 minutes to add the remap feature to your game?
If you loved it - buy it to get some nostalgia.
If you are old af - buy it so your kids would know how you spend your fun times back in the days.
If you never played it - this game is good for your old games collection, but if you just want to play PacMan, you may consider looking at all the other Pac-Man variations on steam.

This is the only review I've ever felt compelled to write. This game is among the best I've ever played not only for its writing, gameplay, or all around polish - but there are conflicting feelings of both completion and emptiness when you finish the main questline. Every choice you make has an impact and in the end, well, you'll find out.
_____
Story
_____
I don't think I can adequately put into words the appreciation I have for the story. The main questline is, at points, predictable, but mixed in are moments of shock. Every choice you make along the way matters as it pertains to your character and your party. It may not seem like it, but even in Fort Joy, think about your decisions. The side quests are fun, challenging, and charming. They also tie into the main story almost seemlessly. Yes, there are moments of quirk that may not mesh with the overall flow, but it's something that is easily forgiven seeing as though there are just too many to count.
_____
Gameplay
_____
Full disclosure, I did play on explorer (easy) to go through the story and see what it had to offer. Much of the combat was pretty easy (duh) but there were still several fights where you have to think about every choice you make because even the slightest mistake and you'll find yourself loading a save. That being said - you will misclick. It will be frustrating. But I tried to chalk it up to a concussion on the battlefield. The variety of approaches to not only combat, but how you get through situations is totally up to you. You can go in, firing on all cylinders - or you can hang back, sneak through, and use the terrain to your advantage. You can steal anything. You can kill anything. But there are always long term consequences to what you do. (I CANNOT STRESS THIS ENOUGH. I had to kind of cheat the system at one point to just keep going as the choices I made put me at a roadblock)
_____
Polish/Overall
_____
This is a well made game. Anyone that plays will not be able to deny this. There are quirks, there are little glitches, but it adds to the charm. There was nothing that was game breaking, If you are a fan of CRPG's, or just games in general, BUY THIS GAME. You will not regret it. There are so many options that you'll find yourself playing over and over again. In fact, right after I write this, I'm going to restart and not rush through. Enjoy the journey.

After releasing   North America on September 16, 2014 ArcheAge gained a massive following, but over time it has dwindled away, so why is that? Arche Age is a open world game with the ability to go anywhere you want in the world, craft weapons and armor, and fight great beasts on your journeys. Although this is not without hinderances, there are 3 main factions the faction of Nuia to the west, Haranya  to the east, and the Pirates of the sea in between. These factions are constantly fighting each other, and themselves.(Although there is now the ability to have a player made nation, though personally these are broken in a way since they function like a huge guild to overshadow the other 3 nations.) This is the main selling points of the game to claim, craft, and conquer, but the ability to get to the top is hindered in this free to play game by its pay to advance nature, driving away a majority of its player base. So those looking for a easy game it takes time and effort to make a place in this online world, whether through riches or fighting skill. Though even so, the fighting is a little un-balanced for new F2P players, they have to work around the system of gearscore. Gearscore is the number of points your armor is worth and how "powerful" you are, so you could be the least skilled player with a high gearscore and still take on maybe up to 4 lower geared players. This is something that also gets in the way of most players and drives them off, but there is a way to get this good gear, the guilds. Guilds are the backbone of the factions and have many a great or terrible players you may run into. From personal experiance entering the right guild makes all the differance in this game, I am leading one myself called the <Royal Griffin Co>. So is Arche Age worth the time and money? Well Arche Age is a free to play game, but it is heavily pushed that you buy their monthly sub service called Patron, which if you do stay in the game and are looking to do a lot, it is worth the money. Though there is a way in game to get the patron with gold in game and that’s to pay(with ingame gold) for player purchased and patron giving item called Apex (which you need 2 to get patron via the credits it gives). As for is it worth your time, well it is up to the player, but playing with a few friends or a guild is totally worth it. Most players that left the game couldn’t take the gear score element, the pushed "pay to advance" of the developers, and increasingly toxic players (as the game shrinks in servers); but for those that remain it’s almost like a second world for them to live in. So come to the world of Arche Age and try it for yourself.

I've been playing this game on and off since launch and its been fun overall. The developers have done alot of shady things that negatively effect hardcore players. Most of these changes have not effected my gameplay experience.
World PvP can be a blast, even if you lose.
The community is about 50/50. 50% salt, 50% nice. I've met some really awesome people and some horrible trolls.

Almost every aspect of this game regarding gear and upgrades is RNG based. It can be quite frustrating when your gear poofs/downgrades into almost nothing when attempting to regrade. Yet so rewarding when the odds are in your favor.
The justice system can be absolutely hilarious to spectate. I've once seen a player get a several day jail sentence.
In the beginning, obtaining land was like finding a needle in a haystack. Now that there are less players and more claimable land, it hasnt been a problem. Real estate bots were also a plague in the early days, they've almost completely dissapeared thanks to the developers.
All in all, my tenure in ArcheAge has been mostly positive. This is one of the few MMOs that i'll always come back to. I cannot speak for the more hardcore players tho. I've heard some horror stories of entire guilds getting completely shafted when new content was released. I feel its best not to invest too much time/energy/money into this game.

Fight off hordes of monstrous mutants created from a strange cataclysmic event in the new tower defense game, Prime World: Defenders. Join a group of exile treasure hunters who have ventured into the capital of an ancient empire, vast with mystery and danger.
Prime World: Defenders merges classic tower defense gameplay with collectible card mechanic. Your towers, your spells, your traps - all are magic cards, that you can collect and upgrade. You'll have to develop your own strategy, because you'll get your random set of cards after each battle.
Freeze, burn, poison, explode and slash countless enemies that will try to stop you from gathering artifacts of old kingdom. Choose your cards carefully, play them strategically and expect some heavy resistance along the way – from small and almost harmless mutated fungi to powerful giant goblins and nagas.
Did we mention? In addition to story-driven single-player campaign Prime World: Defenders has randomly generated missions, newly added endless mode and New Game Plus!

- Pick up your towers for each level

- Many types of opposide units
- Gambling on treasures

I couldnt decide what to write in this review , so im gonna share with you guys my favorite apple pie recipe Enjoy! :
Pastry
2 cups all-purpose flour
1 teaspoon salt
2/3 cup plus 2 tablespoons shortening
4 to 6 tablespoons cold water
Filling
1/3 to 1/2 cup sugar
1/4 cup all-purpose flour
1/2 teaspoon ground cinnamon
1/2 teaspoon ground nutmeg
1/8 teaspoon salt
8 cups thinly sliced peeled tart apples (8 medium)
2 tablespoons butter or margarine
1) In medium bowl, mix 2 cups flour and 1 teaspoon salt. Cut in shortening, using pastry blender (or pulling 2 table knives through ingredients in opposite directions), until particles are size of small peas. Sprinkle with cold water, 1 tablespoon at a time, tossing with fork until all flour is moistened and pastry almost cleans side of bowl (1 to 2 teaspoons more water can be added if necessary).
2) Gather pastry into a ball. Divide in half; shape into 2 flattened rounds on lightly floured surface. Wrap in plastic wrap; refrigerate about 45 minutes or until dough is firm and cold, yet pliable. This allows the shortening to become slightly firm, which helps make the baked pastry more flaky. If refrigerated longer, let pastry soften slightly before rolling.
3) Heat oven to 425°F. With floured rolling pin, roll one pastry round into round 2 inches larger than upside-down 9-inch glass pie plate. Fold pastry into fourths; place in pie plate. Unfold and ease into plate, pressing firmly against bottom and side.
4) In large bowl, mix sugar, 1/4 cup flour, the cinnamon, nutmeg and 1/8 teaspoon salt. Stir in apples until well mixed. Spoon into pastry-lined pie plate. Cut butter into small pieces; sprinkle over filling. Trim overhanging edge of pastry 1/2 inch from rim of plate.
5) Roll other round of pastry into 10-inch round. Fold into fourths and cut slits so steam can escape. Unfold top pastry over filling; trim overhanging edge 1 inch from rim of plate. Fold and roll top edge under lower edge, pressing on rim to seal; flute as desired. Cover edge with 2- to 3-inch strip of foil to prevent excessive browning.
6) Bake 40 to 50 minutes or until crust is brown and juice begins to bubble through slits in crust, removing foil for last 15 minutes of baking. Serve warm if desired.

Out of nostalgia I bought this game in a discount. It's definitely not worth ~7€ on normal price.
It offers not enough content for that price at all.
It copies the simple concept of Populous rather good. But there are too many issues, so I rather not recommend this, not even for nostalgia or on sale:
There are no tooltips whatsoever, you have no idea what the buttons do.
They get mentioned at some point but if you miss it (or forget it, because the UI feels cluttered), you're screwed.
Menus are confusing, to end the game you need to click "options" in the bottom left.
The game starts with a kind of a tutorial style, it gives you the very basics of the game, with as less information as possible.
You get more powers overtime. Still, terraforming and let your people fight is pretty much the only thing you do in the beginning. It's very repetitive and gets boring very quickly.
You ofen times missclick, make land higher/lower than you want because the game lags but if it works as intended it works smooth.
Skirmish mode is locked for some reason and there's no reason as to why, because no tooltips. I assume you have to play the campaign (where it starts with a tutorial) first to be able to play skirmish or up to a certain point. But really, no idea.
Maps are tiny.
Others mentioned it in their reviews: The fire casting of your opponent is annoying. It's casted almost constantly when you get "near" your opponent or rather in his reach.
But most of all, the game seems to be locked at 30FPS.
The fun thing here is, it only gets the 30FPS at the loading screens. As soon as the game starts, framedrops to 25 and usually below that. If you get to populate not even half the tiny map you won't get more than like 16/18FPS.
It's laggy all the time and the gameplay suffers heavily from it.
I wonder how awful it gets in case the maps get bigger and you get more powers with more abilities graphically "straining" your hardware. Of course this issue may be different for every person with their hardware being different to mine.
But 16GB RAM, an ASUS Strix GTX 970 and an Intel i7-4770 should easily be able to give this far beyond 60FPS at all times out of the box.
The design is actually very pretty and there's absolutely potential for this game, so one should maybe keep an eye on it but I won't recommend this game as of yet.
