It's no boring click-click-click-click-click fest of a monotomous MMO like the others.
You actually have to do all the work in this game, including aiming your weapons.
95% of all the items in the game have to be crafted by you. Weapons, armor, items, vehicles. And you have to LEARN how to do this by practice, practice, practice.
If you're looking for a spoon-fed-hold-my-hand game, you will not like this.
Only patient hard workers need apply.
The game has a very steep learning curve.  That can be seen as a good thing and a bad thing.
The good is it feels rewarding overcoming it, the bad thing is the in-game rewards for overcoming them are quite a letdown. Also, a steep learning curve filters out the casual crowd -> less people total in the game. Good or bad?  Your call.
In a perfect world the game would have enough content to cater to both the casual and hardcore crowd, but since the dev team on this game is so small, fixes (which are very few) happen sporadically and the casual crowd gets nothing worthwhile to stay longterm and gets bored eventually. There are so many minor issues that have been around for years with no sign of ever getting fixed.
I'm purely a PVE so I can't say anythign about PVP.  But it was enjoying getting from lvl1 to lvl55 endgame.  But that is where the game ends. There is no decent PVE endgame content for casual gamers. The Dome is......different. I suspect many won't like it or be interested in its rewards. It's definitely not for the aformentioned casual crowd.
But crafting and exploring simply ends when you reach end-level and that is a shame if that is the main reason you are playing FE in the first place, for its HUGE area rife for exploration. You could start over with a new character and make a different build and take different quest-related choices just to experience different dialog and join opposite factions. But once that 2nd character is also at end-level you really are finished with all the PVE content Fallen Earth has to offer. But you will have sunk in hundreds (if not, thousands) of hours by then. And that is not a bad thing, is it?
It's a shame that endgame content takes a 180 turn and turns into a generic boring grindfest with very little options on how to proceed, as opposed to the beginning of the game where you had choices aplenty.
The game has peaked a long time ago, the devs simply don't have enough resources or time to add more content to revive the game to the glory days.
I would in overall give the game a neutral rating if I could.  6.5 / 10. it's not a bad game, but it had too many missed opportunities to become something greater for everybody, not just a selective group of players. By now I have changed my recommend to a non-recommend. The game actually managed to keep getting so bad, its quality is just sub-par now. The community is clearly not a priority to keep satisfied anymore by the publishers. You start playing it now, you will not experience what older players experienced when the game peaked years ago.

Pros:

Get ready because here are the cons that many high gearscored and experianced players like myself have experianced.
Cons:
- Hitting a high gearscore will likely take thousands of real life dollars to invest within gold sellers that are non-endorsed by the Archeage community. On that note, Archeage does not ban players typically for using them if they have spent many hours of gameplay and invested within the game itself. However, a new player is likely to be banned for using them.
- Once you hit top gear you're likely to quit due to the lack of interest in killing low geared players. (This happened to me)
- The game is dieing out due to the fact that many players find the game unbalanced when it comes to trying to achieve a high gear score. For instance, I make about six figures keep it low compared to a high school graduate that makes 0. My gear will obviously be able to two hit him when we compete in pvp.
- The drops from dungeons will never be able to compared to high tier gear or ayanad.
- Servers are typically dominated by a main faction or group of guilds that farm high valued bosses which more then likely a new player will never be able to join due to their gear requirements.
-  Needless to say, a new player will have a very difficult time in attempting to make gold and achieve a high gearscore unless a veteran player were to quit and give them their gear.
- The braggers: The few high geared players that still play will typically feel as if they need to link their weapons or armor to feel acomplished in making other players quit. (Lol I usaelly just whispered back my linked mythics and made them shut up). They also will basically spawn camp or Nuia camp players are low gear scored so that they can't progress in game.
- Drama: Sure drama exists typically with stupid matters but it's mainly because their is nothing else to do within the game.
All in all if you want to start playing a game where you might enjoy investing many hours exploring a new world, then archeage is for you. Just be warned that when it comes late game and you will have to fight other players then you're probally going to need a couple grand to buy new gear. If you enjoy the farming aspect, know that you will probally need to spend many hours and a couple of hundred dollars to start on it to achieve profit.
I have since then moved on from this game to focus back on work and my family. I would recommend for anyone wanting to spend mass of amounts of time on this game to look towards other aspects of your life and question if it's really worth it spending over thousands of dollars just to be able to be number one.

Has lots of "grind" - suggest you buy it cheap and don't plan to finish it.
This feels like it was designed as a free-to-play game - premium currency, random loot, destroying multiple cards to get slightly better ones, lots of grind on the same levels, lots of achievements, remote server - but they chickened out at the last minute.
However, it is complete, and it is playable - albeit slowly. After the tutorial it has a "hub" design where there is a difficult plot level, and several easier levels you grind on until your cards/towers are good enough. This can take dozens of steps, but you only get rewards for victory so there is little incentive to push yourself. There are only a few different maps, but the monotony is broken up by randomized booster / obstacle placement.
Despite the flaws, the combination of CCG and tower defense is very strong and there is a good variety of cards/towers. Looks good, performs well, runs stably. Writing, music, and sounds are okay, but not great.

After seeing the 58% metacritic score, I was hesitant to pick this up ... and now I'm seriously baffled what game the reviewers were playing.  User reviews over at strategy informer give it a 8.8/10 average, which is more in line with where I'd put it.
The CCG mechanics are well implemented, the difficulty range for side missions goes from yawn inducing easy, to fiendishly difficult, with ample reward for toughing out those harder levels in the form of chances at rarer cards.
It's well polished, excellent visuals, and adds interesting mechanics to a somewhat stale genre.  Features a long campaign w/some interesting boss battles, and repeatable semi-random side missions.  There's a vast variety of towers and spells available, and a number of ways in which to acquire and improve on them.  There's an in game store (using IN GAME credit, not a cash store), drops from side missions, drops from official missions, daily rewards and to top it off a crafting system of sorts for 'forging' and 'evolving' towers/spells, to make good use of duplicates or obsolete cards.
I can only assume the 'grindy' complaints were people wanting ALL of the various towers and spells available *quickly* ... but then that would kill the replayability, knowing there's nothing new to drop - and no new strategies to be born from a new tower/spell in the mix?
I'd give it a 9/10 ... only complaints I can think of - back story was weak, and while the voice overs were done well, they could use more variety.  Highly, highly recommended hidden gem of a game - if you like tower defense, don't hesitate.

First off - the metascore baffles me, but then again, I hate the idea of "scores entirely". However, the important question is, is Prime World Defenders worth your time?
Yes, I say, if you like tower defence and collectable card games. Prime World Defenders does an amazing job of mixing the two genres (two of my personal favourites) into one, a collectable card tower defence! I have had a huge amount of fun with this game, and I think any tower defence fan will too. It has some great mechanics and is aesthetically pleasing.
One of the biggest gripes amongst reviewers for this game, is the grinding. Not going to lie, there are "grinding" elements to it, and you do replay certain levels, however they are mixed up each time, with different obstacles in the way, with just enough variety to get by. Personally I didn't see it as a big issue, however some might.
Personally, I would highly recommend this game!
+ Well pulled off merge of tower defence and collectable card games.
+ Pleasing aesthetic.
+ Great variety of towers.
+ Some unique and interesting mechanics.
- "Grinding" may put some people off.
- Information on some of the "Forging" and "Evolution" GUI isn't explained properly.

Do NOT let the metacritic score fool you! This game is an absolute gem for Tower Defense lovers everywhere, but may as well appeal to a broader fanbase in that it has a trading card style mechanic to it. Parts of the game especially after the first few missions can seem kind of grindy at first, but doing missions over and over and collecting different cards and upgrading your towers and spells is what keeps me hooked on the game for hours. I have always enjoyed games where you have to slow down and power yourself up. Keeping you from running through the game altogether. There isnt a vast amount of maps but the replayability is insanely high. Really enjoy the game, the metacritic score is very innacurate. Dont believe me? do yourself a favor and check the user reviews and play the demo! I very well would have paid the 9.99 for the game but the Autumn sales price at 3.40 as of now should be an instant purchase for many! I would give the game a rating of 8/10.

Okay first of: Is this a good game? Yes it is, definatly so.
If you enjoy games like baldurs gate, fallout 1,2 and tactics, Pillars of Eternity and so on then you will definatly enjoy this game. But what surprises me the most is the amount of fantastic well written meaty goodness the story has.
A few bugs are present sure, and there are some other things i dislike about it but that wont affect you one bit.
the only note worthy "bad" thing is that as amazing as the start and mid part of the game is, the ending seem a bit well weak. not directly bad, just rushed perhaps. But the guys made a fantastic tactical rpg with rich story, amazing music, well written romance side quests (at least the ones i have tested). It is just sad that their epilogue doesnt really appeal to me, mainly because of the lack of a few choices to wrap things up with.
Combat: Combat is fun and fast paced, tactical and can be hard as well as long. The whole Elemental magic, terrain exploiting, combining spells for maximum omph and so on is fun. Having a Geomancer make the ground slick with oil, only to have a pyromancer to set it ablaze alongside the enemy. Or have the Aquamancer flood the battle field with rain only to have an Aeromancer send down lightning bolts to electrify everything thats in liquid... yes liquid this means massive blood pools from critical hits or killed mobs can also be used for this. But do not take Warfare, Hunter or Scoundrel lightly these martial skills are not worse than spells, they have definatly their own uses to even the battlefield with knockdown, sleep, aoe damage and more.
Overall better than Divinity: Original Sin at least in my eyes, infact the mid part of the games beat the crap out of any other game i have played in the last few years or so. I am tempted to go 10 of 10, but there are those few little bits of meh that pulls it down to a 8. so yeah 8 of 10 (but could so easily be a 10 if the ending got a bit more polish)

The game starts with a tutorial and some easy levels. As you progress in the story, it keeps getting more and more challenging. With time, you'll have to think at least 15 minutes at only one puzzle to understand how to solve it, which is why I don't recommend this game to people that are impatient or to those few who would set their house on fire only because they've died a few times in Flappy Bird.
Three Dead Zed was meant to be a challange to gamers, so expect to die a lot, at least till you've finally understood the mechanics.
The concept of the game has a very interesting idea at the base of it. I saw some games with zombies, but I never saw a single-player game in which you could actually control the zombie in it. And not only that, but you have the chance to solve puzzles with 3 different forms of zombies at will. The default form that can climb ladders and interact with objects, a heavy form that can deal extra damage and break certain blocks, and a light form that is agile and can walljump, but doesn't attack.
What could be more fun than this? Trust me, if you're a zombie lover like me, you'll like this game!
- If the single-player wasn't enough for you, you'll still have to complete the challenges that will unlock after you finish the game.
- An friendly and adorable artwork that catches your eyes from the very first time you check it's store page.
- An humorous story with cats included in it.
- Support for Achievements and Trading Cards.
- Support for Steam Cloud which will save your♥♥♥♥♥if something happens to your Windows.
- If you have a bad day, you'll have the chance to kill people in this game while they are trying to live their pathetic and meaningless life.
- The music is similar to 8-bit gaming, which makes it compatible to people from the nostalgic era.
- The puzzles are very light, almost all levels are about finding the right switch or destroying the right generator to unlock the path forward.
- It's almost practically impossible to finish the game with less than 30 deaths, at least for me, which makes the achievements harder than it sounds for achievement hunters.
- A lot of rage quitting is included with the purchase of the game.
- Controls feel a little unnatural.
While the game may get at your nerves sometimes, it's a thoroughly enjoyable puzzle platformer with a humorous story that will keep you pumped the entire game, cats that will make you smile and challenges that will make your brain's life hard. If you care for your neurons, buy this game and give it a chance. I'm giving it an 3.5 out of 5 for all the hard work the developers put in making this game.

Prime World:Defenders seems like an interesting mix of RPG and Tower Defense but unfortunately you will find yourself grinding for exp/coins/stars A LOT during the last couple of missions and bosses.
Don't even think of doing the last two missions and the final boss without grinding up a level 3 Lighting tower and Dragon Fire tower, they are impossible without them and you'll have to grind for hours if you aren't lucky with opening booster packs.

The artstyle drew me in, but was surprised to find out that it was a turn based strategy with fps combat. You get a 2D map layout of the area and then you move individual units in 3rd person, which was unique. Although I find it fairly fun, it's both a mix of too easy and too grindy.
For the PC, you can use the mouse to aim. You have unlimited time to aim your shot, and with the mouse, headshots become incredibly easy. Most units you will kill in 1 or 2 actions because of this.
Levels are too long. You control 20 units each level. And the enemy has a large number of units as well. Combined with the long animations switching the 2D map to 3rd person and combat animations, most of your time will probably be spent watching these animations or unskippable cutscenes. And some levels have artificial time constraints. For example, there is a boss that you have to wait at checkpoints for. And if you get killed by an ambush, that's 40 minutes that you have to redo.
Classes are unbalanced. I almost found no need for the Sniper class (their accuracy is terrible, they can't cover fire like other classes, and their damage is not worth the accuracy) or Engineer class (they are the support units, but they are not necessary since many of the other units can heal themselves and you won't really run out of ammo). That's 2/5 of the classes that are useless in a strategy game.
Nevertheless, if you enjoy the art style, turn based shooting, and some difficulty (you may be caught off guard by some ambush in a new level, but you can also often times abuse the bad AI), then I would recommend this game.

Right now the game is pretty bare bones especially in single player which is what i play. Animations freeze up alot with human enemies being the most noticeable as they glide across the land when attacking instead of doing a walking or run animation. No hit impact animations when i hit an enemy with weapons so it looks like they are not even phased or effected by my blows. Combat animations are very stiff,clunky and unnatural as if fighting zombies from the horribly animated game 7 DAYS TO DIE.
There are times when they dont seem to notice me at all then there are others when am really far away and they can spot me easily.
Food and water which you need to survive is used rather quickly as the player's hunger/thirst bars go down very fast killing immersion as your constantly looking for food resources eventhough this can be adjusted a little in the server settings.
Game personality wise i really dont see anything new here that has not been done before in a similar manner and better by other games. The crafting is similar but not anywhere near as polished as it is in games like ARK. Graphics are underwhelming alongside the mostly empty landscapes with only the adult nudity looking very nice which is also the only thing that makes this game stand out otherwise its been there done that with nowhere the amount of content a early acess release should have.
Considerring how am seeing more and more early access titles pushing the sex and nudity angle without ever finishing their games am starting to take this as a sign of buyer beware and wait for the finished product. Such a shame considering how nudity can set a excellent tone to an already mature game setting.
There is also the horrible save mechanic where you can only save afer your character has slept but to do this you have to craft a bed which unrealistically your character does not know how to do until they learn the proper crafting skill to make twine out of fiber eventhough your character is a full grown adult. The save bed is also only good for one use so you will find yourself having to make a bed over and over which just seems like needless busy work and tedious when connected to the save system.
Whatever happened to just being able to save when you want especially when real life calls. Another thing is on default server settings you will lose all your items everytime you die even if you saved your game so you have to start absolutely from scratch again eventhough your character stays at level five or whatever they were before they died.
Another issue is how the player seems to be the center of attention. When getting attacked for example by a crocodile i would try to lure it into the vicinity of other creatures (hyenas,giant turtles,monsters etc) or humans so they will attack it or vice versa yet nothing ever happens instead everybody goes after me as i run around like Benny Hill with a whole village of different species suddenly united to take me down.
Framerate wise it is running pretty smooth on both my older i5 3470k cpu which has just been upgraded to a i7 3770, 8gb ram, Geforce 970 with 4gb vram.
The dedicated Devs are constantly updating the game with fixes at least three times a week.
Unfortunately right now i cant recommend the game. When one pays money for a product even early access it should be fit for consumption in the same way as other early access games have come out the door such as GRIM DAWN, THE LONG DARK, THE DARKEST DUNGEON, THE FOREST etc.

Honestly, I was pretty excited for this game. I got it, day one, even pre-ordered it, bought the soundtrack DLC, kept up with the buzz and updates.
And man... this game is good. There some faults I do have, such as pre-rendered cutscenes (means that new outfits don't show, weapons remain the same), but my love for this game so heavily outweighs the negatives.
So what are the positives? Fun and fast gameplay, brutal gibs and weapons that feel great to use, interesting skill system that lets you change them on the go, and the game even challenges your setups at times, meaning that you can't just stick with the same meta over and over.
Oh and the music and sound design. By cyberpunk god, the music is good. At first I was more hyped for Sidewalks & Skeletons' music to be plastered all over the game, back-to-back, but I was surprised to hear Zamilska and even Susumu Hirasawa in this game. And y'know what? It makes this game so much more flavorful.
And yes, it is very linear with a couple of secrets that can be hard to miss, but it feels like a cyberpunk Hotline Miami (a series I ♥♥♥♥ing love). With the addition of a healthbar and without the annoying one-shot deaths.
To top it off, there's difficulty settings (Looking at you, IGN and Polygon), a speedrun mode, outfits, and the new fatality system in place, which gives you health and energy, along with a speedboost that can stack.
If you're wondering about price, I'd say it's worth it. Amazing art, music, fun and just enjoyable gameplay. And cyberpunk. So much cyberpunk.

The fact that you cannot benefit from farmland or labor regen already removes two aspects to gaining gold on the server. Without gold, one cannot buy gear or upgrade it to be able to do Ocleera Rifts, Ayanad Library, or even the occasional Grimghast. Without gold, it would be hard to gain a trade wagon to earn more anything. Even if you do gain the gold, the labor skimp would be hard to ignore. There is also a big risk, as many players are lurking around to steal your trade packs, even people from your own faction. Since the release of the Dwarven and Warborn races, there has been an influx of people playing those characters for the sole purpose of using their transformations, which are pretty unbalanced. This game is a complete cash grab, and I quite regret spending the money I did for the game. There are other games out there that deserves your time, this isn't it.

One of my favorite pastimes is playing miniature golf. I have decided to review the various places I have made the attempt to play at and set them up here. If you have a comment, please send it to me and I will add it. I will rate all of the locations on four options using a scale of one to ten. The facilities will be rated on:  Challenge, Variety, Fun and Overall Value.There will also be a brief description of the facility and the amenities offered as well as prices as remembered from past experience. Some prices may have changed since I was there.

Challenge is a ranking of how difficult the course is to play. There may also be a factor for how much skill it takes vs how much luck is involved in playing the course. Try to view it as if you don't play often when using this rating.
Variety is a ranking of how many other things are available to do at the facility. Does it have any extras like batting cages or go-carts. I generally will keep courses that have a good variety of holes but nothing else around a 5-6 range. The more amenities, the higher the score.
Fun may be my most subjective item. Is the golf course too difficult to have a good time, or to easy. Is there a good balance between difficulty and challenge. How much do you enjoy this course vs. some others? Would you take a date there?
Overall Value is based on the price to play vs the fun had. It should reflect some composite of the other factors.
Feel free to try them out and tell me if you agree or disagree with my ratings. I am, by no means, an expert. I just know what I like.
Also, a note for the owners of the locations: If you find I have made an error in reporting your location or prices, drop me an email and I will correct it at my first opportunity. My opinions are my own regarding value for dollar, but Idon't want to provide incorrect factual information.
Please note that, unless otherwise stated, all prices are for one round adult admission. Children's pricing and specials may vary.

A lot of the reviews for this game have been a bit difficult to follow, or not ultimately very helpful. So let me give it a try.
The game still has a number of bugs, and it's not complete. Not all strategies are equal, and the game still has a ways to go before being 100%. But it's not a bad game. Part of the problem is people were expecting a direct improvement off Dungeon Keeper 2, to which this game more responds as a spiritual successor with features added or modified to better suit modern demand.
I can't say much for multiplayer at the moment, but the Skirmish AI require a lot of practice and learning to beat, and even the Easy setting will challenge players a bit. Playing different configurations of maps will help bolster your skills and it's easy to find maps you love more than others. But that's part of the appeal, finding what works for you. I solved the campaign far differently from how a number of others have, and that's also to the game's merit. While some strategies are all but impossible at different points in the game, others quickly compensate for the lack.
This game definately feels like Dungeon Keeper for about an hour or two at a time, but at the end of the day, it's something much more. The devs are doing an amazing job, and I can't recommend this game enough.

I couldnt decide what to write in this review , so im gonna share with you guys my favorite apple pie recipe Enjoy! :
Pastry
2 cups all-purpose flour
1 teaspoon salt
2/3 cup plus 2 tablespoons shortening
4 to 6 tablespoons cold water
Filling
1/3 to 1/2 cup sugar
1/4 cup all-purpose flour
1/2 teaspoon ground cinnamon
1/2 teaspoon ground nutmeg
1/8 teaspoon salt
8 cups thinly sliced peeled tart apples (8 medium)
2 tablespoons butter or margarine
1) In medium bowl, mix 2 cups flour and 1 teaspoon salt. Cut in shortening, using pastry blender (or pulling 2 table knives through ingredients in opposite directions), until particles are size of small peas. Sprinkle with cold water, 1 tablespoon at a time, tossing with fork until all flour is moistened and pastry almost cleans side of bowl (1 to 2 teaspoons more water can be added if necessary).
2) Gather pastry into a ball. Divide in half; shape into 2 flattened rounds on lightly floured surface. Wrap in plastic wrap; refrigerate about 45 minutes or until dough is firm and cold, yet pliable. This allows the shortening to become slightly firm, which helps make the baked pastry more flaky. If refrigerated longer, let pastry soften slightly before rolling.
3) Heat oven to 425°F. With floured rolling pin, roll one pastry round into round 2 inches larger than upside-down 9-inch glass pie plate. Fold pastry into fourths; place in pie plate. Unfold and ease into plate, pressing firmly against bottom and side.
4) In large bowl, mix sugar, 1/4 cup flour, the cinnamon, nutmeg and 1/8 teaspoon salt. Stir in apples until well mixed. Spoon into pastry-lined pie plate. Cut butter into small pieces; sprinkle over filling. Trim overhanging edge of pastry 1/2 inch from rim of plate.
5) Roll other round of pastry into 10-inch round. Fold into fourths and cut slits so steam can escape. Unfold top pastry over filling; trim overhanging edge 1 inch from rim of plate. Fold and roll top edge under lower edge, pressing on rim to seal; flute as desired. Cover edge with 2- to 3-inch strip of foil to prevent excessive browning.
6) Bake 40 to 50 minutes or until crust is brown and juice begins to bubble through slits in crust, removing foil for last 15 minutes of baking. Serve warm if desired.

Valkyria Chronicles is a story based anime tactics game in the style of WWII. You play as Welkin Gunther (son of a hero from the first Europan war) and after saving a town with a tank, he become leutanant of squad 7. From here you take part a large variety of missions.
Each mission starts with you placing your select chosen troops that all have their own likes & dislikes (whic can give them buffs) like being in cities, near tanks, ect. After choosing your troops the mission starts and you are looking at a hand drawn map. Circular pieces represent each individual troop. By clicking one of these peices the screen zooms in, and the map become 3D and you are controlling the character in 3rd person. From here, you have a movemant meter which goes down as you run. Once done, you can take cover, heal, shoot an enemy. Be careful though, because if you get to close, the enemy will shoot at you! You can then end your turn. Using a troop uses a command point, and there's a limit to how many of those you have.
There are a variety of classes, and as you progress through the game you can level up a select few
Scouts - Can walk a very long distance, and can hit for a medium amount of damage w/ rifles
Engineers - Fix tanks, re-suply ammo. Terrible for combat
Snipers - derp. Short distance runners
Lancers - They are bascially dudes with rocket launchers in the shape of a lance
Shock Troopers - High damage, and up close machine gunners
While I really liked this game there are definitley some critisisms I have.
-Tank controls by default are terrible on PC. WASD AND THE MOUSE control the tank. So if you want to move your screen to the right just to see whats over there you will move the tank. If you move WASD and the mouse at the same time by accident, it can swing you in a way you don't intend. I have lost missions because of this.
-Story (while touching and enjoyable) wasn't really striking. There's quite a few plot twists that I either saw coming, or just did not phase me at all. Thankfully, you do get somewhat attached to characters. So I did grow to like them.
-Some missions (especially late game) don't feel "Tactical". Some missions here and there have to be beaten in very specific ways, and sometimes this felt a little detracting to me. Especially the final throwdown with Jaeger where I had to go North, and couldn't go West because there were only short alleys with no cover, and enemy tanks at the end of it.
-Not having really high level classes, can make the last few missions much much harder. By the en, I got my snipers to lvl 12. If I had gotten them to 15, I would have had an incredibly powerful ability to make te finals missions easier.
All in all. Good game. I had some frusterating moments with the last few missions, and the tank controls made me angry on multiple occasions.

If twitch reflex, action/puzzle-platformers are your forte, you will love the light hearted humour, beautiful, hand drawn art style and annoyingly, addictive gameplay of Three Dead Zed. For me however, this game had too many frustrating deaths and not enough puzzles that really challenge the player's problem solving skills. I enjoyed my time with Three Dead Zed and was very satisfied after completing the main story levels but am in no way committed enough to push through the challenge rooms that remain. Three Dead Zed is a good indie title and has earned 6.5 out of 10 from me.
STORY
Three Dead Zed tells the story of Subject Zed, a scientifically engineered zombie that must escape the confines of the lab in which it was created, by rescuing cats in tinfoil hats. The player is guided through each level by a mysterious telepathic entity, that has lost touch with its cat infiltration team. As Subject Zed you must use your ability to change forms to traverse extremely dangerous and increasingly difficult areas with the overall goal being, to remove the tinfoil hat of the cat trapped there. I enjoyed the story on the whole, and had a good chuckle at the office warning posters and the very funny line delivery of the science lab PA announcer.
GAMEPLAY
Controls in Three Dead Zed are extremely basic and easy to get the hang of, but are a real challenge to master under pressure. The three different forms of Subject Zed have their own purpose in each level, and it's in this high paced, form swapping the game really gets difficult. The classic form is able to attack with low damage, jump small distance, flick switches and climb ladders. The sprinter form moves extremely quickly, can jump higher and further but is unable to attack or interact with in level items. The final form, the brute, is able to soak up damage well and deal large damage but is unable to interact with in level items or jump. Changing between the three forms is quick and easy, but  with everything in the levels designed to kill you, it isn't always straight forward picking the right zombie for the job.
The level design as a whole is good, with the game being based more around the challenge of high speed and accurate platforming than it is around the solving of puzzles. There are enemies dotted throughout the levels to keep things interesting and a few box stacking, and switch flicking challenges, but for the most part, the way you'll die is through movement mistakes like miss-jumps. This game can be brutal in some sections where the player has to repeat a series of difficult jumps and climbs, which can causing frustration very quickly. I got stuck in some sections and ended up repeating it 20 plus times before getting to the next check point, and I am not too proud to admit that I took advantage of the rage quit option this game offers on several occasions.
Even with the rage quit incidents, I still completed the main story line within a couple of hours, but for the price this is a decent length and does not detract from the experience. After completing the main story the player is able to take on challenge rooms, which are far more difficult than those found in the story mode. I am happy that the developer included the challenge room as an option after the main story missions but due to this game being based more around the platforming than the puzzles I was not motivated enough to push through these levels.
VISUALS & MUSIC
The art style and sound featured in Three Dead Zed are a real strength of the game. I never grew tired of the orange blood splatters throughout the levels that showed my errors from previous attempts. The levels and characters have a beautiful hand drawn look, and the transformation and movement animations are great fun to watch. The sound can get repetitive in some of the more trying levels, but on the whole fits well with the rooms and changes pace accordingly in difficult locations.

Let’s talk about platformers.  My favorite of all time is Super Mario 2. It gave you the option to pick one of four characters, each of whom had different abilities.  If you chose the correct one, you got through the level a lot easier than if you chose poorly.  In Three Dead Zed, you not only get to swap characters, you get to do it mid-level!  It becomes not only necessary to choose the right Zombie, but it also becomes a skill one must master in order to proceed further into the game.  Not only is this ingenious, it’s a hell of a lot of fun!
The puzzles increase in complexity and difficulty as you progress (Which is what you would expect), and it keeps you entertained.  I especially love how a nice splatter of your former self remains after you die and are reborn to try the level again.
The Controls are great if you have a controller.  Xbox360 recommended, but if you are familiar with playing FPS games on a keyboard, you won’t find any difficulty here.  The controls are mapped out in a good way and you can change them if you like.  I switched it to Minecraft controls and found it was easier to go with the defaults so I switched back.
The Artwork is amazing!  I love the zombies and the detail that went into the animations of the game.  The background animations and static images are well placed and look great.  I don’t know much about the difficulty in lighting games, but the shadows and lighting seemed to be really well done.  This helped to provide a really enjoyable and differing environment throughout my gameplay.
The sound effects are well suited for the game and can be quite funny at times.  The music is similar to 8-bit gaming, which rings my nostalgia bell so I enjoyed that as well.
3DZ is a lot of fun and adds something new to both the platformer and zombie genre… which in this day and age, is something to admire.  Three types of zombies means three times the fun!  If you are a fan of zombie stuff, get the game!  If you are a fan of platformers, get the game!  And if you are a fan of both, why haven’t you already gotten the game?

Alot of the negative reviews talk about a lack of explanation concerning game mechanics. Sure, there's a few game mechanics that aren't explained,
It was as simple as trying out new mechanics in future levels that gave me a sense of accomplishment. Especially when I felt satisfied knowing I'd come up with a God-like (no pun intended) strategy that decimated enemies all on my own, sans tutorial.
Understand that, and you'll see this game has very good strategy elements, an incredible GUI, and lovely pixel graphics.
Once you get the hang of the tricks to building fast, expanding, and conquering, everything becomes a timing game IMO: When should you expend resources to attack? Or build more houses? Or use a God power and send a hail of fire upon an enemy city!?
Best of all, if the game starts feeling easy, turn off kindle populants (the ability to basically summon units at will), or increase flag speed (when a unit naturally spawns for either you or the enemy; speeding up real time gameplay).
And hell, there's 30 levels, and that's just the first universe! I've only yet to scratch the surface of this incredibly long campaign.
So go on! Lead your people to victory I say! Your reprisal begins!

There are some serious faults to the game that I am sure will be solved before the official release. The team at FunCom are doing their best to work with the community to solves these issues.  If you have already purchased the game and have had trouble, I'd recommend giving the game another try.  Most connectivity issues and server issues have been resolved.

I honestly anticipated a golf game. I don't know why, it's clearly a puzzle-platformer trapped inside of the rotting husk of golf. A cheeky and fun idea that rapidly overstays its welcome with increasingly over-complicated and poorly implimented level design. The design elements continue to require more and more precise and developer-intended (in that, 90's adventure game kind of way) solutions you'll continue to fail to execute.
Played with friends the first level is bearable, but the experience fell apart so fast as levels continued to spiral out of control into the more precise-platform style gameplay a physics engine powered game cannot provide. Frustration mounts as you hit the swing limit or the time limit, and the jank throughout even the more basic components of the game ruin an otherwise promising looking experience. I don't even see the point in trying to implement customization features when the levels are just try-hard exercises in janky an time-pressured futility.
If you're expecting to pick up and play this game without a thorough understanding of developer intent, you're going to probably fail repeatedly and embarassingly. Skip this game, the level design isn't worth your time and doesn't respect your time.

While I would usually wait for a sale on something like this, happy to pay full price in light that the developers seem to be making big efforts in listening to feedback and continuing to support the game (which seems though it might of suffered from launching too early perhaps.)
So far it is scratching the dungeon keeper itch better than anything else I've played, something I've been waiting for 15 years to happen. I appreciate it seems to be staying close to the atmosphere/tone and design of that game as it seems like other games have never been able to best those specific qualities from original DK. Impressive considering the game doesn't feel like a DK rip off but its own game.
It's obviously hard not to make comparisons given how specific this genre is to a single game, so some things it doesn't feel like it does as well as a 15 year old game are impossible not to notice. Though thankfully these are (relatively) small things like inferior animations or the lack of a "restart mission" option in level.
I initially had some issues with the hand pointer while playing across multiple monitors, though that seems to have either resolved itself, or the game was just patched. I still feel it could animate a little better in certain scenarios, but well done devs. Multi monitor support is a struggle/afterthought for most developers it seems and is highly appreciated when it is payed attention to.
I'm still early days in the campaign, but overall early impressions are positive. Thanks to the Devs for bringing this to life and i'm looking forward to seeing future projects.

Overall Rating = 8.5/10
This game will remind you of Dungeon Keeper almost immediately, and does a good job of keeping things fun and interesting, but it does need more content and polishing.  However, it is still worth the purchase right now, and I'm convinced the development team is dedicated to improving the gameplay and world, especially after reading their state of the game updates.  Give these guys a chance, they really "get it" and aim to please all dungeon keepers out there.  I mean... underlords! :)
What really needs improvement?
-Large scale battles on large maps like the Campaign map "The Kenos" are still choppy.  The game seems to be very RAM intensive on larger maps, so efforts to correct this are very highly recommended.  I have a very high end machine with 32GB of 1600 DDR3 RAM, i7 Quad Core 3.6GHz, and 2x GeForce 780ti's in SLI, and it was choppy for me.  Most likely this has to do with how the game handles memory/processor usage.
-Possession combat is wonky currently.  It's hard to really control the attacks, and you can barely tell if you used one of the creatures abilities or not.  The animations are not prominent when you attack during possession.
-Need more reason to possess a creature, as currently it doesn't seem to make any difference in combat whether you possess a creature or not?
-Not sure if heros or evil heros are implemented or not, but that would be a no-brainer for possession mechanics, assuming it will be in the game at all.
-When building structures like pig slaughter, lair, barracks, etc.. it would be nice if there were visual queues that helped the player visually understand how much bigger their barracks needs to be to increase the army size.  If i build a 3x3, and I have a 10x10 slaughter/lair, maybe when the user mouses over the barracks, it shows them what they are missing by just having a 3x3 barracks?  You get the idea, even if maybe I used the wrong structures in my example!
What would be nice to have?
-I think the game needs a more elaborate sound track/sound effects, as while there is music, it's not dark and dungeony enough for my taste.  I like the current feel of the game, goofy and dark, just continue that theme with more dramatic music during attacks from dwarves, or the discovery of artifacts.  While it's cool to hear the guy say "You have discovered an artifact" maybe a prominent noise specific to artifact discover would be nice, because you tend to tune that voice out after awhile.
-I'm not sure if there is a hotkey system, but if there is, make it more obvious via the tutorial.  I'd rather bind things to my own hotkeys menu, especially the rally flags for minions and beasts, and reveal fog of war ability, lightning ability, etc.
-Add more randomness to digging blocks of earth.  Maybe occassionally I discover a trapped worker from a previous underlord, or a passageway to another area filled with secrets (that appeared as ROCK via reveal fog of war), or stout dwarven enemies, or neutral merchants that sell potions, whatever.  Fog of war should not be able to tell you everything you need to know before digging - add that element of surprise, as it makes the overall game mechanics of digging itself far more interesting.

So, now that WftO has had a few months to cook after its disastrous (and incomplete) launch, what do we have now at version 1.1?
Well, if you're looking for a Dungeon Keeper 3 that actually works this time, WftO is now it.  The game takes the premise of its spirtual ancestor, and expands it with new units, tools, and various other goodies.  Not all of this is for the best, however; many units and tools still feel underdeveloped and underbalanced.  Again, however, WftO now stands out as the best and the brightest of the DK-alikes out there (although, with Dungeons 2 as its only real competitor these days --with maybe KeeperRL as a very distant 3rd -- that's not saying much).
+ Tried and tested Dungeon Keeper gameplay with its own spin.  That's the biggest plus right there.  After many patches, the dev team pretty much nailed what makes the DK formula special.  This single plus pretty much covers up for the game's myriad sins:
- Campaign needs another pass.  One big quibble is the way that new units and tools are dumped willy-nilly on the player, with no warning or explanation, as the campaign progresses.  DK made sure that new stuff was properly introduced -- and necessary! -- at the end of each campaign mission.  WftO doesn't.
- Poor use of all this new and different stuff in the campaign.  You get a lot of different toys and units, but you will not end up using some of them at all in the campaign.  (See: stone bridge).  This may be useful when playing multiplayer, but it's just clutter in the campaign.  Even read a book that cries out for better editing, for elimination of dross and a better focus on what is important?  WtfO needed a better editor, as it were.  There's just too much redundant stuff in it.  DK2 stripped away a lot of DK1's units and tools, as was the better game for it.
- Much more MP focused than the DK games were.  WftO was evidently created by folks who thought DK's MP was the high point of the game, which is arguable.  As a result, you get less of a contemplative, polish your dungeon to a high sheen gameplay in favor of... zerg rushes and click-click-clicky around the map.
- I was wondering if the devs were trolling me when I "won" the game.  Abrupt and unrewarding to say the least.  Not as bad, say, as an old NES game that just displayed "CONGRATULATIONS" on a black screen, but close.
- I hate timed missions in a game centered on building stuff.  The campaign has a few.
TL;DR: WtfO is close, but not quite, for those who waited patiently over the decades for a DK3.  It's definitely still worth a shot, though.

PROS:
+ extremely interesting theme (769 to 1453)
+ great wealth of historical information (persons, dynasties, provinces, rivers and so on)
+ smart, versatile abstraction of core feudal mechanics that fit different locations and timeframes
+ very engaging, it's easy to be sucked in and not want to stop playing, even against your better judgement
+ extremely good visuals, starting from a wonderful map that you can fall in love with and very nice hand drawings
+ usually great sense of humour and optimistic mood in the dialogues
+ masterpiece soundtracks by Andreas Waldetoft
+ its own Wikia site for reference and guidelines, plenty of experts in the community to answer any questions very quickly on the forums
+ a lot of After Action Reports and Let's Play videos from more experienced players
+ somewhat good, stable technical condition (very few CTDs or launching problems, although they do happen)
CONS:
– awful AI, more like barely sketched in than properly developed (Sultans of Tunis will march to Sicily overland through Gibraltar, Provence, Rome, Naples etc. after declaring a war on the basis of proximity of distance over sea)
– realism decreased by missing features or rigid mechanics (e.g. you can't free a Mongol khan's concubine (sex slave) if your soldiers gain custody of her in a siege, you can only return her to her tormentor or keep her in your jail idefinitely — this is just one example of stuff the company doesn't seem to care about)
– situational dead-ends, for example ending up in regency (e.g. witch a child ruler) can break your game, because sufficient mechanics have not been provided to enable you to cope with all situations the game can lead you in (this means e.g. a regent who will sit on his♥♥♥♥♥and veto all decisions because of 'Base Reluctance', i.e. not wanting to do anything)
– lack of consistency in quality levels (quality dips with some portraits, due to varying skill levels of individual artists and lack of consistency in lights and other parameters they use in rendering their work, or event texts/dialogues or event logics) and concepts sometimes (e.g. numbers that don't seem to follow the same scale of values but are absurdly high)
– generally more bugs and bad design decisions than you would expect from a professional company, with Paradox generally unphased by this and PR department blowing its own trumpet with enthusiastic releases, there seems to be a cognitive dissonance in place about the need to fix some stuff and the priority of doing this
– forum staff that are company employees (community volunteer moderators are mostly fine) can be very touchy, act immaturely, become rude, bully you into shutting up or only speaking positively about the company and the product  — you are generally expected to be an obedient an enthusiastic little minion that believes in their fairy tale or at least keeps quiet, despite their assurances to the contrary
All of which generally comes down to a visible and annoying lack of professional standards, including the company acting like a primadonna and not respecting the customer. A brilliant idea and even brilliant product that can't reach its full potential because of the company developing an attitude. Still very much worth playing (and paying) but extremely disappointing at times. The game itself is not as disappointing as the company's attitude is.
** BUY IF: **
THE GAME ITSELF: You are a hardcore mediaeval fan like me. Unphased by poor design logic or able to get over it. Don't mind using debug console (i.e. cheats) or save editing to fix your game, or rolling back to an earlier save if you encounter some serious weirdness or your game gets broken. If you don't mind playing an expensive game released 3 years ago that still feels like a beta and all the more so with subsequent releases of DLCs and patches.  If you ar not obsessed with Steam achievements, which require running the game in Ironman mode, which means no reloads and no console cheats, which means you're stuck with bugs and awkward design etc.
COMMUNITY/SUPPORT: If you don't care about forum life or are thick-skinned, unphased by rude or unfair staff moderators (volunteer moderators are generally more reasonable).
In any case if money is not a pressing concern and you can afford finding out on your own if you like it. This is probably mitigated by frequent Steam sales (up to –75% sometimes).
** DON'T BUY IF: **
THE GAME ITSELF: Your tolerance level for poor design logic and bugs is low. If you expect professional developers to adhere to high professional standards and just can't play a released product that often feels like a beta.
COMMUNITY/SUPPORT: If you expect to be actively involved in community life and be somewhat respected by staff for your contributions — they entertain no such notion. The measure of your worth to them is how much hype you generate for them. Don't be deceived. And don't expect fairness in moderation when you criticize them or the product. If you don't mind this kind of thing, you probably should buy the game because this is like the single biggest problem with CK2/Paradox.
MY OVERALL 'NOT RECOMMENDED' RATING SHOULD BE READ AS: 'DON'T BUY UNLESS' (I.E. UNLESS YOU CAN LIVE WITH THE COMPANY'S ATTITUDE OR CAN AFFORD LOSING MONEY TO TRY AND FIND OUT).

This just isn't a good game.
Three Dead Zed is a puzzle-platformer game where you can switch between three different forms at will; a default form that can climb ladders and interact with objects, a heavy form that can deal extra damage and break certain blocks, and a light form that is agile and can walljump, but can't attack. The puzzles are very light; it's almost all about finding the right switch or destroying the right generator to unlock the path forward.
The problem with the game is the controls just don't feel right. Since the heavy form can't traverse anything and the normal form is still relatively slow with poor jumping abilities, you'll mostly be platforming as the nimble light form. But the platforming just doesn't feel good. Jumping and landing accurately feels like it's much harder than it should be, and there are some absolutely ridiculous spikes in difficulty that just seem unfair. At one point I had to quit the game to do something else, but I was in the middle of a level and thought "I better just finish this first because there is no way I ever want to play this level again." That is a bad sign for a game, period.
The main game took 90 minutes to beat, but it unlocked a challenge mode. But really, when the story mode was just a complete slog to get through, there's no way I'm going to want to play a more frustrating version of that. Don't buy this game.

*Come playyy... We're just getting started...*
This game is a wonder.
The adventure unfolds with the cards given by the story teller.
Will luck be on your side or against you? Who knows... and this is all the fun in this game.
The more you play and the more token you get. And the more token you get, the more cards you get for your deck.
And the more cards you get, the more token you have to unlock. And the more you play!
There's Equippement cards and Encounter cards.
Encounter cards are used to build the adventure and all of them got a Token to unlock but you only unlock it if you complete the challenge offered by the Encounter card successfuly. Some cards will offer you a text story where you have to give a certain amount of your money/food/health to accomplish something while others will offer you the opportunity to fight enemies.
Equippement cards are pretty self-explanatory but let me explain anyway.
At the end of most encounters you will recieve cards to help your journey.
They may give food, health or equippement, the later being weapons, shields, helmets, gloves, artifacts, rings, trinkets...
This equippement is mostly used in the action segments, helping you in combat.
There's equippement slots on your characters, Diablo-style, but with cards, no inventory management.
You can select what you want equipped by choosing any card you recieved in your inventory or sell your extra loot when you find a shop for some gold to buy other stuff.
At the end, that's what makes the game a lot of fun to play, the cards and text adventure coupled with action gameplay.
It's already immersive with the teller talking you through your decisions and, even though I wouldn't say that it's the best combat gameplay ever made, all the action aspect makes you feel feet deep inside the adventure and, also, adds some skill to be use instead of solely be based on luck.
*Now you're not going anywhere...? ...Are you?*
*...Let your destiny... unfold...*

This is a Single Player review only.
Obvious question to start....is this better than ARK?. Yes and no. ARK is 18 months further advanced than Conan so ARK has more content and ironed out many of the teething bugs BUT......Conan (despite the server issues) is a MUCH better game than ARK was when ARK was 2 weeks old.
Why? To list a few immediately obvious to a single player : Conan is super stable, not so CPU/GPU intensive hence looks better as the settings can be higher - I'm running it on an ACER laptop i7 4710 quad core, 8GB RAM and a GTX860M with all settings on ULTRA. Conan also has a number of genuinely unique concepts such as Thralls (human slaves) to help with item production (eventually thralls will add new items based on ethic origin as well as speed and cost reductions) and corruption (longterm character damage resulting from going into baaaaaad places). The building system is ARK 2.0 (the mechanics are similar but the pieces are immensely more beautiful and OMG they figured out a SUPER CLEAR way to tell you which way the piece is facing and you can clearly ROTATE CEILINGS !!!) as well as the inclusion of numerous decorative items to beautify your base. Character customisation - almost  at full RPG levels. The levelling up system is also interesting as it gives possible access to a skill or workstation and that may let you immediately craft 2 or 3 different things.Another nice detail is mining rocks - which makes the rock slowly crack up before completely breaking up as you mine all the ores from it.
Two wonderous features worth singling out since I mentioned ARK  - in Conan, when you pick up something it tells you how many of that thing you now have in inventory (no more guessing 'Do I have enough stone now?') and...wait for it......NO PILLAR NIPPLES....yes, FUNCOM figured out a way to keep the entire pillar between the floor and ceiling - a miracle.
Price: At €/$30 this is a little pricey for an EA survival - but it looks good and so long as Funcom don't have some sort of brain freeze, the price is fair for what could/should be a great game that will entertain you for hours and hours.
As a SP you can at the start of the game tweak all the key factors (speed of XP gain, resource harvesting, thirst drain etc) to make the game less grindy. My first play through I left everything at the default settings and it was a grind, really grindy. But with the tweaks (XP at 2.5 and resource harvest at 4.0 ) things move along and progress comes. I use a quad core i7 laptop with a GeForce GTX 860M card and can run this easily on high+ settings and the world looks great with no FPS problems except (I think) for a stutter when changing map tiles.
In SP the game has a heavy focus on obviously surviving, building and exploring. First off surviving is pretty normal in Conan. Water is freely available but only in certain areas as the map is mainly desert (as in Scorched Earth) and there is enough food around the water to stay alive even without killing things ( although late game advances allow players to obtain water even in the dryest of desert areas). The wildlife and NPC humans both represent a danger - this is universally true when your character is low level, but even at higher levels an angry mob of Dafari cannibals are seriously hard to handle alone. The fight or flight principle also is problematic in Conan as some creatures will slow you, other will stop you moving altogether meaning getting into combat may be a one way experience. Exploring is all done of foot - no flying dino to survey the whole map in 5 minutes. The map is obviously not finished - underwater looks like it is a bit placeholder graphics and the edges of the map all look like we may eventually be able to go there but are currently shielded by the 'Green Cursed Wall' of instant character death ( the area beyond the cursed wall is huge, perhaps 5 or 6+ times the current map area, but it is virtually all empty atm). The devs have said more biomes are to come, but there are already the river valleys with waterfalls, many oases, a savannah, sulphur lakes, the 'forbidden city', the Stygian city, rocky desert and the sand dunes. The map seems about the size  or perhaps a little smaller than the original ARK map, but of course being all on foot it feels huge. Finally building - as I said earlier this is just better than ARK (and with 3000+ hrs on ARK, I love ARK building). Conan's basic building system is simply superior - easier to use and looks MUCH better when comparing the base pieces from both games (sorry for always comparing Conan and ARK). Although mods will undoubtedly add many new things to build, the base game already comes with the ability to build hexagonal and triangular towers and the pieces are all (largely) 'no contact' so building up a cliff face is possible immediately.
Another feature worth noting having already mentioned grind - in Conan the torches don't need fuel - yes, it is illogical and unrealistic - but it is great not having to run around topping up the wood or coal in your torches to keep the lights on.
The creatures in game are currently somewhat limited (probably about 20 or so) ranging from barbarian tribal groups, crocodiles and hyaenas to more mythical undead dragon-like monstrosities - the setting is of course a low-magic fantasy world. Currently their AI is damaged (for example they don't swim - even the crocs) and their animations are very broken (often teleporting, sliding over the ground rather than walking etc) - EA problems that will go shortly I am sure. Resources available seem fairly normal for the genre, also there are a number of items that currently seem to have no purpose (ale and wine kegs) as well as a few recipes that you can discover where we don't have access to all the ingredients (eg malted seeds are apparently not yet in-game).
As it is very early EA there are issues - some items won't place or use a generic image (barrels when placed become sharpened stakes), the thrall system is only partially implemented, the sandstorm is largely a graphical event and does only limited damage to your health and so on. In SP though the game is stable, high FPS, no rubberbanding, no major crashes. Patches come fairly regularly but TBH they seem to break as much as they fix in SP at the moment and they are focused purely on bug fixes and exploits. Funcom have said they anticipate only making 6-8 content patches between now and final release but that they will all be big ones and the game intro has a list of promised features to look forward to. The devs also seem to have quite an active group of community managers and communication through the forums is imho quite good compared to many EA companies.
One flaw the game has in SP especially that hopefully will be addressed is a reason to explore - if you can find a sweet spot on the map (and there are a few) you have currently little incentive to go off to the far side of the map as everything you need is close at hand - as I said I hope this will change as new (geographically specific) features, NPC's and resources/treasures appear.
Mods are coming - the devkit was released mid-Feb so we can expect this game's workshop to provide the imaginative variety of choices and cool stuff that the gaming community has now come to look forward to.
In summary - this is a good EA. If you like the whole Conan thing and/or survival/building games this will satisfy even at this early stage. And lets face it, anybody who has seen Arnie's movies has always wanted to take a poisonous snake, turn it into an arrow and fire it at your enemy - well now you can.

I honestly anticipated a golf game. I don't know why, it's clearly a puzzle-platformer trapped inside of the rotting husk of golf. A cheeky and fun idea that rapidly overstays its welcome with increasingly over-complicated and poorly implimented level design. The design elements continue to require more and more precise and developer-intended (in that, 90's adventure game kind of way) solutions you'll continue to fail to execute.
Played with friends the first level is bearable, but the experience fell apart so fast as levels continued to spiral out of control into the more precise-platform style gameplay a physics engine powered game cannot provide. Frustration mounts as you hit the swing limit or the time limit, and the jank throughout even the more basic components of the game ruin an otherwise promising looking experience. I don't even see the point in trying to implement customization features when the levels are just try-hard exercises in janky an time-pressured futility.
If you're expecting to pick up and play this game without a thorough understanding of developer intent, you're going to probably fail repeatedly and embarassingly. Skip this game, the level design isn't worth your time and doesn't respect your time.

I have played ArcheAge for about over 1,500 hours off the Trion launcher, long before it ever came to Steam. It was good, then. When it first launched...But then the Trion-Management-Team invaded. They have decided to focus all efforts on nothing but a credit-card oriented game. But, for the purpose of review, I'll do a full one, by splitting it up into categories: Graphics, Gameplay (PVP and PVE), and Community.
GRAPHICS
The graphics are actually pretty nice. At high, they're pretty decent, armors are in no way historically accurate (this is a Korean MMORPG, nothing makes sense most of the time), you have the usual huge-cleavage outfits with female characters locked at max chesticle size, but the weapons do look pretty good, and end-game weapons actually look like end-game weapons, not an upgraded reskin of what you started with. Vegetation is there, but usually pretty bland depending on what zone you go to. PVP Zones are pretty much empty which is nice, so you don't have to run circles around trees trying to get that CC combo off. Mounts are also pretty cool. Overall, I'd give it an "average" on its graphics. Nothing spectacular, but still better than a lot of other MMORPG's out there.
GAMEPLAY
A. PVE
PVE is literally the only thing you do from level 1-55. Bosses are bland, and most require multiple people to actually kill. Some world bosses need a full raid or a simple 5-man party depending on its level. Overall, PVE is not really rewarding at all, except for two bosses: The Kraken, and The Red Dragon. The Kraken drops a half-way decent shield, and I think a spear? I'd have to check on that. The Red Dragon drops the motherload of weapons. I've constantly just drewled over having a Red Dragon weapon. They were so good...So...Pristine...So....Perfect. HOWEVER, you'll be lucky if you can find a guild to do Red Dragon, because that's what it basically needs. Unless your entire guild is extremely built up into end-game, you'll need 2 full raids to take down Red Dragon. 1 full raid if you've done it before and you've got it down, or your heavy-hitters in the guild are just damn overpowered. Either way, PVE isn't very fun...Like...at all...Especially at early levels. But once you get to the raid/world bosses, it's hell of a lot better.
B. PVP
I should start off with saying that there are three skill trees you pick to make a class. For example, I play a Darkrunner: Battlerage, Shadowplay, and Auramancy. It's a rogue-style glass cannon DPS class, built for extreme burst damage and VERY fast mobility, almost as fast as some archer classes (which go faster than a lot of mounts). Anyways, only CERTAIN, not ALL, but CERTAIN AND LIMITED combinations of these skill trees actually work for a class to be effective in PVP. To dive more into it, I have Battlerage and Shadowplay, my two main skill trees that give me my Stealth abilities, my CC combos, and my overall damage. Then I have Auramancy, my supporting tree that gives me all my mobility, helps me with getting rid of debuffs, providing me with my own buffs, etc. However, not all skill trees when paired together work like this. A lot of off-spec and weird classes get absolutely SMASHED in PVP. It's said that you're allowed to "play what you want to play"; yeah you can, but you're practically worthless on all accounts most of the time. For example, the class of....Damn I forget it's specific name...but it's Battlerage, Shadowplay, and Archery. That is three damage classes all smashed together. You have no mobility, no CC breaks, nothing. You basically run at normal speed with literally almost no defense, and die within 3 seconds if you're doing any 1v1s. Group battles may be alright but they're still horrible. What I'm trying to say is that, in so many words, there are cheese classes that will easily trump and beat other classes (Darkrunner and some magic-based classes are like that). There's no way to beat them unless you have EXTREEEEMELY better gear.
Now I'm gon'na get into the gear part of PVP. Gear is mainly bought with real cash. Back in 2015, 2016 thereabouts, I was a max-level Darkrunner at 4000 gearscore (gearscore being all your items contribute a "gearscore", all of these item's gearscore added up will be your total gearscore, i.e. mine of 4000). Now, I've pretty much always been a FTP, for a couple months being paid but anyways, that takes a long♥♥♥♥♥time to get, especially if you do it on your own. The Cat Machine is incredibly fun, having the time of my life.
It's a puzzle game reminiscent of SpaceChem, in that you must build paths for certain objects to traverse in just the right way. But in The Cat Machine the thing you're guiding is a train... of cats.
The mechanics are simple and intuitive, and the graphics, music & text are hilarious. I can't get enough of these cat trains, and the scientist cats programming up a storm in the background.
In detail, you have a train of cats where each cat is a different color. You have to make the train go across tracks of the same color as the cats, in the same order. To make matters more complicated, the same set of tracks you designed has to work for several different cat trains.
Often it feels like designing a finite automaton to accept a given set of strings. At a complexity level the game is clearly in NP, and moreover it is straightforward to encode planar Hamilton path in it, so it's NP-complete. (I.e. guaranteed challenge!)
Level design is very good too; brute forcing will not work, you must notice regularities & patterns in the cat trains you're going to have to guide and devise some high-level plan first.
Highly recommended.

One of my favorite games ever. Wasn't just another themepark, generic wow clone. The class system was cool, you'd combine different skill trees to make a class. Crafting, housing, and professions were interesting. Crafting my own boat and going out fishing/exploring was really cool, unlike any other game I've played in this aspect. The freedom to explore with gliders was amazing. Hit the sweet spot that WoW seems to struggle with; you couldn't fly permanently so you were forced to interact with other people.
There was a crime system as well and in the beginning people were planting hidden gardens all over the map due to the limited amount of buyable land. Trees could randomly get hit by thunder during storms and become "thunderstruck", which would yield incredibly rare crafting materials and were probably the most valuable mats in the beginning. So the result was that people wre planting hidden tree gardens all over the world and the entire server would get involved pretty fast if a tree farm was discovered. It would turn into an all-out-war.
Unfortunately it's one of the most p2w games I've ever experienced and was promptly ruined. You could pay to progress and pretty much had no limit to how strong you could get. As long as you kept spending money you kept getting stronger. Within a few weeks of release the entire blanace was destroyed and the game was unplayable without a creditcard in-hand at all times.
Scumbag Trion and greedy devs strike again. It's a shame too, I would have easily been willing to pay a monthly sub if it meant neutering the p2w cash shop and restricting it to convenience/asthetics. I would have had 1,000+ hours no question and would probablty still be playing today. Oh, did I mention you could buy a monthly sub on top of the broken cash shop? Doubly p2w in that regard, it wasn't "required" but in reality in really was.

So... this is the conclusion to the 'epic' story of a girl that stands up to an oppressive regime of martial arts fighters by gathering 12 martial arts fighters to challenge the current government, because that's the only way to win an election...
I've played through all five games and while after the first one I didn't have much motivation to carry on, the second and third game are actually decent and offer a good amount of exploration, secrets and somewhat interesting characters. Still the main story and companion comments aren't good, but at least the gameplay keeps it together. That changes in game four. Not only does the game fall apart into lengthy dungeons with annoying secrets and almost nothing else, the story takes a turn for the even worse.
Introducing time pressure into an RPG Maker game doesn't work. It simply doesn't. The main character turns into a psycho forcing people to fight for her by burning down their house. The companion dialog gets overwhelming and so thin that it's just plain annoying. At the end of the fourth game my motivation that was kindled by the second and third game was running very low again.
Now it's time to talk about the fifth game. The game splits your characters into *5* groups quite early on and then happily jumps back and fourth between the groups without any real reason except for padding the game out a bit more. By now it's clear that the game was separated into five parts and then padded out to have the proper amount of 'content' in each of them. The story consists of endless and pointless rantings by all characters. It's by now really painful to read the overly lengthy and completely non-relevant dialog.
The dungeons are as to be expected long and boring, but (mostly) filled with enough monsters to train you for the big showdown. It feels tedious to drag through the game knowing that you only do it to train for the final battle. The worst bit though is when the game makes you play the exact same dungeon five times in a row. It's mind-numbingly boring.
Afterwards it's the 'good' old fight-99-dragons showdown with another round of meaningless dialog thrown in. If you hit a small window of grinding the right amount you get the better ending of the game, otherwise if you train too less or too much you get a worse one. That's it.
I still admire the amount of work that went into this game and there is a lot of good in the presentation (minus the horrible 'manmade' sound effects), but overall it just doesn't work. Make it a two part game, cut a lot of the ballast and you have something that is fun to play and that isn't dragged out this much. As it is there's just way too much dead weight for it to be a good game.

One of my favorite pastimes is playing miniature golf. I have decided to review the various places I have made the attempt to play at and set them up here. If you have a comment, please send it to me and I will add it. I will rate all of the locations on four options using a scale of one to ten. The facilities will be rated on:  Challenge, Variety, Fun and Overall Value.There will also be a brief description of the facility and the amenities offered as well as prices as remembered from past experience. Some prices may have changed since I was there.

Challenge is a ranking of how difficult the course is to play. There may also be a factor for how much skill it takes vs how much luck is involved in playing the course. Try to view it as if you don't play often when using this rating.
Variety is a ranking of how many other things are available to do at the facility. Does it have any extras like batting cages or go-carts. I generally will keep courses that have a good variety of holes but nothing else around a 5-6 range. The more amenities, the higher the score.
Fun may be my most subjective item. Is the golf course too difficult to have a good time, or to easy. Is there a good balance between difficulty and challenge. How much do you enjoy this course vs. some others? Would you take a date there?
Overall Value is based on the price to play vs the fun had. It should reflect some composite of the other factors.
Feel free to try them out and tell me if you agree or disagree with my ratings. I am, by no means, an expert. I just know what I like.
Also, a note for the owners of the locations: If you find I have made an error in reporting your location or prices, drop me an email and I will correct it at my first opportunity. My opinions are my own regarding value for dollar, but Idon't want to provide incorrect factual information.
Please note that, unless otherwise stated, all prices are for one round adult admission. Children's pricing and specials may vary.
