A very simple game that is relaxing to play. It may take you a little bit to get used to the mechanics of the game, but for the most part, it will not be that difficult for you. OVIVO is a platformer that is quite different from others, in that it seems grounded in metaphysics.
All of the game's visuals are in the colors of black or white. You control a little ball (named as OVO) that has what could look like an antenna coming from the top of its head. You only have 2 actions to perform: move left or right with the arrow keys, or perform a color switch with the spacebar.
When you press the spacebar, OVO will alternate to the opposite color of what it currently is, and this will also alternate the direction of gravity. The gravity will make you stop when OVO hits an object of the same color as itself. Otherwise, OVO will simply fall forever (or fly upwards forever) through the opposite color's background. If you fall out of bounds, OVO will eventually respawn.
Doing these color changes and reversal of gravity allow you to actually perform jumps and other mechanics, because you can fall through hills and come back up through even larger hills, for instance.
There is an introduction level to the game, as well as 9 other levels. Each new level tends to add new mechanics to the game, such as black hole objects which will suck you in and then shoot you back out, or other obstacles that will make you respawn.
Note that the game is not that difficult because there is a large amount of checkpoints throughout the game, so you are not sent far back through the level whenever you respawn. Further, the levels are mostly linear, except for some collectibles which will be addressed shortly.
As can be seen in screenshots or videos, the levels are very artistically-designed. There are many different types of objects you can encounter, many of which are hidden out of the way or are somewhat difficult to recognize because of the game's use of only black and white.
Lastly, the game has some collectibles for you to find, which are not extremely difficult. Each level has 3 symbols that you can find, as well as an arbitrary number of dots. When you are in a level, you can look at the Pause screen and see the number of dots that are in the level. As you collect the dots, they will grow larger on the Pause screen, going from left to right, and will color themselves as black or white. Once all of them are larger than the initial size, then you will know you have collected all for the level.
The only detail I can say about the collectibles is to pay attention to them - take a little bit of time to think about them and what the game tells you when you find them.
Overall, OVIVO was a very interesting game to play. While it was only a few hours to fully complete, I enjoyed it very much, and hope that more will come to it in the future.

Pros:
- (More) sprawling, immersive setting. The conflicts that had previously just been mentioned are brought into the foreground with side characters' arcs.
- (More) iconic original soundtrack.
- (More) likeable and deep characters. A LOT of them. There's someone here for everyone to enjoy kicking♥♥♥♥♥with.
- (Another) intriguing plot, which actually starts to make sense of the motivations of the series' antagonists. Although to get there, the game does railroad you a bit, using a character I won't spoil but who I like to refer to as Ronald Reagan. At least you can complain about the railroading?
- (More) fantastic voice acting.
- Shepard is still a badass, customizable protagonist with a convincing personality. The increasing length of the franchise adds a lot more nuance to the character. You get rewards for importing a character from the first game, which are rather nice.
- Importing an old character changes many minor details of the story and unlocks a few side quests.
- Seven potential romance subplots - four for each gender of protagonist. Can also avoid romance entirely.
- A solid sequel. (Not included).
- An intense, difficult and dynamic conclusion. It feels like an epic science fiction in and of itself.
- We are free of the Mako!!
- I've heard that the DLCs for this game are universally fantastic, but alas, I have not played them.
- I hate fighting them, but it's probably a plus for the game that Husks suddenly got scary.
Cons:
- Again: Aged graphics.
- Again: I have a 15"+ screen, and the game crops itself - lots of black border space, but only in cutscenes.
- Again: Male Shepard's voice acting. Sorry, Dude Shep, but it's gotta be said.
- Again: The implied homophobia of having no queer LI available for Dude Shep. We see what you did there, BioWare. Six of the seven potential romances are gender-locked, with the bisexual character not even being a squad mate; this is impressively worse than the last game.
- I know I'm a rarity in preferring the first Mass Effect to the second - as fantastic as all of the individual storylines in the second game are, only the finale is continuous in gameplay and story, and that leaves the game feeling very disjointed for me.
- Importing a Mass Effect 1 save over the PC is a major pain, involving digging into computer files and should probably be accomplished with a guide.
- Why did we get rid of the Overheat feature, again?

If you know of this game you've probably heard it refered to as a "sibling murder, incest, warmonger, and religious intolerance map simulator" or something of the like. While this is a humurous synopsis of the experience - and mostly true - it's not very helpful if you're trying to decide whether or not to dump copious amounts of cash into this thing. I mean, just look at all the DLC. It's at least 160 something odd dollars for all of it. So, is it worth it?
The short answer: maybe. I know that's a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ short answer, but hear me out. This game is niche. Very, very niche. It's unique certainly, but that does not change the fact that you could very well absolutely hate it. For starters, if you're thinking of making this purchase and have not played other games like this one (Europa Universalis etc.) then go watch Arumba's guide on how to play it. Also, pay attention to the fact that it's 22 videos long of about 18 minutes each. Granted, they are very in-depth, but this does not change the fact that understanding how this game works is not easy. It's an experience, and you will have to put time and effort into this game to get any sort of rewarding feeling for playing it. However, once you reach that point it becomes something very fun. Suddenly your son dieing of small pox leaving your daughter the only one to inherit becomes a challenge, rather than a guaranteed game over. Your neighbor converting to a different religion becomes an opperunity, not a reason to cower hoping that they won't declare war. The Pope becomes your "friend" rather than the guy that excommunicates you so your neighbor can steal your♥♥♥♥♥♥ It goes on and on.
Now, I like this game. I want that to be clear. However, this is not a game for everyone. It's not a game made for everyone either, hence the price point. This game in itself is a bit of a hobby, and while the price is stupidly high, it's about 6 or 7 expansions of decent content and a butt load of not so decent penny grabs. However, playing without all the dlc is very different from playing with all the dlc, and the game with dlc is objectively better most of the time. It's got more content, a bigger map, more events, religions, etc. As such, if your on the fence about this game, I'd suggest waiting until it goes on sale - as it does usually every so often - and pick up the whole thing for about 25~30ish dollars. At that price I'd hands down suggest this game to anyone with even a remote interest, but whether or not it's worth the full 160 is your decision, and you might regret it.
Onto what this game actually is. In essence, you play as a family, not a single character. You do play as one person at a time, but you are survived by your children or relatives. You build power through war - which is not as exciting as it sounds - and intrique - which is. This game is not about the combat. It matters, yes, but playing a warmonger is only fun for about the first 80 hours put into a dynisty before you own all of Europe and are expanding into uncivilized lands. It is - above all - a game about the sibling murder, the incest, the bribing, the corruption, the intrigue, the homosexuals, the lovers, the concubines, the children, the murdering of the children, the arranged marriages, the raiding, the power struggles, the underlings -  the dirty, dirty unloyal underlings - the castle building, the character improvement, the ruling, and - above all - the characters. This game has no story, and yet the best story of any game I've ever played. Everything that happens is your legacy. You murdered the duke and stole his titles, well that's now part of your family legacy. Married into Royalty. That's there too. The whole game is about building your own alternative histories where the Scottish get invaded by the Moors and become Muslims, where Russia is formed early and fends off the mongols, where the Viking Pagan Empire stretches from Iceland to India. It's about doing whatever the hell you want, and it's glorious.
This game is fun, and half of the fun is figuring out why it's fun. But for the love of all that is watched over by Zun, don't spend 160 bucks on the thing if you're unsure it's your cup of tea. It might be the best tea you've ever had, but wait until it's on sale.

Desktop Dungeons might look like a roguelike, but don't let that fool you. It is much of more a puzzle game. With a LOT of maths. But the good thing is that if you enjoy mathsy puzzle games, this one is amazing.
Like all good puzzle games the mechanics are very simple but leave enough space for a massive amount of variation. The amount of different character classes, monsters, and dungeons, that QCF managed to put into the game is staggering and gives the game with a huge potential playtime.

It's great! The puzzles start off easy, with light quirky humour to ease you in, and then the tricky puzzles come along - something to get one's claws into. The beginning puzzles might take a few minutes but it didn’t take me too long to arrive at levels where I’m sitting there for 20 minutes puzzling away. Some levels are a nightmare and I had to temporarily give up – even on these puzzles I wasn’t annoyed at the game, just annoyed at my own stupidity. It’s certainly a clever type of puzzle system and enjoyable, if you like puzzles. The gentle presence of cat humour is welcome.

The soundtrack is perfect and really suits the game. The main theme is catchy and the ambient gameplay music is in the same vein as SimCity, it's nice to listen to but can easily loop for a few hours without becoming annoyingly repetitive.

So, this isn’t a catastrophe of a game, quite the opposite. If you like intricate and well-designed puzzles I highly recommend it.

Providing empirical evidence that I am not simply a curmudgeon who hates artsy puzzle games, OVIVO! Its bold, minimalist, black-and-white visual style was really evocative, its music was just right, and the level design was excellent. Its simple premise -- switch the gravity of the black-and-white world by pressing the spacebar -- evolved in such interesting ways, skillfully building on itself as time went on. I liked that it was flush with checkpoints, letting me do crazy things with the gravity without having to worry about being sent back to the start, and the symbols were cleverly hidden but findable. It's almost miraculous to have a game where I can find everything without a walkthrough that explains you have to hold your computer out a window while counting backward from 10 and sacrificing a chicken to get the last gem, but here we are: actual competent game design. OVIVO definitely isn't for anyone, but if visual interest and clever mechanics are up your alley, and you don't mind the artsiness of it, this is one to check out.

Most of the objectives are 'capture this point' 'defend this guy' 'knock down this door' and offer limited to no change in the game-play. Personally I love that this game isn't as soul-crushing as CS:GO, WOW, RL, Diablo, Halo/COD or any other games you see people investing thousands of hours in. It's fun, not addicting. As a side-note the game also allows you to choose from 1st or 3rd person.

The Cat Machine is easy to categorize.  It's a catchy entry in the catalogue of puzzle games, and will draw you in like Catholics to a catechism.  You simply place rails, and cat trains drive along them like caterpillars, with a goal of preventing a catastrophe from befalling the earth.  Avoiding the cataclysm is as simple as flinging cats off the train in the correct order.  Levels become increasingly complex, and some of the more difficult ones have left me feeling catatonic, but finally solving them can feel cathartic.  If you get too stressed out, just take a catnap, have some catnip, and try again.  If you like puzzles, The Cat Machine caters to you, and is a real cat treat.

I never had a Computer, or Internet for that matter during the time when WoW was popular. A lot of my friends and many people I know played WoW for many years and it obviously was the best MMO as no other were even spoken of. In this regard with most people falling off WoW I feel as though I am in the same situation when it comes to finding something new and fresh in the MMO genre but It always seems to ends in the same way where its fun for a few days but in the end... the same as before with nothing new on the surface.
I like the idea of an MMO. A game with a massive world, 1000's of players, countless Quests, Epic gear & towards the end game content Dungeons & PvP. However to get to that end game level where you can farm high level dungeons for the best gear and have a chance in PvP requires 100's of hours of playtime which in this day and age where a new game comes out almost every week committing that much time to something that you might not really end up even liking is hard to do.
Getting to ArcheAge in general though, I started when the Revelations/ New Start servers came out and played through the storyline as a Dwarf. The story was so bland and uninteresting by the end I was just confused as to how that could be it. It then connected to the main story which took me too many areas that were considered "in conflict" or "unrest" some colors dark red others light orange. I assumed that because it was our races State or Island there would be pretty much no enemy players around.
I do a couple of side quests which I just need to kill a few AI and behind me I see a max level player riding past. He stops, comes over to me and spams like 50 different abilities and I die instantly, then just continues on his way. I respawn and go back to what I was doing, complete the side quests and move into the MAIN STORY QUEST. I get to the town gate and pass by another enemy, I ignore him and hope he just keeps going. For a moment he does, then turns around kills me and continues on his way. Once I meet a few high level players who helped me get to where I needed to go I realized there was so many enemy players there because it was a medium level/ popular dungeon in the same area. I CAN'T EVEN PLAY THROUGH THE STORY WITHOUT GETTING KILLED IN RANDOM PVP ZONES!?
I get the idea behind different areas going into conflict but if I'm doing the story I'm still learning and have no idea what specialist class I even want to build let along have a chance at PvP. The problem is theres no penalty for killing low level players so they just kill everyone! WHY!!!!
The combat system is nothing special but I did pick a mage so maybe it just felt slow because Mage has a lot of cast time spells.
No one plays low level dungeons so it's hard to even be able to experience them atleast once unless you get a high level player who is just there for the daily which IMO is no experience at all as they just run through one shooting everything.
The Gear system I do like. It’s very RPG like, you collect armor for your specific class and it’s all about maximizing your damage/ defense output which for me was Magic Damage.
All in all I tired WoW to late and found it repetitive and boring, Guild Wars 2 was better but again lots of repetitive quests, traveling But atleast there was no BS PvP zones in your Races state and it had massive bosses that required 100+ people to fight which is an impressive site to behold.
I think I'm just done with MMO's and they are just not my thing.

Rich story + RPG strategy + third-person shooter game? OMG. This game has really interesting gameplay.
Well, I'm not really playing this game till the end, since I played the sequel on PSP first... (The sequel have more classes and it's a lil bit confusing that the speciality of each class is like a "downgrade" when you played the sequel first)
A. Story
There are stories for each character beside main stories. And you could unlock special ability for each character. The story itself is good. The dub is also amazing. The art itself also really good. All these aspect make this became interesting game with rich story. Unlocking the ability for each character, make you want to use all the characters.... It makes me like playing a VN without option to choose. But I feel the relationship between MC and other characters is building up step by step.
B. Strategy Game
There're many classes that u could choose. Try different weapon, choose your own squad for each mission.... There're so many characters in this game with different ability and speciality that make this game became really interesting strategy game.
C. RPG+Third-Person Gameplay
While the gameplay still use a turn-based game, You're moving your character like a third-person-shooter. You choose who's moving, and it become third-person gameplay. There's still "limit" on your movement like other Strategy RPG game. But the enemy can shoot you while you're moving if you're in their sight-area. This third-person gameplay + turn-based gameplay make this game more interesting.

I really like this game.  It's more complicated than Dungeon II which I also really like.  I do feel that the tutorial in Dungeon II campaign is better though because it explains each little item as you go.  War for the Overworld does not do this.  For instance on Level 7 you really need to build the bombard traps and lots of them but the game does not teach you that you need foundries to get toolboxes to build defenses.  I had a lot of defenses but none of them were building so I had to watch a video online and not only did it show me that you need foundries but that you can pick up toolboxes and put them directly on the defenses to speed up their building.  The game also did not teach me how to use the screen that lists all your monsters and click on it to pick up guys.  I learned that from watching a youtube video.  On level 7 I found the lack of gold to be my biggest obstacle but using blood money and a big prison and turning all their guys into gold statues did the trick.  Infinite gold basically.  Actually it might be level 9 where you have the gold problems looking at my notes.
One problem I have with the game is that moving around on the screen does not work well with the mouse.  In Dungeons II the mouse moves around on the screen really well but in War for the Overworld you really need to use the arrow keys instead.  It works really well with the arrow keys.  Another problem is the game is a bit dark and so it's harder to see the screen.  I understand underground is supposed to be dark but I would really appreciate a little more light for visibility.  Overall the game does a really good job in that you have many minion choices from Succubus to Vampire , etc.
I guess I should be writing this review from the perspective of advertising to someone who has never played a game like this before.  In that case you build a dungeon to defeat the do gooders that come to destroy your dungeon.  You do this by carving out rooms in the underground and then putting things in them like vaults to store gold, Barracks to attract    low level monsters, Prisons to put enemies in, torture chambers for Succubi to convert them to your side or turn them into Ghosts, Beast chambers to attract beasts, etc.  Then you build an army out of these creatures to attack your enemies.  You can also use traps and doors to slow down the enemy or kill them.  All in all this is a very good game.

Have never written a game review before, but aside from all the public stigmatism of "P2W" it is not true.
First some facts:
I have played 1000+ hours on steam alone, that doesn't include the 1000-2000+ before steam integration.
I purchased Patron and played with it for the entire longevity of my playtime.
I have played World of Warcraft for 11 years, Warhammer online for its short lifetime from start to end, Aion, Rift, AoConan, Ragnarok Online 1 + 2, FFXIV, Everquest 1 + 2, the failed NEXT alpha, Landmark,  4000hrs + EvE online, tons of runescape. Yet nothing can even come close to the model and operation of Archeage. It is singlehandedly the best crafting and timewasting MMO possible. As far as PvP goes it takes a lot of dedication and commitment to rise yourself to even to begin to be able to compete with the big boys. Most of these people who nark PVP or Pirate have been playing this game since the beginning, understand the game well, and have worked hard for all their gear.
PvP in this game is a whole nother genre in itself. It's hard, breathtaking, and god dont let me mention the ships.
Naval Warfare in this game is even comparable to the once great Pirates of the Burning Sea. Wishing there was more options for vessels but the ones available are gorgeous.
This game will allow you to literally do anything you want.
Want to spend 1000 hours planting seeds in a circle then reaping it for its crops and selling it? Yes.
Want to spend 500 hours diving to the depths of the ocean to look for treasure? Yes.
Want to ride around on your sexy red farm wagon while taking finely aged cheese for gold? Yes.
Want to run around and kill your own faction and laugh as they cry? Yes.
Want to know more? Play.

The missions are small-unit tactics, usually with a tank. It's a lot of fun - you individually control each soldier, and each of the battles feel like a lot of fun. It's not overly deep, but it's FUN.
It's also, surprisingly, for a game about fantasy-WW2, a game that decides to tackle racial genocide. I respect that.
Valkyria Chronicle feels like a game that handles war even-handedly. The theme song still makes me tear up, and the ending is great.
So yes, it has that weird obligatory swimsuit episode and random busty women in skimpy clothing, but don't let that stop you from trying this game, because it's amazingly good.

After playing the original version on the PS3, I was very wary of this PC port, and how the controls would translate from console to PC.
After my first mission, my worries turned out to be unfounded. This is every bit a reliable port of the amazing turn-based srpg (strategy RPG). The game itself has aged gracefully with graphics that don't manage to seem too dated and a story that rivals a quality anime.
The story itself explores many of the tropes and themes of war (specifically WW2) and acts as a heavily fictionalized retelling of the second World War, specifically exploring the topics of racism and genocide.
The gameplay is a magnificent blend of turn-based strategy and real-time action shooter combat. It's both challenging and rewarding - the visceral "chunk" of getting a headshot is comically satisfying. There's little gore, so the game is very PG-13, aside from the gruesome aspects of the story.
The progression system is fairly simple - you never feel like you have to grind a lot, but a little grinding can be helpful at times. Level ups are tied to classes instead of individual units, so if you level up one of your classes, every unit of that class is leveled up. Equipment can also be upgraded or found on the battlefield - including the rarest equipment.
You also get a tank to mess around with and upgrade. It's very unwieldy and slow but extremely powerful, so as with everything else, you need to find when and how to use it to your tactical advantage.
Overall, a wonderful game that I'd whole-heartedly recommend that everyone should try.

ATS may be much smaller in scale than ETS2 but its environments are better designed i.e., prettier and more believable. It is also a bit more challenging with harder drop-off points that you can select for bonus in XP. Smaller gas stations would give you problem to navigate your long trailer in requiring you to be mindful when entering them. There are now police and emergency vehicles that roam the streets which are nice additions for better immersion. The Police would sound their sirene should you violate traffic rules and get yourself fined as a result. Towns and cities are bigger, prettier, and believable in ATS. There are also fewer trucks in ATS but with time there may be more trucks coming as SCS resolves their truck license issues.
To me since the game has  Kenworth W900 that alone is enough reason to buy it.
The downside is that the fps in ATS varies quite a bit. It goes from 60 fps on highways to 40s at towns' intersections and some portions of cities. It's probably due to its reliance on DirectX9. There are some rumors that SCS intends to port both ETS2 and ATS to DirectX11 but until that happens there's little you can do to mitigate this wild variation in fps, unless perhaps you have an older computer.
If you love American setting and enjoy ETS2 you should buy this game. If you love American trucks then this is the game for you.
SCS is known to set its DLCs and expansions at fair prices. I'd definitely give my support to these people at SCS. I hope they will port the game to DirectX 11 engine. The sooner, the better.

Prime World Defenders gets a lot of flack for being "unbalanced" but I've never really gotten that impression from the game.  There were maps that were difficult, and maps that were easy; but none of the game mechanics lead me to believe that this game was inbalanced enough to hinder enjoyment.  In fact, the hardest part about this game was navigating the series of crashes that riddled the game towards the later stages.  These have since been fixed, but at the time they were very cumbersome.
The premise of the game is like any Tower Defense game:  stop the zerging monsters from reaching your core by any means possible.  This game is different from others in its genre through it's use of currency and experience points to add meta-game character development aspect.  Use Silver or Stars (earned by completing levels perfectly and acquiring achievements) to unlock Talents which improve your abilities or let you hold more cards (which are Towers or Spells) in your hand or deck, and improve your cards by leveling them up throughout the game.  Upgrading Towers is a standby in all Tower Defense games; but in Prime World Defenders, you have to improve your tower's card before you can improve it in each match.
For Tower Defense enthusiasts, this is a must-grab title.  It's not without faults, but it's one of the more enjoyable games that I've played this year.

Mass Effect 2 is an excellent follow up to Mass Effect, in almost every possible way.
The shooting mechanics have been completely overhauled, the villains are more interesting, the graphics are better, the biotic powers and the UI are more entertaining and easier to use, heck even the Normandy is cooler than before.
That's also the only problem with Mass Effect 2. BioWare retooled this game into much more of a third person shooter with RPG elements than the original, which was an RPG with third person shooter elements. You can no longer freely explore planet surfaces, but are forced into the invisible walled areas they've designed for the game. You also no longer control the equipment your party uses or their skills to as great of an extent as the first game.
Fortunately those limited areas have been crafted to produce some great experiences, like when you first get Jack.
The paragon/rogue system is also pretty much meaningless in this game. You have to intentionally be a jerk at every possible opportunity in order to not get paragon.
Even so, the game is still good fun with a great story and great voice acting, with characters you can care about. If you aren't already using it, please get the ALOT mod as it makes this an entirely different experience than playing it on console (even though it is just textures).

Most people will compare this instantly to the Fallout series, the only thing they share in common as far as I'm concerned is the Post Apoc setting for the world. The game plays more like Neocron, Hellgate London or STALKER.
The game play requires some getting used for people who've never played a hybrid interface game as there is a toggle between Aim/Fight mode and RPG mode. In Aim/Fight mode the game behaves like a FPS. While in RPG mode the mouse cursor is free so you can click on menu items, objects, and such. Many people make the mistake of skipping the tutorial, a really big mistake as a lot of the basic how to's are taught through the tutorial.
Fallen Earth literally has a spider web of story especially in Sector 1 (the beginners sector) where various stories from starter towns and the later higher level towns actually come together or are related enriching the experience. Much more to say, but not much space left to type. . . give it a honest try and enjoy it for what it is

This game bares the same similarities that make Hotline Miami and Furi so fantastic. It's funny, it's not like they're of the same genre, but they're all built the same. Incredible soundtracks, by independent European developers, with a unique artstyle, quick-paced, action-oriented gameplay, clear inspiration, and a simple story that's almost purely "show don't tell".
As of writing this review, I still haven't finished it, but I believe what I've already experienced is enough to warrant it an incredibly positive rating. It's fun. It's rewarding. It's unique. It has a world you want to explore. It has features that let you customise your gameplay experience. It has a rank system for all you score-based diehards out there.
But it's the price-tag that needs to have you persuaded here -- at least for me it was. $20 always feels a little steep for an indie action game, but trust me, the value is there. It has cutscenes, it's well-optimized, there's attention to detail in the world, and in-depth combat that doesn't make you feel the need to cheese situations -- it just feels really well padded and brushed. And, hey, Hotline Miami 2 and Furi are the same price, and I bought them at launch, so what would make this any different?
So, in saying that, this game earns my figurative badge for being a staple of what a baller as ♥♥♥♥ indie game should be. If you want another small, solid game to fill up some of your time with its love and care, this is one of them.

OVIVO takes you into beautiful black and white art pieces where your goal is simply to traverse them.
As well as being beautiful, the art also guides you through the level in a really smooth way. It's pretty much always clear where you need to go and not even a single word is used.
To move around you often move in and out the artwork. Switching can be a bit counter-intuitive at first, but you'll got into a flow soon enough (though sometimes it can be hard to keep flowing). Once you reach the end of the level, the camera zooms out all the way and shows you a nice overview. pretty satisfying. I think I played about half an hour per level and that's a good time to just jump in a few times.
Nearly every level offers some new mechanic and it's pretty crazy how much there is. Even on the last level new mechanics get introduced.
The music was good, but nothing mind blowing. The audio design seemed a bit lacking, but it's not a huge deal.
All in all it's an incredibly well made game. I can wholeheartedly recommend it.

If you're craving a God game that is a spiritual successor to the 1980s hit "Populas", then Reprisal Universe is what you're looking for. First, and most importantly, the programmer is actively monitoring for feedback and tweaking the game to improve the overall experience. Secondly, it provides interesting innovations that warrant grabbing this instead of just going back and playing the original Populas game. Third, and most important, it's not by Peter Molyneux. (That may seem like the least important element, but go give Godus a look over and really dig into the commitment and how many of those commitments have been broken-- then come back and compare against this game where the developer is actively engaged with his community. The difference is night and day.)
The game ramps up steadily in difficulty. (plus)
The game is at its core a God game. (plus)
The AI is not overwhemling in any map, yet offers a decent challenge in the latter maps. (plus)
This was not always the case (in the initial release, the AI over utilized one of its free powers resulting in an unplayable game-- but the dev fixed this in the first week of player feedback.)
It's inexpensive (plus)
It has a lot of campaign content (30 maps, plus.)
It has an even larger number of "Universe" maps (not sure about the total, plus)
Some of the negatives:
This is a retro pixel game (negative for some, not for me)
You have very limtied control over your populants/peeps (negative for some, not for me)
No music (but new sounds that go with the game play, and you can always use the Steam Beta Music Player to play the original Reprisal Soundtrack, if you like. Negative for some, not for me.)
Scrolling is rough (keyboard tapping required, or a newly introduce mouse scroll which still needs some work. This is a negative but the dev is working to improve the overall experience so a plus for me.)
Map visibility is limited (this is a negative, but it is an homage to the retro Populas UI. There are some differences. Some find this frustrating. I can let it go.)
The only item that is a real negative for me, the author has committed to working on a fix. (The most likely is center-mouse-button-click-and-drag to move the camera around.)
So I don't really have any problems with the game. I'd give it a 8.5/10 personally. And, I expect further development will be done to address remaining issues.
If you're looking for the spiritual successor to Populas, or just looking for a God game to scratch that itch... Buy this, it'll be a number of hours of retro fun. (If retro is not your thing, give it a pass... but I'm telling you, you're missing out.)

I really liked the game, it captures most of the spirit of the original Dungeon Keeper games + some improvements and that alone is a feat that any indie game should be really proud. I was pleasantly surprised, because Im a total fan of the series.
If I dont give it a 8 or 9/10 is because the "sim/soul" part of the game is still lacking compared to all the other things. The creatures are different in appearance and some even in combat, but what about personality's? In the DK games you had the bile demon wanting tons of food, the dragons lots of gold, spiders hating flies, wizards wanting silence in their library's, dogs fertilizing your cementerys etc... Those things not only made you think about how to place rooms or witch creatures try to summon for X or Y lvl, but added a lot to the feeling of your dungeon being "alive" and populated by creatures with desires and/or uses for non room activity's.
The other thing is polish and pacing, but that is probably easier to fix with feedback and the experience the devs already gained by making the game. All in all, its a really good game that can be recommended to any DK fan.

This is a pretty faithful reproduction of the old school game Populous, with the addition of worlds that brings in a touch of Populous: The Beginning. For new players, this is a God game. You can manipulate the land to allow your autonomous citizens to build bigger houses, generating more mana and allowing bigger God powers, such as fire, lightning and marshes. The general idea is to collect totems containing new powers and to wipe out your opponent! There are plenty of islands to keep you occupied and you are even able to partially amend the way later levels start once you complete them (this affects the islands for everyone as the changes are saved online)
You don't directly control your people. In fact there are only 3 actions they can perform: Settle (where newly 'born' people create buildings to increase population growth & mana rate), Gather (they head to the marker that you place as one of your powers), Fight (pick a fight nearby). Combining gather with the other two actions gives you enough control as you need. You can also force people out of houses, but this leaves the house open for invasion.
The game is much harder than I expected. The AI seems to very rapidly build up it's strength (I'm not sure how, but expect I'll learn with time) and begins attacking early. Thay naturally also have access to God powers and can lay waste to your houses if you're not careful. I've just started a world with all 4 tribes on it (apparently all against me!) and it's pretty much chaos! Fun, but chaos! The new update has introduced the option to turn off the 'kindle' option (which allows you to produce people from houses early), this makes the game much more playable and less of a click frenzy.
The latest update has also improved the UI in terms of allowing edge scrolling (phew). In addition there are some keyboard shortcuts but only for high level selection of the group of spells, not individual ones. Click sensitivity also seems to be a bit off, if you don't click the upper part of the spell icon it doesn't register. One gripe is that the ESC key turns off fullscreen mode, rather than the expected standard of opening a menu and skipping the intro (which you apparently cannot).
The terrorforming tool (which you use constantly) is normally available and automatically selected (e.g. launch some fire and you switch back to terrorforming immediately), except sometimes it's not (e.g. lay some marsh and you apparently have nothing selected). So there's a bit of inconcistency which may just be a bug that gets fixed later (hopefully).
The graphics are simple pixel art, but nice to look at, check out the pics & video! It can be unclear at times exactly which square your cursor is on, due to its shape, and as a result launching powers at exact points can be tricky (although exact aim doesn't really matter *that* much. The map edge is tricky to visualise because there is a blurred effect, particularly at the bottom of the screen, and anything built there is slightly obscured (again not *that* bad but could be clearer). The power effects are fairly reasonable although things like fire and lightning storm can obscure things behind them.
The sound effects are basic but well suited to the feel of the game. There is no music, surprisingly, but I never have the music on anyway. Find yourself some good tunes to listen to and forget about in game music!
So in summary, it's a good remake of the classic Populous game, fun and challenging, looks and sounds ok. The latest update has made the game more playable, with the edge scrolling and no kindle option. For the price it's definitely worth it. I expect it's going to bring many hours of fun and frustration and what more can you want!!

It looks like Dungeon Keeper, it sounds like Dungeon Keeper, but it doesn't obey your dark will like Dungeon Keeper.
One of my favorite things of the Dungeon Keeper series was actually building the dungeon, fortifying it, training my host of evil, and THEN attacking with it.
My least favorite thing in War for the Overworld is that it forces you to play the game at its pace, and doesn't allow you to dictate the pace of the game based on your own tactics.  You are often facing a ticking down timer, or faced with an AI opponent that has a fully built dungeon and starting minion compliment that happily bum rushes directly toward you within five minutes of the level loading with no reguard for its own level 1 minions.
This means that for most of the campaign you're distracted from building your dungeon by having to deal with a constant horde of weak pointless minions constantly trying to make a bee line to your dungeon heart.  On most maps, save for the one the game specifically expects you to create them on defenses generally feel pretty worthless as well, not like you'd even have time to build them on later missions anyway since the game just devolves into planting the All Minion/Beast flags down and spamming heal monster as fast as your mana can support.
I also don't like how once the AI has decided it is going to attack you, there is basically nothing else to do except deal with its suicidal tendencies since it somehow always magically has a full host of minions to keep pouring into your territory, no matter how many you seem to kill/capture.  You can't drive them back and take a breather to let your minions sleep, eat, and get back to their tasks like performing rituals, converting prisoners and raising the collected corpses.  Your only choice is to keep an unrelenting drive directly to the dungeon heart even as more enemy minions run their little level 1 legs into your minion ball.
If I'm not mistaken, Dungeon Keeper had a finite minion pool available on each map, and each portal would only allow a limited number of minions through.  When a minion died, it was gone for good and not available to either you, nor your enemies any longer.  This is what made portals matter, prisons, graveyards and torture chambers vital and scavenging pits so annoying.  It also ment you could slap the ever loving♥♥♥♥♥♥out of worthless creatures and kill them (or sacrifice them in the temple to make something better) so they wouldn't be constantly taking up a slot a better minion could be filling.  This also ment you could win a war of attrition as long as you killed more than you lost.
Still, I don't hate the game.  I just get frustrated with the way it makes you play it.  I wish Steam would introduce stars instead of just a Yes/No.  My feelings on the game aren't that binary.  But I guess at the end of the day I'd still say it is worth a try, as long as you don't go expecting pure Dungeon Keeper out of it.

Prime World: Defenders is a challenging tower defense with card collecting and rpg elements, where the story is told through comic book art sequences with full voice acting. 23 repeatable story levels, as well as randomized levels for grinding, are laid out on an overworld map. When you play a level you’ll have a rotatable, zoomable and pannable isometric view of towers and enemies. Towers cost “prime” to build and upgrade, and you only begin levels with a small amount. Killing enemies will earn you more prime, as will summoning additional waves of enemies before they’re due--though in many cases this will increase the difficulty and possibly overwhelm you. Where towers can be placed on the field there are sometimes helpful anomalies which increase their range, power or firing rate. There is also a handy toggle for 2x battle speed.
Towers and spells in the game are represented by reusable cards in your inventory, and you can only carry a set number with you into battle. You can see which enemy types populate a map before you enter so you know how to build your deck. There are towers for both land and air enemies, invisibility detection, snaring, poison, fire, mortar and more. Destructible towers which buff or heal the enemy may also exist within levels.
Spells don’t cost prime but are instead on a timer, and consist of targetable AoEs which snare, stun, reveal invisible enemies and/or do flat damage. Spell and tower cards can be combined with other cards in the forge to level them up--increasing their base damage, range and/or secondary effect intensity--and tower cards can be combined with their duplicates to make the towers upgradeable to tier II and tier III during battle, doubling and quadrupling their damage respectively.
Currency is awarded after battle and can be used to unlock talents for your hero, purchase cards from the store and pay for forging costs. Each story map you complete will earn you 1-3 stars as well, depending on your performance. These stars can be used to unlock high level talents and purchase rare cards. You’ll also be numerically scored on every story map depending on how much damage you take and the amount of prime you have left over at the end, and these scores can be compared with friends’ for each map. You’re also given a total game score which can be compared both globally and with friends’ on the leaderboards.
The difficulty can be frustrating and requires some grinding before bosses, but it tends to be a gear check rather than a matter of skill. Everything about Prime World: Defenders is surprisingly solid for a title that came out of nowhere, and that’s even considering my time with the game was mostly in its beta state and the fact I am not remotely a fan of tower defense.

Warframe is a futurist TPS in which you play space ninjas, called Tennos, who travel all across the planets of our Solar System to protect humanity.
After the human species colonized all the planets of our Solar System, they called themselves the Orokin, an all-powerful race ruling over all. Until thinking machines, the Sentients, brought humanity to its knees.
Defeated, the machines fled, but humanity was left weakened, and divided into factions.
Now, centuries later, you, a Tenno, arrive to save what remains.
Who will you fight against? Against the Grineer, a military empire of clones dedicated to conquering every planet if their path. Against the Corpus, an organization seeking profit and power by selling advanced technology to anyone who can pay. And against the Infestation, a biological plague consuming all life-forms it encounters...
Against these powerful foes, you control your Warframe, an armor with special abilities and powers that you choose, depending if you wish to use fire attacks (Ember), water (Hydroid), ice (Frost), electricity (Volt), poison (Saryn), illusions (Mirage), the list goes on and on.
Start with a basic Warframe like Excalibur, use high-powered guns or deadly sword strikes to destroy your foes. You choose your Warframe, and your weapons, gun or blade, katana or giant hammer, sniper or rocket launcher.
Play solo if you wish to get better, join with friends to battle the boss that waits for you at the end of each planet. I find the community to be quite helpful: for each troll, you'll find 10 players willing to help you on missions or to sell you stuff.
Improve your Warframe and weapons, earn Credits (basic money) and Platinum (the money you'll use to trade weapons and Warframes with other players).
And here's the Warframe Wiki, it'll answer a lot of your questions once you start playing!
No matter if you're listening to music on your ship, fishing on Earth, fighting on Mars or Jupiter, or exploring that mysterious dimension we call the Void... have fun, and protect humanity! :)

**This review is based on the base game**
A great grand strategy game from Paradox.  The first in their 4 strategy series, this game is set in the medieval period, streching from Ireland to India and Iceland to Mali.  The base game ranges from 1066 (norman invasion) - 1453 (fall of constantinople).  In CKII you try to continue dynasty - trying to make it the most prestigous in Europe!  The game is centered around your dynasty and succession.  If your heir is not of your dynasty, it's game over.
You start as a count/earl, duke, king or emporer controlling one of the counties, duchies, kingdoms or empires on the map.  Without any DLCs, you can only be a christian ruler and not a merchant rebublic.  You cannot be a theology (pope/bishop).  The game also features baronies, cities and bishoprics but that cannot be your primary title.  As a ruler you manage vassals (rulers below you) and try to please - or overthrow - your leige (ruler above you).  The feudal ranking is as below (above = liege; below = vassal):
- Emporer
- King
- Duke
- Baron/Bishop/Mayor
You can be a liege to someone below you, but not equal or above you.  Your vassals are only below you - not equal to you.
A Catholic (usually) follows the pope, and the pope can orders crusades.  The crusades can be based on real historical crusades (such as many of the ones for Jerusalem) and crusades to rid infidels/heritics.  Any catholic ruler can join a crusade, and the winner of the crusade is defined by how much they contributed to the crusade.  Winning the crusade will sometimes grant the winner all titles (including baronies).
Each character has traits.  Your traits affect peoples opinion of you and your diplomacy, martial, stewardship, intriuge and learning level.  Traits will be passed on by the guardian of a child and by events occuring to an adult (16+).  Few traits will be passed on through birth (such as genius) but there is only a small chance.
One of the games biggest features is Casus Beli (CB).  A CB is a justificaiton for war - something you need to attack a ruler of your own faith. CBs can range from De Jure claims to Overthrow ruler.  A claim is just that - you or one of your courtiers is related to the ruler of the title you want.  Whether that relation is a blood relation, or through marriage it doesn't matter.  The independence or overthrow ruler CBs are against you liege, and are self explanetory.  Holy wars can be declared on heretics/infidels.  Another type of claim is the de jure claim.
De jure is where is the title is traditionally in that duchy/kingdom/empire.  For example, the duchy of cornwall is de jure Wales, but is owned by England.  It takes 100 years for de jure to change, and it will only change if you have the whole duchy.

I totally want to slap the developers. They made a fantastic game, which is nearly perfect, but only nearly. The closer something is to perfection the more frustrating are the tiny flaws.
The idea is so brilliant: An adventure-RPG card game with real time fighting, where you and your "opponent" influence the card decks and you continuously expand your available cards by playing (i.e. questing).
The atmosphere is great, the comments of the dealer work as a key element like in Bastion. He tells you a lot of things, sometimes kind sometimes aggressive, sometimes purely informative.
The artdesign is beautiful.
The gameplay is a bit repetitive but the replayability is huge. With every run you can unlock more encounters and equipment.
However there are two flaws, that bothered me somehow, because they probably could have been solved by not very much work:
- The real-time fights are a key element of the game, but they become tedious pretty quickly, because your move set is VERY limited. Slash or Bash, Dodge, Counter, sometimes special effects of weapons (which I never use, because the counterattacks are too powerful). That's it. You cannot combo, there is nothing to master. All weapons work the same way. The fighting works and looks great the way it is, but it is just not diverse enough to keep me motivated (maybe because I love games like God of War, Devil May Cry or Bayonetta).
- You do not have any possibility of customization, although it is an RPG. You can't even choose your gender. Your character looks like a bearded barbarian or sailor and you have to stay that way. This is very likely one of the points the developers simply overlook when creating such a game. Everyone is polishing the important aspects of the game so that these unimportant, immersive ones are forgotten.
In the end there is this feeling that I play such a gem of a game but also this frustration, that it could have been perfect if only...
P.S.: I got this game in the recent Humble Bundle. I am unsure about 20€ for it, as the story mode is pretty short. I guess it would also make an excellent 1v1-Boardgame. :D
Edit: Just saw there is already a boardgame adaptation, Hand of Fate:Ordeals.

When I first saw the game, I felt like they may be using the cuteness factor of cats to sell a subpar puzzle game. I was wrong. The game offers some real challenge, demanding that you build an all purpose solution to several different problems. The Cat Machine requires crafty thinking and some patience in order to solve these complex conundrums. Anyone looking for a great strategy game for the weekend could do much worst than this thoughtful and cute game. I’m proud to say that The Cat Machine is more than welcome to has a cheezburger.
The titular contraption is a sophisticated piece of machinery that uses unimaginable technology, maintaining the stability of the Earth as it rotates the sun. Yes, it turns out it’s all thanks to a series of colorful cats being thrown off of train tracks that keeps our life-giving planet on its orbit. Thanks a lot Newton; it doesn’t have anything to do with gravity at all. It was cats.
The game is relatively easy to understand. You’re given a train of cats, made up of a random selection of three different colors (blue, yellow and red), and ending with a white cat. The cats follow the leader, its color deciding which extensions the train will go down. After they go over one of the bridges that you’ve placed, the lead cat flies away, leaving the next in the train to go down another colored path. The goal is to end the journey with the white cat flying off the solidary white path.
Doesn’t sound too hard, and it feels especially easy in the earlier stages, but this gets dramatically harder as you progress. The game throws more complicated level designs at you, and sometimes you’ll have up to five different trains you’ll need to map out. So, not only will you have to make a route for one train, but you’ll have to build it to accommodate several other different paths as well.
With that being said, you will slam your head into your keyboard several times while playing this game; but it’s okay. You’ll eventually figure it out, and you’ll feel very satisfied as the cats triumphantly circle the screen, meowing out a jaunty little song. Again, it’s cute, and its playful attitude doesn’t intimidate those who may feel like a ‘dum-dum’ when they struggle with problems.
The 50+ levels simply get too repetitive for its own good. Its minimalist approach is fine, but the levels end up feeling two-dimensional, and possibly adding some height or obstacles to the paths might’ve given the experience more diversity. That’s not to say the challenge isn’t there, because it is- I just felt like I was solving a different version of the same puzzle each time. Even the scheme of the levels are mostly the same, with a similar ocean background occupying every platformed level.
Overall, this isn’t a bad game, but it’s lacking that something to make it truly memorable. The puzzles are engaging, so if you’re someone who likes getting your brain twerked for twenty minutes as you try to solve a puzzle, this will satisfy that part of you that likes torturing your noggin. While its ten dollar price point is on the higher end of where a game like this should be, I can honestly say it gave me a few chuckles, and a rewarding experience when I solved something I started to convince myself was impossible. Plus, it has cats; so if that’s a buying factor for you, I’d say pick this game up meow. Sorry, couldn’t resist.

After my initial review was met with downvotes, I went back to the game to see if I had missed something.  Yes I had.  I missed heck of a lot of things that were not sufficiently explained by the interface of the game.  So unless you go into the game understanding its basic premise and mechanics you may have a hard time as I initially did.  Look, I'm the kind of player that doesn't want to know too much going in and I expect the game to communicate critical information to me.  After a bunch of Googling which I never like to do in a game I understood a little more about getting going.  You may need to do this as well.  The rest of the review continues after I muddled through the less-than-helpful interface (mystery meat navigation) and did a bunch of Wiki reading.
The game plays as some kind of board game / card game hybrid.  You have some input on how the "board" is composed based on some card choices you put into your deck (more are randomly added by the "dealer").  Once you play for a while the illusion breaks and you realize that the card game is just an illusion covering up an RNG.  The problem is the illusion doesn't help it just slows the entire game to a crawl.  If, for random example, you find a treasure chest, instead of RNG just telling you if you got lucky, you have to play this pick-a-card game... but since it is all random your choice has no bearing.
In the end most of this game is about pressing (A) over and over while watching stupid cards flip around and reading lame, tacked-on flavor text.  The same goes for navigating around the 'board' which is made up of face-down cards.  There is no reason to even pick a card or for the cards to really exist because it is all just RNG.
Then the variance of the RNG is just out of whack.  It's nothing for the game to deal out an entire game board, then have the exit be the first or second card you pick.  Same thing on the next board, same on the next.  Now you're out of food with no opportunity to get more, and nothing's happened.  Game over you died of hunger.  That is just one example of what seems to happen almost every play, be it with food, gold, or other conditions such as the RNG deciding that after you won an epic fight, all of the loot gets denied to you because RNG LOL
All of this could be overlooked, but the fighting is boring as sin too even on hard difficulty.  Just watch what you're supposed to press then press it to win.  Boooooo-rrrrrrrring.
All in all, this is a cool idea with profoundly bad execution.  The mouthy narrator doesn't really help either... I guess he is supposed to add mysticysim, but I honestly felt like most of his comments were just jerky... one of the things was something like ... "Really?  That's the course of action you chose?  Live with it then..."  Sheesh... relax dude.

Within an hour of playing the game I can mostly speak to the horrid game mechanics which have left me with only regret of spending the $16.99 CAD I did when this game was on sale. The game houses a top down Diablo esc view with a cyberpunk like setting. The visuals and soundtrack leave me stunningly impressed and really set the mood for a game like this. Though looks aren't the entire game as this is an amazing example of. You'll find that most of the time while you play the game that when you die, it'll be out of lack of responsiveness to your input then being bested by the game, which almost seems like a mechanic since there is a system that tracks and rewards you for dying a large amount of times. The skills system allows you to set up a loadout with various equipment and tools to use in each fight but doesn't really allow for any indepth development of a specific playstyle. Your skill points can be placed and refunded so that you can build new kits and try out new things without punishment but unfortunately you are /REQUIRED/ to reorganize to fight each boss or set of enemies. So there is no way to focus purely on a melee build or a run and gun build, there are tools that are absolutely necessary and some which are trivial to even have other then to make the skill page seem more plentiful. Speaking of bosses, they all possess a rinse and repeat styled fight sequence, if I had the time or the interest you could set a macro to run the boss fight for you, and by the time you finish it you'll have lost interest to continue playing besides just wanting to finish that boss and get the next checkpoint.
I'll still try to beat the game but to any people looking to purchase I'd advise against it. The only thing you'll be doing is slamming your head against the wall.

A charming and witty puzzler, one I keep coming back to!
The game has a unique theme compared to others: it turns out our earth is kept in orbit by cats riding trains and it's your job to make sure the tracks are laid out correctly... It appears science has changed a bit since I was at school! Your journey through the levels is accompanied by a science cat who makes humorous comments as you go along.
Beyond the fun and light hearted theme/presentation of the game (the cat pictures are a nice touch), it has a simple set of mechanics and rules but still provides a challenging and positive experience. There are many levels to keep you occupied and the difficulty steps up as you go along, providing a clear introduction to the key concepts as you progress. Extra depths of complexity also exist aside from basic track placement - for example laying out your tracks so the larger cat trains don't crash into themselves or end up in infinite loops. Eureka moments on the harder levels make the game very satisfying to play, however, the first set of levels are very easy - stick with it and the difficulty gets to a good level soon after.
The music, although limited, fits the theme of a logical cat machine very well and doesn't get in the way of your train (heh) of thought - I end up muting some puzzlers but not this one.
If you like Cats, Trains or puzzlers then this game shouldn't disappoint. If you like all 3 then what are you waiting for?!

This game has cartoon, brightly primary colored cats.  They ride around on colored tracks you build.  If you build the tracks right, the cats fly off into space, thus keeping the Earth from going off orbit and killing us all.   All of this is underscored with a zippy, upbeat soundtrack that is oddly infectious on its own.
This might lead a casual observer to conclude that this is simplistic game targeted towards children.    That observer would be wrong.  The puzzles seem like they would be straight forward enough.  You can see the trains of kitties that will have to navigate the machine you must build.  So just build colors of tracks that match the kitties that must ride them.  Simple?  Not so much after the first few puzzles.  I got stumped four or five puzzles in.  Solved a few more puzzles, since the game progression isn't completely linear and that is an option.  My brain grew a bit smarter at this, and I was able to go back and finish the one that stopped me.  As much as I like the soundtrack, I soon disabled it to better focus on the mentally engaging gameplay.
The answers aren't always obvious, at least to someone with my brainpower.  Still, the puzzles do seem doable.  It's refreshing to find a puzzle game mechanic that straddles the line between challenging and thought provoking without crossing over to exasperation.  All with a cheerfully looney premise, adorable oddly colored cats, and a lighthearted cheerful soundtrack that bring capital letter "F" fun.
About the only negative criticism I can really think of right now is that there really is only just the puzzle build aspect of this game.  As far as I can tell no score is kept, solving the puzzles and progressing to the next one is it's own reward.  There are, I dunno, 50-ish levels I believe?  I'm not looking forward to the day I run out of them.  Hopefully in the future there will be some DLC with more puzzles.  Also.  it would be super if there were steam workshop support so that players could create share puzzles with the community.
All in all this is a very nice little title that seems worth the price.   If you like puzzle games I doubt that you'll be disapointed with this one.

For me, the game is a negative.  For you, it may be exactly what you're looking for, so read on.
Screenshots and videos on the Steam store page are slightly misleading as to what type of game this is.  I see the screeshots and "Rogue-lite" description and immediately think it was going to be something with some strong RPG elements combined with some tactical strategy (since there is no forced rush during gameplay).  It's nice to be able to think out your next move without something bearing down on you, but the game is designed in a way that will force you to fail no matter how methodical you think you're being if you don't do things in the correct order.
I'm sure that you can pour hours into the game and "figure it out", but the reality is that the game isn't as engaging as the Steam store page would make you believe.  Re-doing the same level over and over again isn't appealing.  The numerous times that I sat staring at the final "boss" and couldn't do anything because they were higher level than me and was forced to restart (becuase I didn't do things "in the correct order") is what forces a negative review.  I'm always down for a good puzzle, but when it looks like an RPG, I want it to play like an RPG; which means that I should have at least some say in how I go about completing it based on my decisions, not the decisions the developers have already made for me.
The "puzzle" in this game isn't the gameplay, it's the hidden framework of killing things in a certain order and is just masked behind an RPG skin.  You may be looking for this type of game, but I was not.

War For The Overworld is a real time strategy game, very similar to Dungeon Keeper, both from a gameplay and atmosphere point of view.
You view your dungeon from a top down perspective, drag-select tiles to order your imps to dig space for you to construct rooms, which attracts various types of monsters through a portal. Give them food and a place to sleep, train them to improve combat skills, and then send them out to kill the heroes. Some minions can research spells or construct traps. You can hold captured enemies in a prison, torture them to convert them to your cause, or let them die so their corpses can turn into undead minions at a graveyard.
There's a fun, dark sense of humour, especially thanks to the advisor, who is the same voice actor from Dungeon Keeper. As a fan of DK, it really does feel like everything I'd want to see from an unofficial sequel.
I wish I could end the review there with a positive recommendation. Unfortunately, my enjoyment of WFTO has been spoiled by terrible technical performance. I've suffered from two significant problems.
The first is a very frequent "stutter", where everything freezes for about a second. Its not game breaking, but it is very annoying, especially when you're moving the camera around the map.
The second - and far more serious - problem, is a progressively worsening framerate, which seems to be related to how much of the map you can see, and how many creatures and traps are active in the map. At the start of a level, everything is covered by the fog of war, so my framerate is a nice smooth 60. But as I explore, the more of the map I uncover, and the more creatures are recruited by myself and the enemy, the framerate starts to die. It doesn't seem to be related to any graphics option - I've got the same problem with every setting at maximum and every setting at minimum. The engine just can't cope with so many moving objects in such a large space.
There are 13 levels in the campaign, and as you would expect, the later maps are larger and everybody has a bigger army. During the first half of the campaign the framerate hit isn't so bad, dipping to around 40, which is still playable. But from around level 8, it got much worse, at times being almost like a powerpoint slideshow. I'm not exaggerating when I say my framerate was dipping into single figures.
I have a significantly more powerful PC than the recommended specs listed on the store page (Win7 64 bit, Quad core i7 2600k @ 3.4Ghz, 8GB Ram, GTX 770 with 4GB Vram) so I should be able to run this kind of game without a problem. A quick search on the forum and other reviews indicates I'm not alone.
Ultimately, in the current state, I have no choice but to give a negative review. Its a shame, because judging by the gameplay alone, WFTO is a good game. But this level of performance is unacceptable. Wait a few months, see if the developers can improve the performance with some patches. (Note: I started playing the day AFTER patch 1.1.15 was released, so 1.1.15, which supposedly improved performance, is still terrible).

Some of the spells have been made more complex, unclear and weird. For example, the fireball spell now has 3 effects, even though the glyph tooltip only lists 2 of them. The added music is pretty nice.
There are various annoying bugs in the menu. For example, the "cloud save" button is greyed out, with no indication whatsoever on how to fix it, and the "login" button does nothing.

Desktop Dungeons is like Mine Sweeper and a dungeons crawler mixed with a rogue like game. You start by selecting a character. You choose the race and class. Then you start at the first dungeon floor. The whole dungeon is covered in a fog if war. By exploring the tile next to you, you uncover the dungeon gradually. Along the way you will find enemies. They have levels. Killing a higher level enemies is hard, but gives you bonus xp. Killing a lower level enemies is easy but gives you less xp. Every time you explore a new square (that is covered by Fog of War) you get health and manna. All the onscreen enemies recover health.
Between each dungeon is a kingdom that can be upgraded. Upgrading the kingdom unlocks new classes, races and items.
Desktop Dungeons is a highly addictive game that I would recommend to any patient gamer.

TLDR, This game is for people who want a semi-casual startegy game that's similar to Xcom
The graphics is nothing to write home about. It will run on a potato. The anime style is nice but you can tell that it's a port because there is a good amount of alaising in this game. Not a deal breaker though, its not a technical marvel in the first place. The amount of weaboo in this game is  virtually non-existant, which is good for people who are not into anime.

The story in this game is actually quite nice and even more enjoyable if you buy (in game currency, no micro-bull$hit) the interviews for all of the characters. I strongly recommend that you do not skip the cutscenes. The characters imo are memorable and I feel invested in them. This game addresses some real world problems like racism and genocide better than some other games cough* cough* callofdutyww2. The voice acting is decent, not too bad. The plot twist in the story is a little too over dramatic but it's okay.
The gameplay is good. It's very satisfying to plan and capture the enemy base(s). In the actual field, your unit will have AP which is used to move your character (Sort of like chess, each piece can move a different amount of squares). It's an RPG, so you have hitpoints and the like. Cover is very important in this game and emphasized a lot. The units you command have actual names and life outside of combat (Think of it like the intro BF1 war stories). This is a very nice feature because it will make think twice about who you want in the field and it also simulates how it feels to send YOUR men out to fight. If a squad member gets taken out, they go unconscious, you must medivac them by having another squadmate touch them, otherwise he/she dies for good. You have 4 classes scout, shocktrooper, lancer and snipers. All these classes have their strongpoints and weakpoints. Lancers are underpowered, they are only good at taking tanks out unless you get lucky with the lance (BTW the lance is similar to the RPG irl). you can train your classes ( No you dont train squad mates individually, it's by class) by using the XP you earn during battle. There is also R&D you can do in this game, for a small fee you can upgrade your weapons and tanks armor. You have skirmishes which you can repeat however many times you like. Overall in terms of gameplay it's really solid and fun. I have to admit that it consumes a lot of time. Its a short game but I almost have 60 hours on it. Not sure if thats good or bad. Also you get free DLC included.
This game however is not perfect. Although it's suppose to be a strategy game sometimes you can simply rambo through everything if you grind really hard in the skirmishes and level up your classes. When you play a really hard mission and your totally immersed you enemy commander will somtimes order stupid order that might benefit you. For example A general I was facing kept throwing smoke at a base i was occupying (yeah thanks buddy). But at other times the enemy can seem like the terminator. The tank is the most vulnerable from the back, If an enemy lancer or tanks hits you there its a 1 hit kill. So one time I positioned my tank in such a way that it's impossible to destroy me with one hit, the back of my tank was against the wall. But still an enemy lancer took me out and i lost( You play as Welkin, the tank commander).

Edit 27-07-2016
I didn't grow up with Dungeon Keeper, in fact I had never even heard of it until I started watching The Co-Optional Podcast so there's very little in the way of nostalgia for me with this game.
With that said, I absolutely adore War For The Overworld. The writing is funny, the characters are amusing, the visual aesthetic is perfect for what they're trying to achieve and the mechanics are thoroughly engrossing.
It's not without its flaws, and I'm not entirely certain if this is a result of the Unity engine or not, but there are times where the game will stutter or "hiccup" and I can't pin down the reason as to why. My CPU is more than enough to handle this game and doesn't go anywhere near capping even during these odd little hiccups, but that's a minor annoyance rather than a dealbreaker.
The original War for the Overworld campaign gives you several hours to play with and acts as sort of an extended tutorial, which may disappoint some but I'm happy to say that with 1.4 and the first expansion "Heart of Gold" there's more for you to do with fewer restrictions. A couple new mechanics are added in as well, so it's more than just an added campaign.
I highly recommend War for the Overworld on its own merits, but don't expect a traditional RTS as it's more of a god game.

It's okay. It's certainly no Hexcells Infinite, but it's fairly enjoyable with a few caveats here and there. I'm not sure I'd pay full price though.
It's much more of a mathematical crossword puzzle than a pure logic puzzler. There is no failure mode, which seems to encourage trial and error. I also felt like some levels allowed for multiple solutions, but on most stages I did pick up on a stringent path to a unique solution. The progression is decently gentle with a few bumps here and there. The 2-3 really hard levels were very enjoyable and probably account for most of my playtime. Content is a bit on the light side with just about 3 hours of pre-made levels. I can see some replayability in a few years, but for now that's it. There is no way to generate additional levels. Hexcells Plus and especially Hexcells Infinite will get you much more gameplay for a comparable price.
The game gradually introduces a few new mechanics. Some of them put nice twists on the formula (introducing zeros for instance), but none of them really blew me away. The way multiplications worked felt a bit counter-intuitive to me (unlike the tile "+4" the tile "x4" does not represent a 4 by itself, only as part of a multiplication).
The UI and graphical style feel like a step back from Hexcells Infinite. The menu transitions are done with fades, which take way too long. By default there is a strange water ripple effect trailing your mouse which was incredibly nauseating and terribly distracting. Thankfully you can turn it off in the launcher, because that would have killed my desire to play. The brightness slider is nice, but not a replacement for an actual dark theme. I'm also not sure why there were no player assists in the UI like the beams and fields in Hexcells Infinite. I would have loved the ability to decrese the target numbers by the tiles you've already marked instead of running the same counts and calculations for the tenth time on some of the longer levels. There is also no undo and no reset from within the level.
In a vacuum this is a decent game, but nothing to write home about. But coming from the brain behind Hexcells Infinite this is a bit of a let-down for me. Still, for what little gameplay it offered, I mostly enjoyed myself and it gave my brain a good work-out. Pick it up on sale maybe?

A very very interesting game in the series created by Matthew Brown. It breaks a lot of conventions that Matthew Brown has set which I believe is part of the reason for the divide this game seems to add. In most Hexcells games, you must think before you act, as an error is marked on your attempt and you only get one free pass, usually taken from an unfortunate misclick. In Crosscells, you can click and unclick as much as you want. While that would create ease, and it does in the earlier levels, the challenge of the individual puzzles becomes much less a seek-and-find for the next move and more of a mind-bending math problems. Hexcells and the series before had sudoku-like logic and math problems, but Crosscells includes actual math.
Hexcells Infinite and Hexcells (vanilla) are still my favourite Matthew Brown games but I was surprised how much he was still able to craft puzzles so well after breaking a lot of his own rules. Definite recommend!
