After my initial review was met with downvotes, I went back to the game to see if I had missed something.  Yes I had.  I missed heck of a lot of things that were not sufficiently explained by the interface of the game.  So unless you go into the game understanding its basic premise and mechanics you may have a hard time as I initially did.  Look, I'm the kind of player that doesn't want to know too much going in and I expect the game to communicate critical information to me.  After a bunch of Googling which I never like to do in a game I understood a little more about getting going.  You may need to do this as well.  The rest of the review continues after I muddled through the less-than-helpful interface (mystery meat navigation) and did a bunch of Wiki reading.
The game plays as some kind of board game / card game hybrid.  You have some input on how the "board" is composed based on some card choices you put into your deck (more are randomly added by the "dealer").  Once you play for a while the illusion breaks and you realize that the card game is just an illusion covering up an RNG.  The problem is the illusion doesn't help it just slows the entire game to a crawl.  If, for random example, you find a treasure chest, instead of RNG just telling you if you got lucky, you have to play this pick-a-card game... but since it is all random your choice has no bearing.
In the end most of this game is about pressing (A) over and over while watching stupid cards flip around and reading lame, tacked-on flavor text.  The same goes for navigating around the 'board' which is made up of face-down cards.  There is no reason to even pick a card or for the cards to really exist because it is all just RNG.
Then the variance of the RNG is just out of whack.  It's nothing for the game to deal out an entire game board, then have the exit be the first or second card you pick.  Same thing on the next board, same on the next.  Now you're out of food with no opportunity to get more, and nothing's happened.  Game over you died of hunger.  That is just one example of what seems to happen almost every play, be it with food, gold, or other conditions such as the RNG deciding that after you won an epic fight, all of the loot gets denied to you because RNG LOL
All of this could be overlooked, but the fighting is boring as sin too even on hard difficulty.  Just watch what you're supposed to press then press it to win.  Boooooo-rrrrrrrring.
All in all, this is a cool idea with profoundly bad execution.  The mouthy narrator doesn't really help either... I guess he is supposed to add mysticysim, but I honestly felt like most of his comments were just jerky... one of the things was something like ... "Really?  That's the course of action you chose?  Live with it then..."  Sheesh... relax dude.

RUINER is this really pretty neon pit that a good game almost crawled out of. The whole thing looks like you're playing through concept art. The setting and ~worldbuilding~ are evocative, but you could say the same thing about every other cyberpunk game on Steam.
Where RUINER loses me is the feedback. Enemies and bosses feel like sacks of hit points with no stun frames. The game wants you to get up close and do cool melee moves but punishes you for trying it. The sound is muted and mumbly -- compare it with Nuclear Throne, a game with sound design that lets you absolutely know when you've connected with an enemy.
RUINER commits to a visual aesthetic over relaying useful information to you. Are those red lights setting dressing? Are they objects to interact with? Or are they split-second markers before an enemy deep strikes from above the map, insta-gibbing you? Can you tell these elements apart in a room with several quick-death threats, sometimes with objects in the foreground obscuring the action below?
I'm going to be That Guy who compares anything slightly frustrating to Dark Souls, but I feel like Dark Souls can get away with monsters offering subtle tells because they're so big on the screen. In RUINER, the camera is too high to give you anything to study. I couldn't tell you what the last two or three bosses look like. At that height, they're all faceless dolls with slightly different kinds of weapons.
This game wasn't for me. If you love neon-soaked dystopias so much you'll chew through janky controls and feedback (basically, if you loved Brigador), then you'll get a lot out of this game. As for me, I feel like I was sold a bill of goods.

Just like Divinity Original Sin before it, this game fumbles the very early hours by not informing a new player why they died. The combination of choosing your class, skills, and playstyle means this is a game you will come back to for multiple playthroughs. Each one better than the last because you understand that you really shouldn't try to fight those magical teleporting crocodiles the second you step out of town. What happens if I would've killed this guy I saved last time? More xp and better items? It's ok to be a jerk!
You can play this game with whatever moral code you like. Those crocodiles don't live by a moral code though, you've been warned.

This game really has potential. It's a really cool blend of roguelike, card-and-deck-building game, and a light action rpg. In theory. The setting is awesome and the atmosphere is great. I absolutely love the way narration is handled.
The problem lies with luck-of-the-draw aspect, the linear paths, and the action sections themselves. The game is really unforgiving later on, and it's almost all because of luck-based gameplay. Your skills, even with building interesting decks beforehand, doesn't matter much. Unless you grind cards. Maybe. At best. Sure, card games in general have luck involved to some extent, but here it feels really punishing. You'll have instances where you get 4 curses in a row only because you might get the same damn Hanged Man 4 times in a row. No fight to save yourself. No second path to choose from. Just "Here. Bam! Cursed". Even if you know the path forward is rigged, you can't avoid it. At all. Sure, you'll get blessings too, but most of them feel pretty underwhelming and don't negate the curses much. Especially in stages where, for example, being cursed on its own gets you punished even more with reduced max health the more curses you have.
The action sections are fought Batman: Arkham Asylum-style, but in really small arenas with not much variation. It's not bad. It's fine. But almost all enemies are tackled in the same way. Dodge, attack openings and counter-attack. Or, at least, that's the easy way to win. Almost too easy. You aren't encouraged to use combos or slow attacks on enemies since they either aren't staggered when hit, or the rest of the group swarm up from behind in seconds on account of the arena being tiny. You end up dodging around like a madman, which works like a charm, but it's not that satisfying. There are spells and equipment to use if you are lucky enough to come across them on the path, but spells and items aren't necessary nor are they especially inviting to use. And equipment feels underwhelming. Sure, a good mace or an awesome sword will make short work of enemies, but once again - it's all luck-based whether you get anything at all.
Also, the hunger mechanic mostly hinders the tiny (read tiny) bit of exploration the game allows. You consume food for each step you take which makes beelining for the exit the only viable option if you don't come across food for a while.
Yeah, it's a roguelike and all, it's supposed to be played over and over again. But the game's blend isn't a perfect match in this case. And the shortcomings are annoying.
Maybe I suck. Hell knows I don't play that many roguelikes in general. But the above reasons are why I cannot really recommend it - even though it has some really good things going for it.
Here's hoping to the sequel being more balanced and gives the player some use for their skills.

While I truly appreciate the labour of love the developers came up with in terms of graphics, music score and atmosphere, the gameplay is surprisingly lucklustre. If I had to choose two words to define this game I'd go with beautiful and boring. A small heads up: although this may look like a plaftormer it is in fact a shooter/platformer hybrid.
I won't delve into the story and just concentrate of what made playing this game an incredibly frustrating experience: from the random backtracking, the boring stealth sections, the shooting mechanics (due to the "weapons" fire rate and unexplicably uneasy aiming), the fact that when you're traversing a challenging section it's easier to go forward for a couple of screens and die rather than try to preserve you energies, because if you went just forward enough (usually just a couple of screens) you'll be revived and fully recharged? Considering that some enemies are just annoying and that Otus can't take much pain before dying this makes the game much *less* challenging for all the wrong reasons.
Most of the puzzles are either too easy or require a walkthrough... beacuse you just get stuck, like in the goold old days. No way to tell that you need to *shoot a candle with a barrel gun* to open a gate that gives you access to a dungeon. You either get it or you're don't, no hints. Did I mention the fact that sometimes you'll just get slapped right to left to right because you're stuck in a small room with several enemies and your character has a falling animation that you can't control when you get hit midair? And each time you get hit you have to re-summon your weapon, which makes for a frustrating experience whenever you're getting hit a few times in a row. I got gangraped by chimps and it was NOT fun.
There are times I'm so bored with this game that I can't concentrate hard enough to beat a boss or an environmental hazard and I get killed again and again. And I love punishing, rinse and repeat, hard as hell retro games. This game just doesn't cut it because... It's simply not fun.
All in all the artwork is beauftiful just as the setting and I'm still trying to finish it just to witness all that pixel goodness, but boy it feels like an irritating chore.
Edit: I'm playing through the final section, which, all of sudden, requires precise platforming with floaty controls. It has the platforming-by-muscle-memory trope found for eg. in Megaman 2's Heatman stage. Except that the section is sloooow and requires a level of precision which is extremely unconfortable with said controls. I'm hating this game more and more and I want it to finish ASAP.

Surprisingly addictive dungeon-crawler, high strategy and low luck -- you only die when you've made a blunder, or backed yourself into a corner by poor planning.
(EDIT: If you're stuck and feel like giving up, google for "DDWiki" from QCF Designs which has info and guides to everything in the game. I avoided it until I was 100+ hours into the game since I wanted the fun of alot of trial and error.)
This may seem like a simple hack-and-slash, but it's not. There's almost no luck and a surprising amount of planning involved. Each dungeon is like a puzzle, and might take 15-45 minutes to complete. You start each dungeon as a lowly level 1 character. Kill the monsters in a certian order and gain the power-ups at the right times and you will be able to defeat the boss-monster and thus "win" each dungeon.  if you randomly charge in like a hack-and-slash game, you won't maximize your powerups and you won't have enough health to tackle the tougher monsters. Same if you spend the power-ups too soon. If you don't defeat the tougher monsters, you don't gain the experience-point bonuses to increase your abilities enough to tackle the boss-monster. As you complete dungeons, you can unlock other character classes (again, you start each dungeon back as level 1). Since there's very little luck involved in combat, most of the time you will know the results of a combat before it happens, and can choose to either delay it until you are more powerful or press on. The game UI shows you how much damage you and your opponent will suffer each round of cobmat, and thus allow you to predict the result of each combat. Choosing to use magic glyphs and potions can also modify how a combat turns out. Therefore you only die when you've made a blunder, or backed yourself into a corner by poor planning.
EDIT: about the only negatives are that the class challenges are somewhat hard and might put off beginners. Also some of the Explorers Giuld puzzles are more like chess puzzles, in that one wrong move and you can't beat it. Again, give the DDwiki a look before giving up.

I am so torn with this title, but when it comes down to it, I recommend RUINER.
Gameplay:
The bread and butter of the game. The most enjoyable part by far, and what made playing it through a complete blast. I have heard comments of the difficulty being too high, but I played after the changes to Mother. And I can say that even on the hardest difficulty it is an enjoyable, fair experience. I have died on a few parts, but it is quick to jump back in.
For those who need frames of reference for the gameplay, think titles like Hotline Miami, Hyper Light Drifter, Binding of Issac, Enter the Gungeon, hell, even titles like Dead Ops Arcade have the same feels to it. Of course there are distinct differences that pull it apart from every one of these titles, it feels like it's found it's place and knows it.
Soundtrack:
Another smack out of the park. Very gutteral, harsh, and broken down mechanical. The soundtrack is up on spotify, and features tracks from artists like  Sidewalks and Skeletons and Zamilska. It is heart pumping but emotionless. Its the type of tracks that give you tunnel vision as you bloody the streets of Rengkok. It is a sweet addition and makes the gameplay even more intense.
Story:
This is what kills me. I
to believe this has an amazing story, but it really hurts. REALLY hurts. There's so much ambiguity even with a dedicated lore tab. A lot of this ambiguity isnt even plot related, but just aims for a "Mysterious" world vibe, but ends up just pulling me away from Rengkok. I dont feel any connection, hell I only wander the streets as random quotes are thrown at me from NPCs as I try to get to my next objective. As "Puppy", I don't even know his drives, and the only time you get any sense of who he is at the end, and even then it's such a cliche. The biggest twists made me feel nothing except to just go "huh. I guess x is actually y. okay.". For such an awesome title to play through, and such a short game at that, the story isnt bad enough that it hurts the gameplay, but it's the worst part in that there is so much that COULD be there, but isnt. It's a Destiny situation here, but without any lorebuilding at least Destiny had.
Difficulty:
Found no problems here, in certain sections it's a little tedious but you will progress at a steady rate, just be ready to die a lot :-)
Visuals (Non-technical):
Ranges from dropdead gorgeous, to meh. I love the character designs. Puppy is probably my favorite looking protagonist in the past 3 years.  Your "Hacker Friend" is such a unique looking ally that I cant help but adore the dynamic duo Reikon Games has delivered. Some levels (Mainly Heaven, and the level before it) are expansive and tuned with the soundtrack are exactly what the game is going for and slam dunks it. However, the other levels are just "Oh, asphault, oh lava, oh metal walkways" and feel mediocre at best.
OVERALL TL;DR:
I recommend this game on what it does best: Kickass combat, kickass tunes, and kickass characters. However, if you're looking for a great story (or anything close), you best look elsewhere.

Although the game was an unplayable mess at its original release, War for the Overworld has become an impressive and fun successor to the Dungeon Keeper series after Patch 1.1.  It truly felt like I was playing the next logical step, or Dungeon Keeper 3, if you will.
For those uneducated and/or unexperienced in the Dungeon Keeper series, War for the Overworld is a strategy game where you play as the Underlord, the master of a dungeon that you build from the ground up.  You dig out the earth surrounding your dungeon core and designate what the tiles that you have dug out are to be repurposed for.  Barracks, lairs, torture chambers, prison, sanctuaries, traps, and many, many other rooms are available, all of which have their own unique abilities that they add to your dungeon and most of which that bring in new creatures to serve you in crushing the competing underlords and those pesky human armies that seek to reclaim their land from you.
All in all a great game and one that I highly recommend those fans who have been waiting years for a legitimate sequel to the Dungeon Keeper series.

Alright! Let's dive in.
First and foremost, it can get slightly laggy at times, even under a decent setup. Low settings will work on most older computers, but others it may freeze on. Keep that in mind before investing money in. In fact, give it about a month of play and then if you like what you're dealing with, then I wholeheartedly suggest setting up as a Patron.
If you like World of Warcraft, you'll like this game. Heck, if you don't like WoW, you'll like this game.
Beyond level 30 can get a bit grind heavy, but there are places you can get experience, public farms, and even mining...and these vocations give your character experience to level up and skill up as well. (You could, technically be a total pacifist aside from any story required quests, raids, etc.)
Everyone gets: A battle pet, a mount pet, and a glider. All in all these kind of vary, but sometimes through events you might get interesting additional pets. (Like the Ember Nymph I got for leveling to 30, which was an event.)
A HUGE thing for me is how the cash element/F2P model is handled. Most stuff is purely cosmetic. While you can access the auction house..you can't really sell anything on there without either a license from the shop, or Patron. There are some expansion scrolls for your bags and storage, but they aren't necessary to fully enjoy the game, and in addition you can get those via the auction house. IN ADDITION, its true..you can't get land without APEX, Patron, etc. HOWEVER, if you know someone in a family...join the family, have them set the land to your use and one person pays..everyone wins. Then later you can contribute tax certificates or help with quests. Win win for everyone. Its all about how you use your resources...and that includes people.
So, one other big plus? The Class system. Any other MMO i've seen when it comes to multiclassing kinda tends to force you in weird directions. When you want to change, you wind up having to pay real world money. NOT HERE. In game money..and something like x amount of silver or copper. This is both for switching out one of your three classes, or reverting a class you've already chosen. I really like this, because you can play around and you only have to worry about the armor statistics that will aid the class of choice. This gives a level of flexibility that is a rare find..they definitely did that one right. There have been a few nerfs so always keep an eye on that.
Servers themselves..not gonna lie, the alt game is strong. Morpheus could use some serious love on the Haranya side, but it is quite possible to get a nation going with the right people. There are some, especially in the Nuian faction that enjoy hiding in towns and then ambusing others in larger numbers...there are of course ways to get around that, which I won't broadcast here. All in all, though, it hasn't been too terribly bad even in those respects.
And regarding labor, it regularly seems to regenerate...more if you are a Patron and offline is included in Patron regeneration. There are some decent areas that you really can spend labor on for xp and goods, and the dailies net you Gilda stars that can earn cool blueprints you can either sell later..or plunk down to have a Mansion or a freakin War Galleon that is a thing of beauty.
So all of that said, while my first impressions of Archeage were clunky, clustered, and plain horrible, they really put their nose to the grindstone and fixed A TON OF THINGS. They have greatly improved themselves since opening day, enough that I went from a skeptical free player and said "heck yeah, i'll support this as a Patron." I'm a picky gamer, mind you, so that is as big of a deal as it sounds.
Hope to see you on Morpheus, hope you enjoy the game, and feel free to give me a shoutout if you're looking for a Haranya family!

**This review is based on the base game**
A great grand strategy game from Paradox.  The first in their 4 strategy series, this game is set in the medieval period, streching from Ireland to India and Iceland to Mali.  The base game ranges from 1066 (norman invasion) - 1453 (fall of constantinople).  In CKII you try to continue dynasty - trying to make it the most prestigous in Europe!  The game is centered around your dynasty and succession.  If your heir is not of your dynasty, it's game over.
You start as a count/earl, duke, king or emporer controlling one of the counties, duchies, kingdoms or empires on the map.  Without any DLCs, you can only be a christian ruler and not a merchant rebublic.  You cannot be a theology (pope/bishop).  The game also features baronies, cities and bishoprics but that cannot be your primary title.  As a ruler you manage vassals (rulers below you) and try to please - or overthrow - your leige (ruler above you).  The feudal ranking is as below (above = liege; below = vassal):
- Emporer
- King
- Duke
- Baron/Bishop/Mayor
You can be a liege to someone below you, but not equal or above you.  Your vassals are only below you - not equal to you.
A Catholic (usually) follows the pope, and the pope can orders crusades.  The crusades can be based on real historical crusades (such as many of the ones for Jerusalem) and crusades to rid infidels/heritics.  Any catholic ruler can join a crusade, and the winner of the crusade is defined by how much they contributed to the crusade.  Winning the crusade will sometimes grant the winner all titles (including baronies).
Each character has traits.  Your traits affect peoples opinion of you and your diplomacy, martial, stewardship, intriuge and learning level.  Traits will be passed on by the guardian of a child and by events occuring to an adult (16+).  Few traits will be passed on through birth (such as genius) but there is only a small chance.
One of the games biggest features is Casus Beli (CB).  A CB is a justificaiton for war - something you need to attack a ruler of your own faith. CBs can range from De Jure claims to Overthrow ruler.  A claim is just that - you or one of your courtiers is related to the ruler of the title you want.  Whether that relation is a blood relation, or through marriage it doesn't matter.  The independence or overthrow ruler CBs are against you liege, and are self explanetory.  Holy wars can be declared on heretics/infidels.  Another type of claim is the de jure claim.
De jure is where is the title is traditionally in that duchy/kingdom/empire.  For example, the duchy of cornwall is de jure Wales, but is owned by England.  It takes 100 years for de jure to change, and it will only change if you have the whole duchy.
CKII is an excellent strategy game - if you have the patience.  It can be quite frustrating at times, and will boggle your mind with all the confusing succession laws.  This game is a great mix of plotting, pleasing and prisoning, not to mention declaring all of that war.  With over $100 worth of DLC, there is a huge base for expansion and the game also has a big modding community.

Hey. I rated this game down before, and I'm willing to change my opinion about it now that I know what I know now.
This game grows on you. Learning to play it takes patience, and mastering it will take more than enough time. I've logged about a hundred hours by the time I wrote this review and I feel as though I'm far from mastering the game.
I started playing with no DLCs at all; for the price they give you on the base game, it's worth it I tell ya. The DLCs add extra layers of dynamics in the game, with each capable of adding hundreds of hours of gameplay---no two games are the same with Crusader Kings. WARNING though, there are a couple of DLCs required to play the bigger factions in the game, but you'll not fall short of game simply by playing all Christian factions.
At first it will come off as an everyday spreadsheet game, Paradox is well-known in the industry for that reason, and this game's a cracker like any other game they have. This leaves room for the imagination to play. One playthrough you can unite all Ireland, take on England, and establish the Empire of Britannia. In another playthrough you can start off as the King of Abyssinia and declare all religious sites for all religions under the Miaphysite religion. The point being, you can take history to where it was afeared to go.
My two cents: Get the base game full price, get the DLCs on sale and let it take your life over.

This game is quite possibly the easiest and most addicting of the Paradox grand strategy titles to get into.
- The base audio that comes with this game really captures the mood of the time, with additional themed soundtracks you can purchase for a small sum. Even the effects really add to the game with relevant sounds notifying you of births, tithes collected, war declarations, etc.
- You put yourself into the role of a ruler ranging from the 8th - 15th century AD with a map ranging from the Indian subcontinent to Iceland, Ghana to the Steppes of Asia. Though this range is smaller than with other Paradox titles, with unique mechanics like the tribal system, the Indian caste system, and such there is a great feeling of variation depending on where you start in the map.
- With thousands of characters to choose from (or you can choose to make your own), tens of religions, cultures, and various ruling styles the replayability in this game is endless.
- The list of DLC that comes with this game is daunting, however most of it is cosmetic. The refreshing thing with Crusader Kings 2 is that with each large patch (such as the one which introduced India) all players will benefit from free content regardless of whether they want to dole out more dosh for DLC.
It's a fun game, especially if you enjoy a bit of roleplay. Go buy it and ♥♥♥♥ around as a duke, well worth the cost.

Just mentioning Zelda, Hyper Light Drifter or Ori and the Blind Forest as comparable games brings me to the downsides of Owlboy: The lack of difficulty on its own would be acceptable, however it also ties in closely with a real sense of progression which comes with the other aforementioned games. Owlboy's levels are overall designed nicely, diverse and all with some unique mechanics, but they also feel highly constructed and "game-y" without a believable architecture or any other surprising elements to back them up. As your initial skills do not really progress much at all, the levels do not increase much in difficulty either.
Secrets may be found, but not with keen eyes or a sense of clear telegraphing, but instead with a lot of trial and error in the form of flying against walls to see if they are permeable. Coins may be collected to increase your HP, but beyond that, finding them for completionist's sake is not really tempting, as the low difficulty makes you breeze through the game anyway. On a very positive note there are some major well-designed secrets which even spread a sense of mystery, in rare cases even leading to further story elements. However those absolutely remain in the minority, and most of the time I stumbled across them by pure accident or trial-and error which is a clear indicator that collectables were not a priority. If you are expecting a "Metroid" in terms of upgrades you will be clearly disappointed.
Many of the points above make it sound like Owlboy is in fact not such a good game after all - but saying that would be wrong. Yes, there are flaws, and some of them are quite apparent. However there are also many many great qualities to this game which you can spot immediately. The presentation and the narrative is really solid, characters are likeable and the game does not have many lengths - it's actually a rather short, concise experience. The musical score is something among the best in the gaming genre and worth a buy on its own. If you can ignore the kinda stale fighting system, lack of progression and low difficulty you can simply experience this game as a highly linear and not too hard adventure catered to beginners of the platformer genre. If you rather see it like an interactive narrative instead of an action-adventure you will enjoy Owlboy a lot. It's not the masterpiece that 9 years of development could make one expect, but it also is far from being a bad game.

*** NOMINATED FOR A STEAM AWARD 24TH November 2016 ***
I purchased War for the Overworld Underlord Edition + Early Adopter Bonus (Early Access) on 22/08/2014.
I put off playing until this month as I wanted to support the development and wait for a more "polished" game.
Following is my review of my experience playing from start to finish (Avoiding spoilers and game play guides).
I have been building, customizing and using personal computers and consoles since the late 80s.
My system is:
AMD FX 9370 Eight-Core Processor @4.7GHz
32GB PC2200 RAM
Samsung 850 EVO 250GB SSD
Western Digital Black 2TB
PowerColor R9 290 4GB GFX Card
Running x64 Windows 8.1 Enterprise
Starting the game I found loading times to be a bit long.
Once starting to play the experience was good.
Each level progression was as to be expected and offered a more robust enemy, however, each level up to and including level 11 took no more than two attempts to finish.
The hardest level from my experience was level 12. I took sometime to complete this level with at least five attempts being racked up.
The final level was very easy. In fact too easy. The only reason I took more than three attempts to complete it was due to a bug that stopped me. This bug persisted through game save and load and system restart forcing me to start the level over on two occasions.
The ending was disappointing. Leaving me, and others, to think the end cut scene was glitched. (I no longer believe this is the case).
Bad:
Loading times are long, especially when launching the game I often had "Program not responding" dialogs pop up. After clicking wait for program to respond the game would start.
Lag, Lag and more Lag! The game lags a lot. Especially when big battles are happening.
Still buggy in parts. Even though the game is now considered a "Release" product.
AI can be very stupid. Good for us trying to beat it. No so good for over all game enjoyment.
Sometimes mid battle you are healing or zapping trying to protect your core and.... ARRRRR.... A cut scene as a new minion enters your dungeon with no way to skip the bloody thing.
Good:
As a fan of the Dungeon Keeper games and having spent many, many hours playing them this game does not disappoint and keeps to the spirit of the DK sieris.
Despite all of the "Bad" above the game is still well worth buying as I am sure with refinement via patches this will fix most of the issues.
Bottom line:
I would recommend this game if you are a fan of the DK games or if you are new.
I score this game 7/10. (This is because I am a fan of the DK games and can over look the issues I had).
I hope the issues are patched and if/when they are the game will be much better.

Aside from the cliche anime style story and dialouge, Valkyria Chronicles is a very unique experience that targets two groups of gaming that for a very long time have been kept seperate from each other. (I say cliche in the best possible meaning.) The gameplay is a combonation of the Third Person Shooter and the Tactical RPG genres. This makes for interesting, albeit somewhat irritating. To give an example, my sniper has a very clear shot of a potential target. A target that, if he doesn't die, will end the mission by destroying my main character's vehicle. Being in a TPS mode, I aim up the shot and pull the trigger. I miss by literally pixels. In most traditional strategy games, I would not have been involved with the aiming and would have had a much smaller margin of error with sure shots. This occurance, however is rather rare and non-intrusive.
The artwork of Valkyria Chronicles is a very eye-catching sketchbook and water color anime style that creates the illusion of seeing the events of the game through a history text book. I for one love the style and find myself looking at some of the artwork online if I'm bored. The voice acting is decent in regards to the English audio. (I don't know about the Japanese audio since I don't speak it.) While the acting isn't Grand Theft Auto or AAA quality, it's perfectly fine for a game that also relies on text based narration.
In regards to the presentation, I would have prefered some more full action cutscenes instead of the overwhelming amount of dialouge that is presented much like an old GBA game. This would have made the story feel much more enjoyable, giving me more time to sit back after a mission that I had trouble completing. (I have a bad habit of not resting between missions, especially in a game I really enjoy.) Another feature that could be very useful for the game is an optional autosave feature. There were many missions that I had almost completed, but due to a tactical error or mispress of some keys on my keyboard, the game would crash or I'd fail the mission. Having an autosave feature would have reduced the amount of rage-quits that I had faced from having to load a save losing 2-3 hours of progress, or having to restart a long and difficult mission.
While it seems that I have said mainly things that have stuck out to me as bad, I must take a moment to say that the game itslef is excellent. The gameplay is challenging, but completable. Casual, yet addicting. I have found myself saying that I'm going to stop playing after this mission, later finding myself an hour later doing another mission. I liken this game to Fire Emblem. The strategy involved and the threat of permadeath is deep. The characters are fun and you come to cheer your team on as they take out long range targets or capture a base that's been allowing the use of your opponents of-screen rockets. The story will make you laugh and make you cry. The music is very good and, although you hear it on loop, is non-intrusive.
Overall, I would give this game an 8/10. The game is worth picking up when on sale and playing through a couple of times. It is best enjoyed with a gamepad because of the comfort over using a kbm. I really enjoy this game and recommend it whoheartedly.

This game is great. Some of the finest war gaming on the market today, featuring gameplay based on Strategy-Tactics-Unit Management with a splash of Shooter.
Build squads from a cast of characters, not just faceless NPCs but with human qualities like preferences, feelings, prejudices, and other personality quirks; even allergies have tactical implications. Dig up your people's secret selves through trial by fire, but take care that the flames don't get so hot that they die; we're talkin' quasi-Fire Emblem conditions; you get a couple of turns to drag them back to a medic, but permadeath is a real risk if you let your subordinates bleed out.
Tanks are sturdier (though not invincible or without weak points), but if they're brought to 0 HP, it's generally an immediately catastrophic game over; plus, you'll need them for things other than daring charges. Sometimes they're the only cover your ground-pounders can get!
The combat blends turn-based strategy and real-time third-person shooter. You can issue orders (read: buffs, certain actions) and assume direct control of a unit. One then moves that unit third-person style, enemy units take their potshots, and the unit's action finishes once you've taken your action and positioned it where you like. Try to stick to cover, they'll appreciate it.
Experience what's effectively steampunk World War 2 from the perspective of the idyllic steampunk Netherlands, and drive imperial aggressors out of your homeland. The plot's almost storybook, the noble Gallians dunking on the superior-in-every-strategic-regard...except for the unquantifiable one that winds up mattering, the human will.
Treat yourself to Valkyria Chronicles. You'll be glad you did.

Not quite as good as the HexCells games, but still a good puzzle game.
Compared to HexCells, you don't get punished for making mistakes. You don't get feedback if a move was a mistake either. The only way to know that you made a mistake somewhere is when you run into contradictions that are unsolvable without reverting the last few steps. In that case, you need to revert manually since there is no undo functionality.
While solving puzzles, you won't uncover new hints, all of the hints (or rather conditions that must be met for a solution) are visible from the start. All puzzles can be deduced without guessing, but some of the puzzles require quite a lot of steps to look ahead. There is no timer, so you can take all the time you need, unless the time you need spans over multiple sessions. The state of individual puzzles is not saved, they reset when you back out into the menu. That shouldn't be a problem though since the puzzles are not very big.
A few of the puzzles were tricky in some parts, but overall the game was rather easy. It took me 3.5 hours to complete in a single sitting (while getting distracted by other stuff), but I did enjoy it while it lasted. Definitely worth it since it is rather cheap. If you enjoyed any of the HexCells games, this one is for you as well.

Crosscells is the one game of the *cells family that I'm a little leery of. Whereas the others put their own deductive spin on established games like Minesweeper and Picross, Crosscells is something of a multiple-choice math quiz. Each puzzle consists of a grid of equations with a handful of blanks and an equal amount of numbered tiles to fill them in with. But whereas the other *cells had you gradually using localized clues to give shape to a visual puzzle, Crosscells ends up as more of an all-or-nothing approach, which shifts the balance somewhat in the direction of random (or at least semi-random) guessing. A neat experiment, but not one that I think really works.
Do note that the levels are specifically designed rather than randomly generated. If you're looking at this, it's probably worth picking up the entire Logic Puzzle Pack. Each game has its own charms, and Hexcells Infinite brings an infinite puzzle generator to go with the pre-crafted ones.

TL;DR: A somewhat interesting indie roguelike game with many technical flaws and horrible combat system. Also, RNG will destroy you.
***
This is basically a roguelike game where encounters, enemies and loot are determined by cards you draw from several different decks (events, equipment, rewards, etc.).
Some cards in those decks are predefined, the rest you can change.
By going through adventures you unlock new cards to use in your decks. Of course, you get better equipment as you go, but enemies also become stronger.
However, fights themselves are not decided via card draw or something like that. The game actually lets you crush the enemies from third person perspective with a battle system resembling Batman: Arkham series and Shadow of Mordor/War. You can move around, chain your attacks, block enemy hits and projectiles (by pressing a button at the right time), dodge attacks, and use powers (like freezing enemies or making them drop gold).
Having said that, the combat is extremely clunky. Controls are bad, animations are jaggery, camera is simply horrible (and you can't even control it manually), so half the time you are attacked off screen either by a ranged enemy or by a trap. That doesn't make much of impact in the beginning, but as you progress and encounters become harder, the combat turns into a rage inducing mess. This is definitely one of the worst aspects of the game.
Another really bad thing is RNG. Aside from combat, most of the encounters are decided by a dice roll. I never finished some of the story arcs because chances of a success were 25%, and you can't progress further if you fail. This is basically double RNG: not only you need to draw the specific encounter card from your deck, but also be lucky enough to hit one in four cards (1 Success against 3 Failures).
The other problem is that even after 3 years since launch the game has trouble supporting many gamepads. If that happens, try using the Big Picture mode and setting your gamepad as either "Generic USB gamepad" or "XBOX Controller".
I wonder why the developers themselves don't recommend trying this. Instead they are asking for controller configuration and promise to patch in support for the gamepad sometimes later.

If you've never played Desktop Dungeons, play the Free Alpha. It's very accessible and very fun.
If you like the alpha, you will *probably* love the retail version, but there are so many caveats that I find it very hard to recommend.
1) There are a lot more items in the retail version of desktop dungeons, most of them feel rather balanced and fun to use.
BUT unlocking these are barred behind dungeon completion quests and silver challenges, neither of which usually highlight the best aspects of Desktop Dungeons
2) Some of the dungeons are like mini-adventures or have very unique quirks that make them feel very different from other ones, and very challenging in their own way. The Alpha would have LOVED to have dungeons half as interesting.
BUT the quests you are usually given and guided toward involve going to the most boring dungeons.
Example: Namtar's Lair involves striking down a reanimating necromancer six times while carrying his corpse further and further down the Underworld, while you both become weaker the farther you descend. This dungeon is dope as hell, but there's no quests for it. Den of Danger is the resident baby dungeon and encourages you to replay it at least 11 times successfully (I think, AT LEAST 9).
Verdict: This game is really fun and has a lot of content; however, the way you're encouraged to play to unlock things is not really the best showcase of the game. If you enjoy it and stick with it, there's a ton of fun you can have.

I was looking for a decent RPG when I stumbled upon this after playing strategy for a while. I'll admit I was 50/50 about it. I expected a fairly typical JRPG. I couldn't have been more wrong. The basic premise is a reworking of World War 2 in that 'half fantasy/half reality' style peculiar to JRPG's. Your country has been invaded and the rest, as they say, is up to you.
The first thing that will get your attention is the comic book artstyle that runs throughout. It's not unique but it is pretty special. Possibly as a result of this the cut scenes get to the point. There's no endless philosophical waffle here. The story *is* the characters and they are well drawn in every sense. It has English and Japanese voice acting and the English works just fine.
The second surprise will be the combat. It's a strange combination of real time and turn based that is both pretty original and very satisfying. Essentially your moves are tightly limited but you can take your time and think about them. When you need 'The Shot' and you get it, the game knows all about it. When the game gets it, you do. Simple but effective. In reality if you do get your butt handed to you you can go again easily. It's the sign of a good game that it's just as much fun the second or third time. None of it is super difficult but it definitely requires some thought as you progress.
The two lead characters you'll stick with throughout but there's a lot of additional ones to pick from as you advance the story. Many of them have specific skills or buffs you'll benefit from. Even so you'll more than likely find yourself using a core team, largely because of the role they play in the story. The overall sense is that all the characters are well thought out rather than interchangeable props to get you to the next objective. This is backed up with an extensive bio which you gain access to as you go.
Advancement is handled very much in the same vein as the rest of the game. It's quirky and slightly madcap, with a variety of game and story elements you can pick up as you progress. But even here there are challenges, as you attempt to earn enough to gain special content and fund a propaganda war. You will almost certainly have to make choices at some point and the game will be more or less challenging as a result.
I'm not really sure what you'd call this game overall. It's part RPG, part strategy and part graphic novel. What I do know is that it works, it's humourous and engaging and definitely worth the time to play.

I was very very excited for this game. I preordered the day I became aware of it's existence. I probably sank hundreds of hours into DK 1 and 2 in my adolescence and every couple of years I play through them even with the terrible emulation of Dosbox. So when I fired up WFTO and saw that it had the best of everything I remembered from both DK's I was ecstatic, the voice of the mentor was back, and it seemed to have the same sardonic humor I could barely contain myself.
Then I started playing.
The game itself has the same dynamics of the originals. Carve out some rooms, beat some minions, watch the enemies impale themselves upon your floor spikes. But as you keep playing you realize this is just a shadow of what made the original DK great. There is little to discover (no special rooms to summon elite minions, no fun combinations of defenses, no fun things to do with posession) and you can win nearly every level of the campaign by building 5 or 6 beast pits and dropping a flag on the enemy core. In fact, through have the campaign that is exactly what you HAVE to do since defenses are practically worthless. I only found them useful in 1 campaign level. Usually the enemies will rush you so quickly you have no time to build defenses or train your minions and if you can withstand their attack you can immediately counter to win.
If you do try and build up and turtle the campaign will just punish you with infinite waves of enemies that rush right passed all your minions to start banging on your core or with the flawless AI micromanagement. Where is the valiant freeing of prisoners? Looting the vaults? Why aren't rooms wrecked up and torched so they need to be fixed?
I kept playing despite the campaign really not being my style. I prefer to spend some time crafting a world then crushing my foes but, hey, it's nice to be pushed outside your comfort area now and again. As you keep playing the rough edges of the game will begin to grate through your resilience causing frustration and agony. The UI is sluggish and the buttons small. I have tried to click the little cancel attack flag circle and burrowed through the wall of my base too many times. Paging through the laggy menus to lighting bolt a worker who is stuttering around my base as the AI simultaneously blasts 6 of my workers while dropping 30 minions onto the square they just took in my base is psychological torture.  Or sometimes the game lags so bad you just drop a flag where you need to be and go make lunch, coming back 30 minutes later to see you won while AFK (level 9).
The final nail in the coffin causing me to uninstall my hopes and dreams of a DK successor are the bugs. Workers standing around doing nothing. Defense parts never being delivered. Walls never being repaired. Dropping an attack flag and watching my soldiers walk into a wall while my core gets demolished. Possession freezing my computer. The game is unplayable in Linux and poorly running in Windows. Probably the worst was when I beat the second to last mission (level 12) and the game just never ended. Apparently there is a bug where you can capture an enemy core without destroying it making it impossible to win. For the record this was patch 1.1.7 which was supposed to be playable. As of now I wish I could get a refund, my 13 hours back, and to wash off this disappointment.

Just finished the single player game. Difficult to give a thumbs up here, as much as I want to give one to the spiritual successor of some of my favourite games, which I loved so much that I actually bought WFTO once on Kickstarter and once in Steam.
In terms of mechanics it mostly works all right, except for that weird bug where prisoners keep dying as they are dropped into prison (just save and reload) and that thing where Revelation never ends so you can't use another ritual. Mostly all right. Performance and graphics wise it's decent. Just don't expect nifty extras like the special torture animations for different characters, here they are all the same.
But the single player campaign missions... so simplistic and skeletal compared to Dungeon Keeper 1 and 2 both. Whoever designed the missions have not benchmarked their work against the predecessors and told themselves they must do better; it is more like they have never tried the old ones. It is a real shame to see all the working mechanics but such poor missions. By the time the game ends you probably won't even have tried half the spells/traps/rituals/potions/ on offer and easily never use several room types and minion types, the mission are just that insipid and easy. Everything is "kill everything".
Balance issues abound as well. It is simply too easy to convert enemies quickly, DK 1 and 2 had the same issue but not quite so strongly. This makes supposedy tough missions trivial - defeat the first enemy wave and you immediately have enough minions to steamroll all the objectives. This goes hand in hand with the bizarre abundance of infinite gold resource on so many single player missions - it makes the game trivially easy! I finished it all and never even tried ghouls, or spirits, or vampires.. because you don't need it when you have 50 monsters fighting a handful.
I have not tried the multiplayer. It is difficult to give it a try when the single player was always wonderful in DK1 and DK2 and so different here.
Overall the campaign felt painfully abbreviated vs DK1 or DK2 and the ending was emotionally a big letdown as well. You should NEVER have a situation in a game where the boss died in 10 seconds and his taunts then play one after another for half a minute! Seriously devs..
I guess it's worth buying if it's on 50% sale, or if they have some kind of free expansion with another 15 missions.
REALLY hope this game becomes moddable so people can step in with proper single player mission designs and rebalance things like how easy torture conversion is. Don't need your voiceovers. Just good missions.

This game is basically a turn-based tactical game (like XCOM) set in a fantasy WWII setting with an anime artstyle. Got that? It certainly is a quite unique mix of usually very different things, but I think that this is its big strength.
The gameplay works similar to XCOM, except you can move your units freely instead of on a grid. This gives you more freedom, but also makes it more difficult to plan your moves, since it's hard to tell how far your units can go. Also, tank and anti-tank combat plays a big role in this game. Overall it's fun, however the difficulty between levels varies greatly. At one time the AI can be forgiving, while in other levels it will attack you ruthlessly.
The story and characters are very anime-like. Whether that's a pro or a con is up to you. I enjoyed the story overall, but I think that by any standard it has some weaknesses (why are the characters overall so unfazed by the, you know, war going on around them?) and there is A LOT of dialogue going on. If you're used to jRPGs, this might not be a huge problem for you, but for me it became overwhelming after some time.
Overall, if you're looking for a good tactical game or a good jRPG-style game (this is not really an RPG though), or even both, you should check this one out.

This game is a breath of fresh air. Risks were taken everywhere, with quality as the sole goal, and Valkyria Chronicles hits so many runs on those risks. The only place it falters is its fairly strict adherance to typical anime story beats and character types (skinny World War 2 goku is the protagonist), but this is offset by a few original curveballs they throw in here and there. All told, this is an incredably solid game, and a must have if you even mildly like anime.
Spoilers:
Going in as blind as possible is recomended, but for those curious of what I meant by risks, here is a little explaniation.
The gameplay is fire-emblem crossed with call of duty, so turn-based RPG FPS would be the most accurate description for how it works. It lacks the frantic pace of an FPS, but it gives the player greater agency then just comparing numbers and rolling dice. It also opens up many possiblities and challanges to the player. Characters can only move so far, so each step is a precious resource. Heavy hitting shock troopers are key in eliminating enemy infantry, but they can be easily kited by swift moving scouts or out ranged by well placed snipers. Then there's the tanks.
Another novel idea the designers had was set the whole game within the framing device of a history book. No joke, this video game is an anime chapter book that is surprisingly intutitive to navigate. There's a Table of contents that takes the player between equipment management, codex's, research, mission select, and all the cut scenes. It is really well done. Then there's the tanks.
As I said before, the story is pretty cookie cutter, but it does have it's bright spots. Conflict between character protagonists is quite well done, and covers a variety of themes. Racism amoung them. This is one of the few World War 2 games that actually deals with the holocaust in a comprehensive and emotionally weighted manner from all sides. And that weight is heavy. Then there's the ruddy tanks.
They control like♥♥♥♥♥♥ I can not tell you how many mission restarts I had because of the stupid things. They are a powerful asset, but costly to use. Messing up one turn with a tank is tantamount to seppuku.
Control issues aside, this is a great game. Buy it. Play it. Cry a bit. Laugh a bit. Learn about fictional bugs. Its a good time.

I recommend this game with one significant caveat. Namely, I consider this the weakest game in the series. So if you have not played any of the HexCells or SquareCells, I recommend those above this game by a significant margin. Only if you've played all of the other games would I recommend this to scratch a similar itch if you feel the need, and even then, it comes as (what I perceive) a step down in engagement.
I don't regret playing it, but I had higher hopes. It's hard to say exactly where this really falls down for me, but I think it's that I had a harder time juggling all the interdependent variables in a way that tipped the scales a little more towards work than pleasure compared to the other games in the -Cells series, or my beloved Picross games. It may well be that smarter players than me might find this more rather than less enjoyable than the other -Cells games. I can't discount the possibility that I lack a large enough working memory to make this more enjoyable to play. That said, I feel that there's a fairly narrow segment of players who want to work harder on their puzzles, but are satisfied with doing so for only two hours. For me, CrossCells sits in an awkward middle ground between the chill-out style puzzle games like its precessors and deeper and more complex games such as those by Zachtronics (e.g. SpaceChem, Infinifactory, et. al.). It's fine for what it is, but I'd rather play something that's more towards one extreme or the other.

While this title lacks some the mastery of the Hexcells series, it's still a lot of fun and worthy of further exploration.
Other reviews have discussed the need for trial and error and the lack of an 'error counter' to let you know when you are branching off into a series of decisions based on an error. I disagree with these somewhat, or at least wish to qualify them with my experience:
- Trial and error: at first it seems like most of your decisions *have to* rely on trial and error. After all, he left something out - didn't he? I actually found my initial trial and error approach to be wrong and after enough concentration realized that all the clues for making decisions were actually right there before me. The point is: you don't need to mindlessly click around to finish the puzzle unless you're just impatient or the difficulty level is too high. The information is there if you look.
- Error counter: while an error counter might be useful due to the fact you can just try different solutions without penalty, consider this: these puzzles are on average smaller than the massive Hexcell maps - I think it would take some of the fun out of the solve. Not only that, even in Hexcells you could cheese the counter by just restarting the puzzle. I don't feel like losing it really takes anything away from the game.
Regardless of your position neither of these issues is worth not recommending the game.
CrossCells isn't the revelation that Hexcells was but it's still worth playing and very indicative of Matthew Brown's style, of which I'm a huge fan. I wish we saw more of his work more often.

I really wish Valve would give a "Neutral" option for reviews. My opinion of CrossCells is thoroughly mixed and while at its core it's a great idea, the major grievances I have with it make me hesitant to recommend it.
To start off, I love Matthew Brown's other games, Hexcells and SquareCells. However, CrossCells is fundamentally different from both of those. In Hexcells/SquareCells, if you mark or clear a tile incorrectly, you are penalized with a mistake, and that encourages you to solve the puzzles with zero mistakes, which is completely doable because everything can be figured out via a series of logical steps.
With CrossCells however, there is no mistake counter. If you make a mistake, you won't know until you run into a contradiction later on. This leads into my main problem with this game. In Hexcells/SquareCells, sometimes two options will be possible, and those lead to their own logical branches. However, those branches almost always converge a few steps later, where you see the branch you took either leads to a contradiction or the right path. These branches can be calculated in your head since they are short.
In many CrossCells puzzles, these branches extend the entire length of the puzzle, making calculation beforehand nearly impossible unless you have a natural gift for it. This takes what could have been a fun game of logic and arithmetic and turns it into a trial-and-error slog where you have to follow the branch all the way to its logical conclusion, and if it doesn't work, reset the puzzle. Since there are no penalties for CrossCells, this further adds to the trial-and-error aspect since you can mark/clear tiles all you want without fear of repercussion. It's a step down in design in my opinion because it does not take advantage of the fact that it's a video game. CrossCells could easily be put on paper, whereas Hexcells and SquareCells by their nature could not.
It's a shame because some things in CrossCells I found really clever. Sometimes I had to use a sort of "meta logic" to solve the puzzles. For example, if there are two tiles, and one or both of them can be cleared, but there are absolutely no other informational clues in the whole puzzle related to those two tiles, I had to make the deduction that since the game would not force me to guess in such an obvious manner, both tiles can be cleared.
However, given the heavy trial-and-error aspect of long logical branches combined with the lack of any penalty for mistakes, I simply can't in good faith recommend CrossCells.

This game is a multiplayer arena with a heavy-handed leveling system that gives you access to weapons. The whacky mechanics and sound effects decorate the battlefield as you eviscerate your foes with axes, arrows, knives, and heavy shoes. Not kidding, they're a selectable weapon. But that's all it really is, just a nearly depth-less flash game that seems to have gotten lost on the way to Armor Games and just kind of ended up here instead.
The game really wasn't bad, but there wasn't a whole lot of redeeming qualities. I played it across two days, one with friends and one without. Thankfully it's entertaining enough to allow me to experience thirty minutes of it without bleeding from my eyes. There's only one map, and the only real variable in the game is what weapon you choose to wield. That's the only real dynamic, with about as much depth of a kiddie pool if you want to try and cheese your opponents with these invisible bombs that everyone gets. Those are pretty cool. But, I guess an important thing to mention is that Battlestick
, and I appreciate that. There are some good qualities about the game.
One of the good qualities is that the developers seemed to have taken time and balance all weapons appropriately, but so that each one has their own unique identity. This is great because weapons are either unlockable via the levelling system, or purchasable using the super-currency. The super-currency runs cheap, and there's no insta-kill weapon. The blatantly strong weapons have punishable downsides and the weaker weapons have some good attributes to make it selectable. However, that's really kind of it.
The game however is riddle with downsides; the environmental items on the primary map do no damage to you. I later learned that the Team Deathmatch map does have some damaging environmentals, but if you see a spike barricade and you run full force into it, you expect damage. On the primary map, that's not a thing. Neither is the hole in the ground; you won't fall anywhere. The sound-track is composed of one song per map that only plays for roughly 7 minutes, then stops. In that case you're left with the beautiful sounds of squishy sound effects, inaccurate sounds of weapons hitting surroundings, and everything you never wished the game to be. The movement controls are kind of clunky -- the aiming portion is okay but I always felt like there was some sort of a delay, which isn't that big of a deal but it's just one bruised banana in my bunch. Then there's the fact that you can't join a friends game through the Steam UI. There's just about 0 Steam integration at all except the bare-barebones minimum.
Anywhoo, the game is cheesy fun but unless you have a hard-on for flash games that are something less than exciting than Pizza Day at your local cafeteria, then you might want to avoid it. But heck, it's free, the investment time is lower than WalMart's low-low prices, and it's an extremely lightweight game to download. You could probably play it in your community college dorm-room if you don't get much more than 2 Mbps up/down.

Hey. I rated this game down before, and I'm willing to change my opinion about it now that I know what I know now.
This game grows on you. Learning to play it takes patience, and mastering it will take more than enough time. I've logged about a hundred hours by the time I wrote this review and I feel as though I'm far from mastering the game.
I started playing with no DLCs at all; for the price they give you on the base game, it's worth it I tell ya. The DLCs add extra layers of dynamics in the game, with each capable of adding hundreds of hours of gameplay---no two games are the same with Crusader Kings. WARNING though, there are a couple of DLCs required to play the bigger factions in the game, but you'll not fall short of game simply by playing all Christian factions.
At first it will come off as an everyday spreadsheet game, Paradox is well-known in the industry for that reason, and this game's a cracker like any other game they have. This leaves room for the imagination to play. One playthrough you can unite all Ireland, take on England, and establish the Empire of Britannia. In another playthrough you can start off as the King of Abyssinia and declare all religious sites for all religions under the Miaphysite religion. The point being, you can take history to where it was afeared to go.
My two cents: Get the base game full price, get the DLCs on sale and let it take your life over.

This game is quite possibly the easiest and most addicting of the Paradox grand strategy titles to get into.
- The base audio that comes with this game really captures the mood of the time, with additional themed soundtracks you can purchase for a small sum. Even the effects really add to the game with relevant sounds notifying you of births, tithes collected, war declarations, etc.
- You put yourself into the role of a ruler ranging from the 8th - 15th century AD with a map ranging from the Indian subcontinent to Iceland, Ghana to the Steppes of Asia. Though this range is smaller than with other Paradox titles, with unique mechanics like the tribal system, the Indian caste system, and such there is a great feeling of variation depending on where you start in the map.
- With thousands of characters to choose from (or you can choose to make your own), tens of religions, cultures, and various ruling styles the replayability in this game is endless.
- The list of DLC that comes with this game is daunting, however most of it is cosmetic. The refreshing thing with Crusader Kings 2 is that with each large patch (such as the one which introduced India) all players will benefit from free content regardless of whether they want to dole out more dosh for DLC.
It's a fun game, especially if you enjoy a bit of roleplay. Go buy it and ♥♥♥♥ around as a duke, well worth the cost.

The boss strategies weren't always as obvious as they could have been, which caused some frustration and in my case opted to check online for strategies. I thought the story was actually really cool, but it was weakened by the fact that the cutscenes are delivered with text, and not VO. There is some VO in the game, but it appears to have only been used for flavour, but the actors all sound great, so would have loved to hear them deliver more of the story lines.
+ Unique and distinct cyberpunk theme
+ Rewarding and challenging combat
+ Great music and tone
+ Ability upgrades really felt like they made a difference
- Boss strategies aren't always obvious
- It felt difficult to understand how or where to do the side quests
- No voice overs during cutscenes
Side Note: If you're on a gamepad with the default mapping you have to use the bumpers quite a bit, so I would suggest the 360 controller over the Xbox One controller, which has much less responsive bumpers.

On a technical level this feels like it should be a good game, but the feeling I got from playing it was frustration and annoyance.
Controls are ok outside combat, but getting hit will sometimes make you drop your partner, sometimes fling you into a wall and leave you effectively stunlocked for a couple seconds, and sometimes do neither. Combine that with the odd decision to make the teleport ability not pick up the companion if you're on the ground, and the fact that the ally system is clunky in general, and the effect isn't good. Combat (especially bosses) alternates between "no challenge" and "extreme challenge" with no middle ground, and when it's challenging it feels like it's because you can't control your character.
The story feels like it should be the saving grace, since it's obvious someone put effort in and it actually has a coherent theme. But it lost any goodwill it had somewhere between the third time in the same dungeon that the same villain pulls the "anger a big monster and then run away so you can fight a boss" trick; and the sixth time in a row that you seemingly complete your major objective only for it to accomplish nothing, while the villains proceed as if you weren't there. Not a single thing your character does makes a difference for most of the game, even when it creates plotholes.
On the plus side, the visuals and music are good and the dungeon design is decent as long as you're not talking about combat. But overall, I did not have fun playing this game even though it checks every box for the type of game I should enjoy.

Alright, So I have purchased myself, Conan Exiles (not the barbarian edition though) There are what seems to be DAILY updates to this game at the moment, which is a double edged sword. Servers have to update themselves once the update is out, which can take a few minutes. There is a bit of Latency Issues with the game, but nothing too horrific at the moment. I have a GTX 970 ACX SSC 2.0+ 4Gb DDR5, 16Gb DDR 3 System RAM, and an 15-4440. I  get on about average 42 - 49 FPS. This game can be a bit of a grind if a server has 1* XP 1* Gathering and Base Crafting Speed. I will say that this game, like many, is absolutely 1000 times better with friends. The game seems really balanced in the tiers of weapony, armor, and crafting. If you have a Teir 3 (highest tier) Base, they will need Explosives to raid your base. Also beware the many dangers in the game. EVERYTHING IS TRYING TO KILL YOU. It's why I like to refer to the game as "Australia Simulator.  There is Full Blown Nudity, Parital, and no nudity as settings options for you, you create a character when you start the game, and there is a bit of a learning curve. This game is rather enjoyable, and if you have friends that play on it, it's a great way to spend some down time. It's probably one of the best early access games that I have played. (The worst probably being Savage Lands due to its inital lack of content and clunkiness at launch, and the fact that it's still clunky a year or so later. However these are two very differently sized dev teams.) So should you buy this game? I'm 50/50 on it. I wouldn't, in all honesty, if you don't have friends to play with. Due to the fact that it can get boring going out to mine iron or stone, end on end, by yourself. If you do have some friends who have it and like it, then yeah I would totally get this game if you have the budget for this game. It's not an absolute MUST HAVE of the  year though. If Crafting-Survival games is not your forté, then I would steer clear of this. IT IS ANOTHER CRAFTING SURVIVAL GAME!

I played Valkyria Chronicles quite a while ago, but it seems I never posted a recommendation.
Overall: I went into Valkyria Chronicles expecting nothing and came out with an experience that I will never forget. I highly recommend this game.
Valkyria Chronicles takes place in a setting that closely resembles WWII. This, along with the anime visuals and themes which I am well familiar  with, is what drew me in to give it a try.
The gameplay closely resembles games like XCOM so basically turn-based combat where you control a squad of soldiers each with different classes and combat roles. Applying these different roles to a specific situation is what will lead to eventual victory. You can apply various loadouts to your soldiers and this can be done class wide or per soldier so for example you can equip weapons with a certain effect to only a subset of soldiers of that class or to all of them. Additionally each class levels together.
The combat is engaging and relies on you reading a particular situation and deploying your soldiers appropriatly. The game requires you to apply the game's rules to particular problem like for example in one mission you had to stop a car in the streets of a city using your squad.
I particularly liked being able to use my tanks as a bulletshields against small arms fire.
To avoid spoilers I'll just say that I enjoyed the story and you might too.
Visuals were good, I particularly liked the pencil drawn painting aesthetic. The graphics is dated but I don't really care about graphics all that much. :)
The soundtrack was also good and I still listen to it almost a year after finishing the game.

is a name I haven't heard since the PSP era. An tactical RPG where you position units, plan your moves to capture the enemy camps, and neutralize their forces. The game is great but like many JRPGs, it's not without its flaws. It's
flaws.
The story of Valkyria Chronicles is a pretty simply one. Gallia is a small sovereign nation between two bordering larger nations: The Empire, and the federation. Both sides are at war with each other over a precious resouce known as Ragnite with Gallia caught in the middle. Our protagonist, Welkin Gunther is the son of an accomplished soldier from a border village in Gallia named Bruhl. When he returns home from school (that out-of-town tuition though), he's greeted by his adoptive Darscen sister, Isara but then the
Empire invades Bruhl. Welkin takes up arms to defend his home from the war, hoping to end the conflict and save Gallia. There's also a sort of side plot to the game's lore. Darcsens (people born with dark hair regardless of skin complexion; doesn't explain why that particular factor makes them an entire ethincity or anything. They just are...) are seen as the cause of a great calamity that wiped out the Valkyrur -an ancient advanced race- long along. The war furthers this stigma against them.
The main cast consists of Welkin, Isara, Alicia (an orphan girl from Bruhl who also joins Squad 7), Rosie (the bigot of the group), Largo ( not as much a bigot as Rosie), Faldio (Welkin's best friend), and Lt. Valot (Squad 7's supervisor). The rest of Squad 7 is a cast of assorted characters. Some like Vyse and Aika from another SEGA title
make an cameo as recruitable members. Others are unique to this game and
are there some "interesting" characters
.
The overall plot itself is a mixup of good and extreme. It's an anime through and through (It even has it's own anime). Some events play out almost
as you would think they would.
Overall, the story can be entertaining but take it with a grain of salt here and there. It's a fiction first and reasonable second.
The design of the game tries to mimic a storybook style with effects that add to its illustrative quality. It's like the viewer is reading a memoir of a soldier or the history of a nation. The cell shading gives everything a great range of saturated color, which as an illustrator myself, is always welcome. There's also a fair amount of detail in the unit and tank models. That being said, there is a very anime-styled choice when it comes to the people of this game. Everyone on your squad is cute by which I mean all the women are wearing uniforms with their breast bulging like they're wearing tights. The men are all either moderately handsome or Largo(Gruff n' buff Old); or Cody (Actually Old). No one wears helmets to hide their incredibly stylized hair that makes them questionably more noticble in a game with snipers and tanks, if you as me. The enemy are all john does w/ full helmets. Their only variety comes form Lancers (different helmets) and anyone important to the plot.Not as much an Eastern standard as it is a universal one though. Aside from a few particular battles, most of the game is generic forest, desert, and suburban battle-torn city. An overall colorful and stylized game but it does leave a bit to be desired from its deisgn.
This game is a lot of fun. You have 5 classes aside from your 2 Tanks:
-Shocktrooper (High DPS)
-Scouts (High Mobility)
-Lancers (Anti-Tank)
-Engineer (Repairs Tanks/Resupplies Troops)
-Sniper (Long-Range)
You can train each class with exp from battles and skirmishes and they can unlock new abilities. Each unit has pros & cons. Welkin can learn new orders that bolster your units during battles and you can also upgrade your equipment. You position units before a mission with how many determined by the mission. General objectives are to capture the main enemy base while maintaining your own, keep Welkin alive, and do so in 20 turns. The freedom of movement sets it apart from most tactical RPGs which often take an isometric route. Units move within a set distance, so planning and positioning is key... is what I
to say. Honestly, you can just cheese it. And by "can" I mean
.
. A unit can move more than once at the cost of their overall distance reducing each time. With Scouts however, most maps can be completed in 1-2 turns provided you avoid the enemy and capture their base unmanned. And considering how the ranking system works (less turns used=higher rank & 2-3 Turns is the minimum for most A-Ranks) the game
this. It's sad because it denies creativity. You
try a random team and might win, but it'll take
. Even with a basic team you're looking at 15-20 minutes of your life wasted when you could 've beaten the whole mission with one unit Sonic'ing their way through. You don't even have to level your scouts to do so!
The AI also seems to have lady luck on their side. It's RNG so
, but chances are that they'll have more luck on shots you believe to be implausible with their "suppsedly"
. Your sniper might easily miss a target 30ft away, but the AI will hit your units from halfway across the map with buildings and terrain in-between. On top of that, accuracy is worthless so weapons with higher damage are encouraged (which trades off good aim and range for power). Some battles are heavily reliant on certain tactics (like using smoke shots to hide your units), forcing the player to either do what the game wants but
or fight a war of attrition. NG+ offers harder missions but even they fall to cheese baker Alicia. Skirmishes hold no value or challenge outside of being able to cheese them for quick exp & money. At the end of the day, the combat is fun, don't get me wrong. But it truly allows you to have that fun when you're not playing the story, which is game.

You start each dungeon/puzzle at level 1 and have to fight your way through monsters until you can fight toe to toe with the boss. Despite being "puzzle-ish" there are a lot of different ways to beat a specific dungeon, even if it does not seem like it the first time you play. Fighting a monster takes away health and mana, though you can replenish it by exploring. However, just make sure to consider in which direction you want to explore the dungeon, as the precious tiles run out faster than you think. There are also a lot of different items that you can unlock, which will help you to smack those monsters around. And to spice it up, you have also 9 gods to choose from. Each one will alter your play style, as they reward and punish(!) various actions. One god is easy to learn, but tough to master, but to use more than one and know when to worship which god will take time, but will give such a huge reward!
In addition, there are some fixed dungeons included, which only allow for one single execution of steps to beat the challenge. They are very smartly designed and will teach you the mechanics of the game (if you are observant). Very well done!
10/10 Definitely recommend
