Half year later I decided to give it another try. Many of the bugs have been fixed, however not all of them and there are a few minor new ones (e.g. sometimes icons above minions not showing).
Workers' AI is as poor as it was - workers sometimes stay and do nothing instead of capturing territory of defeated enemy so generally you can forget about playing on large maps with multiple enemies.
Graphical bugs have been fixed and performance has been improved, however there are still FPS drops and the game freezes/crashes when changing textures quality in the options.
Minimap is as useless as it was. There is no large map and it is not possible to zoom out the main view. Still no auto-close on doors. Generally, there is too much micro-management and no easy way to handle it.
The game is great, it is really Dungeon Keeper improved. It looks very promising, however as it currently is, there are too many bugs and flaws. On the good side, developers seem to care, they read the feedback and improve the game and I cannot wait to change this review to positive. I have played a few skirmishes and campaign up to mission 10, which was the biggest one so far and it has really revealed too many problems.
- it is impossible to load certain saves, the game gets stuck while loading
- performance - with decent graphics adapter and on lowest settings the game becomes unplayable on medium size maps (and it's not just FPS, the whole interface becomes slow and unresponsive)
- sometimes the fog of war is not revealed correctly on some tiles so you have creatures moving through the dirt, if you hover over it it displays "fog of war"
- sometimes graphics of the creatures is not displayed correctly, creature looks like if it was teleporting, it is once displayed in one place, a second later in another
- sometimes a button to scroll through the list of the creatures disappears
- creatures are dropped in different place than you click and although it is highlighting where the creature will be dropped is very annoying in torture chamber when you first click on the device to change its purpose and then drop the prisoner next to the device instead of onto it, effectively releasing the prisoner...
- sometimes when casting spell (summon imp) the game says there is no sufficient mana even though the bar on top says something else
- 5 workers free, extra workers lock your mana (theoretical limit 35, practical 20)
- workers' AI is very poor, on large map when I created 50 extra imps with potions they still didn't want to capture enemy territory
- the doors don't have auto-close option, they can be either opened for everyone or closed for everyone
- there is no sound warning when enemies are destroying your defenses
- minimap is useless, pixelated and difficult to see anything on it, it often displays pings in places where nothing happens
- there is no large skirmish maps, the biggest is something like 80x80
- you can recreate earth tile (!)
- a lot of different types of terrains (sand, granite, chasm, blood, some non-mineable explodable thing + at least 10 more I don't remember)
- you can reinforce (make a wall tile which is harder to dig for enemy) gold tiles
- shrines that provide various bonuses when captured (vision, faster mining, cheaper spells)
- call to arms doesn't require mana any more, you can have multiple rally points for different types of creatures
- potions - pay for it upfront, wait for the minions to brew it and then use it
- constructs - imps can build various objects (bombs, gold teleporters, a thing that claims distant territory, earth tile)
- rituals - decide which one, wait for the minions to do their prayers in the special room and then use it
- minions build the traps/doors upfront as manufacturing packets, different objects require different number of packets but they will be delivered immediately after setting a trap blueprint if only you have some in store. You can also manually pick up construction parts and drop them on the selected blueprint
- you can click on traps for special effects (cannon shoots faster, slowing trap freezes enemies, spike trap gets hidden)
- the number of creatures depend primarily on the rooms built (i.e. room 3x3 will attract only 1 creature, room 5x5 will attract max 4), I don't think I have ever hit portal limit (it shows only its capacity usage as e.g. 35%)
- multiple ways of earning gold - spell that changes creature into gold statue, ritual that converts mana into gold, a potion that turns earth tiles into gold (which is worth using even if you have to recreate earth tiles with the constructs)
- technology tree - you don't have everything available upfront, you have to wait for your minions to research a technology point in the library which you can then use to unlock certain room/potion/spell/construct/trap/ritual
- some doors are made of two diagonals of a tile allowing it to be constructed anywhere, this in turn allows wider gates or even diagonal gates

A lot of the squadmate abilities(if not all) actually operate from your line of sight, meaning that the positioning of your squadmates will not interfere with their abilities being used and you cant use squadmate abilities with something blocking your view, otherwise you will just see Concussive Shot just hit the wall right in front of you.
You have one button that has 3 different functions which can be a pain. (Interact, sprint, take cover). This may often get you killed or cause you to miss out on some loot because the safe cracking process got interupted.
Your squadmates will also have a lot of difficulty taking cover where you want them to. If you want them to crouch down behind cover, they may just squat there instead and get shot, sometimes they will even just stand up and not try to hide at all.
Besides those little issues, the game is very enjoyable. I reccomend playing Insanity difficulty when you can because it feels completely different than the lower difficulties, each firefight feels like a hard fought battle, giving you that feeling of accomplishment.

is a name I haven't heard since the PSP era. An tactical RPG where you position units, plan your moves to capture the enemy camps, and neutralize their forces. The game is great but like many JRPGs, it's not without its flaws. It's

The story of Valkyria Chronicles is a pretty simply one. Gallia is a small sovereign nation between two bordering larger nations: The Empire, and the federation. Both sides are at war with each other over a precious resouce known as Ragnite with Gallia caught in the middle. Our protagonist, Welkin Gunther is the son of an accomplished soldier from a border village in Gallia named Bruhl. When he returns home from school (that out-of-town tuition though), he's greeted by his adoptive Darscen sister, Isara but then the
Empire invades Bruhl. Welkin takes up arms to defend his home from the war, hoping to end the conflict and save Gallia. There's also a sort of side plot to the game's lore. Darcsens (people born with dark hair regardless of skin complexion; doesn't explain why that particular factor makes them an entire ethincity or anything. They just are...) are seen as the cause of a great calamity that wiped out the Valkyrur -an ancient advanced race- long along. The war furthers this stigma against them.
The main cast consists of Welkin, Isara, Alicia (an orphan girl from Bruhl who also joins Squad 7), Rosie (the bigot of the group), Largo ( not as much a bigot as Rosie), Faldio (Welkin's best friend), and Lt. Valot (Squad 7's supervisor). The rest of Squad 7 is a cast of assorted characters. Some like Vyse and Aika from another SEGA title
make an cameo as recruitable members. Others are unique to this game and
are there some "interesting" characters
.
The overall plot itself is a mixup of good and extreme. It's an anime through and through (It even has it's own anime). Some events play out almost
as you would think they would.
Overall, the story can be entertaining but take it with a grain of salt here and there. It's a fiction first and reasonable second.
The design of the game tries to mimic a storybook style with effects that add to its illustrative quality. It's like the viewer is reading a memoir of a soldier or the history of a nation. The cell shading gives everything a great range of saturated color, which as an illustrator myself, is always welcome. There's also a fair amount of detail in the unit and tank models. That being said, there is a very anime-styled choice when it comes to the people of this game. Everyone on your squad is cute by which I mean all the women are wearing uniforms with their breast bulging like they're wearing tights. The men are all either moderately handsome or Largo(Gruff n' buff Old); or Cody (Actually Old). No one wears helmets to hide their incredibly stylized hair that makes them questionably more noticble in a game with snipers and tanks, if you as me. The enemy are all john does w/ full helmets. Their only variety comes form Lancers (different helmets) and anyone important to the plot.Not as much an Eastern standard as it is a universal one though. Aside from a few particular battles, most of the game is generic forest, desert, and suburban battle-torn city. An overall colorful and stylized game but it does leave a bit to be desired from its deisgn.
This game is a lot of fun. You have 5 classes aside from your 2 Tanks:
-Shocktrooper (High DPS)
-Scouts (High Mobility)
-Lancers (Anti-Tank)
-Engineer (Repairs Tanks/Resupplies Troops)
-Sniper (Long-Range)
You can train each class with exp from battles and skirmishes and they can unlock new abilities. Each unit has pros & cons. Welkin can learn new orders that bolster your units during battles and you can also upgrade your equipment. You position units before a mission with how many determined by the mission. General objectives are to capture the main enemy base while maintaining your own, keep Welkin alive, and do so in 20 turns. The freedom of movement sets it apart from most tactical RPGs which often take an isometric route. Units move within a set distance, so planning and positioning is key... is what I
to say. Honestly, you can just cheese it. And by "can" I mean
.
. A unit can move more than once at the cost of their overall distance reducing each time. With Scouts however, most maps can be completed in 1-2 turns provided you avoid the enemy and capture their base unmanned. And considering how the ranking system works (less turns used=higher rank & 2-3 Turns is the minimum for most A-Ranks) the game
this. It's sad because it denies creativity. You
try a random team and might win, but it'll take
. Even with a basic team you're looking at 15-20 minutes of your life wasted when you could 've beaten the whole mission with one unit Sonic'ing their way through. You don't even have to level your scouts to do so!
The AI also seems to have lady luck on their side. It's RNG so
, but chances are that they'll have more luck on shots you believe to be implausible with their "suppsedly"

On top of that, accuracy is worthless so weapons with higher damage are encouraged (which trades off good aim and range for power). Some battles are heavily reliant on certain tactics (like using smoke shots to hide your units), forcing the player to either do what the game wants but

I'm immensely grateful that people like Matthew Brown exist. Guy's a real genius with level design, and he has a massive cult hit with HexCells - who would blame him if he kept releasing more handcrafted Hexcells level each year? I'd certainly buy them, for that matter :)
But Matthew wants to move further, and keeps experimenting with new gameplay mechanics in the same general genre. Last year's SquareCells had an interesting fusion of several mechanics, and while it was enjoyable, it simply wasn't such a completely satisfying experience as HexCells. So this year, we have a new (or simply evolved?) mechanic from Matthew in the form of CrossCells - now you don't only have to count the cells, you also have to consider their values.
I imagine the adding of maths may not appeal to everyone, but for me, it absolutely re-invigorated the formula, and provided the same fun as HexCells. Actually, despite the different core mechanic, it very much feels like the first HexCells game, and there comes its only fault - there are too many "learning" puzzles, and there's no real challenge before the last 15-20% of the game. Even so, level 47 was a real bee-tard - it took me quite a while, and I started not to believe that the same relentless logic will lead to results. But eventually, it did :)
Most heartfully recommended, and looking forward to the announcement CrossCells Plus, which, in HexCells fashion, should start in difficulty where the initial game ended.

As opposed to Hexcells and Squarecells which were 100% logic, this game seems to be 3/4 logic, 1/4 trial and error (Unless you have very high skills of thinking SEVERAL moves in the future and calculating multiple equations at the same time) Often times I just have to put in something in the puzzle to see if it will work out with the other parts of the puzzle or not.
One of the game's mechanics is that it does not follow the standard order of operations (PEDMAS) but instead goes in written order. Therefore +3 +2 x4 +1=21 according to this game's logic. And sometimes it will have you look at a problem from right to left (or bottom to top) so for the line above, the total would become 9 instead of 21.
Also to note, the game seems quite short. Even compared to the Hexcells and squarecells games. I don't normally go through games that quickly and have not been rushing through this either but I completed the first 25 levels out of the total of 50 in about an hour. And that includes me doing research in the forums to understand some of the Mechanics that the game did not explain well enough for me to understand. For someone who's a bit faster than me and who doesn't have any problems with the minimal instructions that the game gives, you may even be able to complete the game and still be able to have it refunded being under the 2 hour play time.
That said, it's still a nice little fun game for a fairly low price. Maybe wait for a sale if you thought the other similar games were priced just right.

I grew up playing dungeon keeper 2. My step dad originally introduced me, and I was immediately hooked. "It's good to be bad" was the game's slogan, and it held true to that. The third title was never released because bullfrog was aquired by every gamer's favorite company, EA. So when I heard EA was making a mobile dungeon keeper game a while back, I was interested, but extremely skeptical. Turned out to be freemium garbage as I expected. No dungeon keeper for like 15 years and you decide to bring it back as a cashgrab shell of its former self? Classic EA. There would never be another great DK game, or so I thought.
Then I found out about WFTO. An independent group of people making a new DK game. Again, I had my heart crushed and stomped on before, so I was skeptical. When I first read reviews, it was from before the game's 1.1 patch, and they were rather mixed. Bugs, glitches, memory leaks, etc. I veered away at the time, but still checked up on it occasionally to see how the developers would respond. Over time, I started to notice that the developers were totally ontop of♥♥♥♥♥♥ They were working hard to fix everything, and genuinely seemed to care about making a true successor to DK2. I became more interested and waited for it to go on sale.
When I finally purchased it and played, I was hooked. I played till like 6 in the morning. This totally felt like what DK3 could have been if bullfrog were still around. They even got the original announcer! It was easy at first because of being a DK2 veteran, but eventually started to challenge me a bit more. I got my  handed to me a couple times on level 9 (Belmourne's pass) and had to start working out different strategies. I played nonstop and got to the final level in about two days, which I could not complete because of a glitch. This was pretty annoying, and I messaged the moderators on their subreddit (/r/WFTO). They were quick to respond and said it would be fixed. A couple days later, they released a patch that fixed everything I had trouble with, and I was able to complete the game in about 15 hours overall.
For those unfamiliar with the series, you play as an unseen and omnipotent underlord. You manage your dungeon from a top down perspective and carve out rooms to attract minions to your lair. You use these minions to wipe out the humans (or other underlords) kind of like an RTS. I have to state though, that this is not a traditional RTS. You do not have to micro tons of units, instead you place a flag and all your minions will rally there. They use their own abilities too, so again don't let your bad micro skills stop you from buying this. You can set up defenses, fortifications, cast spells, rituals, and create constructs. There's a ton of different ways to succeed. Once you've eliminated the campaign objective or the human/cpu player's dungeon core, you win.
PROS:
- Original Announcer from the old DK games
- Funny
- More content than DK2
- Countless ways to go about winning
- Gameplay is unique from other RTS
- Take control of a minion and join the battle in FPS mode
- Satisfying to build things
- Developers genuinely care about game
- Multiplayer (Fight with or against your friends)
- Campaign, skrimish, survival, sandbox, plus multiplayer. 5 Modes boys.
- More content on the way
- Challenging
CONS:
- Ending is awkward and unsatisfying at the moment (They will fix)
- You may run into a glitch or two (Again, they will fix)
- Little pricey
- AI still needs a little work (AI won't build traps or defenses guarding their dungeon core, so you can just send all your units directly at it and 90% of the time you'll win. This is mainly a problem in multiplayer/skrimish.)
OTHER:
- You might have to mess with the graphic settings a bit to get it to run smoothly
- To host a multiplayer game may require port forwarding
VERDICT:
If you played the old DK games and liked them, I highly reccommend this. If you want a taste of the gameplay before you're sure, go get DK2 and play a few missions of that. While the campaign is great, I also reccommend getting a friend to buy it and trying out multiplayer.
8/10.

I have not played Mass Effect 1 and since Mass Effect 3 is not available on Steam, I will not be playing that either. I played without guides, walkthroughs, wikis and without knowing what is going on in general. I played on Normal difficulty, finished all the quests I was able to find, hired full squad and did their loyalty missions.
Played on PC with Win 10, i5-6400, GTX 750Ti.
Combat
I had not that much hope for combat since shooters are not my thing but it was surprisingly enjoyable and fluid. The squad members were helpful and once I got some tankier ones, did not even die too much.
The better weapons with more punch had less ammo which balanced it nicely. Then again, ammo was usually plentiful everywhere so I rarely ran out of it.
I did all the upgrades to every weapon I managed to find but I am not sure how much these actually changed anything. Some weapons felt more like new skins instead of different weapon. Want 5% more firepower to shotguns? ok, I guess, but it won't change anything.
All the combat missions were basically single path from starting point to finish point without much branches to explore or different paths to find.
Graphics
After playing Witcher 3 this game was disappointing. Combat animations and models were actually good enough since you rarely have time to look around. But some of the cutscenes were really bad. Illusive Man looked horribly creepy and made it tough to trust anything he said. Most humans had trouble syncing facial expressions with voice acting, in general aliens looked better but perhaps because they had less moving stuff on their faces.
The environments felt empty and bland. In major hubes all the NPCs just sat or stand on their place, nobody was moving around doing their stuff. Everything felt large and empty. Long empty corridors and big empty rooms with nothing to do and no items to interact with. Even your own ship was big and pretty much completely empty even with full squad and it took forever to go around talking to your squad.
Game had very little graphics options, you can pick resolution and fullscreen/window, change brightness and couple ticks to modify shadows. That's it. Then again, it ran smooth and I did not feel any lag or slowdown.
Story
Well... It was pretty boring in the end. There is this evil alien race who wants to destroy everything and human hero to stop them. Why they want to destroy everything? No idea. Cause they evil, I guess.
There is actually quite a lot of alien races, and they suppose to be all different, but most of them felt very similar. I had trouble understanding who was who and I actually did not care enough to figure it out. For example main evil aliens were using another aliens who used to be different aliens in the past. Ok then...
The same issue hampered the squad too. Half of them felt like copies of each other and not enough alien to make much impression. Their powers and abilities were quite similar too so I did not bother to swap much. Not even once during combat mission did I feel, this is not going to end well, let me try with other squad setup. I died several times, sure, but then I loaded with same squad and won easily.
Sound
Was fine. Nothing to complain about. Nothing spectacular either. It worked.
Technical Issues
uhuh... In my 40 hours playthrough this game happened to crash more then during 400+ hours playing Witcher 3. Not only managed it to crash but it also had nasty broken ramp bug where you could get stuck on any slightly angled floor. And then you could go up in the air. Up and up. And had to reload.
The game was clearly not made to be played with keyboard and mouse. Think you can just double click on menu item? Nop. Want to use arrow keys instead of WASD? Can't do it. Some doors opened when you went close, others you had to manually open. Some things you click with mouse, some other things require Space key, complete mess.
Now we get to parts that really annoyed me.
First, you get no map on combat mission. You have map in non-combat areas but nothing when exploring and fighting. Why? Because some developers are lazy or they think disabling map is best way to make game more "challenging"? No idea.
You also can not save game just before boss fights. I mean you can usually save the game between fights, which is normal and proper way, but then you spend 15 minutes cleaning huge room from several waves of enemies and you want to save before big bad boss pops in with new and interesting ways to kill you. Not allowed. If the boss you only fight once in the game kills you, you have to waste time cleaning that huge room again from all the random enemies. Fun? Not really. Annoying? You bet.
Finally, when do developers understand that quick time events are horrible. Nothing is worse then reading/listening through some dialogues about history of galaxy or personal problems some alien has, just to be asked to press random key very fast. Why. Would. You. Think. That. Is. Any. Fun?
Steam
The game has no Steam integration whatsoever. All you can do is to buy it from Steam. To activate DLC keys to need to register on some other site, create new account there and then have access to download extra content. Which I never bothered with.
You do not get any Steam achievements either. See, the game actually has bunch of achievements but they are not connected to Steam. Because... I dunno, to annoy your paying customers perhaps?

CrossCells is an ambient logic puzzle game. Much like other [something]Cells games by Matthew Brown.
Ambient music, minimalistic visuals and brain overheating, these are three things you can expect from Matthew's games. CrossCells is no different. What's it all about? Numbers. It's kinda like sudoku, with a twist. You must match numbers shown on the borders adding and/or multiplying the numbers provided in the table.
If you don't know any other XCells games start with  Hexcells first, these are still the best. This one, in comparison, might require a bit of luck and/or thinking several steps ahead instead of on the spot logic reasoning you used to progress in the former games. But if you're like me and love these games and finished all of them already you should give this one a try. It's not as good as the previous ones, but still quite enjoyable.
I liked:
* some levels are really excellent and can melt your brain
* this is everything you'd expect from a game by Matthew Brown
I disliked:
* more times than I would expect logical thinking gets you nowhere and you just have to blind guess
* two or three puzzles are awfully simple
Get this if:
* you liked any of the previous XCells games
* you like minimalistic puzzlers
Don't get this if:
* you don't like numbers
* you're annoyed by a little guessing in your puzzling

We're ninjas, in space, controlling an armor controlled by a kid.
We can be an all-around swordsman, an ice cube, a necromancer, a fairy, a phoenix, a k-pop singer, an Egypt god, a chinese dragon and a monkey god.
We hunt cloned soldiers, space-infested-zombies, tech mercenaries and ancient beings while equipped with rifles, grenade launchers, bows, swords, frisbees, a portable vacuum cleaner, a cat and a jetpack that can either be used like a plane, a submarine or in space. Sometimes instead of killing, we capture them so that they can become Skynet's test subjects.
We get space aids, your best friend is the cross-breed of Cortana and Marvin and suffers from multiple personality disorder, we're haunted by a doppelganger specialized in jumpscares, your spacemom orders you to beat the #### out strangers until they give information to her.
After a hard day work, you can finally enjoy the night fishing in Europe with a colossal ancient being by your side while you look up to the sky to watch Star Wars' Death Star obliterate a major trading hub with lots of people inside or try to pop a pimple originated by a meteor that contains a house-sized half-smart 3-headed alien with a scythe.
The most brutal, most challenging enemy isn't a head mounted on a drone mounted on an exoskeleton that shoots rockets, nor a goth guy that wears black spandex and threatens you over twitter. No. The true horror is your teammates looking down at you because the colors you chose for your pants don't match your cloak and gun or are out of fashion. That, my friend, is the true endgame.
10/10 would recommend it.

Pros:
-Great General Movement and Shooting Mechanics.
-Awesome art-style and graphics (I've got a mid level rig and it ran on Max 1440p 60fps constant)
-Solid progression mechanics - Large varied skill try that allows you to reasign your skill points on the fly, dependant on the enemies you are facing.
-The soundtrack and sound effects are spot on.
-Large array of arsenal at your disposal, in a Hotline Miami "1 clip then throw away" style. Unlike Hotline Miami, you have a permenent melee and ranged weapon, which do the job most of the time.
Cons:
-The story isn't brilliant, but honestly the gameplay makes up for it.
-There is very little voice acting at all, mostly one liners each time you die or complete a section. All the story is done through text, including the cutscenes. Characters just stand there and subtitles appear below them. I didn't find it engaging in the slightest.
-The quest system is really pointless imo. There are side-quests and such that you can pick up from the "hub" zone, but the game puts little emphasis on them.
-Might be a bit too challenging for some (However, the devs have dumbed down the difficulty a bit in a recent update). If you like a difficult game then this shouldn't be a concern.
If you're looking for a good top down action game, similar to Hotline Miami, and aren't fussed about story, this one is for you.

The description says it's a card game and that it is rogue-like. That's wrong. This is an Action RPG (NOT a card game) with rogue-like elements. Quests, equipments and buffs/curses are represented by card decks. These decks are shuffled and dealt to produce your next session. You also need to pick a boss for each session. Once you defeat all bosses, you "finish" the game, or you can play until you unlock all cards which is the actual point of the game. Overall, It's a good game, but not a "must play".
Good:
- Presentation is pretty unique. This game is like DnD with tarot cards, but each fight is actually played like in an action RPG.
- There is RNG, but not in a frustrating way. You have some control over the RNG and you almost never lose just because of bad luck.
- Play session time is between 30-50 min.
- Most quest cards, when beaten, unlock new quest or equipment cards. Unlocking new cards is one of the best parts of the game.
- DIficulty starts very easy and ramps up after each boss. By the end of the game some fights are very hard.
Bad:
- I like good stories in my games. This one has a bunch of small stories, but not a big overarching plot.
- Battle system is okay and fun, but nothing spetacular. It mostly comes down to dodging attacks and trying to fit in a few hits before having to dodge again. Most spells are very underwhelming.

The gameplay consists of drawing cards, those cards are then placed in a pattern on the game board, and then you move a play piece along a linear path through cards. There can be some paths that are optional but it's pretty easy to find the end and there is no dungeon exploration. After you move you look at the card that you drew and deal with the results. If it is a monster card then you get put into an arena with the monster type that was on the card. The combat is pretty simple and has been a bit boring so far. It definitely goes up in difficulty but there is not much challenge. I expect the challenge in the later game comes from being able to survive combat while rationing your food and health appropriately.
A+ experience so far but I felt a little bit misled by what the developer gave us in the screenshots. The description at the bottom of the store page also seems a bit misleading. Just don't come in expecting a full roguelike dungeon crawler.
As far as combat goes: Pirates, Vikings, & Knights is/was better by a long shot...
Game looks great but lacks substance - not worth the price, and not worth the time.

You start each dungeon/puzzle at level 1 and have to fight your way through monsters until you can fight toe to toe with the boss. Despite being "puzzle-ish" there are a lot of different ways to beat a specific dungeon, even if it does not seem like it the first time you play. Fighting a monster takes away health and mana, though you can replenish it by exploring. However, just make sure to consider in which direction you want to explore the dungeon, as the precious tiles run out faster than you think. There are also a lot of different items that you can unlock, which will help you to smack those monsters around. And to spice it up, you have also 9 gods to choose from. Each one will alter your play style, as they reward and punish(!) various actions. One god is easy to learn, but tough to master, but to use more than one and know when to worship which god will take time, but will give such a huge reward!
In addition, there are some fixed dungeons included, which only allow for one single execution of steps to beat the challenge. They are very smartly designed and will teach you the mechanics of the game (if you are observant). Very well done!
10/10 Definitely recommend

is a name I haven't heard since the PSP era. An tactical RPG where you position units, plan your moves to capture the enemy camps, and neutralize their forces. The game is great but like many JRPGs, it's not without its flaws. It's

The story of Valkyria Chronicles is a pretty simply one. Gallia is a small sovereign nation between two bordering larger nations: The Empire, and the federation. Both sides are at war with each other over a precious resouce known as Ragnite with Gallia caught in the middle. Our protagonist, Welkin Gunther is the son of an accomplished soldier from a border village in Gallia named Bruhl. When he returns home from school (that out-of-town tuition though), he's greeted by his adoptive Darscen sister, Isara but then the
Empire invades Bruhl. Welkin takes up arms to defend his home from the war, hoping to end the conflict and save Gallia. There's also a sort of side plot to the game's lore. Darcsens (people born with dark hair regardless of skin complexion; doesn't explain why that particular factor makes them an entire ethincity or anything. They just are...) are seen as the cause of a great calamity that wiped out the Valkyrur -an ancient advanced race- long along. The war furthers this stigma against them.
The main cast consists of Welkin, Isara, Alicia (an orphan girl from Bruhl who also joins Squad 7), Rosie (the bigot of the group), Largo ( not as much a bigot as Rosie), Faldio (Welkin's best friend), and Lt. Valot (Squad 7's supervisor). The rest of Squad 7 is a cast of assorted characters. Some like Vyse and Aika from another SEGA title
make an cameo as recruitable members. Others are unique to this game and
are there some "interesting" characters
.
The overall plot itself is a mixup of good and extreme. It's an anime through and through (It even has it's own anime). Some events play out almost
as you would think they would.
Overall, the story can be entertaining but take it with a grain of salt here and there. It's a fiction first and reasonable second.
The design of the game tries to mimic a storybook style with effects that add to its illustrative quality. It's like the viewer is reading a memoir of a soldier or the history of a nation. The cell shading gives everything a great range of saturated color, which as an illustrator myself, is always welcome. There's also a fair amount of detail in the unit and tank models. That being said, there is a very anime-styled choice when it comes to the people of this game. Everyone on your squad is cute by which I mean all the women are wearing uniforms with their breast bulging like they're wearing tights. The men are all either moderately handsome or Largo(Gruff n' buff Old); or Cody (Actually Old). No one wears helmets to hide their incredibly stylized hair that makes them questionably more noticble in a game with snipers and tanks, if you as me. The enemy are all john does w/ full helmets. Their only variety comes form Lancers (different helmets) and anyone important to the plot.Not as much an Eastern standard as it is a universal one though. Aside from a few particular battles, most of the game is generic forest, desert, and suburban battle-torn city. An overall colorful and stylized game but it does leave a bit to be desired from its deisgn.
This game is a lot of fun. You have 5 classes aside from your 2 Tanks:
-Shocktrooper (High DPS)
-Scouts (High Mobility)
-Lancers (Anti-Tank)
-Engineer (Repairs Tanks/Resupplies Troops)
-Sniper (Long-Range)
You can train each class with exp from battles and skirmishes and they can unlock new abilities. Each unit has pros & cons. Welkin can learn new orders that bolster your units during battles and you can also upgrade your equipment. You position units before a mission with how many determined by the mission. General objectives are to capture the main enemy base while maintaining your own, keep Welkin alive, and do so in 20 turns. The freedom of movement sets it apart from most tactical RPGs which often take an isometric route. Units move within a set distance, so planning and positioning is key... is what I
to say. Honestly, you can just cheese it. And by "can" I mean
.

this. It's sad because it denies creativity. You
try a random team and might win, but it'll take
. Even with a basic team you're looking at 15-20 minutes of your life wasted when you could 've beaten the whole mission with one unit Sonic'ing their way through. You don't even have to level your scouts to do so!
The AI also seems to have lady luck on their side. It's RNG so
, but chances are that they'll have more luck on shots you believe to be implausible with their "suppsedly"

On top of that, accuracy is worthless so weapons with higher damage are encouraged (which trades off good aim and range for power). Some battles are heavily reliant on certain tactics (like using smoke shots to hide your units), forcing the player to either do what the game wants but

Holy crapy is this game good. I honestly think that anyone who even remotely enjoys RPG's should have to play this game ONCE. The characters were GREAT, I felt like I was actually working with them and building relationships, along with building there trust. The combat is a big step forward from Mass Effect 1, but I would still prefer Mass Effects 3 combat over this games, The combat IS still great though. There is a huge variety of locations, from the post apocalyptic deserts of Tuchanka, to the advanced civilization of the Citadel. Your constantly upgrading your powers, weapons, character, companions, or ship, but its never annoying to constantly upgrade. Theres a ton of optional content, and the final mission is IMHO one of the best final levels in any game I have ever played. The whole game builds up to this epic final moment, and if you put a decent amount of time into the game, you will enjoy the ending so much. Honestly, this is probably among my top 10 games ever. Its the perfect blend of RPG and third person shooter, and will keep you intrigued and entertained for hours. If you haven't had spoilers for this game yet, don't even bother. Keep it to yourself and see how the games story is. All in all, this game is a 10/10 for me, and I think it takes its place deservingly above ME 1 and 3.

A numbers game where you select or hide cells/squares based on special rules shown by numbers on the sides or brackets. Levels get harder each time with new rules appearing. These rules could be better visualized as there is not much of a tutorial for them after level 20. Relaxing music is present again with the same style as the other Cells games. What is not present is the dark mode, which seems like a downgrade from the previous game - SquareCells. There are colors you can choose but nothing that would make the game less white/bright. Ripple effects are annoying but you can turn them off. I imagine it was supposed to look more interesting but for me it just felt distorted and weird. No stars system to reward the player either. So this makes brute force approach the best, which is unfortunate considering the point seemed to be to carefully try each puzzle. The "Select Puzzle" menu is a bit off where you instinctively want to do the first block but the numbers are split between the two blocks (you need to go per row). No level generator, after doing the 50 levels there is almost no replayability. Some of the above was nitpicking but I have a reason. As this game is part of a bundle of five games it cannot avoid the fact that it's inferior to the other four. I think Matthew Brown has done some great work with these games but this one lacks some polish and so just falls under the edge of recommending. If it gets updated I will totally update the review. But as it stands now it's not recommended.

In Sum: A dull Facebook game that is unbearably slow without microtransactions, and suffers from apparent controversy by the dev.  It just isn't fun.  0/5
-----
This is basically a Facebook game on Steam.  And it brings with it the failings of a Facebook game.
The biggest issue in design, as far as I'm concerned, is the time.  This is not a game that you sit down and play.  You do an action, then have to wait hours, sometimes, days, for it to happen.  The game uses real time for this.
Games such as this are not designed for fun or competition.  They are made for compulsion.  And that is the psychological strategy of this game.  You can build or upgrade something and wait from 10 minutes to 24 hours (maybe longer), or you can whip out the credit card and do it instantly.  The design of the game isn't necessarily "pay-to-win", but rather to make not paying so annoying and frustrating, that you pay repeatedly just to find the enjoyable game in here.  Meanwhile, those who do pay can progress essentially without limits, as every aspect of the game can be instant with purchasing.  To be fair, it is possible to play this game for free.  If you only play sporadically and are willing to progress painfully slow.
I realize this is common practice in mobile games, but it is out of place on Steam.
Coming from a number of strategy games before playing this, I found the soldier's actions to be irritating to watch, due to the stupidity.  Sometimes you see them actually do something intelligent, like stopping just outside of howitzer range but in general, attacking troops will run into danger, then proceed to attack buildings while being fired on.  They also will try to group together in a clump, which makes them easily killed as a group.  Due to the slow progression, it is probable that defenses will develop faster than attack power, which causes a sudden bottleneck in progress...unless the credit card comes out.
Overall after playing a few hours, I have to say, I'm not having fun.  I don't feel this was a particular good waste of my time.  I don't feel I have much in the way of positive feedback, because the issue is ultimately the design of the game.  It is truly a casual game in every sense, that not only is it meant for people who only check in every so often, but it requires you to approach it casually.  As for the game, it's not broken, it's just not fun.
I have some concerns as well, about the developer's reputed actions on the community hub.  Apparently, criticisms about the game are being deleted, critics of the game are being banned, and recently a dubious set of community rules was posted on the forum superceding Steam's rules that, along with reasonable prohibitions (which were already against Steam's rules), states that "spreading misinformation" will result in a ban.  This could reasonably be construed as any information contrary to the developer's statements, which would include criticism.  Adding this clause lends credence to the reputation this game has been developing.
Do not spend money on this game. Dev's do not fix bugs. They only steal your money.

What I found difficult at the beginning is the movement in which you move according to the world and not where the player is pointing at which makes fight a movement two different elements that you need to put attention during battles.
Multiple dash in battles is great because you can use it to slow time for a bit and think quickly your next move. I must admit that I played on easy and I didn't have to use it that much, but it greater difficulties that slow time can save you from dying dozens of times.
Is not really that long (5 hours in my case) and if you want to go for the 100% you must complete the game without dying once and that is big no for me, too much stress.
The story is there and it tries to be deep at the end but not really, something simple to serve as an excuse to kill and kill nothing more.
I recommend it but maybe you could wait until sales if you are not sure.

Not bad. I mean, not THAT bad. Graphics, atmosphere and music are nice, and you get some amount of fun from playing.
But… this game is ruined with the thing, which, in my opinion, is the main problem of all modern games – awful balance. At the beginning it isn’t visible, since the most imbalanced stuff is locked until you level-up, but when you do… just spam-deploy barrier and spam-call supply drop to get XAAR weapon. And that’s all.  The first slows down enemy guys and deflects their shots, the second gives you infinite amounts of ranged weapons for no cost at all and with good timing – oneshots everybody.
You can get all those stuff in the very middle of game, and from that point – all fights are the same. Game actually becomes easier as you progress. The final boss battle, which is meant to be the hardest part of the game, was really “just stay and shoot” for me. All previous (miniboss) battles was “move in circles and shoot”. And yes, I tried to play differently – and never succeeded. This is not Hotline Miami, there is no room for strategic thinking – just pure reflexes with which I have problems.
As you can guess – I got bored nearly in the middle and continued played only to uncover the story (which turned to be quiet mediocre). Doesn’t help the fact that devs were spent most of their imagination at this point too, and main challenge from that point was quantity of enemies, not their special abilities or complicated attack patterns. There are only three enemies here – melee guy, ranged weapons guy, suicide guy/thing. Minibosses are all the same – mostly ranged guys with different weapons. Only ability guys as you progress – dash (later teleport) which would be a big problem, if deployable barrier wouldn’t slow them down. Also they sometimes get new 3D models so they look nice – until you stop caring.
So, in the end – Ruiner is a game were good is everything except main – gameplay. And story, but who, except me, cares about that in twin-stick shooters? About story – I expected there will be some kind of twist in the end, but I didn’t expect that it will be boring and uninteresting twist, after which I felt only “what?!” and when it all was explained in encyclopedia entries – only “whatever”. I finished it in nearly 12 hours (some time steam was offline so official statistics a bit different) and I not regret about buying it. But I have no good feelings either so thumbs down.

First off, lets address the elphant in the room. Yes, this game is heavy with RNG, but it's the good kind. One way to sum up this game would be digital deck building with batman arkham style combat thrown in. Top it all off with amazing boss fights and enemy variaty, make this a must for anyone wanting to do some dungeon delving and have the dungeon different every time you play. Think Darkest Dungeon only with real time combat instead old school turn based combat.
There are different card decks for every aspect of the game, from enemies and events to items and special abilites. Each time you take on a dungeon, you will unlock new items, encounters by way of reward tokens. Once you have cleared enough dungeons to complete a set, you will gain an upgrade. Upgrades allow you to start each new run with better grear but also tougher enemies.
This game has a lot going for it, however there are three big issues you need to be aware off.
1 - The mazes can be pain due to clunky controls.
This isn't too much of a problem in the sense that maze runs don't pop up that often and can be removed from the encounter deck.

2 - Skill checks are done with a game of 4 card chance.
This is a bit more annoying as the odds will also change depending on the encounter card. Some will have three successes while others will have only one. This is made worse by the fact that some failures can kill you outright. This will be very outputting to some and I can uderstand that. It is one thing I really hope does not make a return in Hand of Fate 2.
3 - lack of character customisation.
While the gear can alter your look and make you look pretty bad♥♥♥♥♥ you still have to go out and find most of it while you are exploring. DLC will give you variations of the base character but he is esentially all we get. This is a big gripe for me as the dude the ugly as sin and I would kill for a better looking female character. It doesn't help that after all the time this game has been out, the developers have never taken the time to activate mod support. They say that it would take too much time but at the time of writing HoF2 is 3 weeks from release. Surely someone could spare a bit time to put out some tools.
Despite these issuses I would still highly recommend Hand of Fate. There is a ton of stuff to unlock and discover with near endless replay value. Before writing this review I had just faced the Lava golem for the first time and loved how epic the fight felt. Having a giant lightning hammer also helped but that is nether here nor there.
The point is, if you like meaningful progression and unlocking content through the old school method of actually playing the game, then I feel confident you will enjoy Hand of Fate.

First of all I'd like to say - IGNORE THE METACRITIC SCORE!!!! It's only the score that it is because people started leaving reviews before the game was finished and before the 1.1 patch was released. This patch has been a complete revelation!
I know what many of you are probably thinking as you trawl through the reviews left for War for the Overworld......"I thoroughly enjoyed the Dungeon Keeper games and I'd really hope that War for the Overworld would live up to my expectations, given that it's not exactly cheap". Well, as a long term Dungeon Keeper fan (I'm 28 now and played it daily when i was a teen, including a few play throughs as I've gotten older), I can assure you that you won't be disappointed.
I actually felt quite sceptical when purchasing this game, simply because I enjoyed the original Dungeon Keepers games so much. I often hype up something in my own mind to the point where it will probably disappoint, but I've been very pleasantly surprised.
This is about as close as you can get to a Dungeon Keeper 3. I think the creators have done a really great job of keeping just enough of the old Dungeon Keeper vibes to satisfy the DK fans (for example the resemblance of many of the units in the game - The 'Workers' are clearly Imps, the 'Chunders' who love to work in the workshop and have the ability to 'fart' as a weapon (much like my girlfriend) are Bile Demons and you also get a female unit that loves to torture your enemies in the torture chamber.....remind you of anything (except without my old favourite spell lightning).
Your creatures still need to eat but have moved away from chickens and now prefer micropiglets, and some of your old favourite spells are still available like being able to create more workers, being able to reveal parts of the map for limited time, and also the 'Call to Arms' spell has a 'Rally' option too.
I think what's really great about War for the Overworld is the fact that the developers etc have taken great care to only change or remove elements from the DK games that actually work to improve this game. Does anyone remember in Dungeon Keeper how if you had enough gold, you could build an unlimited amount of traps and doors all over your dungeon, while you sat back and used the sight of evil spell in conjunction with the lightening or cave in spells to kill all of the enemy units? yeh you can'y do that anymore, you now actually have to think a bit more and strategy plays more of a part. Your mana pool is actually now split between the number of workers you have, the number of traps you have and any spells that you wish to cast. This means that you have to find a balance between those things because you have loads of workers, you wont be able to lay any traps or cast any spells, alternatively if you have loads of traps, you won't be able to create many extra workers or cast many spells. This was a welcome addition to the game because it's makes things more challenging, but not too difficult.
The graphics are nice and crisp, even if the frame rate can take an occasional hit on a very busy map (nothing that'd bothered me too much mind), the sound effects are very good and actually quite funny in terms of the things you hear your creatures randomly say, and there's more than enough content to keep you playing for a while with multiplayer, the campaign and a survival type mode.
Overall I've been really, pleasantly surprised by this game and what I also think is great is that the developers are really looking after it when it comes to releases/patches/updates. They regularly make sure that they respond to requests from people in terms of improvements etc and they aren't just light touches either. When i first got the game, I felt a little sad that your workers aren't able to level up. After a few days they'd released another couple of updates which added the ability for workers to level and i noticed they'd fixed EVERY other minor bug that I'd experienced.
You get exactly what you'd want and would expect from this game and the aftercare provided by the regular updates etc. It's fun, challenging, addictive and you still get to feel very nostalgic if you loved the original Dungeon Keeper games. If you never played those games and are instead just contemplating buying this game - do it, you won't regret it.

Desktop Dungeons is a very peculiar game which plays like some kind of puzzle game.
One half of the game you are buying upgrades in your town which will aid you in future adventures.
And the other half is you adventuring into caves and dungeons to slay the biggest baddest baddie available and return with the loot.
You are tossed out on a map which you explore square by square. Time standing still when you don't move.
Which gives the idea that you're supposed to stop and think for every move you make.
Resources are scarce, enemies aplenty. You have to decide which enemy to take down in which order and balance that with exploring and using potions and spells to your advantage.
Even if it appears bite-sized it still a game where a single adventure could leave you scratching your head and doing a move every few minutes while you do something else entirely.
I'd say definitely try this out if you want a more laid-back experience which rewards patience and decisionmaking!

Valkyria Chronicles is a game that i'm pleased to say it doesn't fit in one of today's main genres. Instead, it's an unique mix of turn-based 3rd person shooter and RPG upgrading elements, with strategic planning. The setting is also unique, depicting world war 2 with an anime style. For this style, the graphics are good, with drawn textures and effects. The music is also good to hear. The story is engaging with interesting characters that develop over time. It's a bit hard to explain the game mechanics, but basically you pick a squad on a map full of enemies, control it's members individually a few times, and then your enemies do the same in turns until you fulfill the mission requirements or fail. The mechanics work well for the most part, but there's balancing issues with the main 5 classes. Still, it's not an easy game, and you'll also need some trial and error and luck to figure out a working strategy at times. When you master the game, you can try the hardest DLC missions, which are really hard but wield some great rewards. They're not needed for the achievements though. And since it's cheap on sale, if you're curious i recommend you to watch some gameplay footage first, and if you liked it pick it up then. It's definitely an unique game that brings some freshness in today's videogame market.

META: This game is entirely deserving of every accolade it has received over the past year... the transition from early access to final release has been not only one of the fastest but one of the most massive jumps in content quality that I have ever seen. Larian Studios has used the current generation's tools   (Early Access, Social Media, and Crowdfunding) to their advantage in such a delicate and positve way that it has restored my faith the aforementioned services. It has been clear from the start tht Sven Icke and Co. at Larian have wanted nothing more than to bring the Isometric RPG into the future, and they have done so with gret aplomb and miraculous style! Divinity as an IP is one that boasts so many original ideas, yet bows reverently to the tenets of past RPG titles. As such, it is with great satisfaction that I saw the title occupy a position in the TOP SELLING PC GAMES OF ALL TIME  on metacritic; along with the greats such as Baldur's Gate, Quake, Portal, Bioshock, The Witcher III, GTA V, and even HALF-LIFE! This coming from a small Scandinavian studio is an achievement that one wishes they could attain MAYBE ONCE in their lifetime.
Aside from my compliment showering, these are the things I would like to talk about in more detail:
The combat and mechanics in this game are FAR beyond the polish and intricacy of D:OS I. The combat encounters are challenging yet more nuanced. I believe D:OS 1 was the icebreaker for Larian, but in this title they have expounded brilliantely upon the conventions and ideas of the first iteration. Encounters feel much more balanced and well thought out. The entirety of the Skill / Talent / Perk system seems refined, and they have removed supercilious aspects while doubling down on what works, a method that all successful AAA studios employ. The origin characters are fantastic, featuring a wide range of classes, playstyles, and attitudes for players to enjoy. Also, the storyline does a much better job of connecting to the actual mechanics of the game, which goes a long way to making the title feel polished and unified,
I don't want to spoil anyting else for future players. If you like ANY sort of RPG, JRPG, Tactical/Strategy game, do not hesitate. This game will blow you away time and time again.

What this game is:
- sort of a puzzle game (explanation follows)
- a well done and story rich anime graphic novel
- graphically VERY appealing with that super awesome CANVAS engine, even on laptops!

What this game is not:
- a strategy game, ABSOLUTELY NO STRATEGY INVOLVED!!!
- a squad based tactics game (at least not a good one)
- enjoyable for players expecting some WW2 strategy, you will be DEEPLY disappointed, even infuriated!
By now you may have noticed my main gripe with this game: It is tagged totally wrong! In the game description by the publisher there is no talk of this game being strategic, and right they are!
To get a good scoring in the missions - and therefore enough XP and money - you will have to focus on the objectives; And this almost always means running past every enemy and capture the flag with your fastest scout as fast as possible. For this you will have to start the mission several times to know all enemy locations. This is why I call this a puzzle game. Game is finishable with a more conventional approach as well though.
If you are here for a japanese approach on WW2 Europe setting with really fresh graphics and story, by all means get it, devs did an awesome job. If you want a squad based tactics or even strategic game, stay far away!

The whole game builds up to this epic final moment, and if you put a decent amount of time into the game, you will enjoy the ending so much. Honestly, this is probably among my top 10 games ever. Its the perfect blend of RPG and third person shooter, and will keep you intrigued and entertained for hours. If you haven't had spoilers for this game yet, don't even bother. Keep it to yourself and see how the games story is. All in all, this game is a 10/10 for me, and I think it takes its place deservingly above ME 1 and 3.

After a few attempts at trying this game out, then playing it to almost completion, I just can't recommend it. It has not been worth my time. Here's my review on Valkyria Chronicles.
The main problem with this game is that it's very scripted. It's very linear, even if it doesn't SEEM to be. Sure, you can choose all your units and position them where you want and all that. But here's the thing that I noticed - I had to replay missions 2 - 3 times over just to complete them with low rankings. Why? Because the game is run on scripts. Basically, the enemy has a predetermined path (with a few exceptions) that they will follow throughout the game's level / mission.
When you start a mission, you can choose and position your units (it's limited to certain areas). You don't actually know where the enemy is (the briefing's usually are not very informative, and the map just shows arrows to where the enemy will be pointed), AND you mostly will not know what types of units they have or if they have tanks, etc, etc. Again, I had to replay missions 2-3 times just to see what the **** is going on at the start of the mission. That's not fun. That's frustrating.
Alright, I know what you're thinking. "It's a strategy game, you aren't supposed to know where the enemy is!". K then. Explain to me this - if the game is a "strategy game", aren't you supposed to be able to make different strategies and see where they lead you? Aren't the enemies supposed to not be on some set path (by that I mean when you reload your save the enemies will LITERALLY do the same exact thing) that will lead to your utter defeat? That's not strategy. You can actually just play a mission, memorize what moves the enemy makes, then reload and go back in. Seems to me like the game only has one way to win the game.
Now for the worst part. You'll get stuck, like I did. You'll wonder "HOW THE **** AM I SUPPOSED TO PLAY THIS MISSION??!?!". You shouldn't be thinking that. You shouldn't be thinking "How am I supposed to play this mission like the devs set up for me to do?". That's not strategy. Anyways, that's not the worst part. The worst part is that in order to get an 'S' or 'A' ranking on missions, you have to do them AS FAST AS POSSIBLE. That means using cheap methods and ways to get at the enemy. In one mission, there is a boss (won't say who) who rains down on you from above with endless bullets. What you can do is smoke off your teammates, then have 3 snipers hit her. Boom. Mission complete! YAY!
I'm not saying this game is terrible. It's just not what I envisioned it as being.

This minimalist puzzle game is as great as any other by Matthew Brown!
As always, the puzzle set starts with basics that are easy to grasp, and then slowly but appropriately works its way up in difficulty and complexity.
The puzzles are great at making you keep arithmetic sums and products in your head along with quantities of tiles and combinations of numbers, and are overall a great exercise in logical thinking.
If you enjoyed this game, I would highly highly recommend the other puzzle games by Matthew Brown, especially the Hexcells series, as I've found them to be wonderfully designed minimalist puzzle games, all with basically the same style of slow atmospheric music that helps relax you as you think, and puzzles that feel intuitive and balanced in their difficulty progression.
The only complaints I'd have is that the ripple effect in the UI blurs the font that is small enough that you might already have to squint to see (thankfully, this doesn't carry over into the actual game). Having "only" 50 puzzles may make the game seem a bit on the short side as well, and I'd like to see more, but otherwise I love CrossCells and the other puzzle games like it!

A fantastic Australian made roguelike adventure card game. Packed with loads of fun and novel mechanics. Both the chance encounters and the combat are exciting; filled with victories and pitfalls, and you are only ever a stones throw away from either.

A fantastic example of what can be achieved by adequately supported Australian developers outside of the fly-by-night mobile genre.

From the outset, whether you're going to like RUINER or not looks like a simple choice: do you like twin-stick brawler-shooters that require a bit of skill, and just a little bit of luck?
It's not that simple, though. You can fall in love with the idea of a thing, but the execution may turn you off of it. I love RUINER's idea: cyberpunk misanthropy, the game. All of that's here, in a package that's part-mysterious, all-gorgeous. The execution, though? Well, you can already see I've recommended the game. So here's the thing: it's good. But is it great? Well... it's not a game that's invested in showing you how to be better at it like, say, Dark Souls. You experiment with what you've got, or you die a lot. Well, that's not quite right -- you're still going to die a lot. But the game's never punishing for the sake of it. It's important to remember you can respec your abilities at will, because without that, you're never going to get far. Some of the bosses remain a bit cheap, though they've toned that down a bit (hiya, Mother), but it's also a thrill to just get 'em done in one when you figure out what to do.
Part of that frustration is why this isn't a clear-cut recommended. Do you enjoy ramming yourself against a wall until you figure out which parts of it chip and crack, then keep going at it until the whole thing comes down? Well, then play RUINER on Hard. Else do yourself a favour and play it on normal. Also: don't go in expecting much of a story here, because that's not where this game's priorities are.
Its priorities remain being a violent, explosive little thing that focuses on tactile combat and chilly cyberpunk aesthetics, and it does those pretty well. Yes, the levels are repetitive, and some of the encounters are too, but it's all painted with a dazzling neon brush, the artists' favourite colour being a bright, lurid red. The animation and controls are silky smooth, somehow responsive yet managing a weighty heft at the same time that makes for an immediately addictive 'let's have just one more go' feel to it.
Plus, it's got an absolutely banging soundtrack. Sure, there's the legendary Susumu Hirasawa track for its Chiba City-ish hub that everyone talks about, but don't let the grinding pound of Zamilska and Memotone's pieces slip by you. It's all well-gauged and an excellent accompaniment to the bloodbaths on-screen.
In summary: if you're looking for a game with a fantastic sense of style and engaging, if slightly flawed, design and combat, you could do much worse than RUINER.

firstly, if you are expecting a CCG the likes of magic the gathering or whatnots, then perhaps you should temper your expectations again, or just look for a different game.
hand of fate is first and foremost, more of a rogue-like rpg, and the cards simply become gameplay elements, dictating your gear, and the story. if you've played games like card crawl on mobile devices before, you'd have an idea of how it's like.
the fun part about hand of fate however, is very much tied to the way you configure your deck itself. you therefore dictate what kind of random items could appear in your game, what kind of encounters you'd face, etc. and of course, the dealer himself (like a game master in pen and paper rpgs), do inject some random elements of his own into your deck. all this put together, would amount to your single session in the game. facing different foes, picking up different loot, and going through different tales. as there's tons of different cards available for you to pick from (and more as you unlock them), it gives the game a pretty decent replayability.
while luck does play a major factor in how your game progresses sometimes, it does get easier as you accumulate more gold, better gear, and some blessings. there's also the matter of balancing your health, with your gold, and your food too, all of which could potentially lead to your demise at any given moment, depending on the scenarios you'll face. some challenges can be truly rewarding, and just as easily it could be fatally punishing. but i suppose like most rogue-like games, it's something you get used to after a while, for better or for worse.
all in all, it's a pretty interesting concept, and an overall fun game that has lots of possibilities, and thus a lot of replayability. looking forward to the sequel, to see what improvements the developers have added.

RUINER has to be my favourite game of 2017 so far. Though it isn't perfect, nor is it extremely innovative; it is an extremely enjoyable game that far. RUINER is a perfect example of "A whole that outweighs the some of its parts".
Pros:
-The gameplay. The mix of twin-stick shooter and beat'em up is one that works extremely well. While not every weapon or character ability feels powerful on its own, the ability to mix and match on the fly allows for some really interesting combinations. Because of this, there is a lot of oppurtunity for replayability.
-The visuals. The cyberpunk artstyle is one that we don't often see done well in games, but RUINER captures it perfectly. It brought back feelings of Blade Runner with a coat of red neon paint.
-The soundtrack. Ranging from booming EDM to eerie synth to emotional choir vocals. Every track is great in its own way, and really sets the tone for the game world.
-The plot. While a lot of people complain that the story is very linear and the ending being a bit anti-climactic. I find that RUINERs plot works great in context to the game. Because the story is very simple and easy to follow, with only a few twists and reveals, it allows for more world building. Thankfully the devs included a Codex to the game, allowing you to stop at any time and read up on the expansive amount of lore the game world has. Even though the hub world felt small and had limited interaction, there was a lot to look at and learn about, resulting in a very believable game world, and overall a more immersive experience for me.
Cons:
-Playtime. The story is pretty short, I completed it in about 7 hours, including exploration of every level and completing the CATS sidequest in the hub world. This wouldn't be as much of a problem for me if there were a New Game+, but sadly as of right now there isn't one included. (REIKON PLEASE!!!)
-Sound Design. This is a weird one for me, since everything sounds amazing, from the ambient noise of each stage, to the explosive sounds of the firearms. But single most important thing I need to hear in an action game is feedback, which this game lacks almost entirely. Feedback is the effect you hear when your attacks connect with an enemy (ex: hitmarker sounds in fps games) and when an enemy attack connects with you (ex: player character grunts/louder impact sounds). RUINER lacks these effects, which can result in some extremely frustrating fights. In the heat of the moment, especially on later stages, you don't have time to constantly check your health bar to see if you're getting hit. This desperately needs to be added.
OVERALL: 8/10

Desktop Dungeons is one of my favorite games.  The mix of roguelike and puzzle gameplay is extremely well-balanced to a satisfying difficulty combined with near-endless replayability.
You control a hero exploring a randomly-generated dungeon, gathering powerups, equipment, and spells (glyphs).  The enemies are purely reactive: they only damage you in retaliation to your attacks.  This mechanic sets Desktop Dungeons apart from most roguelikes, and your ability to plan ahead results in gameplay comparable to a puzzle game.  Situations can become increasingly complex as you progress further and obtain more unlockables (such as the various gods you can worship in the dungeon).
You (and the enemies) regenerate your health and mana through revealing unexplored tiles, allowing you to recharge between encounters.  Your resources are all finite, so you can't simply grind your way to victory.  Instead, careful play is needed to gain bonus XP from killing higher-level enemies without exhausting your ability to recover before you face the boss (or bosses).
The skill ceiling is extremely high, and the more difficult scenarios are quite brutal.  When you first start playing even the easier "Normal" dungeons will provide a challenge.  You can tilt the odds in your favor by spending kingdom gold (essentially your winnings from successful runs) on preparations that should make your hero more effective.   I will note that the most difficult dungeons are unnecessary to complete the main storyline, but beating them unlocks powerful items as well as four monster races.
Dungeons are reasonably short (my runs are roughly 10-40 minutes depending on the situation), but the game is extremely replayable.  The wide selection of classes, races, and items allows for a wide diversity of viable builds.  I have played over a hundred hours and completed the main storyline, but it will be quite some time before I feel that I have exhausted the postgame content.  The Enhanced Edition additionally introduces a 'Daily Dungeon' feature allowing you to compare your results to other players.

While HexCells is still probably my favorite from this dev, CrossCells stands out on its own as a fun puzzle game. It's a bit complex in the sense that one has to keep a lot of mental notes about each board while solving it, with no in-game option to tentatively mark squares à la Minesweeper's question mark. I'm not particularly good at that, so each puzzle felt like my brain trying to balance ten spinning plates at once. This aspect made the later puzzles feel weirdly intense, in stark contrast to the much more laid back nature of the other *Cells games. It's not what I expected, but I enjoyed it nonetheless.
I played through CrossCells over the course of about a week, and during that span the developer fixed my only two real complaints about the game: the intro to multiplication is a bit more intuitive than it was originally, and there is now a toggle to switch off the ripple effect on the cursor. Useful, timely patches, what an amazing concept. Some might take issue with the unforgiving nature of this game--the player is immediately kicked out of a puzzle as soon as a mistake is made. That's how I played the other *Cells games, so it didn't bother me.
A note on playtime: I left the game running in the background a few times, actual playtime was closer to about three hours.
These games are some of the only ones I buy blindly nowadays, and they're always a treat.

I'm recommending this game for one, very big reason: the gameplay is absolutely terrific. It is fast, frenetic, fun and just fantastic. Sprint, swing, slide, shoot and beat your way to victory in a parkour-with-weapons style game against 3 other opponents across myriad of maps, including many, MANY user-made ones.
As opponents fall too-far behind in the race, they are eliminated (when they fall so far behind as to be just out-of-screen). Once this happens to the first opponent, the screen begins to shrink slowly, making it progressively more difficult to keep up and stay in the race. It's all very tense and exciting. When there is only one runner left, they gain a point, and then everyone respawns to do it again. The first runner to reach 3 points, wins. Simple, yet extraordinarily effective.
Throw into this a variety of fun and inventive weapon pick-ups (ice-lasers that freeze those ahead of you, dropping crates behind you for opponents to trip over, and so forth), and the whole shebang becomes hilarious, as players switch positions from first to last and back to first again, over and over. You can play against bots, local multiplayer or online in ranked matches. If you can manage to get 3 friends together in your living room, with a few drinks, entertainment is guaranteed.
However, there are some drawbacks, as things stand. Firstly, to point out,
, so bear that in mind. I'm quite positive these will all be fixed in the future. But they're frustrating nonetheless. To start with, the matchmaking system is quite appalling. You can wait many, many minutes to be matched up with 3 opponents, even this weekend when the game was free, and there were tens of thousands of concurrent users.
The initial loading times once you find your opponents can be ludicrously long, too, for such a simple game. And once you begin, you may find that half (or even on rare occasions, all) the game may already be over, as the game has started before you've loaded in. This works the other way too, unfortunately, and i've won a game while watching my 3 opponents stand stock still, as they hadn't loaded in yet. Though to be fair, once you've eventually found 3 other players, the loading times reduce significantly and the desync ends, even when choosing different maps (with those same opponents)
Also on rare occasions, you can be so far ahead on a map that YOU are eliminated from the round instead of your opponents, which completely defeats the objective of the game.
Like i said, i'm quite sure these problems will be fixed when the game hits 1.0.
So with that, i give this a big thumbs up. If the game is lucky, you could even see it go the way of Rocket League in its popularity, and it even reminds me a little of Nidhogg in how it makes something so involving out of a seemingly simple idea. Lots of fun indeed.

If there's one downside to this game it's that after playing it for the 128 hours I have on record as of this writing the music seems awfully repetitive, but seriously after all that time I cannot complain about something so trivial.
The combat is also mediocre, not terrible by any means, just not fantastic. It's totally functional and there are hardly any annoying bugs, and nothing I can think of as totally gamebreaking. There are even enemies that have varied abilities and attack patterns that keep things from going too stale, but at later combat levels you just know what to expect, and nothing's really going to surprise you.
There are a number of heroes that play uniquely, though, so you can find something that works with your play style ideally, and you can also mix-and-match which heroes play on which days through every playthrough.
