While enticing trailers shows a fast paced game with brutal combat, makes the game look awesome. It is broken, simply by the game not being able to keep up with the combat.
My Biggest gripe with the game is that enemies deal damage before their animation starts, this means that you will take damage from things you cant event possibly react to. This means you have to ♥♥♥♥♥ around instead of taking the fight to the enemies. Along with this the controls are quite horrible. Now i played the game relying heavily on the slowdown dash + slash combo, with the dash causing the enemies to get staggered while i could land a hit or 2 before having to dash again.
Having to hold right click (simply clicking make you normal dash), then left click, then left click again as soon as you release right click to then again hold right click and then repeat. This is works well... untill it dosent. Heres is why. First off sometimes the game slows down to let you know you hit the enemy so that you stagger them, except sometimes the enemies arent staggered. This means you take a face full of damage without being able to respond well to it since you are in the state of wanting to deal dmg since they should be staggered.
Othertimes when you left click to put down a dash point and release right click, you dont dash and is then killed, not fun.
Another problem is when placing down a dash point, if you cannot dash to that exact location, no marker will be placed not even one, close to where you are aimning, this again means that you just stand there like a retard taking a shotgun to the face. This could easily be solved by either having the dash point close to where you were aiming or by having the game make it clear, like with a loud sound n stuff that you did NOT place a dash point, so you dont exit bullet time before being able to react and redo the dash marker.
This wouldent be all too bad since you can keep trying to play more and more carefully, constantly overdoing everything so that you dont get ♥♥♥♥ed by the game. Except a lot of the difficulty comes from arenas where you are just figthing the same enemies over and over again, making more and more likely that you get killed due to the game ♥♥♥♥ing you over before the encounter ends.
This means that i either get S/S+ after a fight or get c-a if the fight goes on for too long.
The mini-bosses are also super easy and no different from normal enemies except larger health pools and a flashy intro.
The other bosses are rather lame since you are forced to use abilities and weapons that you dont normally use (cause they are boring). And then when you have beaten the boss you have to manually switch back all the skills since there isent even a skill "loadout" that you can return to. (Looking at you Mother (>_>)  )
for the record i played on normal difficulty and wouldent even wanna try hard, since it would just be even more one shots due to the game completely failing to follow the flow of combat.

This game may only be of interest to you if you are interested in American trucks but don't want to use the mods for Euro Truck Simulator.
For a game that has only been recently released, the content included isn't as much as I expected. Driving with only three trucks and two states does get boring quite quickly. However, the developers are working on new trucks and more states for the game, however I feel that they should have postponed release until they received the licenses from the truck manufacturers and at least a few more states developed. At the time this review was written, a new state is in public beta testing stages, however this did come four months after the game's release.
In-game, you cannot fault the gameplay. However if you have played Euro Truck Simulator 2 in the past, you may feel as if this is just a re-skin, since it shares the same base as Euro Truck Simulator 2. You may feel as if it's a deja vu, as you are seeing the same UI design as Euro Truck Simulator 2.
However, this isn't all a bad thing. The gameplay from ETS2 has had a lot of work been put into it from its release in 2012, and every single feature that makes the game good can be found here. SCS Software, the developer, have stated that both games will receive any new feature they develop, so you can be assured that you aren't left out on updates to the game.
Driving is a pleasure. Cruising through America was more relaxing than I thought it would be. It's obvious that SCS have put a lot of time and effort into the game's world. Though the lack of content hindered this pleasure a bit, I still got a few days of joy from it.
In conclusion, I give it a 7/10. The gameplay of this game is magnificent, and you can never go wrong at a rather low price. However, this doesn't hide the fact that the lack of content hinders your continuous enjoyment from driving through beautiful American scenery. I recommend this, however I would say wait a bit until more content gets put into the game.

Hard Reset was going good until I ran into a Level 12 spawn bug. Once it occurred, I could not progress. This bug is so bad I wrote an email to the Flying Hog. However, they have not solved the issue and so I have to give this game a negative review so that others will not have to buy a flawed game. I would have given this game a positive review if they didn't have a gamebreaking bug. You just press Q and E to alternate between a kinetic projectile weapon and an energy weapon. Fundamentally, both guns are extremely similar.
Gameplay-wise, it's repetitive but the boss battles are intriguing enough. You go around killing little bots, medium bots and big bots. You pick up red boxes for the projectile weapons, blue boxes for the energy weapons, green boxes for health regen and orange boxes for credits. Shields regenerate on their own. The story is just boring and the closest game you can compare it to would be Deus Ex, which is way better than Hard Reset.
Conclusion, do not buy this game until the bug is fixed. Considering that this game was released in 2011, you can guess that they sat on the bug for a very long time.

Point and shoot, WASD keys

Games are forced saved at check points. You can't choose to save the game at any point of time.

You just run into one location, fight a combination of the following bots. Rinse and Repeat.
a. Little bots

You start at level 1 in a one screen dungeon, and try to get strong enough to beat the lvl 10 boss.
In the meantime, you will have to explore, get equipped, beat lower level foes to gain experience and get stronger.
During the process, you will constantly juggle risk vs reward since every decision you take will probably burn some precious  ressource or some other. You will always run the risk of driving yourself into a corner.
But since the dungeon is quiet short, any mistake will only set you back 10-20 minutes at most and you will itch to try again one more time.
As you chain the  dungeons, you will be able to unlock new classes, races, loot, dungeons and options. Each of these expand the ways you might tackle the next dungeon, adding variety and more difficult decisions to the mix.
I found the process very addictive as you always have the impression to improve in meaningful ways; and each run is short enough to fit in a coffeebreak.
In short: very enjoyable game.

The First time I ran into this game was years ago when it was a contender in the Independent Games Festival. I remember downloading other contest entries as well, but the alpha of this game was the one that really grabbed my attention.

So, its Saturday night, around 1 Am, i just completed my second playthough of Kotor1, i wasnt tired, so i checked out some Steam sales, and there it was, Hard reset, with a price tag of 1,40€, the reviews were about 60% positive, it looked Sci-fi which i love, and well, i knew what to expect, but with that prize tag, it didnt really matter.
And now having completed the game and the DLC included, heres what i think.
The word that comes into mind is painfully mediocre, i mean just about everything, the plot, combat, looks, ai, its all really really mediocre, the game is kinda like a warm bottle of Coca cola, it wont make you sick or anything, but its not good (except this game was cheaper then a bottle of Cola)
It really reminded me of a Terminator FPS game i got for PS2 a loooong time ago...
So the good:
hm, its pretty hard to come up with just about anything, the enviroments are filled with enviromental hazards, so you can plan around with them, some of the guns are okay, theres a few things to upgrade. What i did enjoy was seeing the evolution, this game came from the studio that would make Shadow warrior 1 few years later, and you can really see that on this game, gladly that game is better too.
The bad:
-This is one of those games that go with the "weapon module" type of thing, like many games, it didnt go too well, you essentially have two guns, one for normal ammo and on that uses energy based ammo, each of the two weapons then can be upgraded into 5 different weapon modules, you got the basic assault rifle, shotgun, railgun, granade launcher etc etc. The problem here is that you run out of ammo fast, since half the weapons use the same ammo, for example, the shotgun and missile launcer draw from the same ammo pool, another problem is that, for me, it rendered some weapons completelly useless, if you had a pistol and an assault rifle, that would use the same ammo, why would you really use the pistol.  And since some weapons were bad and some weapons really good, and they used the same ammo,  i just basically did the whole game with about 3 or 4 weapons out of 10.
- The plot is really REALLY weak, its told with these comic book style sheets, with text bubbles in them that were voice overed , and well, there were few characters, all of them weak, the plot made no sense at all, your basically a guy working for this PMC company or so, after a while you are send out to kill a guy, you reach the guy, he tells you not to trust the company, and youre like "okay" and then proseed to not trust the company. The main character is a proper edge lord too.
The game included a DLC that continuet right after the main plot and i didnt even realize that i had transitioned into the DLC area, i only noticed that when i started to get DLC achievements. I googled where the main game ended to find that out. So its really some next level weaknes.
-Combat is not done too well, it completelly lacks the "flow" and synergy that Shadow warrios combat has, you have a bunch of different typical enemies, i played it thogh on hard, and many of the enemies were really bullet spongy, when i started i was wondering if i even did the right thing, unloading my starting assault rifle on them, but the just take time to kill. You can jump, but not over most obstacles, so thats useless, and getting cornered will kill you every time since the only mobility you get is Straight, back, left or right.
- Ridiculous level design, many levels consist of you doing some meaningless objective, and really often you run into some obstacles, which can be neutralized by pressing a button, after you have cleared the area,  MANY of these obstacles could be climbed or jumpet over, if your character could do that. So it just feels like you have objectives for the sake of having them.
- Lots of minor things that were weird, like how the game has interface to read PDF´s, which only appear in the DLC, and there were about 5 of them there. So through the main game i was wondering where the hell do you get them, some bugs like getting stuck on things, invisible walls, spring that lasts for about 5 seconds, absolutelly dead world even tho its a city.
This is a game where nothing is done well, nothing redeems it, with this plot it might aswell just be an arena based shooting gallery, i really have no reason to recommend it, theres a ps4/xbone/pc remake of this game too, which i have no real intrest of checking out, but i guess if you liked that and want to play the original, get it with a cheap price.

TLDR: If you're into logic/puzzles, math, and rogue-like elements, the games don't get more entertaining than this.
The Good:
-The necessity to use different strategies and builds depending on the levels. There's no single strategy that will beat the game for you.
-The difficulty is almost spot-on throughout the entire game. It's only easy in the beginning. By the end it's brutally hard, but you feel accomplished.
-Fun in small spurts or for long periods of time.
-There are a ton of upgrades that keep the game fresh.
The Bad:
-The more you lose on one level the harder it is to remain patient and play well (more of a personal flaw, but it applies greatly here).
-The randomness of the "boss", glyph drops, enemies, etc. can break/ruin a run for you.  Takes some luck on harder levels.
Verdict: If you can deal with feeling dumb as you try to figure out the best strategies and are patient enough to not blow a fuse as you repeat levels multiple times, the game is great.  The upgrades keep the game and strategies fresh and you feel great accomplishment as you make your way through the harder levels.  For the price they are asking, you get great value for your buck.  I'd give it a solid 9/10.

I think the main reason I didn't really like Desktop Dungeons is that it is not at all what I expected. I thought this game was going to be a rogue-like dungeon-crawler rpg, but after a few hours of play I realized that the game simply isn't this at all. It is actually an rpg skin over top of a resource optimization puzzle game. The dungeons aren't really about battles, equipment, or spells (though all these things are in the game), they are about whether you can exploit the idiosynchrasies of the game mechanics to squeeze a few extra xp out of the dungeon so that you can ultimately beat the boss.
Let me explain: There's a limited (and small) number of enemies in each dungeon, as well as a limited amount of gold and healing. You start at level 1. The boss is at level 10. You've got to level your character up and accumulate stuff to have any chance against the boss. But here's the rub: if you simply kill the enemies in order from lowest level to highest, you don't stand much chance. You need to take advantage of the battle mechanics to kill higher level monsters than you really should be able to in sneaky, gamey ways. Then, you'll get bonus experience and reach a higher level faster. Hence, the whole game becomes a puzzle of how you can squeeze all the resources out of a limited supply. This kind of puzzle is just not what I signed up for, and I found playing this way to be very effective but very tedious and dull.
If you are looking for a puzzle game combined with rpg elements, you might like this. Otherwise, I'd skip it.

I've been playing Desktop Dungeons since the alpha, signed up during the beta, happily redeemed my key on Steam and have put in countless hours. It's genuinely one of the best puzzle games ever made - it has a roguelike sheen and borrows heavily from Dungeon Crawl Stone Soup (which is my roguelike of choice anyways) but it follows a certain iterative structure, and builds into something that requires a lot of math, resource management, and long-term thinking with short-term heuristics on trying to figure out the best choice when you don't have all of the information in front of you. It's genuinely good, more than well worth the price point, and I'd suggest it to anybody who asked and try to push it on a few people who didn't either.
Don't go in expecting a formal RPG - it does get hard, fast, but it's much much more forgiving than it seems, and while the learning curve is steep, it pulls you right up along it. I would only refrain from recommending it if you're looking for not even a more casual experience, but just something that doesn't require you to do a weird amount of math on the fly. Otherwise, it's a game that could happily belong in everyone's library.

I really don't know what the description of this game is going on about, calling itself an "Economic studio". While the economic model is interesting: unowned laborers decide where to live/work based on distance and cost/salary, the AI games have no settings or options, just everyone thrown in together on one tiny map where the AI will always make roughly the same decisions and outcomes, and build some strange-looking, tiny industrial blob. The tools to view the in-game economy that has developed are underpowered and unhelpful, and it is basically impossible to find the information you would need to micromanage your production.
Aside from that, the game, in its current state, is very limited. There are only a small handful of production chains, and a pathetically small maximum map size. The game advertises multiplayer, but my client wasn't able to connect to their matchmaking servers.
Running the game just to see what kind of economy the AI will set up can be mildly interesting the first time, but once that point is reached there's nothing to do aside from look at vague, scattered charts for an individual building's production, without any proper context of its relation to the economy as a whole, and without being able to discern any useful information for its impact on the game's economy. Once the AI fills up the incredibly tiny map you just have to sit around tweaking numbers and hoping one of the other companies goes out of business eventually so that it clears up a few tiny plots of land for whatever you had planned next.
Maybe I'm not supposed to look at this as a "Game", but given the lack of feedback for what's happening, I can't imagine it being a very useful "Economic simulator" either.  It feels very unfinished, with very little to do and a terrible UI. The developer doesn't include any sort of tutorial or guide, and while it's not too hard to figure out what's happening on your own, this period of learning for yourself is very conveinent for the dev, since Steam has a no-refund policy past 2 hours of playtime.

I've been playing warframe for a long time, and it's a fantastic F2P.  Great visuals, AAA level gameplay, great storyline and fantastic VAs make this a truly enjoyable game.

Note: I played the game about 80% through prior to the 1.1 patch that fixed a few things. I finished it post-patch and replayed a few levels to see if my original concerns were met.
This is another enjoyable and well designed puzzle game by Matthew Brown.  If you've played any of his games already (HexCells, SquareCells) and enjoyed them, chances are that you are the type of person that would enjoy CrossCells as well.
CrossCells takes the basic foundation of a nonogram puzzle and adds it's own new mechanics, as well as a heavy dose of arithmetic.  Each puzzle is well designed and will have you really churning out logical ways to elminate squares to work through the puzzle.
This may end up being Brown's most devisive game, and I can see how some players may be put off from the heavy emphasis on equations.  The player may end up stopping for long periods of time working out possible equations and how those may fit or not fit the puzzle multiple steps down the path to the solution.  It can feel like a lot more work than the more straight forward HexCells or SquareCells.  I think it will come down to personal taste on whether or not you enjoy this type of puzzle as much as others, but there is no doubting they are well designed and challenging puzzles.
There are 50 puzzles total and while they are all great, I always wish there were more.  I understand how difficult these must be to design, but I'll keep my fingers crossed for an expansion or something one day (and SquareCells and HexCells too!)
I want to add (to help explain to potential players) that pre 1.1 patch I had an issue with one of the mechanics and many other early reviewers did as well.  The way multiplication was introduced was a bit mishandled in my opinion.  I was able to figure out the rules within the game, but doing so required a bit of trial and error to "prove" the games rules so to speak.  When dealing with equations, order of operations is important and the game wasn't quite clear on how it handles the order of addition and multiplication.  Thankfully this is all cleared up post patch, so please keep that in mind when reading other reviews that mention this as a negative.  The slightly tweaked levels do a great job showing the player the way multiplication works without blatently spelling it out.  Another minor thing was the ripple effect is quite distracting at first and looks quite bad when it goes over text.  Thankfully, it doesn't interfere with the puzzle blocks or numbers and post-patch can now be toggled.  Thank you to Matt Brown for quickly addressing these issues, I think the game is much better for it.
CrossCells is another fine addition to a great library by Brown and I'd recommend it to all puzzle fans.  Please keep in mind if reading other reviews that I believe the early problems have been answered by the patch and you can play without any concerns.  Thanks again to Matthew Brown for a great puzzle game and I'll be looking forward to his future work.

At last, Hand of Fate has been dealt. I... couldn't resist. In any case there is some truth to that considering how long it took me to finish the game versus what I expected, but I'll get around to that in due time. For now let's see how this rather outlandish action/card game hybrid works out in action.
Thing is I've already told you the basic structure of the game and its main hook – dual nature of an action RPG married to a card game. I wouldn't call it CCG because that constitute a whole different set of parameters Hand of Fate [thankfully] doesn't indulge in, but allow me to break it down a bit further mechanically in how it works. You only assume direct control over your character in situations that call for combat scenarios, most of what you'll be doing, or in rarer cases when you have to maneuver through a trap-filled level. Other than those most of Hand of Fate's gameplay is relegated to a game board where you move from tile to tile ever weary of your dwindling food supplies lest you go hungry. Major attraction lies in how these two segments interacts with one another in a symbiotic relationship. There are dozens of cards with different effects ranging from quest chains that will take a while to complete as you gradually unlock new stages, straight up combat skirmishes like ambushes or alike, etc but most cards have a SITUATION to deal with. Keep in mind you also get to make decisions and they're not all positive but there's usually the best one for most cards that will either unlock a token aka rewards you get when you finish a round or have a decision to make. For example, one of the few entirely beneficial cards is The Maiden that simply asks you what do you want be it food, gold, more life, etc. These are rare and few in-between seeing as most cards can have a negative outcome or outright refuse to play out for you unless you've met some prerequisite.
What I'm trying to say is cards are varied and remain a mystery until you come across them in game proper so they can reveal themselves. Keeping in mind this also extends to things that have more tangible impact on your character like gear or curses/blessings you can easily see how the game maintains this air of mystique until you unlock most of the cards and know exactly what to choose for best outcomes. Sadly, there's also another factor at play here – dreaded RNG. Good majority of cards contains a choice between four cards, which can have varied number of successes and failures, and you have to choose the correct one after they're shuffled. Speed with which they're shuffled varies and can be affected with certain equipment or level of difficulty which depends on your character, but goddamn if it didn't feel like the world was out to get me at times. This is simply the name of the game with RNG systems, though.
You'll note I've skipped my usual blabbering about story which is something I do first in reviews, but it's valid in this case considering there effectively is no story to Hand of Fate. There is the Dealer and you're there to play his game, that's it. That's not to say the entire thing isn't incredibly moody the way he narrates based on how the game is developing, what your character's status is, whether enemies are returning after you've defeated them, etc. Very much like in Bastion having an interactive narrator adds a ton to the game, but I especially found it intriguing how he gets more antagonistic towards you as you progress and gets bitter when you defeat his cards or when “these things are too good for you”. Considering the Dealer is the only real character in the game and so much hinges on his delivery I'd say it's a job well done.
While being powered by Unity engine doesn't spell doom and gloom, despite what we hear from people who know about it even less than I do, game does have some minor performance problems as it tries to hide the loading screens by seamlessly transitioning from the board into combat for couple of seconds accompanied by jitters. It never went away for me and I just had to accept it. Speaking of combat I was disappointed to see a very, very basic Arkham-style one present and you don't get much variety outside of two abilities that depend on your weapon/artifact. Enemy roster fares a bit better and benefits from having four factions with couple of units each in addition to bosses you'll be facing to fill in your cabinet of cards along the way. I do wish combat could've been expanded a bit more in some way because even had I played the game in 2015 when it was released old BamHam combat had already worn out its welcome.
Presentation itself is more than acceptable as far as I'm concerned. Once again it's the Dealer himself who steals the spotlight with his emoting and gesticulation, but what game lacks in sheer polygon count it most definitely makes up for in art style and employing an intelligent color scheme to color code things for the player. It could have of course benefited from more common enemies, but once you're up against a larger number based on what the cards throw at you combined with level hazards you appreciate what's there. I would be remiss if I didn't mention the outstanding soundtrack which sadly gets relegated to the background more often than not considering you're either focusing on what the Dealer is saying or you're rushing past it all. Shame because some of the songs are criminally good and you just hear short clips.
In conclusion, then. Would I recommend Hand of Fate? For sure I would, just keep in mind a game of this type brings with it a random factor that might annoy you. I know it's highly frustrating to breeze through combat encounters, until the finale when game sadly stumbles and puts you through a predictable boss gauntlet, only to be gypped by chance cards and lose your health when food runs out with no shop in sight. Not to mention there also happened to be sudden rise in difficulty in the last two-three games as you get burdened by harsh conditions that keep pilling on.
This is definitely the kind of game I might keep around on my hard drive for a bit longer if only to try out the Endless mode and other characters.

Unique and fascinating game in which your hero navigates dungeons (monsters, traps, and chance-based encounters) based on cards you accumulate, mixed in with random ones based on the scenario. The narrator, a master of fate, creates your dungeons by flipping over cards as you choose a path. The more advanced the scenario, the more deadly the cards he mixes in. Players can let the computer decide what's a good mix, or you can choose your own deck. You'll need chances to get equipment, health, and so on as each scenario you begin with only the basics. Also, many cards have built in quests, so when you complete those, it opens up another card in that quest line. Keeps the game fresh (even if you die, you may have made progress toward a quest line.)
Death can be frustrating, you die and the entire dungeon is over. Combat is a little tricky to master as there isn't a major tutorial (and some monsters require a specific maneuver or you'll never beat them, e.g. lizard men with shields). Still, it's worth it.
Finally, the narrator's voice and dialog is fantastic and really makes this game shine. It was a blast.
Two Cons:
-  difficulty when you get to the higher tier scenarios. They are insane
-  RNG plays a huge role. In the higher tier ones, a single bad random number and you're screwed.

text: Have you ever tried to prove your worth, yet seem like anything you do isn't good enough in the eyes of others? This game represents the feeling of seeking validation, and it does so flawlessly. Owlboy is a game about an owl-human hybrid named Otus, who tries to prove himself to his master by saving his world from a band of pirates searching for three ancient relics. Not surprisingly, you play as Otus, flying around multiple dungeons and meet new friends along the way. These characters come with abilities that will be essential to puzzle solving. The cast of characters is definitely this game's strong suit. And the way Otus interacts with these characters is heartwarming, because that is what this game is about--not doing things alone. Because your friends will lend you an extra hand or two. I have some small nitpicks; the lack of a map made navigation a tad bit cumbersome, and controls will take some time getting used to. But overall, this game was definitely worth playing 10 years in the making. With a relatable protagonist, gorgeous visuals, stellar sound and a touching story, Owlboy will be sure to leave a lasting impression.

It's Dungeon Keeper 3....and it's AWESOME!
The good:
War for the Overworld is Dungeon Keeper 3 in all but name! Richard Ridings (of the original Dungeon Keeper games) is back voicing the mentor, telling you to get building glorious dungeons to house your minions. The Empire is banging on your dungeon doors and you need all the help you can get.
This all add's up to a lot of fun than fans of the original Dungeon Keeper games never thought we would see again all because a small but very solid dev team Kickstarted this game and I'm so very glad they did.
There has been a constant stream of patches and interaction from the devs since I purchased the game and to be honest, they are putting big comapny names to shame in how fast they are to respond to issues.
The bad:
The game is still a bit rough around the edges and unfinnished in parts. Certain parts of the game have yet to be finnished fully (such as skirmish mode which is to be added later this year) and there is still a lot of ingame tweaking done by the devs. Save games can also be a risk as a quick patch can render a save file unuseable (though thankfully it only means restarting a level). It's also one of those games where you'll find yourself binge playing through the whole thing if you're not careful.
So..should you buy this game? Most certainly. The main campaign is finnished and multiplayer works. The unfinnished parts are just..extras. It's great fun and it's one of those rare titles where the devs are acctually doing what they say they will do.

-Combat is pretty bad, and seems more gear than skill based at the moment. I also read a chart about what damage the different weapons do and the stats are all wonky. - Awesome sandbox mmo that isn't worth playing free to play and is pay to win.
After skipping over this mmo for a while due to hearing about all the pay to win aspects and seeing the mixed/negative reviews on steam I finally decided to give it a go, and I'm really glad I did. The combat is your typical mmo tab target style (ie World of Warcraft), but with a combo system that makes abilities work off one another, and it works fine. Where ArcheAge really shines is in its sandbox elements. You can attempt to kill most players, regardless if they are from your faction or not in zones that allow it. You can sail the enormous ocean on a clipper with a small group of friends doing PvE content, or looking for other vessels full of players to murder and plunder. You can sail the ocean on giant warships with your guild doing those same things, engaging in naval battles, boarding enemy ships, doing PvE content. You can find a spot to call your home and build a house, a farm, raise crops and animals. The housing zones aren't instanced either, so while finding a spot can be difficult, once you do it really feels like you're living in the game world, with other players as neighbors and a community that you contribute to. The free to play should be treated as just a free trial, as you are extremely limited in what you can accomplish. Also, this game is a huge time sink. Since it heavily focuses on pvp, to stay relevant in gear you need to commit large amounts of hours or large amounts of real life cashmoney, or both. So while you can't buy actual gear with micro transactions, you can buy certain items that sell for heaps, giving you the ingame gold to aquire better gear. Definitely worth playing if you have the time and money.

META: This game is entirely deserving of every accolade it has received over the past year... the transition from early access to final release has been not only one of the fastest but one of the most massive jumps in content quality that I have ever seen. Larian Studios has used the current generation's tools   (Early Access, Social Media, and Crowdfunding) to their advantage in such a delicate and positve way that it has restored my faith the aforementioned services. It has been clear from the start tht Sven Icke and Co. at Larian have wanted nothing more than to bring the Isometric RPG into the future, and they have done so with gret aplomb and miraculous style! Divinity as an IP is one that boasts so many original ideas, yet bows reverently to the tenets of past RPG titles. As such, it is with great satisfaction that I saw the title occupy a position in the TOP SELLING PC GAMES OF ALL TIME  on metacritic; along with the greats such as Baldur's Gate, Quake, Portal, Bioshock, The Witcher III, GTA V, and even HALF-LIFE! This coming from a small Scandinavian studio is an achievement that one wishes they could attain MAYBE ONCE in their lifetime.
Aside from my compliment showering, these are the things I would like to talk about in more detail:
The combat and mechanics in this game are FAR beyond the polish and intricacy of D:OS I. The combat encounters are challenging yet more nuanced. I believe D:OS 1 was the icebreaker for Larian, but in this title they have expounded brilliantely upon the conventions and ideas of the first iteration. Encounters feel much more balanced and well thought out. The entirety of the Skill / Talent / Perk system seems refined, and they have removed supercilious aspects while doubling down on what works, a method that all successful AAA studios employ. The origin characters are fantastic, featuring a wide range of classes, playstyles, and attitudes for players to enjoy. Also, the storyline does a much better job of connecting to the actual mechanics of the game, which goes a long way to making the title feel polished and unified,
I don't want to spoil anyting else for future players. If you like ANY sort of RPG, JRPG, Tactical/Strategy game, do not hesitate. This game will blow you away time and time again.

Let me preface this by saying; this was the first game that actually got me interested in the genre of Rogue-likes. Previously I had played around with Vulture for Nethack, The Binding of Isaac (although it doesn’t necessarily fit my idea of Rogue-like), Don’t Starve, and some various flash games that just never sparked interest.
Now here is what Desktop Dungeons does right
- Great for beginners:
If you're willing to waltz throught the tutorial, which I recommend you do, you'll begin to believe that you understand the game a lot more than you do, but the tutorial drops you off at a point where the learning curve is much less steep.
- Captivating and Hilarious:
Each of the missions that you run through, each have taken me around 3-5 runs before completion, have left me thirsty for much much more, and considering the expandability of your kingdom and the available upgrades, I believe I haven't even sank my teeth into the first quarter of this game and I love it. Going back to the tutorial,  the narrator is hilarious and there are always little things they add into the game that make me giggle. Never a full on guffaw, but a solid giggle.
- Difficulty:
Beyond giggling to the moon at the minor jokes that are at hand, Desktop Dungeons has set an immense level of difficulty, which parallels its learning curve. If the dungeon begin to feel too easy for you, go ahead and try out the puzzles up the mountain, I promise it won't be at all a cake walk. The puzzles really make you go indepth with the mechanics of the game and how each item affects how your character attacks.
And here is what I think has gone wrong (only one thing)
- Price:
I don't believe the price point is necessarily a fair one. The only reason I have this game now, is because I got it in a humble bundle, which is still going on until 7/12/16 where I paid a little over half for this game, and plenty of others, rather than its full price. I don't think I would have bought it otherwise, but I believe if you're on the fence about buying it, you absolutely should.

I could not recommend this game in its' previous release state. However, now I actually can. After its' 1.1 patch, the majority of what this game was missing in its release verison has finally been added.
War for the Overworld, as a game, is...dungeon keeper 3. There really isn't another way to describe it. If Peter Molyneaux and the Bullfrog team were still around today, I feel the game we would have gotten would not be too far off from this. Are there flaws in this game? Obviously. Every game has flaws. But as far as managing to capture the feel of dungeon keeper and make an all-round fun game, this kickstarter title succeeds where higher-budget games such as the Dungeons series failed. With EA making no attempt to actually capitalize on a once great series, and in fact ruining it for a new generation by slamming a free to play business model that shames the series GREATLY (even paying off reviewers EA style couldn't keep dungeon keeper mobile's critic rating up high enough to appear worthwhile), it's nice to see we still have fans of the old game out there who want to see it made new.
Am I rambling a lot on what Dungeon Keeper was? Yep. For those of you unfamiliar with what I'm talking about, this is a game where you manage a...well, dungeon, from the perspective of an evil overlord. Throughout the campaign, rather than being the hero who explores and brings death to dungeons, you build the dungeon and fight back against the good. You can accomplish this through the use of powerful minions as well as various traps and such that your enemy won't (hopefully) see coming, and of course a little bit of god power for good measure (*zap*). You have minimal control over your minions, so this isn't exactly an RTS and it sure as all hell is NOT an actions per minute game - in fact, trying to go all MLG clicky-clicky on this game would likely just hinder you more than anything else. Your control consists of picking minions or imps up and throwing them where you want them to be and...well, hoping they do what you want. You can lay down rally flags to get everyone's attention to a specific spot, but if you try to keep them out for too long you'll end up with a bunch of unhappy minions telling the flag to♥♥♥♥♥♥off and going to bed. You also have to keep them regularly paid with gold, which handily is also the resource you use for literally everything else. Fail in this aspect, and minions will just pack up shop and leave to go elsewhere.
Map design is what made Dungeon Keeper and, as a result, War for the Overworld, extremely unique. There is not a lot of map when you actually get in - it's just a bunch of dirt, some impenetrable rocks, water, lava, maybe a chasm, and gold in the dirt. Oh, and your central dungeon core. Don't lose that...seriously. You have to dig out your own map, tile by tile, and lay down rooms in areas to correspond with what you want and your minions' needs - a lair to sleep, a slaughterpen to eat, a tavern to provide money for you and make people happy, a barracks to train, etc...and of course the arena where you can have minions fight to the death for no reason outside of entertainment. It appears to entertain the other minions to watch their brethren get slaughtered too...and of course, the other benefit to building your own map is deciding when and where to dig to place down traps and such, and if you happen to sight enemy traps...you can dig around them.
By now you may think this is a twisted, evil game where everything is gruesome and terrible. And you'd be right and wrong. While you do play as evil, this is a very lighthearted game as the original dungeon keeper games were. Featuring awesome voice narration from the original DK's narrator, you'll find yourself often having a lot of fun just from hearing some of the things minions have to say, or the random (but amusing) pop culture references made by the narrator.
And when you're done with the campaign, you'll find it is still very fun to play in skirmish or multiplayer modes. In these modes, you and up to 3 other AI or players will duke it out, each building their own dungeons and attacking one another for no reason other than ♥♥♥♥ you, my ground. Unlike the original dungeon keeper, War for the Overworld actually does a decent job of working properly in skirmish and multiplayer. While it was possible in Dungeon Keeper 2 to do the same, the game just didn't quite feel the same as it was very campaign-oriented. WFTO implements some new systems that help the game to work properly in either situation. There is also sandbox mode where you just build in a big, empty map free of gold or mana issues, and survival mode which is...honestly still being worked on and I have very little experience in it, but it's self explanatory.
Overall, this game is easily worth your $30. Hell, go the extra $10 and get the $40 version just for the soundtrack if nothing else - the soundtrack is pure evil and outstanding and it fits PERFECTLY with a game of this theme. This kickstarted game more than deserves your money (after a rocky launch).

I tried my hardest to really like ArcheAge. Even so much so as to force myself to overlook every flaw its produced throughout my "merry" experience. Honestly, I actually typed out a novel in this review, but then realized that no one's going to read a wall of text, even if said wall was broken into paragraphs.
So here's my summary mish mash...
ArcheAge is like the Arch Deluxe that McDonald's proudly promoted with a driving force back in the 90's. Unforunately, that driving force was straight into the ground. The game's clearly not meant for everyone, It's an "acquired" taste.
---
:: For Better Understanding ::
On paper, the game sounds like every MMO Vet's dream. It has an "intricate" crafting system , sandbox building, classic grinding experience, and a worthwhile struggle to late game. It sounds like it's literally a fantasy version of Pre-CE SWG mixed with hints of Everquest, Dark Ages of Camelot, and Guild Wars; all neatly wrapped in an Eastern MMO engine.
BUT! As I said, this is only on paper, the actual truth is that it half-asses everything that it could be. It took all the best features from other games and used only a fourth of what those features originally were, so you wind up with this unusual pile of scrap.
For those of you that can stick it out, good for you. I've clung to my fair share of dying MMOs, so I empathize, but I don't see this game going anywhere anytime soon. This ship is slowly sinking and only the dedicated fans are willing to go down with it. Newcomers will come and go, but the dedicated will remain.

The latest in the *cells puzzle game series. This one feels different, much more so than Squarecells differed from Hexcells. There's an arithmetic focus here, with additions and multiplications.
The puzzles remain good and challenging (In that regard it is more like Hexcells Plus than Hexcells), but there are two problems:
1) Unlike previous games not all the rules are given clearly, some have to be deducted by trial and error. The designer has thus tried an approach akin to The Witness, but it doesn't work as well, and can lead to needless frustrations.
2) The way the game treats errors is awful: any mistake wipes your progress  in the puzzle and takes you back to the main menu. I didn't like how it worked in previous games, but this is even worse. I'd much prefer if the game let you make your mistake and let you realise it yourself when you end up reaching an impossible situation. EDIT: I can gladly say that two of my three caveats have been patched out -- you can disable the shimmer and the puzzles no longer automatically fail upon your first mistake. Great to see a developer listening to feedback! Here's my original review when the game was released:
It's a Matthew Brown game, so you probably have some idea what kind of puzzles to expect: CrossCells is a math-based logic puzzle that's a variation on the basic idea of the Japanese kakuro (essentially a numbers crossword). And, for the most part, it delivers exactly what you want. But this is a recommendation with some caveats:
- The game is badly in need of a tool to mark cells as "maybes/maybe nots" instead of forcing you to commit to either locking in or deleting a cell.
- This is exacerbated by the game abruptly booting you back to the main menu upon a mistake. Let us play it through! It's tough to learn from your mistakes when the puzzle vanishes as soon as you make one.
- A minor one, but the shimmery effect on the white background can be somewhat visually irritating.
I still recommend it, particularly if you're a fan of Brown's previous games, but I would also rank this as his weakest game yet.

My god, was I torn between a good and a bad review. Why, you ask? Because of the final "boss". Hand of Fate challenges you to defeat 12 regular bosses, most of which are rather easy, but still somewhat fun, but the final boss pitches all 12 bosses against you. 3 at a time. With no chance of healing in between. Fun times. Since the game is also based around chance a lot you can simply have a run in which you are pretty screwed. While - in theory - you could win that fight even with your starting equipment and 1 health, that's the same as saying DS can be beaten that way. Yes, it can be done, but 1 mistake and that's it. Back to the pit. Start all over again. Basically I was hammering away at the final boss longer than at all 12 other bosses combined. About 3-4 hours or so on normal.
Now, more about the game. It's basically a card RPG with real time "Arkham-style" combat.
The good stuff:
- Great presentation and narrator. You're actually playing, well, a game of fate on a real game board against the dealer.
- A ton of variety - from different quest cards you can complete to unlock new cards, to equipment cards, curses, blessings, etc. there's pretty much something for every situation. And unlocking new stuff and reading all those fun stories is what kept me going.
- Bosses are all unique and at least sorta fun.
- Game can be played rather quickly.
- Endless mode with a lot of individual modifiers to test out.
The bad stuff:
- Sometimes the RNG just ♥♥♥♥s you over completely, which is "ok" in Endless mode, but was really annoying in story mode. For example, there are certain cards in the game, which have high requirements or require you to acquire another card in the run first, such as the metal ore and the monastery. Well, bad luck when the monastery is on a preceding floor than the ore. Then both cards are absolutely worthless.
- Chance cards are terribly designed. Basically you play a game of guess the correct card with success and failure states. These cards are then shuffled in front of your eyes. If you are lucky you can spot the correct card if the game lets you. Other times you just have only 1 success card and that one is shuffled so obscurely that you can only guess. Then the game may shuffle the cards two, three or four times and increase the shuffle speed, making it just a guessing game. And ob boy, those failures can completely kill a run, but attempting these cards is vital to get new equipment or get out of a bad situation, which you could not have avoided in the first place. I just feel like the design is taunting you and makes this unnecessary. A % chance would have seemed fairer.
- Trap cards are the worst. The camera is so wonky and the controls so terrible that it's hard to avoid damage in the more difficult ones. Especially when you then just stumble from one trap onto another. Fun times. And often there's not even anything to gain.
- Speaking of which, cards that only have negative effects and no way of avoiding them aren't "fun".
- Combat is extremely lackluster. You can attack, counterattack, block and dodge, as well as use a weapon ability and a character ability, if you have those. Some attacks are unblockable, some shields need to be broken to attack enemies. All very basic, but not executed well. Not only does it look terrible it also plays terribly and will be the one thing that will bore you very quickly.
- About encounters: ♥♥♥♥ you for throwing me into an arena with 2 bosses, 10 mobs and lots of traps on a CHANCE encounter. On the second to last floor. Yay.
Ultimately this game can be a lot of fun, but also somewhat frustrating at times, especially since you need to remember what each card does, lest you want to get cursed or lose Health or Food or Gold or Items...I'm gonna play a bit more in endless mode, but I don't see too much more long term fun to be had here.

If you are heavily into "strategic" Card Games (like Magic The Gathering) and expecting something like that: Hand of Fate will disappoint you. While the game demands choices from you, the concept is pretty much NOT MTG, not even Hearthstone.
But if you are a classic P&P-roleplayer, familiar with "solo-adventures" (usually released for The Dark Eye, but I assume others have published them as well), and/or somebody who grew up with those "Choose your own adventure"-books then I can truly recommend this game. And - as those "Choose your own adventure"-books - this game can get very addicting, even if you have to fight against the Ratman Hunting card for the bazillionth of time.
Basically you have 2 deck of cards - one forms your "dungeon" ( = the path to your goal which is to slay "the Jack of somethingsomething" or "king/queen of somethingsomething" like e.g. the Jack of Plague or The Queen of Dust), the other is your equipment. At the beginning of each adventure you can choose which cards you'll take along - some, however, HAVE to stay in the for the sake of the Story.
You sit opposing to the Card-Dealer, a shady man in a "ninja"-mask - or something The Elephant Man would be hiding under. He is basically your "enemy" - he lays out the cards, which form a path (sometimes a straight one, sometimes you can choose which faced-down card you want to look at); each card represents an event - like e.g. a goblin showing up, or you are entering a town where something happens. Some of those cards are even part of "mini-stories", so, while you are playing the game, you can unlock more parts of that story, earning bigger rewards, like equipment. These unlockable "tokens" you keep even when you die - which means that even a round where you don't get to defeat the King/Queen/Jack (or you got killed even before) you might have won something.
I like the little animations and the voice of the Card Dealer. Also I like the spider running around (you can turn the spider off), and I would not mind if the Spider would do more things (attempting to steal a token or a card) or something like that.
The Card Dealer is also a rich source of comments - sure, there will be a point where he is repeating himself, but often his remarks are kinda funny, like when he is bringing up subtle nerd-clichés (and yes, sometimes they are really surprisingly subtle for this kind of game).
The difficulty of that relatively simple concept is increased by you consuming "food" as a resource everytime you take a step. If you run out of food and your health drops to 0 you'll die. So yes - you can die from starvation. If there is a challenge you can overcome it successfully by choosing the right card in some form of "shell game" - only that you don't follow the little pea under the shell with your eyes, but the success-cards. You'll rarely die of you lose such a challenge, but penalty might be the loss of some HP, or a fight gets conjured up, or something like that.
The fights are done differently: your hero appears on a map (I call it "Arena") along with the enemies in "normal" 3D-fashion, meaning: you use the controls to actively bash and kick and block and evade your way out.
That being said - here comes my MAJOR complaint about this game: the controls are buggy as hell. Very often I found myself unable to either move (keyboard not detected) or to fight (mouse not detected); if I tried the controller...well... sometimes controller was not detected.
You can overcome this bug by pressing ESC, going into the "Controls"-menu, and resume the game; however, sometimes I had to do this 2 times, before it worked. This made me losing about 1/4 to 1/5 of the battles, because if there are many ranged fighters attacking you or you fight them in a "trapped" area and your health is already very low...well... they hit you before you "unbug" the controls.
Another thing that bothers me is that I belong to those who can't play it fullscreen. It was already a struggle to start the game for the first time. Luckily the internet (also the Steam-forum) provides solutions; I just want to add here - I needed to restart my computer after applying the recommended changes.
All in all - those are relatively minor things (to me). I can recommend this game, and I think I'll soon have some more hours on my counter.

American Truck Simulator offers a variety of playing ability in the world of owning a Trucking Business.
This simulator allows the player to start off their trucking by working for other companies in order to make money. OR. Players can borrow a bank loan, to immediately make money, which simple deductions being made over time. Grow and develop your own company (which you can name, buy trucks for, and buy garages for) to become the ultimate trucking company in the U.S. (California, Nevada, Arizona so far)
WHAT I LIKE -
-The defualt trucks are the "kings of the road"
-Both Steam and exotic mod support
-LOTS of customization for the trucks
-Default trailers look amazing
-Realism includes fines for disobeying the law, speed limits, traffic lights, traffic, other truck traffic, landmarks (e.g. Golden Gate Bridge) (PLUS A LOT MORE)
-Free map expansions (Arizona)
-Little to no crashes (unless using a corrupt mod)
-No "super-computer" needed (runs smoothly on mostly anyting)

WHAT I DON'T LIKE-
-Too many police cars around
-Very high citation prices (raised if police are involved or around the incident)
-Only 3 default truck designs (unless modded)
-Speed limits are high on very twisty roads
-Some drop off points are annoying

I recommend this game, there are some draw backs. I'll go over these pros and cons and you decide for yourself.
Pros:
This game is very addictive with a skill cap which only yourself limits you. This game through reviews may seem like "Spinning Stimulator" but I'll tell you it's not, though spins are involved it's because the game mechanics though sometimes buggy and slightly exploitable rely on fluidity to combo attacks successfully and gracefully. There are things where you drag your swing to slow it down, or accel your swing (accelerated attack) to speed it up. There are ways to hit around blocks, because blocking covers a limited area and not your sides you have to look at the weapon to block it. This game takes a while to master, I am no where close, around 200 hours is where I personally increased in skill rapidly, then at around 460 which is recent, the peak and valleys of learning are evident in this game. Word of warning, everyone thinks they're bad at this game, well most do, it's because there are a lot of people who may be better than you even though it's a small, albeit slightly toxic community.
Now, about to community, as previously stated it is slightly toxic but that's the normal trolls who are in any game, there are very skilled genuinely nice players who are willing to help new players, I'll tell you my story in this game after the reveiw if you're still around. Now, it is a small community, at least in comparison to most games. Everyone seems to know one another, I personally know many people and I know who a lot of the trolls are. Hacking really isn't much of an issue in this game, server admins of private servers can make themselves do hacking like things through console commands. But there are a decent bit of active admins especially in the EU servers whom TornBanner has put into commission for their official servers. The community can be very entertaining.
There are more pros but they are more on the minor side so I'll go to the cons.

Small community that seems to be dying, though, I have seen an influx of new players as of late.

While this game has potential in its idea, it has some serious issues that stopped me from enjoying it. The game mostly doesn't fit my stylistic preferences but still I think has some objective flaws. It also has, in my opinion, a major lack of features and depth both in its gameplay and story.
Pros
+Graphics are pretty good and it has a good art style to it.
+Map design in its appearence is good and varied, but not in a gameplay sense, see cons.
+The gun play is only decent. But a plus none-the-less.
Cons
-The animations. There are none. Just 2D portraits of people talking. When I say talk, I mean the picture just alternates between two different photos with slightly different mouth positions. Dreadful.
-The characters. There are none. The protagonist(and every other) is only seen in cheap comic book-like cut scenes. He doesn't even have hands that you can see while playing.
-The voice acting. Cringy. This is more preference, but I hate the voice of the main character. He tries so hard to be overly badass and hardened. I felt the same way about the main character in BulletStorm. It just is so cliche and akward to listen to for me. Most of the time I just wanted him to shut up.
-The guns. There are two (technically). While they slightly change shape when switchting between "modules" among the two weapons, the guns just don't feel that satisfying to use and sometimes just♥♥♥♥♥♥me off on their balancing. There are only two ammo types and the modules just take different amounts per shot.  The only cool gun is the Smart Gun. It shoots guided projectiles throw walls.
-The effects. They are distracting and annoying. For example, when you sprint, or say walk slightly faster, the screen blurs so much its like you litterally poored vasaline in your eyeballs. WTF. When using the normal machine gun, the muzzle flash and such is so disorienting that I can't see what I'm aiming at! Explosions and other screen effects are just too much too in my opinion.
-The story. What is even going on? Maybe it was the cheap cut-scenes or the bad voice acting that prevented me from getting involved in the story. Or maybe there is just such a lack of developent and variation that the whole time playing this I just felt confused. Now this clearly isn't the selling point of this game, I get that, but I fell they almost tried to make it one but stopped short to fulling fleshing it out.
-Gameplay. Very repetetive and restricted. Not a always a bad thing in all games, but in this one, it is. You are pretty much forced into these small to medium sized areas and forced to kill everything there. No problem, but it wont let you go back or forward into another area until you have killed every last enemy, which 3 times took me a couple minutes to find becuase it glitched out. The areas are okay mostly but some are just poorly designed with combat in mind. Between these larger fights you just walk through halls and streets solving repetive tasks/puzzles to unlock the next area (if killing them doesn't). You also have to backtrack a few times which I HATE.
-Difficulty. Not consistent. I grew up playing Serious Sam, which by the way, is also a "old-school" styled shooter but does everything better than this, and that game wasn't too hard for me on normal. But this game I found very difficult for normal difficulty. Some games when you die its no big deal, but after a while I got very annoyed. There is also very inconsistent autosave points. Sometimes they would be right before something, and others they would be way back at the beginning of the level.
Overall this game just feels cheap and poorly done. I know it is old but that doesn't change anything. I mean look at half-life 2. That game has aged great and thats over a decade old.

I played a ton of Desktop Dungeons back in college, when it was a freeware game. It had everything I loved most about roguelikes - the balance between short-term tactics and long-term strategy, resource management, and replayability. Then it put all that into a puzzle sort of format that made it easy to learn and quick to play whenever I had some time between classes. Best of all, it was designed such the RNG had little influence on your outcome. Your victories, and your failures, were your own.
This release maintains the solid gameplay and tight balance of the original, while adding a metric ton of content. There are so many dungeons, monsters, races, classes, gods, and so on now that even I'm overwhelmed. Fortunately, it's meted out to you in a very mobile-game sort of way, which in any other game I'd find distasteful. If anything, I'd say the pace of content unlocking is almost too fast. I'm unlocking way more things than I can try even once.
Desktop Dungeons is well worth your money and time. After watching the gameplay videos I wasn't convinced they had done enough to turn this freeware classic into a $15 product, but now that I've played it (for 6 hours straight, glued to my chair) I can confidently recommend it.

I am extremely dissapointed with this game. It takes such a fun idea and completely buggars it over on many levels.

Now that that's clarified, I'll move on to the fun part. Archeage is an openworld with an undeniably dense and lively feel. It's not all barren wasteland with unusable landscape like most MMOs; there is plenty of content both above and under sea level including quests, hidden quests, npcs virtually everywhere, and close to EVERYTHING is harvestable. If you've ever seen a map of the game, you'll notice a huge ocean that separates the three continents, and

If that isn't enough for you to try the game out, let me talk about the crafting/profession system. There are 25+ professions ranging from smithing weapons and armor to dungeon delving to farming and harvesting. On top of that, nearly every profession can craft over 150 items that may or may not require an item from another craft tree. These trees progress separately and very drastically. (So a fresh tailor will not be able to craft the same gear as a tailor with 10k points in.)
Which brings me to yet another profession, trading.  Across all continents, there is trade potential for every province, and each province has its own specialty crates and they can be taken to any other province IN THE GAME. Which means, you can carry your crates from one end of the world to the other and actually profit from it; that's absolutely dope.
My last point is Trion and XL's customer service, which absolutely blows. They're most likely good at heart, but they can't keep up with the constant demands and requests. It's a running joke that they don't care about their players, but I highly doubt it. I haven't experienced any game-breaking bugs, so they have won on that level.
TL;DR) Games free, but not. Definitely worth the money.

Stilton, Pear and Walnut bread
(Makes one small loaf)
Ingredients:
500g Strong White Bread Flour
10g Salt
7g satchet instant yeast
20g Unsalted Butter, diced and softened
320ml water
200g Stilton Cheese
100g Walnut Peices
1 pear, peeled, cored and diced
1. Tip the flour into a large bowl. Add the salt to one side, yeast into the other. Add the butter and 3/4ths of the water, then turn the mixture with the fingers of one hand. Add the remaining water a little at a time, continuing to mix untill all the flour is taken in and the dough is soft and sticky; you may not need all the water.
2. Coat the work surface with a little oil to prevent the dough sticking. Turn out the dough and knead for at least 5 mins, until smooth and no longer sticky. Lightly oil a bowl, return the dough to it, and cover with cling film. Put in fride for an hour, so it has doubled in size.
3. Line a baking tray with grease-proof paper. Scrape the dough out of the bowl and fold it inwards again and again until all the air is knocked out and it is smooth. Add the stilton, walnut and pear peices to the dough and work them in well.
4. Shape the dough into a rectangle 30 cm long, roll it up into a sausage, then flatten it out again and roll it up a bit tighter this time. Tuck the edges under and neaten the loaf by rolling the edges to taper them slightly. Put the dogh on the baking tray with greaseproof paperwith the join underneath. Place the tray in a plastic bag and leave to prove for about 40 mins, until the loaf has doubled in size. Heat the oven too 200C, or Gas 6.
5. Just before baking, gently rub flour over the loaf, then make deep diagonal cuts along the top, first in one direction, then the other, to make a criss-cross pattern. Bake for about 30 mins, until well-risen and golden brown. Cool on a wire rack.
6. Place into oven once more then wait until it has begun its abortion. Then give the developers a pile of brocken piezo speakers and ask them to refund your money or you would fix the speakers. Wait for reaction, take the bread's abomination then force feed it to the devs. Wait for reaction. If death occurs then you have finished. If not: rinse and repeat.

A very fun and well made game which I compare to Xcom. I like the running meter which measures the movement. This meter is used instead of squares etc. Story is great (but a bit predictable): it's not black and white and some scenes are very emotional without being pushed. Some missions are very frustrating, because the enemy gets suddenly reinforcements right behind you and they take your leader down with one shot. So in some missions you just have to know beforehand where the enemy comes from or you're toast. Also the defense mechanism during enemy turns is insane: sometimes the enemy soldiers run right under your soldier's nose and they do nothing and you scream "SHOOT IT YOU #¤%#¤% piece of ¤%#%#!!!!!", sometimes enemies in defense kill your moving or just active soldiers from impossible distances and angles. So, sometimes the game is VERY frustrating, so if you're the impatient kind of people – don't play. You will throw the monitor out of your window.
Also sometimes the game doesn't make sense: an antitank shell straight to face? Zero damage. Walk in front of the enemy and shoot with a submachinegun? Maximum damage! In some mission you just have to try every weapon available and find out, which actually works, unless you read the walkthrough. One time I shot a gate with everything I got but the answer was to drive through it with the tank... Also the ranking of mission successes is stupid, because in many cases it just depends if the shot fired were all hits: one miss can ruin the whole plan, you have to take second turn to finish and then it drops from A rank to B rank.
Even with these little and bearable faults the game is excellent and fun to play.

This is by the same man who created the excellent Hexcells and Squarecells.  This is sadly not nearly as good as the others. There are only 50 puzzles, which I finished in an hour and a half. The concept is interesting - using numbers of cells and basic math to figure out which should be highlighted, but the interface has a basic flaw that ruins most everything.  One mistake and you're done; it kicks you out to the level select screen. That means that any progress you made is lost, and also, since every cell can either only be on or off, it tells you what that cell should be, giving you an extra hint (if you can remember where you were). This interaction both make the game very frustrating and very easy to 'guess' your way through. Practically any other approach would have made things more satisfying. It is a fundamental flaw to an otherwise challenging logic game.

Updated as of June 8: Brown has released an update for the game which addresses my main issues. The user experience is much improved, and I am pleased to now be able to recommend the game.
I am a fan of Brown's previous games, and have over a thousand puzzles solved in Hexcells Infinite. So I was really looking forward to trying his latest effort. Unfortunately it is not up to the standard of his earlier work, and I can not recommend it (at least in the current state, hopefully some changes will be made).
Some of the mechanics of the puzzles are not explained at all clearly, unlike in his previous work where each new concept was demonstrated with an introductory puzzle or two. Instead one is forced to trial and error to work out how the mechanic works. This frustration is increased because the result of making an error is to be thrown back to the main menu, forcing a restart of that puzzle. I much preferred the system in Hexcells, where the error was flagged but you remained in the puzzle and could think through where you went astray so you could learn from your mistake. Then you could restart the puzzle from scratch and try for a clean solve.
There are some good ideas in CrossCells, and I hope Brown makes some changes to address these issues. But in its current form this game is quite a disappointment.

Dungeon Keeper 2. The game that captivated the attention of many a gamer and left a solid mark in their minds for all eternity. It was a game that left a monument difficult to match - with a fun campaign, great pacing and truck loads of charm. With its sequel cancelled and EA hogging the rights, people waited and waited for a spiritual successor.
So in came War for the Overworld. A game promising to be Dungeon Keeper without being Dungeon keeper. You've got your rooms, your dungeon heart, your minions, your imps... everything is there. Traps, doors, spells, gold... and a deviously evil yet satisfyingly supportive advisor. The charm is there. The atmosphere is there... but one can't help but feel like... something is missing.
Gameplay just seems... lacking. The pacing feels all... wrong. The campaign feels a little offly-paced and building up your own dungeon feels... a little unsatisfying. Minions seem less... personal than in Dungeon Keeper as well. You don't get the 'oh look, there's one of my goblins having a good time with a rogue!' feeling you get with DK2... nor do you have the urge to take control of one of your favourite minions to do scouting, fighting or just exploring your dungeon. Your troops feel more like... insignificant insects. Foot-soldiers.
So just what is missing? The game has the content. It has the charm. It has the atmosphere... but it just doesn't have the soul. And until it captures that soul... I dunno... I just don't feel satisfaction from playing...

If I had to describe the overall vibe of Recettear it would be that it feels like Monster Rancher, but with more story and less grinding.
The story goes more in depth, but the basic premise is that your Dad mysteriously disappeared and you now have to pay his debts, so you open an item shop. Different types of customers (old man, merchant, various adventurers, other main characters, etc) come in to buy and sell items, and your job is to maximize profits and have enough for your debt payments at the end of each week which increase over time.
At a high level, the strategy is to figure out the pricing tolerance of customer types through experimentation and haggling and how they change as your reputation changes, hiring (and playing!) adventurers to go into dungeons to find crafting ingredients and rare items not available in the market, how variables affect short and long term sales, and balancing them in various situations.
This all starts off nice and simple, but as you progress increasingly complex variables are introduced. A couple of examples are managing the atmosphere (i.e. the "feel" of your shop) based on what items you place where and your decorations which attract different types of customers, and taking advantage of random events such as supply and demand changes and news broadcasts. Also as you progress, more things can happen other than just a customer buying/selling which makes the gameplay more interesting. Playing as the adventurer and going through dungeons is also fun.
Overall I like it a lot. There's enough complexity to make it interesting and it does a good job of simulating a real market, but not so complex that it's overwheliming. Once you're a few hours into the game, I'd recommend keeping a pad of paper and pencil handy. It's not necessary, but sometimes it's nice to be able to track what items you've bought really cheap that you want to push more, things like that.
The only criticism I have of this game is that there's no auto-save.

RUINER is one of the tougher games when it comes to Steam's YES/NO duality, because it seems like every good point comes either with a downside, or with an unrelated flaw that subtracts the brownie points it has earned.
+ Beautiful cyberpunk setting, which nails the whole "neon slums" setting vital to the genre.
- ...all of which is disappointing given only the level hub and parts of the first two levels utilize it, with dungeon settings being what feels like the meat of the game.
+ The protagonist is a very interesting character, with his mask being a great concept in itself. This extends to a few enemies and NPCs, who are very well designed for the most part
- ...but like the settings, a lot of this goes out the window as the game goes on, with the enemies in the final chapters of the game being pretty bland and generic (and in some cases shamelssly recycled) by comparison.
+ The levelling system is great, with a range of different attacks and skills for the choosing, further complimented by the ability to add and remove upgrade points on a whim depending on what you wish to try
- Once you have a few points, however, this becomes extremely exploitable, as you can instantly change abilities on the fly rather than being limited to between battles or whatever; there is no point investing in the supply drop skill when you can simply pause, remove all your points from a passive skill, invest in all the supply drop levels, call in a new ranged or melee weapon, and then shift all your points back again once you're loaded up.
+ The plot starts off interesting enough, with the nameless protagonist being guided towards revenge by a hacker named HER, and the stock cyberpunk tropes about social status and humanity naturally make an appearance.
- The plot is let down by an arbitrary Act 3 twist that is just confusing and comes across as forced more than anything, especially given a few character motivations don't seem to make much sense. The "silent or amnesiac protagonist who clearly has a few secrets" trope is so stale that it's not even a spoiler to say there is an Act 3 twist.
+ Boss battles start out interesting enough, with each needing a certain approach (which can be adapted to depending on what skills you invest in).
- ...that is until you have to fight a specific boss three seperate times across the story, who is very easily beaten considering you're told what skills to use against them. And that isn't even as bad as the worst offender: you're pitted against a mini-boss you've fought twice already, only this time they have a reskin, a bigger health pool, and said boss needs killing thrice without checkpoints lest you start it over at the beginning.
+
The game absolutely deserves bonus points for the soundtrack, which is both intense and an interesting selection from a number of artists; the OST DLC is totally worth considering if you like electronic music. All that said, it's strangely missing the track
, which I consider one of the highlights of the soundtrack.
- The only irredeemable aspect are the side-missions: you have to collect the i-ching coins in the levels for a nonsensical fortune telling, hack the cats around the hub level for a few weapon caches in the next level you play, and the game has a bounty listing for the bosses and sub-bosses you have to kill as part of plot progression anyway. All of which are tedious or pretty pointless unless you want the achievements. And that's even before getting into that the side-mission listings basically spoil that there's only four areas in the game.
Is the game bad? Absolutely not, it's gripping and intense, the soundtrack is terrifc, when it's good it's great; it's definitely worth a look, especially if it's on sale. The issue is that it feels like the developers aimed to make another
but accidentally made another
; the game starts out strong, but it really starts to peter out and get repetitive as it nears the end, with certain aspects like dull side-missions and checkpoint starvation pointing to late-game padding.
With all that said, I'd be lying if I said that I didn't find the playable epilogue gripping, or that the disappointing ending didn't leave me a little curious for a sequel. It's just a shame that the game becomes somewhat of a chore in the later stages, or that the game couldn't have been longer without all the padding and late-game tedium. Should you get RUINER? Yes, but only when it's on sale.
