It's pretty good, I'll recommend it, but it has some issues. First off the positives. The game looks great and plays very smoothly. The world is pretty cool (at first, more on that later) with a nighttime futuristic city setting with lots of neon and stuff. Very nice to look at and explore.
The main issue is the difficulty. It's not a hard game per se, but it can feel a bit cheap and frustrating at times. The core of the challenge boils down to you enter a room, a flood of enemies rush in, and you quickly get surrounded. Enemies just love to charge you constantly and get right up in your face. They can start to feel a bit bullet-spongey too, so a lot of the combat just boils down to mastering WASD to stay mobile while trying to fend off this aggressive hoard. But a lot of objects in the environment explode and you can quickly find yourself instantly dead if you get caught in the blast, which is easy to do considering how hectic things get. Again, not really a *bad* system, but the final area of the base game takes it to an extreme and it gets absurd.
The game also has DLC that continues on immediately after you kill the "final" boss, but oddly they do a complete 180 and suddenly it feels like you're playing a totally different game. Instead of the dark rainy cyber city everything is sunny, brown, and you're roaming around an ugly barren junkyard. Definitely not as cool. It introduces a few new enemy types, but bizarrely it really likes to push this new flying one on you when it feels like your weapons were not originally designed to deal with fluttery, agile aerial enemies. I mean, they really weren't, since you never fought them in the base game. But you also never get a new weapon to deal with them to balance it out so it feels like a hassle whenever they fill the skies. But the DLC is now included automatically when you buy the game and is a seamless continuation of it, going right into the new chapters after the defeat of the boss. So thanks to the developers for including them together now so the game feels more complete.
Last thing I want to mention are the guns you get. You have two types of guns built into one that you switch between as needed. One is focused on electricity/energy shots and the other is more traditional ballistic ammunition. There are 5 "guns" included in each category that you can unlock with upgrades, and most have a secondary fire option too. So total that's like almost 20 guns you can switch between, but it can get very confusing and awkward when you're in the heat of battle and getting swarmed with all types of robots. It also takes a very long time, relatively speaking for an FPS, to switch between guns, like the whole animation of switching has to finish playing out before you can go to the next one. In a game this hectic and fast paced this can lead to frustration and confusion when you need to switch in a hurry and accidentally pick the wrong one, adding further to your panic. Basically what I'm saying is this game might not be the best choice for someone who is brand new to FPSes. Start them on something a little slower and simpler. My advice, buy the electric mortar's secondary weapon ASAP since it shoots out a dome of energy that freezes any enemy inside it, something you will definitely want when the enemies' whole strategy is to charge you like a rampaging bull.
Good game overall though, I liked it despite some frustrations here or there. I'm not even a big FPS fan and had fun.

A first person shooter in a cyber punk environment. It is a bit aged, but still playable, although it shows at least three restrictions modern games probably shouldn't come along with any more:
- There are no cloud saves, the player cannot just replay a level different from the one he/she is actually in. For example, if he/she is playing Level 10 and wants to replay Level 8, the player has to restart the whole campaign and play till Level 8 again.
- There are not more than 10 different types of enemies. The game becomes repetetive very fast.
- Forget about the story, it seems to be a translation from Japanese and the essence was lost in translation.
But the positives prevail, that is a fast paced action shooter where the player has to manage his/her ressources well to survive the given difficulty levels. Therefore he/she is equipped with 10 different weapon types and upgrades (one for each enemy type it seems, but it's not true). It's likely to be called a present on discount.

Unlike both M&B and WotR, Chivalry has no mounted combat at all, although it's not a huge drawback, it's still something relevant. Maps in Chivalry are small and the game offers a lot of game modes: deathmatches, capture the flag, king of the hill and many more. During the game the player chooses one of four classes - an archer or light/medium/heavy infrantry. They play quite differently - their speed is different and weaponry differs as well. However, the game suffers from terrible hitboxes - some weapons hit the enemy while they seem to be still far away from him, while other seemingly go through enemies harmlessly. In addition, there seems to be some kind of autoaim when playing archers, it seems very easy to just headshot a lot (or I am very good at it, which I doubt a lot as I'm not a good FPS player). There is a huge amount of graphical bugs or half-baked meshes and textures. Overall, the game is fun and I recommend getting it, albeit after some time it gets a bit stale. I definitely enjoy it more than War of the Roses and vanilla M&B, but cRPG servers in M&B Warband still remain my favourite swordplay action game.

Let me start talking about Mass Effect 2 by talking about Mass Effect 3.
If ME3 were to follow any other second-part, it would have been regarded as a pretty decent game, save for some people maybe being a little cheesed-off by the ending and the inevitable comment by some fruitcake who thinks that a game where you kill thousands of people and at several points have the option to commit the genocide of an entire race is fine, but the moment you throw gay romance into the picture, it's gone too far.
By all rights, ME3 was actually a fine game.
However, Mass Effect 2 set the bar so high that people couldn't help but be disappointed by 3. They were a victim of their own success, in a manner of speaking.
The reason for this is the compelling story for which the outcome varies significantly based on how much effort you put into it, the strong endings, the interactions. The sense that everything has meaning. You feel emotionally invested in the story, in every gunfight as much as every conversation.
It's not really a surprise that people were disappointed by even as decent of a game, comparitively speaking, as ME3 after just how fantastic 2 was.
Brilliant game, strong storyline, fantastic score.
Controls are just a touch awkward on keyboard, but gameplay scales very well to difficulty and the graphics have aged well.
If you're a fan of over-the-shoulder shooters with RPG elements, and for some reason you still haven't played any of the Mass Effect games, then you're in for a treat.

So uh, I finished this game recently, and here's a brief review of this game.
Story: The story was not bad at all. It started off a bit slow, but it began to pick up speed fairly quickly. There are some good twists within the story that are sometimes small, and big. It is a bit short, but it is worth reading.
Gameplay: My experience with the game was really pleasant. Moving around the environment felt different pretty unique. When I watched some videos of the gameplay, it felt underwhelming, but after playing it. It was a good decision to buy it because it's really fluid. Some platforming sections are challenging, but they are not frustrating to complete. To make things short, it is fun to traverse in the environment and fight the enemies.
Graphics: It has some great moments that make you appreciate the amount of work that went into creating the game. Overall artwork is done well. It is colorful and feels like you are playing one of those old school games during the SNES era.
Sound: I really enjoyed the soundtrack of this game. It had the right soundtracks being played at the right moments. At no point during the game, I felt that they used a wrong track for boss fights or levels.
Overall, I recommend this game to anyone looking for a good 2D action game. You will enjoy the easy, difficult, and regular moments in this game. They are great! If I had to say one negative thing about this game. It would have to be the dark sections of the game. They are not fun to engage in, and I did not enjoy them. Other than that, it was a great experience. If you are a numbers person, I would give this an 8/10.

Despite having played this game to buggery and back on PS3, when the PC version released I felt it was well worth buying again just to support the developers decision to bring it to a wider audience. Valkyria Chronicles is an exceptional and unique turn based tactical RPG with an engaging story, interesting characters you'll grow to care about, a soundtrack perfectly fitting the game's mood and a beautiful pencil drawn sketchbook art style unlike any other game I have played. This art style serves a dual purpose; aside from providing a very special aesthetic it serves to present the story as if drawn by the hand of the main character, a naturalist who spends his free time sketching in his notebook. This presentation style lends the game a sense of believability, as though you are reading genuine accounts of past events, as experienced by those who lived through them.
For its artistic presentation alone Valkyria Chronicles is a stand out title well worth your time. The same is true for it's story which parallels mid 20th century world history and explores genuine social issues both past and present. Add to this a cast of relatable, likeable characters who grow on you as they develop over time, then top it off with unique mechanics which raise the bar for turn based tactics and you have a title that I just cannot recommend enough.

There's a lot of potential here, but I feel like the game launched at least three months too soon. Save your money, people.

I've been going through the backlog, trying to finish games I bounced off first go round. Hard Reset is an FPS in which you play some guy (I think he's a sort of corporate security officer) and you shoot robots until they stop moving. You can also shoot barrels and other explosive / electrifying environmental hazards to help in your quest to make robots stop moving. I think this is a story about competing AI's, but Person of Interest it is not. I've seen Hard Reset described as cyberpunk, but I'm not sure that applies either - it's just a generic future with bad robots.
You only have two guns, but you can upgrade them to shoot differently so it ends up being 8 or 10. They do different things (rockets, rail guns, tracking ammo) but I spent most of the time just using the default "a gun" setting, at least until I hit "you go boom with lser guided rockets" mode.
I found the game quite hard, but your mileage may vary if you don't actually suck at shooters. I swicthed to the easiest difficulty before the end, just to finish it so I could justify uninstalling. That turned it into a game about shooting robots as they try to tickle you which may not be much fun for the full game, but was about all I could be bothered with near the end.
Speaking of the end, I got to the end of the original game (the story, such as it is, is told by a series of voiced comic book pages) and started the Extended Edition parts but just thought, well, I'm still not really enjoying this, am I? So I stopped and uninstalled.
Hard Reset isn't a bad game, it's just not one that really did it for me, so on that basis I really couldn't recommend it.

Hand of Fate is a fantastic rogue-like that mimics the experience of going through a D&D campaign. The game differentiates itself by having the player choose what enemies to face, what events to see and what equipment will appear. It's an interesting twist on the typical randomly generated dungeon because you get to pick your fate *no pun intended*. Unfortunately even after two years of its' release, Hand of Fate is still mired by buggy framerate and an extremely difficult end game.
Hand of Fate is a game where most of the action takes place in your imagination. There are no beautiful cut-scenes, no elaborate storylines and no memorable characters. Instead you're responsible for crafting the story on how you will defeat the Jack of Dust or the Queen of Scales, or another boss. Do you choose to construct a deck full of enemy encounters and fight your way to the end or try to play your luck with chance events?
While mentioning the chance events, I will make a poignant note that they are not purely random! Cards are splayed in front of you and shuffled Three Card Monte style (except it is with 4 cards). Sometimes you will get 3 success cards and 1 failure card, other times it will be the complete opposite. Depending on how well you can read the cards, the chances of getting a success is higher than you would expect. Personally with 3 success cards and 1 failure card in play, I got it right about 90% of the time.
In contrast to the rest of the game, enemy encounters feel like they belong in a different genre of game. The player is suddenly transported into a battle arena and you fight various enemies using Batman Arkham Asylum combat. I found the combat to be completely serviceable and not exceptionally complex given that it is not the main draw of the game. There is a basic attack, parry, stun, special move and magic spell. The combat can be hectic at times in later parts of the game where enemies will block your attacks or throw fireballs from afar.
I enjoyed my time with Hand of Fate but the bugs definitely soured my experience and limited my gaming sessions to about an hour. The main issue is the framerate. I have a moderately powerful video card that can run most games at a consistent 90+ FPS in medium settings. When I played Hand of Fate, the frame rate was choppy whenever there the game transitions from the card field to the battle arena. I also found that the frame rate tends to become more inconsistent the longer the game runs. This problem is especially bad after playing for almost 45 minutes, reaching the boss and experiencing sudden frame dips every 5-6 seconds. Other bugs that are concerning, are cut-scenes where the Dealer appears to be talking without audio or when there are subtitles on the screen that aren't synchronized with what the Dealer is saying.
Even without the bugs, Hand of Fate has a severe difficulty spike in the last act. I was forced to farm most of the tokens (roughly the equivalent of completing side-quests) to even come close to defeating the final boss on the regular difficulty. If you Google "Hand of Fate boss", there are multiple threads complaining and discussing how ludicrously unfair the final boss is. The difficulty comes from the curses that are unavoidable no matter how you build your deck. I was shocked to Google that the best strategy to defeat the final boss is to use a character only available in DLC.
Overall, I can recommend playing Hand of Fate, but maybe not finishing it (unless you like a challenge). The game has obvious flaws but still stands above its' rogue-like competitors for its' unique D&D inspired gameplay.

I almost feel bad leaving a negative review because on paper it seems like a game that I should love. But having played it for three hours total I decided to call it quits for the time being because I'm just not having fun anymore. There's too many fundamental problems that I'm just not able to ignore.
The game's "intended" difficulty according to the difficulty selection is hard. Of course I want to play the mode the game was balanced around, that probably got the most dev-time and must be that curated experience that they want you to have. Since I'm playing on the intended setting it would be unfair to say that I should play on a lower difficulty.  I don't want to say I'm a hardcore♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ who's beaten and enjoyed some of the most notoriously hard games in existence with ease because that would make me seem like some elitist pro-g4m0r who unironically uses the phrase "git gud". But basically I'm trying to get across the point that my complaint is not how difficult the game is, but the way the "difficulty" makes me feel.
Because while I don't think that mode is too hard, I don't find it hard in fun ways. When I die I often don't feel that it was my fault. I am frustrated more than I feel encouraged to do better next time and when I beat a challenge I don't feel satisfaction but instead relief that the next overly long arena encounter has finally ended. I'm then shown some stats about my performance and a rating between E and A, and then S and S+ (maybe it goes higher, but I haven't achieved anything better than that in my limited playtime). Normally I'd feel encouraged to try again and get a better rating but here I just view it as a thing to ignore.
Furthermore, the game's difficulty curve seems out of whack. The first (or one of the first, I don't quite remember) encounter of the second area (excluding the intro level) had me die 33 times. But all encounters after that have been much easier, even easier than some of the encounters of the previous set of levels. Even boss fights encountered since then haven't killed me that many times. It was just a sudden difficulty spike that made me believe "Ah, maybe this second section of the game is much more difficult and I have to step up". But nah, You could conceivably just beat your head against a wall here until you eventually break through by dumb luck and the following challenges will be back to normal.
At its heart the game is a very twitchy twin-stick shooter. There's guns, there's swords (and other melee weapons) and there's skills. The game gives you many an option. Only the game seems to discourage you from using most of them. Most guns are worse than your default one. And there's skills that, while they aren't iterations, are just similar enough to another skill while being objectively better than the other. For example, there is a shield that surrounds you like a bubble but gets turned off if you use a weapon, then there's a shield you can place in a convenient location, that lets you fire through it and also slows down enemies that move through it. The only drawback is that it's stationary, but with clever placement you can hold out without having to worry about getting hit for quite a bit. Then there's a part where you are expected to use a specific skill or die, if you don't happen to have that (inferior, by the way) shield active at the time you are likely to get vaporized. You can survive without but it's much harder.
Guns feel weak (after they got buffed, mind you), and save for a few, they feel even weaker than the default gun. Melee, which according to most people seems to be the way to go, also feels weak to me. Essentially, to kill an enemy, I can either unload an entire clip of my default gun into an enemy or hit them three times, it takes about the same amount of effort but really isn't satisfying at all, which is really what the game should be going for, but neither the way the game implemented its difficulty, nor the combat itself feel satisfying to me.
I suppose they try to enhance the feel of the game and make it more fair by adding a slow-motion effect if you're being attacked. The problem with that is that that whenever this effect activates it has the exact same visual and aural tell as the bullet time you can trigger manually, and they stack. So every time I notice slow-motion, I press the button to turn it back off, only to realize I didn't turn it on in the first place. The thing is, it's really easy to turn on on accident because the default keybinding for it (which as of the time of this writing cannot be customized) is clicking in the right stick. The automatic slow-mo is a conscious design decision, but not a well thought out one. It throws me off more than it helps me and happens frequently enough to be an issue.
And while this doesn't seem to be anything that's occurred to anyone else I've sometimes had the game ignore my inputs. Despite being on full battery my shield would not activate when pressing LT/L2 (and yeah, I know the game recognizes my DS4 as a DS4 because otherwise I wouldn't have to turn off Steam Controller support to not get double inputs, at least give me appropriate controller icons, it should be an industry standard for PC Ports at this point), or my melee wouldn't charge despite me clearly holding the button, or my dash would simply not happen, prompting me to mash the button in frustration only to suddenly use up all my charges at once.
At the end of the day what made me stop playing was one particular encounter with one particular enemy type. In fairness, this might be a freak occurrence because neither is this the first meeting with this enemy type, nor did they act like this before. It is however the straw that broke the camel's back for me. There is an enemy that has glowing orange regenerating armor. Every time I destroyed that armor he'd teleport somewhere and regenerate before I could readjust my aim to shoot, or get close enough to hit him. I fooled around with him for 2-3 minutes before I got impatient and just died because I tried way riskier approaches. I stopped having fun before that, but after that I really didn't feel like going on, isolated incident or not.
The developer, while obviously passionate, misunderstood what makes a difficult game fun and while they do give you options to handle situations, there is one that is more correct than others. Not making everything viable and fun, especially on higher difficulty settings is an easy mistake to make but a hard one to fix. Most weapons and skills would have to be reworked to make the game fun for me. With what some of the more positive reviews say I almost feel like I'm playing a different game somehow. Because I'm already after the refund window I might give it another shot eventually, hoping some of my issues with the game get ironed out. But I honestly kind of doubt it because several of the issues I have seem deliberate.

A nice albeit really short FPS, even if you replay it after completion, I wouldn't expect it to last more than ten hours. To some extent it even feels like Flying Wild Hog's tech demo for their in-house engine, albeit unlike Demon Daggers or other tech demos it still comes out as a solid game even if plot has few major developments despite the premise and enemy type count is quite limited.
Anyways, the combat is great. It's this somewhat popular nowadays hybid of old 90ies era shooters and more modern gimmicks, so your health is one part regenerating shield and one part pickup requiring armor/health. Weapons can regenerate ammo too, although at a certain amount and slowly, with particular upgrades. Talking about upgrades, you technically spend the entire game with just two guns. Yeah, just two guns, the ballistic and energy. Though, they have some incredible modular capabilities and come with many firing mode upgrades, 5 per each, plus an alt-fire gimmick, so in the end you have like ten weapons with all the modules purchased. And all these weapons are pretty cool while at it, too. Some are cliche - like railgun or homming missile launcher. Then others are even more cliche like a plinky machinegun and shotgun. The rest are pretty original though, like a close-range tesla cannon or a mortar that creates lethal to enemies electricity fields. And the alt-fire modes spice up every single gun too (except for machinegun that just gets a sucky useless zoom) - the shotgun can stun, the railgun gets wallhack vision and penetration. Enemies aren't that diverse ad they prefer to rely on melee, but they're still fun to fight, with lots of dodging and shootgin while running backwards. Which I assume may not be your cup of tea if you weren't fond of, say, Serious Sam.
As for the experience outside the gameplay, the story is mostly presented trough comic intermissions during loadscreens, but the story doesn't offer much in real developments - most are just diversions trying to stop the robot menace, and no plot threads get resolved. I guess they left all the real plot for the sequel? By the way, visuals are pretty neat, it's all cyberpunk streets and wrecked factories, but the designs are still real cool and locales are interesting to visit. Sound design and music are neat too, unless you hate bit-crushed audio as quite some combat scene tracks have that thing going for them.
So yeah, feel free to buy it if you like more old-school-ish FPSes, wanna crack some robot skulls and this thing is on sale - the length will be a massive disappointment if you buy this at full price. Also feel free to check out Flying Wild Hog's games overall, they seem to be pretty competent at developing fun shooters.

Every new rule makes sense instantly, and I feel like the knowledge of how quickly a player could grasp them made for stronger puzzle design. There are only 50 puzzles, but new elements are introduced regularly and I felt like it took complete advantage of the overall concept.
Worth a few bucks if you've bored yourself to death playing the more standard logic puzzles, even if it only lasts a few hours.

CrossCells is a puzzle and logic game that requires just a little mathematic thinking (summation and multiplication of single-digit numbers).
The game contists of 50 increasingly challenging levels and introduces new puzzle elements every few levels. Overall the game is not too challenging and can be completed within a few hours. All 50 levels are immediately available and can be played in any order.
In the current version, the difficulty is heavily reduced by the fact that every wrong guess will interrupt the level and bring you back to the level selection menu. Thus, every wrong guess is immediately clear and can be avoided the next time playing the same level. I would have prefered a system like in Minesweeper where you can put a flag on an uncertain tile as a visual aid.
Another flaw is the not-so-clear introduction to the MULTIPLICATION RULE. As a hint:
- The position of the goal number indicates in which direction the numbers have to be added and/or multiplied.
- A multiplication tile multiplies all numbers that are in front of the factor, e.g. 2  4  x2 would equal (2+4)x2=16.
Altogether it is a short but enjoyable puzzle and logic game, which, hopefully, will be a little improved by the devs.

text: I almost never write reviews, but even in the few 12 hours that I've played (which has only felt like 2-3 hours) this game has shown to be a true master class in the RPG genre. Imagine D&D with one of the best story-telling and smart dungeon masters, and that is the feel of this game. Combat is incredibly in depth and tactical, hard modes require grinding and ingenuity. Sound design, voice work, character designs, class systems are all next level. If you're looking for constant action this might not be the game for you, but if you want to be absorbed into a world, experience an incredibly rewarding feeling when finally beating a fight, and spend hours exploring and shooting off on side quests this is the game for you. Lovers of RPG's this is a must buy.

Owlboy, the story of a young…well, owlboy, named Otus. This 2D platform/puzzler game is short, sweet, and pretty darn beautiful. The game follows Otis, the titular owlboy as he looks to redeem his past mistakes in the eyes of his townsmen and mentor while saving his hometown, and possibly the world. The metroidvania style world has a number of branching areas with their own unique quirks, a collection of interesting power-ups and travel partners, and consistently stellar pixel art throughout. A simple, easy, and enjoyable romp through a world simply too small and too short to be fully enjoyed. Owlboy is a game with promise at it’s core, but maybe not enough fulfillment to keep everyone happy.
Pros: The first thing anyone looking into Owlboy will notice is the very very pretty art style. The pixel art is great, and the cutscenes, what few of them there are, is where the art really takes over. A few select locations, purposefully designed to be points of reflection, really take the art to the next level. The spaces in between these moments are just as pretty though, and each location is satisfyingly unique and keeps the eye focused and interested into the changing environments. Similarly, the characters are designed just as well. The owl people in particular have both wonderful colour palettes, and interesting and unique shapes which keep them both human-like and still clearly based on owl species. The soundtrack is sweet, whimsical and fitting of the air themed gameplay. While not my favourite soundtrack, it should be given a nod for it’s soft and feathery feel. The gameplay itself could be considered a point of contention, but in the pro’s I will say that it is smooth and was, for the most part, very fun to play around with. Later power-ups make the flying even more enjoyable, and by the final levels I was deeply enjoying every moment I could get in the sky. The combat could be awkward in the beginning, but it has a very gradual difficultly spike and is perfect for casual and medium level players. Especially towards the end of the game, once again, things go from trying to just fun having. Finally, the story and lore of this game is very interesting as well. Without going into spoilers all I can say is it’s interesting and maybe a bit more sci-fi out there then you might expect. There are also some twists here and there you may or may not be caught up by. Surprisingly, I also found the humour of the game fantastic. There were a few moments when I truly laughed at the jokes. Not everything hit, but I was pleasantly surprised by how little eye rolling I did. Overall, I can say that after one-hundred-precenting the game, and seeing all the extra bits, the lore of this world was leaving me wanting more.
Cons: Wanting more is the theme of this game it seems, and want is not always a good thing. For example, I want to love this game, I want to play it more, I want to read the lore and meet the characters and see the sights, but I can’t. The game is wonderful, but after only 16 hours I completed every level, collected every item, beat all the bosses, saw all the extra bits, and never have to play the game again simply because there is nothing left. The world is wonderful, but some areas just feel empty and pointless. Some places are mentioned, but you never get to actually go to them. It is such a shame too, because the beauty of what you do see makes you think what you don’t could have been such an amazing sight. The lore is promising, but in the end it leaves you having to guess on things. It really feels like so much more was planned for this world and the developers just ran out of time, money, or both. The ending even felt a little rushed. At the end I was left wondering if it really was the final level, and that, to me, is a sign of an anti-climatic end, unfortunately. In the same vein the gameplay just petered off in the end. I’m no king of metroidvania’s but even I was finding the final levels to be just too easy. The upgrades to powers made things fly by too quickly in the end. It’s a great game for players just getting into this style of game for the very first time, but I suspect even they may find this a bit on the easy side by the end. For a game with adult themes, the difficultly treats you like a child. Even the bonus game, a cute little track you run through, was only just that, a single track. I would have loved to play more than one track, and maybe that would have given people at least a little more to keep them playing longer. The collectables are optional too, you do not need everything to unlock all the achievements, and that to me is just too easy. Once again, it reminds me of a child’s game. If you don’t need the items, why are they in the game? I don’t need to be thrown a bone in the last levels, or if I want to hundred percent the game, I want a challenge. Owlboy did not deliver on that promise.
In conclusion, Owlboy is so beautiful in so many ways. Its colourful pixel art highlights the quirky characters perfectly. The sweet melodic music enhances the fight and action of the game. The side characters are interesting, the main character is even more so. The world feels deep and ready to be explored. The story is unique and coupled with the lore is a real treat to experience. It is fun and funny, sad and empty. It is void of the juicer meat you want to sink your teeth into. The game holds your hand more than you need by the end and leaves you wanting more but not in a good way. It is far too easy for advanced gamers so if you’re looking for a rush it will not be found here. If you’re new to this stuff this is a great starting game. There is very little wrong with it if you’re new and you just want something to play. If you want the deeper lore I’m afraid you’re out of luck like I was. However, the surface level lore is amazing and such a treat to experience. There just isn’t enough to really feel like the world is more than a painting and skin deep though. I know there’s an ocean of story there somewhere, but for whatever reason this game does not allow you to swim in it. In the end I came away from this game with a smile on my face, hence the positive review, but I will say it’s more of a middle of the road game than a standing ovation. It is great in so many ways, but is so many it is just not enough. The goods outweighs the bad in my mind, but be wary going into this game, as it may be too little for advance gamers. I can only hope someday a sequel is made which can expand on this world and maybe make it a little more difficult. I think the idea is solid, and the execution a little shaky. Still, a solid game, and one most gamers can enjoy.

At a first glance, the thought of a game being based off of a famous novel does sound intriguing. However, that also depends on what type of game it is, and how the concept works for the said game. There is an Interactive Fiction game for Journey to the Centre of the Earth, but not a platformer.
Without stating any spoilers, let us start off on what exists in both the game and novel. Otto, Axel and Hans are featured in this game, as well as Options/Credits/Select Level listed on the menu. You can also read a mini-bio for each character by clicking them!
I did find the 3-character play a bit superfluous at first. Once I noticed the perk that each individual had, and how they would complement certain parts of the level, that’s where cooperation was needed. Axel’s ability to jump long distances helps him get across larger obstacles that the others wouldn’t be capable of. Otto’s ability to use tools helps him in breaking obstacles that would block your way. Hand well … he can carry fill up water bottle so there’s that. I’m still not sure how beneficial he is, out of all 3 though.
The game has that cartoon outlook, which more than not has fine detailing - especially in the rocks and blurred background, but there lacks shading and gradient. It gives the overall art a flat, bland design. I’m surprised that the developers had used Unity to program this game, too.
No BGM exists either, so that sweeps the atmospheric feel off the table. Little to no sound effects are included.
The controls are fine, but the Auto-save is ick. Truth is, this function only works when you reach check points on the level, and if you do close/re-open the game you’re starting back to level 1. That is not how an Auto-Save works …
I do not think this was executed well as a platformer game. Regardless, this game (aka project) looks well made for a team of students.

Owlboy is an average game that has been rated highly by people who are enamored by its graphics rather than actual important elements such as gameplay, story, characters, or dialogue.
The story starts out simple enough.  You're a disliked mute owl apprentice named Otus who lives in a small village populated by some owls and some people.  A thief steals something and while tracking him down in a cave, the village is attacked by pirates.  You spend most of the rest of the game trying to stop the pirates from acquiring some relics that will make the head pirate all powerful.
The game mostly consists of you exploring new areas, fighting enemies, solving puzzles, occasional stealth sections, and listening to dialogue...... lots of pointless dialogue.  Your main character is sort of useless on his own as all he can do is fly, pick things up, roll, and do a spin attack.  You'll find 3 characters that join you.  Each character must be carried to use their abilities and can be swapped on the fly.  One let's you shoot enemies at range, one let's you shoot a close range shotgun and light certain objects on fire, and one lets you trap enemies or zip across areas while making you invincible.
The game looks good and the music is pretty decent.  The game controls alright, except for the occasionally frustrating flight controls.  There are some bright spots in the game but they are few and far between.  The game isn't bad, it just doesn't excel at anything or stand out in any real way.
So the game suffers from a myriad of problems.  Firstly, the game itself is very easy.  Prepare to fight easy enemy after easy enemy and “solve” simple puzzle after simple puzzle (mostly, push this switch to open this door or pull this switch and get into the door before the door slams shut).  Bosses barely provide a challenge as well, unless you happened to stumble into one while low on health.  The game doesn't seem to know how to handle it's health system.  You have a health bar, which can generally only be refilled by finding and eating food.  There will be large areas in the game where you will barely find any food.  Sometimes you'll wonder into a boss with no food or very little provided to you prior to fighting them.  The game does have some areas where you can instantly die.  The game checkpoints a lot so you usually respawn at the same part with all your health restored, so death is not a big deal.
The plot for most of the game isn't anything new or special and it completely changes out of nowhere towards the end of the game and makes little sense as it's full of plot holes.  It was clearly rushed and is less than satisfying.
The main characters are mostly forgettable and there's no reason to care about any of the side characters.  One of the dumbest scenes in the game takes place in a graveyard, but you don't care about any of these people so I don't know why it's there.  The guy you think is the main antagonist barely appears and you don't even fight him at the end.  The dialogue for the game isn't anything special either, it's barely middle of the road and rarely entertaining throughout the game.  This contributes strongly to you not really caring that much about any of the characters.  The dialogue can often get annoying due to the the next issue.
The game constantly wants to interrupt your gameplay by forcing you to watch unnecessary cutscenes.  Characters constantly want to stop and talk for no reason and rarely say anything useful or interesting. Near the end of the game, I was doing a platforming section, got to the end of it and the game interrupts with a cutscene.  Otus falls down, your teammates pop out and say something like “Get up Otus, we're not quite there yet, let's continue on” and then you get up as you watch them run off to the right before you can move again.  Why was this necessary???  There are scenes like this constantly occuring throughout the game.  Put all the relevant cutscene dialogue in 1 or 2 spots in each area and stop interrupting my gameplay every 2-5 minutes.  It's akin to watching a movie with bad editing.
If you want to explore, your second companion lets you burn through vines and your third companion lets you zip through waterfalls or harsh wind (which prevent you from flying through those areas).  There's not much of a reason to explore though since there are only 2 things for you to find.  There are treasure boxes containing coins or circle rings that you fly through which give you coins.  Every time you get 250 coins (up to 2000 coins), you can visit the shopkeeper to get a health upgrade, a hat that does nothing, or an upgrade for your first two characters.  There's a 9th item but I guess you have to hunt for every single coin and I certainly wasn't going to waste my time doing such a thing.  The only other thing you'll find are 3 hidden golden coins which let you access some special cutscenes.
I won't go into this much but the flight controls can get finicky and annoying at times, especially in combat after taking a hit.  There's a minigame you can unlock about midway through the game that controls horrendously.
The game does screen transitions in an annoying manner such that enemies can be right on the other side and hurt you through the screen transition with you having no way of knowing they're there.  Doesn't happen often, but certainly annoying when it does occur.
Owlboy is an alright game.  I don't dislike it, but it's simply nothing better than average and does nothing to warrant such a high rating.  The gameplay provides little challenge.  The plot, stories, characters, dialogue, etc are all forgettable.  The game is very linear and the few times you can go off path aren't worth doing since there's nothing worthwhile to find anyway.  There's nothing new or interesting here.  It's a game that lacks a soul, even though it tries to give off the appearance that it has one.  It's extremely overrated and not worth your time unless you really enjoy mediocre gameplay experiences.

Hardware:
Core i5 6600K 3.5Ghz
AsRock B150 Gaming K4
2x8GB DDR4 Hyper X Fury
EVGA GeForce GTX 760 2GB
Settings:
All Medium(Textures high)
No AA

1080p

As someone who hates abuse of the EA system (Day-Z for example) I tend to be wary when purchasing EA titles. However,♥♥♥♥♥♥physics ultimately caught my attention, and the developers got me to stay.
TL:DR - Potential,♥♥♥♥♥♥Physics, pleasantly surprised by dedicated devs. Better launch status than any EA (maybe some AAA) game I have played. Lovely building, great usage of graphic engine. No sign of slowing down. #nobrakes #windsweptdicks
Pros:
-The game itself is interesting, with a much better feel to gameplay and GUI than similar titles in the genre.
-The focus on the Conan universe CAN bring a unique and fresh environment to the survival genre IF the devs do it right.
-Enemies aren't scaled, but maxing out doesn't make it a cakewalk. Crocodiles still bite hard at level 50.
-Tedious experiences in some games aren't present here. For example, you don't need to fuel light sources, "Thralls" do not need fed/maintenance, and crafting benches can be filled to do multiple stages of crafting in order. (Ironore -> Iron -> steel because you loaded the forge with steelfire). Basically no need to micromanage constantly.
-Limited, but MASSIVE and GORGEOUS map.
-Lovely and realistic graphics.
-Sand physics (where it is deep enough).
-Tons of room for improvement, devs left doors open for them to develop through.
♥♥♥♥♥♥physics. Boob physics (for dudes too!).
-First person with immersive inclusion of feet... and assets. No more disembodied head disorder.
-Third person that works as good as first (minor hitbox errors, explained later).
I felt there are some VERY important pros that needed seperate lauding.
SUPERpros:
-Amazing building potential (I spent about 20 hours building a castle)
-Very active devs that regualarly stream and interface with fans. (Twitch and Twitter to reach them best)
-Regular patches
-Devs keep players informed on decisions, such as moving away from inadequate server providers.
*The developers are uniquely dedicated to this game, I think they actually will use EA PROPERLY and are capable of diong something great. Help em out! The Gamepedia wiki needs some loving, and they made it EA for us to break it and report bugs!*
Now for the detractors:
-There are some optimization problems some complain about. My rig is a monster, so I rarely have issues, and my WiFi is fully capable of hosting without lag. I however am not the majority, so wanted to let potato users know.
-Currently there are some minor hitbox errors, so you may need to fidget with third person aim. (SUUPER, minor, barely there in first person). Specifically you might have trouble harvesting a resourse/corpse on the ground.
-The game doesn't allow you to get all of the crafting recipes legitimately, meaning there WILL be some choices. Some people wont like this, but it isn't set in stone and you CAN add points with cheats/admin menu without much effort.
-Some items and objects require a metric ♥♥♥♥♥on of materials to assemble, or take literal minutes to craft. Only a few things are like this, and you can work around it via server settings (set crafting speed multiplier LESS than 1), or speed gathering by increasing it's multiplier (again, in server settings, which is a singleplayer settings tab (last one, same menu with graphics and audio settings).
-Thralls can take a long time to "break". This is affected by crafting time multiplier and usage of "Taskmaster" thralls in the wheel of pain, but will annoy the impatient.
-Servers can lag quite badly for people with high ping.
-Some recipes have NO ingame explanations. I don't mind this, but maybe the devs will want to add them in. For example, there is limited NON-LORE explanation on how to make Hardened bricks, which you need for all tier 3 buildings and most endgame placable structures. More importantly is the game not explaining how to get steel.
-----
For sake of thouroughly addressing how to fix things, I will provide these recipes for those who fear google.
Steel (furnace):
5:1 ratio of Iron Bars and Steelfire make ONE Steel Bar
Steelfire (cauldron):
2 Tar and 1 Brimstone make 2 Steelfire.
Hardened Brick (furnace):
1 Brick and 1 Stone Consolidant make 1 Hardened Brick
You can get Tar as a byproduct from tanning leather.
Brimstone is found in caves as a yellow ore rock.
Standard Bricks are made from baking 10 raw Stone in a furnace into 1 Brick.
Stone Consolidant is made in a cauldron by combining 5 Twine and 2 Ichor (dropped by spiders).

I bought this game and its expansion "Wildcards" on a sale yesterday and I'm enjoying it a lot. It's a roguelike that's kind of a mix between a card game and an RPG. I'm not usually a huge fan of card games in general but this game works differently, the deck of cards contains both equipment and such for you, and the encounters, locations, and games of chance for you to experience throughout your adventure. It plays a lot with the concept of using a deck of playing cards to represent each aspect of the game, with different types of enemies being represented as "suits". Even your character is represented as a tabletop miniature, moving between cards making up the layout of the current leg of your journey.
When you get into an encounter the playing table changes into a small arena where you engage in combat with enemies drawn as cards in real time from a third-person perspective, effectively becoming an action game for the duration of the encounter. The combat mechanics are simple but well-done. As a game on their own they'd probably get stale before long, but when used to shake things up from the text-based gameplay that serves as the game's backbone the're quite fun, and just might have you on the edge of your seat.
The whole thing is narrated by the guy dealing the cards, who is voice acted very well and rarely feels repetitive. His commentary and conversation really sets the tone for the game, and while you're naturally aware that he is simply a character model and collection of voice lines he is dynamic enough that his speech always feels relevant to what's happening. I wouldn't go so far as to say that he feels like a real person, but he definitely feels like a solid character and I find his presentation quite immersive.
Initially I was a little worried that the game was feeling a bit easy and moving by too quickly, but with every victory the dealer ramps up the difficulty a little, and now each attempt is truly a challenge. Each time you succeed in a new challenge you'll win "tokens" from the dealer which will reward you with new cards for your deck, which you have the option of customizing before you start your next adventure. I know that makes this sound like I'm setting up to talk about microtransactions, but this game is entirely free of them, which is quite refreshing. The tokens the dealer wagers on your success are merely part of the game's progression mechanics, untainted by the modern game industry's intent to milk your wallet dry.
I can vouch that the Wildcards expansion adds a lot of extra depth to it, by changing your starting conditions and adding specific quests for the path you've chosen, so if you've got a few extra dollars grab that too. I bought it on sale for cheap of course, but if you're buying this game full price I'd say buy the game first and then grab Wildcards if you like what you've already got and want to make the game more interesting.
In short, Hand of Fate earns a solid recommendation from me.

Okay so this is a game where two hours of gametime gives you enough to review it.
Hands of Fate is a videogame based on the old tabletop RPG's you played with your friends, much like Dungeons and Dragons, but this time the gameplay is mixed with cool deck building and your playmate wants to kill you.
HoF isn't a one big story, it's a series of random mini dungeons the Dealer makes for you, the first dungeons are about two floors, and it becomes really huge quickly. The big dungeons consist of long side quests or one time events, all of them are engaging and tell a nice story. Also the Dealer, your new best frenemy gives you a good chitchat and will talk all kinds of fun things on your journey and your actions.
You have three decks, equipment, encounters and monsters.
The Dealer makes the floors of the dungeons by placing down random encounter cards from your deck, so you can make the game easier or harder by fiddling with the deck, but new "packs" are earned by doing new and increasingly harder encounters.
A battle encounter makes the Dealer draw cards from his monster deck, with luck your fights will be easy, but in average they can be kinda hard. The battling system is much like the fights in the Batman series or Shadow of Mordor, though they are not the main point of the game, so if you don't like the RPG experience you'll not enjoy the game only for it's fights, but they do reward people with skill, so a good player will be good even though the game is mostly RNG.
The game is diverse, but if you mainly enjoy a good written story and continuous dungeon crawling this will be right your alley, the game will teach you to play the fights, but if you are
at the arkham style combat you will die, a lot.
But if you're good at the fights, you will be able to win a fight against 12 enemies even if you've been already punished. So it's a really rewarding and fun experience if you can adapt to the RNG modifiers.

It’s odd these days as people cite Doom and Wolfenstein: The New Order as reviving the action-centered twitchy FPS genre that has been in steady decline since Call of Duty decided to ground everything in more realism.  That’s because Hard Reset gave us all of that classic run-and-gun explosive gibbing (do robots gib?) all the way back in 2012.  Well, technically 2011, but the game wasn’t really finished until Hard Reset: Exile was added in April of 2012.  Still, that’s two years before Wolfenstein shook things up backed by one of the most well-established IPs in PC gaming.
Hard Reset isn’t a game that’s going to bludgeon you with complexity.  You only have two actual guns in the game, which up front sounds terrible.  However, what you find out early on is that these guns have the ability to be upgraded and modified to have different fire modes that feature unique traits, fire rates, ranges, and projectile types.  So while you’re only picking up two ammo types, you can have several different types of weapons available to you as you progress through the game.  One weapon, the C.L.N. Firearm, features physical projectiles and can be augmented to produce things like grenades while the other, the N.R.G. Weapon, is an energy based weapon that can transition to things like a railgun.  There’s not a great deal of difference in the nature of the damage these weapons do, though to me it seemed like the physical nature of the C.L.N. would provide more raw stopping power for charging enemies and the N.R.G. would make quicker work of exposed enemies.  That could just be my imagination though.
You will progress through mostly linear levels that still offer some secondary exploration to find secrets and extra ammo/upgrades.  Enemies are often the product of triggers that happen when you get to certain areas, which can provide some moderate jump scares.  I’m not a fan of jump scares, but for the most part I didn’t find it too egregious in that department.  Fights can range from quick spats where you blast robots to pieces in a matter of seconds to much longer affairs with larger enemies that can feel a bit too spongey at times.  Beyond that, you do encounter a small number of boss fights that I think are set up quite well and require some dynamic thinking to resolve.  FPS boss fights are always a unique treat for the player and, when done well can really prop up games that may not otherwise be notable.  Hard Reset is not an exception in that regard.
Hard Reset does include some story elements that justify your need to blow up all of these AI controlled robots that is told through animated comics with voice.  It’s not the most amazing way to do so, but the art style is decent and the story is easy to follow.  What really works for the game though is the environment.  It’s very dense with all sorts of cyberpunk accoutrements that dig you in to the immersion of the game.  Whether it’s the flashing neon signs of businesses, the scurrying little friendly robot doing its job peacefully, the random bits of trash that an enemy may or may not pop out of, or just the towering buildings that make up the background, you always feel like you’re part of a bigger universe.  Every interaction with screens, whether it's turning on power, turning off a laser gate, or accessing one of the fancy 'upgrade machines' you'll need to unlock your firing modes and character abilities, keeps you fully integrated into the game - so you’re not drawn out to some face-covering window that feels like a wholly separate part of the experience.  It is probably the case that the environment itself does a better job conveying the story than the parts that are designed to.
I can’t say that Hard Reset is perfect.  It’s better than it was originally, and there’s a mixed response as to whether the “Redux” version is actually better or worse than the original.  Yet I can say without a doubt that it was a fun game to play prior to the release of more polished and functional games like Doom.  Whether someone would get as much out of it today after playing those is a mystery to me, but given that the game has been well under $5 on many occasions, there doesn’t seem to be much reason not to give it a chance.  I hereby recommend this game (if you can get it cheap enough)!

TL;DR: Entertaining game for about 5 hours, after that it's just as fun as throwing a 1 three times in a row with a D20 to win.
If your one of those, who normaly want to grow with a game, to finally beat and finish it - this is not the game for you.
The first 10 (out of 13) levels are fine, and even on higher difficulties very well managable - but they only clock around 4-6 hours of gameplay.
After that, the game suddenly throws all the previously kept balance and steadily increasing challenge over board, and just stacks everything against you, until the game becomes just a "try and try again", with you having minimal to no influence on the outcome of each try. And when you finally get to what seems to be the end - you get an endless battle with fckin QUICKTIME EVENTS (c'mon, really?) and bad camera angle.
And taking to accord that after every failure you have to start from scratch, 'cuz the RPG elements only count for a turn, this repeating just is tedious and unrewarding.
Oh, and random frame dops/lagging makes the fights sometimes unplayable. That means even IF you have a tiny bit of luck on one point and you think you could make it - BAM, try fighting with like 10 fps.
So if you get this on a sale and just want to have some fun for an evening, this game might be fun (because the overall concept is very intriguing, the art stunningly beautiful and voice acting very well executed) - but don't think this is a game you can master in the end or even finish, because it becomes just unfair randomness.

If anyone, like me, has recently come into the possession of Hard Reset and Hard Reset Redux, this review is for you. After playing Redux for a while, I decided to give the original a try and what a difference. Combat feels far more grounded. It is very clear what engine this game was designed for. Moving from Redux to the original, enemies that felt bullet-spongey are now fast, savage monstrosities that are a real threat rather than a tanky target. Fodder enemies become an overwhelming swarm that requires fast aim and many bullets.
Point is, combat is just as fast, but it handles even better. Would you add a dodge mechanic to Bioshock? How about F.E.A.R.? Combat was tuned for this engine, without a dodge mechanic. You can't just speedy zoom away and dance back down all the corridors you came up while hosing away at enemies. Aim well. The visuals are far better (wtf!? Why would you downgrade your visuals that much in a new engine?). I have no FPS drop; I actually have less screen tear (w/out V-Sync on).
But it even goes deeper than that. When interacting with machines in the game, Redux has you mash 'E'. The original has a touchscreen interface with different things to click and see. Sure, ultimately, all you can meaningfully do is push a button, but the details add depth and however small, it matters. I mean, Redux has a flashlight (pointless, seriously. All meaninful pickups glow with a distiguishing light, making them easy to find and see in the gloom), and it's hard to find the right atmospheric vibe in a different lighting engine, however similar.
Even the story, the 4/10 story gets better! Audio quality gives richness to the character's voices (since the still panels don't lend much to that), and the timings on lines is even better. Hell, the Redux version couldn't quite get my exact resolution, but the original can.

The plot takes place in
, year 2091. You are a gruesome cybernetically augmented man on a quest to find your brother who was abducted by the Behemoth Corporation:
.
Sociopath at best, there will be no dialogue or negotiations. As a matter of fact, you can’t even talk and only communicate through images going out of your mask. With your weapons, pipes, katana and the help of the cute girl who hacked your brain (yes). You will become the Cyber Street Samurai getting answers from HEAVEN.
What is interesting to note is how little control you exert over your own life. You are nothing more than a dog. Referred to as Puppy, you go fetch, you are ordered to kill big dogs, some other characters are your masters and you go on side quests to hunt cats.
RUINER is a twin-stick shooter where hoards of cyborgs, robots, creeps, trained soldier and security details will try to kill you with all they have. Your only way out is through and you will have to paint the town red and let the bodies hit the floor.
To help us in our endeavor, the game will give you the possibility to unlock different skills ranging from shields, to stun grenade or some sort of berserk mode. Your capacity to adapt to the situation will make the difference in the game and will determine whether you will die 27 times on the same boss or not (true story).
Aesthetically, the game is more than pleasing. Cybered-criminals in leather jacket and denim are all out of bubblegum and ready to kick♥♥♥♥♥in a neon-lit and violent town. This will remind you of Ghost in the Shell without a doubt. The soundtrack, mostly electronic is gorgeous, rarely repeats itself and really matches the intensity of the game.
If there is only one downfall to RUINER, it really is the lack of content and the impossibility to start a New Game+ and the low replay-ability this title offers. Content-wise, with such a great atmosphere I would expect the side quests to offer more insights on the world of Rengkok, they are facultative at best, but won’t succeed in cutting out the linearity of the game and it is particularly complicated to explain what are the rewards they offer.

Hard Reset.  Well let's start there.  Guys you literally have the most generic title in all of video games, it's so bad it's almost impossible to search online and not get something about rebooting a phone.   I mean, wow, that's a real pain in the butt.
But overall Hard Reset is a reasonably good game with some oddities on it, almost like a beautiful yacht that doesn't glide through the water because of barnacles.  It's not a horrible game mind you, but it definitely has some rough edges.
The first issue I have with the game is the story, or what the developers call the story.  The issue is the "Story" in this game is cutscenes shown before a level.  When you get in the game, the game promptly forgets it has a story and you run around running through a doom like level.    The story is almost never referenced in game, after a couple levels I skipped the cutscenes (As loading is wicked fast on a SSD) and ... I didn't feel like I missed much.  This isn't really a game that respects it's story, but it feels like it's there, so I feel judging it is valid, even if it's so lacking.
The other thing in this game is it's a doom like shooter, the entire time you're going to run, gun and dodge enemies.  And dodge in "moving to the side" not hitting a special button.   The end result is pretty damn glorious, though not with out it's mistakes.
The only real problem with the level design is that there's very little variety, quite often you'll go through the same area that you've gone through before, it feels like you're going through it in reverse, but in fact it's in another area, so you're supposed to proceed, quite often you'll have situations where you think you are going the wrong direction.  If you persevere you'll find the next "new'-ish area.
The other issue for the levels just "end" quite often, and start in random spots.  There's really not that much that ties the game levels to the story.  A shame.
But ignoring the level design (Which isn't repetative most of the time) the game revolves around the player fighting waves of enemies, similar to Doom, where the player enters an area, takes out enemies, and goes to the next arena and beats the hell out of the enemies.  There's the ability to blast environmental objects that help you kill the enemies, but quite often you'll just have to dodge attacks and deliver a destructive force to beat the enemies.
The fact is that mostly works.  Honestly there's really only two enemies that kind of annoy me.  The Gorilla enemy that charges the player will usually hit the player.  And that's a real shame, because when you continue in the game they appear more commonly.
The other issue I have with the game is the final boss, which just feels cheap.  It's a shame because I beat 99 percent of the game on Normal but the final enemy I just couldn't get a handle on even knowing HOW to beat him, the damage just comes to fast.  The good news, is switching to easy makes the game VERY easy, exactly what it should do, but it's a shame, because up to that part it's quite fair with the difficulty.
Overall though the game is solid and fun.  It's just random action, and while there could be more enemies, the levels feel varied enough (at times)  to make it feel fun to keep progressing and see what happens next.   The game seems to have a few missteps but nothing to make me stop playing it (though the hard final boss almost did it).  There's an expansion (Exiles) that's gives more content.
I like the game quite a bit, but I only recommend the Extended Edition, apparently the redux version that just came out wants to charge more money for a very similar looking game.  Weird.  Hard Reset Extended Edition on the other hand is the same game minus one small weapon.
I might not recommend this over a ton of other games, but if you want another game like Doom this fits the bill.

As someone who hates abuse of the EA system (Day-Z for example) I tend to be wary when purchasing EA titles. However,♥♥♥♥♥♥physics ultimately caught my attention, and the developers got me to stay.
TL:DR - Potential,♥♥♥♥♥♥Physics, pleasantly surprised by dedicated devs. Better launch status than any EA (maybe some AAA) game I have played. Lovely building, great usage of graphic engine. No sign of slowing down. #nobrakes #windsweptdicks
Pros:
-The game itself is interesting, with a much better feel to gameplay and GUI than similar titles in the genre.
-The focus on the Conan universe CAN bring a unique and fresh environment to the survival genre IF the devs do it right.
-Enemies aren't scaled, but maxing out doesn't make it a cakewalk. Crocodiles still bite hard at level 50.
-Tedious experiences in some games aren't present here. For example, you don't need to fuel light sources, "Thralls" do not need fed/maintenance, and crafting benches can be filled to do multiple stages of crafting in order. (Ironore -> Iron -> steel because you loaded the forge with steelfire). Basically no need to micromanage constantly.
-Limited, but MASSIVE and GORGEOUS map.
-Lovely and realistic graphics.
-Sand physics (where it is deep enough).
-Tons of room for improvement, devs left doors open for them to develop through.
♥♥♥♥♥♥physics. Boob physics (for dudes too!).
-First person with immersive inclusion of feet... and assets. No more disembodied head disorder.
-Third person that works as good as first (minor hitbox errors, explained later).
I felt there are some VERY important pros that needed seperate lauding.
SUPERpros:
-Amazing building potential (I spent about 20 hours building a castle)
-Very active devs that regualarly stream and interface with fans. (Twitch and Twitter to reach them best)
-Regular patches
-Devs keep players informed on decisions, such as moving away from inadequate server providers.
*The developers are uniquely dedicated to this game, I think they actually will use EA PROPERLY and are capable of diong something great. Help em out! The Gamepedia wiki needs some loving, and they made it EA for us to break it and report bugs!*
Now for the detractors:
-There are some optimization problems some complain about. My rig is a monster, so I rarely have issues, and my WiFi is fully capable of hosting without lag. I however am not the majority, so wanted to let potato users know.
-Currently there are some minor hitbox errors, so you may need to fidget with third person aim. (SUUPER, minor, barely there in first person). Specifically you might have trouble harvesting a resourse/corpse on the ground.
-The game doesn't allow you to get all of the crafting recipes legitimately, meaning there WILL be some choices. Some people wont like this, but it isn't set in stone and you CAN add points with cheats/admin menu without much effort.
-Some items and objects require a metric ♥♥♥♥♥on of materials to assemble, or take literal minutes to craft. Only a few things are like this, and you can work around it via server settings (set crafting speed multiplier LESS than 1), or speed gathering by increasing it's multiplier (again, in server settings, which is a singleplayer settings tab (last one, same menu with graphics and audio settings).
-Thralls can take a long time to "break". This is affected by crafting time multiplier and usage of "Taskmaster" thralls in the wheel of pain, but will annoy the impatient.
-Servers can lag quite badly for people with high ping.
-Some recipes have NO ingame explanations. I don't mind this, but maybe the devs will want to add them in. For example, there is limited NON-LORE explanation on how to make Hardened bricks, which you need for all tier 3 buildings and most endgame placable structures. More importantly is the game not explaining how to get steel.
-----
For sake of thouroughly addressing how to fix things, I will provide these recipes for those who fear google.
Steel (furnace):
5:1 ratio of Iron Bars and Steelfire make ONE Steel Bar
Steelfire (cauldron):
2 Tar and 1 Brimstone make 2 Steelfire.
Hardened Brick (furnace):
1 Brick and 1 Stone Consolidant make 1 Hardened Brick
You can get Tar as a byproduct from tanning leather.
Brimstone is found in caves as a yellow ore rock.
Standard Bricks are made from baking 10 raw Stone in a furnace into 1 Brick.
Stone Consolidant is made in a cauldron by combining 5 Twine and 2 Ichor (dropped by spiders).
-----
I am actually quite hopeful for the post EA future of this game. The way the devs have worked endlessly to release patches, and won't shy away from the community (or cut themselves off) is a change of pace that could work for the benefit of EA, the players, the game, and the devs. IF Funcom does this right, Conan Exiles has the potential to rise above the competition, and become something great. You have your communities' attention Funcom, make use of it.

Okay so this is a game where two hours of gametime gives you enough to review it.
Hands of Fate is a videogame based on the old tabletop RPG's you played with your friends, much like Dungeons and Dragons, but this time the gameplay is mixed with cool deck building and your playmate wants to kill you.
HoF isn't a one big story, it's a series of random mini dungeons the Dealer makes for you, the first dungeons are about two floors, and it becomes really huge quickly. The big dungeons consist of long side quests or one time events, all of them are engaging and tell a nice story. Also the Dealer, your new best frenemy gives you a good chitchat and will talk all kinds of fun things on your journey and your actions.
You have three decks, equipment, encounters and monsters.
The Dealer makes the floors of the dungeons by placing down random encounter cards from your deck, so you can make the game easier or harder by fiddling with the deck, but new "packs" are earned by doing new and increasingly harder encounters.
A battle encounter makes the Dealer draw cards from his monster deck, with luck your fights will be easy, but in average they can be kinda hard. The battling system is much like the fights in the Batman series or Shadow of Mordor, though they are not the main point of the game, so if you don't like the RPG experience you'll not enjoy the game only for it's fights, but they do reward people with skill, so a good player will be good even though the game is mostly RNG.
The game is diverse, but if you mainly enjoy a good written story and continuous dungeon crawling this will be right your alley, the game will teach you to play the fights, but if you are
at the arkham style combat you will die, a lot.
But if you're good at the fights, you will be able to win a fight against 12 enemies even if you've been already punished. So it's a really rewarding and fun experience if you can adapt to the RNG modifiers.

I was always fond of ETS2, I have somewhere near 200 hours (of course some have way more, but that is still a lot of time). TL;DR: Entertaining game for about 5 hours, after that it's just as fun as throwing a 1 three times in a row with a D20 to win.
If your one of those, who normaly want to grow with a game, to finally beat and finish it - this is not the game for you.
The first 10 (out of 13) levels are fine, and even on higher difficulties very well managable - but they only clock around 4-6 hours of gameplay.
After that, the game suddenly throws all the previously kept balance and steadily increasing challenge over board, and just stacks everything against you, until the game becomes just a "try and try again", with you having minimal to no influence on the outcome of each try. And when you finally get to what seems to be the end - you get an endless battle with fckin QUICKTIME EVENTS (c'mon, really?) and bad camera angle.
And taking to accord that after every failure you have to start from scratch, 'cuz the RPG elements only count for a turn, this repeating just is tedious and unrewarding.
Oh, and random frame dops/lagging makes the fights sometimes unplayable. That means even IF you have a tiny bit of luck on one point and you think you could make it - BAM, try fighting with like 10 fps.
So if you get this on a sale and just want to have some fun for an evening, this game might be fun (because the overall concept is very intriguing, the art stunningly beautiful and voice acting very well executed) - but don't think this is a game you can master in the end or even finish, because it becomes just unfair randomness.

Hand Of Fate is like Mad As Hell, extremely underrated and oddly Australian. Yet here I am in the Australian steam store, paying American dollars to play a game that is co-produced by Screen Australia.  Irony writ very large indeed, eh Valve?
The ‘Dealer’ or narrator if you prefer looks like the merchant from RE4 except somehow less necrotic, the accent sounds like some Melbourne art student trying their absolute best to not butcher a mixed British-Muslim accent… its somewhere between cringe-worthy and cult.
I’ve only really committed about 8 hours to this game, and I’m not entirely bored with it, on the contrary I picked it along with its DLC on sale for roughly $8. Have I gotten my money’s worth? Hell yes. Would I recommend it to friends? Yes.
It looks quite cheap and charming seeming to combine a dungeons and dragons style feel with bog standard arkham asylum combat on a budget. Hit detection is a bit iffy though not enough that it becomes a problem.
It is a short, quirky and very interesting game from a mechanical and experiential standpoint.  What makes it sometimes fun, sometimes annoying and sometimes hilarious is that no two play throughs are the same. Everything is randomly generated by the deal of the cards.
The dealer-narrator-dungeon master like character seems to really enjoy torturing you, offering unique dialogue with every twist of the knife. The problem with every dungeon being procedurally generated is it can go from being too easy to impossibly hard.
Replay value is theoretically infinite, doubly so with the first DLC and all of its ‘modifiers’, if you’re really that in love with it. I have every intention of finishing Hand of Fate, though at the same time, its best played in short bursts on a weekend as it feels very short.
I know it’s an indie, and its half TCG half arkham knockoff on a budget, but would it have killed the developers to put in a little more voice acting? I don’t play ARPGs to read walls upon walls of text.
However, I will give the art direction props for the insane European tarot card style artwork on the dealer’s cards, it looks atmospheric without being needlessly colourful.  It really makes you feel like you’re playing against a real person.
A person who, like you, in some strange meta way has become a slave to the game within the game so to speak. There’s a subtle hint of Dorian Gray in the storytelling and the way the Dealer taunts the player at the conclusion of every move is just spectacular.
More interesting still, he levels with you and the more of his ‘Champions’ you send to the graveyard the more he seems to hate yet respect you for beating him at his own game. I wonder if there’s a ‘Fight Club’ style plot twist once you defeat his final champion.
And did I mention the resource management? You can die in combat, you can die of starvation… god help you if you don’t have enough money to buy food and weapons, then it’s pretty much an instant game over. Tactical, unpredictable and intense.
I’ve only finished about 25% of it in 6 hours or so and for those of you who are feeling truly masochistic there’s also an endless mode I dare not touch for fear it could become more addictive then smack. What’s on the cards for you? Try your luck, buy Hand of Fate today...
