Erenor Eternal is the name of the 3.5 update for ArcheAge, this time bringing new changes to a number of features.
Wisps have been removed and are no longer required for crafting.
The RNG element of unsealing your weapon or armor for a Flame/Lake/Wave/Earth has been changed in favor of a cloaking system. The way it works now is when you uncloak a piece of equipment, you have the option to choose if it's Flame/Lake/Wave/Earth. This results in a much linear progression path that will always guarantee you can upgrade, and players can choose to re-cloak their item if they wish to sell it.
There is, of course, a trade-off for this more linear progression.  As a result of crafting being more linear, in order to make the next tier an item needs to be at the appropriate grade. What this means is in order to craft an Illustrous item, you need to regrade the Apprentice item to Rare. To get to Magnificent you need to have a cloaked Arcane Illustrious, and so on. The regrade rates have been adjusted as well in favor of a more successful regrade, and success change is listed in the regrade window.
As with the main tier, wisps are removed. Apprentice items are no longer required to start crafting Obsidian equipment; all that is required to start this tier is Archeum and the materials required from Auroria mobs. So to start crafting a basic Obsidian Sword all that is requred is 15 Sunlight Archeum Crystals and 10 Malevolent Obsidian. Obsidian equipment does not need to be at a certain grade in order to progreess to the next tier.
The main trade-off with Obsidian gear is that it's now the hardest tier to regrade. Also it still remains cost effective to regrade the base tier of Obsidian as far as you feel comfortable before upgrading to the next tier.
Dungeon Equipment is the easiest equipment to regrade. Crafted equipment from the main tier is the second hardest, including Lost Garden and Auroria equipment drops. The hardest tier to regrade is Obsidian-equipment and world boss drops. Pet accessories and ship components have different regrade rates than equipment, can make use of charms, and can reach the Eternal grade.
This updates introduces a new Main Tier - Erenor. Obtaining this requires a Divine Ayanad and results in a basic grade Erenor item. Upgrading Erenor equipment involves a synthesis-like system using equipment rather than stones. As a result this makes this tier an expensive one to upgrade, but makes sense to do so since it's the strongest tier in the game right now.
A new grade is introduced as well. Eternal is the grade beyond Mythic, and as one would imagine has a very low chance of being reached. As a result, this grade provides even better stats than Mythic.
From a technical standpoint, the level cap in ArcheAge is now 62 thanks to Ancenstral levels. Once a character reaches level 55, then can use Vocation and/or Honor to acquire Ancenstral medals to reach these levels. Starting the Ancenstral levels grants access to Ancestral Skills; variants of certain skills that provide new effects.

Two new zones and an addition to the questline are available.
Many players who used Larceny as a primary method of earning gold have voiced their dissatisfaction in the past, especially once changes to the mob's loot system were made in 3.0. With the 3.5 update, mobs in Whalesong Harbor and Aegis Island drop Ancestral Coin Purse and Ancestral Crate. The coin purses will provide a bit over 1g for 30 labor. The crates, however, have the potential to drop between 2-4 Mysterious Garden Powders, up to 9 Regrade Braziers or Radiant Archeum Tree Saplings, and Lunarite. Opening 14 crates is enough to make 100g from just selling the braziers and saplings to an NPC vendor, and selling 15 MGP can net you 110g on the auction house. It's safe to say those that enjoy mob farming as a way of earning funds have a more reliable way of doing so again.
The way commerce and oversea trading works has been changed as well. Because of kind of changes made, it's better to view the livestream to see how it works:
Regardless, Trion has noted that the current system isn't working as well as it should right now, and are currently discussing options with XL Games to make the system more functional.
As always, there's additional features to the game not noted in this review, and are better viewed in the patch notes and sites managed by players that go more in-depth with the game's update. Surprisingly the greatest issue with this update is just the current problem with the trade system and not acquiring equipment or crafting. That said, I would still recommend giving ArcheAge a go, and look into finding a guild that fits your playstyle to get the most out of the game.

I am a big fan of 4x games and I've played them all starting from Master Of Orion I, II, III, The new MOO; Imperium Galactica I,II;  Galactic Civilizations I, II, III; Star Ruler I, II; Stellaris; Distant Worlds; whatever you name it.
I have hundreds of hours in all those titles...
I've bought polaris sector before the Lumens DLC By that time, this was Polaris Sector was a mediocre 4x.
But with Lumens, I am very surprised. The tactical depth of the game got insane. And the game progressed very well.
Pros:
1. The learning curve is steep but rewarding. Space battles are much more enjoyable compared to other titles such as Stellaris or Galactic Civ. III. Every ship has its purpose and balanced fleets that can counter different fleet configurations are a must to win.
2. Planet automation is very well done. Except that several UI tweaks can be made to make it easy for the player to better control the assets of his/her space empire.
3. The way the empire borders expand is simple, efficient and amazingly done.
4. Research & Development is unarguably the best I've seen in any 4x game.
Cons:
1. I personally didnt like how the races are represented. Especially the humans. Race portraits, stories could be made better and cooler from my viewpoint. But this doesnt affect game play
2. You could spend much of your time in Ship Designer mode to come up with a good design. From time to time placing every single module one by one (and to fill big ships) can be boring. Also the game does not preserve your designs from one game to another.
3. Exploration becomes uninteresting after mid game. But its not a big deal as you can easily convert your exploration ships to epsionage ships.
Final Note:
There is of course much to be improved about the game but even in its current condition, I must say that this game is one of the best 4x I've played in my life.

I love a lot about this game - it is really well thought out and allows the player unmached flexibility in ship design, diplomacy, empire development with a good intuitive GUI looking over the whole theater. The galaxy can be huge with different shapes and OK graphics.
Unfortunately the flexibility comes at a price - micromanagement. If you like getting into the details you will love this game. Every time you want to add, or update, a ship you have to get into ship design and place every weapon, generator, etc. by hand in a rather arbitrary/convoluted ship framework.
Exploration is also a bit tedious. If you want to see the planet's properties while exploring you have to dive/click into the system. I find myself moving the scouts around as fast as possible, and then looking at the economy screen for preferred planets. Where is the fun?
Although the planetary governors are OK, and the planned colonization procedure is great, there are exceptions to the rule that give headaches. For example, developing a world with a research resource. You have to set the governor to mining (or production) and then remember to return later to build the one research center allowed.
Research/technology is a mixed bag. IMHO there are way too many technologies with minor differences between them. Comparing the different engines/generators/weapons by mid-game becomes a nightmare.
Star Lanes: I never like them, and here they seem more restrictive than usual.  Too few linkages between the various strings. Whole sections of the galaxy, even neighboring sections, are sometimes impossible to get to .
Tactical Battle - I think is quite good, but needs more post-battle details.

Suggestions -
1. auto ship design and updating (that can then be optimized)
2. Idle ship and planet notifications option on ships/planets.
3. The gren triangles are nice for colonizable planets, perhaps double green triangles  for high quality planets?
4. Trading is not very transparent - you don't know the details of the technologies that are for sale and you don't have your stockpile inormation available when trading goods.
This game was a wonderful experience for me, and I highly recomend it for anyone considering buying it. This is an example of what a well crafted indie game should strive to become.

I acutally wouldn't consider this game a roguelike. While it does have the trappings of one, such as leveling, equipment, classes, gods, etc. it plays more like a puzzle game.
You enter a one-screen (sometimes with a basement) dungoen with one or more bosses hiding in it. Your objective is to kill all the bosses. However, you will have to level up your character enough in order to be able to stand a chance against the boss. You do this by defeating lesser enemies in a logical order, using your class and racial abilities. Enemies don't move, so you have plenty of freedom to think out your moves. Strangely enough, you gain HP and mana by exploring the dark areas of the screen, so you'll have to manage this resource carefully.
Overall, this game fits the bill for those who like puzzles, but also enjoy random elements and roguelikes or rpgs. Don't expect an exploration-based experience, though.

It is a crime that the reviews on average for this title are "mixed". Although there is certainly room to criticize Polaris Sector (no game is perfect) it succeeds on so many levels, where all others have failed, and most importantly, Polaris Sector has that "X-Factor" missing in nearly every space 4x game made in recent memory. Where Polaris Sector succeeds in particular, is in capturing the true epic nature of what you would expect intergalactic warfare and expansion to be. Efforts to colonize worlds, travel to distant star systems, and even wars, can span hundreds, even thousands of years. The cost of constructing large interstellar vessels and armies, in both time and resources is astronomical in game terms, and the loss of a fleet or army can set your strategic goals back by centuries. Meanwhile, the research system and ship design systems make for exciting gameplay long into a particular game and provides for excitement deep into a session, where other games would begin to stagnate. Technologies consistently have interesting uses, and new modules frequently unlock new tactical and strategic possibilities, which are limited only by the player's imagination. This is one of the few games where real tactical and strategic challenges can be creatively tackled by the player through wise ship design. Finally, the tactical combat system is fantastic. I can think of few games where fleet composition truly matters like it does in Polaris Sector. Bring large capital ships to a party without sufficient fighter screens or point defense systems and that "killer" fleet that just took you a millenium to construct can be vaporized. This game deserves high praise. If you are a fan of the genre,and don't mind options that reward critical thinking and creativity, don't think twice. Pick this one up...you won't regret it.

I don't normally do reviews, but I believe Valkyria Chronicles deserves one.
This game is a true gem for people that relish in creative strategy games and is unique in the strategy game genre since it is a first person turn based strategy game. I won't spoil much of the background of the conflict behind this game but it is in many ways similar to World War II mixing with just a tad bit of fantasy into the mix. The game actually is surprisingly mature in it's stories with plot twists and heartbreaking moments. Don't get this game if you're looking for a fast paced, really easy game though. I can't tell you how many times I loaded up a save because I ****ed up a mission with one simple mistake. The game does an amazing job with the missions they throw at you and it never really feels repetitive with interesting scenarios of each mission (some are very frustrating due to difficult odds). I will say the beginning starts of a little slow but after maybe 4-5 battles in, you are going to be in for a difficult ride. Also the characters are lovely and not really what I expected from an anime-esque game.
Try the game for what it is - A story driven game where one mistake can cost you the entire battle and where the characters have superb voice acting. If you are in need of a game that is unique in terms of gameplay and requires thinking up of multiple plans, Get this. Good luck and Have Fun!

Should you play Desktop Dungeons?
Desktop Dungeons is a rogue-like turn based RPG that plays out perfectly. Definitely a one-of a kind. Honestly, the game is fun, strategic and has received a lot of acclaim and approval from the gaming community. But getting past that, is it really a game you want to play? You start out as a Human Fighter trying to beat dungeons, steal their loot, all for the rightful mission of building your own cities. On the way, you meet fearsome monsters and plots that could end your city..Or fund your wealth. A lot of story-telling is involved, for example, you can even call forth the power of the ancient deities to aid you in your quest, or make a Pact with another to become more resilient. There are a lot of customization and combinations one can try to beat the levels.
This game is definitely worth its price. If you doubt my words but still want to give this game a whirl, you can always wait for it to go on sale, then give it a try.
Should you play Desktop Dungeons? Yes, you should definitely play it.

UPDATED 6/18/2015 v.1.1.5
What comes in this $30 full release game:
War for the Overworld follows a similar formula to Dungeon Keeper and Dungeon Keeper 2 in being a god-mode (watch from above, unable to issue direct commands to your units) real time strategy game.  Build rooms to entice specific creatures and provide services for them and you by proxy, and then lead them on a dark crusade to do whatever it is your dark heart desires.
Unlike its Dungeon Keeper compatriots, War for the Overworld takes a faster paced, Starcraft-like approach which focuses less on watching and catering to a small number of elite, well trained creatures and more on building and using the perks of a massive dungeon to amass large numbers of minions quickly.  Followers will blur together and become nondescript as dozens of them stampede around the dungeon, and there is little time or even reason to watch your underlings go about their business due to the constant necessity to always be expanding and building.  This is especially true since the maximum unit cap is extremely generous and imps (your workers) work at light speed.  Matches turn into a breakneck race to see who can build the most rooms with the most equipment to lure the most creatures in, which results in most of my play time being focused on issuing dig commands and building rooms instead of on the many other (often much less useful) tools they provide.
I'm probably a little jaded due to the half baked release, but overall, War for the Overworld is decent but not quite good in its current state.  The game's pacing feels off, as most of my time playing is spent digging and building random rooms instead of enjoying whatever other charms War for the Overworld may have.  It will probably get better over time as the developers have expressed their devotion to improving the game and releasing new content, which may make it worth the price tag in the future.  War for the Overworld is worth buying for extremely hopeful fans of the genre who want to support this project or if it's on sale.

Valkyria Chronicles is a turn-based game which has a very good story. It tells the story of Welkin, Alicia and their Gallian friends who joined the Militia to protect their homeland from the invading Empire. Along the way, there's a lot of struggles, setbacks, betrayals and deaths.
The story is told by means of a 'comic book format' in which you click the boxes from one page to another. The story is worth following and don't forget to wait for the mid-credits and post-credits to watch the conclusion of the story!
The problem with the game is the controls and the gameplay. During the game, you will be pressing the spacebar for a million times! So often that my spacebar became loose! Japanese games are often like this. An action can be performed by a click or a tap, but they just have to add two or more clicks or taps etc. The cutscenes and 'orders' are so repetitive that they become so irritating. Be prepared to do other stuff when these happen.
The AI of the game is really bad. Maybe it's because of the turn-based style but the enemies don't do anything if they are not of the correct role. For example, a sniper and a lancer will not shoot at you even if you walk pass them in front.
This game also prepares you well for round 2 (new game +) if you are into the achievements. They even made a nice Statistics page in your second playthrough so that you won't miss any of them.
Overall, the game is good thanks to the solid story and the beautifully acryllic-painted graphics. If you like a good story and turn-based actions, you should try it out.

TIme to throw in my two cents...
Conan Exiles so far for ease of understanding can best be compared to an ARK type experience in basics. You start out a lone exile pinned to a cross naked ( unlike ARKs start as a naked survivor, depending on server or local setting you really are naked.. graphically naked )
Your Avatar creation is much like a solid RPG game, height, appearence etc..
From the beginning the crafting starts about like ARK. Grind some resources and as you level you enhance your character with level up points to stats and unlock crafting recipes with points. A major difference is that the recipes start in ' sets '. IE Survival set gives you campfire, bedroll.. Mason give you stone working basics... No need to purchase each thing seperately. Upgrades etc are by different choices you make in streamlining your character
It also runs really smooth. I ve only been playing a non dedicated server with a visit by 2 others who had no issues game wise. There are a few bugs still yet, but considering at this time the game has only been EA a few days.. not surprising. Nothing yet is game breaking or deadly to your hard work on surviving.
I ve read some bugs that have appeared in the MMO servers that I ve not seen, the biggest is the alters seem to despawn on a restart. I have no doubt that sort of thing is not backburner.
On servers, FunCom had to drop the original official server host for a new one. That is detailed in an update news.
Gamewise, its fun for solo or coop or local host / non dedicated server play. It has Conan lore type enemies, including NPC's who have been said will be expanding their roles further. It has friendly NPC's, and the ability to utilize slavery.. you can create not only followers.. but enslaved followers. Who also contribute with skill's etc.  On that, I ve not done it myself yet. But further reading says it works well. Big surprise having Dancers around seems to be a hit. ;-)
Survival side, you must eat, drink etc. Being able to cook food is of course better. But you can find things in the wild to keep you going. Water is your biggest need really being a desert... but its plentiful. The problem is, low end you need to be careful getting to the major water.. because a lot of things that want to kill / eat you hang out by water. The majority of the creatures you may run into are easy to take care of in ones and two's with only your basic 'stuff'.. but dont train them.. dont mess or even let the crocodile see you.. and for gods sake.. dont mess with the humans camping on the shoreline. They are not your friends..
Dieties play into this. Crom wants nothing... and gives you nothing. Others give benefits / can be summoned ( not a low end ability ) by constructing alters and tending to them. Bonuses in healing, food / drink, and poison / antidote type things..  But be warned. If you choose Crom at first, to unlock the other Alters is a hefty fee in level points. OR you can find the NPC priest of that religion and learn from them. Crom is your basic opt out of the religion issue.
Its a fun game, that doesnt feel like a big grind. My character so far is not even gone far into the lands. I am basically living off my bedroll and campfire, just roaming the areas around this waterhole, and working on beating up things to eat and harvest while I learn not only the game, but level up in the process.. The deeper desert is not a friendly place, so I am perfectly content at the moment in living here off the land, hunting, gathering.. and covering myself in the blood of those things that would eat me. ( literally.. chopping things up is pretty messy, and you wear your enemies blood proudly... )  No urgent feel to build some giant base, the world provides for now all I need here, but soon.. very soon I will embark to find those who left me on that cross... and I will take the very hearts from them. By Crom!

I got this game as part of a bundle a while ago, but only just got around to playing it. my first impressions of this game in the first few missions was that this would just be a fun shooter. Even though it had just started, the story didn't grab my attention, and for a game like this I feel it doesn't matter as much.
However, having completed the game on the Normal difficulty, I find that the gameplay is quite dull in a lot of areas.
First, the good:
Weapons - You have two primary weapons which you can upgrade to fire differently (RPG, Shotgun etc.) and most of them are pretty fun to use. Throughout the game I probably used the weapons an equal amount of time.
Levels - For the most time the areas look good and are fun to play in, but on a lot of occasions the areas do feel the same especially in certain Missions.
The bad:
Enemies - The enemies are just boring in this game. In the vanilla missions, there's I think 3 different enemies with different variants of charging at you, shooting you, or launching missiles. This gets old pretty quick. The DLC missions add a few more, but it's more of the same thing in a different mechanical body. The boss fights are pretty fun, though.
Gameplay - Pretty much every level consisted of turning on/off power for a door, getting attacked and repeating. Sometimes the door might require another switch which you have to backtrack to get to, but you'll just be attacked on the way. Once you've done one mission, you've pretty much done them all.
Story - I wasn't too bothered with the story coming into the game, but followed it a bit and felt the parts I did were quite boring. Maybe it got better later on, but I just wanted to clear this game from my backlog.
Overall, if you're a fan of old school shooters and just wanted about 8-9 hours of killing stuff, go for this game. Though I'd wait for a sale, even if it is pretty cheap right now.

Owlboy is a very enjoyable pixel-art adventure hinting on a deep backstory, though not quite getting into it. The history of Owlboy's world is told in a way that shows some effort towards being consistent where other game narratives tend to leave the player wondering.
Insofar, it's curious that telling the now-story holds some irritating character portrayals - at one point you use the main character to fight multiple monsters at once only to have him frozen stiff (apparently out of fear) when encountering the next monster; at another point a side character effectively starts a very short countdown on a bomb but then talks excitedly through that countdown "preventing" everybody seeking cover.
Those two instances of what I consider lazy story-telling and a short list of further problems (see below) can clearly fall into the category of nit-picks and wouldn't have prevented me from buying the game had I known of them in advance.
+ Beautiful fluid pixel-art graphics
+ Nice story and music
+ Good attempt at consistent over-arching story
+ One-button switch between fullscreen and windowed mode
0 Cutscenes: can be skipped after the "first" time around
0 Controls at times a bit floaty (not really a problem)
0 Cannon race
- No map, no minimap, almost no guideposts in a world slightly too big for me to memorise
- Some inconsistent moment-to-moment developments
Hint: When you are stuck, remember pushing down twice can let you fall through ledges.
Cutscenes can be skipped after you watch them the "first" time around but quitting the game resets cutscenes to "unwatched" giving you multiple "first" times.
Controls are pretty tight but I've gotten used to "ugh" moments when I actually needed to jump of a ledge and missed the jump because my button press was deemed too late.
I very much enjoyed being able to fly, breaking free from the usual vertical handicap.
There's a fast-paced cannon race (you'll understand when you get there) that seems designed to make you rip your hair out. Until you figured out how to complete the race each race will take 10 to 12 seconds on average with a few more seconds setup time between attempts. For me it made blood pressure and anger rise to the point where my nose and feet started to itch and I wanted to throw stuff through the room. I think, I spent an hour until I actually completed the race.
There is nothing in the way of a map only a few guideposts pointing out major areas in the world which I didn't want to keep in mind. When you're in need of a map start with the only slightly spoilery
by apocalyptech.
Additionally, I would have liked the pause menu to tell me what area I'm in right now.
I saw two glitches (in the same place) among otherwise amazingly clean graphics.
Again, all the negative critique given here can be considered nit-picking. Those points were irritating but didn't take away from an overall very positive experience.
I recommend Owlboy.

Alright. Ruiner.
Well, for starters I'd like to say this is a nice and relatively short game.
It has a compelling atmosphere and the gameplay is fun... Depending on the difficulty you choose.
Most weapons are fun to use, even though some seem a little unbalanced.
The music is really fitting and complements the gameplay and atmosphere quite well.
Honestly the best thing about this game, at least to me, was how good it felt to use the dashes and plan where to jump to in advance, just to kill multiple enemies in one rush. Really fun mechanic there. The little hacking "minigame" if you can even call it that was almost perfectly integrated IMO. It was just pressing some keys on the keyboard, but somehow it fit. It didn't break the flow of the game too much, but you still felt like you did something. One thing I might've liked though, would be that the time limit was even shorter. I never really failed at unlocking anything the first time.

However this game is far from perfect. The story is rather standard I'd say. I'm quite a fan on dystopian settings and all, and the setting is rather impressive, yet the story is, uh, well, standard. Without spoiling anything, certain points of the plot seem rather clear from the beginning. Those plotpoints that are not haven't really caught my interest too much. This might very well be due to my biggest problem with the game. I started playing it on the hard difficulty and went to about half of the game. Some of the bosses were almost unplayable for me, mostly because everything was way too fast to realize what mistake actually killed me. I'm not sure which boss it was, but I think it was the first one using grenades and a grenade launcher. At that point in the game you don't have enough health to survive anything from him and the damage your dealing is unsatisfyingly low. I had to retry that boss about 25x until he bugged in a wall and didn't move anymore. That was just no fun. A few bosses later I was just completely out of the game. Unlike in Dark Souls for example, where you instantly know what mistake you made, most of the time you're just♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off when you die in this game. At that boss I turned the difficulty to Medium and managed to kill the boss quite easily. From then on the whole game was way too easy. The fights with Mother and the Angels were kind of repetitive and no real challenge. Also, as I previously mentioned, many of the weapons seem unbalanced. Also, once you pick the supply drop skill, the rarity of these weapons instantly dies off, and you can just use whatever you want all the time. Oftentimes I hacked one of the weapon lockers just to remind myself of the supply drop and then just get a better weapon than that I just "earned" by hacking.
A good point to finish this review though, I really liked the challenge at the epilogue. Maybe it was because of the hard difficulty at the beginning, but I felt really strong and badass during that fight.
So, if you'd like a challenge that might be rather frustrating at times, in a weird and cool dystopian setting, I'd recommend Ruiner. It certainly has style and a great atmosphere.

Hard Reset is an old school first person shooter. You play as Major Fletcher and you need to shoot your way through hordes of robotic enemies in the Cyberpunk city of Bezoar.
The game looks decent enough and the futuristic environments are well realized, if a touch derivative. The enemy designs on the other hand are quite bland and repetitive.
The sound effects are pretty solid and most of the weapons sound quite good. The music is somewhat forgottable but it fits the setting at least. Voice acting on the other hand is rather poorly done.
Hard Reset has a decent variety of weapons with some interesting alternate firing modes. There's a lot of opportunities to use the environment to damage your enemies, too.
Unfortunately the game suffers from rather poor enemy design. Many of the enemies are boring bullet-sponges and there's way too many melee enemies that just blindly try to rush you. Some more variety with the enemies would have been nice.
The level design is by far the greatest weakness of the game, however. The maps are ridiculously linear and most of the combat takes place in small rooms and corridors that are locked whenever you engage in combat. Even more insultingly the levels are full of invisible walls to ensure you stay on the predetermined path. This is nothing like the glorious sprawling and complex levels of the classic shooters.
Finally, the game relies on a checkpoint system over traditional saves. This is another baffling design choice in a supposedly old-school shooter. On a positive note the game engine does actually support quick saving/loading, you just need to bind the approriate keys yourself using the in-game console.
The difficulty level felt pretty good on normal difficulty. The Exile DLC is slightly more difficult, but not excessively so.
For the most part the controls are quite good. Sprinting is implemented in a rather annoying manner, however.
The story is rather weak and the writing is pretty terrible. Not that you should expect much in a shooter like this.
The free Exile DLC pack adds a few more levels to the end of the story. It has some new environments and enemies, but doesn't really change the core gameplay much. It's a solid enough addition to the game, especially since it's free.
Overall the game is reasonably bug free. The physics implementation is pretty terrible, however, and objects often behave in extremely unrealistic manner.
Personally I found Hard Reset a really disappointing attempt to recapture the magic of the classic old school shooters. The enemies are rather bland and the map/encounter design is truly atrocious (and nothing like those classic games!). I wouldn't recommended the game.
There's also a redux version available on Steam which supposedly fixes some of my complaints. As far as I'm aware it doesn't do anything to fix the terrible map design, however.
I played through the game on normal. It took me little over four hours to finish the main game and then 2.5 hours for the Exile DLC.

I was hesitant at first to play this because I thought it was a simple card game. I couldn't have been more wrong. Yes, it has cards, but it's more of an outer layer that sets the tone and story. At it's core it's a straight up action/adventure dungeon crawler with RPG elements. The best part though, is it has the same famous fighting style of the Batman Arkham series and Shadow of Mordor.
As I said, the cards more or less set tone for the game, and even has a story why you are 'trying your hand at fate' with this mysterious game master. The card dealer himself is a very interesting character with a fantastic top-notch voice actor. Seriously, this guy does an incredible job. The goal of each level/dungeon is to defeat the top-tier card, Jack of Plague, Queen of Rats, King of Skulls, etc. I was most surpised by the way the levels were executed. The cards themselves ARE the dungeon. Spread out across the board in a labryinth format with multiple layers, you choose which card and direction you want to transverse in to find the exit to the next floor. But you never know what each card holds in stock for you. Some good, some bad, some give you coins or items, others are shops or traps. There are cards that can give you several different quests or lead to multiple decision making moments. Some of these moments though are RNG based so you never know the outcome. The battle cards switch you to a 3d environment, where the Arkham style combat kicks in. You take full control of your character to fight foes and dodge traps, using spells or weapons and armor you've collected throughout.
Even though the labryinth is in card format, it sucked me in and felt like I was actually in a dungeon crawler. There is also a rouge-like element where each mission starts you with basic gear having to earn more weapons, gold, items, ect. When you're 5 layers deep it can get pretty intense. Overall, this game caught me by surprise. Some people don't like RNG, but the game wouldn't make sense without it. I had a great time playing it. If you like games where you battle your way through multiple floors of a dungeon, never knowing what to expect, or if you really like the Batman Arkham/Shadow of Mordor fighting style, then you will most likely enjoy this game.

There are a some things to like about Polaris Sector.   Tactical combat combat is fun & interesting.  Planet management forces tough choices on the player - science, industry, or agriculture?  But these good points do not make up for the negatives.
1.  Ship design is a game of fitting rectangles into irregular holes.  Btw you are not allowed to rotate any of the rectangles even though it would make sense.  Your scientist are too dumb to figure out how to make a 6x4 shape into a 4x6 shape.  I found this part of the game frustrating and tedious, even so that eventually grew to hate redesigning my ships for new technology.
2.  Technology - Your scientists will spend decades researching a hi-tech item that all too often turns out to be inferior to the lo-tech item you researched a century ago.  Descriptions of techs often don't have any useful information about what the tech actually DOES.
3.  No rally points?  How could the designers overlook this?  If there are rally points, it wasn't mentioned in the manual or the tutorial.
4.  Immersion,  The tactical combat could use some better sound and graphic effects.  But this is really a minor complaint, compared to 1 and 2.

By far the best game I've played in years. The pixel art is refined, elegant, intricate and enormously atmospheric, all without becoming a mosaic of flashy colors. The music is absolutely phenomenal. It has incredible depth and variation for each scene it presents, and truly evokes an evolving, cinematic experience. (Seriously, it goes from chiptunes to droning choir and string sections.)
It you don't buy it for the sheer beauty in audio-visual appeal, the gameplay and character design will seal the deal. Gameplay is simple without being repetitive, because combat and movement requires more than just mastery of the skills given to you over time. The game requires you to think about how best to use those skills in changing environments, making for an engaging, creative experience. And wow, I am so happy to not be playing the stereotypical RPG protagonist over again. Characters in Owlboy each have their strengths and weaknesses, both in technical ability and in personality. This includes the protagonist (for once), whose balance of bravery and insecurity is really a breath of fresh air. I personally cared about the wellbeing of these fictional characters.
The plot was a definite 6/10, for me. You don't learn what the real motivation for all this drama and danger is until very late in the game, if not in the post game. The lore was largely hidden, even though understanding it is vital to grasping the imperative nature of the problems presented to you throughout the game. On my first playthrough I felt like the plot was progressing without me - I just happened to be in the right place at the right time. That said, when all was finally revealed, I still felt like there were too many unanswered questions. Maybe this is supposed to be realistic, though: at Otus's age, I wouldn't really expect to understand why most of what's happening is happening. Regardless, I enjoyed the whole "ancient technology" / "advanced civilization of the past" trope that the plot pivoted around.

This is an excellent little title!  It's light on the Colony Management piece for a Space 4X, but the combat is extraordinary and meshes well with both the research and ship design pieces of the combat to come up with a unique feel for combat.  This game also really gets down the EPIC feeling of empires spending entire human generations at war with one another--the time scale is done just right and nothing happens too quickly.
What is most different about this game is the research system.  The emphasis on Fundamental and Applied science as a path to unlocking technologies will be fun surprise to anybody who's not already familiar with Space Empires 4 (I think), which pioneered this approach.  That research system gets a little cumbersome in the later game, but is still a welcome change from the "Research Mega Blasters / Then research Ultra Blasters" pattern most of us know from the days of Civ I.
What really sets the research system apart is how the introduction of new technologies and components can radically change the way battles should be fought.  A fleet full of carriers with lots of fighters can go rampaging through star system after star system, until the enemy obtains and deploys MIRV technology to shred those fighters in a hurry.  The game also allows you to build highly customized ships (e.g., an anti-fighter killer MIRV missile boat) for almost any occasion.
It's those two things, rather than the research system itself, that truly sets the game apart.  It doesn't have nearly the complexity, nor quite the immersion factor of Distant Worlds: Universe but this is a great little game.

So this review is going to be pretty simple I'll start by looking at where this game is weak, then I'll go over the good points.
What this game isn't is:
Pretty - The graphics are dated and pictures are retro and there's nothing mind blowing in the interfaces its all very basic and very dated looking. If you want a game that looks pretty this isn't it.
What this game could do better;
Exploration, while finding planets and the occasional caches are in, as far as 4x games go this is pretty weak on the explortation side.
Civil Techs and planetary building, again its very basic and while you need to plan your planets carefully there's not much to explore in terms of techs or cultural development.
Invasions, to be fair its better than those found in pretty much any current 4x title at least that I've found but Invasions are very basic and there's no strategy or combat tactics its purely a logistical challange.
Micromanagement - This game needs a ton of Micro, from combats, to ship designs, to fuel supply, cargo hauling and repairs/replacements especially of tiny vessels which could be several thousand in a single fleet. (some of this is getting optionally handled by the game in the coming DLC).
What this game does well:
Tech - There's lots and more coming.
Races - The back stories are really funny and the races are all really different especially when you look at the various options they have for there ships.
Huge - The Galaxy on the largest size is huge and takes 100's of hours to finish.
Empire management - This game will catch 4x space players off guard as you really need to think about resources in the long term rather than just what's at hand. Wasting resources needlessly early on will really come back with game ending consequences later. Then you have fuel, spies and haulage which will take some getting used to.
It's Hard - No I mean its really bloody hard, I cannot think of a 4x game where in I did not win the first map I played on normal difficulty. This game I didn't come close to winning on my first 5 plays, it took me at least 50 hours to realise what I needed to do to keep an empire afloat let alone stay competitive with the other  races.
What this game does better than anything I've played from the current 4x space genre.
Combat - This games combat is detailed and then some, there's layers of strategy and you need balanced fleets, reserve fleets, defence forces, militiary or refuelling hubs and you really can't just dump the best of everything on a  ship, you need tiny craft, escorts, cruisers and battleships to actually function along with support ships. This games combat is really good, but its hard and will really mess your plans up if you go in unprepared.
I currently own Gal Civ 3, MoO, Stellaris, Stardrive 2 and Horizon, yet not one of those games comes close to the combat of this one, its really in a league of its own in that department.
So to conclude I love this game but its not without flaws and its not for everyone but if you want something that has good combat, a lot of logistical thinking and that's a real challenge I cannot recommend this enough.

This is one of those games that you can tell if you like it very early on. It is  riddled with micro transactions. I have most of the DLC which really helped me get started early on but I got all of my DLC for free  from giveaways. I can imagine that it probably would have been a lot harder at the beginning without the DLC. Micro transactions aside, its fun. Its a strange turn based, side scrolling, plants vs zombies, hybrid thingy...There is also a story, its  nice to have a break from all the side scrolling action and read a little bit of what the characters have to say after you complete a level.
There is also an element of multiplayer, which I think has been implimented quite  well. You can fight other peoples teams and also uses their heroes in battle. You also earn special points from PvP which you can spend on crate thingsto get new characters. The crate system is  like any modern game with micro transactions i.e. you have a box that you can open using a currency hard to earn that you can buy. Its how micro transactions work.
There is also a very nice evoling and leveling up system. You can use all the trops  you dont want and  'fuse' them together to level up any desired character. The  leveling up system is very nice, it requires two creates of the same type and an egg and  normally a wierd slug, tenticle thing. How ever everything does have a level lock, so sometimes, it feels like a bit of a grind to get certain things.
There is  also a castle thing that you can take over with mines and things that you can get buffs from and other nice goodies. This part  is very simlilar to mobile RTS games like Clash of Clans etc... and is a very nice addition.
All in all, its a good game that is fun to waste a few spare hours on  with some nice story elements and action.

Aside from this, the gameplay was fun, I did enjoy it as I love RTSs and it also had funny moments. I have yet to play any other modes or skirmishes but it was a shame that it's so buggy.

TL;DR: Nope, not so good, why?:
poor collision with the mapobjects, laggy, almost nobody plays it anymore, huge gap between new & "old" players in skill while there are almost no "middle-skill" players, some of the here showen screenshots are not from actual ingame footage and a lot of the stuff used ingame, like sigeweapons, climbing a ladder and such pretty much looks & feels like it got ripped straight out of a game from 2002.
And apperantly it is/was possible to hack with cheatengine in multiplayer.
--------
Longer version:
After almost 18 Hours and reaching level 16 3/4 ingame this is my experience:
For 23€ this game is a joke. However if you happen to get it for less than 5€ on some sale or other retail site, it might be worth its money. (or for 1€ from Humblebundle, like alot of people did recently, but more to this later.)
The game does a good job in providing a tutorial & teaching you the basics inside of it. However if you want to go back to the tutorial you basically have to walk throu the entire basics of: how to walk, how to hit, block etc. again every time.
So if you do the tutorial, do everything at once.
Settings are good too, you can remap every key, it supports & even by default uses mousewheel up/down, mouse buttons 3,4,5,6,7, and so on.
Only thing that put me off was that apperantly "depth of field" in this game is pretty much: off = crappy texutres, on = HD textures.. but oooookay, seen worse.
Now to the actual gameplay:
you do the tutorial, see that they provide "noob servers" aka max rank 15, which you join and start using what they taught you in the training tutorial on other players.
It kind of works, until a smurf(or maybe even hacker) who most likely got the game from said humblebundle for 1€ recks you and everybody on the server going 20:2 or equal while everybody else barely manages a 1:1 kd/r.
So as a reasonable gamer, you figure well lets go to youtube and watch some tutorials on how to play like the higher lvl guys.
Once you do that you realise that at least half of what they taught you in the ingame-tutorial is pure garbage and nobody even uses it because it is weak, useless & some is even badly implementet(like f/e: alternate attacks cant riposte). On top of that, being good means you have to, as I call it, "abuse the engine". Even though the game is from end of 2012, the actual movement of the characters like in ducking, bending back/forth, feels more like a game from 2005, as to see here:
(note: this is not my channel, I do not know that guy, it is just what I found while trying to learn the game). What you see in this video, is basically how every good player will play, spasming around like this or even worse with questionable tactics. The purpouse of this is, if you want to block an attack, you more or less have to put your crosshair on/near the tip of the enemy weapon. However if they bend, turn, duck or do a combination of said things properly it is close to impossible to see what kind of attack they are going to use and from what direction, so you can not parry it and will get hit unless you get a lucky block or can back off in time to get out of theyr range, which usualy wont work unless you play a fast class aka archer or MAM, which almost nobody plays.
Other examples would be this:
and this:
Another nice engine abuse, essentially you block an attack, do an 180° turn to have the enemy behind you, while using the riposte(aka block) speed to do and speed up an overhead attack which starts from behind your body, to hit your enemy whom is standing behind you pretty much instantly while you jump and therefore have a chance to hit him on the head which deals more damage all while wearing fullplate armor and in less than 2seconds time.
Soooooo.. there is that, if you like this kind of gameplay, good for you. I do not. This was most certanly not in the devs mind when they made the game but due to the poor and old engine they used to create it, it is here now and the most effective way to play.
Now to further this up, after putting myself through almost 2 hours of "how to tutorials on Youtube" from this and that, whirlwind, riposte, overhaead-backhand or however all those "spasming" attacks are called & practicing them I have gotten to the point where, at least on the "New player servers", I could easily hold a 3:1kd/r overall while often heading into 2vs1 fights and winning those aswell.
Once I've reached lvl 15 and therefore abandoned the newbie servers, I've literatly got sat down, skillwise. I got reckt and so did everybody else who was noticable new(ish) to the game.
As mentioned in the TL:DR version, there is a hughe gap in skill. Obviously with the recent humblebundle sale of this game there are a lot of new players but next to all those newbies the only other playerbase in this game are mostly guys who put 300h+ into it.
So virtually I got from being almost always on top of the scoreboard to pretty much being at the bottom with at the best a 1:1 KD/R.
Now the next thing I noticed very often are laggs and/or hacks. Seeing as I've been playing with players from freaking Canada on a server located in Germany and equally disturbing combinations due to the really small playerbase, I would guess it was mostly just laggs... BUT a quick "chivalry hacks" google search turned out that you can literatly speedhack in this game by just using the speedhack feature on cheat engine which can also speed up your attacks slightly, like 20% which does not sound like much and is hard to really notice but it is a incredible big difference... so yea. Weather that is fixed or not I do not know, but just that it is/was possible, says nothing good at all IMO.
To bring this to an end, lets just go fast over the actual movment, animations & map object collisions. In one sentance: they are garbage. Moving your own character feels ok and somewhat reasonable, however using & moving siege weapons, shooting bows, throwing weapons, climbing ladders feels like it was made in 2002. Same goes for the map-object collision, especially trees, tree-branches, carts, outer-edges of stairwells, will get you stuck / stop you from walking very often.
In conclusion:
if you are willing to put up with a often laggy game that is based on abusing the engine, has barely any players left to play with, requires an tremendous amount of practice to become a above-average player & has half of its coding borrowed from the year 2002, this is your game.
If not, I suggest you look for alternatives or get it when it is really really cheap, like in the recent humble bundle (at the time of the review) to get a bit of fun out of it until you are faced with the reality of how the game really is not what it is advertised and hence supposed to be.
You might aswell try War of the Roses, which is free2play and will get you an approx feeling of how this kind of FPS-Knight games work.

So far, this game is mostly what I hoped it would be. I waited until the bumpy release to buy it, and so far, I haven't run into any bugs other than an occassional spike in lag when I use the ritual which reveals the whole map at once for ten seconds.
The art is mostly pleasing, though I tend to like how the hero faction's theme was designed more than the standard Underlord theme. The game so far does a good job at introducing you to key concepts without making the tutorial seem dull, even for an RTS/Dungeon Keeper 1/2 player like me. The campaign can be challenging at times, but a little easy at others. As of now, there are few skirmish maps, but there will be a patch soon that will supposedly add quite a number of maps, which has me pleased. The best thing, though, would be to release a map editor to conjoin with the steam workshop or something so that the game makers can allow the community to create their own maps.
For personal tastes, I like and have a hard time accepting this game at times. I like how diverse you can make your forces on the campaign, but limiting things in skirmish maps based on technology (Sin) trees seems silly in the sense that if I play long enough, I'd like to have access to everything available, rather than be limited in what I can do longterm. Along with that, I have a problem with the types of available creatures in the game- nothing seems to be like an "end-game" level creature other than the super-creatures, which you can't upgrade or train at all, and you can only ever get one. While I LOVE the hero units because I like the idea of having my own super minion, I'd like for the "1" on their HP flower to be a non-number icon, or to allow the supers to level to 10. This would clear up confusion like how I had when I spent a massive amount of time on XP potions in an attempt to level up my Eternal minion. Continuing on this creature-focused section, I think there should be more "high-end" creatures. Right now, the best creatures at the further points of the Sin tree are mostly casters or support-type creatures. The exception to this are the Shadow/Bafu, which in all honesty are not THAT beefy (I'm thinking Black Knights from DK2), and are difficult to train since the Beastmasters can't train the creatures as quickly as some of your intelligent minions can train. To be fair, though, it seems that the beast talent path is designed for aggro strategies, which means their high-end units won't be that incredible. The neutral tree basically only offers casters, which are all nice to have at times, but they don't offer a real frontline other than with the horde of ghouls your Necromancers can build up over time. That being said, the necromancers themselves are incredibly vulnerable to well-placed lightning strikes from your opponents, which can make all of the hard work from your ghoul farming go to waste in a matter of seconds. The defense tree offer the Augre, which is as close to a true tank of a non-super minion. Even so, they are not exactly what I was hoping for. What I hope for in the future, is an addition of the variety of creatures in both theme and purpose. Right now it seems that the main design of the creatures is "beast/beast humanoid," with a couple of demons and a human and a couple of undead for spice. While I love the addition of the beasts and all, it would be great to have more "dark humans," demons, and undead to accompany the beasts abd beast-men.
~~~~~~TLDR:
Pros:
-Keeps the Spirit of DK2 gameplay
-Campaign has good pace for the most part
-Few Bugs now
-Gameplay is mostly fun
Cons:
-Rocky release
-Lag when using a very specific ritual
-Lag if you keep the game runing on the main menu for too long (occasionally)
-No map editor
Would be cons if they weren't being fixed:
-Low amount of Skirmish Maps (adding more soon)
-Bugs in Survival Mode (fixing soon)

I've seen a lot of fan art of this game on DeviantArt so I was curious about the game itself. from the trailers I've seen it looked interesting and so a friend bought a copy for me. I gotta say this game is actually really fun.
Valkyria Chronicles is a WW2 themed game set in a fantasy anime world. you play as Welkin, the commander of Squad 7 and the son of a recently deceased general. Welkin is actually only 22 years old and was drafted into the army when the Empire attacked his home country to take its natural resources. Welkin is a strange guy, a nature lover who sometimes talks to animals. but he has proven to have a natural skill of strategic planning. your goal is to force the Imperial invaders out of your country and build up strength to launch a assault on the Empire's capital. however the Imperials have several aces up their sleeves and your war against them will be even harder than you originally thought.
Gameplay.
If you've played Warhammer 40K: Space Hulk then you should have a pretty good idea of what you'll be doing here. Valkyria Chronicles has a board game style gameplay where you must take turns with the enemy to move your soldiers across the battlefield and position them to attack the enemy. you can only move one unit at a time, and that unit can only travel so far before you have to end your turn. think chess but the pieces are armed with guns. this will require you to think of a good strategy because fighting your enemy head on will be a great way for your mission to end in failure. keep an eye on all your units because if you leave a soldier behind or forget about him/her, that trooper will be an easy target for your enemy. however if you know what you're doing and pull off your plan just right you'll be able to clear missions with ease. I once defeated a boss battle with one shot because I had a soldier in the right place at the right time holding the right weapon.
Level up system.
Just like in most Square Enix games, you can level up your soldiers to make them stronger. you earn Experience Points by completing missions and you spend those points at your HQ to increase each soldier class level. increasing their level will allow them to brush off bullets easier so that your troops can keep going after a long and hard battle. you can also upgrade their weapons so they can do more damage and make the body piles even bigger. leveling up your troops is very important because as your progress through the story mode your enemy will begin to recognize you as a great threat to them and will send tougher and more experienced soldiers with more powerful weapons after you. this game also has boss battles that'll rip your battle formations to pieces with ease so you must make sure your soldiers are kept in shape because the battles will get harder and harder as the story progresses.
Your soldiers.
There is a large selection of characters to choose from to have enlisted into your squad. but you should know right now that even though you have these soldiers in your squad they'll only be background characters in cutscenes and nothing else. so you wont see them interacting with the main character cast. each of your soldiers have specialties and strengths you can use to make each battle a little easier, however they also have downsides and weaknesses that could cause problems for you. some of your soldiers have allergies which means if they are in certain environments or near something they don't like then their health will automatically be lowered. a few other soldiers you'll have are complete cowards and will chicken out when the enemy is nearby or when you tell them to execute a certain order. several soldiers will have their battle states increased when in a good position or near someone they like meaning they'll fight better and do extra damage to the enemy. however... some of your soldiers are racists... their battle states will lower if they are near someone they dislike which could cause problems during battle. each soldier has a profile for you to view so you can study their character, their abilities, and strengths and weaknesses so you'll know when you should include them in a battle or not. but I've never had too many problems because I've always forced my soldiers to deal with it. if there is someone they don't like, too bad because I brought them here to fight and that's exactly what they'll do.
Important tips.
What you could always do to get through this game easier is to look up walkthroughs on YouTube. but one important thing you must absolutely make sure to do is to save your game as often as you can. just like in Space Hulk, not all plans go perfectly. sometimes your soldiers will be able to take out the enemy easily, but other times they have the aim of Stormtroopers meaning if they threw rocks at the ground they would most likely miss. I cant tell you how many times I've had to start over because one of my units messed up and cost me Command Points. another reason to save often is because whenever you start a mission there is no quit button. which means that if you forgot something or decided you don't want to do this mission yet, you cannot exit the battle until it ends. the only way you can exit is if you load a save file where you are in Book Mode. so that's a bit of a inconvenience. so please make sure to save often.
But overall if you like Japanese anime and World War 2 themed games then I recommend Valkyria Chronicles. it can be a little frustrating in the beginning but once you've gotten used to the controls this is a really fun game. I'm excited to get my hands on the next one.

My first ever review...
Ok, Early access game, so that means that it will not be 100% working or finished, bugs remain, mechanics not yet place, balancing to be finalised and everything else associated with that stage of development (essentially open beta).
Pluses.
Nice customisation options when creating your character (including some for those who want bragging rights....) - process is straight forward and simple.
Graphics - very good overall so far.
Crafting - simple to do, simple to use, for major projects can be grindy to collect all the materials. But... you decide how epic you want your place, or places, to be.
Combat - currently simple
Homestead/castle/shack/shed/villa/bungalow/mansion - absolutely freeform building possibilities.
Neutrals
Character development - not particularly complex and all toons have to follow the same paths (religions offer some small differences between them, but my knowledge of this aspect is not comprehensive enough to offer anything  other than that).
Poor
Survival is extremely tough at the start, unless you have read up on what you need to do before playing the game (not many people do this. This was my first 'survival' genre game, so perhaps others will not get this impression).
My expected list of improvements as the game develops from Early Access to 'Complete, but future expansions/additions to follow'.
1) Some servers are suffering from rollbacks that wipe out a large portion of your progress,or all or all of it, which is extremely frustrating. Note, not all servers have this issue, so something in the setup is screwing it up, but from looking at that part myself it certainly does not seem straightforward an issue to solve,
2) Game map - to me appears too small for the clan environments to develop fully - too many people squashed into too small an area. Again, early days and players do need a homestead very early on, so this may disappear as time passes.
3) Small irritations like not able to move items (eg storage boxes) once placed, but not including buildings in that!
I do recommend this but with the 'early access' heavily underlined - if the unfinished aspects annoy you, then post constructive comments as feedback to the developers not whinges please :)

ah, old fps games and the buzz around them... don't get me wrong, they deserve it. as a guy who caught up with the fps craze of the early 00's as a teenager, and played  lots of the early 90ies "golden age of fps" generation of games as a child, i believe i can suummerise this game the best: really good. not great, definitely not wonderful. but much better than a meager "good" and hard as fuuuuuuuuuu... yeah the game is hard, really hard, especially the earlier levels. is there a contridiction here good ol' demanthor, yes! yes there is. because you see the gaming logic dictates that the difficulty is something that should rise gradually. and the reason behind this is simple and can be explained in two legs; 1. you don't want to lose the gamers interest by presenting him/her the hardest challenges before the said person is comfortable with the game mechanics ( i'd like to call this hydrophobia effect) 2. in relation to the first reason in order to help the gamer to be comfortable with the game mechanics you should slowly present them to the gamer and let him/her to familiarize with some easier challenges and gradually throw his/her way harder challenges thus creating an immersive experience for the said gamer.
and hard reset misses both of these fundemental reasonings behind the game design. and the challenges it presents are not well tought challenges either, they are hard because the enemies are attacking you in swarms but unlike good examples of these sort of games ( i.e. serious sam, painkiller etc.) they attack you in great numbers yet the space you are given is so freaking small that you find yourself cornered in some dark alleyway and getting a huuge asswhoopin from some mean♥♥♥♥♥undead lookin robots. and yes, they simply don't freakin die. the ramming robots( i dunno if they have an official name, i named the ramming robots like couple of seconds ago so go with it) are takin like four or five ♥♥♥♥ing granades and/or rockets. five rockets! and these guys are the third enemy type you've yet encountered. another thing that makes this game hard very early on is the fact that almost %90 of the enemies are melee combine this with the genius " too many hits to kill" mechanic you die, you die so freakin much that you lose your mind and sweat like ♥♥♥♥ing psycho in some talking heads song.
yet when you level your guns up and master the weapon system, and understand how to move in the mentioned above small areas, thats when this game freakin shines. and starting from the mid point of the game, all things come together and each and every area you clear you get this great sense of fullfilment, because you know that this game is brutal, you know this game is challenging you fair or not, there is a freaking great challenge and you, the guy who was getting his♥♥♥♥♥kicked by some wimpy robots like literally 30 mins ago, now turned into this killing machine whos changing weapons and scrolling firing modes like a freaking boss.
and i should add they "improved" the problems adressed in this review with the redux, but, after playing this through, i will recommend this one over the redux edition, because since this one is far more brutal the sick masochistic enjoyement you get out of it is far more fulfilling, also extended version is far more cheaper than the redux version and the extra stuff the redux adds ( other than the difficulty curve thing) is not that important ( imho) also i should add the last level of the exile dlc is this kind of game done right. a wide arena where you fight waves after waves of robots. thats the fps i want man.
and there is also a story.
buy this one. if its on sale, DO NOT MISS IT!
ps: the saving system will also frustrate the ♥♥♥♥ you out. cheers.

Cyberpunk games are so rare that when one gets announced it immediately grabs my attention as a lover of the literary genre. And that's strange, 'cause developers could really do a lot with this kind of setting, too bad it doesn't sell greatly since a lot of kids don't even know who Philip♥♥♥♥♥♥(don't censor it Steam, it's a name!!!), Sterling, Effinger or Gibson are. That said, when I first saw Ruiner gameplay in a trailer I was hooked! An action Cyberpunk game where you control a ♥♥♥♥in' killing cybernetic machine? Published by the great Devolver Digital? Sign me in! Finally someone decides to take the sci-fi megacity sprawl setting and do something right with it! Screw the last Deus Ex, what an epic failure that game was. That and the anti-charismatic Adam "I am a good boy" Jensen. Ruiner may not be a perfect game, but boy it surely delivers!
It is action packed, violent, brutal and fast. Mind you, it's not as hard as some people claim it to be, you've got tons of powers to overcome difficulties. Plus you have to manage your weaponry: you have a basic ranged weapon (that can be upgraded through the skill tree) and a melee weapon. The cool thing is that you can grab those dropped by the enemies or found throughout the levels, which are incredibly powerful. They range from normal shotguns, to fire spitting guns, railguns, elemental weapons, katanas that make enemies EXPLODE and saw launchers!
Combining powers, weapons and movement is the key to victory either you play on normal or hard. There are infinite continues like Hotline Miami, so it's just a matter of skills or how you approach a situation. Of course at the beginning it can be a bit confusing, but once you figure out the perfect cybernetic powers combo you'll gain the upper hand. Personally, I think that some of those powers are really overpowered and can get you through boss fights without any problem, so the developers may want to patch up some things or add a more difficult mode for players that want a real challenge (not me, I am too old to curse against a screen).
Graphically speaking, they nailed it. Every level feels like a suffocating metallic mess, a sprawl of cables, elevators and technology that would make every cyberpunk fan happy. Even Rengkok South, the main hub, feels just right, taking inspiration from the Blade Runner movie. The gun effects and the explosions are great, and it's satisfying to stand still after a battle watching the corpses of your enemies lie down at your feet.
Storywise, Ruiner is pretty weak, maybe 'cause it is pretty short. And that's my only complaint, the game is far too short and some of the story gets rushed to the end. Honestly I was hoping for something more, but hey, it's still better than Deus Ex: Mankind Divided. Too bad that there is NO voice acting, which is kinda odd for a modern game with very few dialogues, maybe they will add it in the future. The GREAT soundtrack compensates for this, it's one of the best synthwave electrobeat♥♥♥♥♥♥I've heard since Hotline Miami. It has that futuristic feeling and it contains aggressive and atmospheric tracks that are very good to listen even if you're not playing the game.
Overall, since the price is honest, I really recommend RUINER to every action game and cyberpunk fan.

Solid game with tons of polish. It's an odd mishmash of a board game, roguelike, and DnD, with real time Arkham-style combat that's all tied together absolutely seamlessly. And I mean that literally. The attention to detail on this game is insane, there are no unnatural jumps or skips in anything. The gripes:
- Controls are badly designed. )

So , with what i've played so far this is my personal opinon.
The game isn't bad. though as some other reviews have said there are definitely other games out there.
the tech tree is okay as a novelty but it doesn't really have much in the way of "random" breakthroughs. it tells you exactly how long the tech will take to research and it shows it for all techs based on current amount of generated research points.
the ship design is kinda lack luster. You have color coded slots where you can put things some things can go in a different colour coded slot but not all things.
the ships are pretty much all locked in their appearance you don't really get much ability to change how they look.
the race customization is minimal increase/decrease what your selected race is, or isn't good at. to do this you get a set number of race points adding a benefit takes them adding a penalty increases them. but in my opinon they don't matter and every race gets the exact same list of traits.and racial points. which isn't inherently a bad thing but aside from their lore and racial history/descriptions which are quite long. theres nothing that seperates them as different races outside of appearance which i find to be lame.
the game plays like some of the more popular 4x games from the late 90s early 2,000s . the graphics are much the same.  the combat while offering a little freedom..suffers from the fact that its extremely slow paced atleast in the early stages. and no matter how far away you move your ships using the slight difference in speed..which is extremely slight..and so slow early on that it can be quite difficult to tell if your "big" ships are moving. the ships explosions , and damages to the ships aren't very detailed each ship/fighter gets a health bar once its depleted boom. but the ships fight at full strength till they explode. theres no component damaging , nothing to overly really draw in the more action oriented gamers.(edit i forgot to finish my initial thought which is ships will retreat directly through the enemy even if you give them speed to move fast enough in the opposite direction to get away. which means your ships will attempt to fly through over whelming fire power to escape being destroyed..even when they don't have to.)
there aren't many story/plotlines that i seen there are some hidden things to 'explore'  like the troupe of searching asteroid, or debris fields an finding a bonus to tech, resources, or ships.
I didn't have any bugs , or glitches in what i've played so far so the game seems quite stable. but for what it offers. it is not imo. worth 40$ so if you are thinking of getting it i would highly recommend waiting for a sale.

This game is a gem.  A rough gem but a gem none-the-less.
First off it is really just a 2x game.  There is no win by diplomacy/tech that I am aware of.  And, in fact diplomacy is broken.. There a a few ways to exploit the AI in order to avoid war pretty much indefinitely.
However past that the game is excellent.  Better than excellent in fact.  The best feature of the game is the what has been coined 'Starship Tetris'.  While frustrating to some this is what creates the uniques natures of the various races.  But this also produces a highly un balanced strategic situation, to which some players are unable to adapt.  Each race has a different geometric layout for their ships and this, in turn, limits the placement of various equipment.  The result is that from the start certain races easily out-gun others.  This, in turn, forces the player to pursue a very specific research path in order to counter.  This game will frustrate player swho are used to RTS style build orders which can give you a dominant presence right from the start. Granted there are about 3 or 4 initial techs that are 'must have' from the beginning, however, after that you will need to commit to small, fast and stealthy or lots of guns until the middle game. Once you make it to the middle game the war becomes more grand strategy and less tactical.  However, by this point the weakness in the tactical AI become a bit too glaring.  The late game generally becomes a balance of defensive choke points and the player building the 'kill stack' of ships to knock down key planets.  then move the defensive bases to the new choke point, rinse and repeat.  This is really a 7 of 10 game, which is impressive for a one man show.  And he is currently performing a major upgrade!  so I must recommend support for this herculean effort and his continued interest in making a good game better.
Final Score: 7/10
Pros:
- Tech system is semi-unique
- Has a Star Wars MOD!
- Ship designing creates variety, so players will have several purpose built ships.
- Resource management requires planning (long term planning
- AI does a good job managing planetary builds.
- Good asymetrical tactical elements
- Stealth and sabotage system is interesting and not too OP
Cons
- Tech system is a bit obscured ( you will need to play through to find out where the necessary techs are )
- Ship design is frustrating for the lazy player and limits species strategies with regard to conquest.
- AI does a lousy job in tactical ship battles.
Notes:
Developer is in the process up creating an update which will address some of the logistical management shortcomings in the game, so I left those un addresed.
-E

I'm kind of torn on this game.  It's obviously well done and gets great reviews.  That said, I don't enjoy it very much.  I was looking for a game that could I could play quickly on the go or as in between other games and based on the reviews, this seemed to be it.
I've played around 15 hours now, and just don't enjoy it that much.  If you like rogue-like puzzlers then it's probably a good game for you.  For me, it just lacks that balance between depth of gameplay and casual mental involvement.  If you approach this game casually, you'll almost certainly never win (other then the few introductory games); and if you approach it to  win, then it's certainly neither casual.
I also found the depth of gameplay everyone talks about to be a bit lacking.  After getting frustrated, unable to beat even the first "normal" dungeons, I read a couple of the brief introductory help guides on the community page.  Yes, there are some nuances around skills and abilities, but once you get the "always kill monsters higher level than yourself", that's about 90% of what you need to understand and succeed in this game.
Is there skill involved in this game?  Absolutely.  Is it well done?  Yes.  Could it be a nice, quick diversion or an entire Friday night's gaming session?  Totally.  Is it for me - no.  I feel bad giving this game a thumbs down, and it feels like I'm totally mission something, but for me it just isn't there.  I am compelled to play it from time to time - but unfortunately just in that compulsive "gotta get the next upgrade" kind of way, not the good "OMG I can't wait to play Desktop Dungeons" kins of way.
