I feel like something's missing and I can't quite put my finger on it. Yet beneth everything I'm about to say, I still found Hand of Fate to be a fun and addictive experience.
Hand of Fate is fantastic as an experimental game. Even the premise is unique: You're a veteran adventurer who has reached the end of the world. A magic fortune teller offers a game that will unlock your forgotten memories. Every card in the game is something that's already happened. That alone is clever. However, the game's style is just as interesting. It's progressive DnD questing in the style of tabletop card game, with interactive combat encounters, a card collection mechanic, and rougelike elements. On the surface, that sounds great.
The progressive quests are, in my opinion, one of the most interesting features. Quests take the form of both cards and game board squares. Each quest has multiple sections which are unlocked by completing the previous objectives. Completing a leg of the quest nets you a token which unlocks weapons, abilities, or the next part of the quest. These unlocks take the form of cards, which you can use to "stack the deck" in your favor. When starting a new campaign, your hero always has base equipment, but unlocks more through event cards. Unfortunatley, enemies scale as the player does to "maintain balance." The result is that you never feel like you can get ahead. Not in combat and not in quests.
The quests themselves are well written and a few of them are laugh out loud funny. Unfortunatley, there's only a handful of ways to complete quests. You either offer or ask for supplies, start a combat encounter, or play 4 card monte.
The problem with the card game is that it's essentially a dice roll disguised as an actual choice. You have 4 cards. Based on difficulty they will be some variation of "huge success," "success," "failure," or "huge failure." This would be ok on it's own, but the game includes a curse debuff that only serves to purposely unbalance this selection process. I'll admit however that I appreciate the fact that the cards are actually shuffled. About 1/4 times you can track the card on top.
However, here's an example of what to expect with the 4 card monte:
* Have unlucky curse that makes shuffles too fast to see.
* Meet "Cursed Gambler"
* Walk away and lose half your food
or
* Play 4 card monte
* 3 cards are "failure," which results in a curse.
* The next card on your journey is ANOTHER "Cursed Gambler" and there's still 2 more in the deck.
The problem with this card design is that it "feels" unfair, which is all that really matters in the question of player retention. Even a rigged dice would "feel" better because there's a wider range of options.
The farther you go, the more obscene these checks become. Higher level quests (White Minotaur and Spice Trader) may require you to complete 3-5 increasingly unlikely rolls. These quickly become both tedious and ridiculous, especially when you chase a quest all across the board, only to fail the last check before the token. Oh well, better luck next time. Not only that, but some checks are actually completed by failing the roll. You never know what to expect because the rules are constantly changing based on the scenario.
So you fail the card selection and enter combat. The dealer draws (2) 4 of Plauges. This means you'll be facing off against 8 ratmen, 2 of them armed with unlimited throwing spears. You enter combat and it's Arkham Asylum style rhythm combat. But there's a problem. Other than pricey artefacts and randomly assigned weapons, you have no upgrades. Standard combat is nothing but smashing the mouse button and raising your sheild when projectiles appear. If you're facing that (2) 4 of Plague, you'll be deflecting poisoned projectiles about every 2 seconds. You gain damage with higher combos and hard mode offers several items that increase your speed and damage so long as you don't get hit, but the projectiles become incredibly difficult to block when faced with more than 5 enemies.
All of this makes the combat needlessly frustrating, especially since (as previously stated) enemies improve as the player does and most of them have a lot more HP than you'd expect. Every single enemy in the game has more health than the player, which is needlessly frustrating and I'd argue unbalanced. A default player character has 100hp. A single goblin has enough health to achieve an 11 hit combo with a 23 damage weapon. Worse, they always appears in groups of three. That is objectively bad game design.
Mad Max got away with Arkham Asylum combat because it had character upgrades, weapon variation, and enemy variation; Hand of Fate has the same button mashing over and over and over and over and over again. The worst is a quest that requires you to land a chain of 30 hits against enemies with shields who have a 100% to block your attack and will always make an unblockable counter attack to your parry.
As a final note, the other problem is the roguelike distribution of event cards on the map. Because a unit of food is used up on each square, you constantly need to replenish supplies. However, you generally have no control over whether you live or die. Non-combat deaths are through no fault of your own. You have no control over your money when a curse (which costs $300 gold to remove) detracts a chunk of your gold at the end of each combat encounter. You have no control of food when the cursed gambler either steals your food or hits you with another curse. Hand of Fate gives the illusion of control through the map and 4 card monte. In reality your choices are limited to stores and how you move in combat. The rest is typically beyond your control or made to look like you're in control when you're just along for the ride. While it does fit with the name "Hand of Fate" it doesn't fit with an interactive game.
I think I finally know what's missing. Player agency. Unavoidable and disastrous events happen too often for long term play. Combat is too simple and relies heavily on the luck of the equipment draw. Since you know what big creature you're hunting, you can stack the deck for that enemy type, but as you approach the end of the game, you need more and more cards which makes it less and less likely that you'll actually be equipped for the coming boss battle.
Pitch Hand of Fate against another rougelike, FTL for example, and see what happens. FTL  put players in a position where they still have options even when they were outgunned and were unable to even damage the enemy. FTL always kept control in the hands of the player, even under the worst conditions.
In Hand of Fate the dealer is always in control and the player is just along for the ride. Because the game will choose your optimum cards and because movement squares and event cards are automatically highlighted, you can literally (though with much difficulty) play this game to the end just by endlessly pressing the space bar. If player input is so minimal that a drinking bird can feasibly play at the same skill level as a human, you haven't created a game of choices, you've created a movie that requires button pressing to reach the next scene.
All that having been said, I would be open to a Hand of Fate 2 that fixed all of these issues or even Hand of Fate spinoffs in different settings. This is a great experiment, just not a great game.

Recettear is a game where you play a young girl whose dad left her with a massive (not actually, if you keep a tally) debt and a tiny French fairy arrives to collect it. They come up with a payment plan and set up an item shop. Sounds boring, doesn't it?
Well, IT REALLY IS NOT! There's a surprising amount of things you can do in this game. You can (and should) customize your shop to attract different types of customer, e.g. young girls won't enter a store that looks like it does blood sacrifice on Sundays. You have 4 ways to get items: The market, where you can buy consumables, treasures, clothing, decorations and books. The Merchant Guild, where you can buy combat gear. Buying random items from customers once you reach a certain Merchant Level. Going into a dungeon and picking up drops. Each day is split into 4 time slots and the customers that you can get (and their quantity) varies based on the time, so for example you're not going to see young girls shopping in the evening.
The dungeons have an entire plot of their own, where you'll meet various characters and they'll become customers for your store or a customer for your store turns out to be an adventurer. You don't HAVE TO go into the dungeons, but the dungeons are the only place to drop items used for Fusion, which is basically a crafting system where you can create new items or more powerful versions of existing ones. The different adventurers that you unlock are all different, with single target or area-of-effect attacks, low or high HP/SP, ranged or melee attacks, different kind of special attacks or just... moving really fast. The game tells you that the dungeons are a good way to get stuff for your store, as you pay nothing for the drops. This is true, and you can find a lot of goodies in there, but it also takes a hella lot of time: Just going into the dungeon takes half of an entire day and exploring can take a lot in terms of real playtime.
The actual selling of items is surprisingly complex, with an experience system where you get experience based on how well you did with the haggling. The Merchant Levels will unlock store upgrades and give you access to more expensive items in the Market and Merchant Guild. Every type of customer has a different way they'll haggle. Some have very little money, so even if you give them a huge discount, they still won't buy stuff. Others are the opposite. Some will haggle based on the percentage of profit you try to make. Later on, items can become scarse or abundant based on how much you sell them. Also randomly, a specific item or item type will become "popular" with a type of character: You can use this to summon a literal horde of customers that will only buy that specific thing from you.
Once you clear the game, you unlock Infinite mode, where you can just keep doing things forever. You also unlock a mode where the debt will keep rising indefinitely as long as you keep paying it.
The characters in Recettear are also quite something. The main character, Recette is a dim, happy-go-lucky little girl who somehow forgot that it's been literally weeks since she last saw her father. Tear is a fairy sent to collect the money Recette's dad owns and she's all business, all the time. Bonus points for French swearing. Louie is the first adventurer you meet and he's a young, hopeful kid who is always poor. Caillou is a young wizard who simply will not accept that Recette owns the shop. Charme is a thief that really likes getting drunk and trying to sell you overpriced items. Alouette is your self-proclaimed rival and eventual heiress to the largest chain store around, who is accompanied by a fairy of her own.
If there is something negative about Recettear, it's that it's too damn positive. You're neck deep in debt, you have like 800 pix to your name, which buys you like one bowl of food and your father is missing. Meanwhile, the in-game music is stupidly chipper and catchy. You are supposed to be in a desperate situation, with a literal loan shark LIVING WITH YOU AND WATCHING YOUR EVERY MOVE... and yet your biggest worry is when a little girl won't pay 800 pix for a sandwich because THEIR ALLOWANCE IS LIKE 300 PIX OR SOMETHING!
Recettear is not a game you play for the story: There really isn't much of a story or a "real" ending. Recettear is a game you play to explore the possibilities that the game gives you. Become a merchant that only sells 3 expensive weapons because that's all you can buy. Become a merchant who only sells one type of item (and perish because you can't feed a starving young man a book). Become an adventurer who only sells +11 Slime. Become an order-only merchant, only stocking items that people have ordered from you. Become a hoarder, making sure that you always have several of any given item type available. Just... do whatever, it all works. More or less. And hey, if you fail, you'll just lose all of your cash and start from the beginning.

OVERALL IMPRESSION: Positive! Pretty fun game, but the graphics and the soundtrack are the main attraction. If you like exploration, colorful environments, and great soundtracks, you'll love Owlboy; if you're looking for a challenging action platformer, you might be disappointed.
PROS:
+ Absolutely gorgeous graphics. Now THIS is pixel art, people.
+ Fun, colorful character design.
+ Excellent soundtrack. The later boss fights in particular had suitably epic music.
+ It's nice to see a character with a disability (mutism) as the protagonist in a game, and that everyone (except the obvious bully) was cool about it and it
affect the story (thus sending all kinds of implicit positive messages).
+ The mechanics of controlling the flyer with no attack capability and switching out different gunners with different offense and utility abilities is fun.
+ Completionists will delight in tracking down all 3000 (I think) coins. I guess I'd have to say I'm more completion-ish, because I was satisfied with getting all but the final reward, which requires finding every single coin in the game.
MIXED:
~ The story was great in that was interesting, had very high stakes, and kept me invested, but the particulars were nothing groundbreaking.
~ Not very difficult overall, but see one of the cons below. This may be a positive or a negative for you; personally, I was fine with enjoying the game for the exploration and the aesthetic experience.
CONS:
- I was invested in the story in general, but the particulars weren't all that memorable.
- Characters' motivations often didn't make sense within the context of the story, especially later in the game. In fact, it was not at all clear why the antagonist
the antagonist, because
In particular,
- Like I said, for the most part, the game was not at all difficult, but the odd times it
difficult, it felt like it was because the developers were being underhanded, not because of real gameplay difficulty. For example:
---> When you get hit, you get knocked back, but by the time you get control of Otus again, you only have about a second of immunity left.
---> When you
get control back, sometimes the enemy is already on top of you and there's nothing you can do about it.
---> There's so much happening on-screen, and the screen is shaking so much, that you can't even tell where Otus is.
---> Maybe I'm crazy, but there was one fight in particular where I swear the game switched the controls on me to summon a gunner after taking a hit (normally R to summon the gunner you just had, E to summon the next gunner in sequence), the end result of which was that I could never get the @#$~%! gunner I needed.
...Certainly none of the above four points ruined the game for me, but it was definitely highly annoying in the moment.
- Finally, three of the equipment rewards are absolutely pointless filler. (Hats that do nothing.) I get that they probably wanted to pad out the reward list, but when the hats disappear almost immediately after leaving the shop (when you take a hit, I think)...just don't bother.
Overall, I'm glad I bought it, glad I played it, and glad I finished it, but I did get it on sale. Not sure I would pay full price for this one. All that said, I do recommend Owlboy.

All is all it's a good game to buy if you're new to the whole citybuilding strategy game type, although it falls short if you want some more depth to your games.
10 euros is a decent price i'd say, for the content and great story you're getting ;)

Desktop Dungeons is an entertaining indie game that combines a variety of aspects from RPG, strategy, and puzzle games.  As the ruler of a kingdom, you construct buildings and recruit heroes to do your bidding for you.  The buildings themselves offer unique perks to improve the efficiency of your kingdom while you take control of a hero as you send them out into the further reaches of your lands on quests.
Each quest that you undertake is an entire adventure in itself.  Your hero starts at level 1 and you are capable of leveling them all the way to level 10 during the course of the map.  Each level drastically improves the capabilities of your character and there are plenty of beneficial boosts and magical items to find along the way.
Your buildings, on the other hand, offer options such as crafting magical gear, unlocking one of the many unique classes, adding additional boosts and content to encounter on your adventures, and even new races - all of which have their own stats that significantly alter the playstyle of -every- class.
The quests themselves are turn-based and give you all the time you need to execute the strategy of your choice.  You'll have to manage your health, mana, and experience as you try to maximize your gains and minimize your losses.  The game is unforgiving, though, very rewarding when you successfully pull off a dungeon and drag home a mountain of treasure.
I recommend this game to fans of turn-based RPGs, fantasy worlds, and strategy/puzzle gamers.  I found it to be far more enjoyable than I was expecting.  If you're on the fence, give it a try!

Can I recommend it? Yes and no (as of April 2015)
Yes:
Wow, they really did it! This honestly looks, feels, sounds, tastes (well, maybe not that last one) like everything you liked in the original Dungeon Keeper series. This is a proper and real successor and I recommend any fan of DK to throw away anything in their hands and try this game. I cannot applaud the developers enough, well done!
No:
Not yet, at least.
The game is simply not really done and ready for proper release just yet. On the positive side the developers are working like crazy releasing patches so I have my hopes up. The current state feels like a beta. A lot of things works very well, it's certainly playable, but you're constantly reminded of the game state by unpolished edges. To name some:
- Performance bugs: Even with a PC above recommended specs, every now and then you'll experience extreme slowdowns making the game unplayable. For now, a workaround for me is to exit the game and restart after each finished level. That seems to fix most of it.
- You'll see developer placemarkers for text, debugging or the like in the descriptions of creatures and rooms, instant immersion break right there.
- The campaign works but is quite unpolished. The campaign has a lot of different types of objectives and introduces new features steadily but often the education of new players gets lost, and they'll never get to try out their newly acquired knowledge before having lost the level and forced to start over.
- Another thing in the campaign is that your trusty mentor will often tell stories or talk to your enemies, though regularly these get mixed up and are played in the wrong order.
- The campaign level difficulty is rather random. You can play the same map twice in a row. The first time might be a hectic, stressful experience, trying to figure out how new things work, getting to know your enemy, etc., only to lose because it's almost impossible. The next time you play the same map, it's a rather peaceful experience, you got lots of time to build your base, explore and react.
I might add more when I remember it but these are, for me, major things that need to get fixed before the game unofficially can get out of beta.
Still, despite all of this and all the frustrations, the game is awesome. It just needs a bit more time to really shine.

I really like the idea of this game, and I even like the game itself, for the most part, but I cannot recommend it.

I haven't decided if the problem is the procedurally generated levels (meaning you can't figure out the right path and then execute it properly on the second run, if you didn't manage it the first time), or if the problem is the tricks you can use to beat things beyond your normal abilities (an expectation that once you've encountered an ability, you'll be able to put it in practice like a seasoned rules lawyer).
Either way, the Normal dungeons are all too difficult for me, even after several runs at trying to solve them.
The result, however, is this: far from being a fun and quirky game you can use to fill ten minutes for a break from your work, it becomes a frustrating problem that has players spending much longer than intended trying to beat a dungeon, any dungeon, before giving up in furstration.
Great idea, lousy execution.

I have to recommend this game because I enjoyed playing it. I love the XCOM series and anime and this seemed right up my alley. Can you hear the but coming? Of course you can. I only have two issues. One is that it's too easy and I think I feel that way because I came into it with an XCOM mindset and this is not XCOM level of difficulty. This is more focused on the story of how war affects individuals, (which is awesome by the way) and less about the brutal difficulty of fighting a war against superior forces with insufficient funds.
The second issue is tone and let me explain what I mean by that. The game tries very hard for this to be about the relationships that will inevitably develop in wartime. From love to friendship to racism and everything in between and it does that well. However, it's anime sensibilities means that there are times that people are happily talking about bread shortly after killing someone, presumably for the first time. It just doesn't fit.
Consider this praise by exception. Everything else about the game I loved and I am happy with the hours I spent with the game as I'm sure you will too.

I only got this game a week ago and I am hooked. Its such a great game to play especially with friends. For someone who's not 100 percent sure whether to download this or not try it out its certainly a really addicting game for the most bit (sometimes even the grinding can be fun).

It has some strong points, but they're actually heavily outwheighted by the weak points. Get it if you really want to/ have already played most other similar (turn & squad based strategy with rpg elements), but better games, otherwise get something else instead - there are some recommendations at the end. I'd also say that by the standards of it's original release in 2008, this was a decent game, but especially looking at the mechanics, it has not aged well.
- The visuals: This game has pretty much timelessly beautiful graphics, which are very well used in various settings and while the ingame animations can be somewhat clunky, i still liked watching the cutscenes and sceneries.
- The idea/ approach of topics: You could call it an appropriate war game, which i think is a stronger point than it may seem. I'd say, unlike a lot of other war games, be it shooter or strategy, this game manages to show war a lot more critical, in that no war is good, but sometimes you might still feel a need to fight, if you want to protect what's dear to you. It shows both the camaraderie and hope which keeps troops together, as well as some horrors of war. And while it struggles to be really good at that, it also tries to show that even aggressors can have reasons behind their actions besides power, or just "being bad".
- It's something different: Well, while i'd say that this by itself definetly isn't something that makes a good game, it still can feel somewhat refreshing, especially in an industry with sequels of  clones of sequels.
- The game mechanics, pretty much all of them. I think it just plays horribly in almost every concievable way. Again, some of this might have been forgivable for its original 2008 console release, but by current standards, i think it just isn't.
This starts at the menus, which are a pain to work through, every menu having a sub-menu, having  sub-sub-menu and you have to work through this button by button. Talking any more about this could just become as tideous as working through those menus itself.
- Next is unit movement, which is just as, if not more painful, considering that a lot of the terrain you'll come across is simply impassable, even though you won't be able to tell most of the time. You want to ambush an enemy around some trees? Too bad, you can't, it's impassable terrain, gotta stay on the path. Want to walk around a wall? Nope, can't go that way, there's a pebble on the ground, they just might stub their toe. Wanna go down that small ledge? Well, there's a 50/50 chance, but generally they can't even take a light step up- or downwards, you know, they might just trip. Want to roll that tank over that little dip in the ground? Well you can't, because reasons!
Since most of the game consists of moving units around, this is a major point and since there are little to no pointers which ways are viable or not, unless you're content with going the single most obvious one, it's a constant game of trial and error and can be a very, very frustrating one at that.
- Also, i'd say that there's actually barely any tactics involved - in a "tactics" game, you know, that's not really good either.
In short, the units are kind of "rock - paper - scissors - tank", with "tank" beating everything, including other tanks. Really, the variety of units, "scouts, shocktroopers, lancers, engineers and snipers" is nice and all, but if most of them are kind of bad, sometimes even at the job they're supposed to do (snipers miss on longer distances, while dying to a harsh look, shocktroopers have to get into enemy reaction fire to hit reliably and lancers can even miss entire tanks, the only unit they're good against) and you have a tank on your team which can beat anything, as long as you're not exposing it to too much anti-tank fire and maybe have an engineer around to repair it every now and then, the "tactics" part is kind of superficial and only comes out as a puzzle, if you really want to win missions with an "A ranking".
Plus, you can not flank anything, there's just crouching near cover, which always negates headshots and by that decreases viability of snipers even more, or standing and hoping that you're behind something that reliably blocks shots and while most of your units have granades, they only can throw them as far as a 3 year old would... with a broken arm maybe. So you want to use your tank.... except that the tank can also get stuck on small rocks or corners and if you play with a mouse, the tank controls like it would suffer from spasms most of the time.
In addition, while they try to mix things up, some missions just aren't very well designed, i found minor to major flaws in most of them. So you're pretty much stuck with mostly bad options, which i'd say doesn't really make the game challenging, as far as i can tell, but just sucks rather unpleasantly.
- And lastly, the game wants to give it an actiony, shootery spin, by leaving it to you to aim, but actually this is completely pointless, as there is barely any skill involved in aiming, as you can switch targets/ use an aimbot by the press of a button, nothing's moving while you "aim" and then you hope for the randomized shots to find the hitbox anyways.
- So much for the mechanics, but the other part, the story isn't really good either. I mean, as i wrote as a strong point, i like its critical moments very much, but you have to look rather hard for them and as far as i can tell, that doesn't really make the story. No, the story mostly is about some Japanese-fantasy WW2 Europe, in which some teenagers, plus some in their earliest twenties become war-heroes, with an "oh so quirky" youngster as the center of all attention and everyone pretty much showing their best stereotypical behaviour. To some degree i'd even say that this counters some of the strong points of the story being about discrimination and stereotyping... while any character in the game with more than one dimension can be called lucky and the game in its entirety is rather culture-insensitive. Nope, sorry, that doesn't really work. If you don't like anime i'd guess that most of the storytelling can seem boring or nonsensical and even if you do like anime, as i'd claim for myself... well it's still not a good story. And the fact that it's always switching between proper cutscenes and click by click narration doesn't help either, that just messes up the flow.
In conclusion, while i kind of want to like the game, the bad parts just so heavily outweigh the good parts that i can't really recommend it. It is often compared to XCOM and Fire Emblem, but in the end both of those just are way better at what they're doing respectively - so if you haven't already, you should get those instead, or maybe try Shadowrun, or Banner Saga, also very good picks concering turn based strategy with a good underlying story.

The attempt on story telling is somewhat quaint, with a thin veil of historical parallel of WWII. However, the story has to Japan-ise it with most solider being a rag tag team of teenagers, and the main character is made commander only by the fact that he is the main character and every female wants to bang him. Other characters with less screen time don't matter and can be replaced rather quickly. Quite frankly, I don't know whether this game is supposed to be a tie-in for the anime, or the anime is supposed to be a tie-in for the game. I haven't finished the game, as the gameplay was for me the biggest downfall for this game.
The gameplay attempts to mix two aspects: turn-based and shooter action. However some things just don't go well together, like chocolate and sewer water. The turn based system is supposed to be for the players to plan their moves, while shooter action is supposed to be high-octane play with more emphasis on quick play. When it is the player's turn, you take control of a soldier and control them manually in third-person, consuming some action-points that puts a limit on how far you can move (this I don't have qualms with). However when you are moving, every enemy within your sights and even the enemies with their backs to you will turn around and shoot you and only you like the robots they are. This happens until you stop and take aim, at which point the enemies will stop firing like this was supposed to be a game or something. Things go back swiftly, however, as soon as you stop shooting everyone that was aiming at you will start shooting you again (even if you're not moving), forcing you to end the turn as soon as you're done with a unit. Call me old-fashioned, but I think in turn-based combat the enemies shouldn't be able to attack IF IT'S NOT THEIR TURN. This is compounded by the fact that AI seems to ramp up the aimbot to the max, for if you're seen by an enemy over 2 miles away through a keyhole they'll start spraying as a squad, pinning you down or at least you won't leave unscathed. Cover system is also strict, with sandbags being the only thing that you can take cover behind. Anything else, like a building corner, a crate or chest-high walls, the teenagers stand their like ducks in a shooting gallery. Also the game doesn't have auto-save, so if you die (and you will) you're gonna have a bad time.
Between missions demand micromanagement, with upgrades, equipment and solider training. This would be ok, as I don't mind the base management and I get to at least interact with the characters a little bit. However, the menu is really tedious to navigate, and it was clear that this game was meant for consoles, as the menu was harder to navigate than a goverment bureaucy. Also, the game forces you to watch a cut scene, and no dialogue can be skipped one by one, and only the whole cut scene can be quit, not skipped. Every cut scene and interaction has a prompt "are you sure", as if the game is treating us like mentally handicapped toddler in a crowded shop.
Overall, the game feels like a visual novel, but SEGA wanted to make it into a game and try to be innovative, but failed. Of course, the story could be engaging, but after watching the anime, I have seen everything that there is to see, and the game has nothing more to offer, other than a small window of personality and dialogue of minor characters and stress. I'd recommend if you're into character-character interaction like in visual novels, but not if you're looking for a game to play

I had anticipated this title for some time .... just like many others in the community.
I bought the game at the first opportunity to do so and was nicely surprised to see the game load into my steam account a day earlier than I expected.
Now there is a case of the older sibling casting a shadow on the new family member and I feel ATS still has to come out from under the shadow ETS2 casts and stand on it's own two feet.
That said, I won't sugar-coat my first impressions .... I was a bit deflated personally. I'd run 450 hrs+ in ETS2 and created over 260 YouTube videos .... I really enjoyed ETS2 and expected to take up from a similar position with ATS from the start. I found that ATS ticked the boxes well initially but seems to lack something that made it a 'standing on it's own feet' title. It really felt very much like an add-on to ETS2 to be honest. The thing is, it's not an addon ... and with a little more time and support from SCS which is already coming ... it'll surely mature into another AAA title for SCS.
But it's not quite there yet for two main reasons ...
1) The map currently is 3 states (actually 2 but Arizona is but a week or two away from release). I don't clearly understand what to expect for the remainder of USA and then what the plans may be for Canada and Mexico.
2) Truck makes and models. We've got Peterbilt and Kenworth today and no clear indications on the roadmap for all the other brands.
On a positive note, SCS have upped the communication with the community. It was always best in class and in recent weeks, they seem to upped their standards again.
Maybe I had too much in terms of expectation but I feel that community has generally communicated a similar message back to SCS based on the size of the map and range of trucks available.
It's mid May 2016 as I write this review and I'm ~60 hrs into ATS.  All signs are pointing firmly towards 100's of hrs in this title.  I've enjoyed the Kenworth W900 truck I'm driving and I've explored a lot of the California and Nevada map that SCS opened with. Arizona will help immensely and I'm looking forward impatiently to being able to drive to the East coast.
Now SCS have always been modder friendly and it's this community that enhances a players experience so often in games today. ATS is no exception and kudos to SCS again for their support.
If I recall the release days of ETS2, way back when ..... and look today at what ETS2 developed into today, I would say that ATS is on a similar track ... so the future looks pretty good. The community wants faster updates and is impatient as ever which in my opinion highlight two things ....
a. a call to action for SCS on ATS
b. confirmation to SCS of the passion and energy the community has for ATS
So if you're looking at ATS reviews and trying to decide if it makes sense for you to buy it, my recommendation is Yes, buy it ... it's another great title in the SCS stable and it really does give the player a sense of driving an 'American' truck in an American landscape.
ATS is the only place that offers this truly American trucking experience and the future is full of potential.

The best character is the trash bot.
Fletcher and his head-pal are pretty close, and there's even berserker robots wearing Viking helmets in here.  Promise!
It's very easy to jump into the game and be overwhelmed by the lack of sprint, bots grinding out your guts in surprise ambushes, and your puny killing power; at the same time, the chicken run design of the first level (and some others) isn't the game at its detailed, surreal best.  By 2017 standards this isn't the prettiest game but it does incredibly well for less than 5GB on your hard drive.
Gameplay-wise, there's a few annoyances, but most are designed into the game and you are expected to figure a way around them.  There's also the occasional bug to enjoy, and some difficult jumping.  Some of the particle and screen effects are overboard to the point it's difficult to see what's going on - but again, smart play will deal with this, and the intentionally cutesy (well, mostly) bot designs are very easy to read for quick reactions.
Memorizing enemy spawns will be rewarded, and there's a heavy focus on cover and strafing here.  The game offers lots of tools that promise to slow your enemy, but (having just finished the game on Heroic) you should focus on survival buffs and sheer damage output (the major exceptions being the shock mortar and the gravity grenade, which are both easy to put into your weapon flow).  Some people suggest every weapon has a use, but buying all the weapons actually makes it slower to switch quickly between your go-to combos.
That's really what it's about:  Figuring out ways to keep doing damage to enemies, and preventing damage to yourself.  I don't know if Flying Wild Hog really succeeded in fitting a System Shock's worth of options into the two weapons (with their firing modes), but it's not hopeless.  There are ways to cheese the game, even on Heroic, and when you realize that Fletcher switches to the energy gun faster than to the firearm you should have a hint that the game isn't just about throwing down a stasis field and switching to rockets.
Overall, it's a truly excellent game with some underrated qualities, at the same time that the developers' inconsistent delivery of promises, a difficult-to-understand scoring system, and the mixed experiment of the overhaul make this a tough sell for many gamers - but if you have the patience to learn the system and the skills to execute them, Hard Reset will be a rewarding playthrough (or five).
If you read this far, here's a couple super secret hints:  Some (typically smaller) NANOs can be grabbed from their hiding places by the gravity grenade, if regular explosions aren't working.  If you use the manual quicksave option, watch for the screen to flash to confirm the game is saving - just the CD icon won't do it.  If you try to quick save on the final level, do it before triggering the doors, not after - else you will get spawned in front of a door you cannot open again.

It's a very interesting game where you go through a D&D style adventure with random encounters and events with various results that can either help or hurt you. Hand of Fate is a game made by an Defiant development, an Australian developer - fitting, because it's essentially a solitaire game that is out to murder you in your sleep.
The concept itself is ingenious if simple - deckbuilding meets roguelike. Build your decks and take on them, resolve combat in third person, pray to RNGeesus to unlock more and better cards (or some really terrible ones), and push your way through a court of twisted suits - skulls/skeletons for hearts, plague/ratmen for diamonds, dust/bandits for clubs, and scales/lizardmen for spades. There's also a few unconventional suits that serve as miniboss (or even boss) encounters.
The gameplay is simple as well. Your spunky adventurer piece moves space by space through a trail set by cards dealt from your encounter deck by the helpful Dealer. Some of them are resolved through simple multiple choices, some through a game of chance (but if you're paying attention you can often see where the card you want will be, or at least the one you really don't want), and some as mentioned through live combat; or of course a combination thereof.
Add resource management into the mix, and the game gets more complex. Usually every move costs a unit of food, and as long as you have any of that you'll also heal damage slowly as you move; but run out of food and each move will bring you closer to the cold embrace of death. Naturally, you're going to have a speed date with the Reaper if you lose all your health, too. You acquire equipment and other bonuses through encounters, or through shops that are sparsely strewn through the paths of cards. That, of course, requires gold which is again acquired mostly through encounters.
It starts off easy enough, a few quick and pleasant runs to give you a taste of the game, but the Dealer is a crafty fellow, and on every stage he adds a bit of his own nasty cards into the mix, the deeper you go, the worse they get. He might treat you as a worthy opponent, even in a cordial manner, but remember that he is not your friend.
All in all, it's quite an addictive and replayable experience, despite the occasional rather frustrating chance fails or cheap shots from the Dealer. I do recommend anyone who has the patience to learn the game, and, if all else fails, fight cheese with cheese. Because turnabout is fair play and beating a game that abuses its mechanics against you by abusing its mechanics against it is quite rewading.
And now onwards to the sequel.

It's hard for me to give an accurate rating to the game. Would I recommend it or not? It depends. And I really can't decide which factors are more imporant when it comes to judging a game like this.
I have heard many things about Owlboy. Some of them good, some of them bad - and I've finally decided to give it a try and get an opinion of my own. What did I come up with? Well...
Owlboy is a beautiful game. It has great, pixel-art visuals, pleasant music and some reasonably memorable characters. And those things are good, or even great. If I were to judge the game based on those alone - I'd easily give it a 9/10.
Playing it was a pleasant experience, for the most part. I've constantly felt a sense of wonder, and had a drive to go ahead and explore that bit further...
Sadly - there is much more that makes up a video game. We can't just focus on the visuals, you have to touch upon the game design, how the character handles, et cetera. And that's where it becomes... More complicated.
Owlboy is one of the only games I recall, which has hit animations that are both too short and too long at the same time - The invincibility is a bit too short, making it possible for you to get caught up in damage chains, while the animation of getting hurt is long enough to throw you off, and lose some of the pace during gameplay.
And keeping up the pace can be really important, because bosses in the game aren't too intuitive to deal with. You need to fall in the right rythm and be two steps ahead of them - otherwise, you are going to end up in a terrible situation. You could - in theory - react to everything as it happens, but that'd unfortunately require additional fingers, to pull off seemlessly.
There are sections of the game that seem needlessly harsh and punishing, followed by sections that offer little challange at all. Which is somewhat understandable, but I prefer smooth difficulty curve in games, rather than difficulty spikes. If they had a followup, maybe the tension wouldn't be gone. But as it stands, some sections just come across as boring.
The biggest gripe I've got with the game, though - It doesn't respect your time. There are countless cutscenes, that will take you out of the game, in order to show you some dialogue. Acceptable, but I think I'd rather have longer and more 'dense' breaks, than small ones every few minutes. Additionally, there is a lot of unskippable animations that really don't matter past the first time - Pirates and the locking doors spring to mind. Once a pirate notices you, a game will stop and play door closing animation. If you move slightly backwards - it will play animation of the door opening. If you approach him again, the animation will repeat. And it takes about 20 seconds every single time. And it's far from the only example of the game just wasting time.
Ultimately - while the game was fun to me, I became frustrated with it towards the end. That's why I didn't really go and look for all the coins, and I weren't interested in searching for secrets. I just... Felt tired of the game, after the 9 hours I've spent in it.
While I'd love to recommend Owlboy as a game, I really cannot. It's a bit too much frustration, and too little reward. Even if it looks beautiful.

Word of advice to folks considering this "fresh start" server. Save your time, and money.
In typical Trion-esque style, they have yet again, destroyed what should have been a seamless and practiced server startup. They have been through this twice already so we should expect them to have this down to a science, right? Wrong, absolutely wrong.
When you start the game, you get black screens. If you make it through the black screens, you get in a 3 hour queue. During that queue, you have a good chance to get DC'd and put at the end of the queue. If you somehow manage to make it to 1 in the queue, you have a 50/50 shot to lose connection and start over. If you manage to slip past the queue, and get to the next stage, character select, theres a good chance you get a blue screen instead of your character select screen. At this point, you have to shut down the game and restart. They say there is a "grace period" which is supposed to save your spot in the queue, well.....this is broken by all accounts.
You are now back in the queue at 2200. It moves at about 650 an hour.
But for hilaritys sake, let's assume you get through ALL THAT and make it in game. Well, there is no land left, because a handfull of folks with low ping have managed to stay in the game, with no problems. They have level 55s, every piece of land on the planet, and are already farming endgame gear, while you have been in the game for maybe 60 minutes total working to get to level 30.
All that being said, the game itself is amazing, and if you can manage the ridiculous startup and login issues then a wonderful experience awaits you. But until then, save your money and time and go buy your kids, or parents something nice for Christmas.

Owlboy ultimately feels like it's the embodiment of ‘style over substance’. The visuals are simply amazing; the mind-blowing level of detail in the enviroment and backgrounds, along with polished animation just filled with character, make the game a joy to behold. The soundtrack is entirely done by a live orchestra and it
- it’s certainly a calibre above most games, let alone indies, regularly making you feel like you’re in the front row of a concert hall.
However, the gameplay leaves a lot to be desired, in my opinion. It’s serviceable at best, bland and boring at worst. The majority of the game has you flying through tight, maze-light dungeons - with exploration, bullet-hell, and light puzzle solving elements. These are then broken up by boss fights, plot events and the occasional genre shift - such as a stealth section, for example. While dungeon mechanics are changed up reasonably quickly, they remain frustratingly simple throughout - puzzles never evolve beyond switch-finding, block-dragging or using companion X on object Y. Outside of bosses, combat remains fairly sedate; dodging and holding shoot, with very little variety beyond the occasional need to knock a shield off. The bosses themselves however are consistent highlights, being interestingly designed and of decent difficulty.
The storyline and characterisation is above average. Your companions are charming and the great writing quality (along with the aforementioned visual flair) helps each character remain memorable and entertaining. There’s an almost unbearable amount of melodrama as the plot is fairly dark and depressing, in contrast to the presentation of the game. The worldbuilding is great - but the plot makes maddeningly little use out of it, leaving several big questions unanswered after the credits, and the ending ultimately felt under-cooked and left me a little disappointed.
All in all, I feel you would enjoy this game if you’re fine with overlooking average gameplay for the sake of beautiful sound and visuals. I'm sure a lot of would wouldn't be able to, but for those that can, I'm sure this game would be a treat.

Tapping into that extraordinarily familiar ground that Clash of Clans first revolutionized, Battle Islands is a briefly entertaining if slow-burning freemium strategy game. It’s a little too familiar to truly warrant much excitement but those keen for a World War 2 themed title will find more enjoyment.
Set in 1942, players control a platoon of soldiers as they attempt to establish bases on various tropical islands in the South Pacific. While the theme is slightly different from the norm, the gameplay remains much the same.
A brief tutorial guides one through the basics, which mostly relate to placing buildings and training troops. A barrier keeps players protected from enemy attack for a few days in order to give them a chance to be more established, but this is easily circumvented by the bloodthirsty. Once the tutorial is out of the way, structure is offered through a series of challenges that can be completed with the bonus being that they offer up gold bricks.
Gold bricks are essential here given that they’re the premium currency that affects how quickly projects are completed, among other things. While Battle Islands might seem initially generous with the gold bricks, they vanish quite quickly – leaving one quite restricted due to the plethora of timers.
Waiting around for various tasks to complete will be a regular part of one’s sessions with Battle Islands. It’s really quite slow going. Competing with opposing players is briefly fun, but it’s nothing new for the genre and plays it very safe.
It’s the theme that makes Battle Islands slightly more noticeable, with the World War 2 theme often proving more endearing than something fantastical. That’s sufficient for a brief play session but I’d be surprised if anyone found the game truly gripping for any length of time. It’s not that it does anything particularly badly, it’s just all too familiar.

I've played this game extensively (off-line), and many features are quite good.  However, I have two main gripes:
1) AI gets unlimited fuel.  This absolutely destroys any attempt at strategy, because small AI ships (Corvettes) can travel over huge distances (while you cannot) and sack your colonies--often while they are still defenseless.  This is most apparent in the critical early game.  Absolutely game-breaking for me.  Some people praising the AI are probably just seeing these AI "super Corvettes" cruising in from ridiculous distances.
2) Feels somewhat unfinished.  There are a lot of features that are not yet implemented in the game (e.g., heroes).  Apparently open to modders, but that's not as user friendly as most games (need to recompile files, etc.).
Could be a GREAT game, but the fuel cheat breaks it for me, and it apparently can't be modded.  Recommend holding off until ths is addressed.

It's a clear morning in California. I'm driving my truck down a lonely road, through the empty desert. In the rear view mirror, I see a car approaching. I keep driving, expecting them to pass me, but they don't. I check back in my mirror, and- it's a police car. Okay, this is no situation to panic. I kept driving, slowly and steadily. But I felt myself growing tired. The road stretched on, seemingly endlessly. I finally could take no more and dozed off for anly a few seconds. When I woke up, I was going slightly above the speed limit, and I slammed my brakes. But it was too late. The police car had already called reinforcements. A line of six or seven cop cars was following me down the highway, sirens blaring. I suddenly get a storm of notifications from my GPS- my bank account is being drained, ticket by ticket. Then the shooting started, and they drove the truck off the road. That was the last thing I remembered, until I woke up. The starving, broke, pitiful CEO of a failed trucking company.

Wonderful art and music design with nice & crunchy gameplay that rests in-between the ultra-high-octane of Hotline Miami and the less-high-octane of a more standard twin-stick shooter. Controls take a little bit to get used to but once you've got the hang of it they're actually more than servicable on M/KB, though bear in mind that as of writing there's no option to rebind keys (devs have stated this will be added in the first patch).
Tons of variety in the weapons and skills you can use, and the ability to change up your skill tree on the fly to experiment with new builds even in the middle of a battle adds a wonderful layer of choice and strategy to the player's arsenal, and the Hard difficulty is pretty well balanced. You'll die quite a bit, but it's the same "die then rewind 30 seconds and get right back to trying" that Hotline Miami had, and it works just as well here.
Enemies have nice visual designs, though gameplay wise they're the Hotline-esque "Functionally identical to the player but with only one weapon/ability per enemy", which certainly isn't a bad thing and works well, just nothing particularly impressive.
Bosses unfortunately fall pretty flat, with gun-based bosses really just being a regular enemy with a far larger health pool, at the very least they do tend to use/introduce the more powerful guns that are otherwise reserved for your own use. Likewise, melee-based bosses at least have a couple unique attacks, but they still mostly just try to dash and use regular slashes against the player.
Both types run into a pretty big balance issue about 2/3rds through the game, when you unlock a gun that can stunlock any boss and makes killing them merely a matter of watching as they sit there helpless and gradually die from lightning damage.
Of the 14 or so bosses, only two break this "I'm just a big NPC" pattern and unfortunately neither are very good, with one being a♥♥♥♥♥♥easy puzzle boss and the other's only attack being "shoot a beam for 5 seconds, then recharge, then shoot, then recharge, etc".
While the ending is a bit abrupt, the story and world are pretty neat. The background lore entries you unlock, on top of all the various NPC dialogue both at the hub and in-mission helps build a convincing and immersive cyberpunk world to beat up dudes in.
Overall a very enjoyable experience despite its flaws whether you're coming in as a fan of cyberpunk or as a fan of Hotline-type games.

TL:DR a unique take on the rogue like genre in the form of a card game. The combat sections are a bit hit and miss but I'd recommend giving this game a try
Hand of Fate mashes up a few genres such as rogue-like, choose your own adventure and hack and slash and delivers the experience through the medium of a card game. It manages to combine and balance all these different elements very well.
Your advesary the Dealer, who is a bit like a sinister D&D game master, lays out a grid or row of cards that you move your piece across, like moving from point to point on a map. Each card you land on reveals an encounter or quest. For the quests you get to choose your action and your success or failure is decided by drawing a card from 4 shuffled cards, a bit like the ball under the cup game. Completing quests and killing bosses earns you more cards for future playthroughs.
For the enemy encounters you get to directly control your character and fight the enemies yourself. The combat sections for me are probably the weakest part of the game as fighting the generic enemies is a bit boring as it breaks down to just hitting the attack button and dodging  as well as hitting the counter button when the on screen prompts appear. The boss battles are a bit better though as they require a bit more strategy and variety. You can also obtain spells and special weapons which give you more combat options though each has varying levels of usefullness.
There are two modes, story and endless. Story mode has 12 bosses that you must kill, with the dealer upping the ante by introducing more of his own cards which he uses to hinder you such as making you lose health, food or gold. Endless mode challenges you to survive as long as you can while you earn points throughout the playthrough which goes on a scoreboard when you finish.
To conclude, Hand of Fate feels like quite a unique game and it offers a fun challenge although the combat sections do detract from the enjoyment a little.
Graphics are underwhelming, and though the gameplay is simple, it's also very solid.  It is a fun game, though 'd recommend you wait til it's on sale in a big way :P

This game is good as a game and amazing as a pop culture entity (wow, how hipster can I get?)
If you see a game with cute anime girls, you go in with certain expectations, and you'll be pleasantly surprised to find them completely shattered by this game. The game is not about the cute anime girls, cute and anime though they may be; the game is about capitalism and economic success, and you'll find yourself caring about the colour of your shop's carpet and which things are stocked nearest the windows.
If you enjoy the healing experiences of games like Animal Crossing and Harvest Moon, this game will give you something similar, although with a decent helping of dungeon-crawling to go with it.
I love the characters. Especially Charme and Nagi. And Tear. Actually, pretty much all of the characters are lovable in their own way, except the scammer ♥♥♥♥♥ who exists solely to ruin your combo and your day. She can die in a hole, but everyone else (even the standoffish demon guy) is pretty cool.
Story: 6.5/10. Standard stuff. No real flaws, nothing to reccomend the game for the story alone.
Writing: 8.5/10. This is a genuinely funny and heartwarming game, with a heaping helping of memes spawned from it.
Gameplay: 7.5/10. Pretty fun. Whether you enjoy the nuances of running the shop or the decent (if somewhat simple) dungeon mechanics is down to personal preference. Personally, I like running the actual shop.
Music: 7/10. The music in town is lively and upbeat, and the music in the dungeon is appropriately forboding. It does what it needs to, but I wouldn't expect you to be sticking it in your MP3 player and listening to it by itself.
Replay Value: 8/10. You may not get properly addicted to this game, but there is a lot to be said for multiple playthroughs, if only to play the game without the debt hanging over you or to amass more treasure. If you're a completionist, you will definitely get more than your money's worth collecting all the items and leveling up all the heroes. Also, you will likely need to consult the internet once or twice, as not everything in this game is entirely straightforward in regards to unlocking things.
Final Verdict: 7.5/10. Well worth the money. Capitalism ho!

First, let me state the goods:  great models and animations, ambient sounds, and core mechanics.
Now, the bad.
1.)  It is altogether obvious in many situations that this is an English port, and a poor one at that.  Stilted language, missing narrations, bizarre unit acknowledgements (one unit actually speaks for a full 15 seconds when clicked on!), and other artifacts let this be known.   For instance, "quit game" quits the mission you are on; it doesn't actually exit your game.
2.)  The game is excruciatingly slow paced:  building a decent economy takes well over 15 long minutes, and you'll need one before you can really do anything.  As such, every near mission requires long bouts of waiting just to start.  Once you've got it rolling, you're good, but it is still terribly slow.  Many missions take around 45 minutes to complete, the first 15 of which are waiting, and the other just cumbersome.
3.)  The soundtrack during game only has one track that it plays over and over.
4.)  Single-player campaign is insipid and dull.
5.)  Clunky UI where it feels you can't zoom out enough.
THIS ISN'T A "BAD" GAME.  It is, though, slow and dull.  I got about 6 missions in before I just quit, not because of difficulty, but because the fun to work ratio was not high.  The game lacks polish, and the single-player campaign just feels like it is a collection of fetch quests.  I feel the Stronghold series did what this game was attempting to do better.
It's a great game in it's own way, some love it, some don't. Give it a try.

Developed by insayn and 4nation5 (two talented students from Berlin), Journey To The Center Of The Earth is a very well polished game. A feat quite worthy of attention since this is the dev team’s first and so far only project to date. The game itself is a homage to the classic 2D puzzle platformers we’ve grown accustomed to, but it mixes enough elements as to stand out from the generic platformer crowd.
Journey To The Center Of The Earth is a most enjoyable game revolving around large cave levels, rife with puzzles and obstacles to overcome. The platforming sections fit well with the different powers each of the three protagonists posses. Although the game is loosely based on Jules Verne’s classic adventure novel, it takes some liberties from it while managing to offer an authentically fun puzzle game as well. It does not get boring and provides quite a challenge.
It is in fact, sometimes too difficult. Or better said, it suffers from some diffculty spikes. But that is to be expected from a game that draws inspiration from the many puzzle platformers which preceded it. Not the case to rage quit, but the first few levels were tricky until you have a clear understanding of the characters you control. It does help, the fact that they can be controlled individually, as sometimes it would be near impossible to keep track of them simultaneously. The effort of completing all 18 levels is worth it and the game can part of a speed run, once you get the hang of it.
From a graphical point of view, the game might seem simplistic at first sight. At a closer inspection though, the character sprites reveal the amount of work they took and the cave layouts themselves are well made. The two-men team made a stellar job from a level design perspective.
The game’s sounds and music could have used a bit more diversity. It didn’t quite live up to the the atmosphere of the overall game.The sounds are somewhat generic and the music is too monotonous during the final levels. Still considering the genre and price point, I do believe the sound department to be more of a secondary priority for Journey To The Center Of The Earth.
+ Classic type of gameplay
+ Level diversity
+ Pleasant graphics and character sprites
+ Steam Trading Cards
- Difficulty spikes require some trial and error.
- Repetitive sounds
- No Steam Achievements
The game is rather fun to play and the level diversity made me overlook the trial and error parts of it, which can be frustrating sometimes. The gameplay is that of a classic 2D puzzle platformer and having 3 characters to control, each with a different set of skills, is an interesting challenge.The game’s sounds can get repetitive at times and I would have enjoyed to see Steam Achievements. But at least the dev team added Trading Cards to it, nine months after the game’s initial release.

Before release Slitherine games said they had a "system" for setting price on games, and they were an expert because of all the games they have released. They said if game was too cheap people would not take it serious. I almost laughed at this.
I personally refunded the game because I felt it was too much money, and certainly would have kept it had the price been more reasonable for what is offered.
So what is offered? Well basically a streamlined combat focused 4x. It has all the elements of a 4x, but simplified. There is still a learning curve, but not a steep one. Combat is where this game shines the best, with a half decent combat viewer and some tactical choices that can be made during battles. I also personally enjoy the fuel system for ships, though last I knew the AI ignored this system (free fuel), so it was only a restriction on the player, which is a bummer.
I enjoy doing a lot of the aspects of 4x's that were streamlined in this game. (meaning I dont want them simplified like this game does) Its kinda hard to explain unless you watch a video of gameplay. I hate to bring it into this review, but (almost) everything this game does, Stellaris does 4x better... pun intended. Though to be fair Stellaris has more people working on it, and Stellaris is not perfect either, but Polaris Sector is missing so much in comparison, I will not even bother to compare the 2 games, except to say that they are the same price, which should say something about the price of Polaris Sector.
One good thing to mention, although I have not been active on the forums recently, is that the developer was very responsive and friendly last time I was lurking about. I also did not experience any bugs while playing the game.

I'm going to preface my review by saying that there are some things that I like about this game.  However, there are more things that I dislike about it.
Pros:
1.  The starmap is quite beautiful and can be expansive.  It is also easy to understand at a glance.
2.  The building automation AI for the worlds is pretty good.  I just wish there were more options to go with or a popup when a planet is done building with the automation.
3.  The tech tree is vast and there is a lot to play with.  However, see "Cons" for further information.
Cons:
1.  The races are not that unique.  They feel fairly cookie-cutter due to easily customizing them when starting a game.  Truthfully, you could choose one race and give it all of the bonuses of another race.
2.  The tech tree might be vast, but it's linear and extremely hard to really plan long-term as there is no real tree to look at.  It's linear in the fact that techs will be learned in the exact same order in every game you play unless you play with the sliders to research different things faster.  However, techs are still in the same line.  The tech tree is also almost impossible to look at ingame to see what to focus on what to get to a specific tech.  The devs provided a website with all the possible techs, but it's also difficult to navigate and plan with as well.
3.  Here is the biggest problem with this game:  Racial ship balance. Suprisingly fresh-looking 4x space strategy, compared to relatively all-the-same 4x titles published in the last couple of years.
Finally:
1. Relatively complex and deep tactical combat system, where every action means possible change of initiative and battle odds. Finally skill and tactical sense matters, and you can either lose your advantage if you make several mistakes, or you can win even against unfavorable odds if you make a few right decisions.
2. The ship cost is very high - they are a long and expensive investment. So, like real battleships of our era - sometimes you make a new design for each new ship, and you feel that every single ship is unique and important for you. No faceless ship swarms here (except fighters and bombers swarms, of course).
3. Long ship production times demand strategic planning. When you meet another race - will you try to build a couple of new colony ships to occupy good spots near their border, and leave them undefended, or will you build a couple of warships and risk losing possible colonization spot?
4. Realistic colonization process, where new colonies initially are a liability to defend, and not a source of easy expansion.
5. Research is unique in this game. Every single discovery you make is known beforehead, and appreciated, and quickly applied to ship designs after it is finally discovered.
Cons:
1. Due to long build and planning and exploration times game is not very fast-paced - so you have to be a bit meditative and patient while nothing else happens.
All in all - a solid and interesting concept, at least after several gameplay hours.

The critics sure did love Owlboy. On first playing the game it’s easily to see why they were so bewitched. Credit where credit is due – Owlboy is a spectacular piece of pixelated art. The animation, world design and attention to detail is absolutely amazing – this probably the best looking 2d game ever made, and that’s in a world where Ori and the Blind Forest exists. Everything, from little incidental licks of flame to the enormous screen filling bosses have been hand crafted with loving care down to the tiniest whirring cog and dust plume.
Despite being a side scroller, Owlboy has one inspiration that becomes immediately obvious as you enter the deceptively enclosed hub overworld, and the twee orchestral score swells. This is hammered home with stylised, cartoonish character design (with seemingly obligatory tumblr noses) and discrete, puzzle filled dungeons. Yep, Owlboy is definitely channelling good old Zelda, right down to the set of three all-powerful McGuffins. This extends to the story, which is compact and moves at a fair clip, and is just about interesting enough to keep things ticking along even if most of the more emotional moments fall a little flat.
I’ve heard this game described as a metroidvania, but it really isn’t – the game is almost entirely linear, with no map screen (though it honestly could really have done with one). The only hidden collectables to dig up via the minimal allowed backtracking are coins – these can be used to buy a variety of rather perfunctory upgrades. You get three health upgrades, and a couple of range upgrades, and that’s your lot.
Of course being linear isn’t in itself a problem as long as the game is fun and well designed. Unfortunately while it’s beautiful Owlboy is very flawed, and in some ways it’s a case study in poor design choices. There are three enforced stealth sections, with each being longer and more tedious than the last. Boss fights, while graphically stunning have random, difficult to avoid attacks which are exacerbated by your character’s unclear hit box. It’s also very easy to lose track of your character during hectic moments due to how busy each screen is, and it’s not always obvious what is foreground and background. This is obviously a game designed by artists, and that’s every bit the backhanded compliment it seems.
Worse than all of this perhaps is that when it isn’t being annoying, Owlboy is often just uninteresting. The dungeons aren’t particularly cleverly designed, and the puzzles are so basic that it’s impossible to imagine even children getting stumped for more than a minute or two. The flight mechanic is not used in exciting ways either – it just feels like a 2D platformer without the platforming most of the time.
However, the game has been crafted with so much obvious love and care that I can’t bring myself to dismiss it completely. I obviously enjoyed it enough to finish it, and even when I was starting to lose interest the desire to see what the artists had cooked up next gave me enough enthusiasm to press on – in this case the lean 7-10 hour runtime works in its favour, and there’s no filler or enforced backtracking. If you can put up with some flabby design, as a showcase of artistic talent Owlboy is absolutely worth your time, and I can’t deny my opinion of the game is a net positive, if only slightly. If as much care had been put into the game design as the art, Owlboy would have been an undisputed classic.

It's a clear morning in California. I'm driving my truck down a lonely road, through the empty desert. In the rear view mirror, I see a car approaching. I keep driving, expecting them to pass me, but they don't. I check back in my mirror, and- it's a police car. Okay, this is no situation to panic. I kept driving, slowly and steadily. But I felt myself growing tired. The road stretched on, seemingly endlessly. I finally could take no more and dozed off for anly a few seconds. When I woke up, I was going slightly above the speed limit, and I slammed my brakes. But it was too late. The police car had already called reinforcements. A line of six or seven cop cars was following me down the highway, sirens blaring. I suddenly get a storm of notifications from my GPS- my bank account is being drained, ticket by ticket. Then the shooting started, and they drove the truck off the road. That was the last thing I remembered, until I woke up. The starving, broke, pitiful CEO of a failed trucking company.

Not a very populair game, the Settlers: Heritage of kings is a classis city building game, set in the old times.
In this review I'll talk about a few things:
- The story
- The gameplay
- The graphics
- Online play
- Pros en Cons in general.
The story:
The story starts with out hero, Dario, chilling alone under a tree. His village gets attacked and mostly destroyed, the only thing that remains is the castle. After you fight off all the attackers, it's up to you to rebuild the village. Once you've succeeded, you're going to move on to a different place, this happens after every city. There are 15 main missions in total, which are all about building villages, making armies, and defeating other villages.
The gameplay:
The Settlers: Heritage of Kings is a strategy game. You start off each map with atleast four serfs, and with atleast one hero. A serf is a worker, they can build the buildings you need to evolve your village. New serfs can be bought in the castle, which is your main base of operations. The hero is a special kind of soldier, they have special abilities, there is a total of 6 heroes for you to play as.
As you start the map, your serf can only build a few buildings. Mines, houses, farms, and schools. In order to make more buildings, you will need a school to research, after that new buildings will be unlocked. To unlock more things to be researched, you will need higher leveld buildings, it's a various circle.
The graphics:
This game is from 2004, so the graphics aren't really the best. It's not minecraft level where it's all blocks, but it isn't far cry 3 either. You'll be able to tell which building is which and what it does, same goes with the heros, soldiers, and archers.
Online play:
Despite the game being this old, there is a multiplayer option.
The only thing availible is LAN play, so if you and some friends are in the same house, you'll be able to play together. There's are a lot of maps to play together, which each player being a colour. Mulitplayer games do NOT have a hero.
Pro's:
- Fun gameplay
- Good music
- Different types of missions.
- Voice acting
- Free play
Con's:
- Gets old after a while
- Repetitive voice acting
- You have to wait a long time for some resources.
- Enemies have ridiculous large armies.
Overal I'd give this game a 7/10, a good buy for 10 euro!

This is a platformer and you control a team of 3 characters. They can move together, or you can choose to control each one separately. The aim is to get past every level's obstacles, and you do this primarily by opening doors & escaping booby traps.
If any of your 3 characters dies in the level, the entire team will have to restart. As you play, you also have to keep an eye on your thirst level - if you run out of drinking water, your entire team will die. So an added challenge is having to look for water sources so you can replenish your water throughout the game.
This game suffers from some major problems. For instance, in the very first level, if you die and have to restart, a stone block that is crucial to allowing you to overcome an obstacle, is no longer present. So how are you supposed to continue?! You'd then have to start a completely new game!
And there seems to be a complete lack of a "save" function. The game claims to autosave, but when I next opened the game, it started me from the very beginning again. What happened to my previous gameplay?!
From my understanding, this game was developed by students for a project or something like that, which may explain the shoddy game development.
I did find the underlying concept and puzzle-solving elements to be quite amusing and fun though, and I also liked the style of the graphics and music.
This isn't some brainless platformer where you charge ahead and mindlessly blast enemies in your path; this game requires a degree of strategising and planning, yet also precision in controls (especially with the jumping) - I found this balance of required skills to be good, and would recommend
to anyone who wants an interesting challenge... if not for the gameplay issues mentioned above.
