There are some idiotic negative reviews for this game. People saying it's too difficult to learn or the controls are horrible or whatever. Maybe those things are true if you're an idiot, but for anybody with 1/2 a brain, the controls are easy to learn & most of the gameplay is also. I always check the keybinds of any new game I play to see what you can do, but there were only a couple buttons I didn't figure out before I checked the keybinds. As I said, very easy controls. As for the gameplay, the game teaches you what you need to know to do alright. The dungeon aspect is very easy to learn, like most top-down action style games. The merchant aspect is a bit more complex, but not much. The most difficult thing to learn in this game is the best price-percent to sell/buy at with each customer. You have 2 ways to do this: 1- Old-school style, where you note every percent you try to buy/sell at with each customer & whether it worked until you find the best percentage for each, or 2- Wiki style, where you simply Google it & use the wiki to read the same information you could easily figure out on your own. Again, not exactly difficult either way, it would merely take longer to figure out if you do it old-school. I initially did things old-school, then decided using the wiki would simply speed up the game some without really cheating because it wouldn't give me any info I couldn't, or wouldn't eventually, get myself in-game.
The biggest down-side to the game? When you sell things in merchant mode, it doesn't pull the items from your stock, it pulls them from the display. In other words, you must put something on display to sell it (or in a vending machine). If you have 5 of the item in stock, the item you put on display is still the item sold instead of using your stock, forcing you to replace every display item you sell before each merchant session & preventing the same item being sold to 2 different customers each session (assuming you have multiple in stock to sell to multiple customers) unless you place multiple copies of it. It isn't exactly difficult to replace the items, it simply takes time. That's the only bad part of this game, and it isn't exactly horrible. It would be much better if they made it so it pulled from stock, but it would only save you a little time & hassle, nothing more.
The rest of the game is very fun & cute. It isn't the most action-oriented gameplay ever, nor is it the most fun game I ever played, but it is fun, easy to learn, & has a cute story with cute graphics. It requires multiple play-throughs to unlock everything, but so what? Each playthrough can be endless until you decide to end it, each restart has the potential to unlock new things depending on how you did things this time through, and dying or failing at worst forces you to restart through New Game + so you don't lose everything.
Is it worth $20? Well, I have 100 hours played so far and will be playing more, so technically yes, especially if you don't mind the potentially repetitive item placing for the merchant system. However, if you can get it for $10 or less, definitely worth grabbing.

Desktop Dungeons is a turn based roguelike with a little bit of a difference; each run in a dungeon takes about five minutes to come to conclusion. You are free to roam around the dungeon as much as you want, enemies will only attack you if you attack them first, giving you the freedom to work out your strategy however you prefer.
Graphics are the usual 2d style which we are seeing so much of these days, but the sprites are nicely designed with some well-known characters thrown in there such as Super Meat Boy. The UI can be a little daunting to begin with but you see all of the information you require within one click.
Each of the individual levels are randomly generated; this adds to the replayability of the game as no dungeon will ever be the same; I believe each dungeon has its own set "theme" but what is included in the dungeon and how its laid out is completely random. The difficulty is something to be said for though, it is very easy to learn how to play, but very difficult to master, you will die, ALOT in Desktop Dungeons, they even tell you that at the very beginning of the game; it is to be expected. It takes a lot of thought out planning and preparation to work your way through most of the dungeons even straight after the tutorial you are thrown straight in at the deep end.
The game length can vary, I have been playing for about five hours and I still haven’t managed to get past the fifth dungeon, there are tons of content available, class challenges, random dungeon runs, extra tutorial lessons for different spells and many more. I have seen some people with over a hundred hours put into Desktop Dungeon. One of the extra plus points I've found is that a potato can run this game, meaning you can stick it on any machine, maybe even your work machine, and load it up on breaks to sneak in fifteen minutes here and there; as it's not resourcefully demanding.
Desktop Dungeons is certainly worth your time, and boy will it suck up your time as it is highly addictive.

I started playing the free version of the game and finally got the steam version. That was a really good choice. My advice: Try the free version, it'll show you the very core of the game. If you like it get the full version.
Pros:
- Problems to solve strategically: Essentially every dungeon is different and you can solve it in many different ways. But, one or two mistakes and you're done. This is the rogue-like aspect of the game. In the start you'll feel very lost but as soon as you play you'll start using the deep mechanics of the game in your advantage.
- Progression and goals to be achieved. Development of your kingdom and uncovering different races, classes, items, etc. through the campaign mode. This is the hook of the game, the RPG aspect, and the way it's done is fantastic.
- Huge replayability. The amount of combinations is just enormous. It's always the same idea: get in the dungeon, kill the boss/es and get out, but the amount of combinations of classes, races, deities, items, layout of the dungeon, level of difficulty of the dungeon, badges achievable, etc make every run different than the previous one.
- Daily dungeon.
- Complex and difficult. This game is all about thinking, the puzzle element is about 70% of the game. I you don't like staring at the screen for a couple of minutes checking your best option then you probably won't like the game. Difficult dungeons take about 20-30 min and you need to be focus all the time.
- Good difficulty curve and very good tutorials.
Cons:
- Can't think of any.
Overall this is an extremely well done game (once you play for a while you'll notice this in the little details). Very original and unique in its way. But remember to try the free version first, this is not a game for everyone.

Hello
As someone who liked the old dungeon keeper games, when I saw this game go on kickstarter I was very excited about it. This genre of game is unique in a sense that you are the evil. You build a kingdom but you cannot control those who join your cause and your style of building defines what archetype of mobs join you.
I must say that for a game that has just released it is to be expected to have a slightly buggy experience, however in this case there really are bugs everywhere. The game feels unfinished. When you open up the menu after installing and click multiplayer the first thing that prompts up is, this will be patched in. The same happens when you click survival mode, and when you click skirmish there is a shocking three maps. The only fully functional mode as of right now is the campaign. This was already a huge letdown, minutes after finishing my download.
I didn't let it phase me and I went for the campaign. Now from the very start I ran into bugs and problems. As a former dungeon keeper player and with many games behind my belt I have a good idea on how to play games. Now this is very important because the tutorial is horrible. They barely scrape the surface of what buildings do, there is no explanation what so ever how the controls work. I was unable to move my camera, had issues with targetting. You'd figure okay, I will read the tooltips but frankly, there are no useful tooltips anywhere in the game to be found. Mostly there are placeholders from an early alpha build. "shrine prop siege" doesn't tell me what it does? The big thing for this game is the micro management of the buildings, however there is no explanation on how the sizes of your exhibits have to be in order to recruit units. The props are invisible. And you can slap units but there is no real talk on how it affects efficiency.
So I went in completely blind. Now the early campaign maps are fairly easy, straightforward objectives and simple tasks. With no time pressure that is good. The only problem is that you cannot build anything else while you have a certain task. Build a X on this tile. Then you cannot continue to do what you were doing, it forces you to do something specific, some of the cutscene 'talks' appear to be unskippable and this is just tiny annoyances everywhere.
I pushed onward, in a quite bad mood now. And then I encountered many little bugs. I summoned a vampire, it went mad. Started killing my units but I had no idea how to fix that. Everytime I cast a scouting ritual my pc froze up completely. Now I have a really expensive modern pc less than two months old. That is just bad scripting. Lag, delay and crashes occurred regulary. I had units bug into the wall and frankly no idea what half of the spells, flasks or shrines are for. The possesion spell, which was a huge thing, is completely broken.
So yes. I did finish the campaign. It took me roughly 12 hours. I only had to restart one map which I failed on my part. So through the buggy experience I can say that the campaign has a good design, it is versatile and interesting. The small storyline has a funny plot to it. But its so dissatisfyingly short, and the experience was a chain hindrance of little problems that I can't say I fully enjoyed it. There was no map that was challenging in the entire campaign and by the time most buildings and plots are revealed you are done.
I then decided to take on the AI in skirmishes just to see what the full experience would be like. Considering I hadn't had that strong opponents in the campaign. Now I took on every AI setting on master, they were challenging. So I will say that the game definatly has potential. It is fun in design, fun in concept and I'm sure that with some more patches and content this will be a good game. For those who have seen the totalbiscuit WTF video, what he says is very true. This game looks like it will be worthwhile, in 6months or more to come. As of right now, I cannot recommend this game. I personally found it fun, but I am dissapointed in what I consider a premature release and I hope the developpers will put effort into this game, and make it great. As I think it can be.

Like any Dungeon Keeper fanboy I was excited when news of this game reached my ears. Here was a promise to pay homage to a favorite game of mine from when I was way younger, a game that has had few of its like since it came out.
This is what I expected: A dungeon building simulator where you build your lair, gather minions, train them, build defenses and then storm the opposition. To say that this is not what I received would be a lie but the thing is the game delivers things so clunkily that all enjoyment is simply sucked out of it.
Yes, you do build your own fully functioning dungeon... assuming you can figure out the actual mechanics of the game, that being the logistics behind the rooms and how the minions interract with them. You can have lots of fun reading through half finished tool tips and placeholders and see if you can make sense of it.
You do employ a workforce of diabolical minions... but again the game is not exactly forthcoming on details on how they function inside your dungeon and in combat which leads to cluster♥♥♥♥ combat scenarios in which you just pile your guys together and hope they come out on top.
You do conquer realms and bring ruination to your enemies... but through a story that appears to be missing half of its cutscenes and animations and this is assuming that the game doesn't crash or go through constant memory leaks.
I guess you could say that this game delivers everything that was expected, but it is done so badly that all the fun gets lost behind somewhere. There's a lot of good ideas here but the game doesn't take its time to explain how they work and some ideas never get used at all.

COMPARISON OF OVERWORLD TO DUNGEONKEEPER
I bought the game despite the negative reviews, and suggest you do the same. I am a diehard fan of DK, having an emulator on my PC for the sole purpose of playing it (and have done so a lot). I am so happy I found a game that brought me what 'Impire' and 'Dungeons' didn't. This game exceeded my expectations enough I may uninstall my emulator for DK.
PROS:
+True DK successor- saturated with eastereggs  that even veteran players may miss (micropiglets have invaded your dungeon)
+Better storyline than DK. You aren't a random keeper trying to get out of hell for implied reasons.
+Perfect voice acting-  Better execution than in DK, which was exceptional to begin with.
+Well balanced.  Good luck finding a cheap exploit against a good player.
+Multiple strategies for victory. DK was won by having a hoard of creatures and that alone. Overworld has many, if you're clever enough to find them.
+Technology tree that allows for rushing, booming and turtling strategies that didn't exist in DK.
+An AI that is actually challenging.
+Elite, boss like creatures that put dark angels to shame
+More meaningful combinations with traps. DK had many traps, but they weren't actually useful like they are in Overworld.
+Constructs for sapping, replacing earth (I wanted that so bad in DK), and more
+More strategy with spells. In DK, pragmatically you could only use the same 2-3. While you aren't forced to be spell happy, spells can be a main strategy for victory.
+Dungeon molds to your playing style more than DK
CONS
-UI needs to be more polished- If you select a potion, you are unable to change your mind; You have to use it. Selecting a ritual to perform is clunky, and is easy to cancel out of by mistake without knowing.
-Was under pressure to ship to market too soon. Fortunately development has been responsive.
-Possesion mode doesn't make it clear what you're targeting, or if you're hitting anything as well as DK does.
-Creature dialogue can distract from gameplay. I know some other players find creatures overtly chatty. Only the Cultist bothers me.
-If there are secret creatures to be gained by combining rooms, I haven't found them.
-None of the minigames that gave the original DK some of it's flavor. But I never played those much anyway. No comical video shorts either
-No invincible, horned reaper. But let's be honest, it probably doesn't belong in there unless they're literally cloning DK.
-Your dungeon isn't filled with yoghurt. The floor isn't lumpy either. No need to order your minions to jump up and down.

TL;DR: Absolutely recommented.
Honestly, I was roped into buying Owlboy because of its pixel art graphics. It looked like a work of an almost forgotten art, and oh boy, was I right. Spotless, creative, Metal Slug-grade graphics right there.
The game has been in development for 10 years by a handful of people, and it is clear how much effort and love has been put into this project. Music, art, story and gameplay intertwine smoothly and help convey the overall adventure and friendship-oriented themes. Everything in this game feels like a light-hearted 90s adventure... at least for a while. Then it becomes darker both in themes and interactions, as the and draws near.
Gameplay-wise, Owlboy essentially tries to combine exploration and puzzle-solving sort of in the same way the Zelda games do. Exploration is rewarded with secrets (pretty much all of those very emotional and touching) and hidden coins to gather in order to purchase advancements for the characters. The puzzles consist 90% of the times in trying to figure out how to open a door or get around an enemy. They are not the most original ever, but they play smoothly.
Combat is very simple, and probaly one of the weakest points of this title. You carry around different characters that have different combat abilities, but eventually you can almost always just kill any creep with Geddy's pea shooter gun. The boss fights are ingenious and sometimes very original, but almost all of them suffer from the same problem normal creeps do. I wish I could only hurt different enemies using a different combination of the characters' abilities, instead of just sticking to the gun and occasionally hurling something explosive when that does not work.
Expect to get from 10 to 20 hours out of this title, since the only replay value I can see is backtracking the levels to find secrets and hidden coins in order to finish the game 100%. Finding the secrets is actually very rewarding though, as they add bits to the overall story.
To sum up, the game is gorgeous to look and to listen to. It is a 90s style adventure to play and chill down. In my opinions the combat flaws can be overlooked by exploration, story and the overall feeling of the game.

I have mixed feelings.
I think this game probably has the best tech tree of any 4X game ever and that's saying something. The tech tree is original, fun, allows for rapid adaptation of strategy, but really, most importantly, it shows us something new that we haven't really seen before in the increasingly tired and already-done-before 4X genre by splitting fundamental and applied sciences and allowing research focusing w/ priorization. True game design innovations don't really happen that often, but this game genuinely has one in its tech tree.
Other people have criticized the game's tendency to go "on the rails" (i.e. the game plays itself), and I don't agree. I played in a galaxy w/ 800 stars and if you don't have macroeconomic automation, that just gets tedious. And most of the automation is around invasion and colonization, which are things I *really* don't want to micromanage. But if you do, the game absolutely lets you. The automated construction of planetary buildings seemed totally fine to me because most planets can only get a very limited subset of buildings anyway and if you wanted to micro it without going nuts, you could use build queue templates to do that. I personally found myself wishing the automation was even more automated than it is. One thing that kept cropping up for me was that some planets would max population and all population would be completely allocated. Only unallocated population can be used to colonize a planet and the automated colony ships would queue up at fully allocated planets, waiting for 1000 population to free up when that was impossible instead of just going to a planet where it was actually possible for population growth to happen. That forced me to micro a bit to unblock my expansion and by late game, that was pretty unwelcome. That said, the population growth mechanics in general just seemed really artificial and strange.
Fleet combat is OK. Not great, not bad, just OK. I'd have liked to see more utility modules that give more variation in strategy. Weapon variety starts to fall over near the end of the game where high damage torpedoes become increasingly critical and alpha damage starts being more important than anything else. Basically I think fleet combat in general needs more variety and balance tweaks. Shields should recharge much more quickly, kiting should be a more viable strategy, utility modules should get more emphasis, broadside combat should get more emphasis for capital ships (i.e. put all the big hardpoints on broadsides, small turrets only for 360). There should be utilities that can only be placed on smaller and medium ships to force fleet variety instead of the usual 4X late game battleships-only BS.
Espionage system is utterly useless and feels like it was tacked on as an afterthought. Diplomacy system is better than average, though I felt like AI was perhaps a little too aggressive diplomatically speaking on Normal and Hard difficulties.
But I think the biggest complaint I have is the end game. I won't spoil it for you, but due to what I believe is a known bug, the win condition can become completely impossible because certain enemies have unbounded growth. That said, as I was getting to late game and essentially steam rolling everything in sight and thinking, "Man, game got too easy all of a sudden", the game flipped things around and made things much more challenging.
I have very mixed feelings though on the end game. It's sort of the opposite of deus ex machina. Out of nowhere, with no prior warning, you essentially get a boss fight that you likely were not preparing for. At least in MOO, you know the Orions are a thing and you probably have to fight them at some point. In Polaris, poof, Big Bad, and now things are going horribly wrong. There's no strategy you just have to research stuff fast enough and then build up a big fleet before the Big Bad gets too big. If they get too big, welp, too bad, you lose. Or rather you don't lose but you can't win. And that sucks.
Should you buy it? Depends on if you can stomach the current just-shy-of-AAA price tag. I think it's a good 4X game with by far the best tech tree of any 4X, but it's crippled by a bad end game and inconstent AI that's either way too hard or way too easy and uninspiring fleet combat. Overall, I liked it. I got a good 30+ hours out of it over a couple games. I think the endgame badly needs a patch. I think the rest of my criticism needs a sequel. I don't think this will end up being a game that I drop 100+ hours on though, and that's usually the point where I feel $40+ is justified.
Depending on what the modding community releases though, I could definitely see myself revisiting the title and getting my full $40's worth.

In my opinion, this is one of the best shooters available on the market these days.
TL;DR
Play the game, it's awesome
Good sides
1) It's completely free, ALL ingame content is obtainable if you spend time in the game, only the cosmetics are paid platinum (in-game currency), but you can get plat without investing any real money, just trading with other players (for prime parts, rare mods etc)
2) Warframes. Unique war exosuits build for destruction, each with it's own powers. You can always find the one that suits you, and mod it to become even better
3) There're plenty of weaponry to choose from, and even if you think it's not good enough for you, just install mods and make the gun perfect for your playstyle
4) Regular updates. The Devs love their creation and they're always supporting it. I've first played Warframe back in 2013, and didn't like it because the game was too raw for me. Now, in 2017 I returned to it because I wanted to play game a bit similar to De Tiny 2, before it was released on PC, and I was shocked about how many things have changed in Warframe. So, I kinda regret not playing it back then 4 years before. And, also, Warframe is much more exiting than De Tiny 2. And it's free.
5) Community. There are always players who can help you get started. If you have any questions, even the dumbest ones, you can always get help (at least in Russian community, since it's the region where I live and play)
6) Rewards. The game respects the time you put into it, so every second you spent there will be paid off
Bad sides
1) Grind. You will need to invest your time into grinding resourses, at least in the begining. Many high mastery weapons require a lot of parts, but most of them are easily obtained, if you know where to farm them. Personally, I didn't notice much problems with resorses, I just play the game for the gameplay itself, so I don't notice the grind at all. I managed to get a lot of resourses just playing quests and opening nodes for the access to other planets. So, if you're a player like me, grind will not be a problem for you
2) High, well, skillcap, maybe? I don't know the right word for it, but the thing is - game will explain only the basics to you in the beginning, and all other things you'll have to figure out yourself. And there are A LOT of things you'll need to know. But there're always other people who can help you get comfortable with the game. Also, don't forget to check the wiki from time to time, ther're a lot of useful information
3) Bugs. They're not gamebreaking, but, you know. bugs.
Wake up, Tenno!

At first I didn't expect much of this game, but it turned out to be a whole lot more fun than I expected.

You ONLY fight ROBOTS in this game, but the game still feels really dark and intense.
Though the game doesn't feature the most hardware consuming graphics, the looks are REALLY good. The use of colours, lighting, shadows and other effects are done extremely well in this game, I haven't seen many games done this as good as this game.
The music may not be the grooviest of music you'll ever hear, but it is used really well in a way that fits the game. As soon as a wave of enemies is gonna attack you, the combat music will start playing, and the SECOND you finish off the last enemy the music comes to an end, which really boosts the atmosphere in a positive way.
The game also features an upgrade system, which allows you to unlock new weapons and suit upgrades throughout the game. Wich each upgrade point you'll unlock, you'll probably be immediately rushing to the nearest upgrade station like a crack addict who just found a penny because the upgrades help A LOT.
The weapon variation is done pretty well, though there are technically only 2 different types of ammo: you have 2 guns of many guns which will form all your weapons throughout the game.
The game also features secrets, though they are mostly just nano (required for upgrade points).
They did NOT go easy on the invisible walls in this game. Though this is usually no big deal since they are placed in rational locations, sometimes it can make secrets "harder to find" which might leave a bad taste in your mouth.
The game has a storyline, but I didn't really feel it. The cutscenes are animated comic-style, which is kinda cool.
If you like run&gunning with loads of explosions, the dark cyberpunk setting of the game and fighting robots you'll definitely like this game.

I really enjoy this game.  It is one of my favorite platformer games and I own over 2,400 games between my two accounts.  Many platformer games that I own are just plain impossible for me to complete due to ridiculously hard difficulty.   This game is very hard but it is not so hard that it is impossible to complete it.   I think the difficulty is fair and I think there is a fair amount of checkpoints in each level.   Talking about checkpoints, the checkpoints in this game are unique.   The first time you walk over the checkpoint it will save the exact status of your game.   So you can use some strategy as to when you want to walk over the checkpoint (which always appears as a sleeping bag on the ground).   You can position your characters wherever you want, and then walk over the checkpoint at the exact point you want to save.   Very neat feature.  Since the difficulty is hard enough in this game that you will die a lot, the ability to control when the checkpoint saves will save you a lot of time.
You control 3 characters in this game, but I presume you already know that from reading the store page or other reviews.   The game is really fun because at later levels you will need to walk all 3 characters in different directions in the level to find the buttons to move levers and doors.   And you have to cross extremely dangerous obstacles in the process.   The difficulty is hard enough that you will feel challenged in each level starting at around level 5.   The first 4 levels are easier, and are meant as more of a tutorial.     There is a small bug with accessing level 5.   To access level 5, do NOT click on the start button.   Instead hit the enter key twice.    This will load the level.    If you click on the start button, it will lock up.   Hitting the enter key twice should also work if you use a controller, or you could try hitting the A button on the controller twice.
I tried the game with both a controller and the keyboard, and I found the game easier to play on a keyboard because you could more precisely control your characters movement with a keyboard then with a controller.    You need that precise control to get over the deadly obstacles in your path.   I normally always play platformer games with a controller, so this is one of the only platformer games that I recommend playing with a keyboard.
As I said earlier, this game is extremely fun.   But I wouldn't classify it so much as a puzzle platformer, as more of an "obstacle" platformer.     You spend most of your time trying to locate the right direction to go, and get over the obstacles blocking your path.   The difficulty is very hard but fair, and it gives you a very good challenge.   Also you are on a time system, where if you run out of water then your party dies of thirst.   Since you are being timed (based on how much water you have left), then you will feel pressured when playing the game to rush and move fast so you don't run out of water before you are able to refill the party's canteen.    I usually play a level or two of this game, when I'm in the mood for something challenging in my day.    I will be very sad when I complete the game, and finished all the levels.   But maybe in a few years from now, once I forget the levels, I will go back and play the game again :)   I enjoy the game so much, that I can see myself playing it again in the future.    Also I wanted to note, that I make sure I find the rune in each level I play.   I'm not sure if it unlocks a bonus at the end of the game or not, but I wanted to make sure that I fully complete each level before moving on, and getting the rune is part of each level.
Would I recommend buying this game at full price?    Most definitely yes.    The full price is very low.   The game doesn't cost very much and you will get probably 8 to 10 hours of fun out of it especially if you search for the rune on each level.

Other than that, there's not much I can add here.  This was a fun little game.

Like most of the game journalism sites, their discussion moved around the big news as well as the big games around the industry. Some point along the show they brought up a new game into their discussion called Owlboy. The game they described did not sound like a big blockbuster game at all – it instantly piqued my curiosity. I confirmed its indie status when they showed some footages from the game. Now there are couple of things to note here. I was a regular viewer of the show and I do not remember the last time they put down an entire segment around an indie game before. From their description, the game sounded great and it looked really retro, yet modern – right around my alley. I ALT+Tabbed back to Steam and instantly put the game into my wish list. It was sitting there for almost half a year until I was able to purchase it. Having only finished it a week ago, I can finally give you my opinion on the game.
In Owlboy you play as a young owl called Otus, who under the guidance of his mentor, is tasked to protect the land from those ever nefarious pirates. One of the first things you will notice is the topology of the world. The world is apparently is split into pieces of land, disconnected from each other and seem to float for some reason. The ancient owls were apparently one heck of a race, which superseded everything in terms of knowledge and technology. These little oddities made me very curious during the early hours of the game. Tonally the game is very light hearted. Although there times the game starts to sink into the darkness, but it manages to break the tension with some comedy soon after. By the time you finish the game, you will be provided with a satisfying level of answers to all the questions you may have.
Let us now talk about how the game looks. The game goes for a 16-bit look like many indie games of its class. Where the others are happy to stop right there after; Owlboy goes all-in with the style and nurtures it to the point it feels something beyond being just being there for novelty’s sake by injecting the style into the game’s DNA. It starts doing that by making it heavily driven by the artists. This low-bit style create self-imposed technical restrictions in the characters, yet the game strives in characterization than most games out there. With the help of some good writing and clever use of body language, the characters in Owlboy may not have anywhere near the polygons of many triple-A games, yet they somehow possess an equal measure of more depth. It would be unfair to say that the game hard locks to 16-bit technical specifications. When instead, the game looks like a game that could have come out from that era; yet it looks much sharper, has more layering, smoother animations and overall looks much cleaner than the actual 16-bit era games. This is the case when our memory romanticizes by making us remember those games in similar way but not exactly how they actually looked.
In keeping with the restrictions imposed by 16-bit, Owlboy has no recorded voice. Instead, the game delivers the lines in text bubbles with a beeping, almost Morse-Code-like sound. It also helps its cause further when the protagonist is a mute. Although it would have been great to hear these characters speak, not once though I missed the lack of it as the delivery of lines synergizes well with the body language. In some ways, I actually find this form of self-expression much more effective.
Where the game does break away from its low-bit limitations is when it comes to the score. The game has a satisfying soundtrack to follow you on the journey. The soundtrack does a terrific job in not only expressing the environment, but also the mood. Then it is not hard to imagine how it can lend another hand in fleshing out the narrative.
The world is fractured and floats across each other. This would have been the ideal scenario for platforming, but they are too random and too far apart at times. With the protagonist being an owl, his main ability is to fly across the world. The topology forces players to traverse both horizontally and vertically. While traversing, players come across light combat and puzzles. The combat is quite shallow and ends soon as it begins at times. Otus himself cannot do everything by himself; this is when his companions step in to provide firepower in interesting ways. The way most combat works is with Otus flying while carrying one character at a time. Otus does all the movement while his companion does all the damage. You will come across multiple characters in the game and can quickly switch between them on the fly. There are also similarly light puzzles in the game, which can be solved without sweating over it for long. While the general gameplay is the weakest aspect of the game, things get better with the boss fights. They often force you out of the comfort zone by escalating traversal and combat with a bit of a puzzle at the same time.
There were two occasions that I found quite frustrating. One of them was a speed run mode, which luckily was optional but clearly not designed with the mechanics at play. The second one requires you to do some precise platforming towards the end. Before this part, the game did not require much platforming, let alone something that requires precision and timing. The floaty and imprecise nature of the controls had made this part very frustrating.
So let us sum it up. Owlboy is a great narrative experience with a wonderful cast. It is funny but also can sometimes be sad. Unfortunately, the core gameplay is too basic for being enjoyable and repetition quickly kicks in. The boss fights break boredom however. Despite being thin in gameplay, I enjoyed the time I had in this wonderfully weird world.

I guess I'm being mean. I have to say no to this game. I can see how this game could be enjoyed by a great many people. It's not a scam, and it's not terrible. It's just kinda boring and several parts of it don't fit.
So first of all, the story. And, by extension, the writing. I really can't understand games that approach character design and dialogue in such a cute, cheeky way but then stuff a TON of talking into the game. Like, if you want to make the story light and out-of-the-way, don't have so much talking. If you don't want to have deep lore or explain anything, don't keep burying us with vagueries.
Second of all, in my opinion this game is not a Metroidvania. Sure there's a central hub and some exploration, but each new area or level or whatever is 100% linear. The only exploring comes from moving about the same couple screens to solve a given puzzle or to find a secret. It's not a giant connected map with multiple routes. No sir.
Third of all, the gameplay is just too awkward. Owlboy can fly, so there's no plaforming (except on the last level, where you can't fly...). It's just a weird way to go about moving through a 2D environment. Different, I guess, but it doesn't add anything cool. It just takes away from the norm without actually giving any reason to move away from it. The weapons and attacks are almost all bad. You have a pea-shooter, a shotgun with no range that takes 7 years to reload, and a twirl that makes Crash Bandicoot look like Brock Lesnar by comparison. Your dodge is incredibly short, but spammable. So guess what? Prepare to dodge everywhere you go once you find out how fast you move! Also prepare to dodge three times just to dodge a attack. Towards the end you get a Spider buddy and he's OP as hell. So that's nice.
Then there's odd... interactions. Not sure what else to call this. Basically, certain things like trying to pick up an object. If you're carrying a buddy, you'll have to toss that buddy across the room first. THEN you can pick up the healing item. And, as I said, Owlboy can fly. If he touches the ground for even a frame, he starts walking. Sometimes you'll barely graze some pixel so he decides to go into walk-mode. This makes you fall like a rock. I found it somehow inconsistent getting him to fly from a standing position. I guess I feel like if I hold A, he should fly. But what you do is press A a second time and that toggles flying on and off. This sounds like a non-issue, until you get slammed into a wall or you slip into walk mode unexpectedly. It becomes really inconsistent when SOME attacks knock you into a wall and you have to press... something... and you shake off the stun and then you have to react to Owlboy falling. Other times he seems to recover without falling, so I instinctively press A which then makes me fall. I think I better solution would be to have Fly and Fall be separate buttons. Then just get rid of his tendency to walk when he gets too close to ground and BOOM! Flying mechanic is now solid.
The game also has very bizarre difficulty. Most everything in the game is super casual-level easy. But then you'll be surprised by instant fail sections. It also has constant checkpoints that restore your health to full. Which is good because they never really figured out a good flow for the player to get health back. You can just charge straight into a boss with 1hp, secure in the knowledge the fight will restart and you'll be at full health.
There's also a stealth section and a bunch of "flashlight" sections. Both of which feel out-of-place and are completely annoying. I guess they felt they had to change things up... but I feel like the main game never hits full stride.
This feels like a game that was made by artists. That's the best way I can describe it. It looks gorgeous and has some surprisingly high-quality music, but it didn't think to grab some writers and GAME DESIGNERS to maybe flush things out and re-iterate a bit. I realize this is an indie game and had limited personnel, but not everyone can be good at everything. Oh! But that reminds me. The game does have good programming! I don't think I encountered a single bug.

Owlboy is outstanding. The storytelling and world-building are bounds ahead of most of the genre. The mechanics are novel, intuitive, and fun - a most difficult hat-trick. The difficulty curve is nearly perfect, and the learning moments are well-placed and very clear. The artwork, especially the backgrounds are beautiful (and, if you've read many of my other reviews, you know how hard I am to please with pixel graphics).
Despite all that, the place the game really shines is in the level design. Every moment seems to be something new, back tracking and repetition are at a stark minimum, and I feel like my time investment is respected. Due to this masterful design, the game was able to shift in feel dramatically from scene to scene. Sometimes it was a dexterity challenge, sometimes a puzzler, sometimes a twin-stick shooter, sometimes a timing-memorizer all without forcing the player to learn new mechanics, or even change the POV.
I highly recommend Owlboy

At first glance, Polaris Sector appears to be a deep and meaningful strategy game, but ultimately it is neither deep nor a strategy game. This is not a 4X game, this is a tactical fleet simulator with a 4X veneer slapped on.
Yes, you can expand and build an empire, but that empire has no meaning by itself, being defined solely by its ability to produce fleets of warships. Yes, you can micromanage your planets to your heart's content, but the problem is that planets only have four roles:
1) Building ships.
2) Producing resources to build ships.
3) Researching new ship parts or ways to make resource extraction more efficient, so you can build more ships.
4) Producing food to support the population that is used to power the facilities that perform the above three roles.
You cannot, or at least, you should not, colonise planets for the sake of colonising planets. You should not grow your population as large as you can for the sake of having a large population. The game mechanics will penalise you if you do, because in order to do what the game wants you to do, you only need JUST ENOUGH population to man the factories, mines and farms that are all geared towards increasing your shipbuilding capacity.
Diplomacy and technology are a joke, both existing solely as a means to further your ship production ambitions. There are NO technologies that perform any role beyond unlocking new ship weapons and modules, or a means to increase your production of physical resources.
Can you research to improve your research ability? Nope. Can you unlock different forms of government with different empire-wide bonuses to production, diplomacy, morale or research? Nope. Just ship parts and mining equipment.
This game is geared entirely towards designing and producing ships and enabling you to design and produce ships. The strategic layer could be removed and this game turned into a purely tactical game that allows you to begin battles from a Skirmish setup screen and nothing of value would be lost.
If you're looking to buy this game because you want a good 4X game, DON'T. This is not a 4X game and it should not be advertised as such. I honestly regret spending money on this because of that one massive lie.
If you're looking to buy this game because you want a good tactical fleet simulator with a anaemic strategic layer that only exists to make tactical battles happen, go right ahead, chief. Have fun. Someone should.

This game was lots of fun.  There isn't much of a story.  And you probably won't want to bother following what story there is...because it's a mess.  But the story doesn't seem to be the point here anyway.  This game seems to be about the intense action.  You run around fighting off hordes of killer robots who try to swarm you, stomp you, and lay into you with buzzsaws.  There are only two basic weapons, a gun and a laser, but they can be modified and upgraded to do a ton of different stuff.  For example, the gun starts off shooting only bullets, but can be upgraded to also fire grenades, rockets, and what not.  Same with the laser -- you can buy upgrades in-game to make it shoot energy rail slugs, EMP blasts, etc.  Plus, there is lots of stuff in the environment you can blow to bits (electrical transformer boxes, gas cans, cars, oil drums) which, of course, can be used against your enemies.  Many of the enemies are tough and it takes a lot to bring them down.  Also, it seems that most of them want to engage you in some type of melee combat, so this is not an FPS for you if you want stealth and sniping.  Most of the combat will be in-your-face, and you'll be running around like crazy, spraying the mobs of enemies with lots of hot lead and laser blasts.  On top of the fast-paced combat, you'll get to enjoy the super-cool cyber-punk setting.  I had fun with this one; hopefully you will too.
P.S. It is a bit short -- I finished it in just over 10 hours.

Graphics and animation are nice and top notch despite its age. That "watercolor" style is simply gorgeous.
Story and lore is pretty rich although all the background text you unlock is entirely optional for those who love to learn all about the world.
Combat system is one of a kind and very solid. I've yet to find any other game that is any bit similar or as refined. It's turn-based, but when you select a unit, you actually personally control that unit during its actions through third-person. Enemies react to your actions during this phase too which was mind-blowing to me the first time. When a unit attempts an attack instead of an actual hit percentage you get a cone of potential directions of fire and the amount of shots the person will make.
RPG aspect is very minimal though since the only real customizing feature are just a couple of unique weapon upgrades and how you outfit your tanks. Regular equipment upgrades work on the entire squad and the class level ups are similar. You'll have more than enough exp and money to buy and upgrade everything so there's almost no risk of choice.
My only complaint is the replayability of the game. Basically, unless you are aiming for absolute 100%, there's no real joy or reason in playing it again. New game plus keeps the enemies exactly the same while retaining your squad's upgrades from the end, so you literally cannot die through over half of the game at this point. Although the story is good, it still gets bland after you hear or see it several times.

Hard Reset is a simple First Person Shooter with interesting graphics. It's set in a "Terminator" style universe where machines have taken over from humans. The graphics are interesting - sort of cartoon like. I played the single player campaign and the robots tend to attack by ambush and at times in waves.  Winning these fights involves (limited) ammo management, health management (finding medkits) and choosing the right weapon for the job. I found the shotgun to be good for the swarm attacks, with the plasma (NRG) weapon, particularly the railgun and smartgun, good for the larger enemies.
On the downside, the dialogue is awful. The designers overused profanity. Some of the cartoon cutscenes are undecipherable scribbles. Some of the plot nuances were a bit lost on me - the protagnist seems to have some ability to absorb multiple personalties?  This wasn't explained very well.
Levelling up in this game consists of collecting orange "Nanos" which eventually allow you to select either a weapon, shield or tactical upgrade. That's it.  This makes the game rather one-dimensional. However, if you enjoy a fast paced FPS then you're sure to enjoy this game. It is getting a bit repetitive/monotonous however. Oh, there are bosses which can sometimes be a bit tricky to work out how to defeat.

There are some idiotic negative reviews for this game. People saying it's too difficult to learn or the controls are horrible or whatever. Maybe those things are true if you're an idiot, but for anybody with 1/2 a brain, the controls are easy to learn & most of the gameplay is also. I always check the keybinds of any new game I play to see what you can do, but there were only a couple buttons I didn't figure out before I checked the keybinds. As I said, very easy controls. As for the gameplay, the game teaches you what you need to know to do alright. The dungeon aspect is very easy to learn, like most top-down action style games. The merchant aspect is a bit more complex, but not much. The most difficult thing to learn in this game is the best price-percent to sell/buy at with each customer. You have 2 ways to do this: 1- Old-school style, where you note every percent you try to buy/sell at with each customer & whether it worked until you find the best percentage for each, or 2- Wiki style, where you simply Google it & use the wiki to read the same information you could easily figure out on your own. Again, not exactly difficult either way, it would merely take longer to figure out if you do it old-school. I initially did things old-school, then decided using the wiki would simply speed up the game some without really cheating because it wouldn't give me any info I couldn't, or wouldn't eventually, get myself in-game.
The biggest down-side to the game? When you sell things in merchant mode, it doesn't pull the items from your stock, it pulls them from the display. In other words, you must put something on display to sell it (or in a vending machine). If you have 5 of the item in stock, the item you put on display is still the item sold instead of using your stock, forcing you to replace every display item you sell before each merchant session & preventing the same item being sold to 2 different customers each session (assuming you have multiple in stock to sell to multiple customers) unless you place multiple copies of it. It isn't exactly difficult to replace the items, it simply takes time. That's the only bad part of this game, and it isn't exactly horrible. It would be much better if they made it so it pulled from stock, but it would only save you a little time & hassle, nothing more.
The rest of the game is very fun & cute. It isn't the most action-oriented gameplay ever, nor is it the most fun game I ever played, but it is fun, easy to learn, & has a cute story with cute graphics. It requires multiple play-throughs to unlock everything, but so what? Each playthrough can be endless until you decide to end it, each restart has the potential to unlock new things depending on how you did things this time through, and dying or failing at worst forces you to restart through New Game + so you don't lose everything.
Is it worth $20? Well, I have 100 hours played so far and will be playing more, so technically yes, especially if you don't mind the potentially repetitive item placing for the merchant system. However, if you can get it for $10 or less, definitely worth grabbing.

Recettear is a management sim about running an item shop with a decently in-depth dungeon crawling levels.
Pros:
+Marketing is pure and simple fun; determining what the customer might be interested in and how much they're willing to pay based on their age and occupation never gets old
+The option to hire and play as an adventurer is well executed, as the dungeon crawling is complicated enough to be fun yet simple enough to be addictive. Think Ys without as epic of boss battles.
+You can choose from many different classes of adventurers, each with a unique play style.
+Charming cast and funny dialogue
+The short length of the days, relatively short lengths of the dungeons, and how fast shopkeeping progresses makes the game highly addictive.
+The game is difficult, both in the shop (IE meeting bills on time) and in the dungeons, but it never feels unfair.
+Multiple game modes are unlocked after beating the game, including a much harder difficulty, a survival mode, a new game plus, and a mode that allows you to continue your cleared game file from where you left off without having to worry about paying bills anymore!
+Incredibly cheap price during steam summer and winter sale for how much content you get.
Cons:
-Some may not like the ten hour playtime.
-The simplicity of the dungeon combat was enjoyable for me, but it's unlikely to be everyone's cup of tea.
-The game could use some more voice acting for how many cut scenes there are
Even if the game isn't on sale, Recettear is worth a purchase for anyone who enjoys RPGs, charming characters, and is interested by the premise.

I wish I could give RUINER a neutral score, because the parts of it I enjoy are really good, but it's lacking in so many other aspects.
The aesthetic and delivery of the game are fantastic. The setting is interesting, the "glitchy" effect is really good and in general it just oozes style.
RUINER was definitely in need of a design pass, though. It has all the elements necessary to be great, but they needed to be re-arranged and reworked better.
First off, the mid-fight resource management is really damn demanding. Your health and energy are in one corner of the screen. Your ammo/durability are in the other and your dash charges are center-bottom. Keeping track of all of these in a frantic fight is ridiculous, especially because the simple red UI blends with everything else in the game. There definitely should have been a better layout and clearer audio/visual cues so you know when you're hurting for something.
Skills have a lot of unnecessary fluff and you'll quickly learn what the best combo is. There are VERY FEW points where the game expects you to have a specific skill equipped, but other than that, you'll probably stick to shield + stun grenade + dash upgrades. It's along the lines of "Why would I have a wall I can place, when I can just have an insta-shield that negates damage regardless where I am". Or "why would I have a frag grenade that deals damage when I can just disable any number of enemies".
This carries over to the weapons as well. Melee is always better, unless you are fighting a very specific boss and then you might want to switch to your ranged weapon. Melee stunlocks and deals more damage than almost any firearm in the game, especially in the first few hours.
It also feels like the devs knew this? For example, melee interrupts enemies for the majority of the game, but then you get an enemy category that all of a sudden isn't interrupted by melee. That's fine, you can stun grenade them. Well, now we have a "flaming" enemy type that is immune to the stun grenade specifically. OK, that's fine, you can still ram them with your shield to stun them? It's a weird progression, but the strategy stays the same: disable, damage, disable, damage, avoid until you have enough energy again, repeat. This is enough to get you S+ rank on almost all fights.
There are other weird things, like energy costs being relayed to you as numerical costs, but your UI is actual icons? I assume each of the icons is 10 energy/health, but I never know whether I have enough or not to do my thing, so, combined with it being hard to track your health/energy, I just never bother thinking about it.
The enemy encounters could have been better laid out. Again, all the elements are there, but the waves are uninteresting. You'll have two melee dudes and two gun dudes. OK, that's fine. Now you'll have a wave that's just suicide bombers. Now a wave that's just mines. Now a wave that's a draining device and one big dude. Why not throw in mines/suicide bombers in the mid of more varied waves? Then you can use them as tools against other enemies. There's very little target prioritization going on, because the actual battles aren't mixed up enough.
Probably the two most frustrating moments for me were a boss battle with three health bars for no real reason (and you can just stun-lock him anyway) and that a very late fight has infinite spawns that the game literally teaches you up until then how to disable completely, and then the fight starts and it's like "nope, they're immune now, sorry".
So, yeah, the game is very stylish, I don't regret buying it, but I think it needed one big design and balancing pass to actually capitalize on all its other strong points.
For reference, I beat the game on Hard difficulty, since it was the "recommended" one.

I'm a fan of roguelikes and their cousins. I'm also a fan of games in which you actually use the resources gained in your journeys to do something, rather than just progress. One of my favorite games on Playstation was Azure Dreams, for example. And now, in PC gaming, there is Recettear.
Recettear is the story of a girl who inherits an item store... and a debt to go along with it. In order to pay off your debt, you need to sell things. In order to sell things, you need to get things. In order to get things, you need to buy things. In order to buy things, you need money. In order to get money, you need to sell things.
"Capitalism, ho!"
So where does my discussion about the 'Roguelike' come in? Well, among the many things you can sell, most of the better ones, as well as a variety of combination ingredients (because like almost all my favorite games, this game has a crafting system of some sort!) are in the dungeons of the game, which are ever-evolving. In fact, if you progress far enough, you will find that the dungeon evolution is an actual *part of the game's storyline*.... but I digress. For your average player, this makes it an endless cycle of getting items, pricing items, selling items, returning to the dungeon, et cetera.
Multiple adventuter characters show up in the game, each with an actual backstory to them. A story that one may have to dig deep to find, or go to certain locations at certain times, but that all exist to some degree or another. It just adds another layer of depth to a game that could be dull if done wrong.... but 'Wrong' is definitely not the case with this game, if my playtime doesn't say that loudly enough.
I have a mental wishlist of what I would like in my perfect game. Recettear ticks better than 3/4 of those boxes, and adds its own spin on them. To that end, I honestly can't recommend it highly enough for people like me who enjoy 'roguelikes with a purpose', particularly when they include good characters and a few mysteries and hidden secrets to go along with them, not to mention after-campaign challenges and reasons to keep playing even *after* you have 'finished' the game!
There may be a day when I finally get everything, and get completely bored with the game. However, I can safely say that this is not that day. Tomorrow ain't looking good, either.

I've played most every space 4x game ever made, and for me this is one of the best.
Things I like:
It has a no-money economy system, so there is no rush buying of things -- which makes every decision about what to build and when to build it very meaningful.
The pace of the game feels real:  travel between stars takes years, if not decades, as does planet development.  So I feel like I'm watching my empire develop over a period of decades and centuries.
The tech system feels like real research, instead of just picking something from a list.
The combat system interacts with the tech system in such a way that there is no one certain tactic that always leads to victory.  (The guys over at Grogheads are loving it, because it feels like real military decisions to them.)
Planet specialization is a necessity, and entails meaningful choices.  No cookie-cutter planets here.
The AI seems to actually know how to play the game.
To me, this game is worth more than I paid for it.

Two of my favourite web-sites reviewed this game and completely disagreed with each other.  One thought it sub-par and the other recommended it.
I recommend it, and I've been trying to work out why.
AI - Good
From what I've played the AI is quite good, both strategically (exploring, expanding, etc) and tactically (diplomacy, space combat, esionage, etc).  And I value that highly; too many games have sucky AI and have to give huge bonuses to AI players to compensate.  In this game it's the other way around, the Human player gets the bonuses except on the Hard difficulty.
Real Time - Good
I've played hundreds of hours of Distant Worlds and I've found it hard ot go back to truely turn based games.  I'm biased towards Polaris Sector simply because it's a pausable realt time strategy game (I don't like twitch games, I like thinking games, but I'm hooked on the real time version of that now).
Simplified - Good
This time an antithesis to Distant Worlds and other games; this is Not a deeply complex game with masses of subtle decisions to make.  It simplifies things down to the fun parts, and forgoes layers of complexity.  That does mean Star Lanes, which some people hate, but I've enjoyed having the constraint because I've started playing quicker "lighter" games.  Over all this makes it feel almost like an Arcade Game version of Distant Worlds.  It's still no whre near a "finished in 60 minutes" game, but it doen't feel like I'm enduring a burden of beauracracy at the end of the game.
The special something extra - Fantastic
Actually, I don't think this game has anything about it that is better than Good.  The reseach system is novel, the AI is good, the simplifications are nice, but nothing strikes me as outstanding.
Overall - Enjoyable, to me
I've had fun so far.  I'm still working things out (I only just realised you can dismantle a starbase and use freighters to move it to another system), so I'll play a lot more of this.  I can honestly say I might even play this as much as Distant Worlds.  It's not as deep, it doesn't have the same degree of freedom, but is does feel more consistently fun to me.

This game, an obvious copycat of Dungeon Keeper (and that's not a bad thing), is very much like a disorienting disco where too many hallucinogens have throttled the experience from the mundane to the overwhelming. It's not that this game is bad. Actually, if they corrected a few mistakes, this game could be very cool. Unfortunately, the couple of problems that this game has makes for a disorienting and annoying experience.
First, the color palette is inappropriate to the genre, and, additionally, it is distracting to they eye. Let's face it, dungeons are dark places that are lit by torches. Fluorescent greens, oranges, and yellows do not belong in dungeons, except in the rare circumstance where magic is present. Most of the time, dungeons are like dungeons. That is, they are cold, dark, and earthy. Just looking at this game for too long can burn your retinas. I advise against that.
Second, the camera control is very limited. I want to be able to get a greater view of the happenings in my dungeon, dammit. Making me stay stay close in scope in relation to the goings on in my dungeon makes me dissatisfied. I'm the CEO of the dungeon, right? Shouldn't I be able to see the greater picture?
Like I said. I don't think this is a bad game, but it lacks insight into the basic wants of the RTS gamer.

is one of those games I've seen years ago announced on a random blog. Even back then the beautifully crafted pixel artwork immediately caught my eye. In fact I go as far to say that it is some of the most gorgeous pixel art I've seen in 2D games so far.
Many years later
was finally released and immediately earned the attention it had deserved for so long. It earned extremely positive critics, even with mainstream review sites such as IGN giving 9 out of 10's.
Is it really that good?
First of let me say again that in terms of presentation
is almost perfect, both visually and audibly. The animations are fluid as they can be, despite the incredible sprites. The memorable soundtrack was even composed by a small orchestra. Controls, interface, inventory and so on are mostly flawless as well.
There are some intense boss fights and scripted events that definitely will stay with you after finishing the game.
The story, characters and world-building are top-notch as well. This could also have been written by Studio Ghibli in their best years.
You see, the small developer team from Norway went to great lengths to deliver an overly polished and perfected product. In this regard
puts AAA games from mainstream developers totally into shame.
So are there any flaws at all at the end of the day?
I didn't like some of the grinding parts in the game. For instance later in the game there's a part in which you can collect three hidden golden coins, which takes quite some effort and time to do so. After you invested almost two hours in finding them, it turns out that all the work wasn't that rewarding at all. Personally I take that a bit as a lazy move from the developers to unnessecarily lengthen the game.
I also wish there were more upgrades and power ups to the existing ones.
therefore wasted a bit of potential to rise its replayability.
A quite similar game that existed a long time before this and which didn't commit the same flaws is
. It has similar gameplay mechanics, not as detailed but still lovely 2D pixel graphics, a good weapon upgrade system, several endings and therefore quite a high factor of replayability. If you enjoyed
and are hungry for more, you will definitely love
which was ported to pretty much every system out there.
To put it in a nutshell,
is really good game, but certainly not a perfect one. It's well worth 10 hours of your life, but it won't be the very end of the line.
I therefore give this 8 out of 10 Boguins.

This is definetely not AAA game, but it is realy addictive to me. Great space combats with hundreds of vessels in one battle, different tactics mastered by AI and available to player (not ideally though). My favourite ship designer where everything matters: size, weight, production and maintenance cost - not only basic parameters.
And there is no money or BC`s in this game, completely! Only mineral resources, food and production.
Starlane movement and single point systems can be serious drawbacks for someone, but I like to focus on strategy and tactics, not micromanaging of my empire. This game offers many options to automate routine actions like colonization and planetary development so I can focus on economy, strategy and tactic combats. Autobattle is strange, use it only with outnumbered fleets. Looks like it simply command "act on your own" to all ships and speeds up time.
Game mechanics is very different from MOO-like mechanics, your limit is not command points or income, your limit is your economy. And be careful with food, earthlike planets do not have population cap and unemployed population in this game is useless and worse - it consumes food. Single earthlike or gaia planet without population limit programm can lead whole empire to starvation.
UI is not always intuitive and polished, in big galaxies there are many endless lists and annoying fighter management, that`s not good. But UI is good enough to concentrate on game, not on UI gaps.
I recommend this game.

The graphics showcase an incredible amount of attention to detail, and the level of fluidity captured in pixel art animation here is astounding.  While I personally found the accompanying orchestral music to be rather forgettable (And I think the OST's fairly small amount of plays on YouTube is evidence that I am not alone in this opinion), it still fulfills its ultimate goal of being tuned to the situation where it plays in-game.
The unfortunate part of Owlboy, however, is that where its aesthetic succeeds, every other aspect of it fails.  And to continue to be fair, it still starts out very promising:  the beginning of the game, which serves as a tutorial, also serves as a montage of all your player-character's past failures, culminating in an exceedingly striking interactive cutscene that drills into your mind,
Flash-forward to the present; Otus, mute protagonist and player-character, and Geddy, guard-in-training and his only friend, have been entrusted with the task of protecting their home village from pirates.  After chasing a shady-looking figure into the local cave system, you get your first dungeon, where the very different abilities of Otus and Geddy are established.  Otus (Being an Owl) can fly, pick up stuff, and when carrying Geddy he can make use of his blaster to fight enemies—but he himself is very weak in combat, only with a spin attack that he can use to briefly stun enemies.  There are some simple, but nice puzzles where you have to use Geddy as a weight to proceed, then figure out another way to carry him forward with you.  Hell, the first boss in the game is also one of the best bosses in the game, because it involves you having to manage both characters' abilities in a clever way—you have to knock its armor off with Otus's spin attack and then get over to Geddy and use his blaster to actually damage it.
...Then at the end of the dungeon you get a trinket that teleports Geddy to you on demand, and he becomes nothing more than a weapon on your scrollwheel.
That's the first dungeon.  The game proceeds in this manner until it's over.
Everything about this game's actual
feels unfinished; every time some interesting gimmick shows up, it's relevant for a few minutes and then never appears again.  Take a portion of the next area, where you have to stealth-segment your way around enemies that are extremely sensitive to sound, so you can't just fly past them because they'll hear you—this is one of two times in the entire game where you're asked to do some actual platforming.  Or a later portion where the capital gets invaded and you have to carry around a wounded soldier who can only bash enemies with her cane—much more fun than it sounds, but
never comes up again.  It's like if every level in Super Mario 3D World ended at the halfway point; your abilities never feel properly tested, not even by many of the bosses.
I could perhaps forgive the slipshod work on the level design if the narrative and characters made up for it, but—spoiler alert—they don't.  The story that Owlboy sets out to tell at the beginning and the story that Owlboy is telling at the end are so different from one another they can hardly even be considered the same story.  The characters are similarly mishandled, with Otus getting no proper development due to being mute, a bland and two-dimensional antagonist, Geddy appearing hilariously inconsistent because his animations and design suggest he is a comic relief character when in reality he plays Bad Cop for much of the game, and the other supporting characters having a similar amount of "attention to detail."
I wanted to like Owlboy.  In fact, when I saw Owlboy for the first time, I thought it was going to be the next Cave Story.  And now, as I sit here and write this review, I cannot believe that a game that is so visually impressive can fail so completely in all other departments.  I cannot believe that a game that has been worked on for eight years can still feel so unfinished.  I cannot believe that a game, touting itself as story-driven, can have such poorly written characters.
I'd give Owlboy
Maybe even five, if I'm being brutally honest.  I bought it for fifteen dollars when it came out and am disappointed with my purchase; I certainly would not recommend it for the twenty-five dollars they ask for now.

Owlboy is a frustrating game. Not because of gameplay, but just because I wanted to like it so much but didn't enjoy a good deal of it.
First off the positives. The artwork, animation, and soundtrack are all top notch and I super appreciate that the music is actually orchestrated and not just synthesized. This game deserves high praise on these marks.
Everything else though? Fair to middling with the biggest sin being that it's just boring. There's no exploration, no world to explore even though there's a hub you return to from time to time. Combat is minimal and bland, the puzzles are braindead, and the game is completely linear. Worse still the game CONSTANTLY stops so characters can talk and emote at each other. Having control taken away screen after screen completely kills any flow the game might have had. The progression mechanic is also completely worthless as you might as well not even have a health bar and you'll barely use the weapon upgrades. And the hats? Why are these here?
The story is fine but feels like there's a lot left unexplained. References are made to things and characters brought up that are forgotten and do absolutely nothing. There's also a terrible minigame that might be the worst part of Owlboy.
There are WAY too many stealth and darkness sequences, the platforming is middling, and flying just feels like moving a cursor around the screen. In the end it feels like all of the care for Owlboy went into the visuals and charm and not nearly enough into the actual game play and structure.
Buy this game if you like great sprite work and music and don't care about engrossing gameplay. Also the owls are all jerks and I'm glad they're dead.

----- February, 2017 -----
This game has the potential of becoming the major survival game, getting over Ark. That's because it is well situated in time and technology. The weapons, constructions, movements, foods, religions, make sense in that context. Ark is lost because tries to have everything, primitive and high technology weapons, structures...
But there is some HUGE problems that sign us it will be a long journey until we arrive in an acceptable level of the game.
- FPS very unstable; loading structures big delay
- Servers doesn't work properly, being reset many times a day to maintain an ok amount of lag
- Devs communicate a lot with community but give no real information about processes of server issues or patches
- Huge amount of patches that doesn't actually solve the bigger problems
So Devs have a great opportunity to dominate survival gaming market, but it seems that we will have to wait like 6 months to worth spending time on Conan Exiles.
- Official servers treated like nothing: they were up for game release and 3 days after they were shut down because they were a disaster. Now, after 7 days they are putting some servers up only in NA and EU, and talk about a few weeks to supply other regions.
That is known that Early Access means that bugs and problems will show up, but pay the game, play 3 days and have to wait almost a month to play again seems ridiculous...
----- November, 2017 -----
After waiting about 9 months, I am able to say that the game is amazing now. There are still some bugs, but the graphics are beautiful with acceptable performance and FPS, the story, creatures, technologies all make sense for the game's age.
We can spend many hours having fun, farming, killing creatures and enemies, constructing bases. The DEVs still need to figure out how to balance god's thing, since it's still too strong and too easy. Some people does no structure, simply rush level, then rush religion and wipe people.
Maybe the servers slots might be a little bit higher, since official servers have 40 slots and the map is a lot bigger.
I can sincerely say now that Conan Exiles is the best survival game I have ever played and if you are wondering on buying it, you should give it a try.

Nice puzzle game, in dungeon crawler RPG form.
You start each dungeon at level 1, and the goal is to power up enough to kill the boss. But you have limited resources. You only heal by exploring unexplored tiles or leveling up (or chugging potions), and you only level up by killing things (which usually depletes health and/or mana). And monsters and items don't respawn or anything like that. So you have to be smart about how you go about killing things, and in what order, and so on.
You can also unlock new classes and starter items and such to take into the various dungeons, and there are special challenge dungeons, and some tightly calibrated puzzle levels. It's pretty engaging overall. Made me late to class because I lost track of time.
Also the music in the dungeons is pretty great.
And the tutorial system is extremely well done. It throws you right into a dungeon that's designed to teach you how to play as you go, without any explicit instructions. And then once you complete it (or, I bet, if you die), it gives you the option to continue on to the rest of the game or to go into some actual hand-holding tutorial levels with explicit instruction.

Otto, Axel and Hans have decided to go on a journey to the center of the Earth. This platformer is a debut for German indie studio insayn. How did it end up? Pretty bad, I have to say; let's classify the reasons.
You control all three characters separately or grouped together, it's up to you but it has its flaws. You can choose each character separately to move through levels redundantly three times (feels more like a boring labor), or you can group them together and risk their death at some parts - the grouping has its bugs and even when they are grouped, they can split but still keep movement locked together. This often leads to unnecessary deaths and requirement for more patience in places with deadly pits.
To justify the character trio existence (to look more complex and to make up the space for puzzles), every character has a unique skill. Otto can use a pickaxe to destroy stones (just specific ones, you can't make your own way through the levels), Axel can jump higher and Hans... can hold a water in his canteen.
As for the puzzles, which are the main gameplay feature, they get harder over time but they also treat the player like he would be stupid. I don't know if that's underestimating of the players or just artificial extending of level length, but it's really boring to see the same repeating puzzle pattern over and over again. For example, you have two buttons in front of the gate to open it, and one another button in back of the gate that keeps it open. Guess what you have to do with three characters.
I don't think there's anything special to tell about sounds and graphics, it just looks ugly on higher resolutions. The characters are weirdly slim and tall but we can take it as a part of the game's aesthetics. Also, menu design feels slightly counter-intuitive with controller.
Journey to the Center of the Earth could have ended up good with higher budget and more experienced developers. While it can offer difficult puzzle challenges and mediocre length, many players will get bored even before they get there. Level design have many dull and boring parts, and repeating patterns. Even with lower price in consideration, I don't think it's a puzzle platformer that would be worth recommending.
