Hard reset is set in a heavily cyberpunk setting where robots have caused all hell to break lose. It can be related to the 'Serious Sam' franchise, and as a fan of those games I thought I'd give Hard Reset a go. There are a multitude of Pros & Cons, but it the end, it felt empty. The Cons side of the list started over-running the pros, the game was becoming too 'rinse and repeat' for me. It was like eating your Aunt's crappy fruit cake, but you don't want to make her feel bad so you keep on eating it anyway. Again, I'm not saying it's a bad game; just tiresome. The game goes by too fast too. After 2 hours of gameplay I found my self already about half-way through.
-
- Appealing Graphics for it's time; about 4/5
- Weapon Customization
- Challenge: it has decent difficulty, even on easy.
-
- Soundtrack, I can handle Techno/Dubtsep/DNB/Whateverelseyouwanttocallit music, used to love it in fact, but as a connosieur for OST's - all I can say is: "what is this trash?". I wouldn't even call it by those name as the majority of the songs sound like some pots being banged together. It's a good thing that even at max volume it's hard to hear the music.
- Gameplay, it can be enjoyable to some people, but mostly iffy for me. It's a little Point-A-to-Point-B-ish and rinse and repeat on killing the same enemies
- The Enemies: Lack of diversity; I think there were a total of 3 kinds of robots at the half-way point I made it to. There was: a ranged enemy. A bull vs. matador style enemy - which ends up being a big push over due to it being so easy to dodge, plus if there's more than one, you can make them damage each other. And finally these small♥♥♥♥♥exploding runts that run faster than light, making them the biggest threat in the game. They seem to never be farther away than four inches from you, meaning you're always hit by their explosion + they have razors if they make contact with you. There movement is usually predictable, so it isn't that hard to hit them, but they sometimes come in massive packs, so if you don't kill 'em fast enough you get overrun immediatly.
- Balance in resources: Now this is absolutely nitpicking on my part, but I thought I'd point it out at the least. You get ammo out the♥♥♥♥♥and never run out, but health starts to become more and more uncommon the father along you go.
- Story: hard to get immersed in. And I personally adore good voice acting, but all this game presented was mediocre everywhere.
O.P.R.- Mixed Feelings. The game is okay. Not bad, but not good, unless you completely adore a game like Hard Reset, then I guess you'd call it good. I would give it a middle revied if I could, but personally I'm swaying a little more to 'Not Recommended'.

This review is mostly for people unfamiliar with Desktop Dungeons. If you played the free alpha, then you already know whether you like the game; this new version features many improvements, but it's still the same type of gameplay.
Anyway, the second video (with the gnome wizard runthrough) does a decent job of showcasing game mechanics. Your goal is to explore a randomly-generated dungeon and ultimately to defeat a high-level boss monster. To beat the boss, you'll need to have leveled efficiently. This (usually) includes killing the highest-level monster that you can at any given time, since you get bonus XP for killing a monster whose level is higher than your own.
That's pretty much the core of what makes Desktop Dungeons interesting: you're always trying to beat a tougher monster. The way you do this varies tremendously; there's a long list of things that can help or hurt you, and you have to deal with whichever ones happen to be in the dungeon you're exploring. It's this variation that keeps the game interesting hours later.
Bottom line: I don't often write reviews. I like Desktop Dungeons enough that I felt I should take the time. I highly recommend this game.

When I bought this game as part of the christmas sale 2014, I didn't know what to expect, apart from a heavily visual-focused cyberpunk shooter. Trying it out showed me that Hard Reset was exactly that; but unfortunately, I put it down due to hardware changes and eventual loss of interest. In the last two days, I've been finishing up what was left of the game, and thus decided to share my opinions on it.
First of all, positive points.
+ Hard Reset packs a visual experience so unique and interesting that I have yet to see a match for it in this point.
+ The game supports surround sound, widescreen and multiple monitor setups. Not many games from this production value category do.
+ The story is intriguing, and had me captured.
+ I always love it when games integrate mechanics into the environment, like the upgrade machines in HR.
Neutral points, for those interested.
#This game bleeds Cyberpunk, (If you don't know what that means: dystopian Sci-Fi. Essentially, Corporations against Humanity.) which was one of the main reasons for me to buy it.
#Whilst having the appearance of a linear game, it felt slightly like an RPG to me.
And finally, the negative points. Sadly, there are not too few.
- The game felt VERY repetitive. Shoot enemies in area A. Go to Area B using Button. Loading. Repeat.
- I had to play the game at easy difficulty because of the sheer mass of enemies. There were some parts of the game where just senseless amounts of baddies were cornering and subsequentially destroying me for no apparent reason. (Protip: the shotgun is very effective against the small and medium enemies.)
- The storyline of the game was very predictable. (Example: "Oh how unusual that there is entity XY in this area." *10 seconds later* welp, time to fight it as a miniboss.)
- The endboss was a pathetic excuse. In the last level you're just being flooded with information about the 30 weak points he has, and they're even pointing them out so you can remember them, even though the vulnerable areas are lit up in neon orange on the boss himself.
- There are many N.A.N.O. Packets (the "currency" with which you pay for upgrades) placed in the environment. Unfortunately, some of their positions seem like they were chosen before the ducking mechanic was removed from the game, which is another negative point.
- The storyline, although nice, feels unexplained in some parts. I wonder if it were possible to implement a codex-like mechanic in which the players could read up on the game workd? It would surely help the immersion.
- The sprinting. You can't upgrade it. The distorted effect on the screen. You can't steer at all whilst sprinting, and it offers absolutely no benefit whatsoever. The heavier enemies crush you, and the smaller ones block your sprinting.
Conclusion: I do recommend Hard Reset despite its' bad sides. It still has some improvement potential.
That's it for now. Keep in mind, this review is based on my personal experience of the game. I hope my review helps in improving the game, given the fact that the developers read, let alone care about these reviews.

Controls are a tad hard since it's a top-down shooter. You have to press the button depending on the way that your character faces, f.e. if Puppy is looking right and you're supposed to go along a corridor, you have to press D to move forward. Following the defeat of Sovereign at the end of Mass Effect 1, Shepherd and crew find themselves in the midst of a grand denial.  The Council attributes the unprecedented attack against the Citadel to the Geth and a rogue agent, blissfully happy to believe that the danger has passed.  Meanwhile, they still treat the true threat, the Reapers, as myth.  Shepherd finds himself in a waiting game; without Council support for a full investigation of the Reapers, there is little else to do but wait for their next move.  When a mysterious ship appears and attacks the Normandy, Shepherd find himself injured, presumed dead, and cut off from the Alliance--at least temporarily.
The highlight of Mass Effect 2 is unquestionably its story and universe, which builds upon the first game's fantastic universe with a tremendous deal of depth and new revelations.  Many of the races that were only hinted at are given far more treatment this time around.  With Shepherd working outside the Alliance, we get to explore the outer rim systems.  It is a realm that ranges from semi-ordered to lawless, and most of its residents are happy to operate outside of Council space.   The Quarians, courtesy of a companion character, are given a tremendous amount of development, including a visit to the migrant fleet.  And, in a surprise highlight later in the game, we even get a healthy dose of new insights on the Geth.  Several other races also are featured heavily, many of which received only a brief mention in the first game.
The story is fast-paced throughout the game, with the feeling of tangible threat growing each step along the way.  It is a good length--I finished the game in 52 hours, and I always play slowly--just enough to feel like you can sink yourself into the story without every feeling like the game was dragging.  It was a very satisfying experience, and yet I was wishing for more by the end.
The combat and RPG system is still fun in Mass Effect 2, but it is definitely different.  Many of the classical RPG elements were streamlined from the first game, which was a little disappointing.  There is very little, if any, choice to be made about equipment, with the exception of one's preferred rate of fire for shotguns.  Furthermore, decisions about abilities are largely relegated to deciding which of four skills (five for Shepherd) to forego.  Controls were similarly simplified, with you needing basically three buttons outside of movement: your trigger, the pause-the-game-breathe-and-trigger-abilities button (I live and die with this button), and the run/take cover button.  It took some getting used to, but by the end I found that combat was pretty fluid, fun, dynamic, and rarely over-dependent on "twitchy" player skills.
The biggest addition to the combat system was a paper-rock-scissors (sort of) system of defenses.  In addition to health, enemies can have up to three other types of defenses: armor, shields, and biotic barriers.  Each defense is best targeted by different kinds of weapons and skills.  Shields, for example, can be attacked by semi-automatic guns of Warp biotic abilities, whereas armor is better penetrated by heavy pistols and fire-based biotics.  I really enjoyed this addition; it made weapon switching important in combat, and, best of all, encouraged me to take along different companions depending on the types of enemies I expected to face in a given mission.
Also gone in this game were the planetary exploration missions of the first game.  You never get the equivalent of the mako tank missions where you get to drop down on a planet and battle your way to a mercenary base.  Instead, in this game, the mission just starts at the door to the base.  The mako's controls might have been bad at release, but by the time I played the game, it was vastly improved and, frankly, really fun.  I LOVED the opportunity to trek across alien landscapes of random planets, many of which weren't directly tied to the main plot.  ME2 seemingly replaced the mako experience with something far less fun: painfully slow, boring scans of planets for resources.  Those scans are mandatory, too, if you want to get enough resources to upgrade your weapons and ship sufficiently to take down the bad guys in the endgame.  I have no idea what the designers were thinking with this part of the game; more than once, they ended my late-night gaming session because I was nodding off trying to find a little bit more iridium.
In the end, ME2 is a terrific game.  Its main failing is that it probably isn't quite as good as the original, which has an argument for best RPG of all time.  If you compare it against ME1, you probably have to take off a star.  But compared to other games, I just can't do that.  ME2 is a blast to play, and I wouldn't hesitate to recommend it to others.  It's not perfect, but it's a 5 out of 5.

I wish there was an 'undecided' or 'conflicted' choice between recommend and not recommended, because that's exactly how I feel about hand of Fate; conflicted. One half of the game feels polished, well-done, inspired, and enjoyable, while the other half of the game feels clunky, frustrating, and greatly disappointing.
Most of the game is played through a large variety of cards which feel like a thoughtful mixture of dungeons & dragons and an at-home tabletop card game. Something like; 'You find an elven maiden in an emerald grove, what do you do?' then, based off your choices(and whether or not you succeed or fail)you are either rewarded with food, health, gold, or items, or you suffer a penalty of one of the above. Or worse, you face a random encounter – which is not to say that random encounters are the most dangerous of penalties in the game, but that they are the most cumbersome and thoughtless segments of the entire game. The combat isn't fun, and it isn't really challenging. At best it' is a bearable distraction, and at worst it's incredibly frustrating.
It almost feels like there were two teams(or people)who developed the game completely separate from each other and that one group wanted the game to be an engaging card-based d&d style game, while the other group just wanted to emulate a sloppy hack-and-slash game styled after the bland combat in Batman Arkham Asylum. “Tap left-click to attack and tap Q to parry”. There is some variation if you have unique weaponry or equipment, but it only serves to make combat in Hand of Fate feel like less of a “chore” which exactly how you DONT want your game's combat to feel.
Honestly, I admire the idea here: “What if a d&d styled card game had interactive combat?” With proper execution in both parts, we might have discovered an incredibly enjoyable niche game. But, while the card game segment is very well done, the combat isn't and the game suffers as a whole because of it. In my opinion the developers should have left combat to the cards and some dice rolls. It would have felt more in tune with the overall theme, felt much less clunky, and the extra development budget and time not spent on 3d modeling and combat coding could have greatly boosted the already enjoyable card segments. More cards, more card-based encounters, maybe even some cool screen visuals for certain effects, etc. In short, if they had scrapped the combat system, this game could have been so much better.
To make things worse, the card-game segment itself is very rouge-like, in that death will end your play and you'll be forced to restart your chapter progress from the start, but with the added benefit of gaining new cards which can bolster your character and add exciting new twists and turns for the next game. That in itself isn't bad at all, in fact it's enjoyable, but the problem comes from RNG and how cards can work in this game. Despite how many new cards you get from playing the game your character will ALWAYS start out a chapter with base equipment and stats(which can get better as you progress through the story but only after key chapters, and the progression is equally tied to enemy strength and difficulty, so the improvements always feel negligible and counteracted). RNG rears it's ugly face in the order by which you draw cards, and playing with the DLC 'characters' which add some new pro's and con's to your playthrough, you might be doomed from the very start thanks to such RNG.
For example, I tried my first Endless mode with a character that can only eat Iron Ore from discarded equipment and during my route(which was entirely linear from the start)I didn't come across a single piece of equipment. My character ran out of food and starved to death before I could find any gear to salvage for sustenance, and I wasn't able to scrap any of my equipped gear as a last resort because that's not a function of the game. I was doomed from the start to fail the match and all I gained were a few measly cards. This sort of RNG isn't absent from other rouge-likes, but-in my opinion-it is poor design. I don't expect the RNG to ensure my victory from the start, or at all for that matter, but I should have more control over my character's “Fate” than hoping I land on the exact cards I need to survive, especially in Endless mode where I have ZERO control over which cards are in the deck and which might appear next.
An idea that could have fixed this issue would have been 'hand cards' which you draw at the beginning of a game and are added to your 'hand'. You could use them at any time to gain supplies or whichever other benefit they provide and they either can't be refilled or can only be refilled on other rare event cards. For example, when playing the character which can only eat Iron Ore, you could start off with one or two random equipment cards, nothing worth equipping(rusted stuff maybe)but for use in case of emergencies. This way you're not entirely at the mercy of RNG if you run into a stretch of bad luck. Something like that could have been a very simple and enjoyable addition to the game which could have provided a bit more player choice and control. Letting players alter their 'hand cards' at the start of a match, for example, choosing from the pile of new cards they have acquired, would have been a great way to support players who really enjoy certain styles of play but might struggle under the fickleness of RNG.
Sadly, the absence of such a feature and the “fate” of your character more often than not relying on RNG isn't ideal for me. I understand that the game is called “Hand of Fate” and that “fate” implies a degree of luck and chance, but that shouldn't mean my character is guaranteed to not survive past the second floor because the RNG layout is entirely non-viable for my character. That isn't just 'fate' that's poor design, and it isn't enjoyable. I'll continue to play this game and I hope that further progression might change my mind, but for right now – I just can't recommend this kind of a game. The card-game segment is well written and clearly a thoughtful and lovingly designed portion of the game, but almost everything else(the combat, RNG, and some card and character mechanics)really ruin the atmosphere for me.
6/10 Slightly above average, but the parts that do work are niche elements and I can't recommend the package as a whole.

Recettear: An Item Shop's Tale follows Recette and Tear (hence Recettear) on their epic quest of... running an Item shop to pay back debts.
What may sound boring is actually a great game. The item shop system is well designed, the characters are funny and the dungeons are... dungeons, I guess. It should also be mentioned that the game's story is told in passages like a visual novel, while dungeons and the shop are played with the sprites of the according characters.
First of all, let's look at the item shop itself. To even have items for sale, you need to buy them first from merchants or find them in dungeons. Some items can only be found in dungeons, others can only be crafted with ingredients found in dungeons. Those items may be valuable, however, they are not essential for winning the game.
To sell items, you have to place them around your shop. Location is key, items placed at the windows will attract customers and have a higher chance of being bought. Furthermore, some items may become more expensive or cheaper for a short duration, so you have to adjust your prices and locations accordingly.
Not every customer will simply buy everything at any price, they will try to haggle to either sell their item higher or buy yours cheaper. Depending on the current values of items, you may even offend customers, causing them to leave. Succesfully selling items will grant experience which is crucial in expanding your shop. In addition, not every customer likes every atmosphere. Little girls like bright shops while thieves and assassins like it a bit more sinister. Using decorations allows you to change the atmosphere of your shop, either attracting or repelling specific customers. Combine this with higher prices for highly demanded items to become rich very quickly.
As for the characters, they are almost all likeable. Most of them have some quirks which lead to funny dialogues or situational comedy, but often it's just Recettes comments that made me laugh. Phrases such as "Holy carp!"[NOT a typo] make the novel part of the game so enjoyable.
The dungeons are nothing special, randomly generated and filled with different monsters with different colours. To enter a dungeon, you'll have to recruit an adventurer first and actually pay them to work for you. Furthermore, going to a dungeon will take more time than running your shop, so I highly suggest you play through the dungeons on your NewGame+.
The graphics are not great, honestly speaking. While characters are well designed, the overall game is not an artistic masterpiece. The music is great, though. The qatchy themes made me stop playing just to listen to the music.
All in all, Recettear: An Item Shop's Tale is a solid game with a few flaws, but tons of fun. I often wanted to play "just five more minutes" and ended up closing the game two hours later. It is a good game and worth it's money, but try to get it on sale, simply because: Capitalism, ho!

I think after 500 hours, I can finally review this game.
Pros:
-Freedom : You have the freedom to do what you want in this game. Farm, build, trade, PvP, etc. It's a great open world MMO.
-Vehicules : You get to ride a decent amount of vehicules. There's cars, carts, boats.
-Graphics : I am going to put this in the pros, as they are good compared to a lot of F2P mmos in my opinion.
-Combat : Simple yet fun. It's not as great as BDO, but I do think it is a good system.
-Time Consuming : This can be a pro or a con depending on how casual you plan to be. The amount of content in this game is amazing.
-Massive PvP : Wars can have massive amount of people, I am not even sure if there is a cap for the amount of people.
Cons:
-Trion Support : Trion's support can be slow and when you finally get a response it can be a very generic answer, almost like you've been answered by a robot.
-Server Downtime : There's been a few times where the servers go down and they stay down for hours more than the ETA. I understand that it happens, but it can still be annoying.
-P2W : Now I don't mean that the cash shop is broken, but buying APEX and selling it can certainly put you ahead. If you want housing, you have to buy the monthly Patron

Polaris Sector is a very interesting game!
When you start a game you can completely customize your galaxy, and trust me, the choices you make here affect gameplay radically.
Then you pick a race, and although some of them look a bit weird (space koalas?! Ahah well it’s funny though! Can’t be worse than Ewoks) they seem intriguing enough and all have very different space designs and quite different modifiers. Then the real fun starts.
Polaris Sector is very combat oriented. It’s more more more warlike than other 4x games. You start from the ship designer tool, which allows you to customize your fleet completely. It adds a whole new strategic layer to the game, which in my opinion sets Polaris Sector apart from the other games of the genre. I had tons of fun just by designing my ships and coming up with crazy tactics for them.
The ship designer is well integrated with the research system, and researching individual theoretical and applied technical branches is a very elegant solution, one I prefer to the old “technology tree” system that other games have.
And then there’s the battles: I really like them. Tactical battles are very hard to master, as choosing the wrong formation or sending the wrong orders make a HUGE difference! You will be soundly defeated if you don’t know what you’re doing, as the AI is really smart.
In short, Polaris Sector is a very combat oriented sci-fi 4x game. If war and tactical combat with an excellent and challenging AI are your cup of tea, go for it and you won’t be disappointed.

I played the original 'Dungeon Keeper' and add on pack to the end back in the day, enjoying them greatly. I bought a game called 'Dungeons' on Steam a few years ago and was dissappointed. It played more like 'the Sims - Dungeon Keeper'.
When I saw this game was out and saw a high proportion of negative reviews I had low expectations. However, with a 10% discount and free DLC and some positive reviews I gave them my money and booted it up, with fingers crossed. Oh I am so glad I did!
This is the Dungeon Keeper clone we have been waiting for. It stays true to the original game whilst adding enough new stuff to keep it fresh. Also this is just an early build with active work taking place, but it still plays great. The game mechanics work here and I didn't realise how important the RTS element was, making the game more competitive and challenging. True you don't really design a dungeon for adventurers to explore (Sword Coast: Legends will allow you to do this I am sure).
You are basically an evil master who encourages minions and sets the hordes against your foes, sometimes stubborn Dwarves and other times your similar skilled brethren. The game plays at a fast enough pace so you don't get bored. I have already gone back to previous campaign missions to chase missing achievements as they are all so much fun. I still have the final two campaign levels to go, and am looking forward to my free DLC
If you are a retro gamer who enjoyed Dungeon Keeper you should like this game; if you are into Fantasy and RTS games you will enjoy this game and if you are both you will LOVE this game!

Desktop Dungeons is a good game for what it is. I played free variant for a long time, before picking up this  release.
The released version adds more of everything, more monsters, spells, classes, quests, rewards ...
This version also has upgraded graphic, making everything more charming.
Game play is turn based, with monster being stationary (some bosses have blink spell, that moves them unless you counter it.). At the beginning dungeon has fog of war. You reveal parts of dungeon by moving to adjacent square. You want to be carefull how much of a dungeon you reveal, since each square you reveal, recovers some of you health and mana. This is the main way you will recover health and mana. This means that exploring too much too early can leave you unable to heal, later on. On the other hand each square you reveal can have beneficial items, that you might want. This makes unrevealed tiles in dungeon weary important resource.
This is a quick game. Once you get used to controls and basic concepts, you can easily complete a dungeon/quest in 5 min. If it will take you longer it will be because you spend time thinking of best move.
Game is also paced quite well, so at the beginning you only have access to one class and one race (human fighter.), but you quickly unlock more.
With all that said, it is important to remember that this game is a filler game. It's meant to be played in short sessions.
If you play it for hours, you will quickly become bored. But playing couple of dungeons every day, while waiting for whatever bigger game you are currently playing to patch itself, it is time well spent.

Desktop Dungeons is a puzzle game that takes elements from rogue and condenses it to a single screen experience. You pick a class, buy some starting items and venture forth into a randomly generated dungeon. Your "hero" always starts at level 1 and you have to find a way to make the best use of experience boosts, glyphs, items and gold to beat the boss (or bosses) of the level. If you're successful you bring back treasures that will help improve your kingdom and allow you to discover new dungeons and monsters.
The goal is to use your resources to beat higher level monsters and get the experience boost you need to level up high enough to strike the boss. Uncovered tiles regenerate you and your foes, so waste as little as possible. Keep weak monsters around to strategically level up mid-fight and gain a full heal. There are lots of strategies and once you master them you can tackle any dungeon with any class. The mechanics are very deep and the advanced dungeons can take you one or two hours to beat them. Some later dungeons also abandon the idea of a single screen map and will offer two or more screens to play with, or challenge you with shifting walls. There's even a minotaur that chases you.
I've been playing the game since beta and there's still more content for me to uncover. The newly added daily challenges adds new motivation to keep playing the game and the absolutely fantastic soundtrack by Danny Baranowsky has been a steady part of my music playlist since release. If you like puzzles and you like strategical fights then this game is a must buy.

This is a great survival game. I played Ark and what I hated there was the total dependancy of big dinosaurs to protect me. This game lets me become the big beast. I have over 74 hours invested since launch two weeks ago, and every time I find game crashing lag or inexplicable death that makes me want to rage quit, I find something that makes me completely want to play again.
Pros:
Open world map that lets you see structures that you have built in the far distance.
Nothing in the game is just for scenery. See a temple on top of a mountain that is unreachable? build stairs and there are interactive things at that temple to discover.
Raid zones that really challenge groups of players to work together.
A giant stone pirate ship
Corruption zones that make areas and challenges tougher the longer you stay in them.
A really steep learning curve at first that pits players against basic concepts. i.e. hunger thirst, crocs, and hyenas
A story line
Cons:
Lag is severely bad when near large player built structures.
When you log in, you have to make sure your spawn is set to your bed as logging out cancels it currently.
When you die, the rendering of said large bases can cause you to rubberband back to your home even after running halfway across a zone to recover your body.
Crafting bug makes you craft multiple copies of an item when you select only one. It ties up the resources that multiple copies would make and ties up the crafting queue as well. This also affects the wheel of pain. Running out of render distance or logging out/in fixes it - temporarily.
Rhinos charge actually glitches them inside of you making them unkillable and you a defenseless target dummy.
Respawn rates are atrocious in some spots like caves or hyena alley but glacial in areas like spider valley.
All in all, I will not refund this game. It has so much potential and I cannot wait to see what they do with it.

Time to edit my review. Once my group of friends and I hit level 30 in Conan. We quickly ran out of things to do and we all moved on to other games. That was approximately one week after I posted this review. Now it is three months later and I feel some more critiquing is needed.
This review will be solely from a solo player viewpoint as I couldn't find a decent server to play on.
The game is still punishingly hard as a starter. The experience farm is rather inconsistent. One simply cannot just go around and kill weaker creatures and the occasional alligator to level up fast. Nor can one just go into grindy gather mode to get experience. Building a base seems to give ok xp, but you are limited to only a few pieces you can build at first. A campfire should take precedence when starting out because there are not enough shaleback eggs to keep you fed. (6 shaleback eggs are good for about 3/4 health or about 10 minutes of gameplay)
I have several hours in on my latest attempt and I have only managed to reach level 6.
Combat is still problematic. As long as you get the sword early on, you can kite the npc exiles in 1v1 and usually win. If they 2v1 you, then you better learn to run and fight and hide in the water since they currently will not go in water higher than their knees.
Don't even mess with archers though. Their range is well beyond what any player can reach and their shots are devastating and punishingly accurate. Their arrows also break down any cover you might find whether it's a tree or a large boulder.
The lag attached to large structures seems to have been repaired as has the inability to loot underwater.
The spawnpoint for bedrolls has not been fixed though. Every time that you log in you have to remember to right click on your bed to set the spawn, which can make for a very long naked mile back to your base. Which is impossible if you have built near hyenas.
All in all, the game is still fun if you are masochistic. If you dont like ultra grind mode, then this game is not for you. I enjoy a bit of grind, but I think I will shelve this title for another three months.

That isn't a problem, but your guy feels sluggish when moving.
Running through the general level is fun, but as soon as you hit subbosses (especially) and bosses (less so, but still present), all pretense goes out the window. There is no resistance to when you get hit, there are no I-frames; you go from full health to half health or less in a matter of milliseconds, and the only way you'd know it is to look. You'd better not be looking, though, because boss enemies are harmful whether they're dashing, shooting, slashing, or looking in your general direction. Most of the bosses can fill the space with area-denial (fire or bouncing projectiles or whatever) and also be everywhere at once, with flawless homing ability. Similarly, even basic mooks with guns can cut you from full to nothing in literally less than a second, and the only reason you'll know is because the screen will flash red and white and you're prompted to restart.
Restarting doesn't always work like it does in Hotline. Against subbosses, rather than starting right up front against the SB, you start up against the last crop of dip♥♥♥♥♥ you took down before he showed up. It's annoying, it's repetitive, and since the crop of idiots isn't what killed me, I'd prefer starting against the subboss who did so I can waste him and move on faster.
You take damage incredibly fast; a single bullet does, say, half a heart of damage, but since there are no I-frames, a three-round burst will hit you in the course of about half a second, and will take away a heart and a half in the time it takes you to blink. This is while other enemies are attacking, some of whom do more than that per strike, which means while you're noticing bullets, you may  move to dodge them and then get hit by two guys doing one move which happens to do half your health, so you still die in the space of about one second, regardless.
Add to that, and this is a minor grip, but relevant; everything in this game is ♥♥♥♥ing red. Like, I get it, guys, motif, but Jesus H. Moses, at a certain point, it gets hard to differentiate what the Hell is on the screen and what the Hell is going on, especially when ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s are throwing firebombs everywhere. The lights are red, the fire is red (and orange), the outlines are red, you dash as a red silhouette, enemies dash red, weapon swipes are red, projectiles are red, the screen flashes red when you're low on health, it all blends together, and I can't BELIEVE the number of times I was prompted to hit "R" and just thought "what the ♥♥♥♥ just happened?  What killed me?" More confused than even irritated, until it happened for the twentieth time.  Even memorizing patterns, it all starts to get so chaotic as the battle goes on that it's incredibly easy to lose track until "YER DED PRESS R KAY". Again, it ceases to be amusing.
It merits saying that maybe you get more skills to mitigate this. It could be a case of Early Game Hell. ♥♥♥♥, I mean, I love XCOM, so I'm no stranger to it, but this game went from suckering me in during the first 45 minutes to absolutely not fun whatsoever by the second subboss fight. I don't care if there's a special or correct way to do it, I don't care if trial-and-error is supposed to be the way you get things done or figure it out. I don't care if just keeping the entire arena between me and the boss enemy and shooting him with my basic pistol, doing chip damage until he dies and hoping he doesn't whip out some kind of almost-undodgeable or unforeseen, devestating attack works on every boss. It isn't fun. I was not enjoying myself once I past the 45 minute mark. And again, maybe it gets better later, but I doubt it, I don't think that's a valid excuse, and I wasn't interested in putting in more time spent irritated to find out if maybe that were true.
I did not PAY for this game and I want it off my Library list. Christ on sale, what a letdown.

Following the defeat of Sovereign at the end of Mass Effect 1, Shepherd and crew find themselves in the midst of a grand denial.  The Council attributes the unprecedented attack against the Citadel to the Geth and a rogue agent, blissfully happy to believe that the danger has passed.  Meanwhile, they still treat the true threat, the Reapers, as myth.  Shepherd finds himself in a waiting game; without Council support for a full investigation of the Reapers, there is little else to do but wait for their next move.  When a mysterious ship appears and attacks the Normandy, Shepherd find himself injured, presumed dead, and cut off from the Alliance--at least temporarily.
The highlight of Mass Effect 2 is unquestionably its story and universe, which builds upon the first game's fantastic universe with a tremendous deal of depth and new revelations.  Many of the races that were only hinted at are given far more treatment this time around.  With Shepherd working outside the Alliance, we get to explore the outer rim systems.  It is a realm that ranges from semi-ordered to lawless, and most of its residents are happy to operate outside of Council space.   The Quarians, courtesy of a companion character, are given a tremendous amount of development, including a visit to the migrant fleet.  And, in a surprise highlight later in the game, we even get a healthy dose of new insights on the Geth.  Several other races also are featured heavily, many of which received only a brief mention in the first game.
The story is fast-paced throughout the game, with the feeling of tangible threat growing each step along the way.  It is a good length--I finished the game in 52 hours, and I always play slowly--just enough to feel like you can sink yourself into the story without every feeling like the game was dragging.  It was a very satisfying experience, and yet I was wishing for more by the end.
The combat and RPG system is still fun in Mass Effect 2, but it is definitely different.  Many of the classical RPG elements were streamlined from the first game, which was a little disappointing.  There is very little, if any, choice to be made about equipment, with the exception of one's preferred rate of fire for shotguns.  Furthermore, decisions about abilities are largely relegated to deciding which of four skills (five for Shepherd) to forego.  Controls were similarly simplified, with you needing basically three buttons outside of movement: your trigger, the pause-the-game-breathe-and-trigger-abilities button (I live and die with this button), and the run/take cover button.  It took some getting used to, but by the end I found that combat was pretty fluid, fun, dynamic, and rarely over-dependent on "twitchy" player skills.
The biggest addition to the combat system was a paper-rock-scissors (sort of) system of defenses.  In addition to health, enemies can have up to three other types of defenses: armor, shields, and biotic barriers.  Each defense is best targeted by different kinds of weapons and skills.  Shields, for example, can be attacked by semi-automatic guns of Warp biotic abilities, whereas armor is better penetrated by heavy pistols and fire-based biotics.  I really enjoyed this addition; it made weapon switching important in combat, and, best of all, encouraged me to take along different companions depending on the types of enemies I expected to face in a given mission.
Also gone in this game were the planetary exploration missions of the first game.  You never get the equivalent of the mako tank missions where you get to drop down on a planet and battle your way to a mercenary base.  Instead, in this game, the mission just starts at the door to the base.  The mako's controls might have been bad at release, but by the time I played the game, it was vastly improved and, frankly, really fun.  I LOVED the opportunity to trek across alien landscapes of random planets, many of which weren't directly tied to the main plot.  ME2 seemingly replaced the mako experience with something far less fun: painfully slow, boring scans of planets for resources.  Those scans are mandatory, too, if you want to get enough resources to upgrade your weapons and ship sufficiently to take down the bad guys in the endgame.  I have no idea what the designers were thinking with this part of the game; more than once, they ended my late-night gaming session because I was nodding off trying to find a little bit more iridium.
In the end, ME2 is a terrific game.  Its main failing is that it probably isn't quite as good as the original, which has an argument for best RPG of all time.  If you compare it against ME1, you probably have to take off a star.  But compared to other games, I just can't do that.  ME2 is a blast to play, and I wouldn't hesitate to recommend it to others.  It's not perfect, but it's a 5 out of 5.

I wish there was an 'undecided' or 'conflicted' choice between recommend and not recommended, because that's exactly how I feel about hand of Fate; conflicted. One half of the game feels polished, well-done, inspired, and enjoyable, while the other half of the game feels clunky, frustrating, and greatly disappointing.
Most of the game is played through a large variety of cards which feel like a thoughtful mixture of dungeons & dragons and an at-home tabletop card game. Something like; 'You find an elven maiden in an emerald grove, what do you do?' then, based off your choices(and whether or not you succeed or fail)you are either rewarded with food, health, gold, or items, or you suffer a penalty of one of the above. Or worse, you face a random encounter – which is not to say that random encounters are the most dangerous of penalties in the game, but that they are the most cumbersome and thoughtless segments of the entire game. The combat isn't fun, and it isn't really challenging. At best it' is a bearable distraction, and at worst it's incredibly frustrating.
It almost feels like there were two teams(or people)who developed the game completely separate from each other and that one group wanted the game to be an engaging card-based d&d style game, while the other group just wanted to emulate a sloppy hack-and-slash game styled after the bland combat in Batman Arkham Asylum. “Tap left-click to attack and tap Q to parry”. There is some variation if you have unique weaponry or equipment, but it only serves to make combat in Hand of Fate feel like less of a “chore” which exactly how you DONT want your game's combat to feel.
Honestly, I admire the idea here: “What if a d&d styled card game had interactive combat?” With proper execution in both parts, we might have discovered an incredibly enjoyable niche game. But, while the card game segment is very well done, the combat isn't and the game suffers as a whole because of it. In my opinion the developers should have left combat to the cards and some dice rolls. It would have felt more in tune with the overall theme, felt much less clunky, and the extra development budget and time not spent on 3d modeling and combat coding could have greatly boosted the already enjoyable card segments. More cards, more card-based encounters, maybe even some cool screen visuals for certain effects, etc. In short, if they had scrapped the combat system, this game could have been so much better.
To make things worse, the card-game segment itself is very rouge-like, in that death will end your play and you'll be forced to restart your chapter progress from the start, but with the added benefit of gaining new cards which can bolster your character and add exciting new twists and turns for the next game. That in itself isn't bad at all, in fact it's enjoyable, but the problem comes from RNG and how cards can work in this game. Despite how many new cards you get from playing the game your character will ALWAYS start out a chapter with base equipment and stats(which can get better as you progress through the story but only after key chapters, and the progression is equally tied to enemy strength and difficulty, so the improvements always feel negligible and counteracted). RNG rears it's ugly face in the order by which you draw cards, and playing with the DLC 'characters' which add some new pro's and con's to your playthrough, you might be doomed from the very start thanks to such RNG.
For example, I tried my first Endless mode with a character that can only eat Iron Ore from discarded equipment and during my route(which was entirely linear from the start)I didn't come across a single piece of equipment. My character ran out of food and starved to death before I could find any gear to salvage for sustenance, and I wasn't able to scrap any of my equipped gear as a last resort because that's not a function of the game. I was doomed from the start to fail the match and all I gained were a few measly cards. This sort of RNG isn't absent from other rouge-likes, but-in my opinion-it is poor design. I don't expect the RNG to ensure my victory from the start, or at all for that matter, but I should have more control over my character's “Fate” than hoping I land on the exact cards I need to survive, especially in Endless mode where I have ZERO control over which cards are in the deck and which might appear next.
An idea that could have fixed this issue would have been 'hand cards' which you draw at the beginning of a game and are added to your 'hand'. You could use them at any time to gain supplies or whichever other benefit they provide and they either can't be refilled or can only be refilled on other rare event cards. For example, when playing the character which can only eat Iron Ore, you could start off with one or two random equipment cards, nothing worth equipping(rusted stuff maybe)but for use in case of emergencies. This way you're not entirely at the mercy of RNG if you run into a stretch of bad luck. Something like that could have been a very simple and enjoyable addition to the game which could have provided a bit more player choice and control. Letting players alter their 'hand cards' at the start of a match, for example, choosing from the pile of new cards they have acquired, would have been a great way to support players who really enjoy certain styles of play but might struggle under the fickleness of RNG.
Sadly, the absence of such a feature and the “fate” of your character more often than not relying on RNG isn't ideal for me. I understand that the game is called “Hand of Fate” and that “fate” implies a degree of luck and chance, but that shouldn't mean my character is guaranteed to not survive past the second floor because the RNG layout is entirely non-viable for my character. That isn't just 'fate' that's poor design, and it isn't enjoyable. I'll continue to play this game and I hope that further progression might change my mind, but for right now – I just can't recommend this kind of a game. The card-game segment is well written and clearly a thoughtful and lovingly designed portion of the game, but almost everything else(the combat, RNG, and some card and character mechanics)really ruin the atmosphere for me.
6/10 Slightly above average, but the parts that do work are niche elements and I can't recommend the package as a whole.

It's honestly a bit hard to explain this game, since it's such a mash of game elements. The general gameplay of moving from point to point and dealing with the events there feels very FTL, but then the combat kicks in and it's assassin's creed/arkham style fighting with counters, and the overarching deckbuilding mechanics are a whole layer of their own. The game is immensely fun, the enemy you face is full of character (with just a few random lines and some scripting they've achieved a character more interesting than most triple-A titles churn out these days...), and unlike most rogue-likes, you can make ongoing long-term progress even if you fail your main quest, in the form of unlocking new cards to encounter or use on your quest.
Honestly if you like rogue-like games at all I would check this one out, as it's overflowing with character. If you happen to be like me, and enjoy rogue-likes, counterattack combat, and deckbuilding, what are you waiting for?

There is no explanation as to what resources are what, no sense of how a deficit in one resource impacts or doesn't impact the player. I also feel that there is a lack of information given to the player about what buildings to build and planet management. The descriptions don't actually convey what the benefit or loss of building one building or another is. I very much had to guess that one building was a military building and so on from the description with no real idea of what it actually does. Also the amount of buildings you can build is not explicitly stated and I found myself fumbling with what to build and why. The ship designer also feels the same way, that I am not sure what to use and where and how much of specific parts. I found it repetitive, boring, and frustrating. The research tree I found as a black hole, basically just a big giant pile of stuff to research with no real goal in sight other than "something" that I assumed was better than whatever I had. I understand they were going for a feel that was for focusing on a certain research path and it would reveal techs related to that path in no specific order but I feel this was the biggest pitfall. Not because this was a bad idea but because of how it was implemented. The research is not really searchable, I'd have to get through 2-3 or more clicks before I would get to a description that really only describes a technology and doesn't tell me why it would benefit me. So I would search the descriptions of the varied researches available looking for something like "shields" or "phasers" but after about 10 minutes of searching, it was the last straw and gave up then asked for a refund.
Overall it feels like it could be a lot better, but it lacks some basic functionality. Like hovering your mouse over for tool tips. Or searching the tech tree. Or the game telling you what to do and why. I have no problem trying to figure out how these things work, but when I feel like I "need" to read the manual or play a tutorial in order to get the basic fundamentals of a game that maybe it wasn't put together well in the first place.
Also the main menu screen has no "Options" menu (or at least it wasn't obvious to me) and the music is terrible and too loud, I wanted to shut it off immediately but I couldn't. So I rushed through an empire creation to get in game so I could merely shut off the music.

I am a person of little words, so writing a review does not come natural to me.  In fact, this is probably the first review I have ever written.  I have just been so impressed that I had to support this team, and this is the way I am doing it.
In a nutshell, I recommend this game to anyone who loved DK and DK2.  I actually think this game is much better.  A small team of programmers made me so happy to play a game again!  The support this teams gives is amazing as well.  You can feel the love and passion of the game they created when playing.

This game has potential. I watched its development for the last 6 months, played several betas and there was huge progress in absolutely right direction (at least for me). I think it could be released later to become more polished, pricing tag is too big from my point of view, but one developer is only one developer and publisher decides this things. As I said, I see here a potential which developer realy strifes to implement and part of this price is a mean to invest in the future of this game.
Current version best sides:
- Challageble AI, which can deliver real pain. It has some gaps in diplomacy and sometimes delusion of grandeur, but in overall it is plesant to play with.
- Ship designer is a pinnacle of evolution in my view. I like to design and customize ships and here each ship becomes unique. I never played twice with same designes. The only gap here is a lack of default designs for lazy players and lack of battle arena for testing, which I think will be fixed soon.
- This brigns me to another major side of this game: tactical combat. Dozens of ships in one combat, hundreds of fighters - easy peasy. Flexible designer grands huge amount of variations in tactic. Carriers, fighters, battleships, anti-fighter ships, torpedo carriers, stations and so on in many variations - you need to adapt your fleet to opponent, his style of combat and technological level. Some technologies can dramatically change combat flow. Animation is nice too - nothing fancy, but plesant.
- External threat implementation in late game :)
Downsides:
- Exploration is most underdeveloped part of this game. I like big glaxies, but there is nothing to do in big galaxy here. Small maps with early opponents are preferrable. Pirates are unconvincing, need something more, like minor races. I think external threat could become huge exploration drive if intoduced sooner in the game.
- Governments are non-existent. I would like to see political/economical systems specific to different races.
- There are no planetary upgrades except of abstract mining techs which are applied automatically. Game strategy itself is too much colonization-driven. No way for some small empire to win concentrating on quality, not quantity of colonies.
- No ability to continue game after external threat. I would really like that, <spoilers> :)

What Crusader Kings 2 provides you with is essentially a toolbox for managing your Dynasty. But what is a Dynasty right? Well you play as an independent country or a duchy in the middle ages and when your character dies you play as their heir, and keep on playing until you have no heirs left. Which can happen if you manage to♥♥♥♥♥♥off the whole of Europe.
What this leaves you with is a game that is based almost entirely on intrigue and plotting. You marry not out of love, but to forge strong alliances so that you can call them into war. You can assassinate people who don’t like you and try and manipulate situations so that you end up in power. In my first play through my daughter killed my son to solidify herself as heir, I then discovered the plot and had her executed. My brother than hated me for killing my daughter and had me killed. It sounds great on paper right? But mechanically it’s quite complicated because there are SO MANY moving pieces to consider. This is the

There are a few really comprehensive guides and wikis on this game, so do have a look at those as well.

Polaris Sector is a space 4x game that I have been looking for in a long while.  Other games held my interest for a while but ultimately fell flat as I got bored with them.  Either those games were overly complex or too simple.  Polaris Sector seems to offer happy medium.  I've only played 5 hours at the time of this writing however this game is very addictive and is not too hard nor too easy.  There is a lot of depth in research, combat, production, ship design, etc.  I could go on but I'll save the details for when I have some more time under my belt.
In short, I would take the negative reviews with some doubt.  I'm not sure why those reviewers hate on the game.  I'm a fairly critical individual but I'm having a hard time finding any faults with this game.
Update (3.Apr 2016):  27 hours in at time of this writing.
I have to say I still think this is a great game for the 4x space genre.  My first game as the humans ended in disaster and it wasn't because I lost to overwhelming firepower or spam fleets of doom.  It was because I overlooked the dangers of espionage and had no way to stop the enemy from sabotaging my mining.  The end result was that I quickly ran out of a key mineral type needed to sustain and build a fleet.  My ships wasted away because they no longer had access to the mineral they needed to keep the ships 'afloat'.  I was impressed and have started a new game as the Logans with this lesson learned.
The research system is presentented in a refreshingly unique way.  It has been lauded by some and criticized by others.  If one takes the time to understand how the system works they will find that it's much more thought provoking than a typical static tech tree found in many strategy games.
Ship design is a joy and is not a tedious chore.  The design system focuses only on the interesting aspects of ship design and abstracts the mundane such as life support, bridge room, etc.  Those components are assumed to be part of every ship and there is no need for the player to find precious space to install those pieces.  Instead the player is going to be faced with many interesting decisions about what components is needed for the ship in question.  The many possible combinations all layed out in a fairly easy to follwo format are impressive.  Ship design is almost a game within a game as you constantly need to assess problems in the galaxy and how to deal with them via a specific ship type.
I experienced no mid or late game tedium.  There is always something to do in this game.  There is no busy work or mandatory tasks that must be performed manually that you find in many other games.  The ai does a good job managing your planets for you if you decide you don't want to micromanage them.  I like how you can also plan colonization automatically and let the ai handle settling in to that nice new planet you found.  In addition the ai does a fairly decent job at planning planetary ground invasions as well.  All in all I like having options to automate certain aspects of the game if I choose.
That's all for now but I hope my feedback helps you decide one way or the other if you want to buy this game.

Recettear: An Item Shop's Tale is a cute little RPG set in a world were you must satisfy customers who require their Fantasy-like items for their own adventure. The game follows a deadline system where every week you must make a certain amount of money in order to pay off your debt and proceed; which is done through none other than selling items above buy cost. You can also go out into dungeons to search for items for free, and verse a plethora of enemies and bosses using adventureres as your guide.
Overall I did find this game very addictive, but by the time I had finished the five weeks of paying off my debt I no longer needed to continue playing. I didn't get addicted to the dungeon gameplay, but I did find it amusing for a short period. The item selling is a unique mechanic which is the core gameplay, which you will find is the only reason people like myself stay to play. Yet after the five weeks it became repetetive and I was done with playing, I had no urge to play through the post-game content. Whilst I do highly recommend this game, I do also say that you won't really want to complete it 100% and there may be some factors in the game which may irritate you. Once you figure out how to use the high cost sales period to your advantage, it is quite easy to make more money than required.

Hard Reset is a sci-fi themed FPS set in desolate, unknown world, possibly our own, where science and technology have advanced to the brink, causing chaos and uncertainty for the human race. You play as Major Fletcher, a security officer of sorts whose tasked at patrolling; the game, however, opens up with major Fletcher at his more preferred location: a dilapidated bar.
The silence is broken by the call of work and Major Fletcher is forced to go meander through an area of town to investigate potential goings on. Cue the dead bodies and deadly robots and you’ve got endless waves of crazed, bloodthirsty machines to destroy. Your arsenal of weapons to wage war and protect humanity is limited to two, but you’re in luck because your machine gun and plasma gun morph into a variety of deadly products: shotguns, rocket launchers, lasers, grenades and even EMP blasts to name a few. With guns in hand, you’re off to be the sole protector of the human race – get to it, Major Fletcher.
There are some major points in Hard Reset that I really enjoyed and other elements that felt lacking. For those of you who expected a story, you’ll be hard-pressed to find one in Hard Reset. With very linear story progression and an even smaller cast of characters, you’ll find yourself very alone; there is not a single human being in the entirety of the game [DLC included] that you meet aside from telecommunications at key junctures. That is, unless a dead body or two will fill your social expectations.
This became one of my major gripes with Hard Reset, but keep in mind I love stories, character development and the like, so for me Hard Reset didn’t deliver those expectations. In a city brimming with life and an opening scene of wanton destruction and death, human contact is the rarest commodity. You feel alone, wandering around, slaying hordes of machines, visiting vast stretches of land, scaling buildings and traversing factories only to find the same thing in every scene: nobody.
While social aspects aren’t Hard Reset’s suite, it does paint detailed environments: changing landscapes, satisfying destructible objects and lots of them and a generally pleasant musical score and great background pieces, which help bring life into a mostly lifeless, linear game.
What Hard Reset does best isn’t immediately noticeable until you progress further into the story. That talent is shown in the enemies you encounter and the bosses you must conquer, providing some unique fights that I enjoyed. Much to its credit, Hard Reset proclaims that it takes a step back into past shooters, removing many of the aspects that have made them dull and too easy; Hard Reset delivers. The game is hard, really, really hard and that’s just the “normal” difficulty. There’s then even more asinine difficulties for those who are truly masochists at heart. Couple that with little to go by and the learning curve can be unpleasant at times.
Hard Reset is devoid of any QTEs [thankfully], but also comes with no real tutorials, instructions, no regenerating health or suggestions on how to defeat any enemy in the game, which, contradictory to how it sounds, is rather pleasant. You’re left to formulate your own plans, devise your own cover [this game has no traditional hard cover mechanics] and decide what tools and weapons will work the most efficiently in dispatching the enemy. The lack of help is something I didn't realize was so prevalent in our games until I was restricted from such features. All in all, this left me dying a lot, but not so much that it became frustrating, as I learned to adapt over time.
As I mentioned above, the game is mostly linear, but there are secrets to collect and you’ll want to find them since this is the key feature in upgrading your weaponry and passive perks. Most secrets are easy to find and a little bit of digging will net you most of them without much effort. However, finding them all will take a bit of detective work if you’re up for the challenge and some will take some delicate fingers because they're hidden in ridiculously treacherous locations - I'm looking at you secret on the collapsible bridge.
Some of you will enjoy Hard Reset for the immense challenge, the sheer destruction and piles of shredded metal you can leave in your wake, while some will find it dull, uninteresting and lacking in substance. I do admit, the game started to become far more interesting right towards the end, leaving a kind of hollow victory inside me as the credits rolled and I left looking for more, only to find I had done all Hard Reset had to offer.


Overall, Hard Reset targets a rather unique demographic, which is probably why it has received such mixed reviews overall. Providing a grueling, unforgiving FPS experience is great for some, but an anemic story and linear gameplay might be too much to overlook for other buyers, leaving them disappointed. While I personally enjoyed the game for what it was, I highly suggest looking into it before you buy it because Hard Reset isn’t for everyone.

Conan Exiles... My partner and I are scouting the desert wasteland for a bandit camp to capture a blacksmith and make him our thrall. (work for us) We come across two other exiles building a base not far from our hidden base in the mountains, so we stop by to investigate/greet them. "Hello there sirs, How goes it?" I ask. Shoooooomth! Im met with an arrow to the arm. I dodge the next two arrows and we run behind a rock. I say to my partner, "Lets do this!" My partner and I rush the attackers.
The one exile breaks his stairs leading up to his tower in progress so we cant get to him and starts hailing down arrows at us. My partner starts firing back. I, not having a bow but having a steel pickaxe, notice another larger base about 100 yards to the east. (obviously theirs) So, I rush over there and start hacking down one of the walls to try to entice the attacker to come down. The other exile has ran inside this base by this time and I can hear him frantically running around. I tear down a wall but cant get inside because the foundations were too high to jump on...
Then comes the sandstorm. Almost immediately, Wind and sand is swirling around, Im blinded at this point, can barely see 5 feet in front of me.
Trying to make out the terrain and navigate myself to a more safe area, I hear running footsteps getting closer, and quickly. SLASH! something slices me in the back, then the front. Blood spraying on the ground, Im at about 60% health. I can barely make out the two exiles circling me. I attack them both the best I can with my sword and shield. One rushes me with a charged spear trust, I block him with my shield and counter attack with a swift slice to his shoulder. I circle around the one and down him with a final charged blow, slicing his arm off in the process. Im now faced against the other exile 1 vs 1. My health is around 30% at this point. I can feel my palms sweating, hands shaky, adrenaline rushing.
The exile lunges at me with his spear, I quickly dodge to the left and then strike his right arm. He backs off, we start circling around, both looking for an opening to strike and regaining stamina. Then, Out of nowhere... Thunk! An arrow sinks in the exiles back. "This is my chance" I think to myself. I start pummeling him with sword strikes. My partner runs up on him from behind and with her huge battle axe slices the exile, ripping his torso from the rest of his body...
Blood and body parts everywhere, on the brink of death, we quickly snatch the exiles gear and loot. Then head off towards our home.

My review is going to be short, sweet and to the point.
First and foremost: A vast, vast majority of the negative reviews are from the very early days of Alpha and were posted by people who fail to fully grasp the concept of what an Alpha stage is and choose to judge a product and its entire development team by the usual bugs that crop up during this stage. That said, the team so far has been very good at not only identifying and working on fixes, updates and more content for the game, but also communication and keeping in contact with the playerbase they rely on so heavily.
The game itself is extremely promising and to echo many others, it's a mixture of Rust and ARK but also has a lot of its own original content like sandstorms and the way rocks break, not to mention the level of character customization that rivals many MMO's / RPG's out there.
There are definite bugs out there such as crafting and AI but they are being worked on and the developers have identified a lot of the more serious, game-breaking ones. Combat is also unorthodox and a bit clunky, especially in comparison with more smoother action-based combat like Skyrim or something, that's really just a matter of taste and the player getting used to it. Right now the biggest thing (as is the case in most early access titles) is optimization, there are some performance issues with rendering, frame rate drops and server lag.
With all that said, I've found the game extremely enjoyable and haven't encountered any bugs that have made me want to uninstall or drop this game. It's a ♥♥♥♥ load of fun when playing it with friends and I'm really excited and optimistic about what the future holds for this title. In closing, I'd like to echo what other players have said -- DEVELOPERS: You have a very good opportunity here, you've got a fantastic game in the making and it's on you to make it work out. Don't ruin it, don't betray your playerbase, stay driven and keep adding content and working on those issues that crop up!

RUINER is a cyberpunk twin stick shooter focused on delivering a first rate visual and audial experience. The art style is gritty and stylish, using comic book style renders to set the pulpy cyberpunk tone, and the soundtrack
... expect a bit more bark than bite, but the game is still fun to play and it doesn't overstay its welcome (expect roughly 7-9 hours on Hard).
+ The art direction is excellent.
+ The soundtrack is excellent.
+ It's fast paced and never really feels like a slog.
+ Some bosses are really satisfying to fight and beat.
+ Once you get past the controls, the mechanics work incredibly well.
+ I personally really liked the story and writing. It's simple, but feels nuanced and
like pulpy cyberpunk goodness.
- While the game has an excellent style, it would have benefited from more environmental variety.
- Some bosses are weaksauce, like Hongshi, which is a shame because I thought he had a very cool design. There were a few like him that turned out underwhelming.
- It lacks endgame content and is short.
- It was easy for me, even on Hard. I would have liked a mode that forced limited retries before full mission restart or something along those lines.
Overall, it's a good game and I recommend it. I look forward to seeing more content for the game.

Owlboy is a pretty great game, but despite that I do not think it's worth the full price. In a sale? Sure. The art and soundtrack are gorgeous, the story is alright, but for me it has little in replay value. I imagine it'd be especially true for any completionists out there or achievement hunters.
Still, I'm going to recommend it because I found it enjoyable overall.
The controls are tight and everything flows smoothly, the boss battles are pretty great (I'm not amazing at platformers and struggled in some cases playing with keyboard+mouse) and generally challenging what with the switching between characters. I really loved zipping around with Twig, and nailing a part of a fight that I'd been grinding my teeth over felt wonderfully rewarding. The areas are interesting enough to make me want to come back and explore for secrets, but while the completionist in me wants to collect everything, I also found the vastness of some of the areas rather tedious and offputting.
Actually my biggest con with this game, despite it being more or less linear, is the lack of a map. For someone trying to actually collect everything, this would be a boon.
The story writing could be better, it's a good concept, and though I figured it out early I was satisfied with the conclusion, bittersweet as it was. I say it could be better because the characters fall a little flat, despite some stellar dialogue and humor. It has some very strong 'Ori and the Blind Forest' or 'Zelda' vibes for me, which is great in the latter case because that's one of my favorite series of games ever, yet doesn't quite make it. There's a lot of back and forth in the dungeons and it feels kind of...I guess, in retrospect, half finished? At least where the story is concerned.
Obviously a lot of effort went into it, but it feels like a cut version of a longer game, which is why I can't find myself justifying the price. I snapped this up as part of a bundle though so I'm not exactly sorry for the pricetag.
The last thing that I found quite disheartening was how much everyone ragged on Otus, telling him he was useless etc when he clearly wasn't, and a lot of the situations were out of his control, even when he had Geddy to back him up, they still didn't believe him. Can't say I'm really a fan of the intensely negative attitude towards the little guy, though it was nice to see that change a bit. (It just took too long to get to the point of respect for being courageous and everything he'd done imo.)

The plot of this game was really interesting but the side quests kind off cut off abruptly in the end, hopefully there will be DLC to tie up the loose ends. The combat in this game is so fast paced and fun that sometimes I found myself completely immersed in the game trying to focus all of my thoughts on it. The shield and dash skills are obviously the best working combo for now, but the timing needs to be perfect in order to use its effectively and once you get the stun upgrade for the shield, the game becomes way easier. The gunplay feels a bit weak and sometimes the guns are completely useless for fighting bosses, most of the time I could just use melee to beat them but it is still fun at times and guns like shotguns are incredibly satisfying to use. Overall I would say that with the gunplay being a bit weak but still fun at times, and everything else in the game being superb this game is another masterpiece and a great experience. 9/10

Chivalry Medieval Warfare is a very intense and frusterting game, yet it also happens to be the most rewarding and stimulating game I have ever played. It's best that I say it now. This game is completely dead even in it's review potential.
Please allow me to explain...
1. Gameplay:
Gameplay is extremely well thought out and precise. To me, there is nothing more satisfying than shooting a Heavy Crossbow Bolt a hundred yards away into a Knight's neck. Or Being on the verge of death and managing to get that lucky stab with my dagger through an enemy's chest. The pacing is quite good and you are always on your toes. However, this game's precision also comes at a price. The way the weapons work in Chivalry is that as long as the weapon it'self hits you, it counts. This means that if I jump and do a 360 of of a bench and my sword hits you while spinning, you will get hurt. Most experienced players use this to their advantage. This results in new players being completely demolished and experienced players being nearly one-man batallions if they are good enough. This however also presents a learning curve. I came from Chivalry on the Xbox (We do not speak of that atrocity) and I was shocked at how people were playing. Twirling around and managing nearly impossible hits. BUT, if you take your time and are patient enough, you WILL learn how to counter-act these people. If not by Sword or Hammer, than by bow. Because what's the easiest way to take out a twirler before they hit you? Shoot 'em.
2. Community:
The comunity goes without the need for explanation, yet I will do so anyway. I have made SO MANY friends by playing this game. So many nice people who are funny, honorable, and just all around fun to play with. I personally haven't met anyone who hates me or vice versa, yet I have seen the ocassional  jerk. I have seen a lot of kicks in my play-time, yet all of these people where either jerks themselves, causing a hostile enviorment (I.E. arguing with people in chat, spouting random insults, ect). The community loves to be helpful and most importantly to everyone, keep the game going. This means that if you are AFK for a while without telling anyone, they will most likely kick you in order for other people who are playing to join. Things like that. Yes, there will be jerks. They are on every game. But if you are light hearted and go in with good feelings and attitude, you will be surprised how many people that you never even knew will become your best friends.
3. Classes:
Each class is dynamic and unique in it's on way. Some out do others in stamina, others out do others in health, ect. But no class is better than the other. Examples; you may be a hulking Knight in full clad armor, but one good shot to the head from a Crossbow and you are done. You may also be a nimble and accurate archer, but if you are caught off guard or with your bow drawn, it's game over. Finally, you may be a Vanguard with a long Polearm, keeping enemies at a distance, but if someone gets through you with a dagger or short-sword, you are at a disadvantage. But what I like most about these classes is tht nothing is impenetrable. Any class can die by any class. A quick thing you will learn in this game is that Stats do not matter at all. Your weapon is only as good as the person weilding it. This means that if you are good enough, you can smash the face off of a Knight with a stick, or kill a Vanguard with well placed axe throwing. No class (Heh) Out-classes the other. Yes, I did a funny.
4. Servers:
There are many servers in this game. Each one is in a certain region or consist of certain mods, certain maps, ect. You will not have any issue finding what you want to play and where you want to play it. Although, make sure you keep an eye on your ping level to the right of the server names. Your peformance may varry on certain servers if you are not within your region, though, that is obvious.
So in conclusion....
1. There are really good players. Some of the tactics are cheap. But if you are patient enough to wait/learn/practice with others, you WILL match them and beat them.
2. There are good and bad people in the world. But a long as you aren't stiring up trouble, AFK without informing the others, or if your ping is too high, you will not be kicked.
3. Each and every class is hard to master. Very hard. But once you do, you can be very dangerous to anyone who crosses you. Also, people have a little disdain for archers. but those people are quickly silenced with a shot to the head! xP
4. Each and every server suits your needs in a particular need. There are so many, game modes, weapons, maps, and mods. Pick whichever fits your fancy.
So that's it. This review was to show anyone interested that this game DOES have it's pros and cons. Some will find it interesting and give it a try and love it. Others may do the same but find it lacking or not to thier liking. As long as you know what you are going in to, it's up to you what you do with the information given to you. I still however MUST recommend this game. For any Competitive, patient, medieval loving gamer out there, this game is NOT worth missing.
Thank you very much for reading. I hope to see you on the battlefield!
