In short: the game has great atmosphere / immersion, but for the current version of the game with it existing feature set (1.0.3), I personally found the price a bit too big.
-	Immersion: the game builds a great atmosphere: if you ever go for a summer walk during a starry night – that’s exactly the feeling that you experience when playing the game
-	Beautiful Art
-	Great soundtrack, relaxing music
-	Innovative approach to puzzles
-	As you progress, puzzles really become challenging
-	First levels really feel to easy: new mechanics are being introduced, but often not explored enough. The „putterfish” levels (after lvl 4) is when challenge begins.
-	At the later levels, there’s so much synergy between elements  that sometimes you just don’t realize how you solved the puzzle: the huge chain reaction starts (especially with dolphins) and then suddenly, the path opens.
-	Hints are useless: if you are stuck, it just gives a generic advice that might not even apply to your situation (instead of showing the next move, like it usually is in puzzles)
To sum it up, if you plan to buy it at full cost: wait until all features are complete (unless you have lots of feedback that you like giving). It’s a decent puzzle game, but the price is a bit steep for now. Definitely grab it at 50% discount, but otherwise: consider waiting to see if developers deliver.

If I had to boil Recettear down to one word, “cute” would definitely be it. The anime-like art style, the character designs, the music, it’s all basically adorable. The premise draws on the concept from your typical RPG of the ubiquitous items shop. But while in most games, these shops are pretty generic, this story takes it from the shop owners’ perspective, selling to adventurers and townsfolk alike. It definitely plays like an RPG, but the majority of the focus is on resource management in the shop. Not that you can’t go dungeon crawling if you want to–and sometimes the variety is nice. While the whole buying and selling thing can be a bit repetitive, you are faced with time-management challenges and an increasingly complex market as time goes by. Plus, there are some fun character interactions mixed in, especially between Recette and Tear. I think the adorable relationship between these two–and the stark contrast in their personalities–is what truly makes this game. It’s certainly what I enjoyed the most. As for sound, the music is simple but cute. There is some minimal character voicing, mostly just set phrases, which is all in Japanese but is quite well done; the timing and quality of the actors really does add to the overall flavor of the game, although none of the actual words will make sense unless you have at least a basic understanding of Japanese. All the written text has been translated to English, though, so it’s completely playable–also, the translation is actually quite good. So yeah, it you’re looking for cute RPG that’s a bit different from the norm, I think Recettear is a fun option to try.

You know... I WANT to love this game. Like most players i came from the old DK series and jumped on WFTO as soon as it was announced. I stuck with it through Early Access waiting for the final release. Now that it has been released and i have played through the campaign i am left with a 'is that it' feeling.
The Campaign levels mostly relied upon rushes, there was none of the patient 'build, probe, attack and assimilate' of the DK series. This was more of a 'build a few rooms, cap out your army then rush'.
Some of the levels required it, you could not beat them otherwise. The lack of thought needed to beat the campaign was a real turn-off for me.
There were so many spells, potions and rituals that i had no need for.
I basically beat the game with just 3 of the available defences (door, bombard and lotus trap), 3 of the spells (heal, lightning and summon imp) and the required Ritual in the last level. That meant that > 75% of the available buffs were unnecessary!
The voice overs were often repeated with machinegun regularity and i wished for a way to turn them off.
It is a lovely game (plagued by stuttering) and i hope the devs can change its course back to what they were clearly aiming for.
At the moment i cannot possibly recommend it either for old DK players or new players.

To start I was a beta tester for this game for several months before it launched so I have many more hours with the game than Steam reports.
I've played tons of 4x games over the years from MOO to Gal Civ to Sword of the Stars to Endless Space to Stardrive to Distant Worlds to... you get the idea. This game offers several unique things that keep me coming back  to it:
+ Importance of long-term planning: In most 4x games if you run low on a resource you can just shift population around to fix things quickly. Not so here. You need to carefully plan out your economy, planetary governor focuses, and so much more. The level of in-depth empire management this game offers is only matched by Distant Worlds in my opinion which is a good thing.
+ Research: Finally a unique approach to research split between developing general fields of research areas that generate specific technologies over time. It takes a little getting used to, but overall it is nice to have something different from the standard tech trees most other 4x games offer.
+ Combat (specifically fighters): Finally a game where I can design and build proper carriers with swarms of fighters and bombers to use in combat to overwhelm my enemies. Point defense systems can shred fighters though, so a constant balance is needed. This is a game where you can study an enemy's ship designs and build counters to those designs which is always nice to see.
+ Strong AI: I've seen the AI expand agressively when appropriate and seek friendly relations when I am in a position of stength. AI can be a weak point for many 4x games, but so far I've happen pleasantly satisified with my computer opponents thus far.
- Exploration: The dev tried to add in some interesting things like anamolies and wormholes to help make the galaxy feel more interesting, but most systems will feel very bland as you search the galaxy. The lack of unique things like minor races and chained events/quests makes exploration a little dull, but then again that is to be expected in a game of this scale with so many systems to explore.
Overall this is an easy recommendation from me. The dev is very active and responsive and they deserve credit for the great game they've put together. If you are a 4x fan who enjoys empire management on a large scale this game is for you.

Expanding is really slow and boring, especially in the beginning. Not really a problem but because there is not that much to do early game, only explore/refuel and repeat, you really need to speed the game up.  You can let the AI manage the colonization process, which is nice to some degree.
Combat is ok, even tho it feels a bit sluggish but you can speed things up for a fast resolve or even auto-resolve. Mid-late game you are kinda forced to use a type of weapon/tech or you can end up with a useless fleet.

A lot of buts for a game that looked really good on paper. I still hope for an expansion or some really good mods.

Crusader Kings 2 is important for a number of reasons. It's one of those games that you can
get on PC due to the sheer amount of depth to it. When you start the game it is very confusing and very baffling, so I’ll start off with
you should play it and then
to get into it.
If you played Total War and you hated the empire management element but loved the battles then this game probably isn’t for you. What Crusader Kings 2 provides you with is essentially a toolbox for managing your Dynasty. But what is a Dynasty right? Well you play as an independent country or a duchy in the middle ages and when your character dies you play as their heir, and keep on playing until you have no heirs left. Which can happen if you manage to♥♥♥♥♥♥off the whole of Europe.
What this leaves you with is a game that is based almost entirely on intrigue and plotting. You marry not out of love, but to forge strong alliances so that you can call them into war. You can assassinate people who don’t like you and try and manipulate situations so that you end up in power. In my first play through my daughter killed my son to solidify herself as heir, I then discovered the plot and had her executed. My brother than hated me for killing my daughter and had me killed. Then I went on playing the game as my brother – who everyone actually liked because he got rid of a terrible king. He then ruled for a ridiculous period (50 or so years), united Ireland and had a ton of children with 3 different wives. Once he died, all of the children started plotting against each other to get themselves into power. The ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s.
It sounds great on paper right? But mechanically it’s quite complicated because there are SO MANY moving pieces to consider. This is the
part of the review. When you start, you want to do as many tutorials as you have the patience to sit through, and then do a learning scenario like playing as the King of Leon. Once you’ve done that a few times, then I strongly recommend picking a kingdom on Ireland and having your short-term goal being the Unification of the Kingdom of Eire. There are a few really comprehensive guides and wikis on this game, so do have a look at those as well.
It’s a treat to play this game once you get into it. Just don’t come in expecting a Total War game. What this is, is essentially dynasty simulation at its finest. So fine that there’s a really awesome Game of Thrones mod for once you’ve got to grips with the game! Oh, and be wary of those Mongols in the 13th Century. Those guys are♥♥♥♥♥♥♥

The only real 'business' part of it is the ability to set prices and bargain with each character. Unfortunately, this gets to be very tedious very fast -- you have to price each item individually for every customer (of which there are only a few types), and can only sell a handful of things each day. The only way to 'survive', in effect, is to crawl the ever-loving♥♥♥♥♥♥out of the dungeons and pray that you got some expensive loot to sell at your store... so basically at its core it's a pretty average action RPG.

I am unsure where to begin with Divinity 2 at this point.
This game has been and still is an amazing journey you can take on alone or with your friends.
I am hardly convinced with most of the games I play but Divinity has me on a collar. I cannot look away or stop playing it.
I already am at 50H and haven't even experienced the whole singleplayer campaign.
The fact that you can talk with every single NPC, including animals (if you got the "Pet Pal" Talent early on), that you can explore every corner, find new clues and ways to secret caves or find treasure chests. All those aspects are a big yes for me to recommend Divinity2.
But was that all? Hell no. I haven't even covered 20 percent of what this game is capable of yet!
I really enjoy freedom. I want to choose what to do, how to do it and, that should I take the wrong path in a conversation, have to deal with the backfire.
Each race reacts differently towards NPC's (as do they. A lot of racism going on in this game) while adding more tags to your character such as "Barbarian""Scholar""Outlaw""Mystic""Soldier""Jester" and "Noble" gives you the options to get more information out of them or successfully persuing them after they saw you stealing.
(I have to add this since it caused me great pain. Do NOT click on a trader while they are walking by. I accidentally stole a bottle of wine instead of talking to the trader and hell on earth broke out. Never steal wine guys. NEVER.)
Each races armor looks different depending on what armor you give them. The same helmet looks differently for each race which means just getting out all the armor sets probably took ages and I am glad they put so much detail and work in this game. You can see the development teams heart in it. A great game that is meant to be so much more.
It is sometimes hard to keep the playerbase or even raise those numbers shouldn't there be options to replay the game after "finishing". Divinity did everything right. I am putting the word "finish" like this simply because of the fact that you will be having a hard time completing this game 100% if not impossible. So many options depending on what you chose while creating your character, while talking, whom you talk too and how. So many options to go, so much to explore, so many ways you can complete a single quest will make it hard for you to not get lost in this wonderful world <3
And I haven't even started to talk about the Game Master aspect. So far I have't been able to look at them simply because of the fact that the moment I have freetime I play the campaign.... I might be addicted at this point.
The option to create your own campaign, invite your friends or upload your work on Divnity's Steam Workshop will give you a never ending adventure.
My friendgroup started to use Divinity as DnD platform. Our GM creates the world and through Divinity you don't need to only imagine it, you can actually see and play your personal adventure.
Since the game is turn based you have everything a little RP heart needs to be happy.
In short:
If you enjoy exploring, a never ending adventure and have a great time with your friends while playing Divnity's campaign, a downloaded one from the workshop or your own this is the game for you to play.
A long awaited tripple A game that has been worth all the wait. Hands up for an amazing adventure I will be enjoying for a long time!

ontop of a curb high ledge. In these cases, I had to use another 'command point' just to move the guy like 3 feet just so he would be save. DAMN, I was tired. Beaten and broken to my absolute core. Like Gandalf after the Balrog fight, I lay like roadkill on Gaming’s Last Stand. Left in the ditch by the ravenous, greedy games industry, all but forcing me to violently amputate myself from my hobby after so many years, my thoughts returned to me through the mist of my mind. Game publishers had made me hate gaming more and more with every Microtransaction, Gambling Lootbox, and übergreedy DLC-pettiness, rubbing their scummy hands together, waiting for their chance to turn me so desperate that I'd sell my mum's wheelchair just to be able to play the story of a single player game wholesale instead of in disgusting piece-meal chunks.
Exhausted.
Ready to let my hobby die.
Clearing my head to drift forever into the mindless, mainstream, middleaged hobbies of pathetic Rom-Coms so bad they have to tell you where to laugh, sports night with a team letting you down for 20 years straight, and pedantic tv-gameshow hosts as full of themselves as the CEOs and board members of todays’ AAA game companies.
I had cried out for Gaben, but he was nowhere to be seen. I called out for him again and again, desperately trying to summon the one time so great mythical Valve Overlord to give me a glimpse of Half-Life 3 or some other new IP, for a last incongruent attempt to restore my faith in The Greatest Hobby ever known. But Gaben had sojourned to the evil gates of DOTA 2 many moons ago, and had never been seen since. Every Valve knave had followed their once and future king, but in their wake had only left silence for those few of us who still cared. Their footprints, all leading to DOTA 2, and not one leading back, had all but vanished.
And amidst the Consumer Forest behind Valve Village, there was talk of another presence, only whispered in fear, between creeping darkness and depressive thoughts; Artifact... Artifact... The wind carried the promise of a terrible omen, of yet another unnecessary card game to come, assuring the deliverance of the final strike into the once golden, now charred, heart of gaming. And Gaben never appeared in this, my darkest hour. The heroic saviour was lost to time and space as he had succumbed to The Void of Game Industry Indifference.
My mind wandered. Valve Village lay in ruins. Long was the time since anyone had fixed anything on the barricades of Team Fortress, and the walls of Counter-Life: Grognard Operations' padded cells had crumbled, leaving demons and hell-outcasts running rampant and harassing any remaining villagers. There were rumors that some of the worst of these creatures had even snuck after Gabe through the gates of DOTA, in the Unholiest of Unholy joinings of good and evil, but none had heard back from them either. The Portals to the temple of Half-Life were rusted to a sad metal heap, and the temple they guarded had lied dormant for centuries with no Programmer Priests or Artist Acolytes left to work on the Half-Life religion. Valve Village was a ghost town. Dying at last, together with me.
I felt my body getting numb. I knew I was close to exhaling my last breath of gaming. Doomed to never experience the warm freedom from corporate game publisher mind£uckery. Never allowed again to experience the sheer joy of a great game not tormented by CEO and board member greed.
I closed my eyes.
I made my peace with everything. Accepting of Bobby Kotick’s miniscule d|ck, mercilessly drilling down the insides of my throat, demolishing my gag reflex for all time. No more protesting Zenimax’ and Bethesda’s Pete Hines lying and lying, his nose getting longer and longer inbetween my a$$ cheeks as he denounced that their new paid mods system was indeed paid mods. I let out a poor sigh as I came to terms with EA’s bukk4k3 horror show, drowning me and their other customers in their blank secrete of filthy business decisions, in amounts so vast they could shave their chiseled d0uche game publisher jawline in the mirroring reflection of my glistening forehead.
Nothing mattered anymore. We, the customers, had lost. And as a single tear ran down my cheek, gaming was dead and gone forever. I embraced the darkness and muttered a final prayer to the gaming gods of old, before feeling a last remaining speckle of life vanish from my veins. My gamer soul was ready. I was to return home to 8bit, 16bit, Playstation and PC; to the 80s and 90s gaming heaven. Far away from the grotesque demonic onslaught hell here, far from the karmic injustice of game publishers burning the industry down until they had extinguished its last pittance of grace. I was ready. And darkness came.
Then, movement.
Not from me. Outside of me.
A feather of light touched my eyes. A vague, finely tuned iota beam, shimmering onto my eyelids. It tormented my weak sight, but it was real! A light, a light! My body jolted as it shone towards me from the distant skies. My a$$crack ravaged, my throat sore, my forehead glimmering with horrible Microtransaction DLC. I was not dead yet, there was a game title coming closer, flapping it's angel wings as it descended upon my old, withered gamer soul. Larian had come to my rescue. They would not let me fall to the demonic creature game publisher overlords. They would conquer this Normandy, they would sail this Pacific. They would go on until the end. And no micro DLC could stand in their way of delivering the atomic bomb which destiny would have in itself the strenght and honour to become 2017s GOTY.
Long live Larian, the New Gamer Wine. The Future World Leader in cRPGs. The Youthful Lords of Gaming.
Support this developer. Sell your kids, dogs, and a kidney if you must. But support them, please. Drop them a bundle of cash from a helicopter, write your will today and give it all to Larian. Or do something else more or less creative. But promise me you’ll support them.

Valkyria Chronicles is a gorgeous, unique hybrid of turn-based tactics and real-time action that doesn't live up to its full potential, but it's still well worth your time if you're interested in games like XCOM or Nintendo's Fire Emblem series. Initially released on the PS3, the game's excellent hand-drawn storybook visuals have aged remarkably well. The story is full of Japanese RPG cliches, but it's still engaging, particularly its stark depiction of war (based on World War II).
The game plays pretty well, and the transition from turn-based to real-time is as smooth as it could be. The unique hybrid nature introduces a few wrinkles that take a while to get used to, like needing to hurry to end a turn because enemies will continue to fire. The biggest issue is that there are too many missions that don't play to the game's strengths. These missions rely more on trial and error, and they can lead to some frustration if you're not sure what you're supposed to be doing.
At its best, Valkyria Chronicles offers exciting and approachable squad-based tactics full of colorful characters with distinct personalities. If you're willing to overlook some difficulty spikes and the occasional frustrating mission, it's one of the best games of its kind on Steam.

If you're into unique and wonderfully executed artstyles you can probably ignore anything negative that I or anyone else has to say about this game. Its fantastic, colorful world is its biggest selling point and, in my eyes, 100% of the reason why anyone would enjoy or really want to play Owlboy. The art IS just that good, although not good enough for me to straight up recommend the game.
The overall gameplay is nothing that anyone hasn't seen before. The protagonist, Otus, can mostly only fly, spin, and lift items. Most of his offensive abilities come from carrying one of his friends around and using their varied attacks. A teleportation mechanic is used to solve certain door-and-button puzzles. Some tiles harm you, and different enemies require different attacks to defeat. Standard fare.
On the more negative it's fairly easy to get lost in the game (no map feature that I could see, either), and I could *easily* see someone getting desperately lost if they were away from the game for a time and didn't remember where they were supposed to be heading. Simply "loading an earlier checkpoint" or looking up a walkthrough isn't good enough in my eyes. A few of the bosses feel extremely weak, while others feel punishing until you figure out the method necessary to make them *super* weak. None of the gameplay *ever* feels especially compelling. This game lives and dies on its art style.
Story is a hodgepodge of tropes from other games and media thrown together with no real value, entertainment-wise or moralistically. It's acceptable, but you'll probably forget it five minutes after you finish the game. The ending is pretty nice, but not enough to save the general blandness. I found the set-piece moments (riding a lava worm, etc.) to be the highlights of the game.
All things considered the highs in this game are pretty high, but they come too few and far between the lows-and-mediocres that the game throws to you at pretty much every turn. Not a BAD game, just a very mediocre one. I can't recommend it except to huge fans of the art.
Given the greatness of the art and the overall acceptableness of the gameplay I'd rate this game a 7.5/10

I have finished the game and unlocked all achievements. I can say without a doubt, this game has a lot to offer and will not disappoint most of 2D/pixel graphics enthusiasts such as myself. That being said, I have read a handful of the negative reviews and have come to realise that most issues other players have with the game are more personal than objective. The one I see show up most often is the combat system. In my opinion, the combat system here is very INNOVATIVE (this is not synonymous with GOOD, I think its a good and interesting one) and the boss fights prove to be unique and challenging at an ideal level, not button-mashing easy nor soul-crushing hard.
The second issue I also see show up a lot is people having issues with the story. I don't see much WRONG with it. It's a simple (SLIGHTLY cliché,
) and direct. I feel as if the power of the story though, lies with the characters, all of them being very unique, not just in appearance, but also in personality and detail, even their manner of speech, (for Odus, his facial expressions).
If you thoroughly enjoyed Shovel Knight and/or Hollow Knight, I highly recommend this title.

It's certainly a very pretty game, one of the nicest looking ones I've seen, but the gameplay doesn't live up to it at all. I'm six hours in and so far it's just been flying from Point A to Point B (and the flying isn't particularly interesting, just movement in eight directions), shooting at weak enemies (which only your first partner can really do practically), and solving very simple puzzles. Feels like they wanted to do a Zelda game but couldn't quite pull it off.
The story is kind of interesting, but I wouldn't say it's twenty dollars interesting at all, and every character feels flat. Your second partner, Alphonse, betrays the pirates he's been working with for some time for two people he's never met, for reasons that seemed shallow to me. His third scene has your first partner giving him a big motivational speech which felt like it should have come at the midpoint or end of the game, not his first appearance.
The game also seems to really like to drive in how Otis the protagonist fails a lot, starting with a tutorial where you literally are incapable of succeeding. But so far, all of the situations where he's supposed to be a bungler are ones he couldn't have done anything about. An example is the first dungeon, which is revealed to be a distraction by the pirates so they could move their ships past Otis' town freely.
Except that Otis was doing his job pursuing someone stealing from the town, and there was only one cannon available anyway; surely it couldn't have stopped an entire fleet? Shooting at them might have even gotten the town blown up by return fire. Obviously they wanted to make Otis feel like an underdog with stuff like this and him being mute, but it just made me dislike the story for bagging on him unfairly.
I probably would have just stopped playing the game ordinarily, but it's a pretty high profile indie game at this point and the screenshots and positive review ratio might be a little deceiving, so hopefully this helps someone.

One of the best games I've played in a while.
Really good music and sound design, combined with some mindblowing sprite-work and background artwork, all in a pixelart aesthetic. The gameplay is classic metroid/castlevania/LoZ style. New gameplay mechanics are introduced in a satisfying way and get more complex as you progress, eventually you gain new companions that allow you to traverse obstacles that you could see very early on, which I think is really satisfying (see blocked path, gain new power, remember locked path that requires said power, proceed through the once blocked path). It's mostly linear with a few optional areas for collecting buccaneer coins that you spend on upgrades. However because of the metroidvania design the linearity is not usually bothersome, since you can see branching paths, just many of those paths are blocked off until you get the required companion, for narrative reasons.
What really amazes me is that essentially each aspect of the game is made by one person, Simon Stafsnes Andersen apparently did all of the visual artwork as well as part of the programming and general design, Jonathan Geer composed the soundtrack and most of the SFX, and Adrian Bauer did most of the level design (not to belittle the rest of the contributors, these are the main ones).
And by being such a small scale production, it maintains a very coherent artistic vision, something that is rarely seen in games.
Huge respect to the creators that made this game, Hope they get/have gotten some proper recognition for it.

A mute owl, tutored and trained by an abusive mentor, tasked with helping safekeep a little village floating in the sky. Owlboy starts off by tugging at the players heartstrings, trying, perhaps a bit heavy-handedly, to make you care for our little protagonist: Otus. For some, that heavy handedness may harm the story of this game quite a bit, but what the game blunders in one area, it makes up for in others.
Owlboy is chock-full of immensely beautiful, finely detailed and lovingly animated pixel art. Everything, blades of grass, floating rocks, boxes, chests, houses, enemies, NPC's and especially the protagonist, Otus, are all so vividly animated and perfectly characterized that I cannot help but fall in love with this game.
To boost the game even further, the music is excellent, flowing tunes and calm themes swelling up into powerful symphonies as you explore your environments, form friendships with some of the NPC's and work your way towards proving your worth and saving your home.
As a game, however, Owlboy ends up stumbling somewhat. A platformer where the very starting point is that you can fly, means there is fairly little in the way of movement-based exploration and the game is forced to use some fairly clumsy gates to keep your progress in check early on. The game is also quite linear and, while it allows you to go back and indulge in some collect-a-thong fun (if that's your thing), it didn't really draw me in enough to justify the repetition, especially in some of the more challenging areas.
Still, despite some slight game-design shortfalls and a story told with some awkward and heavy-handed themes, Owlboy is an endearing adventure with plenty of charm, style and good-natured fun to be enjoyed, with the early parts of the game especially providing for some fun little puzzles and challenges to enjoy.

Polaris Sector is a very good game and I would recommend it to any 4X space strategy fan. What makes this game interesting is how it manages your empire without a lot of work and lets you focus on whatever part of gameplay you enjoy. The ship building is fun, the science research is interesting, and the exploration and expansion system makes you feel like you are playing a game in space, where planets are very far apart.
Some people don't like new ideas, or changing up what they are "use too" in a 4X game, Polaris mixes up a lot of the standard ideas and adds in new and updated systems that makes it stand out from the crowd. This game is for a new generation of 4X space players, with new ideas, new ways of doing things, and a good interface that allows you to focus on the fun and let the game manage the stuff you don't want to mess with. Highly recommend this to any space explorer out there interested in playing something new and interesting.

Excellent game. Polaris Sector really stands out from the current crop of 4X games through a combination of tight balance and strong AI, leading to a genuinely challenging and interesting experience. Casual players may be a little turned off by the difficulty and non-flashy graphics, but any serious fan of 4X or Grand Strategy games really ought to have this game on their shelf.
Pros:
* Innovative and well-balanced mechanics
* Excellent strategic AI that will slaughter you on your first couple of playthroughs
* Automation done right - you can trust the governor AI to do a good job, but can always intervene and overrule it
* Spying in particular is a very cool and original concept
Cons:
* Combat AI fairly average
* Not always intuitive
* Graphics are OK, but not top-notch - if you really think that's important in a game where you're staring at a map for 99% of your time
* difficulty may be intimidating for non-hardcore players

Another dud.  I just may be done buying in this genre because "space" seems to be a marketing buzzword that substitutes for polish or balance.
The AI is so heavily cheated that you'll either stomp it or your empire will be a hopeless case.  There is no balance at all, and what I'm calling the "AI" really consists of a function that spams stuff at you.
The interface is confusing.  The parts you could probably stand to be reminded of show up on your first playthrough and never again, but you're reminded of the easy stuff every playthrough.  It's overly complicated and fiddly, time has almost no sense of meaning at all, and trying to plan your technological development alongside your production means you'll always be upgrading fleets that you never get to field, and the AI's will always be better.
In battle, sometimes your ships don't attack at all.  You have to use autoresolve to stand a chance because it's that bugged.  You'll command your ships to attack, or even tell them to act on their own and tell them to attack, and they'll just kind of fly near the enemy and do nothing, even when they're fully mounted with weapons that have no ammunition requirement (ie, missiles need ammo; lasers don't).
Your corvettes are made of tissue paper, but from the very first pirate fleet you encounter, enemy corvettes are made of the strongest stuff imaginable, with the best weapons.  Or, so it seems.  No matter how you outfit your ships, the pirate corvettes tear through them like nothing.
The settings menu for the launcher is so bugged on 4k screens that it manages to crash twice at the same time, unless you disable the Steam overlay.  Yeah, that should be impossible, so this one actually has cutting edge, ground-breaking levels of failure.  If you don't disable high DPI, the settings menu for the launcher will only appear offscreen.  If you have a modern system, you'll need to edit the settings CFG manually, which isn't really pleasant because it's a jumbled mess.
Research is divided into theoretical and applied sciences, which is nice.  Sadly, the interface is so badly designed with such an obvious lack of thought or effort that it's next to impossible to plan your research.  It's as if the developers forgot that players don't know the source code. Ship modules in the tech tree don't show their stats, so even when you manage to find them, you can't tell what you should be pursuing first.
Settings for the galaxy are hard-coded such that you don't actually have options beyond the space between your primary planets ("Earth-like," and oceanic, typically).  Want a big galaxy, where the distance between empires is enormous, as if space is big?  Too bad.  If you lower the number of opponents, the maximum number of stars you can set it to is lowered as well.  On top of that, the AI cheats so heavily that while your empire is wasting decades or centuries building and dispatching fuel ships, the AI just kind of teleports around the map free of cost.
The colony management system violates its own rules sometimes, blocking you from building things like factories on Earth-like planets that have nothing else built on them, even if you have the population to build them.  This bug happens if you initially set the planet to "agricultural" and let the AI fill it up with farms.  Even if you destroy every building on the planet except the base colony building, the game will never let you construct another building there.
The AI is the most war-loving I've ever seen.  You'll meet them, and unless the RNG decides they're already at war with each other, you will usually very soon after have them demand half your resources and declare war on you when you don't provide them.  The developers claim that only happens on "hard" mode, but I've seen in repeated games that it happens on "normal" difficulty.  They ignored my posting that.  These developers don't even know their own game, which suggests that most of the development was outsourced to the lowest bidder.
You can't defeat enemy fleets because retreat can't be stopped.  In the rare case when you do manage to do well (which involves zerging very small fleets), there will always be at least one remaining enemy ship that you have to chase all over the map, will never be able to kill, and if you don't keep chasing it then it will go destroy your orbital infrastructure.  So, battles ultimately can't be won at all.  The appearance of an enemy means you've already lost, either thanks to the massive buffs and cheats the AI has, or because the game will never permit you to destroy all their ships anyway.
The forums are filled with developers for the game outright lying about the mechanics and rules of the game while demonstrating in regard to bugs that they don't actually know how their own code works.  It seems like most of the developers' work on this game involves using sockpuppets to convince players who complain that they're basically hallucinating and what they see happen in the game doesn't happen.  Rather than develop a game, they try to use the forum to con the would-be buyer into thinking it's already developed.
And this, you get for $40.
So, here's what's happening with this genre.  Developers slap "space", "4E", and "Grand Strategy" labels on it, release unpolished, unbalanced, lazily thrown together garbage, hire a PR firm to post good reviews, sockpuppet their forums to shout down anyone who has problems with it or (if they go the polite route) simply lie about the game, and by the time you know you've bought yet another dud, it's too late for a refund because the games are designed to take a long time to find out whether they're ultimately playable, with nothing but timesinks.
This genre is dead.  Steam killed it.  I just wish I could get back all the money I've spent trying to find one of these that's actually fun without it ending up just a blatant clone of the bare minimum design first created twenty years ago.  In all honesty, it seems that if you see "Space" together with "4E" and/or "Grand Strategy" tags on Steam, you might as well withdraw your money from the bank and light it on fire because you'll get more for your buck that way.
I don't know why I'm bothering to post this when the devs, the PR firm they hired, and a few fanbois and friends are just going to rate it down.  Hey, if you can make a small set of pixel art or some low poly spaceships, you have a month to learn a little about Unity, and you have a few friends willing to help with fake reviews, then now you know how to con nearly free money through Steam.   And because nobody knows for sure if they've been scammed until it's too late for a refund, you won't have to worry about anyone catching you.

Like most adults who work for a living, I have very hard limits on what I am willing to spend on particular items. Take a bottle of wine, for example: I've found that there is no difference between a ten dollar bottle of wine and a thirty dollar bottle of wine. Anybody that tells you otherwise is trying to impress you. With wine, you get very little return on your investment past the 15-20 dollar price point. There's a reason that many sommeliers refuse to do blind tastings, and that reason being that sommeliers have all agreed to subscribe to the same groupthink that says X vintage and Y grapes grown in Z reason are superior, and none of this information would be available to them if they were prevented from looking at the label on the bottle. Have you ever met anyone who's a certified "master sommelier"? They're truly insufferable people. The next time you meet one ask them a question about wine - any question, it doesn't matter how dumb, will send them into a desperate panic while they fumble to form an opinion, any opinion, about the matter in question. It doesn't matter what their answer is becuase they will be certain to couch it in arcane wine terms like "tannins" and "finish" and other completely subjective abstract concepts that you won't understand.
Desktop Dungeons is like an overpriced bottle of wine. Sure, the label is fancy and the guy trying to sell it to you is telling you about how great it is, using words like "replayability" and other nonsense, but as soon as you taste it you realize "hey, this tastes just like a $5 iphone game?"
Just look at the screenshots. There's a reason that they only expect you to play this in ten minute bursts. $15 is just way, way, too much.

This is a "Wait-for-Sale" game, as much as I hate to say it. But I say that because by the time it goes on sale, it should have more content and most of the bugs out of the system. But if you've been waiting for Dungeon Keeper 3, look no further than this.
At the time of review, I had completed the campaign and dipped a little into the skirmish mode. As far as tech problems, I've only had two of note and both happened on level 10. I had the game freeze for 10 minutes when I did a ritual that revealed the enemy dungeon. And I tried to reload a save for it and it didn't load. Other than that the only other tech problems I've had is really nothing that cannot be solved with graphic adjustments in the options menu. If you're experiencing game breaking bugs, you might want to consider the age of your hardware and upgrade the parts that are over five-years old.
Despite the bugs and the lack of content in the skirmish, I've had a fantastic time with this game. The campaign, while a glorified tutorial, is quite good whether you're an old player or new to this type of game. I played Dungeon Keeper 2 for comparison and my verdict is that it is pretty much DK 2 with the polish that didn't exist in 1999 and with addtions that add to overall experience rather than detract. I found the use of Potions and Rituals to be an interesting addtion to the formula. And you'll come to love the Narrator, who is from the original game, as the way that he delivers his dialouge is such a joy to listen to. I would put him the Hall of Fame where they reconigze voice talents like the narrators from "Stanley Parable" and "Basition".
This game definately is going to be worth having but it's going to happen several patches down the line. To their credit, they are coming out with patches at a quick rate but this game definately could've used another month in Early Access to polish up their assests. Heck, you can still see the Unity engine titles when you hover over units. I don't know whether it was money and/or the bad reputation Early Access has gotten the past year that prompted them to release it in this state, but it thankfully doesn't detract from the overall game experience and the game is backed by a good studio. We haven't really gotten a good successor to Dungeon Keeper and this is by far a worthy successor to the concept.

Until I realized it wasn't fun - and it hadn't been since about the first half hour.  Oh... have I mentioned no saves, and some of the stupidest places for checkpoints I've ever seen?  Beyond awful placement.  Be prepared to redo ages of fighting, hope you enjoy that - cause it will happen - all the time.  Don't care if it can be hacked to be saved, that just means you can put a bandaid on their god-awful game design.  Yeah, great.
3.  Seriously, this is just plain stacking unfair game advantage on you to simulate difficulty.  Difficulty is not giving the player junk tools and enemies that make the player feel about as effective as a toddler with a pellet gun.  Guns don't hit worth a darn, enemies will soak vast amounts of your ammo store barring specific guns.  This game is a good idea that either they got lazy on or just couldn't test with non-"I am leetzor I WILL PUT UP WITH ANY NONSENSE TO PROVE HOW BIG MY DIGITAL REPRODUCTIVE ORGANS ARE RRARR!" people.
4.  Before the usual "Git gud scrub" crowd starts in, games I do like and handle just fine are things like Serious Sam.  I tend to play my shooters on hard - and I've been playing this kind of thing since Doom.  But back in those days we had hitscan because it was all the tech could handle, and monsters and placement were carefully balanced to account for this.  In this case... not even close.  Not even a handwaved attempt at getting close.  Just "We're gonna overwhelm you with stuff everywhere that is stronger than anything you could ever manage, roflcopterbbq. "   This is a failed attempt at reproducing oldschool unless you want oldschool complete with all the bad elements the tech difference required added to a complete lack of care in level design beyond "Swarm them with stuff.  No, 10X the stuff with 50X the hitpoints.  That'll teach 'em!"
5.  Unfortunately, the problems with this game remind unpleasantly of Fear 3 - another shooter I refunded pretty quickly for many of the same reasons.  Hitscan, unfair numbers and placements, bulletsoaking enemies beyond the point of laughability even, and a near complete lack of level design - replaced with sheer overpowered enemies and numbers of mobs well beyond any sense of fun.  Sorry about the length of this, but the level of disappointment here was vast - this coulda been interesting.  Instead, once you get past the shiny at the start you've pretty much got a travesty.  This just digs up oldschool's corpse, sticks a party hat on it, and poses it for some Weekend At Bernie's style action.

- occasional glitches that apparently affect the PC version specifically. was relatively minor for me.
- some frustrating mission design. might not have been so bad if I remembered to use certain abilities that I forgot I had.
- similar to the last point, tanks seem problematic. especially your main tank, supposedly your greatest asset; it's actually a forced liability. 90% of the time you lose will be because your tank dies; it's just a giant clumsy target that takes like three hits, is often placed intentionally in vulnerable positions, and/or enemies will spawn behind it without warning, and it's always instant game over if you lose it. some missions will have enemies that can 3 shot your tank infinitely spawning, and you also can't heal it. artificial difficulty like that really irritates me, but while it's a little annoying, it's not as bad as it could be and it's not game breaking by any means. again, pretty much everything else about the game is extremely good.

First of i'll just say this is one of my favorite games to come out this year. Its atmosphere is incredible, the cyberbunk aesthetic combined with the soundtrack make the game very immersive and very replayable. Gameplay is fast and well balanced at most times.
Pros
-Sound track is excellent, it both fits and enhances the gameplay while also being great to listen to on its own.
-The gameplay is fast paced fun and, at higher difficulties, very rewarding. The wide range of waepons make it so combat never becomes stale (mele is particularly cool)
-The characters, while not incredibly deep, are still very interesting and entertaining. Her's taunting apon failure and praise apon success is....pleasant.
-The abilities are fun, they foster a sense that you have tons of options to defeat each enemy and the skill tree is well constructed to be easy to understand
-The enemy designs are all very unique, each area comes with new and interesting foes. I particularly liked the intro cards when encountering a boss or a  new enemy type.
-The environments are linear. Its not the worst thing, a few more side areas wouldve been nice but its not supposed to be an open world game or anythign like that.
-Insert other things I love about the game but cant think of
Cons
-Its short. 6-8 hours is enough to finish the storyline. It fits the deffinition of "short and sweet", i would have loved to see it hit more around the 15 hour mark but for $20 its just fine
-Playing through the game there are points where the difficulty spikes like crazy unexpectedly. Its beatable but very jarring when you go from kicking♥♥♥♥♥ezpz to dying 30 times in one boss. and these spikes appear pretty randomly. For example the final fight took very little effort on normal but the boss in the first level is much more difficult (this happens once or twice in the whole game)
All in all I loved it and anyone who likes cyberbunk aesthetic, games with great soundtracks and perhaps enjoyed Hotline Miami will too.

My parents didn't like the idea of first-person shooters because they didn't like the violence and gore. However, they had no problem with me sending hundreds if not thousands of unnamed men (and sometimes women) to brutal deaths at the hands of better armed and armoured foes. This was the wonder of Age of Empires II.
Later I graduated to Rome: Total War and Knights of Honor, both excellent RTS games where you take a more holistic look at the world and it was with these games that the challenge of real-time combat was coupled with the slower, methodical empire-building and administration side of gameplay. In the search for that AoE type of game, I found the marvel that is Stronghold 2, another excellent game that is very much in the spirit of classic Age of Empires.
Then I discovered CK2 and oh boy, I don't regret it for a second. I can't quite remember what led me to buy it, I think it was during a steam sale. I had watched/read a let's play about a year before, but at the time I bought it I don't think I had quite twigged that this was the same game that had looked like such amazing fun on YouTube.
So CK2. If you enjoy starting from humble origins to slowly climb the greasy pole to the top, before realising that you're actually terrified of heights so that you slip and fall to the bottom, breaking both your legs and crushing any hope of your dynasty holding any true power ever again, then this is the game for you. Just remember that the fun is in losing. It may sound perverse but it's true, becoming the Emperor of Britain, France, Spain and the Rest of Europe is do-able, but it kicks the fun out of the game damned quickly. It's fun conquering all that territory, but once you have it, things get dull really fast. Fortunately, by the time you've just conquered an empire to rival Byzantium who should turn up but Genghis Khan and his merry men! Which really mixes things up a bit.
Unfortunately, unless you buy the Sunset Invasion DLC (which I highly recommend), then once you've beaten the mongols, it quickly turns into the same monotonous slog.
So my suggestion is this: Buy the game. Buy the DLC, all of it (make sure you do it during a Steam sale or you'll be going without food for a month or so). Then build your massive empire (which will take a while because the game is brutally difficult to get your head around for the first twenty hours or so), then make sure you have a massive family with lots of unlanded sons and give the most ambitious ones the bulk of your kingdom titles. Congratulations! When you die, your throne shall pass to your eldest son/daughter and a bunch of really powerful vassals, with super-strong claims to the throne will be all around you. This is when the true fun begins.
As a wonderful TV character once said: "You know what takes real strength? Holding it all together when the stakes are this high!" Enjoy!
P.S. Like I said above, the game is brutal to start with, but stick with it. The more you lose, the more you learn and the better you will do next time. It may take 20-30 hours of playing before you feel really confident, but once you do you will have hundreds if not thousands of hours of fun with it.
P.P.S. And the fun doesn't have to end in 14-whatever-it-is! Get EU4 and the EU4 save converter, and you can port your CK2 save over into EU4, where there waits another 400(ish) years of history to live through. But that's a review for a different day.
P.P.P.S. Why are you still reading this? Buy the damned game already!

A lot of people have been giving this game negative reviews, and I can understand why. However, to me this game isn't necessarily a "game" in the traditional sense. Owlboy presents to you a heart-warming and sometimes tear-jerking narrative full of vibrant settings, masterfully crafted characters, and breathtaking visuals and music. The characters feel like real, personal people, that actually have feelings and opinions, and change through the course of the game. Talking to them doesn't feel like a chore, it feels like a real conversation, granted Otus (the protagonist) can't speak, so it's a little one sided. Here's the only problem with the game. The controls can feel a bit clunky at times and sometimes, in order to complete some levels, backtracking. However the characters will distract from the gameplay issues. The game gives you characters that truly react to the world around them, and Owlboy does an outstanding job of presenting a story amazing enough to make you keep playing for hours and hours. The game could be great if the core - the combat system - didnt suck so hard.
It took me some time to realize but after that I came to understand that.
At first I was fine but in higher levels you will encounter very skilled players that exploit the system in a way I think it wasnt meant to be used.
The key component that destroys the game is the fllowing:
Arm and torso movement is directly linked to the mouse so if you move your moue in certain ways you can make an attack out of moves that werent supposed to be attacks.
I will give an example:
While wielding a long 2h Sword your character will reach back with the weapon over your shoulder to make a powerfull swing to the front. So the arm and sword movement is: reachback for the swind -> swing to the front.
Clever movement allows you to damage the enemy behind you if you look up while reaching back with your sword. That is since your torso bends backwards while looking up and the tip of your sword is at that point directly behind you. That is possible since the torso movement is liked to te mouse.
Very good players attacking you will use that to turn away from you and look up while reaching back with their sword and you will get damaged by their sword. The second they swing out they look down again and spin to you and damage you again.
This looks utterly stupid and there are many different ways to exploit the mouse system in that way.
(For example you can turn while making a leaping attack and if you are good, you leap past the enemy to swing in his side or back while he still looks the direction where you leaped from)
This leads to enemies spining and flailing with their arms and torsos while the player brandishes with his mouse.
This not only makes no sense but also looks extremely stupid and steals all sense of fighting atmosphere.
For me it destroys the combat system since I am not willing to play in that moronic way and make myself look like a total idiot while actually beeing very efficient and dangerous.

This game has not aged well and I wouldn't recommend it for a serious RTS fan. I like that the maps are huge and that you have unlimited construction resources (though limits to how quickly you can collect them), but in many other ways Supreme Commander fails. For starters, Supreme Commander is missing basic audio cues like telling you when you are low on resources or that some of your units are under attack. There's a setting that is supposed to enable a resource warning, but it doesn't work, so I found myself frequently running out of energy or mass without realizing it.
There are three factions, but with very minor differences they mostly have the same tech trees and units, so there isn't enough variety between factions. Unit balance is fairly broken - many of the units are not worth using, either because they take too long to build or because they are so weak that all they accomplish is wasting slots in your unit cap. Some units immediately stand out as too good - gunships (attack helicopters) are by far the best unit for wrecking bases, and a fleet of cheap level-1 submarines will easily defeat any fleet composed of level 2 and 3 surface vessels.
There are a variety of pointless strategic options. You can build strategic submarines with the potential to launch nukes, but it takes something like
for a submarine to build a nuke - even if you manage to hide your sub for 4 hours, the game is going to be over long before those nukes are ready. You can eventually launch nukes from your base, but the enemy will always shoot them down, so this is also pointless. 95% of bombers will be shot down before they reach their target, so bombers are pointless as well.
Gameplay emphasis is very much on base-building and broad strategy rather than unit tactics. Combat boils down to sending large clumps of units into the enemy to do their own thing; combat is too chaotic and units die too quickly to try to issue orders to individual units once the bullets start flying.
The AI is dumb to nonexistant. In campaign missions, the "AI" follows 100% scripted behaviors and is unable to adapt to your behavior. In some campaign missions, the enemy doesn't even build new units, and since you never run out of resources you will automatically win by attrition. The only thing that makes the campaign missions difficult is cheap shots - most missions have 3 - 5 objectives, and completing an objective often reveals some immediate new threat that you could not possibly have been prepared for without already having played the mission. So campaign boils down to save-scumming before you complete each objective so that the game can't kill you unfairly.
In skirmishes, where the AI can't be 100% scripted, they only build land units. That's right, they'll construct shipyards and air factories but never use them. Once they have upgraded enough to build experimental units, they even stop building land units. There are many levels of Skirmish AI, but they fall into two categories: the ones that play fairly are too dumb to be worth playing against, while the harder diffulties simply cheat and are impossible to defeat.

For those who loved Dungeon Keeper, this game is for you. There are a few bugs to be worked out... and I believe the game probably should have stayed in Beta for a few months longer to work them out. It's small things really, information about units/tiles which isn't fully there, no capability for more than 2+ opponents in multiplayer/skirmish and the odd random crash due to things I'm not even sure of. These however are being worked on by the Dev's from what I can read.
But the game itself is still pretty good regardless of all that I've mentioned. A plethora of minions, the voice over/game tutor with attitude, the spells and good use of the Unity engine presents the game in a very graphically pleasing way. It's a very worthy spiritual successor to Dungeon Keeper that's for sure... and if like myself you still have a bad taste in your mouth from EA's attempt to milk money from the name, this should help wash it away.
I'd be lying though if I would call this a "complete game". As I said earlier, it probably could've done with staying in Beta a little while longer and I have a feeling you'll feel the same if you buy this game now. That being said I would still recommend it, it is very deserving of your money, but be prepared to ignore a few incomplete aspects of the game.

Really great game in so many ways. Fantastic story, characters, gameplay, unique game mechanics, almost everything about the game is just excellent. Reminds me of a ground based WingCommander game, except as a TBS with multiple units. (The commonality is being a part of a team/family of soldiers, fighting together, getting to know each other over the course of the game.)
There's only a couple of weakpoints, everything else is top-notch. The weakpoints are:
- occasional glitches that apparently affect the PC version specifically. was relatively minor for me.
- some frustrating mission design. might not have been so bad if I remembered to use certain abilities that I forgot I had.
- similar to the last point, tanks seem problematic. especially your main tank, supposedly your greatest asset; it's actually a forced liability. 90% of the time you lose will be because your tank dies; it's just a giant clumsy target that takes like three hits, is often placed intentionally in vulnerable positions, and/or enemies will spawn behind it without warning, and it's always instant game over if you lose it. some missions will have enemies that can 3 shot your tank infinitely spawning, and you also can't heal it. artificial difficulty like that really irritates me, but while it's a little annoying, it's not as bad as it could be and it's not game breaking by any means. (the AI doesn't actually capitalize on your vulnerabilities as much as it could; otherwise the game would be impossible. so most of the time you're just worried that they will destroy your tank, because they could if they wanted to, but they will often not take the opportunity.)
again, pretty much everything else about the game is extremely good.

Turn pirates off unless you like swarms of ships that kill all your early game tech based ships in seconds and appear at random one system out from your settled worlds. Seriously I had not even researched the first few weapons techs and my home world was attacked by a fleet of 15 pirate ships with 90 fighters.
When they say they don’t use a tech tree, they mean they use a tech tree that doesn’t look like a tech tree. Ok, yes it’s not the old standard of basic laser> ok laser> good laser> OMGWTFBBQ laser. Instead they fill the list with numerous meaningless middleman techs that are prerequisites for several other useful techs. The path you take to get the a better laser may also result in you getting some other tech you didn’t expect but its convoluted enough that the end result for gameplay is you ignore the various sliders and simply tell the system to auto prioritize the tech you want leading you right back to the old standard of basic laser> ok laser> good laser> OMGWTFBBQ laser.
There are a few new ideas in the ship design function but I didn’t get far enough into the game to see if they are well executed.  One thing I did not see was any way to easily update ships from one design to another. Unless there are better ways with better techs in the later game it looks like you have to send each ship to a system with a ship yard and tell each hull class to upgrade. That will get time consuming if you have a huge empire with hundreds of ships.
Overall the game feels like it could use a lot more time in the oven.

I've written two reviews, one bad over the bugs and glitches, after a few days when they fixed many bugs I deleted that and wrote a good one. I removed them both for this one.
I am completely and utterly enraged by how the story develops and ends and even if there will be a DLC to twist the plot somehow, this is utterly inexcusable.
This of course is accompanied by my struggle (yes, struggle) against the game-breaking bugs, memory leaks, crashes, freezes, save-corruption and many others.
SPOILER ALERT SPOILER ALERT SPOILER ALERT SPOILER ALERT SPOILER ALERT
Right, so by mission 10 or 11 you are starting to realize that the disembodied voice is not your helper, but rather your master, as opposed to being a tyrant, you're just an executive clerk doing whatever your strong and powerful masturr is telling you to do.
This is reflected by the fact he repeatedly tells jokes "If your minions ask for your superior, tell them I'm taking a nap.", by the fact he apparently "controls the aether" hence controls you, by Mira saying you're his tool and by him calling you "My Underlord", as if a pawn of his. And, by mission 13's outro, which will be elaborated further next. Unlike the intro video sequence where you might mistake to think he found your presence and revived it, he is in fact your master.
Alright, that is a bit crappy - but not story-breaking for me.
Oh, but then comes mission 13. The final mission. You besiege and break through the last hero compound in order to butcher the emperor himself. Pretty neat mission, 3-4 optional objectives - a bit of a droll but wrapping things up knowing the world is pretty much doomed by your hand and will be ripe for the taking by you makes it worthwhile.
You breach the inner chamber, kill off the emperor's guards and the emperor, but then MAJIQ! his corpse disappears and then proceeding sequence loads you into your home realm, your main core, where the wretched scum just pops out of nowhere while that ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Mendechaus (w/e his name) says how he found a new pawn and how you're no longer of use to him and that sort of generic crap, then you die.
tl;dr Game over.
No conquest, no "cliffhanger" for an upcoming campaign in the overworld, no outro depicting how terror and misery have struck the goodlies. Not even a chance to fight. Just sit there and watch how the pompous moron just kills you and tyvm for playing. How your campaign ends with a defeaning silence of helplessness. That's the antithesis of being a Dungeon Keeper/Underlord.
I've fought against game-breaking bugs, I've triumphed terribly long loading-screens and save-destroying bugs (wall tiles changing nonstop causing FPS to drop to 5 on a mission vs 3 enemy Underlords)... This is the last straw. This game has the mechanics of its spiritual father, Dungeon Keeper, but not the essence. Maybe multiplayer fans will rejoice in this, but in that case, GL waiting a couple of months until that function will be released properly.
I've uninstalled this game and hopefully this review will be noticed so other people won't feel cheated like I do.

Where do I even begin with a game like this? There’s so much to talk about in all of the things that work together to make this game just absolutely fantastic. Well to start off i’ll say that this game is one of the few games I actually felt so invested in that I wanted to max it out to 100% completion(and I did with lots of grinding and hours of pain). Now here’s the rest of what I believe makes Valkyria Chronicles just an absolute masterpiece.
+Story: You play as Welkin Gunther ,the leader of Squad 7, in the second World War that’ll determine the future of the fictional land of Gallia. The stakes are already set quite high as your Squad is the determining factor of whether or not your home will be a free, independent nation or fall under Imperial control. Now early in the game is the part where your squad kicks tons of♥♥♥♥♥and takes names as the up and coming tactical genius ,Welkin Gunther, does absolutely crazy things to take back the land currently under Imperial control and everybody has a good time.However, the real strength comes from the major development of
and the effects of it ripple throughout the rest of the game as all characters now realize that yes this is war and with it comes sacrifice. This in turn separates Valkyria Chronicles from standard games where the protagonists can just do whatever the ♥♥♥♥ they want without much getting in their way and makes the game’s story all the more  impactful.
+Soundtrack: Wonderful, whether you’re fighting an army that massively outnumbers the rag tag militia under your control or you need to slow things down and have a touching moment between squad members the soundtrack always fits the mood and helps investment in the overall story.
+Characters: All the soldiers under your command have their own diary entries to explain  why they have a certain quirk and why they wanted to join the war as well as the things they do with their lives after the war is over. Now for your main cast they have certain special missions you can unlock to help you understand their motivations and have insight into their pasts that make them act the way they are now. Overall, these features help overall investment into the game as you want them all to succeed and have their dreams come true and it makes it all the more crushing when I explain to you what can stop that.
+Gameplay: First and foremost this game is a mix between tactical turn based Rpg and third-person cover based shooter. The formula works relatively well as your troops level up they’ll be able to aim much better than when they first start out and the game does a good job at explaining the mechanics in the beginning. Also, it helps give you the commander feeling as you’ll want to position your troops so they can shoot at moving troops when your turn is up and vice-versa. To help with the tactical Rpg sense you can also issue orders such as artillery strikes or heal up to assist your squad in combat. Now here’s the most important part, this game does have permadeath for your squad (this is war remember!). However, it’s a lot more lenient than say a game like X-com, you’ll have about 3 turns to rescue a squadmate after they fall in combat and they’ll be safely evacuated but if you’re unsuccessful they will die and will no longer be usable for the rest of the playthrough. This helps build tension as your actions will impact who will be able to survive this war. The gameplay provides a good balance between a little fun run and gun with a slow paced tactical positioning for more strategy oriented players.
+Artstyle: You’ll notice that the character designs are very anime like but it doesn’t distract too much from the main game and it helps blend with the color palette of the background environments when you’re fighting on the battlefield. Pretty pleasing to the eye and helps them have a defining design for gameplay clarity purposes.
-Cover System: While there are other objects that can provide cover ,such as boxes, you can only duck and cover behind sandbags which in certain missions can be really detrimental to your objective as the Imperials will shoot you down very quickly if you can’t reach cover.
-Challenge Missions: Now if you aim for 100% completion like I did this can be absolute headache as the missions are entirely based on how many turns you can complete the mission as opposed to other factors such as kills or minimal loss of squad members. This means that if you want an A-Rank on these special missions it’s entirely dependent on how well Alicia’s skills will activate making the missions less about being a tactical genius and more about how lucky you are with RNG.
-Graveyard: The graveyard is a bit lacking because if a squad member does die instead of actually being able to examine their grave to pay respects you can only talk to an old man for more orders making it less immersive overall.
There’s so much more i’d like to write about but the review is getting pretty long now so to sum it up the game is a solid 9/10. If you're a fan of tactical rpgs rich in story then this is a game that must be picked up.

So far, it's an enjoyable game, started from the very beginning on Hard mode and actually have had a pretty decently easy time until the third boss or so, and then the sudden difficulty spike really killed my enjoyment after the 50th or so time of trying to beat him. It has great visuals, but the controls are poor and not currently rebindable. At least from what i could tell, it always appeared as though my character would always traverse diagonally even when i'm just pressing up. The off-centeredness of the movement controls seem to be contributing a lot more to the games difficulty than the enemies/levels themselves. Getting spammed with firebombs while also dodging buzzsaws and having to manage your weapons on that third boss was a little more tedious and unfun than i wanted it to be. It felt like i was losing moreso at the fault of the game than my inability as a player. What annoys me most I suppose is that it really doesn't do a good job of telling you when you're taking damage, and with everything moving so fast it's hard to bother glancing up at the top left to check your health. All that complaining aside, i do actually think it's a really solid game, but one that needs some adjustment to be a really great twin stick shooter.
The environments are cool, the enemy designs and art direction in general is phenomenal, and the music helps make the combat scenarios feel tense. I'm not that far in but so far the story is pretty generic, but for this type of game I think that's okay. All in all, it's currently a pretty flawed, but fun game. Will more than likely update my review when later patches arrive. I'd say for the time being, wait on it. Given the love that was put into this game I doubt the devs would leave things broken. 6.5/10

As far as First Person Shooters go, Hard Reset is really quite generic in flavor. You traverse very linear levels and use your two guns to kill several varieties of homicidal robot. Despite this, something about it keeps charming me back for more. That "something" is more likely the difficulty. Hard Reset is exceedingly difficult, and getting through any given fight without taking a death carries a certain amount of satisfaction.
The game could be described as "old school" style. Your health doesn't regenerate, requiring you to find healing pickups. The action is fast-paced and aggressive, favoring a DOOM-like method of remaining constantly mobile as you fight. Generally speaking you travel from fight to fight, with a few smaller fights in between the larger ones. However, unlike many shooters of this type, success is not tethered to reflexes because frankly, the player character has no reflexes. Although his movement speed seems fast, he is easily outran by most enemies. Sprinting increases speed by 25% at best and lasts for about 3 seconds, making it largely useless. Jumping is poor and used almost exclusively for getting over scripted obstacles. Instead the game favors strategy and planning, often requiring at least one death in the larger battles to get an idea of the better method of handling things, where to take the fight, what order to kill enemies, ideal weapons to use, and so forth. This is why it's so satisfying to survive a battle on the virgin attempt. The game seems to know this, as there's an achievement for surviving any one level other than the first without dying. Curiously, the player cannot crouch. This wouldn't be a big deal except for the large number of instances where you're told to find a way to get past an obstacle when you can plainly see that it'd be possible if your character would just bend down, slightly. It happens so frequently that at times it almost seems like the game is making fun of its own mechanics.
Technically you only carry two weapons throughout the game, a more standard type and an electronic type, but each one can be upgraded in a variety of ways to give it very different functionalities. By default your regular gun is something of an assault rifle and your electronic gun is a close approximation of DOOM's plasma rifle, but as you add more bells and whistles to each gun, you'll find yourself with weapons such as a shotgun, rocket launcher, tesla cannon, railgun, and more. The electronic weapons are usually the more useful of the two types, but every weapon has its pros and cons. several weapons include a secondary fire which stuns and/or immobilizes foes which is a must if you hope to be successful, as the machines tend to be much faster and more maneuverable than the player.
The level design is fairly good and atmospheric, especially if you're a fan of cyberpunk themes. I'm not, but it's still a pretty good environment, many of the stages taking on a seedy inner-city feel loaded with cheap advertisements and littering. The game includes secrets but often times, these "secrets" are nothing more than money-items hidden behind a large object. There are several instances where an item will be counted as a secret and an item hidden in an almost identical way will not be. Despite the secrets, the level layouts are very linear and don't lend themselves to much exploration. Most of the time you're heading from point A to point B, maybe stopping to check out a few nooks and crannies on the way.
The story is told between levels through animated comic book-style artwork with not-so-great voice acting and swearing that almost seems forced. The story itself is, frankly, almost incomprehensible. In fact it is this seemingly impossible blend of confusingly complicated and yet entirely uncompelling. You know really know what's going on and yet, you don't really care to know. The ending creates more questions and answers and seems like it might have been meant to set up for a sequel that is probably never coming. Perhaps the story was poorly translated, but whatever the reason, it's arguably the game's weakest point and can almost entirely be ignored with little ill effect on the gameplay.
But all the same, despite the game's very middle-of-the-road quality, I found myself repeatedly coming back to it in order to try and step up to the challenge. For that reason I would recommend the game to anybody looking for a fast and simple shooter with a steep challenge, though I might suggest getting it on sale.

Absolutely excellent game! I only have a couple hours on it, but from playing it I love how the game handles.
You play through a deck of cards magically generated with cards you collect and cards the dealer holds. Each card has either a good or bad effect on you, and you explore these slowly elaborately growing dungeons to find the exit. You can go from talking to a merchant and equipping gear you own to fighting an army of bandits. The combat is very fluid, tight and easy to pick up. You are slowly put into the ringer and shown everything you need to know before the real challenges come out. Trust me, the difficulty picks up fast, but at least you can better equip yourself as you progress, because you unlock more useful encounters/equipment cards from beating the dealer at his own game.
