Dreadout is the kind of game that is a cheap fatel frame. Is cheap good? Well I will go over dreadout with a pro/con style and end with my final conclusion.
Pro:
The game has a pretty spooky atmospher. There were moments that the game put me on edge while i scan the room in every direction to find the ghost. That mixed with the pretty decent horror ambiant sounds creates a horrific mood that most big name games can not get.
Some of the enemies or bosses look creepy. Mainly the lady in the red dress, she spooked me the most when she appeared in the mirror with this demonic smile if the player looks left but inside the mirror she looked normal.
Con:
The game has no direction. When the player plays the game there needs to be some hand holding by the game helping the player alone the levels. That is not the case here, all the puzzles are vague and confusing to solve. This leads to the player fumbling around till they give up and look up a youtube tutorial.
The bosses are unfair and very cheap. The bosses like the sissors and the guy that can only be seen in the mirror was very cheap. They were very fast and spawned in random locations. Yes it is very scary but leads to many frustrating deaths and many bad checkpoints.
The checkpoint system is awful. When the player dies they spawn mere moments before their death. In the case of a boss fight near a moment when the boss is attacking. The most annoying moment has to be the endless hallway moment. If you die to this giant enemy you spawn in an endless hallway with no clue as to what to do. Apparently you need to use your camera to find a hidden door but the game does not tell you what to do.
Bosses are cheap. The most bosses have a stun lock ability where they land one attack and constantly attack over and over again untill the player dies. The nursery boss is notorius for this. The big boss near the goddess is another case but it is more of a bug. When he attacks and you get wedged to a wall then you take touch damage till death. Another annoying boss is the boss that can only be seen in the mirror. He moves fast and in later stages because he is harder to see because his colors blend in with the background. The invisible boss is unfair because he is invisible and fighting something you can not see is loads of fun.
The story is near to non-existent. Through the game there is traces of a story and potential but the later you go the less things make sense and that is a bad thing. I dont understand about the spirits or my charact or the other characters. There is no understanding as to what is going on. Maybe the story is explained with documents but that is horrible. Documents should expand on the story or fill in some of the plot or leave hints. Documents should not tell the whole story.
The characters are uninteresting. I remember that this one boy was possessed by a spirit and that spirit snapped his neck right in front of me...I felt nothing because that character had no development so i had no connection to them. It felt forced and kind of humorous at the attempt. That happens like 2 times as far as I remember. The only character to survive for me was the teacher and I did not care for her either. What happend to the fat dude? That is another issue this game has, without interesting characters I wont feel a connection with them and I certainly wont remember their names.
The dialogue is so bad. The dialogue lines might be bad but I can not say for certain. The thing that makes it bad is because it is hard to hear. Either the music or other audio is competitng with the voices or the quality of the voices is so awful. If playing the game use subtitles so you as the player can follow along with the dialogue. Also some of the in game dialogue has fall off which is cool but it definently causes major potential in missing opportunities to hear maybe a fragment of a story because you were too far away.
The NPC animations are very strange. Lets be real it is an indie game but there were many moments where the animimations in the cutscene were very spastic or when in game NPC's were floating. I can not tell if this was a joke or were they not really trying. There were moments where a character would spaz out throwing their arms all over which was funny to watch but overall distracting to the general mood of the game. Also the patty cake moment was funny but out of place as well. If you watch the NPC walking in the city heading to the school..you will see the best magic trick ever, people walking in mid air.
Conclusion:
All and all the game has much potential but ultimately fails at so much. If I can give props to anything it would be just make the comics. The comics are pretty decent to look at. The game however is just a dull experience and something that needs alot of work on to even come close to a solid experience like fatal frame. The game does have a few good scary moments but it over shadowed by the ammount of frustration and confusion that the player must endure in order to complete the game. Even after that the game does not feel fulfilling because it explains nothing and you ultimately feel no connection to any of the other characters or understand what is going on. It could be a good game and I certainly hope the sequal is better but this was not a good experience.

Definitely worth playing for survival horror enthusiasts.
's presentation isn't AAA.  Graphics are serviceable, but dated looking. Menus look unprofessional.  English translation is spotty at best.  The musical soundtrack is goofy and amateurish.  Visual design is good - monsters and ghosts look spooky, and environments are dark, cluttered, and creepy - and ambient sound design is wonderfully weird and scary.  So it's a mixed bag.
There's not much of a story, and what there is isn't very coherent.  This is a world in which the ghost of a pregnant
lives in an abandoned school, next door to a pig demon that can steal money through walls; and a mummy protects his baby with a pair of scissors from a half-dead, half-alive spirit woman that lives outside.
And that's all that's explained about that.
Fine!  Good!  "School kids trapped with a bunch of ghosts."  That's the story, and that can be enough for a game of this type, but the narrative isn't exactly riveting.
Okay, so if presentation and story are mediocre, why play this?  Two reasons:
1) Atmosphere.
Second-rate graphics or no, the environments are unsettling, and the sense of isolation so necessary to good horror is spot on.  The disjointed story and incongruous cast of monsters mentioned above actually
in that they amplify a sense of protagonist vulnerability.  Disembodied skull demons rolling down a staircase?  How am I supposed to deal with that?  And what on earth is coming next?
I don't want to give the impression that it's one over-the-top crazy monster after another.  There certainly are those, but the game also makes strong use of "negative space".  Usually, what you find through the next door is
, which makes for great suspense.
Will

you?  I think that's up to you.  A lot of reviews describe it as "not scary", but, dammit, I was scared!  What kind of player are you?  I think if you "buy in", play with the lights off and headphones, and say, "OK game, how weird can you get?", you'll have a good time.  If you go in with the lights on, trying to be a tough guy and say "Bah!  I've seen scarier," you'll be disappointed.  This game isn't going to give me nightmares, but it did (enjoyably) jerk me between creeped out, tense, thrilled, exhausted, and relieved; and yes, flat-out frightened a few times.
2) Gameplay.
's design does things very right, both moment-to-moment and in terms of overall pacing.
First and foremost, the encounters with the ghosts are tense, memorable, and diverse.  Some enemies are hard to find at all; some are visible only under certain circumstances; some come charging right at you; some do damage before you're even aware they're there; some are invulnerable except for weak spots; some
no weak spots; some simply never attack you at all ... but in general, figuring out how to beat a monster (or escape it) is always challenging and usually surprising.  And once you've beaten a monster, that's usually it; there's no fighting zombies over and over here, so every battle is a fresh new experience, which is a wonderful design decision.
This economy also applies to the usual survival tropes of itemization: finding keys, managing ammunition, assembling puzzle pieces and whatnot.  There is almost none of that here.  You're never "collecting" anything.  Sometimes you will have to find a simple tool to perform a simple task, and there are maybe 3 or 4 keys in the whole game.  Occasionally there may be some backtracking and scrounging when a critical item or puzzle can't be found, but "ransacking" is
the focus.
This all adds up to an experience that is very "to the point", making its 8 hour play time much more eventful than 8 hours of, say, a
with all the backtracking and key searching.  Not that I despise
, but it's refreshing to see so much genre fat trimmed here.  In
there's some unsettling, atmospheric exploration, a great collection of weird monster encounters, a few simple, offbeat puzzles, and that's it.
Good value for your money
your time.  Go for it.  Full price is worth it!

I really wanted to like this game, but after about 8 hours I'm realising the things that irritate me outweigh the good things.
I find the tech tree uninteresting, often spending years to unlock a new piece of research that does very little. It didn't give me a good sense of progression.
Planetary management is somewhat unwieldy, it's hard to get a good overview of the position (but see my further comment below), and the stuff you can build on planets is quite bland. The fuel management system doesn't appeal to me personally , because there's too much micromanagement of the logistics - not a flaw in the game, per se, but it's something I didn't like.
Overall, I'm just not having fun, and I can't see myself playing the game again, although I might give it another try in a couple of months, to see how it's been improved. It's not a terrible game by any means, but it's not for me right now.
Update to take into account Iain's comments below:
1. I take back my point about getting an overview of planet management. I hadn't noticed there was a button to expand the view. To be fair I don't think it's shown in the manual, so I'm guessing it's a relatively recent addition, but it is welcome.
2. On tech, my complaint isn't that it's too fast or too slow, it's that the system doesn't give a real sense of excitement about getting new techs. There's no great sense of 'oh, I've got this tech now, and now I can do these cool things I couldn't do previously'. I'm not saying there are no techs like that, but there are too many that are just a stepping stone to something else, or provide a tech which isn't all that useful.

Research is done uniquely with two separate fields; theoretical and applied sciences.  Ultimately you want to research applied sciences to get all the neat technologies, but to get there you need to get through the theoretical aspect.  To be honest I don't touch the sliders much.

I had the fortune to play the Beta before release and have been pleasantly surprised after initially being unaware of the game. I’m now totally hooked on Polaris Sector to the point that I would rate this game more highly than any Space 4X release in the last 12 months, including Galactic Civilizations 3 and Stardrive 2.
Here are the top reasons why:
1. There is a competent AI which is impressive for a new release. The AI builds decent colonies and uses well designed ships. If you are too aggressive too early an invasion will often falter and you have to think about what you are building against the AI and how to best deploy them in combat.
2. The game is well balanced and avoids out of control exploitation. For example, you can't build early game unbeatable doom fleets, you don't find huge amounts of weapons late game that are worthless and so on.
3. The colony governors are really good. I don’t feel the need to excessively micromanage colonies which vastly reduces the tedium mid to late game. In fact the game shines mid to late for various reasons including the ability to significantly speed up the game.
4. There is a surprising amount of content for a new release. The game includes an end game threat that had me starting at the screen with my mouth open in shock (noting that I consider the Shakturi in Distant Worlds to be total wimps), a novel ship based espionage system and a good ship design system where component selection matters in-game.
5. There are some really cool Spiral galaxy maps to play which can make the game really interesting strategically. For example you might start in an outer ring and find yourself blocked by other races from accessing inner rings or the core without using star tunnels and tankers to provide enough range for early to mid-game fleets.
6. During the beta I have had no crashes at all and just a couple of bugs which the developer promptly responded to.
Some cautions to consider:
1. It’s primarily a war game and although there is some variety in the domination victories (e.g. technology), there aren’t a wide variety of victory conditions.
2. The innovative research is great but it takes a game or two to really get used to it so some patience is recommended.
3. There is some exploration but it could use more events and anomalies to spice it up.
4. The combat is fun and tactical but isn’t as pretty as some other games.
5. A Battle Arena to test designs would have been great but unfortunately not in the game.
6. The tutorials are very limited so checking some Youtube videos might help.

One of my favorites but I feel this a very tough game to rate. I cannot think of any other like it and it succeeds on so many levels that I am blown away by the amount of time and energy it must have taken to create this. That being said many of my friends would (and have) toss this aside very quickly. The best comparison I can think of for this game would be chess, crosswords, or suduko not because this game operates by the same level or rules but because of the amount of mental energy required to play well (or poorly but with maximum effort in my case).
On a high note this game does an excellent job of rewarding progress. Even nearly 80 hours into the game I am still unlocking new aspects every couple hours. The high difficulty factor and this make every finished map lead to both a sigh of relief and quick inhale of anticipation as to what might be next. There are not too many titles you can find that can or will provide this.
The game is a puzzle/roguelike/rpg with a steeeeep learning curve. It goes from fairly easy, to somewhat challenging to difficult to "okay quit smacking me in the balls" tough in a span of about 2 hours or playtime each at which point the challenge continues to escalate as you progress through each map after. I personally enjoy the challenge but I think this is a balancing issue that is likely to turn away alot of people before they really get into the game. This is a shame because of the amazing amount of possiblities and strategies you can and will need to master to get through it. I have to grudgengliny give it a slight knock for this.
The only other major criticism I have is that the tutorial is a bit limited. In a game that gives you such progression the mechanics of many of the aspects are not clearly explained. There are puzzles that come with many of the unlocks that are obviously suppose to help out with this. Unfortunately they are pretty limited (and freakin hard as hell themselves) and do not provide you with much help. This can add on to the frustration level pretty damn quick.
The graphics are obviously not the draw here but the cartoony and light-hearteness of the game provide a nice counterpoint to the toughness factor.
All in all if you own or play mostly titles that contain the tags "board games, tcg, puzzles, strategy, tactical" there is a really good chance this is a gonna be one of your favorites. If your looking for something light-hearted and dislike high difficulty you are likely better off walking the other way.  Objectively I rate his high for orignality and length of content as well as awe-inspiring game design and detract slightly for the poorly explained mechanics and balancing issues.

Update after forcing myself to finish the game at least once (refund got rejected).
So did i enjoy my 20 hours of play time? Well. It is a 4x. So meh. I always SOMEWHAT enjoy them. This has to be the worst 4x game in my library tho, by far. And the most expensive as well.
Compared to Master of Orion: MoO has A LOT less features, like really... it sounds and plays so much simpler. BUT the few things you CAN do are real choices. You can decide what you do, when you do it and how you do it. And multiple ways are possible to advance and win. Polaris Sector has one way and the automation does it for you.
So no, i will not recomment it. A 4x on rails just shouldn't exist.
The game does not get any better like i hoped at the end of my review. It stays a pure illusion of freedom. There is always that ONE best way to do something. Most of the time it is perfectly clear so you just do it, or let automation do it.
As the game progresses you are more and more a watcher only. You do some fights here and there and thats about it. The rest is done by the AI and automation. And really you simply can't do much the AI is not doing on its own.
Few minor adjustments come into play lategame once you get all the techs. You can do some minor tweaks to planets then. At that point it does not matter anymore tho.
My playtrough ended with the "endgame threat". Let's just put it this way: The ONE thing you can choose yourself is how your ships fire. What they fire with. At up to this point i believed that. WRONG again. DON'T even hope to do a lategame ship without missiles. The endgame enemy is immun to anything but a special variation of a missile. Don't use it? Bad luck.
Let me put this into perspective. I had 3 armys, each one as big as the biggest 2 AIs had combined. So pretty much invincible, right? Well no. The endgame enemy jumped in, attacked one army. I killed all their ships within seconds,... all but 2. 2 Battleships. They are immun to all but that one missile type. Those 2 battleships destroyed 30 of my battleships without any return fire.
So that is what happens if you think there is that ONE thing you can choose yourself. All my 3 armadas destroed within 5 ingame years (a few seconds), without being able to shoot back.
By the time i rebuild an armada with the right weapon choice (silly me to use something else then what the game pushes onto me),.. the endgame enemy grew out of proportion. 200 Battleships, 500 Destroyer... needless to say my playtrough ended there.
Also you better love fighters.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Start of original review after about 3 hours played:
The game has many features and looks awesome for any 4x fan on paper. I will happily admit that and i have fallen for exactly that.
Let me call the game "an illusion of freedom". It fits pretty good.
All those features and "stuff" for a lack of a better word:
Basically clutter on the UI without doing anything. Hear me out on this one: The game does an awesome job at making you THINK you can control so many aspects,... but you actually don't control anything. My whole playtime has been a kind of autopilot so far. You can turn of automation on planets, but there are no alternatives anyways. There is that one clear way to go and you just do it, or cripple yourself. Automation works just as good. Illusion of freedom.
Ship battles:
Looked so awesome in those videos. And turned out to be simple rock, paper, scissor fights. Your enemy has this one ship tye? Better send in THIS first, or be destroyed. Auto resolve is less of a pain because you have this one way of doing it again. Do it that way, or fail. Automation does it better then me, since i dislike playing rock, paper, scissor in space. Illusion of freedom.
Ship building:
Key aspect. Stardrive like building. Real freedom, right? No. Weapons only go into yellow slots. Any reason to plug something else in there? No. So... just plug in weapons. 3x3 take small turrets...4x4 take medium turrets,... 6x6 take 4 smalls,... you get the idea. All weapons are of the same size as well. But the other slots are freedom, right? Well... yes. If you dislike your armada and want to destroy it in your first battle. If you don't follow a strict focused approach, the ship will be worthless. So,... well. You gotta plug in x, y and z. If you can fit two x or two y,... great! Thats the real freedom. If you find a layout that takes one more module in all the wasted space. Real illusion of freedom.
AI:
Not. Exactly. Smart. I don't know yet if the AI is just dumb or it is "roleplaying" silly. The agressive guys wanted open boarders... the "never go to war" guys declared war like 30min in without having a single ship i noticed. They did have half a dozen freighters in my space when they declared war tho. Sounds smart, right?
Planetbuilding:
Tackeled it in my first point, but let me alaborate a little: You can focus your planets and you should do that. If you build something, you lock space for other stuff. Building ONE FARM out of 100 slots... locked 24 slots out of my 36 industrial slots on one planet. God knows how or why. But "balanced" is not going to pay off. Illusion of freedom again.
So i don't know. Ill still play for a while and hope i just did not "get it". Or it grows on me,... kinda sad i have spend 33 bucks on this and hope i will stop hating myself for it. Obviously a refund is no option because a 4x game is nothing you can judge after 2 hours.
Stay away for now. Unless you don't mind the illusion of freedom and choice. If you like a 4x on rails, give it a go. It is like watching a movie. And everytime something happens the pause key is pressed. You can read what the AI did, nod a bit and let pause go.

My parents didn't like the idea of first-person shooters because they didn't like the violence and gore. However, they had no problem with me sending hundreds if not thousands of unnamed men (and sometimes women) to brutal deaths at the hands of better armed and armoured foes. This was the wonder of Age of Empires II.
Later I graduated to Rome: Total War and Knights of Honor, both excellent RTS games where you take a more holistic look at the world and it was with these games that the challenge of real-time combat was coupled with the slower, methodical empire-building and administration side of gameplay. In the search for that AoE type of game, I found the marvel that is Stronghold 2, another excellent game that is very much in the spirit of classic Age of Empires.
Then I discovered CK2 and oh boy, I don't regret it for a second. I can't quite remember what led me to buy it, I think it was during a steam sale. I had watched/read a let's play about a year before, but at the time I bought it I don't think I had quite twigged that this was the same game that had looked like such amazing fun on YouTube.
So CK2. If you enjoy starting from humble origins to slowly climb the greasy pole to the top, before realising that you're actually terrified of heights so that you slip and fall to the bottom, breaking both your legs and crushing any hope of your dynasty holding any true power ever again, then this is the game for you. Just remember that the fun is in losing. It may sound perverse but it's true, becoming the Emperor of Britain, France, Spain and the Rest of Europe is do-able, but it kicks the fun out of the game damned quickly. It's fun conquering all that territory, but once you have it, things get dull really fast. Fortunately, by the time you've just conquered an empire to rival Byzantium who should turn up but Genghis Khan and his merry men! Which really mixes things up a bit.
Unfortunately, unless you buy the Sunset Invasion DLC (which I highly recommend), then once you've beaten the mongols, it quickly turns into the same monotonous slog.
So my suggestion is this: Buy the game. Buy the DLC, all of it (make sure you do it during a Steam sale or you'll be going without food for a month or so). Then build your massive empire (which will take a while because the game is brutally difficult to get your head around for the first twenty hours or so), then make sure you have a massive family with lots of unlanded sons and give the most ambitious ones the bulk of your kingdom titles. Congratulations! When you die, your throne shall pass to your eldest son/daughter and a bunch of really powerful vassals, with super-strong claims to the throne will be all around you. This is when the true fun begins.
As a wonderful TV character once said: "You know what takes real strength? Holding it all together when the stakes are this high!" Enjoy!
P.S. Like I said above, the game is brutal to start with, but stick with it. The more you lose, the more you learn and the better you will do next time. It may take 20-30 hours of playing before you feel really confident, but once you do you will have hundreds if not thousands of hours of fun with it.
P.P.S. And the fun doesn't have to end in 14-whatever-it-is! Get EU4 and the EU4 save converter, and you can port your CK2 save over into EU4, where there waits another 400(ish) years of history to live through. But that's a review for a different day.
P.P.P.S. Why are you still reading this? Buy the damned game already!

Crusaders Kings 2 is a strategy game  including a bit of roleplay. Indeed you control the decisions of your character, try to improve his stats, marry him and breed him to have the better offsprings. Your ambition: make your dynasty the most important, rise to the higher ranks and rule your empire.
The historical database is huge and the replayability is immense, provided you buy the many DLCs .At the current time of 2015, with DLC you can start at the age of Charlesmagne ( a bit before 800), and with the DLC to convert your game to Europa Universalis IV, well you end up in the 18th century.  You can play a wide range of civilizations from the arabs to the Indians and the vikings.
I personnally enjoy all this content even though much of it comes through DLCs, but since there are some sales time where you get the game and all the DLC for an affordable price... Thank you steam.

I enjoy how well crafted and original the world of exiles feels, the attention to detail and the map. There is so much you can do and all the time to do it.

Finished this game the same day I bought it. It was one of those games that I just couldn't put down once I picked it up, which should serve as a pretty good indicator of the game's quality by itself. Although it was not all roses, I had a blast and I very much recommend this game to anyone who likes twin-stick shooters. Let's break down the pros and cons.
Pros:
* The artstyle. While fairly generic cyberpunk by some standards, in my opinion it does just enough to stand out. The main character's holographic mask is a wonderfully weird feature, as are the occasional flashes of "GET EM PUPPY" or "HELLO DARKNESS" when fights begin.
* The combat. Some weapons feel clunky and underpowered, some make you feel like God himself, but on the whole it's all well balanced and engaging. Zipping around like a grasshopper and seamlessly switching between shooting and melee attacks kept me entertained the whole way through.
* The skill system. You won't unlock everything in one playthrough, so making choices and finding your preferences is a must. Fortunately, you can also move points around at any time - even in the middle of fights! - which makes it easy to adapt if a particular strategy isn't working.
The cons:
* The checkpoints. While most are just fine, a couple of them are placed in such a way that you'll have to fight a few mooks or even just wait a while before a miniboss or similar threat appears, which can become very tedious if you're having trouble with that particular section.
* The story. It's a decent "Save your beloved X" story, but it seems rather detached from most things you find out during the course of the game. The world building is great, especially with the in-game database fleshing out details about every single weapon, enemy and location, but it feels somewhat unrelated to your overall goal. The ending is cathartic, but doesn't give a lot of answers, and I felt like it was setting up for a post-credits stinger that never came. It should be mentioned that I have only completed the game on normal difficulty, and thus remain unaware if higher difficulties reward you with extra story details.
Conclusion:
RUINER is a great game with a couple of flaws that, while individually annoying, doesn't RUIN the overall experience. It is a great first showing from Reikon Games, and I'm excited to see what they can achieve in the future.

Pros:
-Amazing pixel art
-Interesting characters and their developments
-Fun gameplay mechanics, puzzles, and bosses
-Good story
-Good soundtrack
Cons:
-Manuevering in very brief segments of the game (one of which is optional) is awkward and unenjoyable
-(personal problem) ending needed just a bit more (It was a good ending but I feel that it didn't completely top off the story)

The Good:
- Soundtrack. Let's get that out of the way asap. Nowadays a good soundtrack for a non-AAA title is almost mandatory, this game has it.
- Gameplay. In general, the combat is fair and satisfying. It is also balanced greatly around wide variety of skills: normally in such a fast paced game melee weapons would rule compeletely, this is not the case here as building a ranged-focused character is absolutely possible.
- Atmosphere. The developers managed to deliver a believable (and likeable) world in a difficult genre as cyberpunk. Strolling around Rengkok was actually enjoyable.
- Difficulty. Ignore modern "video game journals" that scream about the game being too difficult. It's not. There's a lot of room for abusing abilities to make your game easier. Just play smart and don't be afraid of dying. Don't forget that sometimes brute force is the easiest way out as well. The "Hard" difficulty is recommended for everyone except people who just want to complete the game and move on.
The Bad:
- Story. Honestly, it was lackluster for my liking. However, I've enjoyed most of the characters presented, so this is not an indication that the whole writing in game is bad. The plot is simple and predictable and the game sometimes fails to extract requested emotions from me.
- Restarting at certain arenas/bosses. This grinded on my gears the most in this game. Two or three major battles in the game has to be restarted including the unskippable cutscene beforehand. Sometimes there are cutscenes during boss stages, which you also can't skip and you have to go through them until you defeat the boss. Frustrating, I don't know why it's in the game.
In general: 8/10, a very solid game, must buy for fans of fast paced action, cyberpunk and collectors of dat karma.

The priest that had begged me seventy times seven for food so the children could survive the winter was on the road ahead of me. I had all the necessary legendary gear required to defeat the king at the end of my quest or some mighty foe that would require a herculian feat; a mace that sharted lightnig, a shield of a defeated skeleton royal that could break skeleton warrios with a touch.
The one thing I did not have was food to share, much less for myself. My choice was simple, refuse the priest's request to feed the children and see him badger me for eternity, or sell all my earthly possessions and forgo my own life to support this guys tireless request to feed the children foundation.
The thought of seeing this priest one more time made the choice easy. I sold everything I had for all the food I could carry. I approach the priest and before he can open his stupid mouth, I hit him with my bag of food. We share words and he gives me some ring. Thanks...
Now I'm starving and I just count down my days until starvation takes me, questioning why I even continue, prolonging the inevitable. Maybe, just maybe the old gods will deliver a miracle and repay me in riches and weapons for my charity.
I stumble into a labrynth. This one seemed familiar... oh wait, there's a titanic minotaur in front of me. Well this is appropiate... I find the minotaur I was hunting all along with nothing to defend myself. "Better than starving I supose" I think to myself and shrug.
I charge it head on to embrace death and glory. He swings his mighty Flail across its torso in almost blinding speed and strength. Either out of habit or not wanting to die (naturally), I roll underneath the attack and ready one swipe at its hoof with a craptastic rusty axe I found, but just then I am blinded by a flash of light. Lightning fell from the sky, striking the minatour and killing it instantly. Standing there with my jaw on the floor in shock I almost couldn't believe it. I can't help but start laughing with joy. The old gods actually came through and I learned a valuable lesson that day.
Sacrifice everything to charity to get the incessant priest out of your deck so you never have to give up your food again.
10/10 :)

Before you flame, read the full review for why I'm giving this game "NOT RECOMMENDED". Firstly, I wish steam had a "Neutral" position, because I definitely did like this game, but I've never played a game before this that has been top-notch and brilliant in so many aspects, and incredibly poor/frustrating in others. I'm giving this a "NO" because the reviews for this game are 93% positive, and while I do think this game is worth considering, to me that is too high of a rating. Overall though, it came down to: "Will I want to replay this game again?", and I can't say I will, at least not now after finishing the game, maybe it will grow on me.
<Spoiler free part>
Graphics:
Let's start with the good stuff. The art direction for this game is incredible. Absolutely beautiful. Beautiful scenery, great environments, great art direction (village themes, enemies/bosses, etc), characters art is well done: cute/quirky/stern/scary/creepy to match respectively. Amazingly done.
Sound:
The sound effects are satisfying (shooting, flying, breaking objects) and sound great. The music is also amazingly composed. I say "composed" carefully, because the person who did the music is truly talented. Some really beautiful themes that will stand out, and do a lot to add to the environments/situation at hand. I expected 8-bit, and while I love 8-bit themes (recently done masterfully by Shovel Knight), but got orchestral/symphonic instead. And rather than being generic and cheap sounding, this was also top-notch.
Gameplay:
I have to start with: WHERE IS THE MAP!!!!! That was a major flaw for me... games like these need maps, and while this game is a lot smaller than it feels, the omission of a map will leave you feeling lost and often times confused. I honestly would have loved to explore the world and find everything (I got everything but the final cape), but without a map, you can be left disoriented. Also, fast travel between particular points of interest also would have gone a long way. The game is relatively linear though, so you'll be able to make your way through it without too many problems, especially if you just stay on the main path.
The controls are tight/responsive, and the game is very smooth. I learned that this game had a decade long production cycle, and that really comes through... It is a very ambitious game the feels like they had tons of amazing ideas, but couldn't fully deliver on all of them. Maybe they needed more time, or more people working on the project, but many parts feel half-baked. Parts of the game feel more like chores to get through. I do like the idea of switching between characters for their unique abilities, but it got a little grating, rather than making moving through the world more satisfying. I did like that all 3 characters had their important uses, rather than them just becoming gimmicks.
This game is difficult, and not in a bad way. You can't just bowl through the game holding shoot, and will need to switch between the 3 characters/and your own character to defeat enemies. The bosses are also fantastically done... to me this was the best part. While the levels were sometimes long/tedious (some interesting sections in each), the boss battles were great -- with some EXCELLENT and exciting set-pieces surprisingly (snake).
Story (minor spoilers):
This is one area that felt very shaky to me. While the game does feel charming, it is on the surface level. We never get to fully meet our characters. There is a lot of set-up, with little pay off. Character arcs are not completed properly (themes like redemption etc) for most characters, and many of the characters fit some sort of stereotype.
In the end, there are some touching moments (I'm a sap, and have shed tears when story telling does "emotional" correctly), but they don't feel earned, and sometimes rushed. Again, the game feels like it needed more time. It is as if they wanted to do a Zelda-type game where you go around the world, meeting new characters, getting new abilities which unlock new areas, characters growing/learning/etc etc, but they didn't have enough time. The game also had dungeons with "relics", but it never felt finished, so they just rushed it. Then at the end, when things were supposed to get touching, I was left confused with who I was talking to and why I should care, it didn't feel earned. The ending leaves itself on a cliffhanger, and while I'm fine with "use your imagination to fill in the blanks", I don't think that was done well here. I did like that Owlboy wasn't who you thought, and that the story wasn't ham-fisted, predictable, and cliched like so many others. They tried to add some twists, but as I said before, everything feels rushed, and the game ends without properly tying up its loose ends.
Overall:
Owl boy is a beautiful game, it sounds great. It shows glimpses of greatness, but it needed more time, or more people working on it (or both). Maybe I was just expecting a larger game, but that's how it was setup and that's how it played. The game is small, and leaves many characters underdeveloped. The gameplay, while tight, has just as many boring parts as exciting parts. There were times where I was considering just quitting, but then something came up that kept me playing. The story was also left half-baked, like they had a "great idea", but didn't know how to flesh it out. It was set up well, it had "the ending", but it was never earned to me. Parts felt tedious, and I think the omission of a map was a huge flaw... they didn't even need to do a Metroid grid that opens up, they could have just made some sort of drawn map that expands as you progress. It is a charming game, with touching moments, but it's not a flawless masterpiece. I wanted to love this game when looking at it, but be aware if you choose to pick it up to keep your expectations in check. If too many people rated the game No, I would have given this game a Yes, but it is not a 93% overall game (where it currently resides). I wish steam had neutral ratings, because that is what this game deserves.
If the devs decide to do an Owlboy 2, I think they have a lot of great things to work with, but there are also a lot of things to improve upon, to make a true masterpiece. Do I regret playing this game? No. But it has its issues.
(Also, the cannon minigame... wtf!!! Since it was optional, I won't hold it against the game, but honestly, did anyone playtest it? I'm all for challenge, but that was just silly.)

Chivalry: Medieval Warfare is a first person melee combat game that features interesting fighting mechanics, epic battles, dimemberment and piles of bodies littering the map. It features a bunch of awesome game modes:
- Team Objective, where you have an attacking and a defending team trying to either complete or prevent the completion of objectives like pushing battering ram carts to the gates, breaching it and murdering the enemy king.
- Last Team Standing, where two teams fight to the death, every player only having one life per round (no respawn).
- Duel, where you can test your skill 1v1 against players of all kinds of skill levels.
- Free For All, where chaos is truly a ladder (amirite, Littlefinger?) and dishonorable backstabbing can take you to the top as fast as being a skilled fighter.
The game is littered with epic and hilarious moments where people bumrush objectives spamming the battle cry button, resulting in an adrenaline fueled charge on the enemy. Using the ingame voices to formally apologize to an opponent when you've just taken their head, respectfully bowing and praising the opponents skill in genuinely chivilrous moments and trolling players by saying "no" everytime you parry their attack, it's really the ingame voices that add that extra dimension of hilarity to this already awesome game.
Just how much fun is this game? Well, I've got 104 hours in on a crappy 2011 laptop running at 20-40 fps (but mostly under 30) with all settings on 'low'. The game is THAT addictive, even if I can't run it well at all. Also, after all those hours, I'm still only a lowly level 25 and at best average at the game. Both those things don't deter me from playing. In fact, they make me want to try harder and learn to become a better player. I can't wait to play this on a good PC (it's coming soon, thank god) to fully enjoy the chaotic, medieval battlefields of chivalry in all their glory.
Pros: Gloriously rewarding gameplay, intense melee combat, epic game modes like Team Objective and Last Team Standing, lots of hilarity, many players actually are chivilrous and the community is one of the least toxic ones I've experienced (of course there are always bad apples).
Cons: Steep learning curve, unrealistic moves are required to become a top player (reverse overheads, spins and other moves that remind more of ballet than swordfighting), somewhat poorly optimized (but not game-breaking).
9/10 - superbly rediculous fun.

Definitely worth playing for survival horror enthusiasts.
's presentation isn't AAA.  Graphics are serviceable, but dated looking. Menus look unprofessional.  English translation is spotty at best.  The musical soundtrack is goofy and amateurish.  Visual design is good - monsters and ghosts look spooky, and environments are dark, cluttered, and creepy - and ambient sound design is wonderfully weird and scary.  So it's a mixed bag.
There's not much of a story, and what there is isn't very coherent.  This is a world in which the ghost of a pregnant
lives in an abandoned school, next door to a pig demon that can steal money through walls; and a mummy protects his baby with a pair of scissors from a half-dead, half-alive spirit woman that lives outside.
And that's all that's explained about that.
Fine!  Good!  "School kids trapped with a bunch of ghosts."  That's the story, and that can be enough for a game of this type, but the narrative isn't exactly riveting.
Okay, so if presentation and story are mediocre, why play this?  Two reasons:
1) Atmosphere.
Second-rate graphics or no, the environments are unsettling, and the sense of isolation so necessary to good horror is spot on.  The disjointed story and incongruous cast of monsters mentioned above actually
in that they amplify a sense of protagonist vulnerability.  Disembodied skull demons rolling down a staircase?  How am I supposed to deal with that?  And what on earth is coming next?
I don't want to give the impression that it's one over-the-top crazy monster after another.  There certainly are those, but the game also makes strong use of "negative space".  Usually, what you find through the next door is
, which makes for great suspense.
Will

you?  I think that's up to you.  A lot of reviews describe it as "not scary", but, dammit, I was scared!  What kind of player are you?  I think if you "buy in", play with the lights off and headphones, and say, "OK game, how weird can you get?", you'll have a good time.  If you go in with the lights on, trying to be a tough guy and say "Bah!  I've seen scarier," you'll be disappointed.  This game isn't going to give me nightmares, but it did (enjoyably) jerk me between creeped out, tense, thrilled, exhausted, and relieved; and yes, flat-out frightened a few times.
2) Gameplay.
's design does things very right, both moment-to-moment and in terms of overall pacing.
First and foremost, the encounters with the ghosts are tense, memorable, and diverse.  Some enemies are hard to find at all; some are visible only under certain circumstances; some come charging right at you; some do damage before you're even aware they're there; some are invulnerable except for weak spots; some
no weak spots; some simply never attack you at all ... but in general, figuring out how to beat a monster (or escape it) is always challenging and usually surprising.  And once you've beaten a monster, that's usually it; there's no fighting zombies over and over here, so every battle is a fresh new experience, which is a wonderful design decision.
This economy also applies to the usual survival tropes of itemization: finding keys, managing ammunition, assembling puzzle pieces and whatnot.  There is almost none of that here.  You're never "collecting" anything.  Sometimes you will have to find a simple tool to perform a simple task, and there are maybe 3 or 4 keys in the whole game.  Occasionally there may be some backtracking and scrounging when a critical item or puzzle can't be found, but "ransacking" is
the focus.
This all adds up to an experience that is very "to the point", making its 8 hour play time much more eventful than 8 hours of, say, a
with all the backtracking and key searching.  Not that I despise
, but it's refreshing to see so much genre fat trimmed here.  In
there's some unsettling, atmospheric exploration, a great collection of weird monster encounters, a few simple, offbeat puzzles, and that's it.
Good value for your money
your time.  Go for it.  Full price is worth it!

Wow.  This was certainly...an experience.  In a good way.
This game seems to have a terrible review score, but 2D platformers with an exploration focus are my thing, and I had the game in my library, so I tried it out anyway.  Besides, it's just 3 MB in size.
It did not disappoint me.  I just finished this game.  I enjoyed this game.  Well, as much as "enjoying" is a word applicable to a pretty darn tense horror game.  And yeah, it's not (yet?) tagged Horror but I'd call this a horror game.  I guess that's the only vaguely spoilery thing I'll tell you.  But maybe this will help you not go into this expecting Super Metroid or something, as it seems some people did.
Sure, the game is something that you can finish in an evening (though I suggest late night for best results), and there's no replay value besides speedrunning it, but...this was like watching a movie that leaves you with a lot to think about.  Again, in a good way.
Incidentally, I'm usually really into game music, but this game completely lacks music.  But I'm also into the atmospheric "feel" of in-game environs...and despite (or due to?) the lack of music, this game delivers its sense of atmosphere quite effectively.  So I didn't mind the silence.  It just made the experience that much more striking.  (This was somewhat reminiscent of this other exploration horror platformer called Holdover.)
Also, the game lacks an in-game map.  I'd normally complain about this but the game world is just the right size that you should be able to remember where you've been -- especially if you're going to finish this in one or two sessions.
A few technical/design comments:
* There's one place where you can potentially get yourself stuck in a nook behind a door you can't open.  Not very good design, but you can easily reset the room by quitting and continuing from the autosave, which takes less than 10 seconds.  The game autosaves every time you enter a room.  So try it again and do something more clever.
* If you've just barely entered a room, you can't immediately re-exit it the same way.  Step outside of the doorway like an inch or so and then you can go back through it.  Doesn't much affect gameplay though, so it's only a minor problem.
* The game BSOD'd my computer (Win8.1) when I closed it after finishing it.  Given what happened in the story, though...it felt fitting.  Heh.  Tried closing it a few more times, including re-finishing the game, but it didn't crash again.  I can't replicate this.  Spooky.
(Disclosure: I bought this game as part of the Indie Gala Greenlight Bundle.)

Let me say first off that I have only played for four hours so far which isn't long enough for an in depth review, it is long enough however for a first impressions and so far those impressions are not good.  I will also say that when it comes to 4x games I am an empire builder.  I strategize and try to see the big picture.  In space 4x I build two or three poweful battle fleets and station them where they can get to probable trouble spots in a reasonable and timely manner.  Polaris sector while appearing to offer similar on the surface actually falls flat once that surface has been penetrated and you get to the soft and not so juicy bits underneath.  You would think that with a map size of 900 stars it would be awhile before you needed to deal with the other major factions, but no.  The game sticks them fairly close so you will start to bump up against them within the first hour of play which makes the map feel smaller than it is, a feeling that is compounded by the stars themselves being quite close to each other and by the pirates that pop up seemingly out of nowhere to harass your worlds and shipping, seriously, turn these off as they are way too common.
The developers really should have looked at another game in the Matrix stable ( Distant Worlds ) and taken a few hints.  Polaris sector has fallen squarely into that old and tired 4x land grab.  Find colonisable world / grab it before the Ai does / try to close off choke points and build huge defences and fleets because you know what's coming.  It's been done to death and it's boring.  You will also find that after a couple of hours the game will auto-pause with nausiating regularity ( every few seconds ) that has you delving into the settings to turn most of it off, which then results in you missing information if the game speed is turned up ( something that you need to do in order to get anywhere ).
One of the main innovations ( according to the developer ) is the research system that boasts no research trees.  Yes there are, they are just displayed differently and research usually devolves into choosing which tech you want next, prioritising it and letting the game get on with churning it out.  Having said that the techs appear many and diverse but with the way the larger game is designed you will find yourself researching the military techs early on so that your ships are not completely outgunned, which is another similarity to many 4x games out there.  Again, perhaps they should have taken a look at Distant Worlds in which techs are split into three different categories allowing for more civilian techs to be researched alongside the military ones.  The ship designer is a variation on a theme first implemented in another 4x game that shall remain nameless but Polaris sector does it better and some interesting combinations can be produced.  I created a fleet of stealth / assassin ships that waited at a choke point for any unsuspecting enemy vessels to wander by.  The pirates got a taste of their own medicine with that lot.
As I said, I have not played long enough for a full review and I will update this when I have a few more hours under my belt.  Hopefully the game will get better as I delve deeper into it but first impressions matter and these have been mine.
Now almost 8 hours in and I'm honestly bored to tears.  I was hoping that the game would blossom and show it's complexity as I got further into it but no, there really is none.  Polaris Sector is one of the most shallow space 4x games that I have ever played and I have played a few of them.  The couple of wafer thin strategic elements that the game brings to the table, the created bottlenecks and the combat have issues of their own and add nothing to the gameplay which is bland and uninspired.  The bottlenecks are created because of the use of warp lanes.  i know why the developers use them, it's to prevent both the player and the Ai from attacking out of nowhere ( mainly the player ) but we are in 2016 here and there are better ways of handling that particular problem.  as it is it just adds one more thing that takes away the immersion and places you on a linear road rather than the expanse of space.  The combat system was quaint for the first few outings but quickly became tiresome and tedious, leaving me to auto-resolve or to tell my fleets to do their own thing, which invariably means frontal assault and tactics be damned.  Simply look at the red / green bar and if you have more than they do then auto-resolve it, you will win.
Matrix produce some decent strategy games if you can get past the decades old graphics but sadly this isn't one of them.  I have clicked 'close and continue' so many %$£^$%£ times in the past few hours while the game pretty much played itself that my index finger has developed a twitch.  If you really must have this in your library then wait for a steam sale.

Valkyria Chronicles delivers an amazing story with interesting, original gameplay.
I simply love how they delivered such a good story without easing on the gameplay; it's not the cutscenes that keep you hooked, but the played parts as well.
The turn-based RTS combat is pretty fun. The game has a unique system, matching together turn-based combat with real-time elements. It also gives you a certain freedom: there are many different strategies you can use to approach a situation, (some better than others I assure you; sometimes one certain approach is forced) and many factors you can play with. For example, some people will perform worse when matched with certain characters; simply because they don't like them. In that way, you'll have to carefully set up the perfect squad that's also matching with the conditions on the battlefield.
You can also level the characters in your squad and individually gear them. These and other factors, like permadeath(!) make the characters grow on you; you don't want them to die, and you'll start to take things personally (well, I did at least).
It's not just the STORY that makes the characters grow on you, but the GAMEPLAY as well. In that way, the gameplay and story are matched perfectly.
Sometimes the AI may perform bad. Though I'm thankful because if it didn't, the game would be too hard.
This brings me to another point: the enemy is overpowered. They will always have better gear than you do. They are designed to actually make it feel like you're a small squad (militia at that, not a full army) just ordered to perfom some missions. Sometimes you actually feel underpowered but you still somehow find a way to beat the enemy, and this makes you feel like you actually achieved something. Again, story and gameplay fusing together very well.
tldr; if story matters to you a lot in a game, buy Valkyria Chronicles. The gameplay does not ruin the story part at all; it's fused together.

TLDR: This is not really a dungeon-crawler... it's an RPG MATHS PUZZLE GAME
I realised the following things when I started unlocking their 'puzzles' which are basically advanced tutorials that don't do any hand holding.
Everyone keeps going on about how awesome this game is, I like it too, but it's not what' you would normally expect froma  dungeon crawler, please let me explain.... forewarned is forearmed....
1st, This is not really a dungeon-crawler... it's a PUZZLE GAME It uses a lot of maths type puzzles - you need to figure out how many minions to kill so that you can level up, and how to do it efficiently... killing higher level baddies gains you an exp bonus, but you need to do it as much as possible so you don't lose XP from minions that are now "lower"... you need to snowball your XP. Levelling up gives you 100%health and mana, and you have to exploit this all game so that you don't use too many potions.... you'll need them for the boss in the level.
2nd, because it's only 10 minutes, things have to be simplified. You move around on a checkerboard style tabletop. revealing a tile (standing next to it = gaining visibility of the next tile) will restore some health and mana.
3rd, this is not a 10 minute game. You can play a dungeon in 10 minutes, sure, so you can play in 10 minute sessions, this can be a positive... but "just one more, it's only 10 minutes" will quickly translate into hours of game play.
4th This is a Rogue LITE - it does have a progression system where you can unlock new classes, abilities, etc between runs, in a similar way to Rogue Legacy. [A true rogue-like features permadeath where you lose everything and start again at level 1.]
For those that like this game, it's addictive. Look at people's play times, the ones that have reviewed this. there are some who have 15-30h, then there are those with 80-120 hours, and the odd one over 200h - that's about the point where you beat the game, from my understanding / reading on the wiki.
Do I recommend this game? That's such a hard one. Yes, If you know what you're getting into when you buy it, but the Store description is deceptive, and doesn't really explain just how this game works, and I was dissapointed about that, I wanted more 'hack n slash', and less 'calculating the next 7 steps to level up without using that mana pot' So for me, Although the game itself seems solid, I do like it, and I will play it some more, but I already know I won't clock it if it requires 200h it's a No.

Inescapable is not a great game. It deserves its mixed reviews. At its core, it's a mostly capable platformer. The controls are fine. It reminds me of Blackthorne, but not nearly as good.
The environments aren't particularly exciting and lack variety. One area is a cavern with orange rocks. Another has green rocks. Another has blue rocks. Aside from the colors, they're basically the same.
The enemies lack variety. There's only two or three types, and you'll soon get tired of shooting the same enemies over and over.
The story is a mixed bag. I must admit that I tuned out about half-way through, but it has a "Cthulu in space" vibe to it that some gamers may enjoy. Unfortunately, the ending is basically non-existent. So even if you get into the story, the ending will almost certainly leave you flat.
Gameplay mostly consists of finding keys and artifacts that allow you to open doors and progress. This would be fine if it didn't involve so much backtracking. And oftentimes, you open a door, thinking you've just made some good progress, and the only thing behind the door are two more locked doors. Ugh!
Even with all these problems, I was ready to give the game a slight thumbs up until the ending. I enjoy the genre, so I played through the game with a forgiving nature. Perhaps too forgiving. Then the ending arrived, and it just wasn't worth it.
I'm not one of those gamers expects the world from a $5 game, but I just can't recommend it at that price. Even if you're a fan of the genre and don't mind keeping your standards fairly low, I'd recommend getting Inescapable only if it's at least 50% off.

It's a sequence of single-screen dungeon crawls, each with a different character, starting at level 1.  Dungeons are randomly generated, plus there are some semi-random quest dungeons and completely fixed puzzles.  The game rules are simple enough, but complex strategies emerge.  It's easy to learn and difficult to master, although I have to say mastery would be a little more attainable if there were better in-game documentation.  There is of course a wiki.
One last warning: it is addictive.  As in: "Holy crap, is it 4:00 tomorrow morning already?"-class addictive.  Highly recommended.

Every time you think you've learned what to do, the game surprises and challenges you to do 1 better. Frankly, this is the only reason anyone should get this game. If you have no interest in storytelling whatsoever, there are much better shooters out there; if you have no interest in shooters, it's not worth being put off. The story is very immersive, with an incredibly fleshed out world, and more than makes up for any flaws the game has in other areas. Characters don't feel neglected, although sometimes there isn't quite enough content for a character you want to experience more of. (Side note: You may get a mixed first impression of "The Salarian", which could prompt you to stop going out of your way to talk to him. This is the sensible option if you wish to preserve your sides later in the game. Some of his lines are just golden.)
If you haven't played Mass Effect 1, I would recommend playing it first, even if it is mechanically slightly inferior to it's sequel, and you
play it without. However, a lot of enjoyment can be derived from taking a single Shepard, with all his actions, choices, and in my case, awful facial hair, through the series.
Satisfying, though slightly repetitive. The cover system can be awkward to use at times, thanks to Use, Sprint, and Take Cover all forcibly bound to the same action - by far the ugliest scar from the console port. If, like I did, you want to play with the same controls as every other PC shooter in the universe, the easiest fix is to use the primary and secondary keybinding functionality to bind the do-everything button to both what you want the Use and Sprint buttons to be. Often you'll be sprinting into cover anyway, so it kind of works, but it's definitely not ideal.
There's a lot of variety to be had in terms of the ways you can build Shepard, but during a single playthrough it can get fairly restrictive, especially if you want to play optimally. That said, the variety in squadmates can allow a few different tactical approaches for the same Shepard, even if you only get to experience their skills and playstyle via the tactics interface, which carries over nicely from Mass Effect 1.
The morality system is extremely black and white, which can be an issue, but if you stick to any non-gamey moral compass for your Shepard, it will probably see you pick up a good few Paragon and Renegade points each. Some important dialogue options require many of one or the other, though, so it's difficult to play a middle man, which is a little disappointing. Additionally, some choices don't really fall under stereotypical "good" and "evil" labels either way, but they assign Parargon and Renegade points to them anyway, so it doesn't always make sense. I didn't find it really hindered me in any way though. The feeling of decisions having an impact in the world is always great, though.

I wish there was a middle ground between thumbs up and down. Because this game has a lot going for it and is worth playing, but it also has a few glaring problems that make it feel...wrong.
Biggest problem is that Dashing seems to have no i-frames. Now, I'm playing on hard, so this might not have much bearing on lower difficulties, but I find myself CONSTANTLY being hit mid dash by both melee and projectile attacks.  And yes, this doesn't make the game unplayable, it just alters how you have to play. Specifically, it means you can't dodge forward through projectiles like a bad♥♥♥♥♥ You have to dodge away. Which  sounds fine on paper but in practice it means the game becomes a lot more defensive  as you constantly attack and then pull back rather than neatly dodging through an enemy shot and continuing to fight.
Half the time you just end up dashing in at an angle, hitting someone with a pipe and stun locking them for 2-3 hits- which often doesn't kill them- and then dashing back out.
And this is fine. The game works just fine. Everything looks great. Everything sounds great. Everything about the game is great but It just seems antithetical to the brutal, hardcore, ultraviolent presentation to make you have to fight with such a defensive, pokey, constantly retreating style.  There's a lot of similarity between this game and Hotline Miami of course, but in Hotline you always had this sense of forward momentum. Because everything in hotline died in one hit there was this capacity to charge down a hall and, with the right actions, kill everything without slowing down. It was all about that one perfect run where you come in and everything dies within a few seconds.
Ruiner...you just don't feel that. Every fight is a chaotic melee that requires you to play defensively rather than agressively. If you cut loose and try to weave through bullets and kill with style, you just get beaten down.  So you sigh and you do it how the game is desgined: you move carefully, you wear the enemies down, you switch weapons constantly to make use of a semi-random slowdown effect, and you deal with the fact that enemies have attack animations that make them literally immune to bullets. Yeah. The jumping attacks of pipe weilding thugs make them invincible at the start and end because they are ducking, and thus the bullets go over them. I think they're even immune through part of the jump itself, on the apex of it, but thats hard for me to say for sure.
I'm rambling. Ruiner is a great game but the actual combat mechanics seem at odds with the style and presentation, at least in hard mode.

Let me start by saying I have nothing against the concept of blending genres. It can work and if done properly it can create a game far greater than the sum of its parts.
, a game which attempts to combine a rogue-like dungeon crawl with a puzzle game, could definitely have worked, if only the elements it chose to borrow from those two genres were actually compatible with each other.
Allow me to explain by way of example. As part of the puzzle aspect of the game, your hero only regenerates health and mana when exploring new areas, not when backtracking over old areas. Blind exploration is dicouraged, as doing so at full health means wasting precious healing. This forces you to think about where you want to go next instead of just going out willy nilly. I know it sounds like I'm praising the game and the truth is it could have been a good gameplay mechanic...
...IF you had any way of actually KNOWING where you should go next.
Unexplored areas are always completely blacked out, and since the dungeons are randomly layed out every time you have no way of knowing where you should go next. The fighter class mitigates this somewhat by automatically revealing the location of enemies that are your level or lower, but that hardly helps out the OTHER classes and even with this, you still have no way of knowing where to find valuable power-ups, equippable items, or spells.
The whole game is like that. In fact the greatest challenge in this game is not any enemy, but the game's own vague rules. I talked about this a little in my review of
but it's even more true here: we really,
need to be given accurate, real information for a game like this to work.
For example, there's a speed stat that determines who attacks first in combat, but you can't actually see what your speed stat is. You can see that some enemies have first strike, but even enemies that don't have first strike and which you would expect to go after you in the combat order - like warlocks and zombies - can often end up going first... sometimes. Other times they go second, and since you can't actually see your speed stat or the enemy's the whole thing just comes across as arbitrary.
And that's why this game fails on both fronts. The puzzle aspects are too strictly demanding and the punishment for even one single misstep is too harsh, so the game fails as a rogue-like. At the same time, the rogue-like aspects add too much randomness and too much hidden information, so the game fails as a puzzle.
The worst part is the game has no idea. It demands care, but then forces you to go out blindly, and then punishes you harshly for doing so. It tells you it's all your fault when you fail (and you will) with condescending messages and taunts, but really it's no one's fault because everything is entirely luck-based.
Like I said, the idea of combining a rogue-like and a puzzle game is not entirely terrible. It could have worked, it just didn't in this case. Maybe some other game will come along and get it right. But this one ain't it.

gamemode, as I generally have most fun exploring a game peacefully.
I have currently played for around 18 hours, and I've had fun while actually playing the game. I've had ALOT of issues with servers. Therefor, I'll split this review into a

section.
As you first might notice, this game borrows
from ARK: Survival Evolved. In my opinion, the world is way more credible as the world isn't overpopulated and the overall atmosphere is very enjoyable. The sounds and music are
good and i leaves me with the feeling you get, when exploring one of the traditional MMORPGs like World Of Warcraft or Guild Wars. The world and setting is beautiful. The map design is epic, and beautiful. It leaves with an epic feeling, and adventuring around that map is awesome.
The inventory, crafting and gathering system is very much like ARK. It works well, but it has its flaws. Generally the system works well, while there are certain bugs, which is expected at such an early state. The game generally doesn't feel grindy, and I actually
going on expeditions to the north to get iron. There are plenty of recipes to craft considering its state.
The wide variety of weapons, armor and shields makes a solid foundation for combat. The mecanichs currently feel decent, however the depth of the combat could be increased in the future.
Building feels alot like ARK, however there is more variety and there are greater costumization options. The building is generally great, however there are certain bugs that can distrupt the joy.
There is a health, stamina, hunger, water and an encumberance meter, Each can be expanded by leveling up your character. There is different religions, each allowing you to gain special items or boons. You can make sacrifices and other ritiuals. It's a nice addition, which should be expanded in the future in my opinion.
There is a variety of wild life. There is not too great diversity yet, but it should not be overdone like ARK is. There are going to mounts in this game, preferably some mount that is faster than the currently available elephant.

TL;DR: Needs tweaking really, really badly. Probably worth a play but it will take a design patch before it's a truly great game.
Disclaimer: I'm only ~3 hours in and will definitely continue playing if only just to see if the problems mentioned below get any better.
The world, characters, and general aesthetic look and feel GREAT. I love what Reikon have done here. Big shoutout to whoever was responsible for the music, it fits in perfectly and there are some real bangers in there.
I love the ability to swap your ability toolset and experiment with different strategies at any given point.
HOWEVER
RUINER in it's current state feels waaaaay too "spongey". The challenge only really comes from bullet sponges for enemies, and AI that feel less like people within a world and more like omnipresent beings (even accounting for cybernetic implants). Most of the boss fights feel more like an akward grind than anything.
There's so much to like about this game, and it's soooo close to being a really great title. I really wanted to like it, but the combat is just such a let down.
As a player I don't feel rewarded when I successfully execute moves that the games seems to be designed around, like slowing time, dashing to dodge bullets and get up into an enemies face to take them down. Instead of being rewarded with the sound of a dead enemy, I'm met with little more than a smaller red bar at their feet, and them somehow reacting instantly to my new location and blasting me in the face. I'm forced to cancel my next move, go back and finish the enemy off, ruining ANY sense of flow within the combat.
I can progress through the level and the game just fine, but the fights are just mundane. Whenever you die (and you will) you feel like the game cheated you and it's just frustrating.
The enemy health bars are really hard to see btw, and having them present by default only seems to distract from the larger picture, which seems counter to what Reikon are trying to do given the number of enemies within each fight. If you pick up this title I'd recommend turning them off.
A lot of people seem bent on comparing this to Hotline Miami, but it's probably the furthest you can get from it. Where HM felt tight, quick, and immensely satisfying, RUINER leaves me disappointed and frustrated. I'm doing everything it seems to want, with little to no reward.
During my time first playing RUINER, I tried Hard initially, found the bullet sponge situation to be unbearable and assumed I would have a better time on Normal. However even after switching still found the combat just as disappointing.
On the topic of in-game settings, not having the ability to remap buttons is less than ideal, but hey we're on Steam so we can do that ourselves I guess. Also would have appreciated the option to change the shield ability to hold-to-use rather than toggle, found it weird that I couldn't change that.
Last thing I will say is that Capt. Bodgan is the worst boss fight I've ever played that I can remember, hands down. Every time I felt like I was playing well I would be punished by some grenade bouncing off the wall and exploding in my face before I could react to it. The blast radius on everything in that fight feels larger than it should be, the AI seems to know where I was going to be at the end of my dash before I did, then proceed to shoot me in the face with a grenade before I get control of my character back, killing me at half-health.
There doesn't seem to be any identifiable hole in his behaviour pattern, making it hard to formulate any kind of plan. When he finally does stop firing, his shields immediately go up, reflecting any projectiles, and when you do get it down he starts launching grenades at your face again. Grendades that can kill you at half health shouldn't travel *that fast* AND explode on impact. One or the other, not both. All the issues with the AI design are very very apparent in that particular fight, because of the nature of his weapons and the environment.
Exploding a barrel when a boss is next to it feels very underwhelming, doing the same amount of damage it would have if I had just fired those bullets at the boss instead. The barrels feel more like environmental hazards than tools to be taken advantage of.
In summary, maybe I'm getting old at the ripe age of 24 and can't play shooters anymore, but to me RUINER feels more interested in punishing the player than entertaining them. Not in the Dark Souls challenging but fair kind of way either, in a ♥♥♥♥ you I'm the computer simulation and you're the lowly human kind of way. If that's your thing then pick it up by all means, but it's not what I'd call a satisfying game.

Owlboy is a 2D platform-adventure game with hints of Metroidvania, and absolutely oozing charm. The game is simply beautiful in every way a video game can be. When you first load up the game you witness the title screen, and I was immediately awed by it. Its an example of how you make a title screen. The game's gorgeous, hand-crafted visuals, and the amazingly well produced musical score are on parade here. When the introduction to the game ended and I found myself taking control in the starting area, the gleeful music and bright, colourful visuals put a huge smile on my face.
Of course its not just about the aesthetics of the game. The story is surprisingly good. Its full of mystery, heroism, has plenty of twists and turns, and was actually surprisingly dark in places. Satisfying to say the least. The gameplay is always the most important aspect of a video game though of course, and Owlboy succeeds in this area too. You could categorise Owlboy as a Metroidvania game; it contains the usual aspects such as: large 2D labyrinth-like areas, new abilities that you unlock which allow you to access new areas, and plenty of backtracking to find secrets, collectables, and new pathways. The combat definitely has a Metroid quality to it too. The main innovation in gameplay that Owlboy offers is that you are able to fly. This completely changes the way that 2D platforming works in the game, creating new challenges, puzzles, and combat scenarios that wouldn't be possible in the average 2D platformer. I also really like how you use your 'weapons' in the game. Its probably taken for granted but I simply have to credit to how clever and different it feels.
Owlboy is one a few games that left me awestruck. I found myself sayng "wow" a lot. Some games leave you with the feeling that you have experienced something truly special, and for me Owlboy was certainly one of those games.
9.5/10

The deck develops as you complete cards, giving more adventurecards (as a story that continues) or useful equipable items. You deal with 12 bosses, that will each appear at the end of a path of individual adventure cards that have to be encountered before the boss can be reached. A new deck can be selected and built before each boss, and changed in between attempts.
The game is extremely casual. Low consequences, many rewards, nice adventures. For layed back play before going to bed and for players who enjoy an adventure without being drowned in reading that adventure, but just want to play it.
Pro's:
-Nice role-playing mechanic. Easy to be absorbed into the story.
-Many (unknown) items to collect and a high variety of story cards make the early and mid part of the game fun!
-Dying has no consequence other than a restart of the level, so the game is not "hard" or frustrating in that sense.
-Rewards from completed adventure cards are also awarded when dying. So when the levels get hard, you still get rewards and are progressing in deckbuilding. Which adds to the casual factor of the game.
-Narrator is fun, not very repetitive (i.m.o.)
-I really enjoy the little metal coins that award new cards or items as you complete a cards adventure. Cool feature!
-Low specs alow for playing on relatively simple laptops and computers.
-Love the heap of artwork.
Con's:
-Game can rely on chance for progress, which can be slightly frustrating at times.
-Combat is quite cluncky and simplistic. (although real-time combat in such a game gives a nice depth and adds to player activity, compared to just drawing cards, and rolling dice.)
-Equipment could be more creative and extensive. Current situation: 1 weapon, shield, chest, helmet, gloves,  (wear multiple rings/trinkets, more gear slots like shoulder/belt/pants or add features like tattoos with small boost effects, add weapon upgrades upon completing adventures, add feature of combining two gloves: mainhand glove/shieldhand glove.)
-No character creation. You are a random dude...
I really love this game. The con's are forgivable and I'm looking forward to Hand of Fate 2, which is in the making. But I hope to finish this version before that.
