Recettear: An Item Shop's Tale is a game where you play as a young entrepreneur with immense monetary-related debt to a magical loan shark. The object of the game is to make enough money to meet each week's deadline and pay off the ever increasing amount. Despite this, Recettear: An Item Shop's Tale is a genuinely fun, cute, and surprisingly relaxing game. The game is split up into two core mechanics, shop management and dungeon crawling. The first being exactly what it sounds like. You decorate your shop, place items in key locations to attract customers, take orders, stock up on items, pay attention to item related trends, haggle, and BUY LOW AND SELL HIGH! The dungeoneering aspect revolves around your partnerships with a couple adventurers whom you control in the dungeons, going through levels in order to obtain loot to sell in your shop. There are 4 periods in a day: Morning, Noon, Evening, and Night. Certain places are only open on certain hours or on certain days. Due to how long it takes (2 periods), visiting the dungeon can only viably be done in the mornings. Due to this mechanic, I felt it necessary to start the game over once or twice because about 3 weeks in, I began to have trouble putting together the amount needed each week. It was only after consulting the wiki and guides that I was able to figure out how to spend each day wisely. Overall it's a very fun game. I would recommend tweaking the controls to your liking if you're playing with a keyboard as the game uses the default japanese layout for it's controls, or just play with a controller (that's the method I prefer).

This is a very fun and addictive game. However, if you don't have the right strategy it can become an extremely frustrating game. First, save a lot. Second, pay attention to announcements. When item prices go up, you can sell those particular items for up to 300% profit! When item prices go down, buy them cheap from the merchants - stock up! If you are going dungeoneering, enter the dungeon first thing in the morning because that takes 2 our of 4 time slots to complete. **Remember to spend your time slots wisely** Have at least 2 of each item-type because you never know when a customer will want them. Get to know your customers and the amount they can pay. To increase your merchant level faster, which is the most important thing to do besides making money, you will want to sell on the first try with back to back customers. Not only does that increase your level faster, it also makes the customers happy. Purchase different types of decor for your space as you will need to modify it to increase the number of customers who stop by to shop. Always ask Tear about the status of the shop's decor before you open your doors. On her grid, you want to be at the center. When certain items are in demand you can sell them for from 200-300% profit, depending on the customer. Finally, place the items you want to sell most by the North-facing windows. As your merchant level goes up, you will unlock new things. Take advantage when you can pay the weaponsmith to increase the size of your shop. I won the main game without purchasing Vending Machines. Not sure if they are a good investment. Is the game worth $19.99? Maybe, if you love haggling like a merchant, Japanese-style games with cute art and dialogue, crafting and making money. Otherwise, wait for a sale. Easily worth $9.99. Peace!

TL:DR version: read the bottom line.
If you grew up playing old school games like metroid or similar "metroidvania" games, or just simply enjoy those types of games you may find yourself looking at this game with curiosity. I certainly did.
I will tell you now, that you will likely be disappointed. The game itself is not terrible, though it doesn't really standout, or even stand-up to those old classics you may have played and thoroughly enjoyed. You will probably not get that proper feeling of nostalgic satisfaction, as this game does not have much in terms of content, no real upgrades, and very few secret or 'extra' things to find, which in my mind is the core part of any metroidvania game. None of the sort of hidden things are cool, or interesting. There are also no bosses. That's right, you simply fight the same enemies throughout the game with no real challenge, no climaxes.
The story itself is ok, but the final nail in the coffin of this game is the ending (no spoilers)...you essentially suffer through some bad level design, and ok gameplay to reach what you hope is some sort of epic, or at least intriguing/satisfying conclusion...instead what you get is, not a bad ending, not an unexpected ending, or dissatisfying ending storywise...no, what you get, is essentially an insult for finishing the game. It informs you of something that most of us already know about playing video games in general. It has nothing to do with the game. I have to say that with that ending, this was in fact the most dissatisfying gaming experience I have ever had. That is saying a lot. I have played thousands of games over the years, and plenty of them were not very good. But the ending to this just leaves an absolutely bitter taste in your mouth. I have to say, I beleive that is exactly what the developer intended.
Don't bother spending a cent on this, unless you enjoy torturing yourself.

A few words of preface: I was a beta tester of Polaris. My initial review was based on beta version, but  i played alrdy 40 hours of the realease one (i think i palyed about 200 hours of the beta, wasnt steeam version so not sure). It mostly reinforces what i alrdy wrote,  no changes needed in my review.
So I really liked Polaris. Its a great 4x war oriented game with good challenging AI. I played a lot of time just for fun during my beta testing, even in its beta state.
Despite liking to a degree both Sd2 and Galciv3 , im pretty sure i played Polaris a few times more then both Sd2 and Galciv3 combined.
+ The AI is good and challenging. Even in mid-late game  the AI can give you trouble. Seriously its one of the better AI i have seen. (I played on hard)
+  Great ship designing and tactical combat.
+  Through all the game there is  something called "doctrine change" . What it means that there is no overpowered weapon/modul/hull/tactic for long.  For example hvy fighters might seem   OP  for a while, but soon new techs/ modules will change the balance back to capital ships. Its really so great, keeps you on your toes and with a varied fleet.
+  The resources management : its pretty uniqe among games. You got  several mineral types and every module on your ships consumes different minerals, you got to plan this.
+ Help with micromanagment: you got governors , who do a fairly good job, and if you are a max efficency micro managing freak like me :) you can define template build orders, then just reuse them. Works grea.
+ Real time  with extensive, configurable notification system  is imho very good.  Im more of a turn based guy myself, but with that many notifications and with pasuable any time, i liked it a lot.
+ Long and varied tech tree.
+ Balanced tech/modules, there is no useless or uber modules like in many games.
The diplomacy is there with many options, but im not a very diplomatic guy :) so wont really judge it. The races art/backstories are pretty good.

So imho if you like war oriented 4x games with ship designing you really should like it.
Imho think twice and watch some more videos if:
1- In depth ship designing and tactical combat isnt really what you like in your 4x

TL;DR
Pros:
Relatively bugfree, easy to grasp mechanics, doesn't fling spreadsheets in your face at every occasion, easy to use UI, plays relatively fast.
Cons:
May be too simple for 4X vets.
Verdict:
For newcomers to the 4X genre I can give a strong recommendation. For most veterans though, this game may be too simple and I would strongly recommend you to take a look at Distant Worlds Universe.
Having played quite a bit of the old Alpha version of this game which used to be available on IndieDB, I think I can write a somewhat informed review of this game.
First of all, this game can be classified as a Realtime Pausable 4X game. It has all those elements into it. Diplomacy, exploration, conquest, empire building, etc.
The game clearly takes on a bit of a lighter footing than most 4X games. It will not shove massive spread-sheet like ui's in your face. It will not have a cumbersome UI which hampers your ability to play. As an added bonus, it has some decent automation features which allow you to focus on what's fun.
You start off with a basic homeplanet, low level technology and a single scoutship. Nothing weird or unusual here. Travel is done through starlanes (consumes fuel, non-instantaneous) or wormholes (occur randomly, instantaneous, don't cost fuel, unpredictable). The systems you will encounter contain several planets, each planet having a planet type and a size. The planet type will enable or disable various buildings, and modify production rates of items and resources. The size mostly dictates construction space available on the planet.
Colonization can be micro'd, but you can also just let the ai find a suitable place to build a colony ship and send it over, just by tapping a single buttom on the ui. This is one of the neat automation features which I like.
Resource management and economy is fairly simple, and will not bury you in spreadsheets. There's just a handful of resources, enough to fit in a small area on your screen. Resource management basically comes down to making sure you don't run out, and this comes down to setting up the right mining facilities on the planets containing these resources. Or you can just let the AI handle this by designating a planet as a mining colony. Nothing really fancy or unique there, except for the total absense of money as far as I could see (which seems logical to me in a space game actually, as USD would have little value to the Gavakens or so).
Research I find neatly done. Instead of picking a single technology to research, you allocate science points to different areas, and can split these between theoretical and applied sciences. I find this system neat because it offers a more logical and natural path of developing technology, compared to picking a single technology at a time.
Ship designing is in my opinion most comparable to stardrive's. You've got space on the hull where you can place modules on. Some will only allow weapons, others might only allow engines, etc. You won't place armor though, or power conduits. It just is the engines, power generators, weapons, shielding, support equipment (fuel tanks, cargo modules, troop drop pods, refueling modules, fuel generators, etc). The system is very straightforward and simple.
Combat is either auto resolved or fought manually. Battles are fairly simple realtime battles where you can order your ships around. To be honest I don't find much interesting of note in this, except for that it is simple, straightforward and it works well.
In terms of bugs, I did not find any so far. Even in its Alpha state it was relatively bugfree (although content and gameplay systems were mostly lacking back then). So not much else to say there.
Compared to the Alpha, this version feels way more enjoyable to play and better fleshed out. While this game is a bit too simple for myself, I do have a good general impression of it.

Though it was likely intended to create a sense of isolation, what Inescapable’s lack of music did to me was give me ample time to think.
Within its audio void, it became easy to see Inescapable’s various parts, how they fit and why they were there. And as I observed and seemed to spend more time analyzing than playing, a pattern began to appear, one which seemed to subliminally cry out “there is no point to any of this.”
Inescapable is a game built-in the image of the greats which came before it, most clearly Super Metroid, but it doesn’t know where to go beyond replicating elements that worked in other games. There’s a suffocating sense of routine running through Inescapable, each piece fitting cleanly in its designated space as if that alone gives it a purpose.
Monsters populate every hallway and cavern, upgrades section off parts of levels, and backtracking is used heavily as if to create an illusion of larger scale. But why? Why am I fighting so many of the same creature when shooting is neither fun nor gives any reward? What is the point of an upgrade with such a minimally used application? Why are levels so large if there’s nothing within them?
I don’t want to say that Inescapable was designed to waste your time, but it definitely feels intentionally drawn out for the sake of it. There is never an end goal to anything you’re doing beyond continuing to explore, to collect, to fight off the incessant monsters whose only real crime is forcing you to stop every few steps to take them out. It’s as if the game desperately wants to keep you playing to give it more time to find the reason you’ve been forced to run around so much. It doesn’t find it though, and what’s been put in place is such an earnestly fabricated attempt at relevance that I just wished Inescapable had come out with it at the start and saved us both the needless journey.

Alright, this is a bit of a wierd game for me to review. Let's start with explaining what the game is like. It's a geo-political historical simulator / real time strategy game. In layman's terms, it's a game where you rule over some dudes. If you've played Civilization, it's like that. If you've played Risk, imagine that but with a more immersive combat system, and more focus on KEEPING your countries, rather than getting them. The main draw to this game is that it has a very, and I mean VERY deep and complex "intrigue" system. This "intrigue" system, as it's refered to in-game, lets you control things from fixing succesion crisises (never was quite sure on the plural for that), killing off people who don't like you, diplomatically inheriting land, or just being a massive♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥to the surrounding countries and going to wars every 5 seconds, although this usually doesn't end too well. Now that I've laid the groundwork, let's look at some fancy numbered points, shall we?
Cons:
1.) A lot, and I mean a LOT of stuff in this game is DLC
2.) The game is $40 to begin with, simple graphical or audio DLCs are $2, and main ones are $8-15, so it's an investment
3.) It's got a BIG learning curve, you gotta put a lot of time if you wanna get good, or sit through hours of optionally tutorials
4.) It's a lot less fun without friends or mods of any kind, and getting friends to buy something this expensive is hard, and the multiplayer is difficult to get working, takes a long time to set up, and crashes from time to time
Pros:
1.) It's very historically accurate
2.) It takes a while to master, so if you enjoy it, you're probably going to get a lot of hours out of it
3.) It's got multiplayer, not the best multiplayer, but it's a thing
4.) It's addicting
5.) There's a lot of replay value, since things never go quite the same between runs
6.) If you're short on money, try tracking down someone willing to host a server for you with all the DLC instead of getting them yourself, since the guests don't need to have the host's DLC, and the server runs all DLC that the server owner has.
So, looking at everything, I enjoyed it, but I'd say unless you look at footage for the game, and maybe play the demo, don't buy it unless you have enough money to spare for you and possibly a friend. If you like Risk or Civilization, or pretty much ANY games by Paradox, you'll probably like this. I reccomend it overall, but this is DEFINITELY a try-before-you-buy.

This game is good. I've spent a lot of time playing it over the past few months (beta testing and all that) and I'm glad to see it has finally been released. I provide 2 versions of reviews, a first impressions video version and a written version. A little something for both camps.
Gameplay Footage:
So let's get right down to business. What is Polaris Sector? Polaris Sector is a 4x Real-time Grand Strategy game in the same vein as Distant World: Universe or a real time version of Space Empires or even Endless Space. It features a real-time battle system where you command ships and fighters against pirates and all manner of Xenos Scum. There are 9 races which all feature unique ship types and can be customized via point distribution in over 13 passive buffs. As is usual with these sorts of games, you have research (an exhaustingly extensive research tree might I add), exploration, espionage and ship customization. You can also rename planets and systems. It's your standard run of the mill 4x Space game.
What sets it a part from other games of the same vein?
Not much to be honest but it does something very well that a lot of 4x Space Strategy games forget... it feels streamlined and the gameplay is relatively fast paced. You always have something to do but because you can just pause the game or slow the speed to a crawl, you never feel overwhelmed. What's better, is a lot of the processes can be automated like planet colonization, invasion planning or just building up your planets so the game doesn't become overly tedious. You've also got about 6 resources that you have to manage. While that may seem like a lot for this type of game, it's surprisingly not. It's fun trying to find planets that produce the resources you need and meeting production. For a one man project, this game feels INSANELY well done.
What's wrong with the game?
Not much. The game itself is pretty fine tuned. There are few things that bother me with this game like the overpowered fighters. It doesn't seem to matter how technologically advanced your ships are, fighters are practically impossible to beat in large numbers. Seriously, just field a fleet with about 10-20 carriers and build 200 fights with heavy ion guns and I guarantee there is nothing that can stop you. I'd recommend bringing down the power of fighters considerably as they are just a cheap tactic at this stage in the game.
The game can also feel a bit tedious later on. For example, in the later stages of the game, it can become a bit tedious having to colonize everything or invading large empires (but remember you can automate that process so that's just me being too lazy to automate it).
In summation, this is a solid 4x Real-Time Space Strategy game that I've really enjoyed my time with. The streamlined and relatively fast pace at which the game flows means I happily spend dozens of hours glued to the screen managing my little Space Empire. I highly recommend this one for fans of the 4x genre.

This is a mild recommendation with some hesitation.
Inescapable is a short (90-120 minute) puzzle platformer in the basic style of a Metroidvania (new areas are unlocked as you get upgrades or items). I would say its look is inspired by early PC or Amiga games, its tone is inspired by lonely sci-fi like The Dig, and its platforming is inspired by games like Flashback, Blackthorne, or Prince of Persia. I liked all three of those things and that's in large part why I'm recommending the game. It tells the story of a mining company ship that crash-lands on a planet and what your player character finds on the surface. Combat is a secondary focus, primarily you just platform and solve puzzles.
My hesitations: The game's default control bindings on a controller are poor, so you'll want to rebind them. The game is short and ends somewhat abruptly. The controls don't quite have the precision they need for some of the late game platforming. But the serious limitation is that the game does not have a map or minimap--for a Metroidvania, this is a problem. Often times, I'd get a new item and say "okay, I need to go find this room to use it"... and then spent a while trying to actually find the room. This could have been mitigated if I kept a paper map, but I didn't because I didn't know I'd need to until it was too late.
I disagree with some of the feedback from other reviews: At the time I played the game, it did not have unavoidable fall damage for most of the game. Items were always clear to me.
I just wanted to end with a little discussion of the plot or theme. The ending is basically an extended quote from David Foster Wallace about the nature of heroism. I did find it interesting, and it did connect to the game in a tangential way... but I couldn't help but feel that the game could do more to earn this critical perspective. It's a pity, because I really liked the text and lore throughout the game and wish there were a little more of it, building towards the ending.
At the time I played the game it did not have achievements or cards, so playing the game is a one-and-done. Again, my verdict is a very mild recommendation and I recommend you read carefully to understand whether you'd like the same things about it as I did.

I had fun with this - its the first game I touched after powering through Breath of the Wild on Wii U for 100+ hours, and it was a great change of pace going back to some 2D roots with easy-on-the-eyes graphics.
The story has its heartbeats, and other moments that fall short of their intended impact, but I was hooked from the very first cutscene when your competence as the character is insulted and it riled up emotions of "oh, just watch this". I felt obligated to carry it through because I felt enough of a connection with the main character even in the first few minutes to carry him through his quest, and to prove to the ones who said I wouldn't amount to anything wrong.
The gameplay has some occasionally frustrating control issues, although not bad. I played through this entirely with an 8bitdo NES30 Pro controller (the one with the analog sticks) and this was the first game I really spent time with that controller on and I had a great time. Its nice that you can spam pretty much every movement control you have, so hammering on the roll button mid-air feels like it really gets you moving, even if holding it down may have had the overall same effect.
This game is definitely worth a playthrough, and for a completionist, you could be done with this game in an easy 15 hours, even taking a relatively easy pace like I did, backtracking and collecting everything you may have missed. A couple of the hidden achievements are timing/event-specific in the story, so I'll need to restart a new game to get those knocked out.
TLDR: Good game with some occasional story flops, minor control hitches, and good cast that you care enough about to see them through to the end of the game. Not sure I'd pay full price ($25 at the moment), but definitely worth picking up on sale at $15 or lower. Have fun!
P.S. I got this game as a gift from a friend, so it was free for me.

Valkyria Chronicles was a hidden gem for me. Shooters aren't my thing and everything with modern weapons such as tanks and machine guns has a rather hard time with me. Not that such games are bad or anything I just don't like them. Just my individual preference. So this game had a rather hard start for me:
I have grown rather fond of the graphics over time but I wasn't impressed at all at the first glance. The painted style turned out to look better and more endearing than I thought both in cutscenes and actual gameplay. The map you choose your characters to move could have been a little differently designed but that's really nitpicking. It was an interessting gamble with the graphics I'd say and it paid off, at least in my books.
The Gameplay takes some getting used to, since I expected a turn based strategy game and Valkyria chronicles has a way of switching between a tactical map (where you can spend your command-points (CP) to move your units and end your turn if you either run  out of CPs or don't want to move anyone) and an action map (where you control the single unit itself moving him/her over the battlefield aiming and shooting yourself). While in action mode enemy units greet you whenever they can with interception fire, while you have to switch to "target mode" first before you can fire back which is kinda not nice. Once you know the ropes however everything falls into place quiet nicely and the game is a lot of fun.
Downsides are in my books that the balancing and rating are off. Speed is everything. You'll get an A-Rank for a mission if you complete it in like 2 turns while other factors like casualties on your side or number of killed enemies do have little effect (if they have an effect at all)  and that motivates only to scout-rush-tactics after all high rankings means more funds and exp. As for the balancing: Good thing is that each class is useful. Considering the rushs scouts are properly the most useful, but the rest can hardly be dismissed. Your protagonist however can use "commands" (special abillities) to do pretty much whatever. he can heal units in calling a medic, boost a units offense or defense (however that works) lower damage from interception fire or give special boosts against tanks or make a unit aim better. While a like it to have such abillities and like to get some noticeable effect out of them in this game they seemed to be a little OP.
The Story is set in an alternate-universe-Europe called Europa and the time is WW2 (here EW2 - Europan War 2) and many links to the real history exist ("ragnite" is a mineral that takes the place of oil/petroleum as a rare ressource and so on) but some things are quite different as well: in this war aerial combat isn't a thing at all.
This isn't exactly my cup of tea either but it was done nicely.
You don't actually fight the war in it's entirety but only a small part of it and your not an all great hero, but a mere squad leader although you are meant to pull off some miracles (but that's a protagonist for you.) (I like that, you can't be everywhere doing everything)
The characters are rather well done and the overall story - while nothing special - isn't bad.
I got surprised by the game in a good way. I bought it only because it was discounted and was like "let's give it a try. If it is bad, then I didn't waste much money on it."
Looking back, that game is well worth even the full price.
It has a few set backs but makes more than up for them.

This is not a masterpiece. The soundtrack is great, the art style is great, but everything else is pretty lackluster. The game is far too linear and lacks any real depth to the story and the combat and puzzle mechanics.
The story is simple. You play Otus, a mute owl who manages to save the day numerous times despite everyone blaming him for everything going wrong in the first place. You battle some power-hungry robot pirates and stop the world from ending, as all good protagonists do. Except, all of this is done in a rush from one plot point to another. There is no open world to explore and learn more about, just several large spaces in between each plot point. The characters you meet don't prop up the story and really add much to it besides one, and even worse, none of them have real backstories. You can't even have conversations with them because Otus is mute. The only real worldbuilding done in this game is the bits and pieces you're fed as you push the plot forward.
The most aggregious thing they do is tease you with the possibility of greater things. There's a particular point where everything felt like it was about to open up and the game was really going to begin. You go through a pretty great action sequence fighting pirates attacking the city of Advent and just as you're getting all excited to see it... BOOM! It's gone. Conveniently, only the few characters you meet fighting the pirates survive, but you get nothing more out of them when it's over.
The combat seems interesting at first, but the novelty wears off quick. You only get three different characters to carry around, and maybe the most interesting one to play with comes pretty late in the game. Honestly, the game would have been far better if Otus just carried the weapons himself. Carrying characters around is clunky, and the sparse challenges you face throughout the game don't compliment it enough to justify it being there.

Owlboy is a game I would honestly describe as "boring." Of all of the things it has going on, none of it is terribly interesting. While nothing is outright terrible, I found that the okay parts didn't carry the game.
People describe it as a "Medtriodvania" but it's so incredibly linear I'm not sure how it earned that title. That isn't a complaint - there's nothing wrong with being linear - but I was confused.
As far as actual complaints go, everything else. Again, none of the elements are completely awful, but none of them are spectacular either. It's a 2D platformer of sorts, except you can fly infinitely. This makes coming up with obstacles difficult, and so the hazards in your basically boils down to either flying enemies or projectiles. You fight enemies by shooting them, and dodge attacks by flying around. So basically, it's less of a platformer and more of a twin-stick shooter, except a bad one. The "bullet hell" just isn't there. I know that's not at all what they were going for, but the enemy patterns seem reminiscent of other platformers, except in most platformers you can't fly, so what they were going for doesn't quite work. Almost every group of enemies is laughably easy to avoid - just fly around them. There are a few rooms where it locks you in until you've defeated all of the enemies, at least. This forces you to use the shooting mechanic, but unfortunately, it isn't super fun. It's rather difficult, but certainly not challenging.
You see, in order to shoot, you need to be carrying a friend who has a gun. But there are certain melee attacks you can only preform when you're not carrying a friend. Furthermore, different friends have different guns. This makes combat a huge hassle. The game largely solves this by having buttons to instantly teleport friends to you, as well as instantly switch between friends, but now you have way too many functions to do what should be the simple task of shooting enemies. This system is way too complicated and accomplishes nothing. The same number of moves could be achieved with a much more intuitive control scheme, except that because the shooting mechanic revolves around carrying allies who have guns (for story reasons I guess?), dropping them and switching between them is a whole new layer of controls without a new layer of actual mechanics. When the controls aren't in the way, the combat is incredibly easy, but this roundabout control scheme often makes preforming simple tasks difficult.
Now, this by itself isn't a total dealbreaker. While it is clunky and unintuitive, you can get used to it. It's not so horrendous that you can't master it anyway and enjoy controling the character. But to master a clumsy control scheme when the combat is mediocore is simply not worth the time. The game does nothing worthy of such a complicated combat system, because the combat itself remains rather simple.
A potential use for this otherwise unnecessary combat system is they could have puzzle mechanics that would require you to drop a friend to carry something else, meaning you're without a weapon, but this is hardly an upside because the puzzles are usually a letdown. It's almost always carry thing from point A to point B with little to no challenge. The one time I can recall ever having to stop and figure something out was because I didn't know what an object did, but once I figured that out the puzzle revealed itself to be another case of carry stuff around until a door opens.
There's also a strange abundance of stealth sections. None of them fun. Some are frustrating, but I was surprsied to find not all of them were. The worst offender was a stealth section were you have to avoid being detected by not flying (because the enemies could hear your wingbeats). This was infuriating, because the jump button and the fly button are actually the same button (you just double press it/hold it down to start flying). It was painfully easy to fly by mistake, which made the entire section almost unbearable. Fortunately, not every stealth section was that bad. Unfortunately, none of them were that good, either.
So at the end of everything, since platforming doesn't exist and avoiding enemies/projectiles is usually easy, the only obstacle we're left with is doors locked either by frustrating combat or boring puzzles, with the occasional unwanted stealth segment. So the only thing left is the story...
It's not great. It starts off with your character being bullied and scolded by his mentor in the most ham-fisted "feel bad for main character" possible so that he can be the underdog who saves the day later. That's basically the extent of the story, and yet the game interrupts you all the time for cutscenes and dialogue and story. I'm having toruble remembering the last time I became as frustrated with how frequent the story interrupts the gameplay. I honestly grew to resent the characters because they wouldn't shut up.
As sad as it makes me, the only nice thing I can say without feeling dishonest is that the game is pretty. Not to say everything is super memorable, but the art is very high quality and looks gorgeous. Otus' design is solid, the animation is fliud, and the sound design is great as well. It's unfortunate that such pretty wrapping is hiding a fairly mediocore play experience.

Fun platforming adventure game that's got just the right amount of challenge.
To start things off, the pace of the game is very consistent, and the story flows well, so there aren't any moments where it feels drab or boring. Even though it took me 9 hours to complete, it didn't feel like it. It's a game that you could probably finish in 7 or 8 hours if you rushed, but taking the time to explore will grant you special unlocks to make the game slightly easier, but nothing that means its otherwise unplayable, and adds some extra story.
The art and animations remind me a lot of Metal Slug, which means that the game is well animated, there's lots of detail, and it's very colourful. Speaking of Metal Slug, this game definitely evokes a 90s game feel, so there's something in it for gamers of that time.
I don't know if there's anything too bad about the game, I mean I certainly have problems with it but they're nothing game breaking, and it's mostly a learning curve with the controls.
To start off with the controls, having the pick up and drop, and attack button be separate is quite frustrating. I don't really see why the left mouse button could've been solely for pick up and attack, whilst the right mouse button is for drop only, instead of it being pick up and drop, so I often found myself throwing my teammates instead of using them, which isn't a good thing in a boss battle.
Speaking of boss battles, sometimes it's a bit annoying when there's still dialogue after you skip a cutscene, because if it's a boss battle you want to jump straight back into it instead of having to wait a bit before you can, although it doesn't happen too often and its a part of the type of game it is.
Gameplay/mechanics wise spawning/teleporting in your teammates with the middle mouse button isn't very ideal if you're trying to shoot quickly, and switching between characters with a different button instead of simply scrolling the middle mouse button can get quite confusing, as not only is it a key (the 'E' key specifically), but it also spawns the other characters, so that gets a bit annoying from time to time when you're trying to spawn in a chracter but accidently hit 'E' so then you have to cycle back to the character you wanted, which often times results in you taking damage from an enemy hit.
Twig can also be quite annoying to use because if his dual-action, action button, so when you're trying to do one thing you can end up doing the other, and in a tense situation it gets quite confusing.
The story isn't as rich as it could've been, but its still interesting and fun.
To end it off, I will say that I don't see myself purchasing this game outside of a sale that makes it ~$15 (~$10 US) or about half off its current price ($30). So if you can get it on sale, I'd suggest you do so, because overall it's a good game. 7/10.

Hard Reset is an old-school FPS shooter with a heavy dose of cyberpunk. As Major Fletcher in the year 2436, you have to defend Bezoar city - humanity’s last sanctuary from an unrelenting hoard of machines, while uncovering a more sinister plot unrevealing in the background. To do so you have two state of the art rifles at your disposal, one based upon kinetic projectiles and the other based upon futuristic energy tech.
There is no cover system and no crouching, this means quick decisive action is the main style of play. By upgrading your weapons with various modules, you can unlock different firing modes; such as shotgun and rockets for the kinetic rifle, or lightning and homing plasma for the energy rifle. There are no handholding tutorials either, so you have to figure out how best to utilise each module against your enemies. Learning to think on your feet is essential.
You can draw good comparisons between this and the Painkiller series, with each stage divided in multiple sections, defended by waves of robots; progress is inhibited until every last bit of those cursed bots are put down for good. So if you never liked playing Painkiller, this probably won’t fare much better with you.
Bezoar is a vibrant city with many dangers lurking every corner, hovercrafts blanketed the skies as neon billiards flickered under the heavy rain. Every stage is unique and distinct from one another, you can tell a lot of attention was placed in level designs. Which is a shame since the cityscape is mostly devoid of life and you will never see many people during game play, the robot menace are fairly uncreative too and they tend to become bullet sponges later on.
The main game consists of 7 levels while the free Exile DLC bought that up to 12. An initial play through lasts around 7-12 hours to complete, while it will take at least 40 hours or more if you aim to complete every achievement. An arena mode exists but it isn’t fully integrated with the Steam leader boards, so I didn’t bother much with it.
Lastly, a “re-mastered” version was released called “Redux”. Logic would assume that Redux will be superior, but with arguable improvements on graphics, a gimmicky “cyber katana” that added no value to actual game play, a seriously dumb down level of difficulty for console babies and no additional modes or levels, you are probably better off buying this cheaper version for now.
In conclusion Hard Reset is an underappreciated gem that can be a bit rough on the edges, but it is ultimately an enjoyable experience to play and a refreshing take on the old school formula. All FPS enthusiasts should look out for it during sales.

Short version:
--------------------------------------
Good Puppy!:
+Challenging, even on normal difficulty. Mobs can kill you pretty easily if you aren't quick to move or block their attacks.
+Very fast combat, Hotline Miami-ish but restricted to 'wave-defense' in a single moderately big room.
+You don't need a controller to play it. I only used keyboard+mouse and it went excellent.
+A good variety of ranged weapons, from pistols to shotguns to miniguns to railcannons.
+You're nicknamed "puppy" :)
+It's actually really entertaining when you learn the controls and dash'n'slash.
+About 15 skills to level up as you progress.
+You can level up and level down each skill with no repercussions.
----------
Neutral Puppy:
Soundtrack could see some improvement in my opinion.
Ending might leave you confused about a few things, doesn't really explain very well what is what and why. Might be on purpose, though.
Level design could've done better.
Normal late-game enemies should be a bit more harder in my opinion, to still present a challenge to the player. Played it on normal, so maybe this point isn't really valid.
----------
Bad Puppy!:
-Flashbang skill affects bosses. Who thought this'd be a good idea? I know you can just not level it, but still :P
-Some guns don't seem to deal as much damage as you'd expect them to, or some others seem sort of useless (or very situational. If you've played the last level you probably know which one I'm talking about!)
-Melee attacks are very powerful in contrast to ranged weapons. Since you can close the distance on an enemy in pretty much an instant, it's way better to go melee than ranged. You'll probably kill them faster and not take that much damage.
-Not long by any means. Finished it on normal difficulty under 8 hours.
--------------------------------------

Long version:
Aight. Finished the game a few hours ago; it's pretty good to be honest.
It's challenging, even on -normal- difficulty (I'll try Hard difficulty later on) you'll die quite some even to the non-bosses, there's about 2-3 skills for each ability hotkey (I think Right click, Q, and shift) and about 4-5 'passives' or 'actives' abilities that give you another hotkey to use.
You can spend AND remove points with no backlash to your decisions, so that's really nice. Storyline seems pretty good- not perfect, but still good. I do feel like the ending could've used a bit of an improvement, as well as the soundtrack?
Don't get me wrong, soundtrack wasn't bad at all, but in a game where you're slashing, dashing, and slashing and dashing, and dashing and slashing- well, you might want something that doesn't seem very ambient-ish and more active, at least in my opinion.
Now- bosses... nothing special, other than them having massive HP and maybe a bit more damage/combos and whatnot. Maybe this could've been polished a bit more, but hey, it wasn't bad either!
Btw. You can flashbang bosses. This leaves them stunned for about 2 seconds or 3 in which you can constantly slash at them, lol. Why. It sorta drains your energy though, but you can upgrade that skill so it drains 50% less. So pretty much, with only that upgraded skill and max energy before initiating boss battle, yep, you can cheese 90% of the bosses. (Except three or four.)
Ranged weapons don't seem all that great compared to melee, except for a few ones which are amazing to use (yes, I'm looking straight at you, Lancer, Sonic Gun and Raijin! I'd have a foursome with you three anyday.)
This game is fun  for everyone, unless you are lazy to read. I am impressed

If you're looking for a game with a definitive and captivating style, then RUINER is for you. The environments are always active with vivid imagery that immerses you in the world of RUINER. The soundtrack hits all the right notes, amping up in combat, coupled with the comforting music of the hub world. The game slows down to show off your moves, bullets flying through the air as you and your enemies dash around the arena.
So, presentation wise, this game hits all the right notes.
But, how does the gameplay hold up? It's intense and fast-paced, so much so you could quickly lose track of enemies, especially in the later half of the game, where enemies gain access to many of your own tools. If you were expecting the sort of gameplay found in Hotline Miami, you'll quickly find that RUINER isn't quite as cutthroat. Enemies and bosses will have lengthy health bars, and won't run mindlessly into your attacks. It's a real test of your reflexes, and when it's good, it's great.
But it isn't always great. I played the game on Hard Mode, as was reccomended. On Hard, some of the bosses become ridiculously difficult, cuing many resets. While this isn't necessarily a bad thing, what I found discouraging was how this difficulty was undermined by playing the game in a rather 'boring' way. Rather than use the many tools that are given to you by the game, the optimal strategy was to simply walk backwards and shoot in the general direction of the boss, dashing every so often and slowly whittling down the health.
There are also some aspects of the game that are lacking, such as the hub world. You don't do much in the hub, as all of your upgrading is done via a menu. You simply do a few 'side quests' here, either turning in collectibles or finding hidden things around the map, and then you're quickly done with the hub, only after returning to it twice during the course of the game. Weapon variety is great, but you quickly begin to choose a few guns over others, as they're simply more effective, and melee stands as the most reliable option for combat.
The story isn't jaw dropping or riveting, so don't expect some narrative masterpiece. You could write it off as simply being a tale of revenge, and the "You are being played," tagline sort of spoils the story. In short, you can more or less expect what's coming next.
Technically, there were some audio issues during loading, but otherwise, the game had ran perfectly. I didn't experience any glitches until near the end of the game, including one annoying glitch where a drop pod that was 20 meters off killed me instantly, and another where I was stuck to a pile swarmed with enemies during the final boss fight.
In summary, the game is great for any fans of the cyberpunk genre. The style is definitely its strongest trait, and for $20, I'd say RUINER is definitely a great experience, though it is definitely lacking in some areas.

As someone that played the original DK from Bullfrog, and the Keeper FX, DK2 I can say that for those old fans looking for some nostalgia this is certainly it.

The voice acting is superb and many comment just for that, lots of humor in the game and quirky stuff. I like that you guys added that when you play after midnight. There is that old nostalgia feeling in the game.
I can see that the developers are taking a huge effort to  listen to us as I have seen on the forums, they are repairing and creating something new along the way. Really good job on the artist for creatures I must say.
Before going to the bad parts, I must say that this game is largerly in development and as it currently is I am giving it a 7/10.
More points scored just because it is what it is. And its a new Dungeon keeper game.
However... The game mechanics are feeling very cluncky and possesing a creature,walking around and attacking certainly needs a lot of work to it.
The creatures themselves are awesome, I would like to nitpick that some of them are really.. Well.. Just not right in my book. Would love to see something like the Bile demon once more, more spiderlings and insect like creratures.
Dragons anyone?
The spells are a huge forward in the game and there is so much to have fun with , but there needs to be balancing in it, Mana is my problem currently as while casting anything makes a delay in your mana pool and waiting for those 5-7 seconds just to have a bit more mana is a little bit frustrating.
The main missions are NOT enough and I hope there will be more added, Most of them get laggy and drop the FPS to a low 20 or 15 for some reason. I have not noticed any problems doing Skirmishes so there must be something wrong in the main missions themselves.
Creature hitbox, Sudden disappearance of my evil minions is frustrtating and some spells need to be checked ( like the alchemy spell that creates gold on dirt blocks)
Last but not least.. One of the things that really frustrate me is the inabilty to actually stay safe in your dungeon, with the added constructs any evil doer or hero can just barge in your dungeon. I would love fortifications in here. Just hold on to my base like in the good old times and come out when I'm ready.. But then again this adds some spice to the game and you can add dirt blocks now,and that is damn awesome!
Overall, if you are that old DK player looking for a fix. Look no further. This is it.
Just don't be surprised of the glitches and bugs that are in here. It may make you a little bit frustrated at times.
They are working hard on the game, consantly patching it up. Wait for a while or simply go play it now.
I am more then certain that you will come back to it all over again.

I might not yet played long enough in release version, but even from my experience as playtester, it is very, very descent game. RP possibilities are endless, starting from the chararcter creation, where you can make your own Human, Elf, Dwarf, Lizard, an Undead version of each (later on the concept of Undead and why it's so greatly implemented), or choose from 6 Origin stories, prewritten and fully voiced, with their unique traits and dialogue options.
The Undead is, perhaprs, the best adaptation of skeletons as a game race so far. Not only you can't use standart healing because you will take damage, but you also must cover yourself fully when near cities or other NPC's for they are afraid of the undead.
The dialogue options are wide, with each line you have at least 4 (minus dialogue ending lines) choices, which differ in tone and attitude towards the person you're talking. Many unnecessary battles can be  avoided with clever answers and success in persuasion attempts. Ah, and if you don't know already - they are fully voiced.
Now to the exploration part. Oh boy, it's endless. You will spend good third of the playthrough in the starting locations becuse "oh, look, a hidden passahe! oh, i can teleport some1 here, so they will loot the chest! what did you say? people in danger? I'm coming!". The last game where I dwelled so far from the main quest because of that was The Witcher 3.
Quest system might look difficult, because of the lack (not to say abscence) of quest markers or straight tasks. Get ready to use all your detective skills to get somewhere, find someone or something. That system brings more joy upon completing the quest, as you figured everything by yourself.
Now, to the combat part. It's turn-based. If you hate that - you will be disappointed. But despite that, it's a great tactical combat, where you have to carefully plan every move. There are plenty of different barrels, surface types and other enviromental aspects which can help to turn combat for your advantage, or be the death of you all if forgotten about.
Graphical part of the game is just beautiful. From character models to animation, everything is masterly done. Game made a great progress since the first part, now it looks refined, polished and detailed, unlike cartoon-like feeling which the first DOS gave me.

TL;DR
Great graphics
Great gameplay
Great questline and writing
Mastercrafted orchestral soundtrack
10/10, helped to cure my post-Witcher trauma

I'll start off by saying I reccomend playing Dreadout, I think the game was a lot of fun, succeeded in creating a scary atmosphere, and showed off a lot of really good ideas. The game has this charm to it that easily wins you over, from the strange script to the unique ghosts to the amusing menu prompts ("Will You Return to the Land of the Living?" makes me smile every time I click to exit the game). There was a lot of work, love, and thought put into this game and I think you'll pick up on that while exploring eerie environments to seek out pictures, items, and rifle through your Ghost Journal.
The game does have it's problems, such as unintuitive puzzles and fights, and I had to restart the game once because of a bug I couldn't find a fix for. For the puzzles even when the answer is revealed it can feel like you've taken a step back in understanding because of just how off the wall the solution was (I think anyone who played the game will know the exact puzzle I'm writing about).
What this game has in issues though it makes up for with all the other features. The combat is smooth and enjoyable, enemies and scares are, well, scary, and the lore is really interesting and provides new insight into the game and the inspirations it pulls from. The game also offers plenty to do and if you like exploring then this game has just enough to keep you interested while also keeping you on track for the main story.
This game is worth your time and money, and the team that worked on this deserve recognition for a well made game. Please try DreadOut!

- If first impressions are important then this game fails. Within the first 10 minutes of the game I experienced a game breaking bug forcing me to look online and then eventually having to restart and try again.

- Puzzles are too obtuse

Conclusion:
This game falls in that grey area between good and bad. It has some good qualities but also has some bad. I have to give this game a thumbs down because there are much better survival horrors game you can play.

Things not conductive to a good Metroidvania experience:
1. Unresponsive controls.
2. No map.
3. A weak inventory system and no idea what items do until you have used them.
4. Instantly kicking you back to the menu when you die to one of the many instant death instances.
5. Unavoidable fall damage.
6. No ability to look down in a game filled with spiked death pits.
7. Unavoidable fall damage while falling between instant death spikes in a game that kicks you back to the main menu when you die. Oh yeah, and you can't look down so it's all trial and error. Seriously, is this a Metroidvania game or a slow, unresponsive, and utterly annoying Super Meat Boy?
All told, I kind of dig the old school graphics and the story (what little there is) seems interesting, but I can only replay the same sections so many times trying to memorize really annoying death laden jumps with unresponsive controls for so long before I have to admit that I'm not having fun. If this game had the ability to look down I would recommend it despite the bad controls, but as it is the bulk of the gameplay is just repeating the same thing over and over while you try and overcome bad controls and bad level design.

This game has no redeeming features, the gameplay is plain and oversimplified, the level design is lazy and repetitive, the puzzles are mostly based on backtracking and serve no purpose other than to make game last longer (it still takes only 2 and a half hours to finish though), the combat is oversimplistic and offers no real challenge at all, the enemies have no AI and are all of only 3 different types and the plot is cut short by an unsatisfying ending right when it was beginning to build up.
The store page says this game has an intriguing storyline and a though provoking ending, but those two things are not true. The plot does not thicken or develops enough to the point were the story becomes complex and interesting and the 'ending' is composed of nothing more than a random quote that (while itself alone is indeed full of insight) hardly has any correlation to the rest of the game and serves no other purpose than to give the game an undeserved sense of depth. If this game had the right to be called intriguing and insightful then if I were to make rom hack of a random NES game and put a quote of Plato in the ending then that rom hack should also have the right to be called intriguing and insightful.
Inescapable is nothing more than a lazy game that makes a generally poor, boring and unfinished application of the old metroidvania formula and that despite it's claims of having a meaningful plot, does not really manages to build a interesting story with anything resembling a climatic ending.

This is a game about Iteration.
If you like attempting a process/workflow, seeing the results and then trying to do it again but better than this game is for you.
I say this because I work for a tech company, love my job, and see a mirror of what I do at work in this game - only it's much more fun!  This is a developer's game.

Want to be an awesome Barbarrian King and conquer the world?  Go ahead!  Oh, you died and now are playing as your spoiled son?  Will the bloodthirsty, barbarian generals your father put in power respect and obey you?  I highly doubt it.  Maybe next time you'll arrange for one of those generals to be your heir insted.

I wrote a somewhat witty and not all that funny review about 2 years ago, after playing about 20 - 30 hours. It's time to give CK2 a proper review.
I recently argued with a colleague if CK2 or EU4 is the better game. He never played CK2 and I didn't play EU4, so it was less about finding a concensus or comparing the games, but who had more passion for 'his' game.
My final argument was, that CK2 would be the "if you are stranded on a remote island and could only have one game with you"-game. Because this game is never the same, it is always different and it is always engaging.
This is a game where you don't win by conquering the world. You don't need to expand your country. If you start as the King of an empire or the chief of some holding in the middle of nowhere, you decide what you want to do. You make your own game and your own story.
Let the stats and traits of your ruler decide your way and CK2 is more like a "Sandbox RPG roguelike" than what you expect from a strategy game.
Only set up marriages with 'lustfull' women and marry off your family members to further your dynasty and lineage and wonder when you get a message from the king of Spain calling you uncle.
War in CK2 is unreliable and messy (one of the few let downs of the game) - so why not foster peace? Make everyone around you a friend and raise their opinions of you, and you don't even need to wage war.
Or unite all norse chiefdoms, create the scandinavian empire, reform their pagan belief into a religion, set up a merchant republic to controll all trade from Estonia to Ireland and have the pope declare holy war on you.
Sure, you can marry your aunt and take your grandmother as a concubine while plotting to have your nephew murdered. That too can be a part of you medieval life. That are the stories you hear about. That isn't what the game is solely about.
It's a game where you tell a new story, everytime you start it.

Otus is a young Owl - member of a proud group that includes both humans with owlike features using special cloaks to fly and athrophormized owls as well. He lives in a small village on one of the floating islands but isn't doing well in his training. In fact, his mentor is so bad that poor boy, already a mute, clearly has a low sense of self-worth. His life, however, changes when one day his village is attacked by the sky pirates, setting him and his best friend Geddy on a quest to determine the fate of the whole world.
Owlboy is a retro throwback to multiple different genres that went kinda out of style with time. On the storytelling side, it's a high fantasy of unlikely heroes saving the world, in style of old Zelda and Final Fantasy (before they became all cinematic) games. But with more inner coherence to the setting, as various things that would usually stand out like robots and guns next to magical creatures all have roots in secrets left by the Ancient Owls, secrets Otus and his friends will discover along the way. The storytelling aspect of the world is completed thanks to both the stunning graphics that give it unique, warm feeling and breathtaking music. The story is basic but told using all the right trick to make you fall in love with the cast of odd characters and feel emotional as the story progresses. It also uses various events you could have expected in this type of tale to make the gameplay more varied, spicing it up with various sequences. Sneaking behind pirate robots, running from a giant robot frog, desperately looking for a light to ward off flesh-eating bugs, the adventure will not leave you bored. The pacing is so good you will, in fact, feel regret the chances for this to become an animated cartoon or anime series that would capture the spirit of the original are so slim.
The gameplay itself is happily borrowing from old titles. It is a platformer that sometimes throws you at a boss in closed space, whose weakness or pattern you have to figure out to beat, not unlikely say, classic Megaman, But it is also a flying shooter where you can defeat enemies and solve puzzles using guns carried by one of Otus' three allies he's literally carrying into combat. But where it differs from games that blindly try to copy old titles (*couch*MightyNo9*cough*) is the inclusion of Otus' ability to fly that completely reshapes the way a player thinks of the field around them and operates in presented framework. It is such an amazing experience that when it is taken away from you near the very end of the game, being forced to return to old paradigm for a longer moment feels jarring and you welcome the boss battle that means it you can spread your wings again.
Great fun, and well worth the wait. Lots to do and tons to unlock... Glad to be finally able to support the original devs of this creative fusion of roguelike and puzzle game.

I beat the game in a sleepless 20 hours after launch!
Overall Ruiner was worth it, and while it was an excellent game, it fell a little short in some areas that would've made it perfect.  I recommend buying this game, although perhaps not as wholeheartedly as I would've wished.
Pros:
-combat is exceptionally satisfying and responsive (I love being able to dash, dodge, and shield, get a stun and some sword slashes in)
-aesthetically, the game is gorgeous in every respect (including the gameplay, video cutscenes, and anime-like dialogues)
-character abilities can be easily changed on the fly (which makes for some cool puzzles where you try to figure out what the optimal build is to beat a certain boss or enemy type)
-brutally difficult, even on normal difficulty (I like games that offer enjoyable challenges)
Cons:
-too many badly designed bosses (bosses only had one pattern and many of them felt like an awkward grind; I would've hoped for multi or alternating attack-pattern bosses with weak enemy adds, as that would be more interesting to make use of all the cool skills Ruiner has to offer, for example, some skills depend on you killing a bunch of enemies to proc, while most boss fights were just you vs boss)
-no keyboard remap (I use a dvorak keyboard layout and had to switch to qwerty just to play this game...)
-max game volume too low (compared to the volume of other games and applications)
-no replayability (for such a beautiful and fun to play game, it feels fairly short; honestly, for such a smooth and fun combat system, I would kill for a full on diablo-sized world to keep playing with such satisfying combat)
-no co-op (this game would be really fun if it was an option)
If you liked games like Hyper Light Drifter, Hotline Miami, or Transistor, then you will adore Ruiner.  I'd give Ruiner a 90/100 for being fantastic game, which is high, but just a little more (maybe a DLC for a rogue-like endless dungeon or co-op) or fixing up the cons would make this game near perfect for me.  In any case, I highly recommend you try this game; it's more than worth it!

Where Hotline and Neon are tense, deliberate action-stealth games, Ruiner is a frantic series of combat arenas linked together by moody corridors and a pretty neat hub world. Fans of Hard Games(tm) are going to eat this up because even the tutorial boss - yes, the tutorial - on Normal difficulty was giving me fits. I don't mnd hard games but they must control well...
Ruiner's controls don't feel good. The WASD movement feels awkward. The shooting mechanics and general user feedback is  awful. I couldn't recall any of the early guns having any sense of impact or weight. Aiming is also finnicky and not helped at all by the auto-reload mechanic on the guns. For a game this frenzied I really wished to unload with some satisyfing-feeling weapons but my expectations were quickly destroyed. The wait the mouse aim both rotates your player and shifts the overhead camera is jarring as heck. Feels unnecessary.
I'll hang on to Satellite Reign as my cyberpunk game show piece. And replay Hotline Miami because that has both style and tight gameplay in spades. Ruiner turned out to be a big disapointment. Great cyberpunk atmosphere but rough gameplay and controls.

You can finish a dungeon in five minutes if you're the impatient sort or if like me you like to mull over optimal moves, a board might take  fifteen minutes or so.  There is a light and humorous background story to give the puzzles a campaign-like structure but War and Peace it ain't.  Which isn't a problem at all as this is the type of game which you'll load up when you have some random time to kill.  You will unlock various ways to customize each dungeon, such as starting equipment, races, classes, gods, etc.  The graphics are cute, the gameplay is tight, the music is not annoying.  If you like puzzle games and think you would enjoy a deconstruction of a dungeon roguelike, then buy this game.  It is practically flawless.

Valkyria Chronicles by its anime adaptation and slightly belated PC portover from the consoles it was originally made to run on is without a doubt one of the better known Japanese games on the Western market with a fairly significant fanbase, and at first glance seemingly well deserved reputation. Shortly after the initial release on Steam, it quickly became popular even among those who have never heard of it before for the setting it takes place in and a peculiar kind of gameplay people often liken to other titles such as the X-COM series. Unfortunately however, while it does have its good points, it is not a masterpiece which only becomes appearant later on.
It all begins with a short but very atmospheric introduction to the story taking place in an alternate timeline, where political struggles and frequent conflicts over the dwindling supplies of a precious resource lead to increasing tensions between the major powers of Europa, either side only waiting for the moment to strike at the other. A conflict which may seem insignificant to those involved in it on the surface, but in a single moment may become the flame that engulfs everything, leaving the ones facing their adversary with seemingly no choice but to surrender. Unless something that counters the invading forces breaks to the surface, a power that transcends the mists of time and within hold the key not only to our oldest legacies, but to who we are as well.
FIRE ONE: COMBAT
Likely not a surprise to say that either in games or elsewhere when you try to shoot someone, they shoot back. This is one of the first points where VC falls short on expectations, because due to some strange design consideration the moment you pick up your weapon, the AI stops completely, allowing you to take your time aiming before emptying the magazine into their heads, sometimes from point blank range. Even more interesting is the fact that 3 out of 5 classes will NEVER try to resist even if you are right in front of them, further emphasizing the problem.
It is also possible and a known exploit to position your troops in a way that will make the AI shoot its own soldiers, since the inherently flawed script cares not if anything happens to be in the way when they attack. One could certainly find this amusing since it gives the player many opportunities to have a good laugh, but after a few times it just becomes sad, especially since many hail this as one of the best features it has.
FIRE TWO: PSEUDO RPG
Another prominent feature is VC's own version of the classic level up system which rewards XP and credits at the end of a mission, that can be used to upgrade units in the training grounds or the garage. The problem with this is the fact that instead of individual units the game raises the stats of entire classes at once there leading to another serious exploit, since by grinding a class challenge from early on in the game you can farm ridiculous amounts of XP and funds which quite literally turns otherwise precious reward into a cheap currency that can be amassed as long as one likes. You also get near limitless access to one of the most powerful scout rifles you can find and enough money to buy everything from the shop for the tanks without ever being close to running low, meaning you can blitz through most if not all missions without much effort even at the very end of the story.
Then we also have the characters who make up Squad 7 with all sorts of interesting backgrounds, which may give the impression that they are all unique sorts of people. They are not.
The traits unlocked at various stages are all variations of the same copypasted abilities, some of which are gamebreakingly strong once invoked randomly or by orders, while others make half the cast a liability, never to see the day they sortie. This is especially obvious with Alicia who can win any mission that doesn't necessitate tank hunters by herself, with complete disregard to enemy fire ranging from infantry rifles to heavy machine guns. No matter how one would try to explain this, it is a very poor design, killing any semblance of challenge and realism especially when the infamous tactic known as scout rush is involved too.
FIRE THREE: THE PLAN
Since the game rates one's success not by how effectively they complete the operation but by how many turns it takes, it pretty much forces the player to hurry as much as possible regardless of danger if they want to get the related achievements. The problem with this is that without advance knowledge of the enemy positions there's little chance of getting A rank on a mission because the tactical map is worthless and until visual contact there's no way to predict what's behind the next corner. As a result the player could get caught in a crossfire out of nowhere anytime, leading to significant delays or possibly loss of troops if you're not quick enough. It is worth to mention that not even fatal head injuries will kill friendly units outright so long as they get a medic which can't be said about the enemy.
There's also the random nature of this game which is the epitome of chaos theory itself with complex mathematical factors inconceivable to mortal men influencing the AI's decision on where to direct every bullet and artillery shell, sometimes right on target, other times going way off the map. On the other hand, if you happen to find just the right spot and direction, it's possible to destroy several targets without actually engaging them, relying solely on shots that were not supposed to happen.
The finishing blow is that while some Gallians can be incapacitated by enemy fire, everybody seems to be immune to runovers from tanks, as any attempt from doing so will only shove them to the side. Most unusual, given what a vehicle of such proportions can do.
FIRE FOUR: PLOTHOLES
While it may be more noticable to some it should still be mentioned how many plotholes and openly presented deus ex machinas can be found here at closer look, turning an atmospheric story into one of great disappointment. These are but a few, as listing all of them would fill a smaller phone book.
The Edelweiss. I'm fairly certain no army would just let a civilian keep a functional tank in their garage with fuel AND ammunition to boot. The ingame explanation for that is insufficient since designing a vehicle doesn't mean they get to keep one. Especially this kind.
In a certain battle one character curb stomps another without even breaking a sweat. There's no logical or even illogical explanation for that to happen with the exception of being protected by plot armor, since the scenario writer decided to make that loss a focal point in the story, regardless of how unreasonable it is.
FIRE FIVE: BEHIND HER BLUE FLAME
The only saving grace of VC at this point is Selvaria's mini campaign which lets the player take control of her and a small Imperial unit around the fortress of Ghirlandaio. It is everything the main storyline should have been actually challenging, a sense of accomplishment and the final mission which could bring tears of joy to the eyes of those who can appreciate it. The difference in quality is so stark, it couldn't be more obvious and raises the question of why not making a storyline for each side, one from Squad 7 and the other from Selvaria's viewpoint. It would have alleviated much of the misgivings about this game without actually giving victory to the Empire.
Valkyria, valkyria
As promising as it started out Sega's popular title turned into only a mere shadow of what it could have been, giving up the possibility of a great chronicle for a game of superficiality that leaves a different kind of lasting impression. Therefore, one should be careful with their expectations before playing it, lest they become disappointed. Only buy it when on sale and only after giving careful consideration.

Hard Reset is cyberpunk themed FPS taking place in the last remaining human city - Bezoar. You are Major Fletcher and you have the job to keep the evil robots out of the city. During your missions you are tasked to find Prof. Percival Novak, who is responsible for the breach, but the truth isn't all black and white. There is much larger threat looming over Bezoar.
Game features fast paced, old school shooter gameplay and plenty of enemies that come with it. You have 2 weapons on your disposal but they can each be upgraded to several different weapon types. Your assault riffle can be upgraded to shotgun or RPG while your energy gun can turn into railgun. Enemies are ranging from small bots to big, missile launching robots. Boss fights require different approach and special way to defeat them.
Game is relatively short, consisting of 12 levels, that can be completed in 4 hours but higher difficulties will prolong it significantly. Story isn't the positive side of this game. It is told through few cutscenes and even then you'll have a hard time understanding it. What is lacking in story, it is fully repayed in graphics department. Visuals are outstanding and you will be compelled to destroy everything on your way just to see those fancy explosions.

Note that while I reccomend it, I must state that it requires a mindset of taking the game on its own terms and not by any other expectations. Sure the term metrovania is used with it but it only loosely its the term.
The game is basically Jameson (you) exploring the planet trying to find out what's going on. Along the way you'll recover suit functions that expand your abilities and deal with what's on the planet.
The graphics aren't exactly complex but they channel the 16 bit days pretty decently. I'd admit the sprites could be better but they get the job done.
Music? mainly ambient sounds, it is a backwater planet after all.
Gameplay will take some getting used to as you're expected to make some pixel perfect jumps, though it's more of a pain early on due to fall damage, but before long you'll get an item that negates that. Still, remembering the lessions the early bits taught you will help as it'll keep you from blundering into stuff.
Unlike the typical metroid game there's various bits of dialogue and text (though it's mainly Jameson talking with the ship's computer)
And i'll be blunt, it is linear in nature, though if you're playing to find out the next bit of plot, you won't mind as much.
This and other things lend this game a certain flavor different than the metrovanias.
in short, if you're looking for a true metrovania with action and exploration glore, this isn't what you want. But if you want to experience a story, 5 bucks isnt' too bad of a price (that and with the upcoming fall and winter sales...)
I do think the developers can make a nice true metrovania if they wanted to, the potential's there.

Inescapable it is an underrated gem, the game draws inspiration from Metroid and many games from the Genesis/MegaDrive era. The game is quite linear with some small backtracking, the gameplay focus on exploration and some light puzzles, the combat is fairly straightforward and doesn't obstruct the flow of the player. The movement of the protagonist could be more refined, sometimes the platforming is not as satisfying as it should be because the jumping motion is a bit tricky.
There are some tense moments, especially the underwater sections, but overall the plot and the atmosphere are well done. It makes you to keep playing and discover the meaning of those logs scattered around.
The duration is short but I think it's a sensible decision, these type of games can drag a lot if they try to force the duration adding zones for no reason.
All in all it was worth my time. Recommended.

The game might be more lenient to start out with which might explain why it never told me how to signal, turn on the wipers (well it never did rain in the states I drove, so that's fair) or even the lights which might be due to road rules in the US being different from where I live (We have our lights on everytime).
And as said, I didn't try it out much - I didn't want to pass the 2hour refund mark, so it might tell how stuff like that works later in the game.
It's not that I dislike "monotonous" games (I played Sims 1.... for way many more hours than I'd like to admit haha), or that the turn signals "broke" the game for me.
It ultimately came down to the steering controls being frantic (I have low DPI, had the in game sens low and I swear I got afraid of doing damage to the steering wheel everytime I turned) and the chunky in game menu.
As said, the game ran fine on my machine, as expected from the requirements and while I find the graphics "bland" others (maybe you) might like it better than I did.
And while even going for a refund, this wasn't the worst 19.99€ I've spent ever.
However I'm unsure if I would've stuck around to play through it, if it wouldn't have been for the refund option.
While a thumb down (we need a middle finger hahaha), I would recommend it to others who enjoy games like these.

Clever and a bit different to anything else I've tried before.
A roguelike that replaces a gridded dungeon with a 'map' of event cards. You collect and spend gold, upgrade items and everything else you might expect from such a descriptor.
Although you collect and use cards throughout, there's no CCG combat mechanics, the combat is handled with 3rd person action style combat (Assasins Creed, Arkham games, Mad Max etc.), which makes for an interesting blend of genres.
I'd actually personally rather the combat be handled by an RNG mechanic based on the equipment etc - or perhaps something like Darkest Dungeon, rather than being 'skill based' and interactive. Maybe something with dice. But it's a mild preference and I don't think any less of the game because of it.

It's actually a really great early access survival game. Really, really well built and much more finished than I expected it to be. Anyway, it would be nice to help out those niche players that just have to use a controller. RB and LB to switch through items, left joystick works the arrow in menus, everything else would be easy and simple first/third person movement controls. I can't really say anything others haven't said, I didn't buy the game the first day, but I was playing on the third day after hearing some trusted reviews. I really believe this might be the best survival game on the market. I honestly believe the devs probably enjoy playing the game, too, and that they really want to make it work. The map is just so vast... And it's really well polished considering it's just a week or so after launch. I really expected much, much worse and was pleasantly surprised. The game is difficult singleplayer, obviously. But I want to get a good grasp on all the mechanics before I jump in other's games. A lot of the problems people are having are supposedly supposed to be ironed out the next couple weeks, and I believe optimization is one of those problems.
